742833.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is a chromosomal disorder whose characteristic craniofacial dysmorphisms include flat facies, up-slanting palpebral fissures and prominent epicanthal folds, small nose with a low nasal bridge, and other facial deformities. The epicanthal folds are a well-recognized diagnostic feature of this syndrome.

673698.long_answer: In PMM2-CDG (formerly CDG-Ia), brain MRI typically reveals marked cerebellar atrophy or hypoplasia—especially of the vermis and hemispheres. This consistent finding is considered a radiological hallmark of the disorder and aids in its clinical recognition.

355218.long_answer: The blood-retinal barrier, formed by tight junctions between retinal vascular endothelial cells (inner BRB) and the retinal pigment epithelium (outer BRB), limits leukocyte and macromolecule movement from the circulation into retinal tissue. This immune-privileged barrier impedes normal trafficking of lymphocytes, so malignant cells can accumulate within the eye, rendering intraocular lymphoma puzzling in the context of systemic immune surveillance.

925803.long_answer: Beyond its approved use for severe acne, isotretinoin (13-cis-retinoic acid) is employed off-label for basal cell carcinoma, the commonest form of skin cancer. As a systemic retinoid, it normalizes keratinocyte differentiation and decreases proliferation, which can reduce the growth and recurrence of basal cell carcinoma lesions, particularly in high-risk or refractory cases.

464938.long_answer: In Epidermolysis bullosa simplex, mutations in keratin 5 or 14 weaken the structural integrity of basal keratinocytes. Mechanical stress therefore causes cytolysis within these basal cells, producing intra-epidermal blisters that remain confined to the basal layer of the epidermis, just above the dermo-epidermal junction.

436314.long_answer: Chronic diabetes mellitus causes diffuse peripheral nerve damage (diabetic peripheral neuropathy) through metabolic and microvascular injury to axons and Schwann cells. The same disease can involve autonomic nerves that supply the anal sphincter and rectum, reducing sphincter tone and impairing rectal sensation, which leads to fecal incontinence. Thus, diabetes mellitus is a well-established common cause of both peripheral neuropathy and fecal incontinence.

600284.long_answer: The phosphomannomutase-2 deficiency subtype (PMM2-CDG, formerly CDG-Ia) frequently involves the retina; electroretinography in affected patients shows markedly decreased scotopic responses, demonstrating reduced rod function.

829671.long_answer: The first-line therapy for Ehrlichiosis is doxycycline, which belongs to the tetracycline class of antibiotics. Tetracyclines inhibit protein synthesis by binding the 30S ribosomal subunit of Ehrlichia species, and early administration markedly reduces morbidity and mortality, making this antibiotic class the standard recommended treatment.

417926.long_answer: Among the clinical features of 3p deletion syndrome, recurrent epileptic seizures are well documented. Loss of genes on the short arm of chromosome 3 disrupts normal neuronal development and excitability, and as a result many affected individuals present with epilepsy, making it a characteristic neurological manifestation of the syndrome.

609911.long_answer: Clozapine, an atypical antipsychotic with strong 5-HT2A and moderate dopamine-D2 antagonism, has been reported in several case studies to markedly reduce the visual trails, halos, and after-images characteristic of Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder when other agents either failed or worsened symptoms. Its serotonergic blockade is thought to counter the cortical 5-HT2A hypersensitivity believed to underlie HPPD, making clozapine the antipsychotic that has shown the most promising benefit for these visual disturbances.

109287.long_answer: Congenital absence of dermatoglyphics (adermatoglyphia) is a hallmark of Naegeli–Franceschetti–Jadassohn syndrome, a rare autosomal-dominant ectodermal dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the keratin-14 (KRT14) gene. The defect disrupts normal epidermal ridge formation during embryogenesis, so patients are born without the distinctive fingerprint patterns normally present on the hands.

126547.long_answer: Iron deficiency in pre-menopausal women is most often due to excessive blood loss during menstruation—clinically termed heavy menstrual bleeding or menorrhagia. This same heavy or prolonged bleeding is recognized as one of the possible menstrual disturbances seen in polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), where irregular endometrial shedding can lead to episodically very heavy periods. Thus, heavy menstrual bleeding is both a frequent cause of iron-deficiency anaemia in women and a documented symptom of PCOS.

694411.long_answer: In VACTERL association, the vertebral component most frequently consists of segmentation defects; the single-sided failure of vertebral body formation known as hemivertebrae is the classic and most commonly reported anomaly, often leading to congenital scoliosis.

960498.long_answer: Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome arises from abnormal genomic imprinting at chromosome 11p15.5. Loss of the normal maternal imprint (or paternal uniparental disomy) removes silencing of the IGF-2 locus so that both alleles are expressed, leading to IGF-2 overactivity and the characteristic fetal over-growth features of the disorder.

727924.long_answer: Unicentric Castleman disease is characterized by enlargement of a single nodal station, and in the majority of reported cases the isolated mass arises from mediastinal (often paratracheal or hilar) lymph nodes. These mediastinal nodes are therefore the classic site involved in unicentric Castleman disease.

500798.long_answer: Trench fever is an acute relapsing febrile illness classically seen in soldiers of World War I. It is caused by the Gram-negative bacillus Bartonella quintana (formerly Rochalimaea quintana), which is transmitted from person to person by the human body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis). The louse becomes infected while feeding on bacteremic humans, and the bacteria are then passed in louse feces that contaminate skin abrasions, leading to systemic infection and the characteristic relapsing fever.

829054.long_answer: Alveolar echinococcosis, produced by the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, is managed primarily with long-term benzimidazole therapy. Albendazole is the drug of choice because it inhibits parasite microtubule assembly via β-tubulin binding, suppressing larval growth and reducing cyst viability. Continuous albendazole treatment—often for months to years and combined with surgery when possible—has been shown to improve survival and disease control in alveolar echinococcosis.

829286.long_answer: In infants, the most frequent reason for persistent inspiratory (chronic) stridor is laryngomalacia, a congenital softening and inward collapse of the supraglottic laryngeal structures during inspiration.

776200.long_answer: Haloperidol is a high-potency, first-generation (typical) antipsychotic whose strong D2-receptor blockade in the nigrostriatal pathway produces prominent extrapyramidal side-effects. Shortly after initiation it commonly causes acute dystonia—sustained, painful muscle contractions of the face, neck or limbs. With long-term use, the same potent dopamine antagonism can lead to ‘rabbit syndrome,’ a rhythmic, perioral tremor that resembles rapid chewing motions. Because haloperidol is well documented to precipitate both of these movement disorders, it is the antipsychotic most closely associated with both acute dystonia and rabbit syndrome.

893445.long_answer: Mowat-Wilson syndrome is a congenital disorder produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the ZEB2 gene. A cardinal clinical triad includes: (1) Hirschsprung’s disease or intestinal aganglionosis, seen in roughly half of affected individuals; (2) distinctive facial dysmorphism with broad eyebrows, uplifted earlobes, wide nasal tip, and pointed chin; and (3) hypoplastic or dystrophic nails—especially of the great toes and fifth fingers. This combination of Hirschsprung’s disease, nail hypoplasia, and abnormal facial features is therefore diagnostic of Mowat-Wilson syndrome.

738795.long_answer: Studies of monozygotic twins show a concordance rate of roughly one-half (≈50 %) for alopecia areata, indicating that if one identical twin is affected the co-twin has about a 50 % chance of developing the disease. This figure is far higher than the general-population risk but well below 100 %, reflecting both strong genetic predisposition and the need for additional non-genetic triggers.

776562.long_answer: The overall burden of lymphatic filariasis is typically expressed in disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), a metric that combines years of life lost due to premature death with years lived with disability, providing a single figure that captures both mortality and morbidity impacts.

376885.long_answer: After inhalation of Histoplasma capsulatum microconidia, symptoms of histoplasmosis typically develop in about 3 to 17 days (roughly 1–3 weeks). This incubation period reflects the time required for the spores to convert to the yeast phase in the lungs, multiply within macrophages, and provoke the host immune response that produces clinical manifestations.

395745.long_answer: The KCNQ1 gene, encoding the Kv7.1 potassium channel α-subunit that forms the cardiac IKs current, is situated on chromosome 11p15.5 and is the principal gene for Long QT syndrome type 1. Pathogenic variants in KCNQ1 prolong ventricular repolarization, producing the prolonged QT interval characteristic of Long QT syndrome.

742741.long_answer: The sight-threatening uveitis that occurs in Behçet's disease is most commonly treated with corticosteroids. Glucocorticoids rapidly suppress the autoimmune-mediated inflammation of the ocular vasculature, reducing pain, preventing structural damage, and preserving vision.

756369.long_answer: Neuroscientist Karim Nader, featured in an NPR segment on memory, described his pioneering research on memory reconsolidation. He showed that when a stored memory is re-activated, its molecular trace becomes temporarily unstable and must be ‘re-saved,’ a process that allows new information to be incorporated. This means a memory can literally be rewritten each time it is recalled.

954827.long_answer: Winchester syndrome—a rare connective-tissue disorder marked by progressive, severe osteolysis (bone resorption) of the limbs and other skeletal sites—is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the MMP2 gene (matrix metalloproteinase-2). Defective MMP-2 disrupts collagen and extracellular-matrix remodeling, leading to the characteristic bone and connective-tissue abnormalities recognized in medical genetics.

760972.long_answer: Nutritional yeast is an inactive form of Saccharomyces cerevisiae grown on molasses, dried, and sold as yellow flakes or powder. Its naturally high content of free glutamic acid gives it a strong savory (“umami”) flavor reminiscent of cheese, which is why it is widely used by vegans and vegetarians as a cheese substitute in sauces, soups, and sprinkled on foods.

423110.long_answer: Schamberg's disease is a chronic pigmented purpuric dermatosis that presents with characteristic copper-brown patches and petechiae on the skin. Because it is a cutaneous vascular disorder diagnosed primarily by clinical inspection of skin lesions (often confirmed with a skin biopsy), the specialist most commonly responsible for recognizing and diagnosing it is a dermatologist.

589286.long_answer: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)—principally ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease—can produce upper-gastrointestinal symptoms such as heartburn because inflammation may involve the esophagus or promote gastro-oesophageal reflux.  More importantly, long-standing colonic inflammation in IBD markedly elevates colorectal cancer risk; patients with pancolitis have a several-fold higher incidence of colon cancer after 8–10 years of disease compared with the general population.  Thus, IBD is a well-recognized gastrointestinal disorder that both causes heartburn and predisposes to colon cancer.

831257.long_answer: Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is a mitochondrial genetic disorder that most often manifests in late teens to early 30-s.  A previously healthy person—classically a young adult man—develops painless, sudden-to-subacute loss of central vision in one eye, and the fellow eye is usually affected within days to a few months.  Thus the disease characteristically produces an abrupt (“immediate” or acute/subacute) onset of vision loss during young adulthood, which is well documented in epidemiologic and clinical studies.  Although the exact timing can vary and some patients present in childhood or later adulthood, the typical presentation matches the statement.

293813.long_answer: Damage to the hypothalamus can impair production of antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also called arginine vasopressin). ADH normally promotes water re-absorption in the renal collecting ducts; when it is deficient, large volumes of dilute urine are excreted, obliging the patient to drink excessively to maintain water balance. Thus ADH deficiency is the classic hypothalamic cause of increased urine output (polyuria) and thirst (polydipsia) characteristic of central diabetes insipidus.

979296.long_answer: Imperforate anus can be part of the OEIS complex – Omphalocele, Exstrophy of the cloaca (bladder/cloacal exstrophy), Imperforate anus, and Spinal defects. In this malformation sequence the bladder is split and exposed (cloacal/bladder exstrophy), directly involving the urinary bladder along with the anorectal atresia.

603779.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type II is caused by pathogenic variants in the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene, which is mapped to chromosome 22q12. Loss or mutation of this chromosome 22–located gene leads to the characteristic vestibular schwannomas and other tumors seen in the disorder.

224012.long_answer: Pulmonary arterial hypertension is often driven by excessive production of the potent vasoconstrictor peptide endothelin-1 in the pulmonary vasculature. Endothelin-1 causes sustained pulmonary arterial constriction and vascular remodeling. Drugs such as bosentan, sitaxentan, and ambrisentan directly antagonize endothelin receptors (ETA and/or ETB), thereby counteracting the effects of endothelin-1 and improving pulmonary hemodynamics.

743949.long_answer: In patients with Wolff–Parkinson–White (WPW) syndrome, a catheter is threaded to the heart and radiofrequency energy is delivered to heat and destroy (“ablate”) the accessory atrioventricular pathway responsible for the pre-excitation. This procedure, known as radiofrequency catheter ablation, eliminates the abnormal conduction route and is the definitive curative treatment for WPW.

772556.long_answer: Intermittent exotropia is a form of strabismus in which one eye intermittently deviates outward. Diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment—whether via glasses, occlusion therapy, orthoptic exercises, or strabismus surgery—are managed by physicians trained in eye diseases. Therefore, a child with intermittent exotropia is typically evaluated and treated by an ophthalmologist, often one subspecialized in pediatric ophthalmology and strabismus.

195280.long_answer: In combined malonic and methylmalonic acidemia (CMAMMA), the most frequently encountered form of methylmalonic acidemia, the earliest clinical manifestations can emerge in the neonatal period—literally within the first days of life—when affected newborns may develop metabolic acidosis, vomiting, and lethargy. Although some individuals remain asymptomatic until later childhood or even adulthood, the disease is first capable of producing symptoms immediately after birth.

570872.long_answer: Foix–Alajouanine syndrome is a subacute necrotizing myelopathy caused by a spinal dural arteriovenous malformation, presenting with progressive neurological deficits such as paraparesis and sensory loss. Evaluation relies on neurological examination, MRI, and spinal angiography, and initial medical management and coordination of definitive neurosurgical or endovascular treatment are overseen by a neurologist. Therefore, a neurologist is the specialist most commonly responsible for diagnosing and treating this condition.

182774.long_answer: Miller-Dieker syndrome is a genetic contiguous-gene deletion involving LIS1 on 17p13.3 that produces classical lissencephaly with pachygyria. Nearly all affected infants develop early-onset epilepsy, and the cortical malformation makes the seizures frequently refractory to multiple anti-epileptic drugs, leading to medically drug-resistant epilepsy.

475125.long_answer: Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II, acid α-glucosidase deficiency) is a lysosomal glycogen storage disorder in which defective acid maltase leads to massive glycogen accumulation in striated muscle, including the muscles of the tongue. The resulting intralysosomal glycogen build-up causes marked enlargement of the tongue (macroglossia), a classic clinical feature of infantile-onset Pompe disease.

863570.long_answer: The TUBB4A gene, located on chromosome 19p13, encodes the β-tubulin 4A protein. Pathogenic variants in TUBB4A are well established as the cause of DYT4 dystonia (also called whispering dysphonia), linking this chromosome-19 gene to dystonic movement disorders.

466281.long_answer: Current clinical evidence does not support the claim that aspirin is effective in reducing mortality in patients who already have acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Although platelet activation contributes to ARDS pathophysiology and some early observational studies suggested that pre-hospital aspirin use might lower the risk of developing ARDS, subsequent randomized controlled trials (e.g., the LIPS-A trial) failed to show a significant benefit either in preventing ARDS or in improving survival once ARDS is established. Major critical-care guidelines (e.g., ATS/ESICM ARDS management recommendations) do not list aspirin as a mortality-reducing therapy. Standard care for ARDS continues to focus on lung-protective ventilation strategies, prone positioning, and other supportive measures, not on antiplatelet agents such as aspirin.

775545.long_answer: Mutations in the SCN9A gene, which encodes the voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.7, underlie both conditions: gain-of-function mutations produce hyper-excitable nociceptors causing familial primary erythromelalgia, while loss-of-function mutations abolish Nav1.7 activity and lead to congenital insensitivity to pain. Thus, SCN9A is the common genetic link between erythromelalgia and complete lack of pain sensation.

789173.long_answer: Following blunt or penetrating injury to the testis, rupture of the tunica albuginea or scrotal vessels can cause blood to collect within the tunica vaginalis sac. This post-traumatic accumulation of blood around the testis is termed a hematocele, presenting as a tender scrotal swelling that transilluminates poorly because it contains blood rather than clear fluid.

580140.long_answer: EEC (Ectrodactyly-Ectodermal dysplasia-Clefting) syndrome is most often caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor. TP63 is crucial for ectodermal and craniofacial development, so its mutation can disrupt normal eyelid morphogenesis, producing the characteristic eyelid abnormalities seen in EEC syndrome.

297447.long_answer: Idiopathic sclerosing mesenteritis is a rare fibro-inflammatory disorder that primarily involves the adipose tissue of the small-bowel mesentery, leading to fibrosis, inflammation, and mass-like thickening of the mesentery.

943866.long_answer: Abnormal and excessive growth of tissue is termed neoplasia. In gestational trophoblastic disease, the trophoblastic cells undergo neoplastic proliferation, giving rise to lesions such as hydatidiform mole, invasive mole, and choriocarcinoma.

438713.long_answer: Vitelliform macular dystrophy (Best disease) is characterized by abnormal accumulation of lipofuscin-rich, yellowish material within and beneath the retinal pigment epithelium at the macula. This buildup of the autofluorescent pigment, caused by mutations such as those in the BEST1 gene that impair RPE ion transport and phagocytic function, produces the classic ‘egg-yolk’ (vitelliform) lesion seen clinically.

937266.long_answer: DiGeorge syndrome, also called 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, is caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 22 and is well known for its strong association with conotruncal cardiac defects, especially tetralogy of Fallot.

492204.long_answer: Several controlled studies have shown that applying anodal transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) to left-hemisphere language cortex, often combined with naming therapy, significantly improves word-retrieval in post-stroke patients with anomic aphasia. By modulating cortical excitability non-invasively, tDCS enhances neural plasticity in perilesional language networks, leading to faster and more durable gains in naming accuracy compared with sham stimulation—hence it is regarded as a promising treatment for anomic aphasia.

349192.long_answer: Valproate (valproic acid/divalproex) is long off-patent and is produced by multiple manufacturers worldwide, so it is fully available as a generic drug rather than being restricted to a single branded product.

925148.long_answer: A cholesteatoma—an abnormal growth of keratinizing squamous epithelium in the middle ear—can erode the bony labyrinth, most often the lateral semicircular canal, creating a labyrinthine fistula. This abnormal opening allows perilymph leakage and abnormal stimulation of vestibular receptors, leading to balance disruption and episodic vertigo.

823420.long_answer: Numerous epidemiological studies have shown that children and adults with spina bifida have a markedly elevated prevalence of IgE-mediated natural-rubber latex allergy—often 20–65 %, compared with <2 % in the general population. The heightened risk is attributed to their repeated early-life exposures to latex-containing surgical gloves, catheter balloons, and other medical devices during the multiple surgeries and catheterizations commonly required for spina bifida care, leading to sensitization and clinical allergy.

685975.long_answer: Ewing sarcoma characteristically harbors a somatic chromosomal translocation, most often t(11;22)(q24;q12), which fuses the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 with the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11. The resulting EWSR1-FLI1 fusion oncogene drives aberrant transcriptional activity and is present in about 85% of Ewing sarcoma cases, making this specific translocation the mutation most commonly associated with the tumor.

562847.long_answer: Dopamine physiologically inhibits prolactin release from pituitary lactotrophs via D2 receptors. Pharmacologic dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine or cabergoline are therefore administered to lower elevated prolactin levels, reverse hyperprolactinemia-induced suppression of GnRH, and correct the resulting acquired hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

969005.long_answer: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is often ordered during the diagnostic work-up for suspected bipolar disorder because it can reveal structural lesions, tumours, strokes, demyelination, or other neurological abnormalities whose symptoms can mimic mood disturbances. A normal MRI helps clinicians rule out these medical or neurological causes, supporting a primary psychiatric diagnosis of bipolar disorder.

998813.long_answer: Paget’s disease of bone has been linked to persistent infection by a paramyxovirus; immunohistochemical and molecular studies have detected nucleocapsid proteins and RNA of canine distemper virus in pagetic osteoclasts. The same virus, a Morbillivirus within the Paramyxoviridae family, is the well-established etiologic agent of canine distemper, thereby connecting it with both conditions.

425954.long_answer: Keratoconus thins and distorts the cornea, causing incoming light to scatter before it reaches the retina. This stray light produces bright circular rings—“halos”—around point-light sources such as headlights or streetlamps, an effect that closely resembles the lens-flare artefact seen in photography.

247094.long_answer: Meleda disease (mal de Meleda) is an autosomal-recessive palmoplantar keratoderma caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLURP1 gene, which encodes the secreted Ly-6/uPAR-related protein-1 important for epidermal homeostasis.

241802.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the NLRP3 gene (also called CIAS1, encoding the inflammasome protein cryopyrin) underlie the spectrum of cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes. These mutations are responsible for the most severe form, neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease (NOMID/CINCA), and have also been identified in patients diagnosed with Marshall syndrome, placing both conditions on the same genetic and pathophysiological continuum.

856277.long_answer: Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis is classically caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the α-subunit of the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav1.4). These gain-of-function mutations impair channel inactivation, leading to sustained sodium influx, membrane depolarization, and episodic muscle weakness precipitated by elevated serum potassium.

250944.long_answer: Shauna Rae, star of the TLC series “I Am Shauna Rae,” developed pituitary-related growth hormone deficiency after chemotherapy for a childhood brain cancer damaged her endocrine system, stunting her growth to 3′10″ despite otherwise normal development.

816469.long_answer: Leukoplakia can show areas where epithelial cells die through necrosis. Necrosis is a pathological form of cell death in which plasma-membrane integrity is lost, leading to leakage of cellular contents into the surrounding tissue. This uncontrolled release provokes inflammation and distinguishes necrosis from the orderly, membrane-contained process of apoptosis.

994966.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the LEMD3 gene, which encodes the inner nuclear membrane protein MAN1, are the established genetic cause of both osteopoikilosis and Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome. Defective LEMD3 disrupts TGF-β/BMP signaling in bone and skin, producing the characteristic sclerotic bone spots of osteopoikilosis and the elastin-rich skin papules seen in Buschke–Ollendorff syndrome.

176539.long_answer: In pemphigus vulgaris, pathogenic IgG auto-antibodies target the desmosomal cadherin desmoglein-3 (and often desmoglein-1), which are adhesion proteins specific to desmosomes of stratified squamous epithelium in the skin and mucous membranes. Loss of desmosomal adhesion within this epithelial layer produces the characteristic intraepidermal blisters and erosions seen in the disease.

412330.long_answer: Porphyria cutanea tarda can occur as a paraneoplastic manifestation of hepatocellular carcinoma; the skin photosensitivity and uroporphyrin accumulation may precede or accompany the liver tumor, making PCT a recognized, although infrequent, paraneoplastic phenomenon of hepatocellular carcinoma.

623772.long_answer: The QT-interval threshold used to diagnose congenital Long QT syndrome in females (≈480 ms QTc) is set at the upper 1 % of the normal population distribution; in other words, the cutoff corresponds to the 99th percentile of QT intervals in healthy women.

755569.long_answer: Mutations in the GDF6 gene (Growth Differentiation Factor 6) cause a form of Klippel–Feil syndrome. GDF6 is a bone morphogenetic protein that directs early skeletal patterning, promoting vertebral bone formation and helping set up the joint boundaries that separate individual bones. Disruption of this gene impairs vertebral segmentation, leading to the congenital fusion characteristic of Klippel–Feil syndrome.

305399.long_answer: Pernicious anemia results from autoimmune atrophic gastritis that destroys parietal cells, producing chronic inflammation, achlorhydria, and intestinal metaplasia of the gastric mucosa. These changes markedly increase the risk of developing gastric adenocarcinoma (stomach cancer), making it the gastrointestinal malignancy classically associated with pernicious anemia.

824549.long_answer: Both duodenal atresia and midgut volvulus may show a “double-bubble” sign on plain abdominal radiography. An upper gastrointestinal (UGI) contrast series tracks the passage of contrast through the duodenum and proximal jejunum; in duodenal atresia contrast stops abruptly at the atretic segment, whereas in midgut volvulus the study demonstrates abnormal duodenal position, corkscrew/twisting of the bowel, or a spiral ‘coiled-spring’ appearance. Thus an UGI series reliably differentiates the two conditions and is considered the diagnostic gold standard for suspected midgut volvulus.

756627.long_answer: Proteus syndrome is caused by a post-zygotic activating mutation in the AKT1 gene (most commonly c.49G>A, p.E17K). The mosaic gain-of-function mutation constitutively activates the PI3K–AKT signalling pathway, driving the disproportionate, segmental overgrowth of bone, connective tissue and other organs that characterises the disorder.

121820.long_answer: A subset of follicular thyroid carcinomas carries the t(2;3)(q13;p25) translocation that fuses PAX8 to the nuclear receptor PPARγ. Because the fusion protein leaves the PPARγ ligand-binding domain intact, activating this receptor with PPARγ agonists can drive redifferentiation and growth arrest. Thiazolidinediones (e.g., pioglitazone, rosiglitazone) are well-known PPARγ agonists and therefore represent a rational therapeutic class for these translocation-positive tumors.

717604.long_answer: Phylogeographic analysis of Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus genomes shows that one genetic clade—the so-called eastern or Novosibirsk lineage—traces its most recent common ancestor to Novosibirsk Oblast in western Siberia, Russia, before spreading to other regions.

957251.long_answer: Fanconi anemia causes defective DNA interstrand cross-link repair, leading to chromosomal breakage and bone-marrow failure. This genomic instability markedly increases the risk of hematologic malignancy, particularly progression to acute myeloid leukemia.

403842.long_answer: Ring chromosome 15 syndrome is caused by the formation of a ring-shaped chromosome derived from chromosome 15. During cell division, the ends of chromosome 15 break and the broken arms fuse, creating a circular (ring) chromosome. This structural abnormality—specifically a ring chromosome involving chromosome 15—leads to loss of genetic material and the characteristic clinical features of the syndrome.

872921.long_answer: An aminoglycoside antibiotic (0.1% gentamicin ointment) is applied to skin lesions in junctional epidermolysis bullosa because it promotes translational read-through of premature stop-codon mutations in genes such as LAMB3 or COL17A1, restoring laminin-332 or type XVII collagen at the dermal-epidermal junction and thereby reducing blistering and improving wound healing.

150970.long_answer: In some newborns, circulating maternal estrogens and prolactin transiently stimulate the infant’s mammary glands, leading to a small secretion of milk-like fluid. This phenomenon is medically termed “witch’s milk” (also called neonatal milk or neonatal galactorrhea). The secretion is harmless, self-limited, and reflects temporary hormonal influence rather than true lactation pathology.

686311.long_answer: DSM-5 defines male hypoactive sexual desire disorder as a condition in which a man experiences persistently or recurrently deficient (or absent) sexual/erotic thoughts, fantasies, and desire for sexual activity for at least six months, on most occasions, leading to clinically significant distress and not attributable to another medical, psychiatric, or substance-related cause.

428040.long_answer: Valproic acid, an anticonvulsant that also functions as a histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitor, has been evaluated in pre-clinical studies and clinical trials to increase SMN2 gene expression and ameliorate symptoms in patients with spinal muscular atrophy.

926351.long_answer: In hypertrophic osteoarthropathy, the disease process includes marked villous (finger-like) proliferation of the synovial membrane that lines synovial joints, producing joint effusions and arthritic symptoms.

348958.long_answer: Subcortical dementia is marked by atrophy and ischemic or degenerative lesions in cerebral white matter and deep gray nuclei, disrupting fronto-subcortical circuits. The resulting disconnection chiefly impairs executive functions (planning, set-shifting, processing speed) while sparing cortical language and visuospatial skills, fitting the pattern described.

644142.long_answer: Individuals with ichthyophobia often avoid eating fish because they fear that small, concealed bones could become lodged in their throat and cause choking. This anxiety about fish bones is a well-documented, common component of the phobia.

957877.long_answer: Reactive arthritis, historically called Reiter syndrome, classically presents with a triad of asymmetric arthritis together with urethritis and conjunctivitis. It is a post-infectious spondyloarthropathy in which joint inflammation follows genitourinary or gastrointestinal infections, explaining the concurrent inflammation of the urethra and conjunctiva.

437004.long_answer: Hepatic veno-occlusive disease was first described in the 1920s in Jamaican patients who had consumed ‘bush teas’ or grain contaminated with Crotalaria/Senecio plants. These plants contain pyrrolizidine alkaloids, which are metabolically activated in the liver to reactive pyrroles that injure sinusoidal endothelial cells and narrow or obliterate terminal hepatic venules. Thus, ingestion of pyrrolizidine alkaloids is the earliest reported cause of hepatic veno-occlusive disease.

374315.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the DCX (doublecortin) gene disturb microtubule-dependent neuronal migration. In affected males this produces the X-linked lissencephaly spectrum, whose neuroimaging hallmark is pachygyria/lissencephaly, while clinically they often display craniofacial dysmorphism such as hypertelorism. Hence a DCX gene mutation is classically linked to the coexistence of pachygyria and hypertelorism.

317312.long_answer: Repeated inflammatory episodes in the ovary/fallopian tube bathe epithelial cells in cytokines (e.g., IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) and reactive oxygen species. These mediators chronically activate the NF-κB signaling pathway, which drives transcription of genes that induce cell proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, create a pro-angiogenic milieu, and exacerbate oxidative DNA damage. The combination of accumulated genetic lesions and NF-κB-dependent survival/proliferation of altered cells promotes malignant transformation, linking chronic inflammation directly to ovarian cancer development.

771176.long_answer: Epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma is an inherited disorder of keratinization that causes thickened, blister-prone skin on the palms and soles. Because it is a primary disease of the epidermis, diagnosis, genetic counseling, and management (e.g., keratolytics, retinoids, wound care) are handled by the medical specialty that deals with skin disorders—dermatology.

630413.long_answer: Muenke syndrome is a craniosynostosis disorder produced by the recurrent FGFR3 Pro250Arg mutation. Although best known for coronal synostosis, the mutation can also lead to premature fusion of the metopic suture, resulting in trigonocephaly. Thus, among the syndromes featuring trigonocephaly, the one specifically caused by an FGFR3 mutation is Muenke syndrome.

681023.long_answer: In humans the HMGCL gene, which encodes the enzyme 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase responsible for the final step of leucine catabolism and ketone-body formation, is mapped to cytogenetic band 1p36.11 on chromosome 1. Mutations in this locus cause 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency.

699663.long_answer: Nitazoxanide is a broad-spectrum thiazolide antiparasitic agent. Clinical studies show it is effective against the cestode Hymenolepis nana, the principal cause of hymenolepiasis, and it is the only drug approved specifically for treating diarrhoeal disease caused by the protozoan Cryptosporidium parvum. Thus, the same medication can be used for both infections.

203463.long_answer: Superficial thrombophlebitis is confirmed in practice with duplex ultrasonography, a non-invasive test that combines B-mode imaging and color Doppler to visualize superficial veins, demonstrate intraluminal thrombus, assess blood flow, and rule out extension into the deep venous system.

477598.long_answer: Listeriosis, caused by the food-borne bacterium Listeria monocytogenes, can cross the placental barrier during pregnancy. Maternal infection often produces only mild flu-like symptoms, but fetal infection can lead to miscarriage, pre-term delivery, or stillbirth because the organism proliferates in the placenta and fetus, provoking severe sepsis.

886185.long_answer: Patients with sickle-cell anemia are especially susceptible to osteomyelitis caused by Salmonella species; defects in splenic function and complement opsonization increase the frequency of Salmonella bacteremia, which can seed bone and lead to osteomyelitis.

192732.long_answer: Muckle-Wells syndrome is a cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome caused by gain-of-function mutations in the NLRP3 gene, which lead to over-activation of the inflammasome. This results in excessive cleavage and secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β (IL-1β), driving the fever, rash, arthralgia and other inflammatory manifestations characteristic of the disorder. Therapeutic blockade of IL-1β (e.g., with anakinra, canakinumab) markedly ameliorates symptoms, underscoring IL-1β’s central role in the disease’s inflammatory response.

152497.long_answer: Lorazepam, a benzodiazepine that enhances GABA-A receptor activity, is the first-line pharmacologic treatment for catatonia. Given intramuscularly or intravenously, it rapidly reduces catatonic symptoms and produces calming sedation, so it is also used in acutely agitated patients with brief psychotic disorder to prevent them from hurting themselves or others.

185992.long_answer: Teduglutide is a recombinant analog of glucagon-like peptide-2 (GLP-2) that is approved for the treatment of short bowel syndrome. By binding to GLP-2 receptors on intestinal epithelial cells, it stimulates mucosal growth, increases intestinal absorptive capacity, and thereby reduces or eliminates the need for parenteral nutrition in patients with SBS.

231132.long_answer: Laryngocele is an air-filled dilation of the laryngeal saccule that develops when intralaryngeal pressure is repeatedly and forcefully raised. People who blow glass for a living habitually generate high, sustained intralaryngeal pressures during the blowing process, and this chronic pressure promotes herniation of the saccule, markedly increasing their risk of laryngocele formation compared with the general population.

550898.long_answer: Parvoviruses place two in-frame AUG start codons on the same capsid mRNA. Because the first AUG sits in a weak Kozak context, many ribosomes bypass it and initiate translation at the downstream AUG. Initiation at the upstream codon yields the longer VP1 protein, while initiation at the downstream codon yields the shorter VP2 protein. This ribosomal bypassing of a sub-optimal start site is called leaky scanning, and it allows different proteins to be produced from one mRNA molecule.

648187.long_answer: The medical term for an unpleasant cutaneous sensation that elicits a strong urge to scratch is pruritus. Pruritus is frequently reported by patients with lichen planus, where immune-mediated skin and mucosal inflammation stimulates itch-specific C-fiber nerve endings, producing the characteristic desire to scratch.

922655.long_answer: Canine Lafora disease, a progressive myoclonic epilepsy caused by autosomal-recessive EPM2B (NHLRC1) mutations leading to polyglucosan body accumulation, is classically reported in and genetically characterized within the Miniature Wirehaired Dachshund breed, making this breed uniquely predisposed to the disorder.

744949.long_answer: Leiner’s disease is an infantile erythroderma regarded as an extreme form of seborrhoeic dermatitis. Because it primarily presents with widespread scaling, erythema and other cutaneous manifestations, its recognition, differential diagnosis and management fall within the domain of dermatology; hence a dermatologist (often with paediatric expertise) is the specialist most commonly responsible for diagnosing and treating the condition.

185980.long_answer: Metabolic crises in long-chain 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency typically arise when the body depends on long-chain fatty-acid oxidation for energy—most commonly during periods of prolonged fasting (or other catabolic stresses such as intercurrent illness). The defective enzyme cannot meet the increased β-oxidation demand, leading to hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and other acute symptoms.

817002.long_answer: Crohn’s disease, an inflammatory bowel disease that occurs more frequently in patients with coeliac disease, produces transmural gastrointestinal inflammation that can involve the stomach or proximal small bowel. Active Crohn’s inflammation disrupts normal neuromuscular function and can cause stricturing or edema, leading to impaired motility and clinically demonstrable delayed gastric emptying (gastroparesis). Thus, Crohn’s disease is the coeliac-associated gastrointestinal disorder that can cause both inflammation and delayed gastric emptying.

480142.long_answer: In 'Once Upon a Time in China III' the character known as Clubfoot Seven (also called Seven Chiu-Tsat) is depicted with a congenital clubfoot deformity, which is central to his nickname and to his storyline within the film.

331222.long_answer: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is an endoscopic-fluoroscopic procedure in which contrast is injected into the bile ducts through the ampulla of Vater, allowing direct radiographic visualization of strictures or masses caused by cholangiocarcinoma. During the same session therapeutic measures—such as brush cytology/biopsy for diagnosis, balloon dilation, and placement of biliary stents to relieve obstruction—can be performed, making ERCP both a diagnostic and therapeutic tool for bile duct cancer.

733883.long_answer: In the 2017 JAMA neuropathology study of 202 deceased American-football players, only 14 had played solely at the high-school level; chronic traumatic encephalopathy was identified in 3 of those 14 brains, yielding a prevalence of 21 percent among tested high-school players.

520806.long_answer: In genetics, penetrance is the proportion of individuals carrying a pathogenic variant who actually express the associated phenotype. When some people with the HOGA1 mutation that causes primary hyperoxaluria type 3 remain clinically asymptomatic, the gene shows less than 100 % penetrance—termed incomplete (or reduced) penetrance.

792706.long_answer: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome (RTS) is a rare genodermatosis caused most often by mutations in the RECQL4 helicase gene. Patients characteristically develop poikiloderma, growth deficiency, and skeletal anomalies such as radial‐ray defects and clinodactyly (curved fifth fingers). Importantly, RTS confers a markedly increased lifetime risk of osteogenic sarcoma (bone cancer), making it the syndrome classically associated with both clinodactyly and heightened bone cancer susceptibility.

378663.long_answer: Among the histologic subtypes of liposarcoma, the myxoid variant is defined by abundant gelatinous (myxoid) extracellular matrix with delicate, arborizing capillaries and scattered lipoblasts. This myxoid stroma is the hallmark feature that distinguishes myxoid liposarcoma from other forms such as well-differentiated, dedifferentiated, or pleomorphic liposarcoma.

521478.long_answer: Both Juberg–Hayward syndrome and Roberts/SC phocomelia syndrome are autosomal-recessive limb-reduction disorders that have been shown to be allelic. Sequencing studies identified pathogenic mutations in the ESCO2 gene (Establishment of Sister Chromatid Cohesion N-acetyltransferase 2) in families diagnosed with either condition. Loss-of-function mutations in ESCO2 impair sister-chromatid cohesion during cell division, producing the characteristic growth retardation, limb malformations and craniofacial anomalies seen in both syndromes.

522218.long_answer: Radiation sickness (acute radiation syndrome) can follow excessive exposure during therapeutic radiation treatments. One of its earliest and most characteristic symptoms is nausea, which arises within hours as rapidly dividing gastrointestinal epithelial cells are injured by ionizing radiation.

113766.long_answer: Acute interstitial pneumonitis is diagnosed by demonstrating diffuse alveolar damage; the standard way to visualise this in vivo is with high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest, which reveals the characteristic bilateral ground-glass opacities and consolidation needed for diagnosis.

496278.long_answer: Ramos-Arroyo syndrome is a very rare multiple-congenital-anomaly disorder originally described by C. Ramos-Arroyo and subsequently catalogued in OMIM (OMIM #601186). Core clinical findings include blepharophimosis/ptosis with characteristic facial dysmorphism, sensorineural hearing loss, intestinal malrotation or spontaneous perforation, growth deficiency and other systemic anomalies. Published case reports and reviews consistently note mild to moderate developmental delay or intellectual disability in the majority of affected individuals. Because the cognitive impairment occurs as one feature of a broader pattern of congenital anomalies, the condition is classified as a syndromic form of intellectual disability rather than a non-syndromic/isolated ID. Thus, the statement that Ramos-Arroyo syndrome is associated with intellectual disability and considered a syndromic intellectual disability is supported by established medical literature.

199585.long_answer: Epidermal nevus syndrome is characterized by hamartomatous overgrowths (epidermal nevi) that originate within and are confined to the epidermis—the outermost layer of the skin. These lesions involve proliferating keratinocytes of the epidermal layer, distinguishing them from conditions that affect the dermis or subcutis.

802978.long_answer: Oropharyngeal dysphagia often arises when the striated muscles of the oropharynx and upper esophageal sphincter are too weak to initiate and coordinate swallowing. The autoimmune neuromuscular-junction disorder myasthenia gravis causes fatigable weakness of these skeletal muscles, leading to impaired bolus propulsion and pharyngeal clearance, and is therefore a well-recognized cause of oropharyngeal dysphagia due to muscle weakness.

732700.long_answer: The U.S. FDA approved tafamidis (marketed as Vyndaqel and Vyndamax) in 2019 as the first disease-modifying therapy for cardiomyopathy caused by transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis (both hereditary and wild-type). Tafamidis binds to and stabilizes the transthyretin tetramer, preventing its dissociation into monomers that misfold and form amyloid fibrils, thereby slowing progression of ATTR cardiomyopathy.

568531.long_answer: In the ICD-11, mild cognitive impairment is classified in the Mental, Behavioural and Neurodevelopmental Disorders chapter under the block of Neurocognitive disorders. The specific code is 6D70, titled “Mild neurocognitive disorder,” which encompasses clinical presentations commonly referred to as mild cognitive impairment (MCI).

206441.long_answer: Mepolizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody against interleukin-5 (IL-5), is used in hypereosinophilic syndrome to lower circulating eosinophil counts. Clinical trials have shown that adding mepolizumab enables significant tapering or discontinuation of systemic glucocorticoids while maintaining disease control, providing a steroid-sparing treatment option for HES.

670297.long_answer: OMIM lists mutations in the X-chromosomal ARX (Aristaless-related homeobox) gene as the cause of the severe fore-brain malformation termed X-linked aprosencephaly (also called hydranencephaly/lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia). Loss-of-function ARX variants disrupt early neurodevelopment, abolishing formation of the prosencephalon and producing the aprosencephaly phenotype that characterises the disorder.

547871.long_answer: Tracing one’s genealogy allows the collection of a detailed family history, revealing how frequently type 2 diabetes and related metabolic disorders occur among blood relatives. Recognizing these familial patterns helps individuals gauge their inherited risk, prompts earlier glucose screening, and encourages preventive lifestyle changes—actions known to delay or mitigate type 2 diabetes progression.

267311.long_answer: Increasing chronological age is a well-established risk factor for both conditions: older adults have markedly higher incidence rates of delirium—especially during acute illness or after surgery—and the probability of developing most cancers rises steeply with advancing age because of cumulative genetic and epigenetic damage and diminished repair capacity.

511652.long_answer: Gitelman syndrome is classically produced by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC12A3 gene, which encodes the thiazide-sensitive Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter (NCC) of the distal convoluted tubule. Impaired NCC activity leads to renal salt wasting, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia, changes that precipitate the characteristic muscle cramps experienced by affected patients.

771190.long_answer: In schizophrenia, loss of normal dopaminergic homeostasis leads to over-activity of dopamine transmission in the mesolimbic pathway and under-activity in the mesocortical pathway. The hyperdopaminergic state drives positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, while hypodopaminergia in prefrontal circuits contributes to negative and cognitive symptoms. Thus, disruption of dopamine balance directly underlies the characteristic clinical manifestations of the disorder.

542242.long_answer: Lichen myxedematosus (also called papular mucinosis) is classified within the cutaneous mucinoses—a group of skin disorders characterized by abnormal dermal deposition of mucin (glycosaminoglycans) produced by fibroblasts.

597166.long_answer: Parvovirus B19 infection is a well-established viral cause of acute, often symmetric polyarthritis that can mimic rheumatoid arthritis, particularly in adults. Immune-complex formation during Parvovirus B19 viremia leads to inflammation of multiple joints, producing the clinical picture of polyarthritis.

909950.long_answer: Patau syndrome, the clinical condition caused by trisomy of chromosome 13, is well-documented to produce multiple ocular malformations, including congenital cataracts. The extra copy of chromosome 13 disrupts normal ocular development, predisposing affected infants to lens opacities alongside other eye anomalies such as microphthalmia and coloboma.

191369.long_answer: Gemfibrozil is a fibrate antihyperlipidemic agent that activates the nuclear receptor PPAR-α, leading to up-regulation of extrahepatic lipoprotein lipase (LPL). Enhanced LPL activity accelerates the hydrolysis and clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins such as VLDL, thereby lowering plasma triglyceride levels and treating hyperlipidemia.

106810.long_answer: Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (AADC) deficiency blocks the decarboxylation of L-DOPA, leading to accumulation of its O-methylated product, 3-O-methyldopa (3-OMD), in blood and urine. Quantifying 3-OMD in dried blood spots or plasma reliably distinguishes affected individuals from healthy controls and is therefore used as a biochemical screening test for AADC deficiency.

601718.long_answer: Randomized controlled trials such as the ATOM1, ATOM2 and LAMP studies have shown that nightly administration of very low-concentration atropine eye drops (≈0.01–0.05%)—an antimuscarinic agent—reduces the rate of axial elongation and refractive change in school-aged children, thereby slowing the progression of myopia without the significant side-effects seen with full-strength atropine.

407706.long_answer: Studies evaluating the in-vivo intramuscular halothane injection test found that only about half of the people with a positive result were truly malignant-hyperthermia susceptible when confirmed by the gold-standard caffeine–halothane contracture test; hence its positive predictive value is roughly 50 %, leading to abandonment of the method for clinical diagnosis.

889221.long_answer: Optic neuropathy is damage or dysfunction of the optic nerve that leads to visual loss. Disorders of the optic nerve are diagnosed and managed primarily by ophthalmologists—often those with subspecialty training in neuro-ophthalmology—because they specialize in diseases of the eye and its neural pathways.

241944.long_answer: After a hip dislocation is reduced, the standard recommendation is to obtain a computed tomography (CT) scan of the pelvis/hip. Thin-section CT images confirm that the femoral head is concentrically reduced and allow detection of occult acetabular or femoral head fractures, intra-articular loose bodies, or other post-reduction complications more sensitively than plain radiographs. Therefore, CT is the imaging technique used to rule out complications following hip-dislocation reduction.

802916.long_answer: Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common sexually transmitted pathogen responsible for cervicitis. The bacteria infect the columnar epithelial cells of the endocervix, triggering an inflammatory immune response that leads to cervical erythema, friability, and mucopurulent discharge. If untreated, chlamydial cervicitis can ascend, causing pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility, underscoring its clinical significance.

954653.long_answer: Statins competitively inhibit HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme that converts HMG-CoA to mevalonate. By blocking mevalonate formation—an essential early precursor in the biosynthetic pathway—statins suppress downstream cholesterol synthesis and thereby lower plasma cholesterol levels.

619760.long_answer: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic routinely prescribed for prophylaxis and treatment of urinary tract infections. A recognized adverse effect of this drug is a hypersensitivity-mediated pulmonary reaction that presents as acute or subacute eosinophilic pneumonia, with infiltrates, hypoxemia, and peripheral eosinophilia that typically resolve once nitrofurantoin is discontinued.

820034.long_answer: CAPOS syndrome (Cerebellar Ataxia, Areflexia, Pes cavus, Optic atrophy, Sensorineural hearing loss) is caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the ATP1A3 gene, which encodes the α3-subunit of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. Dysfunction of this neuronal ion pump disrupts cerebellar and brainstem circuitry, producing cerebellar ataxia and the associated ataxic dysarthria observed in affected individuals.

456813.long_answer: In Orofaciodigital syndrome type 1, central-nervous-system malformations are common, the most characteristic and variably present abnormality being agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum. Different individuals with OFD1 may show complete, partial, or no involvement of this midline cerebral structure.

270175.long_answer: In Adams–Oliver syndrome, the aplasia cutis congenita presents as congenital scalp defects localized over the vertex of the skull, involving the overlying skin and underlying parietal bone in that region.

741282.long_answer: Dietary retinyl esters are hydrolyzed to free retinol, which enters mixed bile-salt micelles. The unesterified retinol then leaves the micelle and crosses the brush-border membrane of enterocytes by simple, concentration-dependent passive diffusion—no dedicated transporter or energy input is required—after which it is re-esterified and packaged into chylomicrons.

569966.long_answer: During the sixth week of embryogenesis, bilateral ectodermal thickenings called the mammary ridges (milk lines) form and give rise to the mammary buds. If these mammary ridges fail to form or regress completely in the pectoral region, no mammary buds develop, resulting in complete absence of breast tissue, nipple, and areola— a condition termed amastia.

209935.long_answer: The ZRS (zone of polarizing activity regulatory sequence) is a limb-specific enhancer located in an intron of the LMBR1 gene that controls transcription of the Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling molecule. Mutations or duplications within ZRS cause ectopic or elevated SHH expression during limb bud development, producing mirror-image or extra digits (polysyndactyly). Thus, SHH is the signaling molecule whose expression is regulated by the ZRS and whose mis-expression leads to polysyndactyly.

404912.long_answer: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia is a hereditary disorder of calcium-sensing receptor signaling that presents with lifelong mild hypercalcemia and inappropriately low urinary calcium. Evaluation of calcium, parathyroid hormone, and renal calcium excretion, along with genetic testing, falls within the expertise of an endocrinologist, the medical specialist who diagnoses and manages metabolic and parathyroid disorders. Therefore, the specialty most likely to diagnose this condition is Endocrinology.

808649.long_answer: Megaloblastic anemia is a blood disorder, and when it arises from the inborn error of pyrimidine synthesis known as orotic aciduria (UMP-synthase deficiency), management focuses on correcting the hematologic defect (e.g., giving uridine). Such evaluation and treatment fall within the expertise of a hematologist, the specialist who diagnoses and treats disorders of the blood and bone marrow.

631778.long_answer: Thanatophoric dysplasia is a lethal FGFR3-related skeletal disorder characterized by extreme micromelia—the long bones of the arms and legs are markedly shortened and bowed (the classic “telephone-receiver” femora). This profound limb involvement is the most conspicuous anatomical abnormality, leading to the dwarfing phenotype and distinguishing the condition clinically and radiologically.

370874.long_answer: Morquio syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV) is a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by severe skeletal dysplasia, progressive airway obstruction, restrictive lung disease, and cervical spine instability. Most published natural-history series and reviews report that death usually results from: 1) progressive respiratory failure caused by upper-airway obstruction, tracheobronchomalacia, and restrictive lung mechanics; 2) cardiac or pulmonary complications such as cor pulmonale; or 3) catastrophic cervical spinal cord injury. Bacterial or viral infections can precipitate decompensation, but they are not cited as the leading, independent cause of death. Therefore, infection is not considered the primary cause of mortality in patients with Morquio syndrome according to established clinical data and expert consensus.

903716.long_answer: Allogeneic bone marrow (hematopoietic stem-cell) transplantation can repopulate the patient with healthy donor-derived hematopoietic precursors, which then establish functional blood cell production even before full intramedullary space is restored. This treatment can correct the bone-marrow failure of infantile osteopetrosis by supplying osteoclast precursors and enabling effective hematopoiesis outside the patient’s sclerotic marrow cavities until normal marrow spaces reopen.

433910.long_answer: In the central nervous system, myelin sheaths around axons are produced by oligodendrocytes. In Cockayne syndrome, neuropathological studies often show marked loss or absence of these myelin sheaths in cerebral white matter, reflecting dysfunction or loss of oligodendrocytes, the cells responsible for CNS myelination.

325259.long_answer: In Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, supportive therapy focuses on hydration, skin care, and comfort measures. For fever control in children, the recommended antipyretic is acetaminophen (paracetamol) because it is effective, well-tolerated, and avoids the Reye-syndrome risk associated with aspirin and the potential renal effects of NSAIDs in dehydrated patients.

308821.long_answer: Marked elevation of serum calcium depresses renal tubular responsiveness to vasopressin, decreasing aquaporin-2 insertion in the collecting duct and producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with polyuria. The same hypercalcemic state can affect neuronal excitability, and very high calcium levels are a well-recognized metabolic trigger for generalized seizures. Thus hypercalcemia is the electrolyte imbalance that can cause both nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and seizures.

897872.long_answer: The ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) gene has been one of the most intensively investigated loci in essential hypertension research. ACE encodes the enzyme that converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, a potent vasoconstrictor that elevates peripheral vascular resistance and stimulates aldosterone release. Increased ACE activity—whether from gene overexpression or common polymorphisms such as the I/D variant—raises angiotensin II levels and reliably elevates blood pressure, establishing its central role in essential hypertension.

637022.long_answer: In HELLP syndrome, placental-derived factors damage maternal vascular endothelium, producing microangiopathic hemolysis, platelet consumption and organ ischemia. In acute kidney injury, ischemic or toxic insults first injure the renal microvascular endothelium, causing vasoconstriction, reduced perfusion and subsequent tubular injury. Therefore, injury and dysfunction of the vascular endothelium is the key pathogenic mechanism common to both HELLP syndrome and acute kidney injury.

679307.long_answer: Gerodermia osteodysplastica is an autosomal-recessive connective-tissue disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the GORAB gene (Golgi-associated Rab2 binding protein). The GORAB locus is situated on chromosome 1 at band 1q24, making chromosome 1 the chromosomal site associated with this condition.

916615.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumours because its excellent soft-tissue contrast allows precise localisation of the nerve-based mass, definition of its extent along the nerve and relationship to surrounding structures, thereby guiding diagnosis and surgical planning.

704704.long_answer: Linkage analyses have mapped both autosomal-dominant familial eosinophilia and susceptibility loci for childhood asthma to the 5q31–q33 cytokine gene cluster on chromosome 5, which contains IL-3, IL-4, IL-5 and other Th2-related genes that drive eosinophilic inflammation and asthma pathogenesis.

999508.long_answer: Fowler’s syndrome is characterized by complex, high-amplitude electrical discharges in the external urethral sphincter. These discharges are detected with urethral sphincter electromyography (EMG), performed using a concentric needle electrode placed in the sphincter muscle. The EMG test reveals the pathognomonic abnormal activity, making it the key diagnostic technique for the disorder.

701740.long_answer: Diverticulitis, the inflammatory complication of diverticulosis, is linked to an increased incidence of adenocarcinoma in the same (usually left-sided/sigmoid) segment of colon. Because inflammation or an occult tumour can underlie or mimic diverticulitis, patients who develop diverticulitis are known to have a higher risk of left-sided colorectal cancer and are routinely advised to undergo colonoscopic surveillance after an attack.

494594.long_answer: Möbius syndrome is defined by congenital palsy of the abducens (VI) and facial (VII) nerves. These two cranial nerves fail to develop fully—typically from hypoplasia or agenesis of their brain-stem nuclei—leading to impaired ocular abduction (VI) and bilateral facial paralysis (VII), the hallmark clinical features of the disorder.

409314.long_answer: Frank–Ter Haar syndrome (caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in SH3PXD2B) produces a distinctive skeletal dysplasia; among its radiographic hallmarks are marked abnormalities of the scapulae, which are enlarged, dysplastic and hook-shaped at the acromion. The shoulder blades are therefore one of the most prominently and characteristically affected bones in this syndrome.

444699.long_answer: Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography (CTA) provides high-resolution images of both vascular structures and the skull base. In cases of carotid agenesis it shows complete absence of the carotid lumen and the corresponding bony carotid canal, making CTA a reliable, widely adopted tool for diagnosing this congenital anomaly.

913773.long_answer: Insulinomas are neuroendocrine tumours that arise from the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. β-cells are the endocrine cells that physiologically synthesize and secrete insulin; when they undergo neoplastic transformation, they overproduce insulin, leading to the hypoglycaemia characteristic of insulinoma.

155613.long_answer: During pregnancy, high-resolution prenatal ultrasonography can reveal the characteristic constellation of findings seen in fetuses with trisomy 9—such as severe intra-uterine growth restriction, craniofacial and limb malformations, cardiac defects and cystic hygroma. Detection of these structural anomalies on prenatal ultrasound raises suspicion for trisomy 9 and leads to confirmatory cytogenetic testing (e.g., amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling).

802699.long_answer: Collins–Pope syndrome has been described in affected siblings born to clinically normal parents, with no vertical transmission, a pattern that requires both copies of the causative gene to be mutated for the phenotype to appear. This pattern is characteristic of an autosomal-recessive genetic disorder.

787959.long_answer: Progressive supranuclear palsy is a 4-repeat tauopathy in which hyper-phosphorylated tau aggregates build up predominantly in neurons and glia of the midbrain (especially the subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra and related brain-stem structures). Degeneration of this midbrain region produces the vertical gaze palsy and postural instability characteristic of the disorder.

838482.long_answer: Dandy–Walker malformation features hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis with cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle. The dilated ventricle expands backward, so cerebrospinal fluid accumulates and markedly enlarges the posterior cranial fossa—the space at the back of the skull that normally houses the cerebellum.

316356.long_answer: Aminoglycosides bind to mitochondrial 12S rRNA, inhibiting mitochondrial protein synthesis. In individuals with pre-existing mitochondrial defects (e.g., m.1555A>G mutation), this greatly worsens mitochondrial dysfunction in cochlear hair cells, producing rapid, irreversible sensorineural hearing loss. Therefore, aminoglycosides are avoided because they carry an unusually high risk of ototoxicity in patients with mitochondrial diseases.

944566.long_answer: SCARF syndrome is believed to follow an autosomal-recessive pattern, meaning both healthy parents can carry one mutated allele and have a 25 % chance of having another affected child in each pregnancy. Genetic counseling helps identify carrier status, explain this recurrence risk, and discuss options such as prenatal or pre-implantation testing, enabling informed reproductive decisions for families with a history of the disorder.

931026.long_answer: The DSM-5 defines obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) as a Cluster C personality disorder marked by pervasive preoccupation with orderliness, perfectionism, mental and interpersonal control, and rigidity at the expense of flexibility and efficiency. Maladaptive perfectionism—striving for flawlessness, excessive self-criticism, and reluctance to delegate—is a core clinical feature and a key reason OCPD is strongly linked to dysfunctional perfectionistic traits.

252795.long_answer: Severe crush injury to skeletal (striated) muscle causes extensive muscle fiber necrosis (rhabdomyolysis), releasing large amounts of the oxygen-binding protein myoglobin into the circulation. Because myoglobin is freely filtered by the glomerulus, the excess load enters the urine, producing characteristic myoglobinuria.

691098.long_answer: In autosomal dominant and recessive forms of osteopetrosis, the dense, poorly vascularized bone is prone to infection; approximately 10 % of patients develop osteomyelitis of the mandible, usually precipitated by dental infections or extractions.

946444.long_answer: Dermatitis often produces a burning sensation in the inflamed skin. This “burning” is not only listed among the classic symptoms of contact, atopic, and other forms of dermatitis, but it is also classified in pain medicine as a specific quality of pain (burning pain), typically mediated by nociceptive C-fibres activated during cutaneous inflammation.

757311.long_answer: Norman–Roberts syndrome, also designated lissencephaly-2 (LIS2), is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the RELN gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein reelin. Reelin is critical for proper neuronal migration and layering of the cerebral cortex and cerebellum; its absence disrupts these processes, giving rise to the characteristic lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia that defines the syndrome.

273616.long_answer: Hydrops fetalis can be immune‐mediated when maternal antibodies destroy fetal red cells. The only immune form that is effectively preventable is Rh(D) alloimmunization (Rh incompatibility) between an Rh-negative mother and an Rh-positive fetus. Administration of anti-D IgG to Rh-negative women during pregnancy and after delivery prevents formation of maternal anti-D antibodies, thereby averting hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn and the development of hydrops fetalis.

788674.long_answer: Hereditary hemochromatosis is almost always caused by pathogenic variants—most commonly C282Y and H63D—in the HFE gene. Molecular testing of the HFE gene in peripheral blood can identify these mutations and definitively confirm the diagnosis in a patient who already shows biochemical iron overload and has a suggestive family history of liver disease.

857513.short_answer: Giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis
857513.long_answer: Large vessel vasculitis predominantly affects the aorta and its major branches. According to international vasculitis classifications (e.g., the 2012 Chapel Hill Consensus Conference), the two prototypic and most common entities in this category are giant cell arteritis (affecting older adults, especially the temporal arteries) and Takayasu arteritis (occurring in younger individuals and involving the aorta and its branches).

696301.long_answer: Alfred Donné first described the protozoan parasite Trichomonas vaginalis in 1836, the causative agent of trichomoniasis. The standard treatment for this infection is the nitroimidazole antibiotic metronidazole, which is highly effective because, once reduced inside the anaerobic parasite, it generates reactive intermediates that damage DNA and other critical biomolecules, eradicating the infection.

828543.long_answer: Turner syndrome (45,X) is classically associated with congenital cystic hygroma. The underlying lymphatic maldevelopment causes fluid accumulation, leading to marked nuchal cystic hygromas and peripheral lymphedema (edema of the hands and feet) in affected fetuses and newborns. Thus, edema is a characteristic symptom of Turner syndrome in the context of cystic hygroma.

467093.long_answer: Co-inheritance of HFE-related hereditary hemochromatosis causes abnormally increased intestinal iron absorption. When a patient with hereditary spherocytosis also carries pathogenic HFE mutations (e.g., C282Y or H63D), the added iron uptake combines with the iron released from chronic hemolysis and any transfusional iron, leading to clinically significant iron overload.

687270.long_answer: Dopamine signaling is central to both conditions: hyperactivity of mesolimbic dopamine pathways is a well-established mechanism underlying psychotic symptoms, while reduced dopaminergic transmission, particularly in mesocortical and striatal circuits, is linked to the anhedonia, psychomotor retardation and other features of melancholic depression.

614806.long_answer: Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis results from impaired H⁺ secretion by the α-intercalated cells in the cortical collecting duct. This segment of the nephron is also a major site for potassium handling—principal cells there secrete K⁺ under aldosterone control—so dysfunction of the collecting duct disrupts both acid–base balance and potassium regulation.

498738.long_answer: Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple osteochondromas) produce osteocartilaginous outgrowths near the growth plates of long bones. In the leg, these lesions most often involve and stunt growth of the fibula, making the fibula the bone classically associated with this inherited disorder.

203343.long_answer: Hemihyperplasia (formerly called hemihypertrophy) is a congenital over-growth disorder that confers a markedly higher risk of embryonal renal tumors, most notably Wilms tumor (nephroblastoma). Because of this well-documented association, children with isolated hemihyperplasia undergo periodic abdominal ultrasonography to screen specifically for Wilms tumor during early childhood.

512176.long_answer: Killer Croc is portrayed as having been born with a mutation that makes his skin thicken into dark, plate-like scales reminiscent of a reptile. The real-world disorder that produces very similar hard, hyperkeratotic, ‘crocodile-like’ scaling—and is classified within the ichthyoses—is epidermolytic hyperkeratosis, a keratin-gene (KRT1/KRT10) mutation resulting in congenital ichthyosis and extensive hyperkeratosis.

303496.long_answer: Mutations in the PKD1 or PKD2 genes cause autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). The numerous renal cysts and distorted collecting system produced by ADPKD promote urinary stasis and stone formation, creating a favorable environment for bacterial growth. Consequently, individuals with ADPKD have a well-documented, significantly higher incidence of recurrent urinary tract and cyst infections compared with the general population.

721685.long_answer: Alexander disease is a rare hereditary leukodystrophy produced by dominant-acting mutations in the gene encoding glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP). These mutations disrupt intermediate filament assembly in astrocytes, leading to Rosenthal fiber accumulation and progressive demyelination characteristic of the disorder.

406516.long_answer: Ascariasis, caused by the intestinal roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, is one of the most common soil-transmitted helminth infections worldwide. According to the World Health Organization and numerous epidemiologic studies, high prevalences are found in regions with warm, humid climates and inadequate sanitation—conditions that occur widely throughout much of Latin America and the Caribbean. Surveys from countries such as Brazil, Bolivia, Peru, Guatemala, and Honduras consistently demonstrate infection rates ranging from 10 % to over 50 % in school-age children, and the region is included in WHO mass drug-administration (MDA) programs targeting soil-transmitted helminths. Because of these documented burdens, Latin America is recognized as one of the geographic areas heavily affected by ascariasis.

768390.long_answer: In neonates and young infants the open fontanelle allows cranial (trans-fontanellar) Doppler ultrasonography to show a midline cystic structure with turbulent, high-velocity flow characteristic of a Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation. Because it is rapid, bedside, and non-invasive, this Doppler ultrasound technique is particularly useful for diagnosing VGAM in infants.

499973.long_answer: Septic shock is a severe, life-threatening condition that develops when a severe infection triggers a systemic inflammatory response; persistent tachycardia is one of the compensatory cardiovascular signs. The combination of a serious infection with marked tachycardia reflects systemic vasodilation, capillary leak, and inadequate tissue perfusion that characterize septic shock.

761827.long_answer: Jansky–Bielschowsky disease, a late-infantile form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in genes such as CLN2 (TPP1). Because the disorder manifests only when both alleles are mutated and carriers are typically unaffected, it follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

458041.long_answer: X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita is caused by mutations in the NR0B1 gene (also called DAX-1) on chromosome Xp21. NR0B1 encodes a nuclear receptor that regulates transcriptional programs essential for proper development and function of the adrenal cortex and the gonads; loss-of-function mutations therefore impair adrenal formation and disrupt ovarian (and testicular) development, producing the characteristic clinical picture of X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita.

659730.long_answer: Benign fasciculation syndrome is characterized by involuntary muscle twitches (fasciculations) that arise in voluntary, striated muscles—such as those of the limbs, face, and trunk. These twitches originate in the lower motor neuron units innervating skeletal muscle fibers; neither smooth nor cardiac muscle is involved.

923724.long_answer: Lucey-Driscoll syndrome (transient familial neonatal hyperbilirubinemia) is produced by loss-of-function variants in the UGT1A1 gene that are inherited on both parental alleles. Because two defective copies are required to impair bilirubin conjugation and cause the neonatal jaundice phenotype, the disorder follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

104493.long_answer: Oculocutaneous albinism frequently causes ocular abnormalities such as nystagmus, reduced visual acuity, photophobia, and foveal hypoplasia. The medical specialty dedicated to diagnosing and managing disorders of the eye and visual system is ophthalmology; ophthalmologists evaluate and treat these vision problems in albinism patients.

901108.long_answer: Lenz-Majewski syndrome is a very rare skeletal dysplasia marked by generalized progressive hyperostosis and craniofacial overgrowth. Genetic studies have shown that it is caused by heterozygous gain-of-function missense mutations in the PTDSS1 gene, which encodes phosphatidylserine synthase 1. These mutations increase phosphatidylserine synthase activity, leading to the characteristic bone overgrowth seen in the syndrome.

556784.long_answer: Systemic capillary leak syndrome (SCLS, Clarkson disease) is a rare disorder marked by sudden, massive leakage of plasma from the vascular space, leading to hypotension, hemoconcentration, and hypo-albuminemia. Because its presentation mimics septic shock, it is frequently misdiagnosed as sepsis.
