PORCN encodes an O-acyltransferase required for palmitoylation and secretion of Wnt proteins, a signaling pathway essential for the proper development of ectoderm-derived tissues such as skin, hair, nails, and teeth. Loss-of-function mutations in PORCN disrupt Wnt signaling, leading to the characteristic cutaneous, skeletal, and ectodermal defects seen in focal dermal hypoplasia.

705125.long_answer: The correct term is “oikophobia,” derived from the Greek ‘oikos’ (house) and ‘phobos’ (fear). In clinical and popular psychology it denotes an irrational fear or aversion to the home environment, including household appliances or familiar domestic objects. In social-political discourse, philosophers such as Roger Scruton have extended the word to describe hostility toward or rejection of one’s own cultural roots. Thus oikophobia uniquely covers both the literal fear of items in the home and the figurative renunciation of one’s native culture.

969269.long_answer: In medical usage the term “birth defect” (or congenital anomaly) is applied to any structural, functional or metabolic abnormality that arises during fetal development and is already present at birth. Mickleson (often written as Michelson/Michels) syndrome is a rare, genetically-determined multiple-anomaly syndrome that is present from the moment of birth and is characterised by a typical pattern of congenital malformations (e.g., distinctive cranio-facial features, ocular and skeletal abnormalities, developmental delay, etc.). Because the disorder originates in embryonic development and the abnormalities are evident at or soon after delivery, it is classified by clinicians as a congenital disorder—that is, a birth defect. Therefore, Mickleson syndrome is considered a birth defect.

964400.long_answer: In distal (type 1) renal tubular acidosis, chronically elevated urinary calcium and phosphate lead to nephrolithiasis/nephrocalcinosis. Passage or impaction of renal stones produces characteristic flank- or loin-localized pain, making loin pain a recognized symptom of distal RTA.

299380.long_answer: In Lyme disease, patients often develop arthralgia—a medical term that literally means pain in one or more joints. This migratory joint pain is a hallmark systemic manifestation of Borrelia burgdorferi infection, reflecting inflammation of the joints during the early disseminated or late stages of the disease.

750919.long_answer: When serum prolactin levels become abnormally high (hyperprolactinaemia), prolactin exerts a negative feedback effect on the hypothalamus, suppressing pulsatile secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). Reduced GnRH output diminishes luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone release from the pituitary, which can result in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

123836.long_answer: Photosensitive reflex epilepsy is most effectively managed with broad-spectrum antiepileptic drugs that suppress the photoparoxysmal response on EEG. Sodium valproate (valproic acid) is widely considered the first-line medication because it enhances inhibitory GABAergic transmission and stabilises neuronal firing across cortical networks, thereby reducing seizures triggered by flashing lights. Clinical guidelines and multiple studies cite sodium valproate as the standard treatment for photosensitive epilepsy.

204745.long_answer: Catalase is a ubiquitous antioxidant enzyme located in peroxisomes that rapidly decomposes hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) into water and molecular oxygen, preventing oxidative damage to cellular components.

240862.long_answer: In Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, dysregulation of the imprinted 11p15.5 region often leads to biallelic expression and overactivity of the IGF2 (insulin-like growth factor 2) gene. Excess IGF2 promotes somatic overgrowth and markedly elevates the risk of embryonal childhood cancers such as Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma, making IGF2 overexpression a central oncogenic driver in this syndrome.

550975.long_answer: Vitamin E functions as a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects erythrocyte membranes from oxidative injury. In deficiency, unchecked reactive oxygen species peroxidize red-cell membrane lipids, leading to membrane fragility and premature destruction of erythrocytes, manifesting clinically as hemolytic anemia.

762215.long_answer: Isoprinosine (inosine pranobex) is an antiviral immunomodulator that, when started early—particularly in stage 1 of subacute sclerosing panencephalitis—can slow neurological deterioration and prolong survival. Clinical studies and neurology guidelines list oral isoprinosine as the principal pharmacologic option for SSPE in its initial stage.

355921.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (also called acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is classically characterized by a combination of craniofacial malformations due to craniosynostosis, limb anomalies that include both pre- or post-axial polydactyly and syndactyly, and shortened digits (brachydactyly). This distinctive triad places Carpenter syndrome among the syndromes in which brachydactyly co-occurs with craniofacial abnormalities and polydactyly.

799276.long_answer: Only three very small series have been published. The syndrome was first described in two Egyptian siblings (Temtamy et al.). A second sib-pair was later reported from the United States (Centerwall et al.), and an isolated case was documented in Canada. No other countries have recorded confirmed occurrences, so cases have been reported solely in Egypt, the United States, and Canada.

240053.long_answer: Passive-aggressive personality disorder (also called negativistic personality disorder) had been an official Axis II diagnosis in DSM-III-R, but in DSM-IV it was removed from the main list and relegated to Appendix B ("Criteria Sets and Axes Provided for Further Study") because of inconsistent empirical support and controversy about its validity. Therefore, it was the disorder moved to Appendix B pending further research.

573879.long_answer: Perceptual disturbances describe abnormalities in the way external stimuli are experienced. The hallmark and most frequently noted manifestation of this disturbance is the visual hallucination—seeing people, objects, or lights that are not actually present. Visual hallucinations arise from aberrant activity in the visual processing pathways of the brain and are classically reported in conditions such as delirium, toxic-metabolic encephalopathies, and certain psychotic disorders, making them the prototypical symptom of a perceptual disturbance.

809608.long_answer: To confirm idiopathic intracranial hypertension, clinicians perform a lumbar puncture—introducing a needle into the sub-arachnoid space between lumbar vertebrae (usually L3–L4 or L4–L5)—and the opening cerebrospinal fluid pressure is recorded. Thus, the procedure involves the lumbar region of the spine.

421906.long_answer: In kidney (renal) transplant recipients, reactivation or primary infection with Human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7) often precedes and stimulates cytomegalovirus (CMV) replication. Clinical studies show that HHV-7 antigenaemia emerges first, and its presence is a strong predictor for subsequent CMV viremia or disease, indicating a causal link between HHV-7 activity and CMV reactivation in this patient group.

902434.long_answer: The protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 22 gene (PTPN22) maps to chromosome 1p13.3. Variants in PTPN22, particularly the R620W (1858C>T) polymorphism, are strongly associated with several autoimmune disorders, including autoimmune thyroid diseases such as Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and Graves’ disease, making PTPN22 the chromosome 1p13 gene linked to these conditions.

300557.long_answer: Labyrinthitis is an inflammatory disorder of the inner ear that primarily involves the membranous labyrinth—the delicate, fluid-filled system of ducts and sacs (cochlear duct, utricle, saccule, semicircular ducts) that resides inside the surrounding bony labyrinth. Thus, the part of the inner ear within the bony labyrinth that is affected is the membranous labyrinth.

900734.long_answer: Bartter syndrome in infants and children produces polyuria, polydipsia, dehydration episodes, failure to thrive, hypokalaemia and nephrocalcinosis—clinical features that closely resemble those seen in distal renal tubular acidosis. The key biochemical distinction is that Bartter syndrome causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, whereas distal RTA causes a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, but the presenting symptoms are sufficiently alike that the two conditions are often considered together in the differential diagnosis.

217978.long_answer: In Northern epilepsy syndrome (the CLN8 form of neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinosis) neurons accumulate intralysosomal material that is immunoreactive for β-amyloid (Aβ) peptides. The same β-amyloid peptides aggregate extracellularly to form the characteristic senile plaques of Alzheimer’s disease. Hence, abnormal accumulation of β-amyloid protein is a pathological feature common to both disorders.

450807.long_answer: Simian virus 40 (SV40) is a member of the Polyomaviridae family. Its large-T antigen has potent oncogenic properties, and SV40 DNA sequences and T-antigen protein have been detected in certain human brain tumors such as ependymomas and choroid-plexus papillomas, linking the virus to brain tumor development.

868686.long_answer: Epidemiologic studies show that frequent consumption of pork—especially in processed, salted or smoked forms—raises exposure to nitrosamines and other carcinogens, and is consistently linked to a higher incidence of gastric (stomach) cancer. The U.S. Department of Agriculture categorizes all pork as red meat, making pork the red-meat dietary factor associated with increased stomach-cancer risk.

975048.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the ADAMTSL4 gene cause the autosomal-recessive ocular disorder known as ectopia lentis et pupillae. This condition is characterised by displacement of the crystalline lens and abnormal position of the pupil; the zonular instability and high myopia that result can precipitate serious complications such as cataract, glaucoma, and retinal detachment.

552587.long_answer: Adrenocortical hyperfunction is an endocrine disorder caused by excess secretion of adrenal cortical hormones (e.g., cortisol, aldosterone). The medical specialty of Endocrinology focuses on diseases of the hormone-producing glands, including the adrenal cortex. Endocrinologists perform hormonal testing, imaging, and manage medical or surgical treatment of conditions such as Cushing’s syndrome or primary hyperaldosteronism, making Endocrinology the appropriate specialty for diagnosis and therapy.

735015.long_answer: Chromoblastomycosis is classified as a subcutaneous (or cutaneous–subcutaneous) mycosis; the causative dematiaceous fungi are introduced by trauma and establish chronic granulomatous infection primarily in the subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis) beneath the dermis.

235042.long_answer: Nail matrix tumors such as onychomatricoma or subungual glomus tumor are effectively managed by completely excising the lesion, including the involved portion of the nail matrix. Surgical removal eliminates the neoplastic tissue, prevents recurrence, and allows the nail unit to regenerate normally, making complete surgical excision the standard recommended treatment.

997097.long_answer: Several case reports and series have shown that interstitial granulomatous dermatitis with arthritis (IGDA) can be precipitated by drugs, most commonly antihypertensive agents. Among these, angiotensin-converting-enzyme (ACE) inhibitors (e.g., captopril, enalapril) and calcium-channel blockers (e.g., diltiazem, verapamil) are the medications most consistently linked to the development of IGDA. Withdrawal of the offending drug often leads to improvement of the cutaneous granulomatous lesions and associated arthritis, underscoring the causal relationship.

464639.long_answer: Hirschsprung’s disease involves congenital absence of enteric ganglion cells and is definitively treated with bowel resection and pull-through procedures, which are performed by surgeons trained to operate on infants and children. Therefore, management of Hirschsprung’s disease–type D brachydactyly syndrome in pediatric patients falls under the specialty of pediatric surgery.

669913.long_answer: Tuberculous meningitis is confirmed by performing a lumbar puncture, which withdraws cerebrospinal fluid for laboratory analysis (cell counts, protein, glucose, acid-fast bacilli smear/culture or PCR) to detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis and characteristic CSF changes.

696076.long_answer: Syndactyly is the congenital fusion of two or more fingers or toes. This digit fusion is a documented phenotypic feature of Jancar syndrome, appearing alongside the syndrome’s neurological and developmental abnormalities.

854117.long_answer: Burosumab is a human monoclonal antibody that binds and inhibits excess fibroblast growth factor-23 (FGF23), the pathogenic driver of phosphate wasting in X-linked hypophosphatemia (XLH). By neutralizing FGF23, burosumab restores renal phosphate reabsorption and increases circulating 1,25-dihydroxy-vitamin D levels, directly addressing the underlying molecular cause of XLH rather than only treating symptoms.

645792.long_answer: High-grade (WHO grade III/IV) astrocytomas are defined histologically by the presence of frequent mitoses—seen as numerous mitotic figures—indicating brisk, uncontrolled cell division. This elevated mitotic activity is one of the key criteria that distinguishes high-grade astrocytoma from lower-grade tumors.

211751.long_answer: In most cases of polydactyly, the supernumerary finger or toe is only partly developed.  When skeletal tissue is present, the element that ossifies first and is therefore most frequently seen is the proximal phalanx.  Metacarpals, metatarsals or more distal phalanges are duplicated far less often, so the proximal phalanx is the bone most commonly found within an accessory digit.

728318.long_answer: Neuro-imaging and neuropathological studies show that the caudate nucleus—a major component of the basal ganglia—exhibits structural and functional abnormalities in both conditions. Children with specific language impairment typically have reduced caudate grey-matter volume and altered activation during language tasks, while enlarged or otherwise atypical caudate morphology is a consistent finding in several genetic and developmental forms of intellectual disability (e.g., Fragile X syndrome). Thus, the caudate nucleus is a common neural substrate implicated in both intellectual disability and specific language impairment.

856597.long_answer: Ifosfamide, an alkylating chemotherapy agent, is well-recognized for causing Fanconi-type proximal renal tubular dysfunction. This injury impairs bicarbonate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, leading to bicarbonaturia and the characteristic metabolic acidosis of proximal (type 2) renal tubular acidosis.

449625.long_answer: Before the 2011 discovery of the somatic activating AKT1 (p.E17K) mutation on chromosome 14, several groups had proposed that Proteus syndrome might belong to the PTEN-hamartoma tumour spectrum because of clinical overlap. PTEN is located at 10q23.31, so chromosome 10 was the chromosomal locus previously suggested to be linked to Proteus syndrome, a hypothesis later disproved by the identification of the AKT1 mosaic mutation.

105213.long_answer: Chlorine, the halogen element employed in sodium hypochlorite and other chlorine-based bleaches and disinfectants used to clean brewing equipment, can be inhaled as chlorine gas or hypochlorite aerosols. This airway irritant is a well-documented cause of irritant-induced and occupational asthma in brewery workers and other cleaning personnel.

376596.long_answer: Parathyroid hormone (PTH), secreted by the parathyroid glands, is the principal regulator of serum calcium. It stimulates osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, releasing calcium into the bloodstream, and also enhances renal calcium reabsorption and activates vitamin D synthesis. These actions collectively maintain normal circulating calcium levels.

228574.long_answer: Reactive arthritis (formerly called Reiter’s syndrome) is classically characterized by the triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. Thus, inflammation of the conjunctiva is a well-known extra-articular manifestation of this form of arthritis.

643453.long_answer: Bare lymphocyte syndrome type II is a severe combined immunodeficiency caused by lack of MHC-class II expression on antigen-presenting cells. Replacing the patient’s hematopoietic system with donor stem cells that can normally express MHC-II reconstitutes functional CD4⁺ T-cell–mediated immunity, so allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplantation is the established therapeutic option.

415499.long_answer: In children who are walking but still in the toddler age range (≈1–3 years), the leading anatomic reason for in-toeing gait is internal (medial) torsion of the tibia. Metatarsus adductus predominates in infants, and excessive femoral anteversion becomes more evident after about 3–4 years, but for toddlers the most frequent etiology is internal tibial torsion, in which the tibia is rotated inward relative to the knee, producing the classic pigeon-toed appearance when walking.

351052.long_answer: The cat-scratch disease pathogen Bartonella henselae is not limited to causing lymphadenitis; it can invade vascular endothelium and cardiac valves, producing culture-negative infective endocarditis—a severe, life-threatening inflammation of the heart’s endocardial lining and valves.

633840.long_answer: Nocardia species (gram-positive, branching, weakly acid-fast bacteria) often begin as a pulmonary infection that can hematogenously disseminate to the central nervous system, producing one or multiple brain abscesses. Because Nocardia grows slowly and relapses are common, effective management requires prolonged, high-dose antibiotic therapy—typically trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 6–12 months—distinguishing it from most other bacterial brain abscess pathogens.

139103.long_answer: Vemurafenib is a selective inhibitor of the BRAF V600E kinase approved for unresectable or metastatic melanoma with this mutation. Clinical trials and post-marketing data show frequent dermatologic toxicities, and hyperkeratosis is a well-documented adverse effect occurring in a substantial proportion of treated patients.

267201.long_answer: Chikungunya virus infection is characteristically accompanied by intense arthralgia—pain in the joints without objective signs of joint inflammation. This non-inflammatory joint pain can persist for weeks to months and is one of the hallmark symptoms used clinically to differentiate chikungunya from other arboviral illnesses.

386590.long_answer: In mammals, excess nitrogen from amino-acid catabolism is converted in the liver to urea via the ornithine (urea) cycle; this urea is then transported to the kidneys and excreted in urine, making it the principal nitrogen-containing constituent of mammalian urine.

211585.long_answer: Oliver–McFarlane syndrome is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene. Clinically it is distinguished by striking trichomegaly (excessively long eyelashes) together with ocular anomalies such as high myopia, chorioretinal degeneration, and progressive macular atrophy. These combined features make Oliver–McFarlane syndrome the prototypical genetic condition ‘characterized by ocular anomalies and trichomegaly.’

855861.long_answer: Pacman dysplasia is a lethal skeletal/osteochondrodysplasia documented in the medical literature (e.g., OMIM #261370) as being inherited in an autosomal recessive manner—affected infants inherit two defective alleles, one from each heterozygous carrier parent.

834021.long_answer: The CFC1 (Cripto/FRL-1/cryptic family 1) gene, situated on chromosome 2q21, has been implicated in syndromic forms of biliary atresia that occur with laterality defects. Pathogenic variants in CFC1 disrupt NODAL signaling essential for bile duct and visceral laterality development, linking this chromosome-2 gene to the pathogenesis of biliary atresia.

925506.long_answer: Galactosialidosis is a lysosomal storage disorder that can produce ocular manifestations such as cherry-red spots, corneal clouding, and progressive vision loss. Management of these vision problems requires an ophthalmologist, the medical doctor specialized in diagnosing and treating eye diseases.

511151.long_answer: Peripheral T-cell lymphomas originate from mature (post-thymic) T lymphocytes located in peripheral lymphoid tissues, most commonly the lymph nodes, rather than in the thymus or bone marrow. Sézary disease is one such lymphoma arising in these peripheral lymph nodes before malignant T cells disseminate to blood and skin.

358933.long_answer: Patients with sialidosis type II frequently develop action myoclonus—sudden, involuntary muscle jerks that are precipitated or intensified by purposeful movement. Action myoclonus is a recognized clinical subtype of myoclonus and is well-documented as a common neurological manifestation in the natural history of sialidosis type II.

544095.long_answer: In von Hippel-Lindau disease (historically called hereditary neurocutaneous angioma), some cerebellar or retinal hemangioblastomas secrete excess erythropoietin, producing secondary polycythemia. The resulting increase in blood viscosity and arterial pressure heightens the likelihood of vessel rupture, making polycythemia a recognized risk factor for cerebral (intracranial) bleeding in these patients.

323707.long_answer: Caroli disease, a congenital dilatation of the intra-hepatic bile ducts (type V choledochal cyst), is frequently found together with congenital hepatic fibrosis (Caroli syndrome). The accompanying portal tract fibrosis obstructs portal venous flow, so patients commonly develop clinically significant portal hypertension.

931553.long_answer: Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21, where individuals have three copies of human chromosome 21 instead of the usual two, leading to the characteristic clinical features of the disorder.

692472.long_answer: Acquired ichthyosis (ichthyosis acquisita) commonly appears as a paraneoplastic dermatosis, and the malignancy most classically linked to it is Hodgkin lymphoma. Numerous case series and reviews have documented that onset of ichthyosiform scaling in adulthood often precedes or parallels the diagnosis or relapse of Hodgkin lymphoma, making this cancer the best-established association.

104035.long_answer: Pickardt syndrome refers to the combination of mild-to-moderate hyperprolactinaemia (the “stalk effect”) and other pituitary–hypothalamic deficits that arise when the pituitary stalk (infundibulum) is compressed. The tumour most often responsible is a non-functioning pituitary adenoma: as it enlarges upward from the sella turcica, it mechanically compresses the infundibulum, interrupting dopaminergic inhibition of prolactin release and transport of hypothalamic releasing hormones. This mechanism produces the endocrine constellation characteristic of Pickardt syndrome.

103485.long_answer: The inherited cancer predisposition formerly called Hereditary breast–ovarian cancer syndrome (HBOC) is increasingly referred to as King syndrome, honoring geneticist Mary-Claire King, who first mapped and identified the BRCA1 gene and, together with subsequent work on BRCA2, established their role in familial breast and ovarian cancers.

325043.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in KMT2D (also called MLL2), which encodes the histone-3 lysine-4 methyltransferase 2D, are the predominant genetic cause of Kabuki syndrome type 1 and have also been classified as causing ‘syndromic microphthalmia 11’ (MCOPS11). Thus, pathogenic KMT2D variants link both the characteristic Kabuki phenotype and the microphthalmia-containing syndromic spectrum.

315450.long_answer: Relapsing polychondritis frequently co-exists with other autoimmune disorders; among these, rheumatoid arthritis is reported most often. Case series show that 10–30 % of patients with relapsing polychondritis have concomitant rheumatoid arthritis, making it the single most common autoimmune association, likely reflecting shared autoimmune mechanisms against cartilage-related antigens.

187008.long_answer: Neoplasia refers to the uncontrolled, abnormal and excessive proliferation of cells that forms a neoplasm (tumor). Such neoplastic changes in the oral mucosa can progress from benign lesions to malignant transformation, ultimately resulting in oral cancer.

359870.long_answer: Gabapentin is an anticonvulsant widely prescribed for neuropathic pain syndromes such as diabetic neuropathy and post-herpetic neuralgia; however, clinical trials and guideline reviews show it has little or no demonstrated efficacy in classical trigeminal neuralgia, in contrast to agents like carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine that reliably alleviate the paroxysmal facial pain.

583717.long_answer: Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) commonly presents with cutaneous involvement, most frequently a diffuse erythematous-maculopapular skin rash, reflecting the systemic immune hyperactivation characteristic of the disease.

103425.long_answer: Achondroplasia is almost always caused by a single point mutation in the FGFR3 gene, in which glycine at codon 380 is replaced by arginine (p.Gly380Arg, c.1138G>A/C). This activating FGFR3 mutation impairs endochondral bone growth, leading to shortened vertebral pedicles and narrowing of the spinal canal. The resulting congenital spinal stenosis frequently produces back pain and neurogenic symptoms in affected individuals.

576971.long_answer: Because the single functioning kidney must compensate by hyperfiltration, individuals with unilateral renal agenesis have an increased risk of developing systemic hypertension later in life.

583807.long_answer: Most genes that produce syndromic X-linked intellectual disability are clustered at the distal long arm of the X chromosome, cytogenetic band Xq28. Multiple well-characterised syndromic XLID genes (e.g., MECP2, L1CAM, IKBKG) reside in Xq28, making this chromosomal region the one classically associated with the syndromic form of X-linked intellectual disability.

550998.long_answer: Brachydactyly is characterized by abnormally short digits, and the shortening is primarily due to underdevelopment or premature fusion of the phalangeal bones (the tubular bones within the fingers and toes). Defective growth of these phalanges leads to the overall reduced length of the digits observed in the condition.

478003.long_answer: Whole-body 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography combined with computed tomography (18F-FDG PET/CT) can reveal increased metabolic uptake in inflamed cartilage before structural changes become apparent on routine imaging, allowing the early detection and assessment of relapsing polychondritis activity.

710756.long_answer: OSLAM (osteosarcoma, limb anomalies, and erythroid macrocytosis) syndrome has been reported in multiple affected siblings born to unaffected parents, with no evidence of vertical transmission. This pattern—affected children of two clinically normal carriers—matches the classical autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

265777.long_answer: PAI-2 is the plasminogen activator inhibitor synthesized and released by placental trophoblasts. Maternal plasma concentrations of PAI-2 rise markedly throughout gestation, becoming one of the dominant fibrinolytic inhibitors in late pregnancy, whereas PAI-1 is chiefly endothelial-derived. Thus, PAI-2 is the inhibitor secreted by the placenta and present in significant amounts during pregnancy.

813321.long_answer: The adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) tumor-suppressor gene is altered in approximately 70–80 % of sporadic colorectal cancers and in virtually all familial adenomatous polyposis–associated tumors, making it the single most frequently mutated gene in colorectal cancer. Loss-of-function APC mutations initiate the classic adenoma–carcinoma sequence by dysregulating the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway, thereby driving early neoplastic transformation in the colon.

713627.long_answer: Annuloaortic ectasia, a dilatation of the aortic root that can progress to aneurysm or dissection, frequently presents with chest pain owing to aortic wall stress and possible ischemia. Palpitations—awareness of an abnormal heartbeat—are often accompanied by chest pain when the underlying rhythm disturbance induces myocardial oxygen mismatch or simply heightens cardiac awareness. Thus, chest pain is a symptom that characteristically appears in both annuloaortic ectasia and episodes of palpitations.

965968.long_answer: Cat eye syndrome is classically caused by a super-numerary marker chromosome derived from chromosome 22 that results in partial tetrasomy of the short arm (22pter) and proximal long arm (22q11). This chromosomal abnormality produces a constellation of congenital malformations—including ocular coloboma, anal atresia, ear tags/pits, cardiac and renal defects—making it the hallmark disorder associated with tetrasomy of the p arm of chromosome 22.

232626.long_answer: Up to 5-10% of women with primary ovarian insufficiency carry a premutation (55–200 CGG repeats) in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. This premutation can expand to a full mutation (>200 repeats) during oogenesis, so carriers have a significantly increased risk of giving birth to a child affected by fragile X syndrome.

128355.long_answer: In the reported case of familial eosinophilia complicated by eosinophil-mediated endomyocardial fibrosis and advanced heart failure, the definitive therapy was orthotopic heart transplantation. Immunosuppressive post-transplant therapy controlled graft rejection while the transplant replaced the irreversibly damaged myocardium, providing clinical recovery despite persistent hereditary eosinophilia.

840364.long_answer: In annuloaortic ectasia the aneurysmal dilatation involves the aortic annulus, sinuses of Valsalva and proximal ascending aorta up to the origin of the brachiocephalic (innominate) artery, but the aortic arch beyond this point is characteristically spared and remains of normal calibre.

429824.long_answer: Pentosan polysulfate sodium (marketed as Elmiron) is the only oral drug approved specifically for interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome. It acts as a synthetic sulfated polysaccharide that adheres to and replenishes the bladder’s glycosaminoglycan layer, thereby helping repair the damaged urothelial lining and reducing pain and urinary urgency.

770532.long_answer: Most cases of the autosomal-dominant Axenfeld–Rieger syndrome are caused by pathogenic variants or dosage alterations in two transcription-factor genes: PITX2 on chromosome 4q25 and FOXC1 on chromosome 6p25. Mutations in either gene disrupt anterior segment and craniofacial development, producing the characteristic ocular and systemic features of the syndrome.

546087.long_answer: Infants with Kniest dysplasia often develop upper-airway obstruction from laryngo- or tracheomalacia caused by the type II collagen defect. Establishing a tracheostomy bypasses the collapsible segment, secures the airway, and reliably alleviates the associated respiratory distress.

198873.long_answer: In dextrocardia the heart lies in the right hemithorax, so to record a normal-looking tracing the ECG electrodes are applied as a mirror image: the precordial leads (V1–V6) are positioned on the right chest in the same intercostal spaces and relative distances (labelled V1R–V6R), and the right- and left-arm limb electrodes are swapped. This right-sided, mirror placement restores the usual anteroposterior and left-right vectors, preventing the false appearance of global infarction or axis reversal that standard left-sided placement would produce.

879263.long_answer: The opportunistic pathogen Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare (collectively termed Mycobacterium avium complex, MAC) frequently causes disseminated, systemic infections in people with advanced AIDS, especially when CD4⁺ T-cell counts fall below ~50 cells/µL. Due to severe cell-mediated immunodeficiency, these patients cannot contain the normally low-virulence organism, leading to bacteremia, lymphadenitis, and multi-organ involvement characteristic of MAC infections in AIDS.

738265.long_answer: Rotavirus is the leading worldwide cause of severe, dehydrating gastroenteritis in infants and young children. Oral rotavirus vaccines (e.g., Rotarix, RotaTeq) are recommended in infancy to induce mucosal immunity against the major circulating rotavirus strains, thereby markedly reducing hospitalizations and deaths from severe diarrheal disease.

965620.long_answer: Starting low-dose aspirin (≈75–150 mg daily) before 16 weeks’ gestation has been shown in randomized trials and guidelines to lower the risk of placenta-mediated complications, including placental abruption, by improving trophoblastic invasion and reducing platelet aggregation within the uteroplacental circulation.

527249.short_answer: Calcinosis Raynaud phenomenon Esophageal dysmotility Sclerodactyly Telangiectasia
527249.long_answer: The limited cutaneous form of systemic sclerosis is classically referred to as CREST syndrome. The acronym CREST expands to the five cardinal clinical features: Calcinosis (deposition of calcium in the skin), Raynaud phenomenon (episodic digital ischemia), Esophageal dysmotility (impaired oesophageal peristalsis and reflux), Sclerodactyly (skin tightening of the fingers), and Telangiectasia (dilated cutaneous capillaries).

278887.long_answer: Acute myeloblastic leukemia (FAB M2) is a malignant disorder of blood-forming cells; its diagnosis, chemotherapeutic management, and supportive care are handled by the medical specialty of hematology (often within combined hematology-oncology practice), which focuses on diseases of the blood and bone marrow.

902209.long_answer: Paramyotonia congenita is an inherited neuromuscular channelopathy caused by mutations in the skeletal-muscle sodium-channel gene (SCN4A). Diagnosis relies on neurologic examination, electromyography, and confirmatory genetic testing, and treatment involves drugs such as mexiletine or acetazolamide plus lifestyle counseling. These evaluations and interventions fall within the expertise of a neurologist—typically one with a subspecialty in neuromuscular medicine—who is therefore the appropriate specialist to diagnose and manage paramyotonia congenita.

286076.long_answer: Urban–Rogers–Meyer syndrome is a rare congenital (present-at-birth) genetic disorder characterized by multiple structural and functional anomalies such as absent or hypoplastic patellae, genital malformations, distinctive facial features, skeletal abnormalities and intellectual disability. Because these abnormalities arise during embryonic development and are already present at birth, the syndrome is classified among congenital anomalies—commonly referred to as birth defects—by clinical genetics references and dysmorphology texts. Therefore, Urban–Rogers–Meyer syndrome is indeed considered a birth defect.

654584.long_answer: Neural tube defects like spina bifida arise when the neural folds fail to fuse during neurulation, the process that forms the neural tube in the 3rd–4th week of embryonic development.

443807.long_answer: Chloramphenicol is well-known for its potential to produce idiosyncratic bone-marrow toxicity. In susceptible individuals it can suppress hematopoiesis, leading to simultaneous decreases in red cells, white cells, and platelets—that is, pancytopenia—sometimes progressing to aplastic anemia.

620499.long_answer: Atrioventricular septal defect leads to excessive pulmonary blood flow and heart failure, producing dyspnea—commonly described as shortness of breath. Dyspnea is one of the top chief complaints prompting emergency department visits across the United States, making it both a hallmark symptom of this congenital heart defect and a leading reason for seeking urgent care.

785233.long_answer: Hypertrichosis of the palms and soles (hypertrichosis palmaris et plantaris, sometimes called “hairy palms and soles”) is a rare genodermatosis. Pedigrees that have been reported in the medical literature show vertical transmission with affected individuals in successive generations and male-to-male transmission, the classic pattern of autosomal-dominant inheritance. OMIM (catalogue number 239200) also lists the disorder as autosomal dominant. Although isolated sporadic cases can occur, the inherited form is not regarded as autosomal recessive. Therefore the statement that hairy palms and soles due to hypertrichosis are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner is incorrect.

408708.long_answer: Hyperphalangy—the presence of more phalanges per digit than the mammalian norm—is a hallmark of the fully aquatic flippers of cetaceans (whales, dolphins, porpoises) and sirenians (manatees, dugongs). In both groups the number of phalanges in the central digits can double the typical 2-3-3-3-3 mammalian pattern, an adaptation that stiffens and elongates the paddle-like forelimbs for efficient swimming.

897819.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the homeobox transcription factor gene ALX1 have been shown to disturb midline craniofacial patterning. Such mutations produce the characteristic median facial cleft, orbital hypertelorism and nasal malformations that define autosomal-recessive frontonasal dysplasia (FND type 3), establishing ALX1 as a causal gene for frontonasal dysplasia.

601093.long_answer: Congenital limb deformities involve structural abnormalities of the bones, joints, or soft tissues present at birth. Evaluation and correction—whether via casting, bracing, growth-modulation procedures, or complex reconstructive surgery—require detailed knowledge of musculoskeletal anatomy and surgical techniques. These responsibilities fall within the expertise of an orthopedic surgeon (often a pediatric orthopedic subspecialist), the physician trained to diagnose and treat congenital and acquired disorders of the limbs and skeleton.

385566.long_answer: Lassa fever is caused by the Lassa virus, whose natural reservoir is the multimammate rat (Mastomys natalensis). The principal route of human infection is environmental exposure to the rat’s excreta—especially urine and feces ("droppings"). People become infected when they inhale aerosolized particles, ingest food or water contaminated by these droppings, or when the excreta come into contact with broken skin or mucous membranes. Although secondary (person-to-person) transmission can occur via direct contact with the blood or body fluids of infected patients, the primary mode of transmission recognized by epidemiologic studies and WHO/CDC guidance remains contact with or ingestion/inhalation of infected rat droppings or urine. Therefore, the statement is accurate.

229737.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, especially when accompanied by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, is frequently caused by mutations in the PRKAG2 gene, which encodes the γ2 regulatory subunit of AMP-activated protein kinase. Genetic testing for a PRKAG2 mutation is therefore part of the diagnostic evaluation of patients with familial or syndromic WPW.

804282.long_answer: Nathalie (Comèl-Netherton) syndrome is classically characterized by a distinctive hair-shaft defect called trichorrhexis invaginata, often described as “bamboo hair.” This abnormality, which makes the hair brittle and easily broken, is regarded as the cardinal clinical sign of the syndrome.

324388.long_answer: Argentine hemorrhagic fever, caused by Junín virus, is acquired chiefly when people inhale dust or aerosols contaminated with the urine, saliva, or feces of its natural rodent reservoir (Calomys musculinus). This airborne exposure to rodent excreta is the principal route by which the virus is transmitted from rodents to humans.

367495.long_answer: If a woman cannot tolerate oral nitroimidazoles because of nausea, metronidazole can be administered intravaginally (e.g., 0.75 % gel or suppository inserted once or twice daily for 5 days). Delivering the drug directly into the vagina bypasses gastrointestinal absorption, minimizing systemic side-effects while providing sufficient local concentrations to eradicate Trichomonas vaginalis.

639236.long_answer: Toxocariasis, a helminth infection caused by the dog and cat roundworms Toxocara canis and Toxocara cati, is recognized as a neglected disease of poverty in the United States. Seroprevalence studies show the highest rates among children living in inner-city neighborhoods where soil contamination with infective eggs and limited access to veterinary care for pets are common. This urban poverty linkage makes toxocariasis the paradigmatic neglected disease prevalent in U.S. inner-city areas.

382444.long_answer: Psoriatic arthritis is a seronegative spondyloarthritis that occurs in patients with psoriasis. A hallmark clinical feature is dactylitis—diffuse, sausage-like swelling of entire fingers or toes—resulting from inflammation of joints, tendons, and their sheaths.

948027.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the PAX2 transcription factor cause the papillorenal (renal-coloboma) syndrome. Because PAX2 is critical for optic stalk and optic nerve development, its disruption produces optic disc/retinal colobomas and, in many patients, optic nerve hypoplasia. Thus a PAX2 mutation is classically associated with the coexistence of coloboma and optic nerve hypoplasia.

551084.long_answer: Flock worker's lung is an occupational interstitial lung disease that develops in workers who inhale microscopic ‘flock’ fibers (typically nylon, rayon, or polyester) used to give fabrics and other materials a velvet-like texture. Chronic exposure to these short synthetic fibers triggers lymphocytic bronchiolitis and interstitial pneumonitis, leading to restrictive lung impairment characteristic of this disease.

386467.long_answer: Homocystinuria can weaken the physis and surrounding bone through altered collagen cross-linking and osteoporosis, predisposing children and adolescents to slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE). Consequently, SCFE is a recognized orthopedic condition that may occur in patients with homocystinuria.

443295.long_answer: Osteopathia striata with cranial sclerosis is an X-linked dominant skeletal dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AMER1 gene (also known as WTX/FAM123B). AMER1 encodes a negative regulator of Wnt/β-catenin signaling; its inactivation disrupts osteoblast differentiation and leads to the characteristic linear striations and cranial sclerosis of the disease.

838918.long_answer: Infections with the cattle-grub larvae Hypoderma lineatum and Hypoderma bovis are routinely treated with ivermectin. This macrocyclic lactone reaches therapeutic levels in tissue and kills the migrating first- and second-stage larvae by opening glutamate-gated chloride channels, leading to paralysis and death of the parasite. A single oral or parenteral dose of ivermectin is highly effective and is the standard treatment recommended in veterinary and occasional human cases of hypodermosis.

421513.long_answer: Paul Karason, known for the argyria that turned his skin blue, underwent coronary artery bypass graft surgery for heart disease. In the period leading up to his death in 2013, he was hospitalized after developing pneumonia, a severe lung infection that can complicate recovery after major cardiac surgery and contribute to respiratory failure. This bout of pneumonia was one of the acute conditions he suffered immediately before his death.

430499.long_answer: Prednisone, a systemic corticosteroid, is first-line therapy in immune thrombocytopenic purpura because it suppresses autoantibody-mediated platelet destruction. The same broad anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive effects make prednisone a standard drug for controlling joint inflammation in rheumatoid arthritis and for inducing remission in Crohn’s disease.

150083.long_answer: Narcolepsy, especially the form with cataplexy, is caused by the selective loss of orexin-producing (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus. This orexin deficiency disrupts the maintenance of wakefulness and REM-sleep control. Wake-promoting agents such as modafinil indirectly enhance orexin signaling and compensate for the missing orexin drive, helping patients stay awake during the day.

597529.long_answer: Mutations in the PC gene abolish or reduce the activity of the mitochondrial enzyme pyruvate carboxylase. Without this enzyme, pyruvate cannot be efficiently converted to oxaloacetate, causing excess pyruvate to be shunted to lactate and resulting in severe lactic acidosis. Therefore, lactic acidosis due to PC gene mutations is characteristic of pyruvate carboxylase deficiency.

906467.long_answer: Cornelia de Lange syndrome (Brachmann-de Lange syndrome) is a congenital cohesinopathy caused most often by pathogenic variants in NIPBL or related cohesin-complex genes. A hallmark is the characteristic “mephistophelian” facies—highly arched, often confluent eyebrows, long eyelashes, and down-turned mouth corners. Typical dysmorphic features also include low-set posteriorly rotated ears, anteverted nares, and micrognathia, making this syndrome the classic genetic disorder described with both a mephistophelian appearance and low-set ears.

295190.long_answer: Carrier couples for alpha-thalassemia can undergo in-vitro fertilization with preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD); embryos are biopsied and only those without the pathogenic HBA1/HBA2 deletions are implanted, thereby avoiding the birth of a child with alpha-thalassemia.

813260.long_answer: Endocarditis is most frequently an infective process caused by bacteria that colonize and inflame the endocardial surfaces of the heart, especially the cardiac valves. Organisms such as Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus viridans are classic culprits, making bacterial infection the condition most commonly associated with endocarditis.

566794.long_answer: In congenital disorders of glycosylation, lectins serve as laboratory probes that bind defined sugar motifs on patient glycoproteins. By comparing lectin-binding patterns (e.g., lectin blotting of serum transferrin) to normal controls, clinicians can detect abnormal or missing glycans and thereby diagnose and subtype CDG. Thus, lectins function as diagnostic tools rather than pathogenic factors in these disorders.

266302.long_answer: Coxiella burnetii is the Gram-negative bacterium that causes Q fever. Although long regarded as an obligate intracellular pathogen, it can now be propagated outside host cells in specialized axenic media such as acidified citrate cysteine medium (ACCM), demonstrating its ability to grow in a cell-free culture system.

495341.long_answer: Trichinosis is contracted by eating raw or under-cooked pork that contains Trichinella spiralis larvae. Jewish dietary (kosher) laws forbid consumption of pork altogether, eliminating this major exposure route and thus helping to prevent the infection.

504877.long_answer: Because treating Pseudomonas aeruginosa often requires prolonged, broad-spectrum or combination antibiotic regimens, the normal intestinal microbiota can be severely disrupted. This ecological imbalance permits overgrowth of toxigenic Clostridioides (Clostridium) difficile, whose toxins injure the colonic mucosa and produce the characteristic inflammatory plaques of pseudomembranous colitis—an important, potentially life-threatening adverse effect of intensive antipseudomonal therapy.

130294.long_answer: In osteogenesis imperfecta, point mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2 often replace the obligatory glycine residue in the Gly-X-Y collagen repeat with a bulkier amino acid; the classic and most frequently cited change is substitution of glycine by cysteine, which disrupts triple-helix formation and weakens type I collagen, producing the brittle-bone phenotype.

967392.long_answer: Dental ankylosis is the pathological fusion of a tooth’s cementum or dentin directly to the surrounding alveolar bone, resulting in obliteration of the periodontal ligament space. This union prevents normal eruptive movement and can lead to infra-occlusion or difficulty in tooth extraction.

859375.long_answer: Proteus syndrome is caused by a somatic, activating missense mutation in the serine-threonine kinase gene AKT1—specifically the c.49G>A (p.Glu17Lys, E17K) substitution. This mutation constitutively activates AKT1 within the PI3K–AKT signaling pathway, driving the segmental overgrowth and tissue dysregulation characteristic of Proteus syndrome.

872048.long_answer: Psychosis precipitated by stimulants such as amphetamine or cocaine produces positive symptoms—paranoid delusions, auditory hallucinations, thought disorder—that are virtually indistinguishable from an acute episode of paranoid schizophrenia. Because the phenomenology, course, and neurochemical basis (excess dopaminergic transmission) are so similar, stimulant psychosis is often used as an experimental model for schizophrenia, and heavy stimulant use can precipitate or unmask latent schizophrenic illness.

541933.long_answer: Pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency results from variant alleles of the BCHE gene, which encodes the plasma enzyme butyrylcholinesterase. Mutations such as the ‘atypical’ (Dibucaine-resistant) and ‘fluoride-resistant’ alleles reduce or abolish enzyme activity, leading to prolonged apnea after succinylcholine or other ester anesthetics. Thus, allelic variants of BCHE are the molecular basis of pseudocholinesterase deficiency.

979327.long_answer: Eugene Merle Shoemaker was diagnosed with Addison's disease, a primary adrenal insufficiency in which the adrenal cortex fails to produce adequate cortisol and aldosterone. Because astronauts must tolerate extreme physical stress and cannot risk an adrenal crisis, this chronic adrenal gland disorder disqualified him from astronaut training, thereby preventing him from becoming the first geologist to walk on the Moon.

125882.long_answer: Mutations in ORC1, which encodes the largest subunit of the Origin-Recognition Complex (a core component of the DNA pre-replication complex), have been shown to cause a form of primordial dwarfism known as Meier-Gorlin syndrome. Defective ORC1 impairs origin licensing during S-phase entry, leading to global reductions in cell proliferation and the extreme proportionate growth failure characteristic of primordial dwarfism.

905902.long_answer: Desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy (desminopathy) is a rare genetic neuromuscular disorder. The primary specialist who evaluates, diagnoses and follows these patients is a neuromuscular physician—typically a neurologist, clinical geneticist or physiatrist with expertise in muscle disease. The diagnostic work-up centers on history and neurologic examination, serum creatine kinase, electromyography, muscle biopsy with histopathology/immunohistochemistry, and confirmatory DES gene sequencing. Muscle MRI or CT can provide supportive information on patterns of muscle involvement, and those images are interpreted by a radiologist; however, radiology plays an ancillary role. The radiologist is therefore not considered the primary specialist responsible for making the diagnosis. Consequently, stating that a radiologist would be the primary specialist involved in diagnosing desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy is not consistent with established clinical practice.

569009.long_answer: Dermatomyositis is frequently associated with the presence of anti-Mi-2 autoantibodies. These IgG antibodies target the Mi-2 component of the nucleosome-remodeling deacetylase (NuRD) complex in cell nuclei. Because anti-Mi-2 antibodies are found in a significant subset of dermatomyositis patients and are highly specific for this inflammatory myopathy, they serve as reliable serological biomarkers for diagnosis and disease subset classification.

896678.long_answer: Multiple well-documented lifestyle factors heighten the likelihood of diabetic nephropathy in people with diabetes. Cigarette smoking accelerates intrarenal hemodynamic changes and independently predicts faster decline in glomerular filtration rate. Persistently poor glycaemic control—often related to unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, and obesity—directly increases hyper-filtration injury and the development of micro-albuminuria. High blood pressure, which can be aggravated by excess dietary sodium, contributes synergistically to renal damage. Epidemiologic and interventional studies consistently show that patients who quit smoking, maintain tight glycaemic control through balanced diet and regular exercise, limit sodium, and keep body weight and blood pressure in recommended ranges have a significantly lower incidence and slower progression of diabetic nephropathy. Therefore, certain modifiable lifestyle habits do increase the risk of developing the condition.

433803.long_answer: When lipomas in familial multiple lipomatosis become large, lie deep, or appear to infiltrate muscle fibres or neurovascular structures, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is employed because it provides superior soft-tissue contrast and delineates the extent of intramuscular or neurovascular involvement, guiding diagnosis and surgical planning.

988951.long_answer: Cockayne syndrome is an autosomal-recessive DNA-repair disorder characterized clinically by growth failure, microcephaly, photosensitivity, neurodevelopmental delay and premature ageing. Pathological studies show diffuse white-matter hypomyelination, basal-ganglia and cerebellar calcifications, cortical and cerebellar atrophy, neuronal loss and astrogliosis. Deposition of β-amyloid and formation of Alzheimer-type neuritic (senile) plaques are not a recognized or common feature of Cockayne syndrome. Amyloid plaques are instead a hallmark of Alzheimer disease and certain other amyloidogenic disorders, not of Cockayne syndrome. Therefore, the statement that amyloid plaques are commonly seen in patients with Cockayne syndrome is not supported by established biomedical evidence.

704659.long_answer: In a megaureter the ureter is markedly dilated and its distal segment exhibits impaired peristalsis; this functional obstruction causes urinary stasis. Stagnant urine provides an excellent milieu for bacterial growth, so patients are prone to repeated ascending infections—i.e., recurrent urinary tract infections—which is one of the main recognized complications of an obstructive megaureter.

248155.long_answer: Most individuals with Nager syndrome carry heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions in the SF3B4 gene, which encodes the splicing factor 3B subunit 4 involved in pre-mRNA processing. Disruption of SF3B4 impairs normal craniofacial and limb development, making these mutations the genetic alteration most often linked to Nager acrofacial dysostosis.

138585.long_answer: Dermatographic urticaria (dermographism) is mediated by histamine released from cutaneous mast cells. While H1-antihistamines are first-line therapy, adding an H2-receptor antagonist can improve control. Cimetidine, a well-studied H2 antagonist, blocks histamine H2 receptors on dermal vasculature and mast cells, thereby reducing wheal formation and pruritus in dermatographic urticaria.

416778.long_answer: Tick-borne encephalitis virus may progress from an initial febrile phase to infection of the central nervous system; involvement of both the meninges and brain parenchyma produces meningoencephalitis. This severe complication is marked by high fever, altered consciousness, seizures, and can leave permanent neurological deficits or be fatal, making it one of the gravest outcomes of tick-borne encephalitis.

351682.long_answer: In eosinophilic gastroenteritis a Th2-skewed immune response leads to over-expression of the cytokines interleukin-3 (IL-3), interleukin-5 (IL-5) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).  These three cytokines share a common β-receptor chain and together promote eosinophil chemotaxis, activation, survival and degranulation in the gastrointestinal mucosa, explaining the tissue eosinophilia characteristic of the disease.

296036.long_answer: Native American myopathy is a congenital myopathy first described in the Lumbee tribe and is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the STAC3 gene (SH3 and cysteine-rich domain 3). STAC3 is critical for skeletal-muscle excitation-contraction coupling, and the recurrent STAC3 p.Trp284Ser variant segregates with the characteristic myopathy and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility seen in affected individuals.

119625.long_answer: Meckel-Gruber syndrome is an autosomal-recessive malformation (lethal ciliopathy) whose core findings include severe internal hydrocephalus/occipital encephalocele, cystic dysplastic kidneys and post-axial polydactyly. Autopsy studies show that affected female fetuses frequently have Müllerian duct fusion defects, most commonly a bicornuate or uterus didelphys. Thus the simultaneous presence of a bicornuate uterus with hydrocephalus internus is characteristic of Meckel-Gruber syndrome.

294708.long_answer: The trauma triad of death is composed of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy. Coagulopathy refers to impaired blood coagulation, leading to uncontrolled bleeding after severe trauma. It develops when massive blood loss, dilution of clotting factors, hypothermia, and acidosis disrupt the normal clotting cascade, making it a pivotal—and often fatal—element of the triad.

969074.long_answer: Over 90 % of osteogenesis imperfecta cases are the mild, Type I form, caused by autosomal-dominant loss-of-function mutations in the COL1A1 gene encoding the α1 chain of type I collagen. These null (often nonsense or frameshift) mutations reduce the amount of normal collagen produced, leading to the characteristic bone fragility of the commonest form of the disease.

574329.long_answer: Apolipoprotein B deficiency results from mutations in the APOB gene located on chromosome 2 (region 2p24.2). Chromosome 2 is one of the numbered, non-sex chromosomes—an autosome—so the disorder is inherited in an autosomal (typically autosomal-recessive) pattern.

855939.long_answer: Benign familial neonatal seizures (also termed benign familial neonatal epilepsy) characteristically present in healthy full-term newborns with frequent, brief focal clonic seizures that may migrate from one side of the body to the other and can secondarily generalize. These clonic motor events, typically starting on day 2–3 of life and resolving within weeks, are the hallmark seizure type associated with this inherited KCNQ2/KCNQ3 channelopathy.

168034.long_answer: Potassium-aggravated myotonia is one of the ‘sodium channel myotonias.’ It is produced by missense mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel α-subunit (NaV1.4). These gain-of-function mutations impair channel inactivation, making muscle fibers hyper-excitable; elevated extracellular potassium further increases this excitability, provoking myotonic stiffness.

525608.long_answer: During general anesthesia, IgE-mediated anaphylaxis is most commonly triggered by neuromuscular blocking agents (e.g., succinylcholine, rocuronium, vecuronium). Their quaternary ammonium groups can cross-link pre-existing IgE on mast cells, provoking rapid histamine release and systemic anaphylaxis, making this drug class the leading cause of peri-operative allergic reactions.

118388.long_answer: Controlled sleep-laboratory studies (e.g., Drake et al., J Clin Sleep Med 2013) demonstrate that ingesting caffeine up to six hours before bedtime significantly shortens total sleep time and lowers sleep efficiency. Consequently, sleep-hygiene guidelines recommend a ‘six-hour caffeine cutoff’—ceasing caffeine consumption at least six hours prior to intended sleep—to minimize caffeine’s disruptive effects on sleep quality.

354010.long_answer: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy) produces progressive distal muscle atrophy and sensory loss. The two most common genetic forms involve the PMP22 gene duplication on chromosome 17 (CMT1A) and mutations in the MPZ gene on chromosome 1 (CMT1B), linking the disorder to abnormalities on chromosomes 17 and 1.

187197.long_answer: Saethre-Chotzen syndrome (acrocephalosyndactyly type III) is an autosomal-dominant craniosynostosis disorder produced by pathogenic variants in TWIST1. Clinically it combines: 1) conductive hearing loss from external and middle-ear malformations; 2) characteristic eyelid ptosis; and 3) skeletal anomalies such as craniosynostosis, brachydactyly and syndactyly. This constellation of features makes Saethre-Chotzen syndrome the well-established diagnosis that fits the triad described.

806042.long_answer: The albino phenotype in guinea pigs is produced by mutations at the classical ‘c-locus’, which encodes the enzyme tyrosinase (gene symbol TYR). Loss-of-function alterations in TYR block the first step of melanin biosynthesis, preventing pigment formation in hair, skin and eyes and thereby causing albinism.

907788.long_answer: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the SKI gene, which is located on chromosome 1p36. Mutations in SKI disrupt TGF-β signalling, producing the craniosynostosis–marfanoid phenotype of the syndrome. Cardiac manifestations of SKI mutations include aortic root dilatation and mitral valve prolapse, linking SKI to both Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome and mitral valve disease.

950328.long_answer: For severe pulmonic (pulmonary) stenosis, the evidence-based first-line therapy is percutaneous balloon pulmonary valvuloplasty, in which a balloon catheter is advanced across the stenotic pulmonary valve and inflated to split the fused commissures, relieving the outflow obstruction. It achieves high success rates, low complication risk, and has largely replaced surgical valvotomy as the preferred treatment when the valve is anatomically suitable.

542461.long_answer: The Ex Utero Intrapartum Treatment (EXIT) procedure is a specialized cesarean-based delivery in which the fetus is partially delivered but kept on placental support while surgeons secure the airway (e.g., intubation, tracheostomy) before complete delivery. It is specifically employed for fetuses with airway-compressing lesions such as large congenital pulmonary airway malformations, ensuring ventilation is established before cord clamping.

470808.long_answer: Ellis-van Creveld syndrome is an autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia characterized by mesomelic limb shortening, polydactyly, and cardiac anomalies. It results from loss-of-function mutations in the EVC gene (or the adjacent EVC2), which disrupt ciliary Hedgehog signaling required for normal endochondral bone growth. Hence, the disease associated with mesomelic dwarfism due to an EVC mutation is Ellis-van Creveld syndrome.

585519.long_answer: Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins in the distal esophagus that develop as a complication of portal hypertension and can cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Their diagnosis (upper endoscopy) and primary treatments—endoscopic band ligation, sclerotherapy, variceal surveillance, and medical therapy with non-selective β-blockers—are all core procedures of gastroenterologists. Therefore, the specialty most commonly responsible for managing and treating esophageal varices is gastroenterology.

297123.long_answer: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in the EZH2 gene cause Weaver syndrome, an over-growth disorder characterized by advanced bone age, macrocephaly and distinctive craniofacial features. Among these facial findings are alterations of the palpebral fissures—typically down-slanting or widened—that reflect the syndrome’s impact on peri-ocular development.

489301.long_answer: In peripheral nerve grafting after facial injury, autologous Schwann cells from a donor nerve (e.g., sural nerve) are implanted because these glial cells myelinate peripheral axons and secrete neurotrophic and guidance factors that direct and accelerate regrowth of injured facial nerve fibers, thereby restoring nerve function.

761714.long_answer: Cartilage–hair hypoplasia is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the non-coding RNA gene RMRP (RNA component of mitochondrial RNA-processing endoribonuclease), which is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 9 (9p). Therefore, the disease-associated gene resides on chromosome 9.

960263.long_answer: Angiolipomas are benign tumors composed largely of adipose tissue; one accepted management option—particularly when multiple lesions are present—is liposuction, a procedure that removes the fatty component of the tumor through suction-assisted aspiration.

570815.long_answer: In individuals with Marfanoid habitus (including many with Marfan syndrome), CT of the temporal bone often reveals an enlarged vestibular aqueduct. This structural malformation disrupts endolymphatic fluid dynamics in the inner ear and is a well-recognised cause of early-onset sensorineural hearing impairment in these patients.

823797.long_answer: Walker–Warburg syndrome is a severe congenital muscular dystrophy characterised by profound brain and eye malformations. Disorders of muscle and central nervous system development are diagnosed and followed chiefly by a paediatric neurologist, who performs the neuromuscular examination, orders brain MRI and genetic testing, and coordinates multidisciplinary care for the affected infant.

974187.long_answer: Cystic hygroma (a congenital lymphatic malformation) can enlarge the neck and upper thorax, and in the neonatal period it may cause airway obstruction, respiratory distress, or other complications that demand immediate advanced resuscitation and surgical or ENT intervention. Current perinatal guidelines therefore recommend that fetuses with a prenatally diagnosed cystic hygroma be delivered in a tertiary-care center with a neonatal intensive care unit and ready access to pediatric surgery/airway specialists (sometimes employing an EXIT procedure). Hence, arranging delivery in a NICU-equipped facility is considered appropriate and standard of care.

621644.long_answer: Familial partial lipodystrophy is characterized by selective loss of body fat from specific regions. The fat that disappears is the adipose tissue located in the hypodermis (subcutaneous layer) of the integumentary system, leaving the epidermis and dermis largely intact.

233652.long_answer: In glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease), the inability to mobilize hepatic glycogen limits glucose availability. When carbohydrates are deficient, the body compensates by oxidizing fatty acids, generating excess ketone bodies; hence affected individuals can develop ketosis (and occasionally ketoacidosis).

608277.long_answer: The American College of Medical Genetics (ACMG) convened an expert panel that, in 2006, issued the Recommended Uniform Screening Panel for U.S. newborns. That list of 29 core disorders specifically includes 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase deficiency, making ACMG the organization that formally recommends newborn screening for this inborn error of leucine metabolism.

315889.long_answer: Broca’s area, located in the dominant (usually left) posterior inferior frontal gyrus, subserves expressive language. Lesions here not only abolish the ability to speak but also eliminate the ability to write (agraphia) because writing is another form of language output. The region lies immediately anterior to the primary motor cortex for the face and arm; therefore strokes or other damage that involve Broca’s area typically extend into adjacent motor cortex, producing contralateral limb or facial paralysis. Thus the same lesion produces both agraphia and paralysis, linking these two deficits to Broca’s area.

833087.long_answer: Central serous chorioretinopathy is caused by focal defects in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Breakdown of the RPE barrier allows choroidal fluid to accumulate under the neurosensory retina, producing the characteristic serous retinal detachment seen in this condition.

120407.long_answer: Cyclosporine A, a calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant, has been reported in case studies to induce remission of steroid-refractory eosinophilic cystitis. By blocking T-cell activation and downstream cytokine release, cyclosporine dampens the eosinophil-driven inflammatory response in the bladder wall, leading to symptomatic and histologic improvement.

432102.long_answer: Bartonella quintana, the agent of trench fever, is well-documented as causing recurrent bloodstream infections and endocarditis in marginalized populations, especially homeless individuals and intravenous drug users who are frequently exposed to body-louse infestation, the main vector of this species.

532850.long_answer: When actinomycosis does not respond adequately to prolonged high-dose antibiotic regimens, hyperbaric oxygen therapy can be added. Exposing tissues to 100% oxygen at increased atmospheric pressure raises local oxygen tensions, directly inhibiting the anaerobic Actinomyces organisms and enhancing the bactericidal activity of penicillins, thereby improving outcomes in refractory cases.

198248.long_answer: Homocystinuria is most commonly caused by deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase. This blocks conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine, leading to accumulation of free homocysteine that readily oxidizes to its disulfide form, homocystine. The excess homocystine is water-soluble and is excreted in large amounts in the urine, making it the hallmark substance detected in patients with homocystinuria.

667557.long_answer: Papillitis is the anterior form of optic neuritis in which the inflammatory process involves the optic nerve head (optic disc), producing disc swelling visible on fundoscopic examination. This distinguishes it from retrobulbar neuritis, where inflammation is posterior to the disc and the optic nerve head appears normal.

526327.long_answer: Midodrine, an oral alpha-1 adrenergic agonist, is commonly prescribed for patients with recurrent vasovagal (neurocardiogenic) syncope who continue to faint despite non-pharmacologic measures such as hydration, salt loading, and physical counter-pressure maneuvers. By increasing peripheral vascular resistance and venous return, midodrine helps prevent the hypotension and bradycardia that trigger vasovagal episodes, and is therefore recommended when other treatments are insufficient.

709446.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), particularly with gadolinium contrast, is the first-line and most widely used modality for evaluating suspected spinal tumors because it provides high-resolution, multiplanar visualization of the spinal cord, vertebrae, and surrounding soft tissues without ionizing radiation.

329656.long_answer: Kocher-Debré-Semelaigne syndrome presents in children with profound hypothyroidism and generalized skeletal-muscle hypertrophy (‘pseudohypertrophy’). The definitive treatment is replacement of the deficient thyroid hormone with levothyroxine; restoring euthyroidism reverses the muscular enlargement and other hypothyroid features.

722245.long_answer: The Ishihara pseudo-isochromatic plate test is the standard clinical tool for detecting and grading color-vision deficiencies. It is routinely used in patients with retinal disorders, including age-related macular degeneration, to document acquired color vision loss.

982459.long_answer: Ellis–Van Creveld (chondroectodermal dysplasia) is characterized radiographically by congenital fusion of the hamate and capitate carpal bones. This hamate–capitate coalition is a well-recognized skeletal marker of the syndrome and helps in its diagnosis.

110356.long_answer: Because the spleen is absent, the person is prone to sudden, fulminant sepsis from encapsulated bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae). A medical identification tag instantly informs clinicians of the patient’s asplenia, prompting urgent empiric antibiotics and other prophylactic measures, thereby reducing the high mortality risk of overwhelming postsplenectomy infection.

999745.long_answer: Nevoid basal-cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome most commonly arises from germ-line mutations in the PTCH1 tumor-suppressor gene, a key receptor in the Hedgehog signaling pathway. Loss-of-function PTCH1 mutations not only predispose to multiple basal-cell carcinomas but are also frequently found in sporadic and syndrome-associated medulloblastomas, especially the desmoplastic subtype, linking the same genetic defect to both conditions.

576851.long_answer: Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome causes venous malformations and limb swelling; wearing graduated compression stockings applies external pressure that improves venous return, limits edema, and reduces pain, making these compression garments a standard conservative measure to relieve KTS symptoms.

959834.long_answer: An atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD), also known as an endocardial cushion defect, is frequently linked to chromosomal abnormalities—most notably trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) and other aneuploidies. The combined atrial and ventricular septal gaps with common AV valve allow a large left-to-right shunt, leading to pulmonary over-circulation and heart failure. This volume overload manifests clinically as tachypnea and shortness of breath in infants and children.

344916.long_answer: Staphylococcus aureus is the classic cause of a skin infection that can progress from superficial lesions (such as folliculitis, impetigo, or cellulitis) into subcutaneous tissue, fascia, and muscle. If not controlled, the bacterium can spread contiguously or via the bloodstream to the underlying bone, where it provokes an inflammatory reaction called osteomyelitis. Its virulence factors (e.g., protein A, toxins, biofilm formation) enable this deep-tissue invasion and persistence.

600801.long_answer: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in the TWIST2 gene have been reported in individuals with Ablepharon-macrostomia syndrome. TWIST2 encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that participates in cranial suture and facial mesenchyme development; consequently, the same mutations have also been documented to cause premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) in affected patients. Thus, TWIST2 mutation links both Ablepharon macrostomia syndrome and craniosynostosis.

156500.long_answer: Léri–Weill dyschondrosteosis is a mesomelic form of dwarfism caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the SHOX (short stature homeobox) gene located in the pseudoautosomal region of the X and Y chromosomes; disruption of SHOX impairs skeletal growth, producing the characteristic short stature and Madelung deformity.

532694.long_answer: Degos disease (malignant atrophic papulosis) typically presents first with pathognomonic porcelain-white, atrophic papules on the skin. These distinctive cutaneous lesions are within the domain of dermatology, and dermatologists are trained to recognize and diagnose such papular eruptions; therefore, a dermatologist is the specialist most likely to make the initial diagnosis of Degos disease.

380808.long_answer: Members of the nematode genus Gongylonema (order Spirurida), such as Gongylonema pulchrum, parasitize the upper digestive tract of mammals and occasionally humans. Infection with these ‘gullet worms’ produces the disease termed gongylonemiasis, characterized by serpiginous tunnels in the oral, esophageal or gastric mucosa and associated irritation or foreign-body sensation. Thus, the pathological condition resulting from Gongylonema infection is called gongylonemiasis.

373743.long_answer: Viral hemorrhagic fevers (e.g., Ebola, Lassa, Marburg, Crimean-Congo) are caused by highly contagious viruses that require specialized infection control, isolation, antiviral therapy, and public-health coordination. These responsibilities fall under the internal-medicine subspecialty of Infectious Disease, whose physicians are trained to diagnose, manage, and contain serious viral infections and their complications.

746875.long_answer: Blepharospasm is a focal dystonia of the eyelid that is treated with interventions such as botulinum-toxin injections and, if needed, eyelid surgery. These diagnostic and therapeutic procedures are routinely performed by ophthalmologists—especially those trained in oculoplastic surgery—making ophthalmology the specialty responsible for managing blepharospasm.

701363.long_answer: During normal embryogenesis the urorectal septum splits the common cloaca into a ventral urogenital sinus (future bladder) and a dorsal anorectal canal (future anus). Malformation of this partitioning or failure of the anal membrane to perforate produces an imperforate anus, often with recto-urinary fistulas, making this the characteristic birth defect linked to the process of separating the anus from the bladder.

325539.long_answer: Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) is regenerated from its oxidized form by the enzyme dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR). If DHPR is deficient, BH4 levels fall, impairing the BH4-dependent enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. This blocks conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, so phenylalanine accumulates in the blood (hyperphenylalaninemia), producing a form of ‘malignant’ phenylketonuria.

535771.long_answer: Exophoria is a latent heterophoria in which the visual axes have a tendency to move outward (away from the midline). When this outward (divergent) deviation becomes manifest, it is termed an exotropia—sometimes called a divergent strabismus or exodeviation. Thus, the specific word that denotes the outward deviation associated with exophoria is “exotropia.”

352844.long_answer: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria causes rapid complement-mediated destruction of red blood cells. When the hemolysis is brisk enough to produce severe, symptomatic anemia, the standard supportive therapy is transfusion of compatible packed red blood cells to quickly restore oxygen-carrying capacity while hemolysis is controlled by warming and treating any underlying trigger.

648635.long_answer: In cases of hypodontia (congenital absence of one or more teeth, excluding third molars), epidemiological studies consistently show that the mandibular (lower) second premolar is the single tooth most frequently missing. Large population surveys rank it ahead of the maxillary lateral incisor and maxillary second premolar, making the lower second premolar the commonest tooth absent in hypodontia.

964366.long_answer: Fragile X syndrome is caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome, leading to methylation-mediated silencing of the gene and loss of FMRP protein. It is the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism spectrum features. Because it follows X-linked dominant inheritance with variable penetrance (full mutation, premutation, carrier states), families benefit greatly from genetic counseling to assess carrier status, recurrence risk, and related conditions such as Fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS) and primary ovarian insufficiency.
