822347.long_answer: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) obtains placental (chorionic-villous) tissue at 10–12 weeks’ gestation, providing fetal DNA that can be molecularly tested for the SMN1 gene deletion/mutation that causes spinal muscular atrophy, allowing definitive prenatal diagnosis.

503148.long_answer: The neuropathic facial or limb pain produced by a syringobulbia‐related brain-stem cavity is commonly treated with anticonvulsant drugs (e.g., carbamazepine, gabapentin). These agents dampen aberrant neuronal firing by modulating voltage-gated sodium or calcium channels and are well-established first-line therapy for central neuropathic pain syndromes, including the pain arising from syringobulbia.

479025.long_answer: MELAS is a mitochondrial myopathy that produces ‘ragged-red fibers’ in skeletal muscle. These abnormal subsarcolemmal accumulations of mitochondria become distinctly red when a muscle biopsy is stained with the modified Gomori trichrome stain, making this histological stain the standard test for confirming MELAS and other mitochondrial myopathies.

785578.long_answer: Teratomas arise from totipotent germ cells; consequently, they can differentiate into and contain mature tissues derived from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. Classic examples include skin or neural tissue (ectoderm), cartilage or bone (mesoderm), and gut-type epithelium (endoderm). Thus, the tumor’s components reflect contributions from all three embryonic germ layers.

400878.long_answer: Patients with chronic granulomatous disease lack a functional NADPH oxidase, impairing their ability to kill catalase-positive microbes. Aspergillus fumigatus is a catalase-positive mold and is the most frequently encountered fungal pathogen in these patients, leading to invasive pulmonary and systemic infections.

160401.long_answer: Leukodystrophies damage the myelin of central and cranial motor pathways, leading to bulbar muscle weakness and incoordination. This commonly produces dysphagia—difficulty swallowing—which is a well-documented clinical manifestation in many leukodystrophy subtypes.

133020.long_answer: In schizoaffective disorder, clozapine is sometimes prescribed when standard antipsychotics are inadequate. Clozapine can suppress bone-marrow function, leading to agranulocytosis or severe neutropenia. A complete blood count is therefore obtained at baseline and monitored regularly to detect any fall in white-blood-cell or absolute neutrophil counts early and prevent life-threatening infection.

515055.long_answer: Budesonide, a locally acting glucocorticoid, is the evidence-based first-line treatment for lymphocytic (microscopic) colitis. The same drug is routinely prescribed, in controlled-release oral or rectal formulations, for inflammatory bowel diseases—specifically mild-to-moderate Crohn’s disease (particularly ileocecal involvement) and for ulcerative colitis via oral MMX tablets or enemas—because it delivers high mucosal anti-inflammatory activity with minimal systemic exposure.

302077.long_answer: Macular (foveal) hypoplasia is typically confirmed with optical coherence tomography, which provides high-resolution cross-sectional images of the retina. OCT reveals the characteristic absence of the normal foveal pit and persistent inner retinal layers, making it the standard imaging modality for diagnosing this condition.

631331.long_answer: Acute dystonia is a well-recognized extrapyramidal side effect of antipsychotic (neuroleptic) drugs, particularly the typical D2-receptor antagonists such as haloperidol, chlorpromazine, and fluphenazine. By blocking dopamine signaling in the nigrostriatal pathway, these agents disrupt the normal balance between dopaminergic and cholinergic tone in the basal ganglia, leading to painful, sustained muscle contractions characteristic of dystonia.

163730.long_answer: Chronic granulomatous disease is caused by inherited defects in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex (most often the gp91-phox subunit). Without functional NADPH oxidase, neutrophils and macrophages cannot generate the superoxide anion and downstream reactive oxygen species that drive the respiratory burst, so ingested bacteria and fungi are not killed effectively.

393075.long_answer: In combined malonic and methylmalonic aciduria (CMAMMA), the mitochondrial enzyme acyl-CoA synthetase family member 3 (ACSF3) normally catalyses the reversible thio-ester reaction between free methylmalonic acid and CoA, i.e. the interconversion of methylmalonyl-CoA and methylmalonic acid (and similarly for malonate/malonyl-CoA). Loss-of-function mutations in ACSF3 prevent this step, so methylmalonyl-CoA is hydrolysed to, and accumulates as, methylmalonic acid, producing the characteristic organic-aciduria.

779438.long_answer: Medication (pharmaco-) phobia is considered a specific phobia—one of the DSM-5 anxiety-disorder subtypes—because the core symptom is an excessive, irrational fear confined to a particular object or situation, namely taking prescribed drugs, which leads to avoidance and clinically significant distress.

694094.long_answer: Within the U.S. National Institutes of Health, the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS) is the branch that supports and funds basic, translational, and clinical research on encephaloceles and a broad range of other brain and nervous system disorders.

498623.long_answer: Two-dimensional and Doppler echocardiography is the standard test to visualise the pulmonary valve, assess leaflet motion, and measure the systolic pressure gradient across the valve; these findings definitively confirm pulmonary valve stenosis.

378803.long_answer: Pompe disease (glycogen-storage disease type II) is caused by pathogenic variants in the GAA gene, which encodes acid α-glucosidase. The GAA gene is mapped to chromosome 17, band q25.3; mutations here lead to deficient lysosomal glycogen breakdown and the clinical manifestations of Pompe disease.

208691.long_answer: After a laryngospasm episode in patients with spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy (SBMA), partial reopening of the glottis causes turbulent airflow through a still-narrowed upper airway. This turbulent, high-frequency, inspiratory sound is clinically termed stridor, a hallmark of upper-airway obstruction following laryngeal spasm.

545092.long_answer: In neutral lipid storage disease—particularly the Chanarin-Dorfman (ichthyotic) form—lipid droplets accumulate in many organs, including the thyroid gland. This infiltration often impairs thyroid function, leading to reduced synthesis of thyroid hormones and a clinical picture of hypothyroidism, which is therefore a well-recognized and frequent endocrine complication of the disease.

406830.long_answer: Moebius syndrome is a congenital cranial nerve disorder classically involving the VI (abducens) and VII (facial) nerves. The VI-nerve palsy produces horizontal ophthalmoparesis/ophthalmoplegia, while reduced fetal facial and limb movement can lead to multiple congenital contractures, i.e., arthrogryposis. Thus, this syndrome links arthrogryposis with ophthalmoparesis.

261072.long_answer: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex is an inherited blistering disorder of the skin; its diagnosis, wound care, and long-term management fall under the expertise of dermatologists, the medical specialists who treat diseases of the skin.

528124.long_answer: In familial hemiplegic migraine, especially with CACNA1A or ATP1A2 mutations, even a minor head trauma can trigger massive, diffuse brain swelling. This malignant or fatal cerebral edema may evolve rapidly after a mild concussion, leading to coma and high mortality, making it a recognized severe complication in these patients.

132691.long_answer: Multiple system atrophy commonly leads to neurogenic orthostatic hypotension because of severe autonomic failure. When a patient also has essential hypertension, antihypertensive therapy and impaired baroreflexes can further widen the blood-pressure swing between the supine and standing positions, making orthostatic hypotension more pronounced and symptomatic.

380678.long_answer: In infants with an interrupted aortic arch, systemic blood flow depends on continued patency of the ductus arteriosus. Intravenous infusion of Prostaglandin E1 (alprostadil) relaxes ductal smooth muscle, preventing closure or reopening the ductus, thereby maintaining adequate systemic perfusion until definitive surgical repair can be performed.

525709.long_answer: Arrhinia, the congenital absence of the nose, arises from disrupted mid‐facial development during embryogenesis. Because it affects the formation of facial structures derived from the craniofacial complex, it is classified as a craniofacial anomaly (a subset of craniofacial malformations).

968235.long_answer: An iatrogenic disease is any disorder, injury, or complication that arises as a direct result of medical intervention—such as surgery, drugs, or diagnostic procedures. Infections like postoperative osteomyelitis exemplify iatrogenic conditions because they are provoked by the treatment itself rather than the underlying illness.

854069.long_answer: Infective endocarditis is an infection of the heart’s endocardial surface and valves, so its diagnosis (e.g., physical examination for murmurs, echocardiography, Duke criteria) and overall management (hemodynamic assessment, valve-related complications, coordination with cardiac surgery) are directed by cardiology specialists, who work with infectious disease consultants for antibiotic selection.

154650.long_answer: Individuals with Down syndrome frequently exhibit delayed exfoliation of the primary (deciduous) teeth. Root resorption and eruption timing are generally slowed in this chromosomal condition, so baby teeth are retained longer than expected before permanent successors emerge.

915916.long_answer: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) is a 4-repeat tauopathy, so abnormal accumulation of phosphorylated tau protein is a core pathological feature. However, the brain regions predominantly affected are the brain-stem (especially the midbrain), basal ganglia structures such as the globus pallidus and subthalamic nucleus, and frontal cortical areas—not the cerebellum. Although the cerebellar dentate nucleus can show some tau pathology, it is not the primary or most severely affected site, nor does cerebellar dysfunction drive the characteristic clinical picture of axial rigidity, vertical gaze palsy and early falls. Therefore the statement that PSP “primarily affects the cerebellum due to tau protein accumulation” is inconsistent with established neuropathological consensus.

970641.long_answer: Cohen-Gibson syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the EED gene. EED encodes a core component of Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2); pathogenic variants impair PRC2’s histone H3K27 methyltransferase activity, leading to the dysregulated gene expression and overgrowth features characteristic of the syndrome.

458077.long_answer: Recurrent aphthous stomatitis (canker sores) characteristically has its first onset during childhood, often before the second decade of life, and new cases are uncommon after about age 30.

901783.long_answer: In Alzheimer’s disease, aggregation of hyper-phosphorylated tau protein inside neurons forms neurofibrillary tangles. PET imaging and CSF assays that quantify tau are closely monitored because regional tau burden correlates strongly with neuronal loss and cerebral cortex atrophy, making tau a key protein tracked for its connection to brain volume loss.

865206.long_answer: In pheochromocytoma, excess circulating catecholamines act on both α- and β-adrenergic receptors. Giving a β-blocker first removes the vasodilatory/chronotropic β-receptor effects, leaving catecholamines to act solely on α-receptors. This unopposed α-adrenergic stimulation causes intense systemic vasoconstriction, abrupt hypertensive crisis, and possible cardiovascular collapse, so β-blockers are avoided unless adequate α-blockade is established beforehand.

428258.long_answer: In this anomaly—also called arteria lusoria—the right fourth aortic arch and proximal right dorsal aorta involute, so the right subclavian artery instead develops from the left dorsal aorta distal to the left subclavian. The vessel then courses posterior to the trachea-esophagus to reach the right arm, making it a classic congenital aortic arch variant.

110461.long_answer: Dystrophin forms a key part of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex, binding cortical actin filaments inside the muscle fiber to transmembrane β-dystroglycan, which in turn connects to the extracellular matrix. This linkage stabilizes the sarcolemma and distributes mechanical stress during muscle contraction and relaxation; its absence leads to membrane fragility and the myofiber degeneration seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

489616.long_answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma almost universally harbors inactivating mutations or deletions in the CDKN2A gene, which encodes the p16INK4A tumor-suppressor protein. p16 is a key regulator of cell-cycle control: it inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6), maintaining the retinoblastoma (RB) protein in its active, hypophosphorylated state and thereby enforcing the G1-to-S checkpoint. Loss of CDKN2A disrupts this pathway, permitting unchecked cell-cycle progression and contributing to pancreatic tumorigenesis.

291071.long_answer: Excess blood ammonia (hyperammonemia) arises when the urea cycle does not function properly. This can occur congenitally from inborn deficiencies of urea-cycle enzymes such as ornithine transcarbamylase, carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I or others. It can also be acquired in severe liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis, fulminant hepatitis), because the diseased liver cannot convert ammonia to urea efficiently. Thus the same metabolic disturbance—hyperammonemia—results from both a genetic enzyme deficiency and liver dysfunction.

337858.long_answer: In dysautonomia, malfunction of the autonomic nervous system can cause excessive sympathetic drive or inadequate parasympathetic modulation. This often produces an inappropriately rapid heart rate—tachycardia—especially when changing posture (as in postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, POTS). Hence, episodic or sustained tachycardia is a well-recognized, common cardiac symptom of dysautonomia.

117444.long_answer: In Wieacker (Wieacker‐Wolff) syndrome, the most severe – frequently prenatal-lethal – presentations are produced by nonsense mutations in the X-linked ZC4H2 gene. These lethal nonsense alleles typically arise from a cytosine-to-thymine (C→T) single-base transition, which converts an arginine-coding CGA triplet into the premature stop codon TGA, truncating the protein and leading to the lethal phenotype.

706411.long_answer: The osteodystrophy seen in DOOR syndrome chiefly involves hypoplasia or absence of the distal phalanges of the fingers and toes—the terminal bones underlying the nails—leading to the characteristic nail and skeletal abnormalities.

754076.long_answer: Tenosynovial giant cell tumor (TGCT)—historically called pigmented villonodular synovitis—is a soft-tissue neoplasm driven by a t(1;2) translocation that places the CSF1 gene under control of COL6A3 regulatory elements. The resulting overexpression of colony-stimulating factor 1 (CSF1) recruits and stimulates macrophages, producing the characteristic tumor mass in synovium, tendon sheath, or adjacent soft tissue.

661072.long_answer: Borrelial lymphocytoma (also called lymphadenosis benigna cutis) is a benign, localized B-cell–rich skin infiltrate caused by Borrelia burgdorferi infection in Lyme disease. Although it more often appears on the earlobe or nipple, in adult males it can develop on the scrotum.

221696.long_answer: Persistent elevation of serum calcium (hypercalcemia) can impair the kidney’s ability to concentrate urine by down-regulating aquaporin-2 water channels in the collecting duct and reducing the responsiveness of tubular cells to antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin). This electrolyte disturbance is therefore a well-recognized, established cause of nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

712494.long_answer: Patrick Henry Hughes was born with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, a disorder causing multiple congenital joint contractures that limit movement of the arms and legs. Management of arthrogryposis— including corrective surgery, bracing, and long-term musculoskeletal care— is handled by physicians trained in orthopedic surgery (often pediatric orthopedics). Therefore, the medical specialty most likely to treat his condition is orthopedic surgery.

965597.long_answer: The hip bone (os coxae) is formed by the fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis. It is one of the skeletal sites where hereditary multiple osteochondromas (also called hereditary multiple exostoses) frequently develop, producing cartilage-capped bony outgrowths along its surface.

637898.long_answer: Turner syndrome is a chromosomal disorder in which affected females have a complete or partial monosomy of the X chromosome (karyotype 45,X or variants). Because many individuals have mild or non-specific physical findings, the diagnosis is frequently made incidentally during evaluation for short stature, primary amenorrhea, or prenatal genetic screening.

428312.long_answer: In lymphangioleiomyomatosis, proliferation of abnormal smooth-muscle cells can narrow small airways and cause airflow obstruction. Inhaled bronchodilators—typically β2-adrenergic agonists or other bronchodilator agents—are often prescribed to relax bronchial smooth muscle and improve expiratory flow, thereby alleviating obstructive lung symptoms such as dyspnea and wheezing.

769915.long_answer: Infection with Sindbis or Sindbis-like alphaviruses (e.g., Ockelbo or Pogosta strains) commonly produces a febrile illness marked by a maculopapular skin rash; this cutaneous eruption is one of the most frequent and characteristic symptoms alongside fever and joint pain.

904243.long_answer: In hyperprolactinemia, elevated prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH release, resulting in reduced anterior-pituitary secretion of the gonadotropins. One of these, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), is essential for promoting the growth and maturation of ovarian follicles; therefore its secretion is inhibited when prolactin levels are abnormally high.

423500.long_answer: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (caused by JC polyomavirus) produces demyelinating lesions that extend from sub-cortical white matter into deep gray structures. Among the basal ganglia, the putamen is a well-documented site of involvement, showing characteristic T2/FLAIR hyperintensity on MRI in PML patients.

574966.long_answer: Paresis is a partial loss of motor strength that arises from injury or disease of the central or peripheral nervous system. Neurologists are the specialists trained to evaluate neurological deficits, perform diagnostic tests such as neuro-imaging and electromyography, determine the underlying cause, and manage or treat conditions that produce paresis.

896626.long_answer: In Rasmussen's encephalitis, the chronic T-cell–mediated inflammation selectively attacks one cerebral hemisphere. This ongoing immune assault destroys cortical neurons and supporting glia, leading to progressive shrinkage of that hemisphere—i.e., unilateral cerebral atrophy—accompanied by hemiparesis, cognitive decline, and focal seizures.

530033.long_answer: In ulcerative colitis, massive inflammatory damage can paralyze the colon, causing marked dilation (≥6 cm), systemic toxicity, and risk of perforation—a condition called toxic megacolon. Because medical therapy often fails and mortality rises rapidly once perforation or sepsis ensues, urgent subtotal colectomy is the standard life-saving surgical treatment.

887159.long_answer: Argininosuccinic aciduria is an inborn error of the urea-cycle caused by deficiency of argininosuccinate lyase. Diagnosis, dietary and pharmacologic nitrogen-scavenging therapy, and genetic counseling for this metabolic disorder are typically coordinated by clinicians trained in medical/clinical genetics (often titled metabolic geneticists or pediatric metabolic specialists). Therefore, the specialty most likely to manage these patients is medical genetics.

746216.long_answer: Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) is clonally integrated and drives most Merkel cell carcinomas, and viral DNA has also been detected in lesions of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (e.g., mycosis fungoides/Sezary syndrome), linking the same virus to both conditions.

257242.long_answer: Blomstrand chondrodysplasia is an autosomal-recessive, perinatally lethal skeletal disorder that results from loss-of-function mutations in the parathyroid hormone/parathyroid hormone-related peptide type-1 receptor (PTH1R). The defective PTH1R impairs signaling of both PTH and PTHrP, leading to premature endochondral ossification and the characteristic skeletal abnormalities seen in this condition.

649018.long_answer: REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is one of the four core clinical features in the diagnostic criteria for dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). In RBD, the normal muscle atonia of REM sleep is lost, leading patients to act out their dreams; its presence strongly supports a diagnosis of DLB because Lewy body pathology frequently affects brainstem structures that regulate REM-sleep atonia.

724187.long_answer: The DYT1 gene (TOR1A) encodes the protein torsinA. TorsinA is an evolutionarily conserved member of the AAA+ (ATPases Associated with diverse cellular Activities) family, and the characteristic GAG-deletion (ΔE) mutation in DYT1 dystonia alters this ATPase, leading to the disorder.

866773.long_answer: Selective mesenteric angiography is considered the gold-standard test for acute intestinal (mesenteric) ischemia because it directly visualizes the superior and inferior mesenteric arterial flow, detects arterial occlusion, emboli, or vasospasm in real time, and can simultaneously permit endovascular therapy. No other modality matches its diagnostic accuracy in the acute setting.

554341.long_answer: Procarbazine, an alkylating-like agent used in Hodgkin’s lymphoma regimens such as MOPP, is well documented to induce secondary myelodysplastic changes and therapy-related (subleukemic) acute myeloid leukemia years after treatment, making it a recognized leukemogenic risk factor in these patients.

725026.long_answer: Cohen syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the VPS13B gene (also known as COH1). VPS13B encodes a large transmembrane protein involved in Golgi trafficking; its disruption leads to the characteristic clinical features of Cohen syndrome, including ocular manifestations such as high myopia, retinal dystrophy and chorioretinitis.

947787.long_answer: Rapid weight loss in anorexia nervosa depletes the mesenteric fat pad, narrowing the angle between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery. This compresses the third portion of the duodenum, producing Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA) syndrome—a gastrointestinal obstruction classically associated with anorexia nervosa.

637108.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant optic atrophy is most commonly caused by pathogenic mutations in the OPA1 gene, which encodes a mitochondrial dynamin-like GTPase. OPA1 is highly expressed in retinal ganglion cells and is essential for mitochondrial fusion and maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential. Loss-of-function OPA1 mutations disrupt mitochondrial dynamics, leading to selective degeneration of retinal ganglion cells and the characteristic visual loss seen in dominant optic atrophy.

596970.long_answer: Hereditary angioedema (HAE) types I and II result from deficiency or dysfunction of the C1 esterase inhibitor. Both forms are caused by pathogenic variants in the SERPING1 gene, which encodes the C1-inhibitor protein; therefore, detecting a SERPING1 mutation is the molecular diagnostic hallmark for HAE types I and II.

670395.long_answer: In the embryonic brain, neural stem cells that give rise to cortical neurons reside along the wall of the cerebral ventricles in a germinal region called the ventricular zone. Mutations causing lissencephaly disrupt these ventricular-zone radial glial stem cells, impairing their ability to proliferate and guide neuronal migration, which leads to the characteristic smooth (agyral) cortex.

427042.long_answer: Brachydactyly-nystagmus syndrome (OMIM #609346) is a rare hereditary condition in which congenital brachydactyly is accompanied by congenital nystagmus. Clinical follow-up of affected families has shown that many patients later manifest progressive cerebellar ataxia, establishing cerebellar involvement as a characteristic component of the disorder’s phenotype.

179023.long_answer: In developed countries, the nodular sclerosis variant of classical Hodgkin lymphoma accounts for the largest proportion of cases—typically around 60–70 %. Its characteristic lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells and collagen banding distinguish it histologically, and epidemiologic surveys consistently show it as the predominant subtype in these populations.

355465.long_answer: In idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension, acute vasodilator testing identifies a small subset (≈5–10%) of patients who are vasoreactive. For these responders, high-dose oral calcium channel blockers such as nifedipine, diltiazem, or amlodipine are recommended because they produce sustained pulmonary arterial vasodilation and improve hemodynamics and symptoms. Other drug classes are reserved for non-responders.

750436.long_answer: Rickettsialpox was first identified after a 1946 outbreak among residents of an apartment complex in Kew Gardens, Queens, New York City. Investigation by Dr. Robert Huebner traced the illness to the mite-borne bacterium Rickettsia akari, making Queens the borough where the initial outbreak occurred.

223641.long_answer: Basilar invagination (also called basilar impression) is a cranio-vertebral junction abnormality in which the odontoid process and body of the C2 vertebra migrate upward through the foramen magnum. This superior displacement narrows the foramen magnum lumen and can compress the medulla and upper cervical spinal cord.

115552.long_answer: The 6th-century BCE Indian surgeon Sushruta, author of the classical treatise Sushruta Samhita, gave one of the earliest systematic descriptions of leprosy (‘kushtha’). He classified its clinical forms, discussed its contagious nature, and prescribed therapies such as purification procedures and chaulmoogra-seed preparations, making him the ancient physician most often credited with the first detailed account and treatment guidelines for leprosy.

896387.long_answer: The human CPOX gene (coproporphyrinogen oxidase), whose variants cause hereditary coproporphyria, has been mapped to the long arm of chromosome 3 (region q11-q12).

531530.long_answer: Froehlich syndrome (also called adiposogenital dystrophy) occurs when a tumor or other lesion of the hypothalamus disrupts its regulatory control over appetite and anterior pituitary function. Damage to the ventromedial hypothalamic nuclei removes the normal satiety signal, producing marked hyperphagia and obesity, while interference with hypothalamic releasing hormones lowers secretion of pituitary gonadotropins and other trophic hormones—reflected historically by very low urinary excretion of these pituitary hormones. Hence, a hypothalamic tumor producing increased appetite together with low urinary pituitary hormones typifies Froehlich syndrome.

932830.long_answer: Bolivian hemorrhagic fever is a viral hemorrhagic fever caused by the Machupo arenavirus. Diagnosis requires specialized virologic testing and management involves high-level infection control, antiviral or supportive care, and outbreak containment—all core responsibilities of physicians trained in the specialty of infectious diseases (often with tropical medicine expertise).

326689.long_answer: Hereditary xanthinuria is a rare purine-metabolism disorder caused by the congenital absence or severe deficiency of the enzyme xanthine oxidoreductase (also called xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase). Loss of this enzyme blocks the conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, resulting in markedly low serum and urinary uric acid and accumulation of xanthine that can precipitate as renal or urinary tract stones. Type I xanthinuria is due solely to xanthine oxidase deficiency, while Type II also involves aldehyde oxidase. Thus, xanthinuria is indeed characterized by xanthine oxidase deficiency, in accord with established biochemical and clinical descriptions of the disease.

208216.long_answer: Lipodystrophy is a syndrome in which adipose tissue is partially or totally lost (or degenerates) in different regions of the body. The resulting severe insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridaemia and renal involvement frequently produce secondary (non-essential) hypertension, so lipodystrophy is recognized as one of the endocrine/metabolic causes of secondary hypertension.

486974.long_answer: Helicobacter pylori is the spiral-shaped bacterium that colonises the stomach lining and is the main infectious cause of peptic (stomach) ulcers in humans. While human-to-human spread is most common, several studies have demonstrated that domestic cats can carry H. pylori in their gastric mucosa and shed the organism, allowing zoonotic transmission from cats to people.

678850.long_answer: Burkitt lymphoma is a high-grade B-cell lymphoma with a well-established association with latent Epstein–Barr virus infection (particularly in the endemic African form). Standard curative regimens (e.g., CODOX-M/IVAC) include the nucleoside analog cytarabine (ara-C), and other nucleoside analogs are active in this disease, so EBV-driven Burkitt lymphoma is characteristically treated with nucleoside-analog–containing chemotherapy.

434424.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the DNMT3A gene cause Tatton-Brown-Rahman syndrome (TBRS), a congenital overgrowth–intellectual disability disorder. Clinical descriptions of TBRS repeatedly note seizures, particularly febrile seizures, in affected children. Thus, TBRS is the DNMT3A-associated genetic disorder that can present with febrile seizures.

340961.long_answer: Leflunomide, an immunosuppressive agent used in transplant medicine and rheumatology, inhibits pyrimidine synthesis and has demonstrated direct antiviral activity against BK virus. It is therefore employed as a potential therapeutic option for BK virus-associated nephropathy while simultaneously allowing some maintenance of immunosuppression.

198080.long_answer: Foix–Alajouanine syndrome is a progressive congestive myelopathy that results from a spinal dural arteriovenous fistula (a type of arteriovenous malformation). The abnormal shunting of arterial blood into the spinal venous system produces venous hypertension, impaired cord perfusion, and ultimately necrotizing myelopathy, which defines the syndrome.

317954.long_answer: Phosphofructokinase (PFK) deficiency—glycogen-storage disease type VII—has an infantile variant in which the enzyme defect affects not only muscle and red blood cells but also heart and brain. Published case reports describe infants with generalized seizures that fulfill diagnostic criteria for epilepsy; this neurological disorder is therefore listed among the recognized symptoms of the infantile form of PFK deficiency.

314340.long_answer: Premature fusion of cranial sutures can restrict posterior-fossa growth, elevate intracranial pressure, or produce a Chiari I malformation, all of which may impair cerebellar function. The resulting neurological complication is cerebellar ataxia—uncoordinated gait and limb movements that arise when the cerebellum is compromised.

534220.long_answer: Although infantile myofibromatosis most often involves skin, muscle, and bone, the tumor can occasionally extend into the central nervous system; when it does, it characteristically forms masses attached to the dura mater, the outer meningeal layer surrounding the brain.

921665.long_answer: Acute myeloid leukemia can infiltrate the central nervous system, most notably the brain. The brain is enclosed and protected by the meninges (dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater), making it the body part that satisfies both conditions specified in the question.

399803.long_answer: Brachydactyly type C is most commonly caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the GDF5 gene (Growth Differentiation Factor 5), located on chromosome 20q11.2. GDF5 encodes a bone morphogenetic protein that is critical for cartilage and bone development; mutations disrupt signaling required for digital growth, leading to the shortened middle phalanges and characteristic hand anomalies seen in brachydactyly type C.

828664.long_answer: Mutations in the TTPA gene, which encodes the α-tocopherol transfer protein, prevent normal incorporation of dietary vitamin E into plasma lipoproteins. Although the individual consumes adequate vitamin E, the defect causes systemic vitamin E deficiency that leads to a progressive neurodegenerative disorder known as ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (AVED).

816728.long_answer: Gardner’s syndrome, a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis, characteristically includes desmoid tumors—also called aggressive fibromatoses. These are benign, non-metastasizing tumors composed of proliferating fibroblasts and collagen that arise from musculo-aponeurotic fibrous tissue. Their strong association with Gardner’s syndrome makes the desmoid tumor the recognized benign fibrous tumor in this condition.

739016.long_answer: Hereditary xerocytosis (dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis) can result from gain-of-function mutations in the KCNN4 gene. KCNN4 encodes the intermediate-conductance, calcium-activated potassium channel KCa3.1 (also called the Gardos channel). Because the channel opens in response to intracellular Ca²⁺, pathogenic KCNN4 variants increase K⁺ efflux from red blood cells, leading to cellular dehydration and the xerocytosis phenotype.

900667.long_answer: In Meige’s syndrome, patients often report photophobia, an abnormal intolerance or sensitivity to light that accompanies the condition’s characteristic blepharospasm and other cranial dystonias.

640345.long_answer: Congenital Dyserythropoietic Anemia type II is caused by intrinsic defects in erythroid precursors (typically SEC23B mutations). Because the underlying marrow produces defective red cells, replacing the patient’s hematopoietic system with donor stem cells can eliminate the disease. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation provides a new, genetically normal erythropoiesis and is therefore considered the only potentially curative therapy for CDA II, whereas supportive measures like transfusion or iron chelation merely mitigate complications.

196704.long_answer: In cutis laxa, the abnormal elastin in connective tissues can involve internal organs as well as the skin. The lungs are commonly affected, leading to early-onset emphysema because their elastic fibers are crucial for normal alveolar recoil and gas exchange. Thus, the lungs—whose primary function is to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide—are an organ that can be compromised in cutis laxa.

916190.long_answer: Split hand split foot-nystagmus syndrome is a rare congenital disorder characterized by ectrodactyly (split hand/foot malformation) together with the ocular finding of congenital nystagmus—an involuntary, rhythmic oscillation of the eyes. The presence of nystagmus is a defining ophthalmic feature consistently reported in patients with this syndrome.

452554.long_answer: High-dose corticosteroids and other potent immunosuppressants used to treat severe graft-versus-host disease markedly impair cellular and humoral immunity, allowing latent or environmental pathogens (e.g., CMV, EBV, invasive fungi, Pneumocystis) to reactivate or invade. Consequently, life-threatening opportunistic infections are a well-recognized complication of the intense immunosuppression required to control GVHD.

487518.long_answer: Liebenberg syndrome is an autosomal-dominant limb malformation disorder produced by deletions or translocations in the regulatory region located upstream of the PITX1 gene. These structural variants dysregulate PITX1 expression during limb development, leading to features such as elbow dysplasia, radial head dislocation, brachydactyly and characteristic finger flexion deformities (camptodactyly).

790262.long_answer: Pulmonary veno-occlusive disease is most readily identified non-invasively by high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest, which characteristically shows interlobular septal thickening, centrilobular ground-glass opacities and mediastinal lymphadenopathy—findings that support the diagnosis without the need for lung biopsy.

963096.long_answer: Cowden syndrome (PTEN hamartoma-tumor syndrome) is characterized by mucocutaneous manifestations such as papillomatous papules, cobblestone oral mucosa, and a markedly fissured tongue. Germ-line mutations in the PTEN tumor-suppressor gene underlie the syndrome. Carriers have a greatly elevated lifetime risk of several malignancies, most notably female breast cancer (up to 50–85% risk), making Cowden syndrome the established link between fissured tongue and increased breast-cancer susceptibility.

865806.long_answer: Propionyl-CoA is first carboxylated to methylmalonyl-CoA, which is then rearranged by the enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase. This mutase requires adenosyl-cobalamin (vitamin B12) as a cofactor to convert methylmalonyl-CoA into the citric-acid-cycle intermediate succinyl-CoA. Thus, succinyl-CoA is the TCA cycle intermediate whose synthesis from propionyl-CoA depends on vitamin B12.

347411.long_answer: The Pakistani type of spondylo-epimetaphyseal dysplasia is an autosomal-recessive skeletal disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PAPSS2 gene (3′-phosphoadenosine 5′-phosphosulfate synthase 2). Defective PAPSS2 impairs synthesis of the universal sulfate donor PAPS, reducing sulfation of cartilage proteoglycans and leading to the characteristic epiphyseal, metaphyseal, and vertebral abnormalities seen in this form of SEMD.

734299.long_answer: Patterson (Kelly-Patterson/Plummer-Vinson) syndrome—characterized by iron-deficiency anaemia, dysphagia and esophageal webs—confers a high risk of malignant change in the upper aerodigestive tract, most characteristically development of post-cricoid and upper esophageal squamous cell carcinoma.

616140.long_answer: AREDYLD syndrome is extraordinarily rare; Orphanet and the NIH Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center list its prevalence as “<1/1,000,000.” At that frequency, fewer than one person per million residents—only a handful of individuals at most—would be expected to have the disorder in the entire United States.

847427.long_answer: Soaking calcium carbonate (e.g., limestone or eggshells) in vinegar (acetic acid) converts it to calcium acetate. Orally, calcium acetate serves as a phosphate-binding agent, lowering serum phosphate levels in patients with chronic kidney disease and thereby helping prevent renal osteodystrophy.

945350.long_answer: In severe or malignant forms, hypertension—especially in obstetric settings such as pre-eclampsia/eclampsia—can trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). DIC is marked by systemic activation of the coagulation cascade, forming microthrombi throughout the vasculature and consuming platelets and clotting factors, which paradoxically leads to both widespread clotting and severe bleeding.

441603.long_answer: Neonatal infection (sepsis) can cause tissue hypoxia and increased lactic acid production, consuming bicarbonate buffers. The accumulation of hydrogen ions drives arterial and venous blood pH below the normal range (< 7.35), producing the acid–base disturbance known as metabolic acidosis.

788141.long_answer: Churg-Strauss syndrome, now termed eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, is an ANCA-associated small-vessel autoimmune vasculitis classically characterized by severe asthma, peripheral eosinophilia, and systemic granulomatous inflammation. Asthma is often the earliest and most persistent clinical feature, linking this autoimmune disease directly with the respiratory condition.

585236.long_answer: Down syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). It is the most frequent live-born aneuploidy, readily identified through karyotyping or targeted prenatal screening, and is routinely managed in medical genetics clinics because of its characteristic physical features, intellectual disability, and associated health complications.

912314.long_answer: In infants with situs ambiguus (heterotaxy), cyanosis—a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes—signals systemic hypoxemia caused by the congenital heart malformations that frequently accompany this condition. Because cyanosis results from inadequate oxygenated blood reaching the systemic circulation, it reflects a circulatory rather than a gastrointestinal or hepatic problem, making it the key symptom that indicates a systemic or circulatory issue in situs ambiguus.

631337.long_answer: Hydrops-ectopic calcification-moth-eaten skeletal dysplasia (also called Greenberg dysplasia) is a rare, usually lethal, autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia caused by mutations in the LBR gene. Diagnosing and managing such congenital skeletal disorders, providing molecular testing, and offering genetic counselling for affected families are the domain of clinical/medical geneticists; therefore, a paediatric medical genetics service would be the specialty most often involved in these cases.

352164.long_answer: Cryptococcus neoformans infection of the meninges (cryptococcal meningitis) is a fungal disease that invades the central nervous system. When the fungus proliferates in the brain and meninges it raises intracranial pressure, commonly producing headache, nausea, and vomiting along with other neurologic signs. This well-documented clinical presentation makes cryptococcal meningitis the fungal infection known to cause nausea when it affects the brain.

983025.long_answer: Developmental dyscalculia is a neurodevelopmental disorder in which functional imaging consistently shows abnormal (usually reduced) activation of right-hemisphere parietal circuits, especially the right intraparietal sulcus that supports number processing. Clinically it produces acalculia, finger-representation problems and frequent left–right disorientation—the very components of Gerstmann syndrome—so it is considered to share core symptoms with that classic parietal-lobe syndrome.

224274.long_answer: The mitochondrial 12S ribosomal RNA gene, MT-RNR1, is encoded entirely within the mitochondrial genome. Pathogenic point mutations in MT-RNR1 (e.g., m.1555A>G) are a well-established cause of maternally inherited nonsyndromic sensorineural deafness, often with heightened susceptibility to aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss.

255543.long_answer: DAVID syndrome (Deficient Anterior pituitary with Variable Immune Deficiency) is caused by heterozygous, typically truncating, mutations in the NFKB2 gene. NFKB2 encodes the p100/p52 subunit of the non-canonical NF-κB transcription factor pathway; loss-of-function mutations act in a dominant-negative fashion, impairing B-cell development (leading to common variable immunodeficiency) and disrupting pituitary ACTH production, yielding the combined endocrine-immune phenotype characteristic of DAVID syndrome.

357565.long_answer: Central core disease is a congenital myopathy in which muscle biopsy examined by light microscopy shows centrally located oxidative-deficient ‘cores’ in the fibers. Almost all familial and sporadic cases with these histological cores carry pathogenic mutations in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor (calcium-release channel) on chromosome 19. Thus, the characteristic light-microscopy finding points to an underlying RYR1 mutation.

720213.long_answer: Both invasive mole and choriocarcinoma fall under gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, which is highly chemosensitive. Single-agent methotrexate (often with folinic-acid rescue) is the standard first-line therapy used to eradicate trophoblastic tissue in both conditions, achieving high cure rates while preserving fertility.

506766.long_answer: In primary ovarian insufficiency the ovaries produce little estrogen and inhibin, removing the normal negative feedback on the pituitary. As a result, gonadotropin secretion rises, and serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) becomes markedly elevated (often >40 IU/L), a key laboratory hallmark of the disorder.

390505.long_answer: Lumbar spinal stenosis is most accurately assessed with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which provides high-resolution, multiplanar images of the spinal canal, vertebral bodies, intervertebral discs, ligaments, and neural elements, allowing visualization of the characteristic narrowing that defines the condition.

515267.long_answer: Glial scars in multiple system atrophy arise through reactive gliosis, in which astrocytes become activated, enlarge, and divide. This astrocytic proliferation (also called astroglial hypertrophy and hyperplasia) lays down dense networks of glial filaments and extracellular matrix that constitute the scar tissue observed in affected brain regions.

393948.long_answer: Coffin–Siris syndrome is most often caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in ARID1B, a core component of the SWI/SNF (BAF) chromatin-remodeling complex. Pathogenic ARID1B mutations account for the clear majority of genetically confirmed CSS cases, so diagnostic molecular testing panels for the syndrome routinely begin with, or focus on, ARID1B sequencing and copy-number analysis.

621180.long_answer: Schinzel–Giedion syndrome is a rare congenital malformation disorder that combines characteristic skeletal defects, notably hypoplastic or shortened ulnae, with central-nervous-system anomalies such as a large retrocerebellar arachnoid (meningeal) cyst. The co-occurrence of ulnar abnormalities and a posterior-fossa arachnoid cyst is regarded as a hallmark radiological–clinical constellation of this syndrome.

813540.long_answer: Musculoskeletal contractures, malalignments, and bone deformities that develop in children with cerebral palsy are most commonly corrected by orthopedic surgery, which includes tendon-lengthening, muscle releases, and osteotomies to improve alignment and function.

583064.long_answer: Menopausal hormone replacement therapy, particularly estrogen-containing regimens, elevates vaginal estrogen levels. Estrogen increases glycogen deposition in the vaginal epithelium, providing a nutrient source for Candida species and fostering an acidic environment that promotes their growth. Consequently, women receiving estrogen-based HRT have a higher incidence of vulvovaginal candidiasis compared with those not on this therapy.

645952.long_answer: Alexander disease is caused by dominant mutations in the GFAP (glial fibrillary acidic protein) gene. The GFAP gene is mapped to band q21 on the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q21), so the pathogenic variants responsible for Alexander disease are located on chromosome 17.

929916.long_answer: The Wenckebach block (second-degree atrioventricular block type I) is named after Dutch physician and physiologist Karel Frederik Wenckebach, who first described the characteristic progressively lengthening PR intervals followed by a dropped ventricular beat in 1899.

365222.long_answer: Under anaerobic conditions, the enzyme lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) catalyzes the reduction of pyruvate to lactate while oxidizing NADH to NAD⁺. This reaction regenerates NAD⁺ needed for glycolysis to continue in the absence of sufficient oxygen.

204520.long_answer: Neu–Laxova syndrome, a rare lethal congenital malformation disorder, consistently features a generalized thickening and lamellar scaling of the skin that resembles congenital ichthyosis. This ichthyosiform hyperkeratosis is one of the characteristic clinical findings reported in virtually all described cases.

509137.long_answer: Heterozygous de-novo missense variants in the EED gene, a core component of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, cause Cohen-Gibson syndrome. This overgrowth–intellectual disability disorder is clinically recognised by dysmorphic facial features (broad forehead, hypertelorism, full lips, etc.), variable developmental delay and other congenital anomalies. Identification of recurrent de-novo EED missense mutations established Cohen-Gibson syndrome as the EED-associated phenotype.

332419.long_answer: Researchers are testing gene therapy for Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy: an adeno-associated viral (AAV) vector is used to deliver a functional copy of the mitochondrial ND4 gene to retinal ganglion cells, aiming to restore or preserve vision lost from the disease.

768470.long_answer: Insufficient ionized calcium in the extracellular fluid (hypocalcaemia) lowers the threshold for action-potential generation in peripheral nerves and muscle fibres. This heightened neuromuscular excitability manifests clinically as painful skeletal muscle cramps and tetany, a well-documented consequence of calcium deficiency.

709775.long_answer: Bevacizumab, a monoclonal antibody that inhibits vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), is well documented to precipitate posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES). VEGF blockade by bevacizumab can produce severe hypertension and endothelial dysfunction, leading to breakdown of the blood-brain barrier and the vasogenic edema characteristic of PRES. Multiple clinical case reports and pharmacovigilance data link bevacizumab therapy—given intravenously for cancer or, less often, intravitreally for ocular disease—to the development of PRES.

152199.long_answer: In Sturge–Weber syndrome, leptomeningeal angiomas cause chronic venous stasis and dystrophic mineral deposition along the cerebral cortical gyri. On CT or skull radiographs this appears as parallel, curvilinear ‘tram-track’ cortical calcifications. Detection of these gyriform tram-track calcifications in the cerebral cortex is a classic, highly suggestive sign of Sturge–Weber syndrome.

772979.long_answer: Proteus syndrome is caused by a mosaic, activating mutation in the AKT1 gene—most commonly the c.49G>A (p.E17K) substitution—which leads to constitutive activation of the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway and the asymmetric, progressive overgrowth characteristic of the disorder.

424506.long_answer: Weaver syndrome is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the EZH2 gene. EZH2 encodes the catalytic subunit of the Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2), a histone-methyltransferase that regulates gene expression. Beyond its role in growth and development, EZH2 is critically involved in lymphopoiesis: it controls chromatin remodeling during B- and T-cell differentiation and germinal-center formation. Thus, the gene linked to Weaver syndrome that functions in lymphopoiesis is EZH2.

573813.long_answer: Bardet–Biedl syndrome is a ciliopathy in which almost all affected individuals develop a progressive rod–cone retinal dystrophy (clinically akin to retinitis pigmentosa). Degeneration of rod photoreceptors causes early night-blindness and peripheral vision loss, followed by cone involvement leading to central vision impairment.

340206.long_answer: Loss-of-function variants in the WNT4 gene are a recognised cause of Müllerian (MRKH) agenesis. The disorder follows an autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern in which several heterozygous carriers—particularly males and some females—show no genital tract malformation, illustrating the gene’s incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity.

851468.long_answer: Patients with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) frequently develop chronic infection with the protozoan Giardia lamblia. The defect in IgA- and IgG-mediated mucosal immunity allows persistent giardial colonisation of the small intestine, leading to chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption. Hence, giardiasis is a characteristic gastrointestinal complication of CVID.

211669.long_answer: Streptococcus suis is a zoonotic bacterium carried by pigs; humans can acquire the infection by handling or eating raw or undercooked contaminated pork. Once in the bloodstream it readily crosses the blood-brain barrier, frequently producing severe neurological disease—most characteristically acute bacterial meningitis, often accompanied by sepsis and permanent hearing loss.

886078.long_answer: Kidneys that develop abnormally in utero—such as renal agenesis, dysplasia, or multicystic kidneys—are classified collectively as congenital kidney disease. These conditions arise from malformation of the urinary tract during fetal development, distinguishing them from kidney disorders acquired after birth.

449509.long_answer: In interstitial, or “atypical,” pneumonia the inflammatory reaction is largely confined to the alveolar septa and pulmonary interstitium; the airspaces themselves remain mostly free of the purulent alveolar exudate that characterizes typical bacterial (lobar or bronchopneumonia) infections.

918149.long_answer: Familial male-limited precocious puberty (testotoxicosis) is managed with the combined use of spironolactone, an anti-androgen that blocks androgen receptors, and testolactone, an aromatase inhibitor that suppresses estrogen synthesis. By lowering estrogen production, testolactone slows bone maturation, while spironolactone counteracts the excess testosterone, together mitigating the precocious puberty phenotype.

818916.long_answer: Most reported cases of Orofaciodigital syndrome correspond to type I, which is caused by pathogenic variants in the OFD1 gene on the X chromosome. Type I is inherited in an X-linked dominant manner and is typically lethal in hemizygous males, making X-linked dominant inheritance the pattern seen in the majority of Orofaciodigital syndrome cases.

624255.long_answer: Langer–Giedion syndrome (trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II) is a contiguous-gene deletion disorder caused by an 8q24.11-q24.13 microdeletion that removes the TRPS1 gene and the EXT1 gene. Loss of TRPS1 leads to the characteristic hair, facial, and skeletal abnormalities, while loss of EXT1 contributes to multiple exostoses. Thus, affected individuals are missing both TRPS1 and EXT1.

997932.long_answer: Hepatology is the subspecialty of medicine focused on liver diseases; hepatologists (often within gastroenterology) diagnose and treat conditions such as hepatomegaly and hepatic cirrhosis, so they would be the appropriate specialists for managing the liver manifestations seen in Senter syndrome.

495238.long_answer: Distal arthrogryposis type 5 (DA5) is a recognised syndromic form of arthrogryposis in which congenital contractures of the hands and feet are accompanied by ocular motility defects. Affected individuals frequently show ptosis, strabismus and partial external ophthalmoplegia/ophthalmoparesis due to limited extra-ocular muscle function. Pathogenic variants in the mechanosensitive ion-channel gene PIEZO2 underlie DA5, explaining the combined limb-muscle and eye-movement phenotype.

964371.long_answer: Epidemiological and experimental studies show that maternal infection with Zika virus during pregnancy can cross the placenta, infect fetal neural progenitor cells, disrupt neurodevelopment, and markedly increase the risk of babies being born with congenital microcephaly.

831283.long_answer: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, fatal neurodegenerative complication that arises years after primary infection with the measles virus (a Morbillivirus of the Paramyxoviridae family). Persistent, mutant measles virus remains in the central nervous system, leading to progressive inflammation, demyelination, and neuronal degeneration characteristic of SSPE.

122942.long_answer: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (often termed arrhythmogenic right-ventricular cardiomyopathy) is most commonly linked to pathogenic variants in the plakophilin-2 (PKP2) gene, which encodes a desmosomal protein essential for myocyte adhesion. Identifying a PKP2 mutation during the work-up helps distinguish this inherited cardiomyopathy from other causes of ventricular arrhythmias in the differential diagnosis.

818361.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis, caused by CFTR gene mutations, produces viscous secretions that obstruct pancreatic ducts. This obstruction destroys the exocrine tissue, leading to exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, and with progressive loss of islet cells many patients develop cystic-fibrosis–related diabetes mellitus.

919209.long_answer: The accessory navicular is traditionally categorized by the Geist classification, which separates these ossicles into three anatomical types: Type I (a small sesamoid bone within the posterior tibial tendon), Type II (a larger triangular or heart-shaped ossicle united to the navicular by a synchondrosis), and Type III (an enlarged, fused ‘cornuate’ navicular).

568203.long_answer: Fine–Lubinsky syndrome is a rare, inherited neuro-developmental and craniofacial disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the CLP1 gene. Because its diagnosis relies on recognizing a characteristic pattern of congenital anomalies and confirming the causative mutation with molecular testing, and because ongoing care involves genetic counseling and multisystem management, the specialty that most commonly evaluates and manages patients with this syndrome is medical (clinical) genetics.

671052.long_answer: Toxoplasmosis is caused by the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. This obligate intracellular apicomplexan infects warm-blooded animals, with felids as the definitive host. Human infection occurs via ingestion of oocysts from cat feces, consumption of tissue cysts in undercooked meat, or transplacental transmission, leading to congenital or acquired toxoplasmosis.

970071.long_answer: Cyclic vomiting syndrome is defined clinically according to the Rome IV functional gastrointestinal disorder criteria: at least two or more stereotypical, discrete episodes of intense nausea and vomiting occurring in the previous 6 months, lasting hours to days, with complete return to baseline between attacks and no alternative medical explanation. These Rome IV criteria are the accepted standard for diagnosing cyclic vomiting syndrome.

592588.long_answer: Saudi Arabia mandates that all pilgrims undertaking Umrah present a certificate of vaccination with a quadrivalent meningococcal conjugate or polysaccharide vaccine (covering serogroups A, C, W-135, and Y) given within the specified period before entry, to prevent outbreaks of meningococcal disease during the pilgrimage.

404066.long_answer: The NF1 gene (neurofibromin-1) is situated on chromosome 17q11.2. Pathogenic variants in NF1 cause neurofibromatosis type 1, a genetic skin disorder characterized by café-au-lait macules, cutaneous neurofibromas and other pigmentary/dermal findings. Thus, NF1 is the skin-condition–related gene located on chromosome 17.

543601.long_answer: The vast majority of primary esophageal malignancies are squamous cell carcinomas, arising from the squamous epithelium that lines most of the esophagus. Epidemiologic data show strong links between classic risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, caustic injury, achalasia, Plummer-Vinson syndrome) and development of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, making this histologic type the one classically associated with esophageal cancer.

932138.long_answer: In cerebral amyloid angiopathy, amyloid-β peptide is deposited within the vessel wall itself—specifically in the tunica media and extending into the adventitia—of small- to medium-sized cortical and leptomeningeal arteries, arterioles, and capillaries. Accumulation in these layers weakens the vessel wall and underlies the characteristic risk of lobar intracerebral hemorrhage seen in this condition.

333646.long_answer: When the renal arteries become narrowed (renal artery stenosis), renal perfusion falls. The juxtaglomerular apparatus responds by releasing excess renin, activating the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. The resulting systemic vasoconstriction and sodium-water retention produce a secondary form of high blood pressure termed renovascular hypertension.

545486.long_answer: The interferon regulatory factor 6 gene (IRF6) on chromosome 1q32 has been repeatedly mapped and functionally validated as a major susceptibility locus for nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate as well as Van der Woude syndrome. Mutations or risk variants in IRF6 disrupt epithelial differentiation during craniofacial development, leading to the clefting phenotype.

495295.long_answer: The presence of a seminoma cannot be reliably distinguished from other testicular tumours by imaging or serum markers alone. The accepted method is removal of the testis through an inguinal approach (radical inguinal orchiectomy), after which histopathological examination of the specimen provides definitive confirmation of seminoma while avoiding tumour seeding that could occur with scrotal biopsy.

561744.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the CA2 gene, encoding carbonic anhydrase II, cause a syndrome that includes autosomal-recessive distal renal tubular acidosis. Because CA II is crucial for CO₂/HCO₃⁻ handling in many tissues, its deficiency also impairs brain acid–base balance, leading to abnormal calcium deposition and characteristic cerebral (intracranial) calcifications.

913550.long_answer: Koilonychia is an abnormal nail finding; diagnosis and treatment of nail disorders fall under dermatology. Board-certified dermatologists are trained to examine nails, identify causes such as iron-deficiency anemia or systemic disease, and manage the condition or refer for additional care, making them the appropriate specialists for koilonychia.

255002.long_answer: Amish nemaline myopathy is caused by a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the TNNT1 gene, which encodes slow-skeletal-muscle troponin T. The truncating mutation abolishes functional troponin T1, disrupts thin-filament regulation, and leads to the severe congenital muscle weakness and nemaline bodies characteristic of this disorder in the Old Order Amish population.

103026.long_answer: Sodium benzoate, widely used as a food preservative, is administered pharmacologically to patients with glycine encephalopathy (non-ketotic hyperglycinemia). It binds free glycine to form hippurate, which is readily excreted by the kidney, thereby lowering systemic and cerebrospinal glycine concentrations. When begun early and combined with other supportive measures, this benzoate therapy can reduce seizures, apnea, and neuro-developmental injury in certain milder or attenuated forms of the disorder, improving clinical outcomes.

478986.long_answer: Urinary urgency, frequency and incontinence that often accompany hereditary spastic paraplegia can be managed with the antimuscarinic agent oxybutynin. By blocking M3 muscarinic receptors in the detrusor muscle, oxybutynin reduces involuntary bladder contractions and improves storage capacity, thereby relieving these urinary symptoms in HSP patients.

376608.long_answer: In infectious mononucleosis, Epstein-Barr virus infects B lymphocytes and triggers marked lymphoid and reticulo-endothelial hyperplasia. The spleen, a major lymphoid organ in the abdomen, consequently undergoes congestion and proliferation of immune cells, leading to splenomegaly that is clinically evident in many patients.

790387.long_answer: The PTGER4 gene, whose variants confer increased susceptibility to ankylosing spondylitis, is located on the short arm of human chromosome 5 (region 5p13.1). Genome-wide association studies have repeatedly linked this chromosomal locus to elevated disease risk.

283480.long_answer: Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is a coagulopathy frequently triggered by acute promyelocytic leukaemia and other leukemic states. In DIC, widespread activation of coagulation leads to formation of microvascular thrombi, consuming platelets and clotting factors; this paradoxically produces both excessive clotting and a high risk of hemorrhage.

954255.long_answer: Hydrops fetalis of immune origin is usually caused by maternal anti-Rh(D) antibodies that destroy Rh-positive fetal red cells. Administering Rho(D) immune globulin (anti-D antibody) to Rh-negative mothers during pregnancy and after delivery binds any fetal Rh-positive erythrocytes in the maternal circulation, preventing maternal sensitization and the subsequent hemolytic disease that can progress to immune hydrops fetalis.

171105.long_answer: The overwhelmingly common genetic cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy is amyloid deposition from mutant transthyretin. Pathogenic variants in the TTR gene destabilize the transthyretin tetramer, leading to misfolded monomers that aggregate as amyloid fibrils in the myocardium, producing the classic stiff-walled, diastolic-dysfunction phenotype of restrictive cardiomyopathy.

476925.long_answer: Glycogen-storage diseases are categorized by the specific enzyme that is deficient. Glycogen storage disease type IV (Andersen disease) is caused by deficiency of the glycogen branching enzyme (also called GBE1). Phosphorylase kinase deficiency produces a different form of glycogen-storage disease, historically classified as type VIII or more commonly type IX (subtypes IXa, IXb, IXc, etc.). Therefore, phosphorylase kinase deficiency does not cause glycogen storage disease type IV.

336288.long_answer: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss) is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis; when it involves dermal post-capillary venules it produces leukocytoclastic vasculitis, leading to the characteristic palpable purpura that can be seen on the skin of affected patients.

310807.long_answer: Patients with Stiff-person syndrome commonly develop persistent rigidity and spasm of the axial and paraspinal muscles, which produces chronic low back pain. This musculoskeletal pain is one of the most frequently reported symptoms of the disorder and is recognized clinically as a prevalent form of chronic pain.

499808.long_answer: Type I citrullinemia results from mutations in the ASS1 gene, which encodes argininosuccinate synthase. This urea-cycle enzyme (argininosuccinate synthetase) is classified under Enzyme Commission number EC 6.3.4.5, catalyzing the ATP-dependent condensation of citrulline and aspartate to form argininosuccinate. Deficiency of this EC 6.3.4.5 enzyme impairs ammonia detoxification, producing the clinical phenotype of type I citrullinemia.

227780.long_answer: Congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) is a rare genetic disorder in which mutations in genes that regulate pancreatic β-cell KATP channels (most commonly ABCC8 or KCNJ11) cause uncontrolled insulin secretion. The resulting persistent, often severe hypoglycemia in neonates and infants can lead to seizures, brain injury, and long-term neurodevelopmental disability if not rapidly recognized and treated.

585039.long_answer: Crigler–Najjar syndrome results from an inherited deficiency of the hepatic enzyme UDP-glucuronosyltransferase 1A1 (UGT1A1), which normally conjugates unconjugated bilirubin with glucuronic acid. Without sufficient UGT1A1 activity, bilirubin cannot be adequately conjugated for excretion, leading to the severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia characteristic of the disorder.

156102.long_answer: Surgical removal of the spleen (splenectomy) is often employed to treat the severe hemolytic anemia in hereditary pyropoikilocytosis, because eliminating splenic sequestration markedly decreases the premature destruction of the fragile, spectrin-deficient red blood cells characteristic of this disorder.

907101.long_answer: Blepharoptosis-myopia-ectopia lentis (BMEL/BHME) is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner: affected individuals carry a single heterozygous pathogenic mutation that is sufficient to cause the syndrome and shows vertical inheritance through successive generations.

998456.long_answer: Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome (a PTEN-hamartoma tumour syndrome) is classically characterized by congenital macrocephaly together with tall, slender ‘Marfanoid’ body habitus, joint laxity and other features such as lipomas and intestinal hamartomatous polyps. The coexistence of macrocephaly and Marfanoid habitus in the same genetic disorder distinguishes BRRS from other overgrowth conditions.

971707.long_answer: Cri du chat syndrome results from deletion of the 5p15 region. Within this critical segment lies the semaphorin F gene (SEMA5A), which guides axonal growth and cortical development. Loss of SEMA5A disrupts normal cerebral development, contributing to the microcephaly and intellectual disability characteristic of the syndrome.

242592.long_answer: Obesity adds extra body weight that places additional mechanical stress on muscles and joints already weakened by prior poliomyelitis. This overload accelerates muscle fatigue, joint degeneration, pain, and respiratory effort, thereby intensifying the characteristic weakness, fatigue, and musculoskeletal pain seen in post-polio syndrome.

973807.long_answer: Lamotrigine is an antiepileptic drug that is also widely used as a mood-stabiliser in bipolar disorder. A recognised adverse effect is a hypersensitivity reaction known as DRESS (Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms), in which striking peripheral eosinophilia is typical. Thus, lamotrigine can cause eosinophilia as a side effect.

157260.long_answer: Mutations in the SPG11 gene (encoding the protein spatacsin) are a frequent cause of autosomal-recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia type 11. Beyond progressive lower-limb spasticity, SPG11‐related disease typically presents as a ‘complex’ form of HSP marked by thinning of the corpus callosum and variable cognitive impairment; many patients exhibit learning difficulties or frank intellectual disability. Thus, SPG11 links hereditary spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability in affected individuals.

887331.long_answer: Mutations in the IRF6 gene (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6) are responsible for Van der Woude syndrome, which is recognized as the most common syndromic form of orofacial clefting (cleft lip and/or palate). Loss-of-function variants in IRF6 disrupt epithelial differentiation during craniofacial development, leading to the characteristic lip pits and clefts that define this prevalent clefting syndrome.

666548.long_answer: Barber-Say syndrome is most often caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the TWIST2 gene, which encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor involved in dermal and craniofacial development. Disruption of TWIST2 alters fibroblast function and extracellular-matrix production, producing clinical features such as redundant or atrophic skin, hypertrichosis, and facial dysmorphism.

336610.long_answer: Removal of a glioblastoma almost always involves a craniotomy, in which a section of the skull is temporarily opened so neurosurgeons can microsurgically resect (debulk) as much of the tumor as is safely possible.

877018.long_answer: Cholestyramine is a bile-acid sequestrant resin that treats hyperlipidemia by binding bile acids in the intestinal lumen. This prevents bile-acid reabsorption, increases hepatic conversion of cholesterol to bile acids, and thereby lowers circulating LDL cholesterol levels.

407269.long_answer: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) is epidemiologically and mechanistically linked to multiple sclerosis; almost all MS patients show prior EBV infection and elevated EBV-specific antibodies, and recent longitudinal studies indicate seroconversion to EBV markedly raises MS risk. EBV can also infect NK/T cells, and its reactivation in these cells underlies the rare but well-documented 'severe mosquito bite allergy,' characterized by exaggerated local and systemic reactions after mosquito bites. Thus, EBV is the virus connecting both phenomena.

766204.long_answer: The ROR2 gene, mutations of which cause the autosomal recessive form of Robinow syndrome, is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 9 (cytogenetic band 9q22.31).

943677.long_answer: Autoimmune hepatitis is primarily managed with immunosuppressive therapy, most commonly systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone. These drugs dampen the aberrant immune response attacking hepatocytes, leading to reduced inflammation, normalization of transaminases, and prevention of progressive liver damage.

338101.long_answer: In children with hemosiderosis, excess iron deposits in endocrine organs—especially the pituitary—impair growth-hormone secretion and other hormonal axes, leading to slowed or stunted physical growth. Consequently, growth retardation is a well-recognized developmental problem in pediatric patients with iron overload (hemosiderosis).

197716.long_answer: Posterior urethral valves are congenital obstructing leaflets in the male infant urethra. Their diagnosis and definitive management—endoscopic valve ablation, vesicostomy, or other urinary tract reconstructive procedures—are performed by physicians trained in pediatric urology, the subspecialty of urology focused on surgical and medical care of genitourinary disorders in infants and children.

339659.long_answer: Hunter syndrome (MPS II) is caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme iduronate-2-sulfatase. Fetal chorionic-villus tissue obtained by chorionic villus sampling (CVS) at 10–12 weeks’ gestation can be assayed directly for iduronate-2-sulfatase activity. Demonstrating markedly reduced or absent enzyme activity in the chorionic villi provides a definitive prenatal diagnosis of Hunter syndrome.

275660.long_answer: Germline mutations in the tumor-suppressor genes BRCA1 and BRCA2 greatly elevate lifetime risk of epithelial ovarian cancer—up to ~40-60 % for BRCA1 and ~10-25 % for BRCA2 carriers—because loss of their DNA-repair (homologous recombination) function promotes genomic instability and malignant transformation in ovarian epithelial cells.

442587.long_answer: Usher syndrome causes progressive vision loss due to retinitis pigmentosa, in which the light-sensing photoreceptor cells of the retina degenerate. Damage to the retina, particularly the rod and later cone photoreceptors, leads to night blindness and constricted visual fields characteristic of the disorder.

823895.long_answer: Thomas Harris’s fictional serial killer Hannibal Lecter is sometimes (incorrectly) cited as an example of a person with elective, or selective, mutism brought on by childhood trauma. In the canon Lecter is only briefly silent after witnessing his sister’s murder; he soon speaks fluently and shows no clinical picture of selective-mutism. Thus the popular attribution of elective mutism to this character is mistaken.

348207.long_answer: The perceived loudness of tinnitus is quantified by matching the tinnitus sound to an external tone and recording its intensity in decibels (dB), typically referenced to the patient’s hearing threshold (dB SL or dB HL). Decibels are the standard acoustic unit for sound intensity and therefore for tinnitus loudness measurement in clinical audiology.

680084.long_answer: Wolf–Hirschhorn syndrome results from a deletion of genetic material on the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p16.3). A hallmark craniofacial feature of this contiguous-gene-deletion disorder is marked hypertelorism, along with a broad nasal bridge and “Greek-warrior-helmet” facies, linking the syndrome to the clinical finding in the question.

347931.long_answer: In lichen planus, activated CD8⁺ cytotoxic T lymphocytes accumulate at the dermal-epidermal junction and induce apoptosis of basal keratinocytes. A key step is the binding of Fas ligand (FasL) on these T cells to the Fas (CD95/APO-1) death receptor expressed on keratinocytes. Engagement of the Fas receptor triggers the caspase cascade, leading to keratinocyte apoptosis and the characteristic interface dermatitis of lichen planus. Thus, the Fas (CD95) receptor is centrally involved in the disease’s immunopathogenesis.

754818.long_answer: In the United States, March is officially recognized by Congress and public health agencies as National Colon Cancer Awareness Month, dedicated to increasing awareness of colorectal cancer screening, prevention, and research.

954209.long_answer: Peritonitis can be definitively confirmed by diagnostic laparoscopy, a minimally invasive procedure in which a laparoscope (camera-equipped endoscope) is introduced through small abdominal incisions, allowing direct visual inspection of the peritoneal cavity and, if necessary, collection of peritoneal fluid or biopsies.

299623.long_answer: The PEP-C regimen is an all-oral combination used for relapsed mantle cell lymphoma; it consists of Prednisone, Etoposide, Procarbazine, and Cyclophosphamide. Thus, Prednisone is one of the medications included in this regimen.

680005.long_answer: In mitral stenosis, left-atrial and pulmonary venous pressures rise, increasing capillary hydrostatic pressure in the lungs. When this hydrostatic force exceeds plasma oncotic pressure, fluid is driven from the pulmonary capillaries into the interstitium and alveoli, producing pulmonary edema.

188115.long_answer: Autosomal recessive GTP-cyclohydrolase I deficiency causes a shortage of the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). Sapropterin dihydrochloride is a synthetic analogue of BH4 that replaces the missing cofactor, restoring phenylalanine hydroxylase and aromatic amino-acid hydroxylase activity. Therefore, sapropterin dihydrochloride is the standard BH4 analogue used in treating this disorder.

170249.long_answer: In advanced lymphedema the limb develops fibrotic, chronic non-pitting edema that no longer responds to conservative measures. The classical surgical option for such cases is the Charles procedure, an excisional operation in which the diseased skin and subcutaneous tissue are removed en bloc down to the deep fascia and the area is resurfaced with split-thickness skin grafts. By excising the fibrotic, lymph-laden tissue, the Charles procedure can markedly reduce the chronic non-pitting edema characteristic of end-stage lymphedema.

938007.long_answer: When a thrombus forms in a cerebral artery, it can block (obstruct) blood flow to brain tissue, producing focal cerebral ischemia. Neurons deprived of oxygen and glucose—especially in memory-critical regions such as the hippocampus and temporal cortex—are damaged or die, leading to symptoms that commonly include acute memory loss. This pathophysiologic event is clinically termed an ischemic stroke (cerebrovascular accident due to thrombosis).

969164.long_answer: Tsetse flies (Glossina spp.) transmit the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma brucei, which causes African trypanosomiasis—also called African sleeping sickness. This vector-borne illness is entirely separate from encephalitis lethargica, a viral-associated encephalitic condition that caused epidemics in the early 20th century.

945365.long_answer: The WT1 (Wilms-tumor 1) tumor-suppressor gene resides at chromosome band 11p13, on the short arm (p) of chromosome 11.
