276288.long_answer: Pressure ulcers (decubitus or bedsore wounds) form when prolonged external pressure over bony prominences causes repeated cycles of tissue ischemia followed by reperfusion. These ischemia–reperfusion episodes generate oxidative stress and inflammatory damage, making pressure ulcers the prototypical wounds linked to this mechanism.

194594.long_answer: In toxic epidermal necrolysis, large numbers of activated cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes infiltrate the epidermis and release granulysin, perforin/granzyme B, and Fas ligand, triggering widespread apoptosis of keratinocytes. These CD8+ T cells are therefore considered the principal effector cells responsible for keratinocyte death in this condition.

965101.long_answer: Blepharophimosis–ptosis–epicanthus inversus syndrome (especially type I, which includes premature ovarian failure) is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the FOXL2 gene on chromosome 3q23. FOXL2 encodes a forkhead box transcription factor critical for eyelid development and ovarian folliculogenesis; when mutated, it leads to the eyelid malformations of BPES and, in many female patients, premature (secondary) ovarian failure.

298991.long_answer: Diseases that cause thickening and stiffening of the interstitium—collectively called interstitial lung diseases or pulmonary fibrosis—affect the lung parenchyma. The interstitium is the delicate tissue surrounding the alveoli, so its scarring directly impairs lung function.

330426.long_answer: At high altitude the fall in atmospheric O₂ lowers arterial PO₂, stimulating peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies. The homeostatic response is reflex hyperventilation—an increase in the rate and depth of breathing—which raises alveolar and arterial O₂ partial pressure and helps restore oxygen delivery, even though it produces a secondary respiratory alkalosis.

392896.long_answer: In Hashimoto’s autoimmune thyroiditis the thyroid parenchyma is infiltrated by autoreactive CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes. These cells recognize thyroid-specific antigens presented on MHC class I molecules of follicular epithelial cells and induce their apoptosis through perforin–granzyme release and Fas–FasL interactions, leading to progressive destruction of the gland.

463336.long_answer: Neuropsychological testing in primary lateral sclerosis commonly reveals subtle but measurable deficits in frontal-lobe executive functions—impaired verbal fluency, set-shifting, working memory and other frontotemporal tasks—while general intellect remains largely intact, indicating the presence of executive dysfunction.

278505.long_answer: Elevated serum potassium (hyperkalemia) can develop after cardiac arrest because global ischemia and cell lysis release intracellular K⁺ and renal perfusion falls, impairing potassium excretion. In metabolic acidosis, excess H⁺ enters cells in exchange for K⁺, shifting potassium into the extracellular fluid. Thus both cardiac arrest and metabolic acidosis can independently lead to the same condition—hyperkalemia.

653418.long_answer: Generalized Arterial Calcification of Infancy causes widespread calcification and stenosis of large- and medium-sized arteries, leading to severe neonatal hypertension and heart failure. Infants typically present with cardiovascular compromise, and diagnosis relies on echocardiography, vascular imaging, and management of heart failure—all core activities of pediatric cardiology. Consequently, pediatric cardiologists are the specialists most often responsible for recognizing and treating GACI, including initiating bisphosphonate therapy and coordinating multidisciplinary care.

900173.long_answer: Primary infection with the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii during pregnancy can cross the placenta and cause congenital toxoplasmosis, which is well-documented to result in miscarriage or stillbirth as well as severe fetal abnormalities. Therefore, toxoplasmosis is the parasitic infection that can lead to stillbirth if acquired while pregnant.

112179.long_answer: Familial progressive hyperpigmentation is an extremely rare genodermatosis, but the greatest number of reported pedigrees originate from China. Case series and genetic studies consistently note that the disorder is seen predominantly in Chinese families, making China the country with the highest documented prevalence of this condition.

904189.long_answer: True diphallia represents complete duplication of the penile shaft, which requires duplication of all three erectile bodies within the penis: the paired corpora cavernosa and the single corpus spongiosum (with its enclosed urethra). Thus, these erectile structures in the body of the penis are the anatomical elements involved in the formation of true diphallia.

444615.long_answer: Mucolipidosis type IV commonly causes eye problems such as corneal clouding, retinal degeneration, strabismus, and optic nerve atrophy. Management of these ocular manifestations is the domain of ophthalmology, the medical specialty dedicated to diagnosing and treating diseases of the eye.

504375.long_answer: Mutations in the gap-junction genes GJB3 (connexin-31) and GJB4 (connexin-30.3) cause the autosomal dominant skin disorder erythrokeratodermia variabilis (EKV). EKV is typified by transient erythematous patches accompanied by persistent or migrating hyperkeratotic plaques, so patients commonly present with areas of marked hyperkeratosis.

680210.long_answer: In the TDx-FLM surfactant-to-albumin (S/A) assay, an S/A ratio of 55 mg surfactant per g albumin or higher is the established cutoff that signifies fetal lung maturity. At this level the fetal lungs contain adequate surfactant, greatly lowering the risk of infant respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS). Values <40 mg/g are considered immature, 40–54 mg/g transitional, and ≥55 mg/g mature.

730145.long_answer: The parotid gland’s excretory (Stensen’s) duct passes across the masseter muscle, pierces the buccinator, and opens into the oral cavity on the buccal mucosa opposite the crown of the maxillary second molar.

209581.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TBX19 gene, which encodes the T-pit transcription factor required for pro-opiomelanocortin expression in corticotrophs, produce congenital isolated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) deficiency. The resulting cortisol lack leads to a characteristic peripheral lymphocytosis that is repeatedly documented in affected neonates and infants. Thus, TBX19 mutation is the recognized genetic cause that links ACTH deficiency and lymphocytosis.

791593.long_answer: Hypoaldosteronism (or aldosterone resistance) reduces Na⁺ reabsorption and impairs distal tubular secretion of H⁺ and K⁺. The resulting hyperkalemia limits ammonium generation, producing a non-anion-gap metabolic acidosis characteristic of Type 4 renal tubular acidosis.

645438.long_answer: X-linked ichthyosis is caused by deletions or loss-of-function mutations in the STS (steroid sulfatase) gene on chromosome Xp22.3. STS encodes the enzyme steroid sulfatase, which hydrolyzes cholesterol sulfate in the epidermis; its deficiency leads to abnormal retention of cholesterol sulfate, impaired corneocyte shedding, and the characteristic generalized scaling of X-linked ichthyosis.

856153.long_answer: Geographic tongue (benign migratory glossitis) presents as multiple erythematous, depapillated areas with whitish serpiginous borders that migrate over time, giving the dorsum of the tongue a map-like appearance. Although its precise etiology is unknown, clinical studies note higher prevalence in individuals with parafunctional oral habits such as bruxism and tongue thrusting, suggesting these habits may contribute to or exacerbate the condition.

204827.long_answer: Klumpke's paralysis is a lower brachial plexus neuropathy (injury of the C8–T1 nerve roots). Disorders of peripheral nerves are diagnosed and managed primarily by specialists in neurology, who evaluate the extent of nerve damage, order electrodiagnostic studies, and guide both medical and rehabilitative treatment. Therefore, the medical specialty most likely to treat Klumpke's paralysis is neurology.

370157.long_answer: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) disrupts development of the third and fourth pharyngeal (branchial) pouches, leading to malformation of the cardiac outflow tract derived from neural‐crest cells. The hallmark congenital heart defect linked to this mechanism is persistent truncus arteriosus, in which a single great vessel fails to septate into the aorta and pulmonary artery. This defect is classically and most commonly cited in association with DiGeorge syndrome.

744044.long_answer: Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type VI) results from inherited deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase B (N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase). Without functional arylsulfatase B, sulfate groups cannot be removed from dermatan sulfate and related glycosaminoglycans, leading to their intralysosomal accumulation and the characteristic clinical features of the disorder.

269724.long_answer: The intestinal inflammation of tropical sprue is driven predominantly by a T-cell–mediated, delayed-type (Type IV) hypersensitivity reaction. Activated lymphocytes release cytokines that recruit macrophages and cause villous atrophy and mucosal injury, accounting for the malabsorption and inflammatory changes characteristic of the disease.

256711.long_answer: Erythrokeratodermia with ataxia is considered a variant of progressive symmetric erythrokeratoderma, one of the two classic forms of hereditary erythrokeratodermias (disorders of keratinization/ichthyosis). Patients show the characteristic bilaterally symmetrical hyperkeratotic erythematous plaques of PSEK together with cerebellar ataxia caused by ELOVL4 mutations.

679761.long_answer: Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme arylsulfatase A. Without this enzyme, sulfatides—sulfated glycolipids (a category of fats/lipids)—accumulate in cells of the nervous system and other tissues. The buildup of these lipid molecules leads to progressive destruction of myelin and the neurological symptoms characteristic of the disease. Thus, MLD is indeed associated with the pathological accumulation of fats (lipids) in the body.

827179.long_answer: Lithiasis is the medical term for the pathological formation of calculi (stones) in the body. Depending on location, it is subclassified as nephrolithiasis or urolithiasis for kidney/urinary stones and cholelithiasis for gallbladder stones, but the overarching process of stone crystallization and aggregation from supersaturated bodily fluids is called lithiasis.

943807.long_answer: Necrotizing fasciitis is a rare, rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection most often precipitated by trauma, surgery, varicella lesions, or underlying illnesses such as diabetes or immunosuppression. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are widely used analgesic and antipyretic agents. A few observational reports—particularly in children with varicella—have suggested that NSAID use might delay recognition of worsening soft-tissue infection or, by modulating host immune responses, potentially facilitate progression to invasive bacterial disease. However, large epidemiologic studies and systematic reviews have failed to demonstrate a consistent, causal link between NSAID exposure and the development of necrotizing fasciitis in the general population. Current clinical guidelines do not list NSAID therapy as an independent, universal risk factor for the disease. Therefore, it is not accurate to state that NSAID use always increases the risk of necrotizing fasciitis; at most, an association is unproven, limited to specific contexts, and remains controversial.

853250.long_answer: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile halogenated anesthetics and depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, not by intravenous induction agents. Propofol, an intravenous anesthetic, does not activate the ryanodine receptor–mediated Ca2⁺ release responsible for malignant hyperthermia episodes, making it a well-established safe choice in patients with malignant hyperthermia susceptibility.

961833.long_answer: Short bowel syndrome usually arises after extensive surgical resection of the small intestine. One of the common reasons surgeons remove large segments of bowel is the presence of benign or malignant intestinal tumors—abnormal proliferations of tissue. Because these neoplastic growths must be excised en bloc with surrounding healthy bowel, intestinal tumors are a well-recognized, common cause of short bowel syndrome.

399332.long_answer: In synovial (osteo)chondromatosis, the cartilaginous transformation originates from metaplasia of the synovial membrane (synovium) lining the joint, resulting in formation of intra-articular cartilaginous nodules.

284560.long_answer: The inaugural description of propionic acidemia (then called propionic aciduria) was published in 1961 by Barton Childs, William Nyhan and colleagues working at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. Their report of two siblings with severe metabolic acidosis and massive urinary excretion of propionic acid introduced the disorder as a new inborn error of metabolism.

884981.long_answer: Carney complex is a hereditary syndrome (often due to PRKAR1A mutations) characterized by spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas, and endocrine tumors. Among its cutaneous manifestations are multiple pigmented melanocytic lesions, classically the blue nevus—especially the epithelioid (pigmented epithelioid melanocytoma) variant—making this type of nevus a recognized feature of Carney complex.

937642.long_answer: Conversion disorder, now formally termed functional neurological symptom disorder, presents with neurological symptoms such as weakness, sensory loss, or seizures that are precipitated or exacerbated by psychological stress. Neuroimaging and other investigations show no structural brain lesion or neurodegenerative process, distinguishing it from organic neurological disease.

728210.long_answer: The established treatment for neonatal encephalopathy due to birth asphyxia (hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy) is therapeutic hypothermia—either whole-body or selective head cooling to ~33–34 °C initiated within 6 hours of birth and maintained for about 72 hours. Cooling lowers cerebral metabolism and mitigates excitotoxicity, inflammation, and apoptotic pathways, significantly improving survival and neurodevelopmental outcomes in multiple randomized controlled trials.

280189.long_answer: The CTSS gene encodes the lysosomal cysteine protease Cathepsin S. Studies of biomarker profiles in Gaucher’s disease—a lysosomal storage disorder caused by glucocerebrosidase deficiency—show that Cathepsin S concentration is markedly increased in patient plasma and tissue, reflecting macrophage activation and altered lysosomal function characteristic of the disease.

894573.long_answer: Aicardi–Goutières syndrome can be caused by mutations in any of the three genes RNASEH2A, RNASEH2B or RNASEH2C, which encode the heterotrimeric ribonuclease H2 (RNase H2) complex. RNase H2 is a trimer made of the A, B and C subunits; its loss of function leads to accumulation of ribonucleotides in DNA, aberrant nucleic-acid sensing and the type I interferon signature characteristic of the disease.

770898.long_answer: CHARGE syndrome is genetically confirmed in most patients by detecting heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the CHD7 gene, which encodes a chromatin-remodeling ATP-dependent helicase. Accordingly, BGI Genomics’ diagnostic panel for CHARGE syndrome focuses on sequencing and analyzing CHD7 to identify pathogenic variants.

643876.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease) results from a deficiency of the hepatic isoform of glycogen phosphorylase, the enzyme that cleaves α-1,4-glycosidic bonds to release glucose-1-phosphate from liver glycogen. Loss of this enzyme impairs glycogenolysis, leading to hepatomegaly, mild hypoglycaemia, and accumulation of glycogen in the liver—hallmarks of GSD VI.

128206.long_answer: Desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy is a hereditary neuromuscular disorder that presents with progressive skeletal muscle weakness and can involve cardiomyopathy. Evaluation requires a neurologic examination, electromyography, nerve-conduction studies, and muscle biopsy—all procedures typically directed by a neurologist (often with neuromuscular subspecialty training). Hence, the medical specialty responsible for diagnosing this condition is Neurology.

508875.long_answer: An infarction within the left Sylvian (lateral) fissure jeopardises the subcortical white-matter fibres of the arcuate fasciculus and adjacent supramarginal cortex that link Broca’s and Wernicke’s language areas. Damage to these fibres produces conduction aphasia, in which speech is fluent and comprehension is relatively preserved but repetition is markedly impaired.

674162.long_answer: Malignant hyperthermia is most commonly caused by mutations in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor calcium channel. Defective RYR1 channels open excessively when exposed to triggering agents such as volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine, releasing large amounts of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The resulting sustained muscle contraction drives rapid ATP consumption, heat production, lactic acidosis, and the systemic hypermetabolic state characteristic of malignant hyperthermia.

314635.long_answer: Kevin Reilly was diagnosed with a desmoid tumor—an uncommon, locally aggressive fibrous neoplasm that arises from musculo-aponeurotic connective tissue. Because the tumor infiltrated the soft tissues of his shoulder girdle and chest wall, surgeons had to perform a radical resection that removed his left arm, shoulder, and five ribs to achieve disease control.

996405.long_answer: Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmia disorder most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SCN5A gene that encodes the cardiac fast sodium channel (NaV1.5). The defective sodium current alters ventricular depolarization and repolarization, producing the characteristic ECG pattern and creating a substrate for malignant arrhythmias, particularly polymorphic ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation, which can lead to sudden cardiac death.

182480.long_answer: Avoidant personality disorder, listed in the DSM-IV-TR, is sometimes called the “anxious” or “panphobic” personality because affected individuals exhibit a pervasive fear of virtually all social interactions and potential negative evaluation. This broad, undifferentiated fearfulness (panphobia) is a core descriptive feature of the disorder, making Avoidant personality disorder the DSM-IV-TR personality disorder most closely linked with panphobia.

495618.long_answer: In hypopituitarism, deficiency of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the anterior pituitary reduces stimulation of the thyroid gland, leading to decreased synthesis and release of thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3). This central (secondary) lack of thyroid hormone production manifests clinically as hypothyroidism.

552798.long_answer: Holoprosencephaly occurs when the embryonic forebrain, known as the prosencephalon, fails to divide into the paired cerebral hemispheres during the 3rd–4th week of gestation. Defective midline patterning signals (e.g., reduced Sonic hedgehog from prechordal tissue) in this organ lead to the characteristic single-lobed cerebrum and associated midline facial anomalies.

191878.long_answer: Botulinum toxin, produced by Clostridium botulinum, cleaves SNARE proteins in motor nerve terminals, preventing presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. This blockade causes flaccid paralysis of skeletal muscles, and weakness of the levator palpebrae superioris leads to the characteristic ptosis seen in botulism.

925242.long_answer: Excess phosphate in the blood (hyperphosphatemia) drives the precipitation of calcium-phosphate complexes, which deposit in renal tubules and interstitium. This calcium-phosphate deposition is a well-recognized mechanism leading to nephrocalcinosis.

891196.long_answer: Syringomyelia secondary to an Arnold-Chiari (Chiari I) malformation is most effectively treated by posterior fossa (foramen magnum) decompression—typically a suboccipital craniectomy with C1 laminectomy and duraplasty—which enlarges the foramen magnum, restores cerebrospinal fluid flow at the craniocervical junction, and allows the syrinx to regress.

626598.long_answer: Sequencing or targeted PCR-based analysis of mitochondrial DNA identifies the characteristic point mutations—m.3243A>G in tRNALeu(UUR) for MELAS and m.8344A>G in tRNALys for MERRF—thereby reliably distinguishing the two syndromes.

360849.long_answer: Pathogenic mutations in the ELANE gene (formerly called ELA2), which encodes neutrophil elastase, are the most frequent and well-established genetic cause of both severe congenital neutropenia (Kostmann disease) and cyclic neutropenia. Different heterozygous ELANE variants disrupt neutrophil maturation, leading either to persistent profound neutropenia (SCN) or the characteristic 21-day oscillations of neutrophil counts seen in cyclic neutropenia.

182042.long_answer: The IDUA gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase whose deficiency causes Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I), is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 4 at band 4p16.3.

928748.long_answer: The IL1B gene encodes the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β. Polymorphisms that increase IL-1β expression enhance gastric mucosal inflammation in response to Helicobacter pylori infection, thereby predisposing individuals to peptic ulcer disease.

136563.long_answer: Blepharophimosis syndrome, formally called blepharophimosis–ptosis–epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES), is classically defined by the triad of congenital ptosis, epicanthus inversus, and a shortened horizontal palpebral fissure (blepharophimosis). These ocular features are pathognomonic for the syndrome and arise from developmental defects in the eyelids, most often due to pathogenic variants in the FOXL2 gene.

918240.long_answer: Prenatal exposure to cocaine can disrupt central neurotransmitter regulation of motor pathways. As a result, some neonates and young infants show hypertonia—abnormally increased skeletal-muscle tone—manifesting as rigid or stiff extremities and exaggerated reflexes during early development.

617987.long_answer: The RET proto-oncogene, mutations of which are a well-established cause of Hirschsprung’s disease, is located on the long arm of chromosome 10 at cytogenetic band 10q11.2—not on chromosome 15. Therefore, the statement that the RET gene associated with Hirschsprung’s disease is on chromosome 15 is incorrect.

832569.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) is an autosomal-dominant tumor-predisposition syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in the NF2 gene encoding merlin. Individuals with NF2 characteristically develop multiple central-nervous-system tumors, including vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and spinal or intracranial ependymomas; thus the syndrome is classically linked to both brain tumors in general and ependymomas specifically.

678991.long_answer: Toxic shock syndrome can precipitate disseminated intravascular coagulation and other coagulative disturbances, leading to a markedly decreased circulating platelet count. This low-platelet state is termed thrombocytopenia, and it is a recognized hematologic complication of toxic shock syndrome.

698643.long_answer:
Strongyloides stercoralis infection can remain asymptomatic for decades but, once a patient becomes immunosuppressed (particularly with corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors or other agents used after solid-organ transplantation), the parasite may proliferate unchecked and cause hyperinfection or disseminated strongyloidiasis, conditions that carry mortality rates exceeding 50 %.  

Because of this well-documented risk, multiple authoritative guidelines recommend that candidates for solid-organ transplantation—or any patient about to receive prolonged or high-dose immunosuppression—be screened for latent Strongyloides infection and treated pre-emptively if positive:
• American Society of Transplantation Infectious Diseases Community of Practice (2020): "All transplant candidates with epidemiologic risk factors (birth, residence, or extensive travel in endemic areas, or unexplained eosinophilia) should undergo serologic screening for Strongyloides and receive ivermectin if positive."  
• Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) parasitic infections guidance (updated 2022) endorses serologic screening of at-risk patients before initiation of immunosuppression, particularly before transplantation.  
• IDSA/AST "Guidelines for Solid Organ Transplant Recipient Care" emphasize the need to identify and treat Strongyloides infection prior to transplantation to prevent hyperinfection.  

Therefore, based on prevailing clinical guidelines and the high morbidity of unchecked infection in immunosuppressed hosts, patients who are about to start immunosuppressive therapy for organ transplantation should indeed be screened for strongyloidiasis.

395433.long_answer: Excess body weight increases intra-abdominal pressure, which in turn raises pressure on the bladder and urethral sphincter. Over time this mechanical strain weakens pelvic floor support and can impair sphincter closure, leading to episodes of involuntary urine leakage—urinary incontinence, particularly the stress subtype. Numerous epidemiologic studies show a direct, dose-dependent rise in incontinence prevalence with higher body-mass index, establishing overweight as a causal risk factor.

796241.long_answer: Holt-Oram syndrome, also called the "heart-hand" syndrome, is an autosomal-dominant disorder in which skeletal anomalies of the upper limbs—especially thumb/radial defects and brachydactyly—occur together with congenital heart disease, most commonly atrial or ventricular septal defects. Thus it is the classic congenital syndrome that links brachydactyly with structural cardiac malformations.

262383.long_answer: Women who may become pregnant are advised to receive the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, which contains a live-attenuated rubella component. Vaccination at least 1 month before conception induces protective antibodies against rubella, preventing primary maternal infection and thereby averting congenital rubella syndrome in the fetus.

578459.long_answer: Gliclazide is considered porphyrinogenic: it can induce hepatic enzymes that accelerate heme synthesis, raising porphyrin precursors and thereby triggering an acute porphyric attack. For this reason it is listed as unsafe and should be avoided in patients with acute porphyria.

658731.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), especially with gadolinium contrast, is the modality of choice for diagnosing spinal nerve sheath tumors such as schwannomas and neurofibromas. MRI provides high-resolution visualization of soft tissues, spinal cord, and nerve roots, allowing precise delineation of tumor size, extent, and relationship to adjacent neural structures.

424536.long_answer: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia—most often due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency—is an autosomal-recessive genetic disorder that impairs cortisol synthesis in the adrenal cortex. The resulting ACTH-driven adrenal hyperplasia leads to overproduction of adrenal androgens. In females this androgen excess commonly manifests as oligomenorrhea, hirsutism, and virilization, making CAH the classic genetic cause of oligomenorrhea linked to excessive androgen production.

823665.long_answer: Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis is characterized by intra-alveolar accumulation of surfactant lipoproteins. The accepted first-line and most effective therapy is whole-lung lavage, in which each lung is sequentially filled and drained with warm saline under general anesthesia to wash out the proteinaceous material, thereby restoring alveolar ventilation and gas exchange.

975353.long_answer: Persistent fear of the dark (nyctophobia), especially in children, is often viewed as a symptom of separation anxiety disorder. In DSM anxiety-disorder nosology, excessive distress when alone or at bedtime and refusal to sleep without an attachment figure are core features of separation anxiety, so nighttime darkness fears are interpreted as a manifestation of this disorder rather than a distinct condition.

455591.long_answer: The transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) procedure is performed to decompress portal hypertension by creating a portosystemic channel within the liver. While effective for bleeding or refractory ascites, TIPS diverts portal blood away from hepatocyte detoxification, raising systemic ammonia and other neurotoxic substances. This increase can precipitate or worsen hepatic encephalopathy, a well-recognized complication in patients—including those with gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE)—who undergo the procedure.

506550.long_answer: Lichen spinulosus is a follicular keratotic disorder; therapy aims to dissolve the compact keratin plugs. Topical keratolytics such as 3–6 % salicylic acid ointment are routinely recommended because salicylic acid breaks down inter-cellular keratin, smooths the papules and improves the rough plaques characteristic of this condition.

518755.long_answer: Mutations in the STXBP2 gene, which encodes the vesicle-fusion regulator Munc18-2, impair apical membrane trafficking in enterocytes, producing Microvillous Inclusion Disease, and simultaneously block cytotoxic-granule exocytosis in NK and cytotoxic T cells, causing Familial Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis type 5.

235064.long_answer: Biallelic pathogenic variants in the AGK gene (acylglycerol kinase) are the established cause of classical Sengers syndrome. Loss of AGK impairs mitochondrial protein import and phospholipid metabolism, leading to mitochondrial myopathy that manifests clinically as generalized muscle weakness and hypotonia, together with the syndrome’s other hallmarks (congenital cataracts, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, lactic acidosis).

903724.long_answer: Achondroplasia accounts for the majority of dwarfism cases worldwide. It results from activating mutations in the FGFR3 gene, leading to impaired endochondral bone growth and the characteristic disproportionate short stature. Clinically and epidemiologically, it is recognized as the single most common form of dwarfism.

611462.long_answer: Germ-line or somatic mutations in the KCNJ5 gene, which encodes the GIRK4 potassium channel, cause familial hyperaldosteronism type III. The mutant channel allows excess sodium influx, stimulating aldosterone over-production. The resulting hyperaldosteronism leads to hypokalaemia, producing muscle weakness along with hypertension.

928497.long_answer: A toupee is a partial wig designed to cover localized areas of hair loss, such as the crown or front scalp commonly affected in androgenetic (male-pattern) baldness. It is tailored to blend with the wearer’s existing hair, providing cosmetic coverage without treating the underlying follicular miniaturization driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT).

529655.long_answer: Levodopa (often given with the peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor carbidopa) remains the gold-standard therapy for Parkinson’s disease because it is the metabolic precursor of dopamine, crosses the blood-brain barrier, and replenishes striatal dopamine levels, providing the greatest and most reliable symptomatic relief of bradykinesia and rigidity compared with any other pharmacologic treatment.

747504.long_answer: Remotivation therapy is a structured group-based intervention used chiefly with confused or cognitively impaired patients, such as those suffering from organic brain syndrome. By engaging the patient in guided discussion of factual, concrete topics (e.g., current events, past interests), it stimulates attention, orientation, and social interaction, thereby helping to re-establish or improve mental functions that have been diminished by the organic brain disorder.

901112.long_answer: The SCN5A gene encodes the cardiac sodium-channel α-subunit (NaV1.5). Pathogenic SCN5A variants are the most frequent genetic cause of Brugada syndrome (≈20–30 % of cases) and have also been repeatedly identified in families with arrhythmogenic right ventricular dysplasia/cardiomyopathy (classified as ARVD10). Loss-of-function mutations in SCN5A reduce inward sodium current, producing conduction delay in the right ventricular outflow tract that underlies the arrhythmic substrate in both disorders, making SCN5A the gene most commonly linked to both conditions.

414167.long_answer: The most common progressive myoclonus epilepsy beginning with the letter “U” is Unverricht–Lundborg disease (EPM1). This disorder is caused by loss-of-function mutations—most often an unstable dodecamer repeat expansion in the promoter—of the CSTB gene, which encodes the protease inhibitor cystatin B. Defective CSTB leads to neuronal dysfunction and the characteristic myoclonus-epilepsy phenotype of Unverricht–Lundborg disease.

384922.long_answer: Patients with familial progressive vestibulocochlear dysfunction frequently experience vertigo—a spinning or whirling sensation that arises from vestibular system impairment. Vertigo is one of the most common clinical forms of dizziness and is therefore recognized as both a hallmark vestibular symptom of this hereditary disorder and a widely encountered type of dizziness in general clinical practice.

833832.long_answer: Brachydactyly is defined by an abnormal shortening of the digits that results from congenital shortening of the phalangeal bones (proximal, middle, and/or distal phalanges) of the fingers; these shortened phalanges give the hand its characteristically short appearance.

184799.long_answer: A balanced translocation t(X;16)(q28;q11.2) can disrupt the FLNA gene on Xq28. Loss-of-function of FLNA causes the X-linked neuronal migration disorder known as periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH). Patients with PVNH, beside epilepsy due to ectopic grey matter lining the ventricles, often show mild craniofacial anomalies such as hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge and high-arched palate. Thus, the genetic disorder associated with the Xq28/16q11.2 translocation and presenting with hypertelorism is periventricular nodular heterotopia.

125455.long_answer: The standard tendon-transfer procedure for persistent foot-drop (loss of tibialis anterior function) is to reroute the tibialis posterior tendon to the dorsum of the foot. This operation is well described for causes such as common-peroneal-nerve palsy, Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease and distal myopathies. The fibularis (peroneus) longus tendon is not the usual or recommended donor in these cases; it is generally left intact to preserve eversion strength and lateral-column stability, and it is itself often weakened in many neuromuscular disorders. Therefore, established surgical consensus does not involve “repurposing” the fibularis longus to act as the tibialis anterior in the treatment of foot drop due to distal myopathy.

228492.long_answer: Deficiencies in early classical-pathway complement components—especially C1q, C2, and C4—impair clearance of immune complexes and apoptotic debris. This promotes loss of self-tolerance and the development of the multisystem autoimmune disease systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). Consequently, inherited or acquired deficiency of these complement proteins is strongly and uniquely linked to an increased risk of SLE.

600892.long_answer: Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disease in which IgG auto-antibodies target desmoglein proteins within desmosomes of stratified squamous epithelium. Loss of desmosomal integrity leads to acantholysis and secondary disruption of adjacent gap junctions, producing fragile blisters and erosions that characteristically involve the oral and other mucous membranes as well as skin.

881534.long_answer: Intrinsic stains from dental fluorosis are often lightened with professional teeth bleaching, typically using hydrogen- or carbamide-peroxide gels. The oxidizing agents penetrate the enamel and break down the pigmented molecules responsible for the brown or mottled discoloration, improving tooth color without removing additional tooth structure.

328209.long_answer: Flint is a hard form of microcrystalline quartz (crystalline silica) that was historically knapped into stone tools and struck to produce sparks for fire-starting. When flint is mined, cut, or ground, respirable crystalline silica dust is released; chronic inhalation of this dust produces the occupational lung disease silicosis.

320839.long_answer: Magnesium physiologically antagonizes voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing calcium influx into excitable cells. Medications known as calcium channel blockers (e.g., verapamil, diltiazem, dihydropyridines) exert the same mechanism pharmacologically, and are therefore used to treat many of the same calcium-dependent conditions such as hypertension, certain arrhythmias and migraine.

986581.long_answer: Kinking hair is a disorder of the hair shaft. Medical doctors who specialize in conditions of the skin, hair, and nails are dermatologists. Their training includes diagnosing structural hair abnormalities such as acquired progressive kinking, pili torti, or other shaft disorders and implementing appropriate medical or procedural management. Therefore, a dermatologist is the specialist equipped to evaluate and treat kinking hair.

242256.long_answer: Parkinson’s disease is characterized by intracellular Lewy bodies composed largely of aggregated alpha-synuclein and is strongly linked to mitochondrial dysfunction in dopaminergic neurons, both of which contribute to the neurodegeneration seen in this disorder.

939072.long_answer: The earliest and most frequent presenting complaint in esophageal cancer is progressive dysphagia—difficulty swallowing that starts with solid foods and gradually involves liquids as the tumor narrows the esophageal lumen. Tumor growth obstructs the esophageal passage, so patients notice swallowing problems before other symptoms such as weight loss or pain.

656115.long_answer: Familial cases of neuroblastoma most often arise from germ-line activating mutations in the ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) proto-oncogene. These autosomal-dominant ALK mutations drive constitutive tyrosine-kinase signaling, predisposing carriers to the development of neuroblastoma in multiple family members.

800932.long_answer: DiGeorge syndrome is frequently associated with congenital cyanotic heart defects such as truncus arteriosus and tetralogy of Fallot. These malformations reduce arterial oxygen saturation, leading to hypoxemia. The clinical manifestation of this oxygen deficiency is cyanosis—a bluish discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes.

847140.long_answer: Large cohort studies show that women who develop preeclampsia—a hypertensive disorder of pregnancy characterized by hypertension and proteinuria—have a markedly higher risk of subsequently developing chronic kidney disease and progressing to end-stage renal disease (kidney failure). Endothelial injury and persistent renal microvascular damage during preeclampsia are believed to underlie this long-term renal risk.

480919.long_answer: Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata type 1 (RCDP-1) is an autosomal-recessive peroxisome biogenesis disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the PEX7 gene, which encodes the peroxisomal targeting signal-2 (PTS2) receptor required for importing specific enzymes into peroxisomes. Loss-of-function mutations in PEX7 disrupt plasmalogen synthesis and other peroxisomal pathways, producing the skeletal, neurological, and ocular features characteristic of RCDP-1.

735420.long_answer: Distal (type I) renal tubular acidosis results from impaired H⁺ secretion by the α-intercalated cells of the cortical collecting duct—the terminal portion of the nephron responsible for final urine acidification.

744025.long_answer: In dual inheritance (gene–culture co-evolution) theory, cultural information can be passed vertically—from parents to their offspring—as opposed to horizontal (peer-to-peer) or oblique (older generation to younger, non-offspring) transmission. The same term, vertical transmission, is used in infectious disease biology to denote pathogens that are transmitted from a mother to her child during pregnancy, childbirth or breastfeeding. Thus, “vertical transmission” is the shared term for parent-to-offspring transfer in both cultural and biomedical contexts.

828542.long_answer: Bart–Pumphrey syndrome, characterized by leukonychia, palmoplantar keratoderma, and sensorineural hearing loss, is caused by heterozygous mutations in the GJB2 gene (connexin-26) and is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion.

506221.long_answer: The great majority of benign familial neonatal seizures are caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the KCNQ2 gene, which encodes the Kv7.2 subunit of the neuronal voltage-gated potassium channel mediating the M-current. Disruption of this channel lowers the threshold for neuronal firing, producing the characteristic self-limited seizures in otherwise healthy neonates. Although mutations in KCNQ3 and a few other genes can also cause this syndrome, KCNQ2 mutations are by far the most prevalent and well-established etiology.

324909.long_answer: In DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion), the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches fail to develop properly, leading to aplasia or hypoplasia of the parathyroid glands. Loss of parathyroid tissue causes deficient parathyroid hormone secretion—i.e., congenital hypoparathyroidism—resulting in hypocalcemia. Thus, hypoparathyroidism is the classic endocrine disease associated with DiGeorge syndrome.

851371.long_answer: Kearns–Sayre syndrome is almost always caused by a spontaneous, single large deletion (typically 1–10 kb) in mitochondrial DNA. This deletion removes multiple contiguous genes needed for oxidative phosphorylation, leading to the characteristic multisystem features of the syndrome.

211013.long_answer: For malignant infantile osteopetrosis, allogeneic bone marrow (hematopoietic stem-cell) transplantation replaces the defective osteoclast lineage with normal donor cells, restoring bone resorption and hematopoiesis. This intervention achieves long-term survival and clinical improvement in a substantial proportion of affected infants, making it the only treatment judged satisfactory in many cases.

728934.long_answer: Pterin-4 α-carbinolamine dehydratase deficiency is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the PCBD1 gene. Because disease manifests only when both alleles are affected, and carriers with one mutant allele are asymptomatic, the disorder follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

413428.long_answer: Intramuscular epinephrine is the first-line, life-saving treatment for any form of anaphylaxis, including exercise-induced anaphylaxis and other severe systemic allergic reactions. It rapidly reverses airway constriction, hypotension, and urticaria by stimulating α- and β-adrenergic receptors, and patients at risk are advised to carry an epinephrine auto-injector.

669408.long_answer: Barrett's esophagus is a premalignant metaplasia of the distal esophagus that commonly progresses through dysplasia to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Numerous studies show that DNA-methylation, histone-modification and other epigenetic alterations accumulate in Barrett’s epithelium and its dysplastic stages, driving the neoplastic transformation that culminates in esophageal adenocarcinoma.

308355.long_answer: Fabry disease, an X-linked sphingolipidosis caused by α-galactosidase A deficiency with accumulation of globotriaosylceramide, classically presents with clusters of cutaneous angiokeratomas (especially in a ‘bathing-trunk’ distribution), making the presence of multiple angiokeratomas a hallmark clinical sign of this disorder.

254546.long_answer: In severe retinopathy of prematurity, peripheral retinal laser photocoagulation is applied to the avascular retina. By destroying the ischemic tissue that releases VEGF, the laser treatment causes regression of the pathologic neovascular tufts and prevents further growth of abnormal blood vessels, making it the standard vision-saving therapy for advanced ROP.

927326.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the ZFPM2 gene, which encodes the transcriptional co-factor FOG2, have been repeatedly identified in patients and families with congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). ZFPM2 interacts with GATA transcription factors to regulate diaphragmatic and pulmonary development; disruption of this gene impairs formation of the pleuroperitoneal membranes, producing the characteristic diaphragmatic defect seen in CDH.

725859.long_answer: To date, the U.S. FDA has granted checkpoint-inhibitor approval only for alveolar soft part sarcoma: in 2021–2022 atezolizumab (anti-PD-L1) was approved for unresectable or metastatic ASPS in adults and children ≥2 years. No other soft-tissue sarcoma subtype has a dedicated immunotherapy approval, so ASPS remains the sole soft-tissue sarcoma with regulatory authorization for immune-checkpoint therapy as of 2023.

218011.long_answer: Olfactory reference syndrome (ORS) is a psychiatric disorder in which individuals hold a persistent, unshakeable belief that they emit a foul or abnormal body odor that others can smell, despite no objective evidence. This false belief (often delusional or obsessional in nature) causes marked distress, social anxiety, and avoidance behavior, and is recognized in contemporary classifications as an obsessive-compulsive and related disorder.

991546.long_answer: Pulmonary edema is the accumulation of fluid within the lung interstitium and alveoli, most commonly precipitated by systemic fluid overload and elevated pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure (as in left-sided heart failure). Loop diuretics such as furosemide are standard therapy because they remove excess intravascular volume, lower pulmonary capillary pressure, and thereby resolve the fluid in the lungs.

905592.long_answer: A profound reduction in central nervous system activity can occur in both severe hypothermia and marked hyperglycemia. When core body temperature falls markedly, neuronal metabolism slows, leading to progressive loss of consciousness that culminates in coma. Likewise, extreme hyperglycemia (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state) produces hyper-osmolarity, dehydration, and acidosis that depress cerebral function, also resulting in coma. Thus, coma is a potential outcome of both hypothermia and hyperglycemia.

348247.long_answer: Jaundice is a yellow discoloration of the skin (and mucous membranes) caused by elevated circulating bilirubin. Because bilirubin metabolism depends on normal hepatic uptake, conjugation, and excretion, jaundice frequently signals systemic disorders such as liver disease, biliary obstruction, or hemolysis.

909679.long_answer: The common cold can cause swelling of the nasopharyngeal mucosa and Eustachian tube dysfunction, which traps secretions behind the tympanic membrane. This predisposes to inflammation and infection of the middle ear, clinically termed otitis media—one of the most frequent complications of viral upper-respiratory infections.

568382.long_answer: Both XX male syndrome (de la Chapelle syndrome) and cryptorchidism commonly lead to azoospermia—complete absence of sperm in the ejaculate. In XX male individuals, lack of the Y-chromosome AZF spermatogenesis regions results in non-obstructive azoospermia. In cryptorchidism, failure of testicular descent exposes germ cells to higher abdominal temperature, causing germ-cell loss and often culminating in azoospermia, especially when bilateral or untreated. Thus, azoospermia is the condition associated with both disorders.

880823.long_answer: Thrombocytopenia involves a decreased number of platelets (cell fragments derived from megakaryocytes). The primary function of these platelets is to initiate hemostasis by adhering to damaged vessel walls, aggregating with one another, and providing a phospholipid surface for the coagulation cascade, thereby forming a blood clot to stop bleeding.

917071.long_answer: The German neurologist Adolf von Strümpell first described the familial form of spastic paraparesis in the 1880s and introduced the designation “hereditary spastic paraplegia” (hereditäre spastische Spinalparalyse). His coinage established the term that is still used to refer to this group of inherited disorders characterised by progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness.

961462.long_answer: Management of diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis is mainly symptomatic. For the characteristic axial pain and stiffness, first-line therapy is the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), which reduce prostaglandin-mediated inflammation at entheseal ossification sites and provide analgesia, thereby improving mobility.

470168.long_answer: When Paget's disease affects the skull, the thickened, enlarged bone can irritate periosteal pain fibers and adjacent soft tissues, producing a dull, tight, band-like pain characteristic of a tension headache—the most common primary headache type.

834447.long_answer: Tocilizumab is a humanised monoclonal antibody that blocks the interleukin-6 (IL-6) receptor. Because excessive IL-6 signalling drives the lymphoproliferation seen in unicentric Castleman disease, international guidelines recommend tocilizumab as the first-line systemic (medical) therapy when the lesion is not amenable to curative surgery. The same drug is widely used and licensed for rheumatoid arthritis, where IL-6 also plays a central role in joint inflammation, making tocilizumab a shared treatment option for both conditions.

900329.long_answer: Myoclonic-astatic epilepsy, also known as Doose syndrome, is an idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndrome whose hallmark seizure type is the myoclonic-astatic (or atonic) seizure, characterized by a brief myoclonic jerk immediately followed by a sudden loss of muscle tone.

231753.long_answer: Bathophobia is listed in Wiktionary, the free-content, collaboratively edited dictionary project maintained by the Wikimedia Foundation. Wiktionary provides open-license definitions for English and many other languages, and its entry for “bathophobia” defines the term as an irrational fear of depths.

201071.long_answer: Non-paraneoplastic (autoimmune) Lambert–Eaton myasthenic syndrome shows a strong genetic association with the HLA-B8 haplotype (often linked to the DR3 and DQ2 alleles). This HLA subtype increases susceptibility to developing the calcium-channel autoantibodies that underlie the neuromuscular transmission defect characteristic of Lambert–Eaton syndrome.

111158.long_answer: Spasmodic dysphonia is a focal laryngeal dystonia, and its diagnosis relies on direct examination of the vocal folds during phonation. An otolaryngologist—often a laryngologist/ENT specialist—performs flexible or rigid laryngoscopy and stroboscopy to observe the task-specific, involuntary spasms that characterize the disorder, making this physician the key professional in establishing the diagnosis.

153470.long_answer: Coagulopathy can trigger widespread microvascular thrombosis and impaired perfusion, leading to failure of multiple organs. The clinical condition defined as “multiple organ dysfunction syndrome” (MODS) is characterized by altered organ function in an acutely ill patient such that homeostasis cannot be maintained without intervention.

130401.long_answer: Vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is associated with fragile arteries and hollow organs that can rupture spontaneously; most patients experience life-threatening complications in young adulthood, giving a median life expectancy of roughly 40–50 years, so overall survival outlook is poor.

470725.long_answer: Although the exact cause of achalasia remains unclear, accumulating evidence—such as lymphocytic infiltration of the myenteric plexus, association with HLA class II alleles, and coexistence with other autoimmune diseases—suggests that achalasia may represent an autoimmune disorder in which immune-mediated destruction of inhibitory myenteric neurons leads to impaired relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter and esophageal aperistalsis.

606779.long_answer: In porencephaly, the cystic cavity most often develops within the temporal region of the cerebral hemisphere. The temporal lobe houses Wernicke’s area, essential for language comprehension, and medial temporal structures such as the hippocampus, which are central to memory formation. Therefore, the temporal lobe links both the porencephalic cyst location and the functions of language comprehension and memory.

987237.long_answer: Increasing dietary intake of omega-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids (e.g., from oily fish or fish-oil supplements) can speed recovery in polymyalgia rheumatica. EPA and DHA compete with arachidonic-acid metabolism, lowering production of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids and cytokines, which diminishes pain and stiffness and can reduce the steroid dose and duration needed for remission.

449563.long_answer: A chloroma, also called a granulocytic or myeloid sarcoma, is a solid mass composed of immature leukemic (most often myeloid) cells. Although these tumors usually arise in bone or soft tissues, they can, on rare occasions, form within the central nervous system, representing an extramedullary manifestation of acute leukemia.

285730.long_answer: After humans ingest Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati eggs, hatchling larvae can enter the bloodstream and migrate to the eye. Their presence in ocular tissues provokes a granulomatous inflammatory reaction, producing the condition known as ocular larva migrans (ocular toxocariasis), which may present as retinal/chorioretinal granuloma, posterior uveitis, or endophthalmitis and can lead to unilateral vision loss.

105543.long_answer: Trevor disease, formally known as dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica, is characterized by unilateral, localized overgrowth of epiphyseal cartilage. This cartilaginous overgrowth forms osteochondroma-like projections from the epiphysis, leading to joint deformity and asymmetry.

798438.long_answer: In Glycogen storage disease type VI (Hers disease), hepatic glycogen phosphorylase is deficient, so liver glycogen cannot be mobilized to release glucose during periods without food intake. Consequently, during fasting these patients can develop hypoglycemia because endogenous glucose production is impaired.

710247.long_answer: Clinical guidelines for epididymitis recommend nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen or naproxen to relieve scrotal pain and reduce inflammation; NSAIDs inhibit cyclo-oxygenase enzymes, lowering prostaglandin synthesis and thereby diminishing pain and swelling.

205456.long_answer: Stevens–Johnson syndrome is a severe mucocutaneous reaction characterized by widespread apoptosis of keratinocytes leading to full-thickness necrosis and detachment of the epidermis at the dermo-epidermal junction, making the epidermal layer the primary site of pathologic injury.

802835.long_answer: Fissured (scrotal) tongue is a benign developmental variation of the oral mucosa. It is usually detected during routine inspection of the mouth and, when management is needed, consists mainly of oral-hygiene instructions and reassurance. The specialists specifically trained to examine, diagnose, and manage conditions of the oral cavity in children are pediatric dentists (the field of pediatric dentistry), so this specialty is most likely to handle fissured tongue in paediatric patients.

626740.long_answer: The most reliable way to guarantee that a hearing protection device (earplug or earmuff) really attenuates workplace noise to a safe level is to perform individual fit-testing (field attenuation measurement) on each worker. Fit-testing quantifies the actual sound attenuation achieved in that person’s ear, yields a Personal Attenuation Rating (PAR), and confirms that the device is inserted or worn correctly; if the measured attenuation is inadequate, the worker can be retrained or issued a different protector. This evidence-based procedure ensures the effectiveness of hearing protection and prevents noise-induced hearing loss.

703574.long_answer: Somatic mutations in the MEN1 gene, which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein menin, are the mutations most often identified in sporadic prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas (prolactinomas). Loss of menin function promotes unchecked proliferation of lactotroph cells, making MEN1 the mutation most commonly linked to sporadic prolactinoma.

744764.long_answer: Holt-Oram syndrome is an autosomal-dominant ‘hand-heart’ disorder caused by mutations in TBX5. It presents with upper-limb skeletal anomalies such as brachydactyly, triphalangeal or absent thumbs, and radial-ray defects, and carries a high incidence of congenital heart disease—most commonly atrial or ventricular septal defects and cardiac conduction abnormalities.

888142.long_answer: The American singer-songwriter Lady Lamb (Aly Spaltro) revealed in early 2020 that she had been diagnosed with Chiari malformation type I and subsequently underwent posterior-fossa decompression brain surgery to correct the herniation of her cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum, a standard surgical treatment for this condition.

865344.long_answer: Plague due to Yersinia pestis is rapidly diagnosed by applying the Wayson stain to a smear of bubo aspirate, blood, or sputum; the stain reveals the characteristic bipolar “safety-pin” appearance of the organism, confirming the infection.

697144.long_answer: When cor triatriatum is discovered incidentally in a patient who has no symptoms and no hemodynamic obstruction, no surgical or medical therapy is required; the condition is simply observed because it carries little risk when asymptomatic.

473078.long_answer: ACE inhibitors block angiotensin-converting enzyme, which normally degrades bradykinin and substance P. Inhibition of this breakdown causes bradykinin to accumulate in the respiratory mucosa, stimulating vagal afferents and producing the characteristic persistent, dry cough seen in some patients.

917930.long_answer: Athetosis is an involuntary movement disorder arising from dysfunction in the basal ganglia and other motor pathways of the central nervous system. The diagnosis, differential assessment, and management of such movement disorders fall within the domain of Neurology, the medical specialty devoted to diseases of the brain, spinal cord, nerves, and muscles.

872254.long_answer: In Glycogen Storage Disease type I (von Gierke disease) the first feature that typically leads to clinical recognition is recurrent, severe fasting hypoglycaemia. Despite very low glucose levels, affected patients show relatively mild neurological symptoms because the disease causes chronic hyper-lactataemia; the elevated circulating lactate (and accompanying ketone bodies) can be taken up and oxidised by the brain, supplying energy and thereby mitigating the usual neuroglycopenic effects of hypoglycaemia.

486265.long_answer: Whole-body radiation doses exceeding ~8 Gy destroy hematopoietic, gastrointestinal and neurovascular stem cells so extensively that even aggressive supportive therapy cannot reverse the damage; death typically occurs within days to a few weeks. Therefore, the prognosis for acute radiation syndrome at >8 Gy is essentially certain death.

963565.long_answer: Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (APS-1/APECED) is characterised by high-titer neutralising autoantibodies directed against the Th17 cytokine interleukin-17 (IL-17A and IL-17F). Loss of functional IL-17 signalling impairs mucosal immunity, contributes to the chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis typical of APS-1, and forms an essential part of the syndrome’s autoimmune pathogenesis.

698957.long_answer: In classic Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) the cerebrospinal fluid shows the characteristic 'albuminocytologic dissociation': an elevated protein concentration with a normal or only minimally increased white-cell count (usually ≤5–10 cells/µL). A true pleocytosis (marked elevation of leukocytes) is not typical for GBS and, if present, should prompt consideration of alternative or accompanying diagnoses such as infectious polyradiculitis (e.g., HIV, CMV, Lyme disease) or meningeal inflammation. Therefore, Guillain–Barré syndrome does not typically present with pleocytosis in cerebrospinal fluid.

856408.long_answer: In Sandhoff disease, deficient β-hexosaminidase activity prevents GM2 ganglioside degradation, causing its progressive accumulation in neurons of the central nervous system, leading to widespread neurodegeneration of the brain and spinal cord.

108509.long_answer: H syndrome is an autosomal-recessive condition due to biallelic SLC29A3 mutations. First documented in a consanguineous Iranian (Jewish) family, the disorder presents with the characteristic triad of cutaneous hyperpigmentation with hypertrichosis and systemic findings that spell the letter “H” (hepatosplenomegaly, hearing loss, heart anomalies, hypogonadism, hyperglycaemia, short stature). Several reported patients also developed progressive renal involvement, leading to chronic renal impairment or failure, making kidney dysfunction a recognised component of the syndrome.

246417.long_answer: The majority of cases of generalized resistance to thyroid hormone (Refetoff syndrome) are caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the THRB gene, which encodes the thyroid hormone receptor-β. These mutations impair receptor binding or co-activator interactions, decreasing tissue responsiveness to circulating T3 and T4 despite normal or elevated hormone levels, and hence are most commonly linked to thyroid hormone resistance.

343844.long_answer: In neurosyphilis, Treponema pallidum infection of the central nervous system elicits a chronic meningeal and perivascular inflammatory reaction. Histopathology consistently shows dense perivascular cuffing by plasma cells—the antibody-producing end-stage B-lymphocytes. This plasma cell-rich infiltrate is a classic hallmark of the immune response in neurosyphilis.

488563.long_answer: Primary sclerosing cholangitis causes chronic cholestasis and reduced bile flow, which impairs the intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Patients may therefore need vitamin supplementation because of UNDER-absorption and resulting deficiencies—not because of over-absorption. Hence, the premise of the question is incorrect.

486395.long_answer: In cystinuria, defective renal tubular re-uptake of cystine causes very high cystine concentrations in the urine. Because cystine is poorly soluble, especially in acidic urine, it becomes supersaturated and precipitates, leading to the aggregation of crystals that form cystine kidney stones.

649749.long_answer: Eosinophilic pneumonia—whether idiopathic, drug-induced, or associated with an underlying malignancy—resolves promptly with systemic glucocorticoid therapy. Corticosteroids suppress eosinophil-mediated inflammation in the lung, leading to rapid improvement in respiratory symptoms, radiographic infiltrates, and peripheral eosinophilia even when the condition is precipitated by cancer.

270922.long_answer: The SPAST gene, which encodes the microtubule-severing protein spastin, is mapped to chromosome locus 2p22.3. Pathogenic variants in SPAST are the most common cause of autosomal-dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia (designated SPG4), leading to progressive lower-limb spasticity through impaired axonal transport and microtubule dynamics.

176983.long_answer: Progressive cardiac conduction defect leads to inexorably worsening atriovioentricular block and bundle-branch disease. No drugs halt this degeneration; the only intervention shown to prevent syncope and sudden death is implantation of a permanent pacemaker to provide reliable electrical pacing when native conduction fails.

209313.long_answer: Infective endocarditis is routinely treated with prolonged courses of high-dose intravenous antibiotics, which deliver bactericidal drug levels directly into the bloodstream to eradicate the organisms adherent to the cardiac endocardium and valves.

744674.long_answer: Auditory processing disorder is not caused by damage to the ears themselves; instead, it involves abnormal neural processing of sound within the brain. Specifically, the disorder affects structures and pathways of the central auditory nervous system—brainstem, midbrain, thalamic, and cortical auditory centers—where acoustic signals are decoded and interpreted. Dysfunction in these central pathways leads to the characteristic difficulties in sound discrimination and comprehension seen in APD.

455429.long_answer: Pallister-Hall syndrome, named after geneticists Philip Pallister and Judith Hall, is produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the GLI3 gene. GLI3 encodes a zinc-finger transcription factor that mediates sonic hedgehog signaling; pathogenic variants disrupt normal embryonic patterning, giving rise to the characteristic anomalies of Pallister-Hall syndrome such as hypothalamic hamartoma, polydactyly and bifid epiglottis.

815084.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the CYP1B1 gene are the commonest genetic cause of primary congenital glaucoma (GLC3A). The elevated intra-ocular pressure produced by CYP1B1 defects leads to photophobia, tearing and reflex blepharospasm, so the same CYP1B1 mutation that produces congenital glaucoma can clinically manifest with blepharospasm.

802160.long_answer: The 45-letter word “pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis,” coined at a 1935 meeting of the National Puzzlers’ League, is accepted by that organization and by major English dictionaries as the longest established word in the language. It names a lung disease caused by inhaling very fine siliceous volcanic dust, and no longer dictionary-listed English word exceeds its length.

210484.long_answer: The FBN2 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-2 and whose pathogenic variants cause congenital contractural arachnodactyly (Beals syndrome), is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5 (region 5q23–q31).

982102.long_answer: In 1643 Evangelista Torricelli filled a sealed glass tube with mercury, inverted it into a mercury basin, and observed that the column fell to about 76 cm while a vacuum formed above it. The only force able to hold that heavy mercury column was the weight of the surrounding air pressing on the reservoir, proving that air has mass and exerts measurable pressure (atmospheric pressure).

930165.long_answer: A pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting neuroendocrine tumor that arises from chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla. Excess release of epinephrine and norepinephrine produces classic adrenergic symptoms such as episodic or sustained hypertension, tachycardia, palpitations, headache, and sweating.

872537.long_answer: Blepharo-naso-facial syndrome is the original descriptive name for Setleis syndrome, a rare focal facial dermal dysplasia caused by TWIST2 mutations. Affected infants present with characteristic facial abnormalities including bilateral scar-like depressions in the temples, abnormal eyelids/eyelashes, a flattened nasal bridge and other mid-face anomalies—hence the blepharo (eyelid)-naso (nose)-facial designation.

818209.long_answer: The chorda tympani nerve, a branch of the facial nerve that conveys taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, has been implicated in burning mouth syndrome. Injury or hypofunction of this nerve can diminish or distort gustatory input, and clinical studies show that such damage is associated with dysgeusia and the oral burning sensations characteristic of the syndrome.

638457.long_answer: Bangstad syndrome is a rare growth-retardation disorder in which patients typically show a characteristic triangular facial shape—broad forehead that tapers to a small, pointed chin. This distinctive triangular face is repeatedly documented as one of the most common cranio-facial findings in the syndrome’s clinical descriptions.

897048.long_answer: Crandall syndrome combines sensorineural deafness and pili torti with hypogonadism. Laboratory studies on affected males consistently show markedly reduced circulating testosterone, reflecting gonadotropin-related hypogonadism. Thus low serum testosterone is a characteristic finding in individuals with Crandall syndrome.

724781.long_answer: The phenotype encompasses all observable characteristics of an organism—morphology, development, biochemical or physiological properties, and clinical conditions. Congenital anomalies such as hemifacial microsomia are part of this outward expression of the underlying genotype interacting with environmental influences, and thus are classified as phenotypic traits.

597350.long_answer: Neonatal herpes simplex virus infection can invade the central nervous system, leading to herpes encephalitis—an inflammation of brain parenchyma that may cause seizures, neurologic deficits, and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment.

714667.long_answer: Paramyotonia congenita is an autosomal-dominant skeletal-muscle channelopathy produced by missense mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the α-subunit (NaV1.4) of the voltage-gated sodium channel in skeletal muscle. These mutations impair normal channel inactivation, leading to the cold- or exercise-induced myotonia and episodic weakness characteristic of the disorder.

616939.long_answer: The VAC combination protocol for rhabdomyosarcoma consists of Vincristine, Actinomycin D (dactinomycin), and Cyclophosphamide; the alkylating agent cyclophosphamide provides DNA-cross-linking cytotoxicity that complements the microtubule inhibition of vincristine and the transcription inhibition of actinomycin D.

342765.long_answer: Mutations in the PAX6 gene are a recognized cause of Peters' Anomaly. PAX6 encodes a paired-box/homeodomain transcription factor that is indispensable for early eye morphogenesis; it controls evagination of the optic vesicle and its subsequent invagination to form the optic cup. Loss-of-function or missense variants in PAX6 disrupt this optic cup development, leading to anterior segment dysgenesis that manifests clinically as Peters' Anomaly.

679383.long_answer: Axial spondyloarthritis is strongly driven by the IL-23/IL-17 cytokine pathway: genetic variants in IL23R and related genes increase risk, IL-23 promotes differentiation of Th17 cells that secrete IL-17A/F, and elevated IL-17 is found in inflamed entheses and serum of patients. Therapeutic blockade of IL-17A (e.g., secukinumab, ixekizumab) or IL-23 markedly improves disease, confirming the pivotal pathogenic role of this pathway.

180261.long_answer: Pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis is a rare vascular lung disease that causes severe pulmonary hypertension and progressive respiratory failure. Its diagnosis, medical therapy, and evaluation for lung transplantation are handled by physicians trained in pulmonary and critical care medicine—i.e., pulmonologists—who specialize in disorders of the pulmonary vasculature.

127259.long_answer: Enlargement of the spleen is medically termed splenomegaly. It occurs when pathologic processes—such as hematologic malignancies like leukemia or storage disorders such as Gaucher’s disease—lead to congestion, infiltration, or hyperplasia of splenic tissue, increasing the organ’s size and weight.

858652.long_answer: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is classically produced by mucin-secreting (mucinous) carcinomas of the appendix or ovary, whose abundant extracellular mucin spills into the peritoneal cavity. The same histologic tumor type—mucinous (colloid) carcinoma—also occurs as a distinct subtype of breast cancer. Thus, mucinous carcinoma is the cancer that can give rise to pseudomyxoma peritonei and can likewise affect the breast.

643114.long_answer: In diffuse neonatal hemangiomatosis, numerous cutaneous hemangiomas are often accompanied by visceral lesions. Among internal organs, the liver is by far the most frequently involved site, typically presenting with multiple hepatic hemangiomas that can lead to complications such as high-output cardiac failure. This hepatic predilection is well documented in neonatal vascular tumor literature.

178589.long_answer: Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal-recessive disorder in which mutations in any of several XPA–XPG genes disable the nucleotide excision repair pathway. The defective DNA repair proteins cannot remove UV-induced pyrimidine dimers, leading to extreme photosensitivity and a markedly increased risk of skin cancers. Thus, the disease is classically defined by a defect in DNA repair proteins and autosomal-recessive inheritance.

168097.long_answer: Nabilone is a synthetic analogue of Δ9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) used as an antiemetic and appetite stimulant. By stimulating central CB1 cannabinoid receptors it can impair cerebellar and vestibular motor control, so clinical trials and prescribing information list dizziness, drowsiness and frank ataxia as characteristic CNS adverse effects.

509368.long_answer: According to the Bernoulli (Venturi) principle, rapid laminar flow in the fetal descending aorta creates a localized fall in static pressure at the aortic end of the ductus arteriosus. Because pressure in the pulmonary artery is higher (owing to the high pulmonary vascular resistance in utero), this pressure drop ‘siphons’ or draws blood through the ductus from the pulmonary artery into the aorta, bypassing the non-functioning fetal lungs.

289485.long_answer: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene (encoding fibrillin-1) underlie several phenotypes. Missense substitutions clustered in the TB5 domain of FBN1 cause acromicric dysplasia, while C-terminal truncating variants that delete the asprosin-encoding region of FBN1 produce Marfanoid–progeroid–lipodystrophy syndrome. Thus the same gene, FBN1, is genetically linked to both disorders.

808236.long_answer: Most dietary iron is absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum of the small intestine. Diseases or surgical loss of these segments cause inadequate iron uptake, depleting body iron stores. Insufficient iron impairs hemoglobin synthesis, producing the characteristic microcytic, hypochromic picture of iron-deficiency anemia.

512504.long_answer: The combination of aniridia, cerebellar ataxia, renal agenesis and psychomotor retardation arises when several neighbouring genes on chromosome 11p (including PAX6 for iris development and other nearby loci for cerebellar and renal development) are simultaneously lost. Such disorders, produced by a microdeletion that removes a stretch of adjacent genes, are classified as contiguous-gene deletion (microdeletion) syndromes rather than single-gene or polygenic traits.

988544.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the SRRT (ARS2) gene cause a neuro-developmental disorder manifested by microcephaly, seizures, hearing problems and other neurological deficits. These clinical signs reflect primary dysfunction of brain development and maintenance, showing that the disease chiefly affects the brain.

638169.long_answer: Chronic helminth infections (e.g., schistosomiasis, soil-transmitted nematodes, filarial worms) can influence the course of HIV infection. Helminths drive persistent immune activation and a Th2-skewed cytokine profile, which can up-regulate HIV co-receptors, increase viral replication, and hasten CD4-cell decline. Epidemiological studies in co-endemic regions have repeatedly shown that HIV-positive individuals who are also infected with helminths tend to have higher plasma HIV RNA levels and progress to symptomatic disease more quickly than helminth-free controls. Small randomized and quasi-experimental trials further support this relationship: anthelmintic treatment (e.g., praziquantel, albendazole, ivermectin) often leads to a modest but measurable fall in HIV viral load and, in some studies, slower CD4 loss. Systematic reviews (e.g., Cochrane 2012, updated 2015) and WHO technical reports conclude that, although the magnitude of benefit varies by parasite species and study quality, the overall evidence indicates that helminthiasis can adversely affect HIV progression and that deworming is a reasonable adjunctive intervention in co-infected patients. Therefore the established biomedical consensus is that helminthiasis does affect the progression of HIV.

488558.long_answer: Benign meningiomas arising at the skull base often carry loss-of-function mutations of the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 22q, which encodes the merlin protein. Growth of an NF2-mutated skull-base meningioma around the cavernous sinus or sphenoid/clival region can compress cranial nerves III, IV, or VI, producing ocular motor palsy and the clinical symptom of diplopia (double vision). Thus, an NF2 mutation is the characteristic genetic alteration linked to these tumors and their ability to cause diplopia.

161434.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the RAB23 gene are the established molecular cause of Carpenter syndrome (acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II). Independent reports have shown that the same RAB23 mutations can present with isolated digit shortening, i.e., brachydactyly, indicating that defective RAB23— a small GTP-binding protein that modulates Hedgehog signalling— underlies both brachydactyly and the full Carpenter syndrome phenotype.

581416.long_answer: Current consensus guidelines and case-series data show that monthly high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG, typically 1–2 g/kg) markedly reduces the frequency and severity of systemic capillary leak syndrome (Clarkson disease) episodes and improves survival, making IVIG the recommended first-line prophylactic therapy.

928924.long_answer: The commonest genetic alteration in embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma is loss of heterozygosity at the imprinted region on the short arm of chromosome 11 (11p15). This LOH, often accompanied by paternal uniparental disomy, disrupts normal imprinting of genes such as IGF2 and H19 and is a hallmark molecular event in this tumour subtype.

392736.long_answer: Crigler–Najjar syndrome (types I and II) results from pathogenic mutations in the UGT1A1 gene that abolish or markedly reduce the activity of bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyl-transferase. Without this enzyme, bilirubin cannot be efficiently conjugated in the liver, leading to severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia and sustained jaundice.

129693.long_answer: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in both copies of the SLC22A5 (OCTN2) gene. Affected individuals therefore carry pathogenic variants on each allele—either the same mutation on both chromosomes (homozygous) or two different mutations (compound heterozygous). Heterozygous carriers have one normal allele and are typically asymptomatic, so clinical disease requires a biallelic (homozygous/compound heterozygous) state.

168163.long_answer: Achard–Thiers syndrome couples type 2 diabetes mellitus with adrenal hypercortisolism (Cushing’s syndrome).
