886931.long_answer: Chondroblastoma, also known as Codman’s tumor, is a rare neoplasm that arises from cartilage-producing chondroblasts in the epiphysis of long bones. Because it is locally aggressive yet lacks metastatic potential, it is categorized within orthopaedic oncology as a benign bone tumor, specifically a benign cartilage-forming tumor.

176418.long_answer: Women with anorexia nervosa commonly develop amenorrhea—cessation of menstrual periods—because severe caloric restriction and low body fat suppress hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal activity, leading to reduced GnRH pulsatility, low LH/FSH, and hypoestrogenism.

613317.long_answer: Pancreatoblastoma often presents with non-specific gastrointestinal complaints, and abdominal pain is one of the most commonly reported symptoms in affected patients. Abdominal pain is also one of the leading chief complaints that bring people to emergency departments worldwide, making it a symptom shared by pancreatoblastoma and a frequent ED presentation.

116539.long_answer: The term ranidaphobia is derived from the zoological name Ranidae, the taxonomic family that contains the “true frogs.” Thus, the specific phobia ranidaphobia refers to an intense, irrational fear of frogs belonging to the family Ranidae.

251070.long_answer: In diabetes, chronic hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance trigger formation of advanced glycation end-products, oxidative stress and inflammation that injure cerebral micro-vessels. This microvascular damage reduces brain perfusion and blood–brain-barrier integrity, while altered insulin signalling facilitates β-amyloid accumulation and tau hyperphosphorylation. The combined vascular insufficiency and neurodegenerative changes accelerate neuronal loss, thereby raising the risk of cognitive impairment.

287524.long_answer: Setleis syndrome produces bilateral, scar-like depressions of the temporal skin that mimic the marks left on a newborn’s face when delivery is assisted with obstetric forceps; hence, the facial defects are described as resembling forceps marks.

105891.long_answer: Pruritus is the medical term for itching of the skin. Generalized or persistent itching without an obvious rash is a recognized ‘B-symptom’ in many patients with Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma, occurring because cytokines released by malignant lymphocytes stimulate cutaneous nerve endings. Thus, the lymphoma symptom referred to as pruritus is simply itching.

766253.long_answer: Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is an EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disorder in which the neoplastic component consists of Epstein–Barr virus–infected B cells surrounded by a reactive T-cell infiltrate. Detection of EBV DNA/RNA in the malignant B cells is a diagnostic hallmark, establishing Epstein–Barr virus as the causative viral agent.

692801.long_answer: Hemiballismus is a movement disorder characterized by violent, involuntary flinging movements of one side of the body. It results from a lesion of the contralateral subthalamic nucleus, which can be caused by vascular events such as rupture or compression from an intracranial aneurysm. Thus, an aneurysm can precipitate hemiballismus, which presents clinically with involuntary limb movements.

916102.long_answer: High-resolution transvaginal sonography has demonstrated the characteristic body-wall and limb defects of Limb Body Wall Complex as early as the 9th gestational week, making 9 weeks the earliest time at which LBWC can be reliably diagnosed by prenatal ultrasound.

933320.long_answer: Castration eliminates testicular androgens, which normally suppress renal urate excretion. Without these androgens, eunuchs clear uric acid more efficiently, so their serum uric-acid levels stay low, making gout—which depends on hyperuricemia—rare in this group.

953363.long_answer: Eosinophilic meningitis is classically produced by helminth larvae that invade the central nervous system. Worldwide, the rat lung-worm Angiostrongylus cantonensis is by far the most frequent culprit: humans acquire the parasite by eating raw or under-cooked snails, slugs, or contaminated vegetables, and the migrating larvae provoke a characteristic cerebrospinal-fluid eosinophilia. Consequently, A. cantonensis is recognized as the most common cause of eosinophilic meningitis in humans.

564412.long_answer: Blood levels of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) are routinely measured to evaluate thyroid function. TSH is secreted by the anterior pituitary and regulates the thyroid gland’s production of thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3); even small changes in thyroid hormone output alter TSH through negative feedback, making it the most sensitive and widely accepted marker for detecting hypo- or hyperthyroidism.

851919.long_answer: Hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is genetically heterogeneous, but the single most frequently mutated gene is SPAST, which encodes the microtubule-severing protein spastin (locus SPG4). SPAST mutations account for roughly 40% of autosomal-dominant and about 20–25% of all HSP cases, making it the gene most commonly associated with the disorder.

426734.long_answer: Onycholysis (separation of the distal nail plate from the nail bed, often called 'Plummer’s nails') is classically associated with hyperthyroidism. In thyrotoxic states, excess thyroid hormone heightens sympathetic nervous system activity and peripheral blood flow changes, weakening the adhesion between the nail plate and bed. This sympathetic overactivity is the recognized mechanism linking hyperthyroidism to onycholysis.

830847.long_answer: The severest form of nemaline myopathy is the neonatal-onset (severe congenital) variant, which typically leads to profound hypotonia and respiratory failure that is lethal in the newborn period.

327312.long_answer: Neuropathic pain from syringobulbia is commonly managed with anticonvulsant drugs such as gabapentin or pregabalin; these agents modulate neuronal excitability and reduce central neuropathic pain.

925866.long_answer: African iron overload (also called Bantu siderosis) has been linked to a missense mutation in the ferroportin-1 gene, SLC40A1. The common African variant, Q248H, impairs hepcidin-mediated regulation of ferroportin, leading to increased intestinal iron absorption and hepatic iron accumulation characteristic of the disorder.

423953.long_answer: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (also called pseudotumor cerebri) is defined by elevated intracranial pressure without an intracranial mass or hydrocephalus. The increased cerebrospinal fluid pressure can transmit pulsations to the dural venous sinuses and middle-ear structures, producing rhythmic vascular noise perceived as pulsatile tinnitus. Thus IIH is a classic cause of pulsatile tinnitus in addition to headaches and papilledema.

584141.long_answer: Myoclonus–dystonia is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in the SGCE gene, which encodes the epsilon-sarcoglycan protein. Mutations in SGCE disrupt the sarcoglycan complex, leading to the characteristic combination of myoclonic jerks and dystonia. No other sarcoglycan genes show the consistent, well-established association seen with SGCE in this disorder.

739447.long_answer: Zamzam–Sheriff–Phillips syndrome has been reported in multiple siblings born to consanguineous parents, with unaffected parents and both male and female children involved, a pattern that fits an autosomal-recessive mode of inheritance.

746701.long_answer: Because the malformations of Limb Body Wall Complex are extensive and easily visualised, high-resolution prenatal ultrasound can identify the syndrome during the routine first-trimester scan; reports consistently show reliable diagnosis at about 12 weeks of gestation (11–13 + 6 weeks), well before the second trimester.

776772.long_answer: The neurotrophic tyrosine kinase receptor type 3 gene (NTRK3) lies on chromosome 15q25.3. NTRK3 encodes Trk-C, the high-affinity receptor for neurotrophin-3 that participates in neural crest-derived enteric nervous system development. Case-control and sequencing studies have shown that variants in NTRK3 increase susceptibility to Hirschsprung’s disease, identifying it as the Hirschsprung-associated gene mapped to chromosome 15.

155407.long_answer: In McArdle’s disease (glycogen-storage disease type V), frozen-section muscle biopsy followed by histochemical staining for phosphorylase activity is employed. The stain normally colors myophosphorylase-positive fibers; its complete absence in the specimen confirms the lack of the enzyme in skeletal muscle, establishing the diagnosis.

435666.long_answer: Perioral dermatitis typically presents with numerous tiny inflammatory papulopustules—small erythematous papules and pustules clustered around the mouth (often sparing the vermilion border). These papulopustular lesions are the characteristic skin finding of the disorder.

628671.long_answer: Synovial sarcoma is molecularly defined by the reciprocal chromosomal translocation t(X;18)(p11.2;q11.2), which fuses the SS18 (SYT) gene on chromosome 18 to an SSX gene (usually SSX1 or SSX2) on the X chromosome. Detection of this SS18-SSX fusion is considered diagnostic for synovial sarcoma.

136820.long_answer: Zenker's diverticulum forms just above the upper esophageal sphincter when the cricopharyngeal muscle (the sphincteric portion of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor) fails to relax or spasms during swallowing. This cricopharyngeal dysfunction increases intraluminal pressure, forcing pharyngeal mucosa to herniate through Killian’s dehiscence, creating the diverticulum.

199051.long_answer: In Once Upon a Time in China III, the character nick-named “Clubfoot Seven,” portrayed by Xiong Xin-xin, is distinguished by having a deformed foot (a clubfoot) that influences both his gait and fighting style; no other character in the film is depicted with this condition.

756013.long_answer: In 48,XXYY syndrome, each cell carries two extra sex chromosomes—one additional X and one additional Y—resulting in a 48,XXYY karyotype. This sex-chromosome aneuploidy disrupts normal testicular development and hormone production, impairing the formation of male primary sex characteristics such as normal-sized testes and sufficient testosterone levels.

494616.long_answer: Sideroblastic anemia often produces marked systemic iron overload, which can be exacerbated by the repeated transfusions many patients require. Deferoxamine is a high-affinity iron-chelating agent that binds excess ferric iron and promotes its renal and biliary excretion, thereby lowering body iron stores and preventing organ damage. For this reason, deferoxamine is routinely used as the pharmacologic treatment for iron overload in patients with sideroblastic anemia.

552975.long_answer: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma almost uniformly shows inactivation of the CDKN2A tumor-suppressor gene, which encodes the p16INK4a protein. p16 normally blocks cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6, enforcing the G1-to-S checkpoint. Mutation or deletion of CDKN2A therefore disrupts cell-cycle control, driving uncontrolled proliferation in pancreatic cancer.

419304.long_answer: In MeSH, the developmental process in which the embryonic neural plate folds and closes to form the neural tube is indexed under the descriptor “Neurulation.” This term covers the sequence of morphogenetic events—neural plate thickening, neural groove formation, elevation of neural folds, and their fusion—that generate the neural tube, the precursor of the central nervous system.

659119.long_answer: In 1949 Horst Bickel and Guido Fanconi first described the disorder now known as Fanconi–Bickel syndrome, which is classified as glycogen storage disease type XI. The syndrome involves mutations in the SLC2A2 gene encoding the glucose transporter GLUT2, leading to massive glycogen accumulation in liver and kidneys along with a generalized proximal renal Fanconi syndrome.

628553.long_answer: Profound hypocalcemia can prolong the QT interval and trigger malignant ventricular arrhythmias that culminate in cardiac arrest. When arrest occurs, the recommended emergency management is immediate cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) with electrical defibrillation to re-establish an effective rhythm while intravenous calcium is given to correct the underlying electrolyte disturbance.

555915.long_answer: Valproic acid (valproate) is an antiepileptic drug that enhances brain GABA levels. It is frequently prescribed to lessen the myoclonic jerks seen in myoclonus-dystonia and is also an established first-line therapy for generalized epilepsies as well as a mood-stabilising agent approved for the treatment of bipolar disorder.

508187.long_answer: Bile duct hamartomas (Von Meyenburg complexes) are typically incidental findings, but in the minority of patients who become symptomatic the most often reported complaint is diffuse or right-upper-quadrant abdominal pain. Abdominal pain is also among the leading chief complaints that drive patients to seek care in emergency departments, making it a shared and well-documented symptom in both contexts.

110942.long_answer: Haemophilus influenzae (especially type b) was historically one of the leading bacterial causes of meningitis in young children, and nontypeable strains commonly colonize the nasopharynx. These same strains ascend the Eustachian tube and are among the principal bacterial pathogens isolated in acute otitis media, making H. influenzae a pathogen that links both meningitis and middle-ear infection.

156927.long_answer: Excess body weight (obesity) is recognized as an independent risk factor for calciphylaxis in patients with chronic kidney disease and is also a well-established major risk factor for developing type 2 diabetes, making obesity a common contributor to both conditions.

603231.long_answer: The word ‘aplasia’ is derived from classical Greek roots: the privative prefix a- meaning ‘without’ or ‘lack of,’ combined with plasis, from plassein, meaning ‘formation’ or ‘molding.’ Hence, aplasia literally signifies the absence or failure of tissue or organ formation, which is exactly how the term is used in medical contexts.

834285.long_answer: Whole-exome next-generation sequencing of families with the characteristic syndactyly, craniofacial anomalies and growth deficiency of Filippi syndrome revealed biallelic loss-of-function variants in CKAP2L (Cytoskeleton Associated Protein 2-Like). CKAP2L encodes a spindle-associated protein required for proper chromosome segregation during mitosis; its disruption explains the developmental defects seen in Filippi syndrome. Thus, CKAP2L is the gene that next-generation sequencing has definitively linked to Filippi syndrome.

173693.long_answer: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler-Weber-Rendu disease) is an autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by multiple telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in organs such as the brain, lungs, and liver. Cerebral AVMs formed in this condition can rupture, and when they do so into the subarachnoid space they produce a subarachnoid hemorrhage.

214798.long_answer: Rheumatology is the medical specialty devoted to the diagnosis and treatment of rheumatic disorders—autoimmune and inflammatory conditions that frequently affect the joints, spine, ligaments, and surrounding tissues. Because chronic back pain can arise from rheumatic diseases such as ankylosing spondylitis or psoriatic arthritis, its evaluation and management fall under the expertise of rheumatologists.

654713.long_answer: Population-based studies from Great Britain and Ireland show biliary atresia occurs in roughly 1 infant for every 15 000–17 000 live births (≈0.6 per 10 000), giving a prevalence close to 1 in 16 000 across the British Isles.

245349.long_answer: The specific phobia characterized by an irrational and persistent fear of amphibians—such as frogs, toads, salamanders, and newts—is called batrachophobia. Derived from the Greek word “batrachos” (frog) and “phobos” (fear), it is classified under animal-type specific phobias in psychiatric nomenclature. Individuals with batrachophobia experience marked anxiety or avoidance when confronted with, or even thinking about, amphibians.

728074.long_answer: According to current scientific and medical consensus, chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) can be diagnosed with certainty only by microscopic examination of brain tissue obtained at autopsy. While research groups have proposed clinical criteria and use brain imaging or fluid biomarkers to identify individuals who may have CTE during life, these tools remain investigational and lack the specificity and validation required for a definitive diagnosis. Therefore, a conclusive, gold-standard diagnosis of CTE cannot yet be made in living individuals.

206768.long_answer: The GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat expansion in the C9ORF72 gene is the single most common genetic cause of frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD), responsible for roughly one-third of familial FTLD cases and a significant proportion of sporadic cases. Pathogenic expansions in C9ORF72 lead to both loss-of-function of the normal protein and toxic gain-of-function mechanisms (RNA foci and dipeptide-repeat proteins), driving neurodegeneration characteristic of FTLD.

237893.long_answer: When strabismus persists throughout much of childhood, the brain suppresses input from the deviating eye to avoid double vision. This chronic suppression prevents normal visual-cortical development in that eye, leading to amblyopia ("lazy eye"), a lasting reduction in visual acuity that cannot be corrected by glasses alone.

196865.long_answer: Situs inversus is usually identified by imaging studies that reveal mirror-image placement of thoracic and abdominal viscera. A plain chest or abdominal X-ray shows the cardiac apex and gastric bubble on the right side, suggesting organ reversal. Abdominal or cardiac ultrasound then confirms right-left inversion of the liver, spleen, and heart chambers, while computed tomography (CT) provides detailed cross-sectional confirmation of the reversed organ anatomy. These three modalities are therefore routinely used to diagnose situs inversus.

204980.long_answer: Becker muscular dystrophy is caused by mutations in the dystrophin (DMD) gene, which is situated on the X chromosome (Xp21). Because the gene is X-linked, the disorder follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance, primarily affecting males while carrier females are usually asymptomatic or mildly affected.

251202.long_answer: Several clinical series have shown that Proteus syndrome patients who carry the heterozygous Factor V Leiden (G1691A) mutation in the F5 gene experience a markedly higher incidence of deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. This pro-coagulant variant increases activated factor V resistance to protein C, predisposing to venous thromboembolism, and when present in the already thrombosis-prone milieu of Proteus syndrome it further elevates DVT risk.

346658.long_answer: Art therapy is an expressive, adjunctive treatment that engages patients in creative activities such as drawing, painting, and sculpting. For people with Bipolar II disorder, these structured creative processes provide a non-verbal channel to externalize complex emotions, reduce mood-related distress, and foster greater insight and self-awareness, complementing standard pharmacologic and psychotherapeutic interventions.

679104.long_answer: Anencephaly is typically detected during routine obstetric ultrasonography, often as early as the first-trimester scan. Absence of the cranial vault and major portions of the brain creates a characteristic ‘frog-eye’ or ‘Mickey Mouse’ appearance on ultrasound images, making the diagnosis clear and reliable before birth.

566311.long_answer: The commonest cause of virilization and ambiguous genitalia in chromosomal females (46,XX) is congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. Loss of this cortisol-synthesizing enzyme diverts adrenal steroid precursors into androgen pathways, leading to excess fetal androgen production and masculinization of the external genitalia.

618974.long_answer: Frederick William Eurich (1867–1933), a British bacteriologist serving the Bradford Anthrax Investigation Board, systematically studied Bacillus anthracis in imported wool and developed effective sterilisation and hygiene procedures for the local wool industry. His work greatly reduced the incidence of cutaneous (woolsorters’) anthrax among Bradford textile workers, making him the key figure in combating the disease there.

733754.long_answer: Methyldopa, an α-2 adrenergic agonist prescribed for systemic hypertension (notably in pregnancy), is a well-documented drug cause of retroperitoneal fibrosis. Chronic exposure can trigger an immune-mediated fibro-inflammatory reaction in the retroperitoneum, leading to ureteral obstruction and other complications.

397214.long_answer: In panhypopituitarism the anterior pituitary fails to secrete LH and FSH, leading to markedly reduced testicular testosterone production. The fall in circulating androgens causes loss of secondary sexual hair, decreased muscle bulk and other male secondary sexual characteristics—clinical changes described as a reversal of virilization in adult males.

564197.long_answer: Exogenous ochronosis is a paradoxical blue-black dermal pigmentation that can develop after prolonged use of skin-lightening creams containing hydroquinone (usually ≥2%). Chronic topical application of this phenolic compound leads to accumulation and polymerization of homogentisic-like pigments within dermal connective tissue, producing the characteristic ochronotic discoloration.

819100.long_answer: Interleukin-1 β is a prototypic pro-inflammatory cytokine that is synthesized and secreted chiefly by activated macrophages. In patients with Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), elevated IL-1β levels have been documented, and this cytokine drives the inflammatory cascade and vascular permeability that characterize the disease.

716038.long_answer: Albinism–deafness syndrome (also called Tietz or Ziprkowski-Krasilnikova syndrome) combines generalized hypopigmentation with congenital sensorineural deafness. The condition is caused by dominant mutations in the MITF gene, the same gene mutated in Waardenburg syndrome type II (WS2). Because of the shared genetic basis and overlapping pigmentary–auditory features, it is generally regarded as a severe variant of Waardenburg syndrome type II.

654893.long_answer: The ZAP70 gene is situated on human chromosome 2 (region 2q11-q12). Chromosome 2 is one of the 22 pairs of autosomes, meaning it is not a sex chromosome (X or Y). Therefore, ZAP70 resides on an autosomal chromosome.

990813.long_answer: The posterior tibial tendon fans out on the plantar aspect of the foot, sending slips not only to the navicular but also to several other tarsal bones, including the cuboid. The cuboid is the bone that becomes malaligned or irritated in the clinical entity termed “cuboid syndrome,” making it the common link between the tendon’s attachment and the syndrome.

936071.long_answer: Analyses of national audiometric surveillance and burden-of-disease data by NIOSH investigators estimate that occupational noise-exposed U.S. workers collectively lose about 2.4 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) from noise-related hearing impairment across all industries. The figure reflects the years lived with disability attributable to permanent hearing loss (virtually no years of life lost from mortality) and represents the total health burden for the U.S. noise-exposed working population.

580722.long_answer: Hypogonadism is the condition in which the gonads (testes or ovaries) fail to produce normal amounts of sex steroids—testosterone in males and estrogen-progesterone in females. This hormonal insufficiency impairs spermatogenesis in men and disrupts ovulation and menstrual cycling in women, so individuals of either genetic sex can experience reduced fertility or complete infertility as a consequence.

575118.long_answer: Fibrous scar-like bands (adhesions) that form between peritoneal surfaces after inflammation, surgery, or congenital malrotation can tether and obstruct the duodenum. This obstruction causes chronic stasis and marked dilatation, producing a megaduodenum. Thus, abdominal adhesions are a well-recognized fibrous-band condition that can lead to megaduodenum.

450069.long_answer: The superior oblique is one of the extra-ocular muscles; its primary action is to depress the eye when it is adducted. Injury to the muscle itself (or to its trochlear nerve supply) produces ophthalmoparesis, leading to vertical diplopia and an inability to look downward effectively. Thus, damage to the superior oblique muscle causes the characteristic depression deficit in eye movements.

594442.long_answer: Holt-Oram syndrome, characterized by upper-limb anomalies such as long thumbs and by cardiac septal and conduction defects, is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner: a single pathogenic allele of the TBX5 gene is sufficient to cause the disorder and it can appear in successive generations with equal frequency in males and females.

384686.long_answer: The CEP290 gene, first identified in Meckel-Gruber syndrome type 4, encodes a centrosomal/transition-zone protein essential for cilium formation. Pathogenic CEP290 variants are also well-known causes of several other ciliopathies—including Joubert syndrome, Leber congenital amaurosis, nephronophthisis, and Bardet–Biedl syndrome—demonstrating its shared role across multiple cilium-related disorders.

271869.long_answer: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPD II) appears in several official rare-disease lists maintained or funded by government bodies. In the United States, the National Institutes of Health—through its Office of Rare Diseases Research (ORDR) and the Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center (GARD)—includes MOPD II in its federally curated Rare Diseases Database. Likewise, Orphanet, which is supported by the European Commission and many European national health ministries, also classifies MOPD II as an orphan (rare) disease. Because it is formally catalogued in these government-backed rare-disease registries, the condition is officially recognized as a rare disease by government agencies.

413775.long_answer: Activating amplification or mutation of the MYCN proto-oncogene, which encodes the N-Myc transcription factor, has been shown to drive a subset of retinoblastomas in the absence of RB1 loss. Because MYCN acts through gain-of-function alterations that promote proliferation, it is classified as a bona fide oncogene, and its mutation/amplification can directly lead to the development of retinoblastoma.

171296.long_answer: Serpiginous choroiditis is classified as a posterior uveitis that primarily affects the choriocapillaris, retinal pigment epithelium, and overlying retina in the posterior pole. In classic descriptions and large clinical series, there is usually little or no inflammatory activity in the anterior segment; if present, anterior chamber cells are minimal and not a defining or common feature. Therefore, anterior chamber involvement is not usually seen in serpiginous choroiditis.

364168.long_answer: Members of the family Poxviridae are among the largest viruses; their brick-shaped (or ovoid) virions typically measure roughly 200–400 nanometres in length, substantially larger than most other DNA viruses.

382323.long_answer: Radiation-induced lumbar plexopathy is a late complication seen after external-beam radiotherapy directed at pelvic malignancies (e.g., cervical, endometrial, prostate, or rectal cancer). The ionizing radiation delivered to the pelvic field can injure the lumbar plexus through microvascular damage and progressive fibrosis, leading to the characteristic delayed neuropathy.

131756.long_answer: Cutaneous listeriosis is usually an occupational infection acquired when Listeria-infected animals (e.g., aborting sheep or cattle) are examined or assisted during delivery. Veterinarians frequently handle these diseased animals, giving them a recognized risk for skin inoculation and localized Listeria infection.

791288.long_answer: Odynophagia (painful swallowing) is a classic presenting symptom of esophageal carcinoma. When the tumor is confined to the esophagus without distant spread, standard management includes surgical resection (esophagectomy) as the preferred curative therapy. Thus, localized esophageal carcinoma is treated by surgical removal.

151332.long_answer: Maternal treatment with the antithyroid drug methimazole (or its pro-drug carbimazole) during early pregnancy is a well-documented teratogen; fetal exposure can disrupt mid-line skin development, leading to the characteristic scalp defect known as aplasia cutis congenita in the newborn.

675014.long_answer: Feingold syndrome type 1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the MYCN proto-oncogene. Independent of the full syndrome, pathogenic variants in MYCN have been identified in patients with isolated or syndromic esophageal atresia/tracheoesophageal fistula, making MYCN a recognized genetic risk factor for this congenital malformation. Thus, the MYCN gene links Feingold syndrome and susceptibility to esophageal atresia.

677392.long_answer: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 (Gordon syndrome) results from mutations in the WNK4 kinase gene that dysregulate the thiazide-sensitive Na⁺/Cl⁻ cotransporter (NCC). This transporter operates in the distal convoluted tubule of the nephron, so that segment is the site chiefly affected by WNK4 mutations, leading to excessive sodium reabsorption, hyperkalemia, and hypertension.

230889.long_answer: If a patent ductus arteriosus is not closed, the continuous left-to-right shunt creates chronic volume overload of the left atrium and ventricle, eventually leading to ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction—i.e., congestive heart failure. Heart failure is one of the most frequent complications of an untreated PDA and is also among the leading causes of cardiomegaly observed on chest imaging.

660033.long_answer: The great majority of malignant hyperthermia–susceptible individuals carry mutations in the RYR1 gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel. Pathogenic RYR1 variants make the channel abnormally sensitive to volatile (inhalational) anesthetics and depolarizing muscle relaxants, leading to uncontrolled Ca²⁺ release, muscle rigidity, hypermetabolism, and the malignant hyperthermia crisis. Hence, RYR1 mutation is the mutation most commonly linked to anesthetic-triggered malignant hyperthermia.

578814.long_answer: Camurati-Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia) is caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the TGFB1 gene (transforming growth factor-β1) on chromosome 19q13. Excessive activity of TGF-β1 from these mutations leads to hyperostosis and cortical thickening of the diaphyses of long bones, producing the characteristic bone pain and limb abnormalities seen in the disorder.

253209.long_answer: In British medical usage, the clinical state of severe thyroid-hormone deficiency is called ‘myxoedema’ (spelled with the digraph ‘oe’). This term refers to the characteristic accumulation of mucopolysaccharides in the skin and other tissues seen in advanced hypothyroidism.

861294.long_answer: In fetuses with gastroschisis, the exposed mid-gut can undergo vascular compromise and twisting while floating free in amniotic fluid. This frequently results in segmental loss or obliteration of the bowel lumen, producing jejuno-ileal intestinal atresia, which is found in roughly 10–20 % of infants with gastroschisis and is the most common postoperative complication requiring additional surgery.

978193.long_answer: Costello syndrome is a congenital (‘birth-defect’) disorder in the RAS-MAPK pathway that was originally described as a Noonan-like condition. Patients show distinctive craniofacial malformations—coarse facial features, large mouth with thick lips, nasal papillomas, and macrocephaly—together with cardiac defects and developmental delay. Because of these clinical similarities to Noonan syndrome, Costello syndrome is classified among the RASopathies but is distinguished by its characteristic craniofacial phenotype.

195760.long_answer: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal-recessive inborn error of phenylalanine metabolism. Absence or deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase causes toxic accumulation of phenylalanine in the brain, which disrupts neurotransmitter synthesis. Without dietary restriction of phenylalanine, affected children typically develop progressive neurotoxicity manifested by intellectual disability, behavioral problems and recurrent seizures. Early detection and strict dietary treatment therefore prevent the seizure disorder associated with untreated PKU.

574800.long_answer: Classic Stickler syndrome is most commonly caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in collagen-encoding genes such as COL2A1, COL11A1, or COL11A2. These mutations produce disease when only one copy of the gene is altered, and affected individuals have a 50 % chance of transmitting the disorder to each child. Thus, the disorder is characteristically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, although rare autosomal-recessive forms have been reported.

959167.long_answer: Familial multiple intestinal atresia is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TTC7A (tetratricopeptide repeat domain 7A) gene. The human TTC7A locus is situated on chromosome 2p16.3; pathogenic variants in this gene disrupt epithelial cell polarity and survival during gut development, leading to the characteristic widespread intestinal atresias seen in affected families.

233920.long_answer: Multiple system atrophy is an incurable, progressively disabling neurodegenerative disorder. As symptoms such as autonomic failure, parkinsonism, ataxia and dysphagia worsen, guidelines urge transition to palliative care to focus on symptom control, comfort measures and quality-of-life support rather than disease-modifying treatment.

324425.long_answer: Microtia is a congenital malformation in which the external ear (pinna) is small or rudimentary. Because the first and second branchial arch structures develop abnormally, the external auditory canal and middle-ear ossicles are often underdeveloped or absent, producing canal atresia and conductive hearing loss. Additional skeletal anomalies that may accompany this defect include bilateral parietal foramina in the parietal bones of the skull.

234242.long_answer: In Latin-based anatomical nomenclature, the term ‘os’ (plural ‘ossa’) is the word for a bone, appearing as a prefix in bone names such as os coxae, os frontale, and os temporale. Thus, the anatomical term for bone that employs the prefix “os” is simply “os.”

451504.long_answer: Type 3 von Willebrand disease is characterized by an almost complete absence of von Willebrand factor because both alleles are defective. Without vWF, circulating factor VIII levels fall drastically and platelet adhesion is profoundly impaired, producing a bleeding phenotype similar to severe hemophilia A. Consequently, patients with type 3 VWD are the ones who most commonly experience deep-tissue and life-threatening internal hemorrhage, whereas types 1 and 2 usually present with milder mucocutaneous bleeding.

779219.long_answer: According to the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and other public-health authorities, placing an infant on their back (supine position) for every sleep is regarded as the single most effective, evidence-based measure to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). The “Back to Sleep” campaign, launched in the 1990s on the basis of this finding, led to a dramatic decline in SIDS rates. While many additional recommendations (e.g., avoidance of soft bedding, room-sharing without bed-sharing, smoke-free environment, breastfeeding, pacifier use during sleep) also lower SIDS risk, none is considered more effective than the supine sleep position. Therefore, stating that putting a child under one year old on their back is only the second most effective method contradicts established scientific consensus.

608842.long_answer: Niacin (nicotinic acid, vitamin B3) is routinely prescribed to treat hypoalphalipoproteinemia because at pharmacologic doses it reduces hepatic clearance of apoA-I and lowers VLDL production, leading to a 15–35 % increase in circulating HDL cholesterol.

535214.long_answer: The case report on the Japanese girl with Pai syndrome described a balanced reciprocal translocation designated t(3;11)(q26.3;p11.2). Thus, the rearrangement involves chromosome 3 (band q26.3) and chromosome 11 (band p11.2), linking these two chromosomes to the phenotype observed in Pai syndrome for that patient.

674348.long_answer: In neurocysticercosis, cysticerci can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid pathways—especially within the ventricular system—leading to hydrocephalus, an accumulation of CSF that raises intracranial pressure inside the skull.

461353.long_answer: Abruzzo–Erickson syndrome is an X-linked intellectual-disability disorder. The causative mutations that have been identified in affected families occur in the ARX gene (Aristaless-related homeobox) located on chromosome Xp22.13, establishing ARX as the X-chromosomal gene responsible for this syndrome.

380670.long_answer: Sézary disease is an aggressive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, a form of cancer originating from malignant T-lymphocytes. The medical specialty responsible for the diagnosis, staging, and treatment of cancers—including lymphomas—is oncology.

563669.long_answer: Factor XIa is a serine protease; its catalytic activity relies on an active-site serine residue (Ser195 in chymotrypsin numbering). This serine performs the nucleophilic attack that cleaves the Arg145-Ala146 and Arg180-Val181 bonds in factor IX, thereby converting factor IX to the active enzyme factor IXa. Hence, the amino acid serine is directly involved in the activation of factor IX by factor XIa.

923841.long_answer: Even in males with Persistent Müllerian duct syndrome, the epididymis serves its normal role: it receives testicular sperm, allows them to mature and acquire motility, and stores them until they are propelled onward through the vas deferens during ejaculation.

238717.long_answer: Familial adenomatous polyposis results from germ-line mutations in the APC tumour-suppressor gene. Frameshift (5-bp deletion) mutations at APC codon 1309 truncate the protein early and abolish its β-catenin–regulating function, leading to thousands of adenomatous polyps at an earlier age than other APC mutations; this codon 1309 defect therefore produces the most severe, ‘profuse’ form of FAP.

353063.long_answer: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal-recessive disorder, most commonly due to HFE gene mutations, that leads to excessive intestinal iron absorption. The resulting systemic iron overload causes iron deposition in multiple organs; when excess iron accumulates in the myocardium it produces dilated or restrictive cardiomyopathy and heart failure, making hemochromatosis a well-recognized genetic cause of iron-overload cardiomyopathy.

762499.long_answer: Schneckenbecken dysplasia produces striking skeletal abnormalities such as the characteristic "snail-shell" pelvis and markedly shortened long bones. These structural changes can be visualised in utero with high-resolution prenatal ultrasonography, allowing the condition to be detected during routine or targeted fetal anomaly scans.

530108.long_answer: Toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a severe illness triggered by exotoxin-producing Staphylococcus aureus or group A Streptococcus infections. The superantigen toxins drive a massive cytokine release that produces high fever, hypotension, rash and multi-organ involvement—clinical features that closely mirror the hyperinflammatory presentation seen in multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C).

897434.long_answer: In tick-borne encephalitis, the infection can progress from isolated meningitis to simultaneous inflammation of both the meninges and brain parenchyma—termed meningoencephalitis. This combined meningeal and cerebral involvement constitutes the severe neurologic complication of tick-borne encephalitis, associated with higher morbidity, prolonged recovery, and risk of permanent neurological deficits.

867436.long_answer: Clarithromycin, a macrolide that binds the 50 S ribosomal subunit and blocks mycobacterial protein synthesis, is the drug of choice for Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare infections when surgical excision is not feasible.

396551.long_answer: Proteus syndrome results from a mosaic activating mutation in AKT1 (most commonly c.49G>A, p.E17K). In addition to its characteristic asymmetric, segmental overgrowth of skin, bone and other tissues, affected individuals frequently show cerebral cortical malformations, and hemimegalencephaly is a well-documented, recurring brain manifestation of the syndrome.

260778.long_answer: Abnormal heart rhythms (cardiac arrhythmias) such as ventricular tachycardia, ventricular fibrillation, high-grade atrioventricular block, or rapid supraventricular tachycardias can drastically reduce the heart’s ability to pump blood effectively. The resulting drop in cerebral perfusion can cause transient loss of consciousness, commonly termed syncope. This pathophysiological link between significant arrhythmias and loss of consciousness is well-documented in cardiology guidelines and clinical practice.

735266.long_answer: Cystathionine β-synthase (CBS) is the key enzyme that converts homocysteine to cystathionine in methionine metabolism. Inherited CBS deficiency causes the inborn‐error disorder homocystinuria. Accumulated homocysteine and its metabolites damage ocular tissues, predisposing patients to lens dislocation and early-onset cataracts, along with other systemic features. Thus, homocystinuria is the metabolic disorder in which CBS deficiency leads to cataract formation.

662899.long_answer: Zollinger–Ellison syndrome causes marked gastric acid hypersecretion from gastrin-producing tumors. High-dose proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole, pantoprazole) are the treatment of choice because they irreversibly inhibit the parietal-cell H⁺/K⁺-ATPase, thereby markedly reducing acid production and controlling the associated peptic symptoms.

946965.long_answer: Infection with the liver fluke Clonorchis sinensis chronically irritates and inflames the biliary epithelium; this prolonged inflammation and epithelial turnover significantly increase the risk of malignant transformation, making clonorchiasis a well-established risk factor for cholangiocarcinoma.

249119.long_answer: A second-degree, or partial-thickness, burn commonly produces fluid-filled blisters in the epidermis/upper dermis, creating thin-walled bullae that closely resemble the vesicles and bullae seen in bullous impetigo caused by Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxins.

122996.long_answer: Because indolent non-Hodgkin lymphomas such as follicular lymphoma grow very slowly and may remain asymptomatic for years, randomized trials have shown no survival advantage to immediate chemotherapy. Therefore, the standard initial management for patients with low-tumor-burden, asymptomatic indolent lymphoma is watchful waiting (active surveillance) until clinical symptoms or disease progression warrant treatment.

311807.long_answer: Primary aldosteronism (Conn’s syndrome) produces hypokalaemia and loss of renal concentrating ability, leading to increased urine volume. This often manifests as nocturia – the need to pass excessive amounts of urine during the night – and is a well-described symptom associated with the disorder.

880679.long_answer: In elderly patients a common hematologic cause of spontaneous hematuria is acquired hemophilia A, an autoimmune disorder in which auto-antibodies neutralize coagulation factor VIII. The resulting severe deficiency of factor VIII impairs the intrinsic coagulation pathway, leading to spontaneous mucosal and soft-tissue bleeding, including bleeding from the urinary tract that manifests as hematuria.

480625.long_answer: In expanded newborn screening, dried-blood-spot samples are analyzed by tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). This technique detects the characteristic acyl-carnitine pattern—especially elevated 3-hydroxy-isovalerylcarnitine (C5-OH)—that signifies 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency.

833986.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is a chromosomal disorder characterized by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 21. A hallmark of affected newborns is generalized hypotonia (“floppy infant”), together with characteristic facial features and varying degrees of intellectual disability. The hypotonia results from altered neuromuscular development linked to the gene dosage imbalance on chromosome 21.

751852.long_answer: Genuphobia is classified as a specific phobia—an anxiety disorder involving an irrational, persistent fear of knees or kneeling. Diagnosis and evidence-based treatments such as cognitive-behavioral therapy, exposure therapy, and, when indicated, pharmacotherapy (e.g., SSRIs, anxiolytics) are overseen by physicians trained in mental-health disorders. These interventions fall squarely within the scope of the medical specialty of psychiatry, making it the most appropriate field for treating genuphobia.

271017.long_answer: Pneumoconiosis is a group of occupational lung diseases that develop when workers chronically inhale inorganic dusts (e.g., coal, silica, asbestos). The inhaled particles deposit in the alveoli, triggering macrophage activation, fibrosis, and progressive impairment of lung function.

714987.long_answer: Chlamydia psittaci is the etiologic agent of psittacosis (parrot fever) contracted from infected birds, and chronic infection with this same bacterium has been repeatedly linked to ocular adnexal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma, a subtype of extranodal marginal zone lymphoma.

575562.long_answer: A drug-induced lichenoid eruption (drug-induced lichenoid dermatitis) produces the same interface-lichenoid histopathology as idiopathic cutaneous lichen planus—including a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate, basal cell vacuolar change, and saw-toothed epidermal hyperplasia—so the two conditions are often histopathologically indistinguishable.

925620.long_answer: The thalamus is the brain’s principal relay station, transferring nearly all sensory information (except olfaction) and many motor signals to the cerebral cortex. Damage to its medial/anterior nuclei disrupts the limbic memory circuits, producing profound anterograde amnesia—as classically observed in Korsakoff syndrome or bilateral thalamic infarcts—while its central role is to relay sensory and motor impulses.

659890.long_answer: A bicuspid aortic valve predisposes to severe aortic stenosis, regurgitation, and—most importantly—ascending aortic aneurysm or dissection due to intrinsic weakness of the aortic media. Definitive management of these complications requires surgical valve replacement and/or repair or replacement of the ascending aorta, operations performed by specialists in cardiothoracic (cardiac) surgery; thus this specialty is most commonly responsible for treating the major complications of a bicuspid aortic valve.

940115.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in SF3B4 reduce the amount of this spliceosomal subunit (haploinsufficiency), disrupting RNA splicing during development and producing the craniofacial and limb anomalies that define Nager syndrome, also called Nager acrofacial dysostosis.

581379.long_answer: Blepharophimosis-intellectual disability syndrome, SBBYS type (also called Say-Barber-Biesecker-Young-Simpson syndrome) is produced by heterozygous loss-of-function or truncating mutations in the KAT6B gene, which encodes the lysine acetyltransferase 6B histone-modifying enzyme. Pathogenic variants in KAT6B disrupt normal chromatin acetylation and gene regulation during development, leading to the characteristic craniofacial features, blepharophimosis and global developmental delay seen in this syndrome.

710008.long_answer: Placido’s disc (photokeratoscope) is a circular plate bearing alternating black-and-white concentric rings that are projected onto the anterior corneal surface. The pattern of the reflected rings is then inspected or analyzed; any distortion or irregular spacing reveals abnormal corneal curvature, making the instrument a classic tool for detecting and diagnosing keratoconus.

398017.long_answer: Pyaemia is a form of septicemia characterized by numerous metastatic abscesses throughout the body. The condition is classically caused by Staphylococcus aureus, a Gram-positive, pus-forming (pyogenic) bacterium whose virulence factors (e.g., coagulase, leukocidins) promote abscess formation and hematogenous spread, producing the clinical picture of pyaemia.

633595.long_answer: Familial progressive hyperpigmentation is consistently reported to segregate through multiple generations with male-to-male transmission and without sex bias, indicating autosomal inheritance. Linkage and mutation studies have identified pathogenic variants in the KITLG (KIT ligand) gene on chromosome 12q21, and affected individuals show disease in every generation, all hallmarks of an autosomal dominant genetic disorder.

347996.long_answer: During the secretory stage of amelogenesis, secretory ameloblasts express high levels of alkaline phosphatase. This enzyme hydrolyses organic phosphate esters, increasing the local concentration of inorganic phosphate and favouring the nucleation of hydroxyapatite crystals. The activity of alkaline phosphatase therefore supports the initial, partial (≈30 %) mineralization of the enamel matrix that precedes the later maturation phase in which full mineral density is achieved.

719171.long_answer: Aase syndrome is characterized by hypoplastic (under-developed) bone marrow, the main post-natal site of hematopoiesis. Because the bone marrow fails to produce adequate red blood cells, affected individuals present with congenital hypoplastic anemia and other blood-cell deficiencies.

871689.long_answer: Menkes kinky hair syndrome is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7A gene, which encodes a copper-transporting P-type ATPase. Defective ATP7A impairs systemic copper transport, leading to the characteristic neurologic degeneration, connective-tissue defects, and ‘kinky’ hair seen in Menkes disease.

579389.long_answer: In pseudohypoparathyroidism, chronic hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia lead to ectopic calcium-phosphate deposition in the brain. The most characteristic site of these intracranial calcifications is the basal ganglia—particularly the globus pallidus and other lenticular nuclei—visible on CT or MRI and associated with movement or neurocognitive symptoms.

708358.long_answer: Malouf syndrome, also known as the dilated cardiomyopathy-hypergonadotropic hypogonadism syndrome, is classically characterized by dilated cardiomyopathy in association with gonadal dysgenesis (streak or under-developed ovaries leading to primary ovarian failure).

326735.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the LMNA gene (encoding lamin A/C) cause a form of familial dilated cardiomyopathy that is notable for early-onset conduction system disease, frequent malignant ventricular arrhythmias, and rapid progression to end-stage heart failure; consequently, carriers have a high incidence of ventricular arrhythmia and often require cardiac transplantation.

960950.long_answer: Plummer–Vinson syndrome is defined by the triad of upper-esophageal webs that cause dysphagia, chronic iron-deficiency anemia, and associated mucosal changes. Patients with this syndrome may also develop systemic manifestations of longstanding iron deficiency, including reactive or congestive splenomegaly, thereby increasing their risk of an enlarged spleen.

351807.long_answer: Shigellosis is spread when Shigella bacteria from an infected person’s feces reach another person’s mouth. Disposable or cloth diapers that become contaminated with stool create a ready source of bacteria; during changing, caregivers’ hands, changing tables, or surrounding surfaces can be contaminated. If hands are not thoroughly washed and surfaces are not disinfected, the organisms are easily transferred to food, toys, or directly to another person, enabling fecal–oral transmission and facilitating outbreaks, especially in daycare settings.

559203.long_answer: High-resolution renal ultrasound is routinely used to pick up nephrocalcinosis at an early stage because fine calcium deposits make the renal pyramids appear brightly echogenic on sonography long before they are dense enough to be seen on plain radiographs or other modalities.

488019.long_answer: Immune-mediated hydrops fetalis most commonly results from Rh incompatibility, in which maternal anti-Rh(D) antibodies attack fetal red blood cells. Administering Rho(D) immune globulin (e.g., RhoGAM) to Rh-negative mothers during pregnancy and after delivery neutralizes any fetal Rh-positive erythrocytes that enter the maternal circulation, preventing maternal sensitization and the consequent antibody-mediated hemolysis that leads to hydrops fetalis.

183697.long_answer: Feingold syndrome (oculodigitoesophagoduodenal syndrome) is an autosomal-dominant disorder most commonly produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the MYCN gene on chromosome 2p24.3. MYCN encodes the N-Myc transcription factor; its haploinsufficiency disrupts embryonic development, leading to the characteristic digital anomalies, microcephaly, facial features, and gastrointestinal atresias seen in Feingold syndrome.

243650.long_answer: Hypertriglyceridemia is identified by quantifying triglyceride concentrations in the blood. This is routinely done with a fasting lipid panel (also called a fasting serum lipid profile), a laboratory blood test that measures triglycerides, total cholesterol, HDL-C and LDL-C. Elevated fasting triglyceride values on this test establish the diagnosis of hypertriglyceridemia.

884056.long_answer: Oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD) is classically caused by heterozygous mutations in the GJA1 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-43. Defects in connexin-43 disrupt intercellular communication within skeletal and otic tissues; in the middle ear this can impair ossicular development or mobility, producing a conductive hearing loss. Thus, a pathogenic mutation in GJA1 is the recognized genetic alteration that links ODDD to conductive deafness.

295809.long_answer: Custom or prefabricated foot orthoses (orthotic shoe inserts) are commonly prescribed to redistribute pressure and improve alignment of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, thereby lessening mechanical stress and relieving the pain produced by bunions (hallux valgus).

538168.long_answer: Myopia is confirmed during a comprehensive eye examination by performing a refraction test (objective retinoscopy and/or automated/subjective refraction). This procedure measures how light focuses through the cornea and lens onto the retina, quantifying the eye’s refractive error; a negative diopter value indicates myopia.

856486.long_answer: Girls and women with Turner syndrome usually have ovarian failure, leading to markedly low circulating estrogen. Administering exogenous estrogen (estrogen replacement therapy, typically low-dose estradiol begun around the normal age of puberty) stimulates secondary sexual characteristics. The added estrogen drives breast tissue growth and the typical female fat distribution that widens the hips, thereby promoting normal pubertal development in Turner syndrome.

449999.long_answer: In infants (younger than 12 months) with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, the single most frequent genetic alteration is a rearrangement of the MLL gene—now designated KMT2A—on chromosome 11q23, usually the t(4;11)(q21;q23) MLL-AF4 fusion. These KMT2A/MLL rearrangements are present in roughly 70–80 % of infant ALL cases, far surpassing any other lesion. Because infants with KMT2A-rearranged ALL often show leukaemic skin infiltrates ("blue-berry muffin" lesions), hepatosplenomegaly and other readily observable findings, the abnormality can first be suspected during the physical examination and then confirmed with cytogenetic or molecular tests.

232430.long_answer: Hemarthrosis—bleeding into joints—is a hallmark of hemophilia A and B, arising from deficient clotting factor activity. Although rare, patients with congenital Factor XIII deficiency can experience the same joint hemorrhages because Factor XIII is essential for stabilizing the fibrin clot; without it, clots are fragile and recurrent bleeding into joints occurs.

313956.long_answer: Muckle-Wells syndrome is one of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS). It is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the NLRP3 gene, which encodes the protein cryopyrin. Mutant cryopyrin hyperactivates the inflammasome, driving excessive maturation and release of the pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin-1β, thereby producing the characteristic recurrent inflammatory episodes of the disease.

485275.long_answer: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 2 (PCH-2) is an autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disorder, most often caused by biallelic TSEN54 mutations. It features marked hypoplasia of the pons and cerebellum and commonly presents with progressive microcephaly, severe motor and cognitive impairment, and early-onset epileptic seizures.

710510.long_answer: The V617F point mutation in the Janus kinase-2 (JAK2) gene is frequently found in patients with splanchnic and portal vein thrombosis. It drives latent myeloproliferative neoplasms, leading to increased erythrocyte and platelet production, hyperviscosity and a pro-thrombotic state; up to half of idiopathic portal vein thrombosis cases carry this mutation.

839196.long_answer: Because the streak gonads in XX gonadal dysgenesis do not produce ovarian sex steroids, exogenous sex‐steroid (estrogen followed by cyclic estrogen-progestin) hormone replacement therapy is given to supply the missing estrogen and progesterone, thereby triggering pubertal development and establishing withdrawal menstruation.

463778.long_answer: A large unrepaired aortopulmonary window produces a substantial left-to-right shunt, chronically overloading the pulmonary circulation. Persistent high pulmonary blood flow leads to progressive pulmonary vascular remodeling and irreversible pulmonary hypertension. Once pulmonary pressures equal or exceed systemic levels, shunt reversal (right-to-left flow) occurs, causing cyanosis and the constellation known as Eisenmenger syndrome.

757667.long_answer: Large amounts of free hemoglobin filtered into the renal tubules during hemoglobinuria precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall proteins and generate oxidative injury, producing acute tubular necrosis. This pigment-induced nephropathy can rapidly lead to acute renal failure (acute kidney injury), a serious complication frequently seen in ICU patients after massive intravascular hemolysis.

364051.long_answer: Nager syndrome is usually caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in SF3B4 and therefore follows an autosomal-dominant model, yet most cases are sporadic while occasional families show multiple affected siblings born to unaffected parents. This apparent discrepancy is best explained by germline (gonadal) mosaicism: a new SF3B4 mutation arises in one parent’s germ-cell line, leaving the parent phenotypically normal but capable of transmitting the mutation to more than one child, producing the observed inheritance pattern.

486144.long_answer: The condition in which a person is born with unusually short fingers and/or toes is called brachydactyly. It is a congenital skeletal malformation in which the phalanges, metacarpals, or metatarsals are shortened, leading to overall reduced digit length.

102003.long_answer: Most patients reported with Kapur–Toriello syndrome exhibit ocular coloboma—an embryologic defect leading to a cleft or gap in structures such as the iris, retina, or optic nerve. Case series and reviews describe coloboma in the majority of individuals with this rare multiple-anomaly syndrome, making it the characteristic eye-related finding.

354313.long_answer: In Sweden, familial amyloid polyneuropathy caused by a transthyretin (TTR) gene mutation is particularly common in and around the city of Skellefteå in Västerbotten County. This ‘Skellefteå variant’ (often TTR Val30Met) has been extensively documented, giving the city one of the world’s highest regional prevalences of TTR-FAP.

740903.long_answer: Ebola virus infection triggers programmed cell death (apoptosis) in many cell types, including lymphocytes and endothelial cells. Viral proteins such as the surface glycoprotein (GP) and VP24/VP35 disrupt intracellular signaling and mitochondrial integrity, activating caspases and leading to apoptotic cell death, which contributes to tissue damage and the severe pathology of Ebola virus disease.

261447.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the PLCG2 gene (encoding phospholipase C-γ2) produce a common-variable-immunodeficiency–like disorder called PLAID/APLAID. A hallmark of this condition is cold-induced urticaria, manifested as wheals and itching that mimic typical hives. Thus, a PLCG2 mutation links CVID with hive-like (urticarial) symptoms.

752657.long_answer: After surgery restores his eyesight, Virgil can see light, color and shape, but his brain cannot transform these raw visual signals into meaningful objects or faces. This higher-order perceptual deficit—intact vision paired with an inability to recognize what is seen—is the clinical picture of visual agnosia, the very condition Oliver Sacks described in the case story on which the film is based.

497305.long_answer: Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) is caused by germ-line mutations in genes such as MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2. These proteins must form MutSα (MSH2-MSH6) and MutLα (MLH1-PMS2) heterodimers to recognize and repair base-pair mismatches and small insertion–deletion loops arising during DNA replication. Loss of functional dimers impairs the DNA mismatch repair process, leading to microsatellite instability and tumor predisposition characteristic of Lynch syndrome.

454984.long_answer: Post-infectious obliterative bronchiolitis due to adenovirus (especially serotypes 3 and 7) can produce unilateral lung hypoplasia with air-trapping and diminished vascularity; this clinical–radiologic entity is called Swyer–James (or Swyer–James–MacLeod) syndrome, a rare complication of adenoviral bronchiolitis obliterans.

934963.long_answer: The RET proto-oncogene, mapped to chromosome 10q11.2, undergoes activating rearrangements (RET/PTC) that are a well-established driver event in papillary thyroid cancer.

353373.long_answer: Among solid tumours, carcinoma of the breast has a particular predilection for metastasising to the axial skeleton. In the bone marrow it seeds discrete aggregates of malignant epithelial cells, producing nodular deposits that can be recognised histologically or on imaging. Thus, nodular formations detected within bone marrow are classically associated with metastatic breast carcinoma.

975295.long_answer: Both Ewing sarcoma and peripheral primitive neuroectodermal tumor belong to the Ewing-family tumors and harbor the characteristic chromosomal translocation t(11;22)(q24;q12), which fuses the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 to the FLI1 gene on chromosome 11. This EWSR1-FLI1 fusion is the defining genetic event common to both tumors.

161601.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome (autosomal-dominant craniofacial dysostosis caused mainly by FGFR2 mutations) involves premature fusion of multiple cranial sutures. This early synostosis produces a small cranium (micro-/brachycephaly), thinning of the calvarial bone, and the characteristic “beaten-copper” or digital impressions—generalized depressions most evident along the frontoparietal and occipitoparietal sutures.

211134.long_answer: Morquio A syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IV A) is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (encoded by the GALNS gene). Lack of this sulfatase prevents proper degradation of the glycosaminoglycans keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate, leading to their accumulation and the characteristic skeletal dysplasia and systemic manifestations of Morquio A.

987631.long_answer: Froehlich syndrome (adiposogenital dystrophy) results from hypothalamic-pituitary damage that lowers secretion of the gonadotropins LH and FSH, causing hypogonadism and delayed puberty. Administering human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) provides an exogenous LH-like stimulus to the gonads, promoting testosterone production and pubertal development in affected children, thereby serving as an appropriate hormone-replacement therapy.

846697.long_answer: Keratitis-Ichthyosis-Deafness (KID) syndrome and many forms of nonsyndromic autosomal recessive sensorineural hearing loss share pathogenic mutations in the GJB2 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-26. Altered connexin-26 disrupts intercellular ion homeostasis in the epidermis and cochlea, producing the characteristic skin lesions and profound hearing impairment observed in these conditions.

908847.long_answer: X-linked intellectual disability results from pathogenic variants in genes located on the X chromosome; because males have a single X chromosome, mutations there readily manifest as intellectual disability with an X-linked pattern of inheritance.

852032.long_answer: In Aase syndrome, the congenital anemia results from bone-marrow hypoplasia, so a bone marrow biopsy (often with aspiration) is the standard diagnostic test used to directly examine marrow cellularity and erythroid precursors.

520419.long_answer: In Cushing's syndrome, chronically elevated cortisol (hypercortisolism) suppresses hypothalamic GnRH secretion and pituitary release of LH and FSH. This disruption of the normal gonadotropin-estrogen/progesterone axis can halt the menstrual cycle, leading to amenorrhea.

597198.long_answer: Large anterior mediastinal teratomas may compress or invade the superior vena cava. Obstruction of this major vein impedes venous return from the head, neck, and upper limbs, producing facial and upper-extremity edema, distended neck veins, and dyspnea. Because it alters venous return and right-atrial filling, the lesion directly disrupts normal hemodynamics— the clinical entity known as superior vena cava syndrome.

943167.long_answer: Swyer–James (MacLeod) syndrome is classically a post-infectious obliterative bronchiolitis that develops after a severe lower-respiratory adenovirus infection—most often adenovirus serotype 7—in infancy or early childhood. The viral damage to small airways prevents normal lung growth and results in the characteristic unilateral hyperlucent, hypoplastic lung seen in this syndrome.

455294.long_answer: Native American myopathy (NAM) is caused by pathogenic variants in the STAC3 gene, which encodes the SH3 and cysteine-rich domain-containing protein 3. STAC3 is essential for excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle; loss-of-function mutations (e.g., the recurrent p.Trp284Ser substitution found in the Lumbee tribe) disrupt calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, producing the characteristic muscle weakness, facial dysmorphism, and malignant hyperthermia susceptibility seen in NAM.

147575.long_answer: Usher syndrome type III is caused by pathogenic mutations in the CLRN1 gene, which encodes the tetraspan membrane protein clarin-1. Loss-of-function variants (e.g., p.Y176X, p.M122K) disrupt clarin-1’s role in inner-ear hair cells and photoreceptors, producing the progressive hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa characteristic of Usher type III.

373781.long_answer: Spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) combines motor neuron degeneration with seizure disorders, both of which fall under disorders of the nervous system. Diagnosis and management—covering motor weakness, electrophysiologic studies, antiepileptic therapy, and supportive neurologic care—are therefore primarily the responsibility of a neurologist (often a pediatric neurologist in children).

576166.long_answer: During embryogenesis the medial nasal (nasomedial) processes fuse with the adjacent maxillary processes to create the vertical mid-line groove of the upper lip known as the philtrum. In Aarskog–Scott syndrome this structure is characteristically elongated or prominent, making the philtrum the facial feature in question.

375414.long_answer: Before undergoing her groundbreaking tracheal transplant, Hannah Warren survived for more than two years in the neonatal intensive-care unit of Samsung Medical Center in Seoul, where mechanical ventilation kept her alive despite being born without a functional trachea.

967510.long_answer: Because the bladder mucosa is exposed to the external environment in bladder exstrophy, enteric bacteria such as Escherichia coli can readily contaminate the open bladder and travel up the ureters. This continual contamination makes ascending urinary tract infection the single most frequent infectious problem seen in patients with bladder exstrophy.

775609.long_answer: Intestinal (mid-gut) malrotation is a congenital defect in which the intestines fail to rotate and fix properly during embryologic development. The abnormal positioning predisposes to duodenal obstruction by Ladd bands and to mid-gut volvulus, both of which commonly present with acute, often bilious, vomiting in neonates and infants.

209996.long_answer: Pregnancy is a well-established host risk factor for progression to severe dengue. The physiologic expansion of maternal blood volume and extracellular fluid in pregnancy amplifies the capillary-plasma leakage characteristic of dengue infection, predisposing pregnant women to haemoconcentration, hypovolaemic shock and severe disease manifestations.

543785.long_answer: Giant congenital melanocytic nevi are large pigmented skin lesions present at birth. Because they are cutaneous abnormalities with potential for malignant melanoma transformation, their diagnosis, monitoring, and initial management fall under the expertise of dermatologists, the medical specialists devoted to skin disorders.

309984.long_answer: Malakoplakia is characterized histologically by sheets of macrophages (von Hansemann cells) that contain round, basophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies composed of partially digested bacterial remnants complexed with calcium and iron. These pathognomonic inclusions are called Michaelis–Gutmann bodies, and their presence is diagnostic of malakoplakia.

413612.long_answer: Burning mouth syndrome occurs predominantly in post-menopausal women, and one leading hypothesis links it to the fall in circulating estrogen after menopause. Estrogen deficiency can alter oral mucosal integrity, salivary composition, and sensory nerve function, creating the persistent burning sensation characteristic of the syndrome.

604134.long_answer: Connective tissue growth factor (CTGF), also known as CCN2, is a well-established downstream mediator of tissue fibrosis that promotes extracellular-matrix deposition and myofibroblast activation. After central nervous system injury, astrocytes strongly up-regulate CTGF, and this protein drives the proliferation and matrix production that are essential for glial scar formation. Thus, CTGF links fibrotic processes with the generation of the glial scar.

154582.long_answer: The disease is osteopetrosis, in which defective osteoclasts fail to resorb bone, leading to abnormally dense yet fragile (brittle) bones. Osteoclasts arise from hematopoietic stem cells, so replacing the patient’s marrow with donor hematopoietic stem cells provides functional osteoclasts and reverses the pathophysiology. Thus, allogeneic bone marrow (hematopoietic stem cell) transplantation is the definitive, disease-modifying treatment.

575214.long_answer: Aldose reductase is the key enzyme of the polyol pathway that reduces glucose to sorbitol. In chronic hyperglycaemia, sorbitol accumulates in nerves and retinal cells, producing osmotic stress and oxidative damage that contribute to diabetic neuropathy and diabetic retinopathy.

724223.long_answer: Primary adrenal insufficiency, known as Addison disease, results in inadequate production of cortisol (and often aldosterone) by the adrenal cortex. Cortisol normally supports vascular tone and responsiveness to catecholamines; when it is deficient, systemic vascular resistance falls, leading to dizziness and blood-pressure drops upon standing—classic orthostatic hypotension.

581031.long_answer: Ligneous conjunctivitis is most commonly caused by congenital type-1 plasminogen deficiency, an autosomal-recessive disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the PLG gene that encodes plasminogen. The impaired plasmin-mediated fibrinolysis leads to accumulation of fibrin-rich, woody (ligneous) pseudomembranes on mucous membranes, including the conjunctiva.

524368.long_answer: Congenital inguinal hernias are frequently seen in patients with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a hereditary connective-tissue disorder caused by defects in collagen synthesis. The abnormal collagen weakens the abdominal wall and inguinal canal, predisposing affected infants to develop inguinal hernias at birth.

104827.long_answer: Immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity reactions—such as anaphylaxis, asthma, and common allergies—are mediated by immunoglobulin E (IgE). Allergen-specific IgE binds to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils; upon re-exposure, cross-linking of these IgE molecules triggers rapid degranulation and release of histamine and other mediators, producing the characteristic immediate allergic response.

435757.long_answer: Stickler syndrome is an autosomal-dominant arthro-ophthalmopathy that arises from pathogenic variants in genes such as COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2 and related loci. These genes encode type II (and related type XI) collagen, the principal structural protein of cartilage and the ocular vitreous. Mutated or deficient type II collagen disrupts normal development of cartilage, joints, mid-facial bones and the vitreous body, producing the characteristic skeletal, craniofacial and ocular manifestations of Stickler syndrome. Thus, abnormal type II collagen is assumed to be the key substance involved in its cause.

653776.long_answer: Organophosphate compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme that normally breaks down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. This inhibition causes acetylcholine to accumulate at cholinergic synapses, overstimulating muscarinic receptors in salivary glands and leading to profuse salivation.

842650.long_answer: Palmoplantar keratoderma-deafness syndrome is most often produced by missense mutations in the GJB2 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin 26. Altered connexin 26 disrupts intercellular communication in both the epidermis (leading to hyperkeratosis of palms and soles) and the cochlea (producing sensorineural hearing loss), establishing GJB2 as the causal gene for this disorder.

146957.long_answer: The Tenth Revision of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10) explicitly lists myiasis under code B87 in Chapter I, ‘Certain infectious and parasitic diseases’, thus providing a specific classification for this condition.

557431.long_answer: Calcium ions are indispensable for skeletal and cardiac muscle contraction because they bind to troponin-C, permitting actin-myosin interaction. Mutations in genes that encode neuronal calcium channels, particularly CACNA1A, produce spinocerebellar ataxia (e.g., SCA type 6). Thus, the element whose normal physiology underlies muscle contraction and whose gene defects cause spinocerebellar ataxia is calcium.

821836.long_answer: 5q- syndrome is a distinct subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome produced by an interstitial deletion on the long arm (q) of chromosome 5. Patients typically present with a severe, isolated macrocytic anemia, relatively preserved or elevated platelet counts, and characteristic dysplastic megakaryocytes. The chromosomal deletion leads to haploinsufficiency of genes such as RPS14, contributing to ineffective erythropoiesis and the macrocytic anemia seen in this disorder.

824203.long_answer: Quadrantanopia classically arises when a lesion involves Meyer's loop—the inferior optic radiations that course through the temporal lobe. Damage here disrupts visual information from the superior contralateral visual quadrant, producing the characteristic ‘pie-in-the-sky’ quadrantanopia most frequently tested and reported in clinical neurology.

331707.long_answer: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is a well-recognized cause of microcephaly, which is defined as a head circumference that is smaller than expected for gestational age and sex. CMV can infect the developing fetal brain, leading to disruption of neuronal proliferation and migration, intracranial calcifications, and overall impaired brain growth. These effects frequently manifest at birth as a smaller-than-normal head size (microcephaly) in affected newborns. This association is documented in authoritative sources such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the American Academy of Pediatrics (Red Book), and numerous peer-reviewed studies on congenital CMV. Therefore, congenital CMV can indeed lead to a smaller head size in newborns.

537873.long_answer: In Nager syndrome (acrofacial dysostosis), congenital radioulnar synostosis frequently fuses the radius and ulna near the elbow, limiting flexion-extension and pronation-supination. This abnormality makes the elbow joint stiff and results in poor movement of the upper limb.

897064.long_answer: In chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction and destruction of pulmonary capillary beds raise pulmonary arterial pressure, leading to pulmonary hypertension. The sustained pressure overload causes right-ventricular hypertrophy and eventual right-sided heart failure, a condition termed cor pulmonale. This cardiovascular complication is among the most common and clinically significant sequelae of COPD.

422304.long_answer: The onion-like concentric rings of alternating demyelinated and myelinated tissue in Baló’s concentric sclerosis are thought to arise from a hypoxia-like ‘tissue preconditioning’ phenomenon: an initial ischemic-type insult triggers protective responses in adjacent white-matter zones, so successive waves of injury and relative protection produce the characteristic concentric lamellae.

830741.long_answer: Papilledema is swelling of the optic disc caused by raised intracranial pressure. In cavernous sinus thrombosis, venous congestion and impaired cerebrospinal fluid drainage elevate intracranial pressure, which can lead to papilledema visible on fundoscopic examination.

429207.long_answer: Sonic hedgehog (SHH) is a developmental morphogen; pathogenic germ-line variants are classically associated with midline developmental defects such as holoprosencephaly, craniofacial anomalies and limb patterning disorders.
