Current medical and genetic literature does not show an association between SHH mutations and mastocytosis, a clonal mast-cell disease that is typically driven by activating mutations in the KIT receptor (most commonly KIT D816V). Likewise, while hedgehog signalling participates in skeletal development, SHH mutations have not been implicated as a recognised genetic cause of osteoporosis in humans; osteoporosis is instead linked to variants in genes such as COL1A1/2, LRP5, WNT1, and others, as well as secondary hormonal and environmental factors. Therefore, genetic mutations in SHH are not considered to be associated with either mastocytosis or osteoporosis according to established biomedical consensus.

656754.long_answer: The definitive confirmation of giant cell arteritis is obtained by histopathologic examination of a temporal artery biopsy, which reveals granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and disruption of the internal elastic lamina. Because this tissue diagnosis directly demonstrates the characteristic vascular lesions, temporal artery biopsy is regarded as the gold-standard diagnostic procedure for GCA.

265579.long_answer: Appendiceal neuroendocrine (carcinoid) tumors can release large amounts of serotonin and related mediators into the circulation, producing carcinoid syndrome. These bioactive substances stimulate fibroblast proliferation, leading to dense fibrosis in the mesentery, peritoneum, and right-sided heart valves. The resulting fibrotic plaques can kink or obstruct bowel loops, impair nutrient transit, and compromise organ function, making carcinoid syndrome the condition in which tumor-induced fibrosis hampers digestion or other visceral activity.

592718.long_answer: A cervical Pap smear collected during prenatal care can be tested for Chlamydia trachomatis. Identifying and treating this often-asymptomatic infection with antibiotics before delivery markedly lowers the risk that the organism will be passed from mother to infant during passage through the birth canal, thereby preventing neonatal conjunctivitis and pneumonia.

351940.long_answer: Diagnosis of congenital disorders of glycosylation relies on isoelectric focusing of serum transferrin. This electrophoretic technique separates transferrin glycoforms according to their net charge, which changes with the number of sialic acid–terminated N-glycans. Abnormal banding patterns on transferrin isoelectric focusing reveal hypoglycosylated forms characteristic of CDG, making it the standard assay to assess transferrin glycosylation status.

485027.long_answer: Cytogenetic studies of products of conception show that extra copies of an autosome (autosomal trisomies—most often trisomy 16) account for roughly 50–60 % of all chromosomal abnormalities found in first-trimester miscarriages, making autosomal trisomy the single most frequent chromosomal anomaly responsible for early pregnancy loss.

299747.long_answer: Neurocutaneous melanosis is driven by post-zygotic, activating mutations of the NRAS oncogene—most commonly substitutions at codon 61 (e.g., Q61K/Q61R). These NRAS mutations are found both in the large/giant congenital melanocytic naevi of the skin and in the leptomeningeal melanocytic proliferations, indicating a shared somatic mosaic origin and underlying the pathogenesis of this phakomatosis.

854038.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the TUBA1A gene, which encodes the α-1A-tubulin subunit, disturb microtubule dynamics needed for neuronal migration, producing a form of lissencephaly ("LIS3"). Because TUBA1A is also critical for corticospinal-tract development, affected individuals frequently show hypertonia and muscle spasticity in addition to the smooth-brain malformation, so the same TUBA1A mutation can present with both lissencephaly and muscle spasticity.

575774.long_answer: Cyclosporine, a calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant, is employed in refractory or severe cases of urticarial vasculitis because it down-regulates T-cell activation and cytokine release, thereby diminishing the immune-complex–mediated vascular inflammation characteristic of the disorder.

634299.long_answer: Vomiting is a classic gastrointestinal symptom seen in disorders such as gastroenteritis, gastritis, and peptic-ulcer disease. Clinical descriptions of pneumonic plague note that, in addition to its hallmark fever, cough, and rapidly progressive pneumonia, patients frequently experience systemic symptoms that include nausea and vomiting. Thus vomiting is a symptom shared by many gastrointestinal diseases and by pneumonic plague.

931570.long_answer: Both dysautonomia—dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system—and reflex (vasovagal) syncope can lead to transient loss of consciousness caused by sudden drops in blood pressure and/or heart rate. This manifests clinically as fainting, the hallmark symptom they share.

520169.short_answer: ≈1 case per 10 million people per year
520169.long_answer: VIPoma is an exceedingly rare neuroendocrine tumour; epidemiologic studies and reviews (e.g., UpToDate, major endocrine oncology texts) place its incidence at roughly one new case per 10 million population annually.

400769.long_answer: Juvenile osteoporosis is a metabolic bone disorder requiring evaluation of calcium–phosphate balance, vitamin-D status, and hormonal influences on bone turnover. These systemic, endocrine-mediated factors are routinely assessed and managed by an endocrinologist (ideally a pediatric endocrinologist), the specialist trained to diagnose and treat metabolic bone diseases in children and adolescents.

414268.long_answer: In POEMS syndrome, monoclonal plasma cells secrete excessive amounts of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF). The elevated VEGF drives abnormal angiogenesis and increased capillary permeability, producing many hallmark features of the syndrome such as edema, organomegaly, skin changes, and peripheral neuropathy. Serum VEGF levels correlate closely with disease activity, confirming that VEGF overproduction underlies the clinical manifestations of POEMS.

775192.long_answer: Elbow dysplasia in dogs is commonly managed by arthroscopic surgery, where a small arthroscope and instruments are inserted into the joint to locate and remove fragmented cartilage or bone (e.g., a fragmented medial coronoid process) and smooth the joint surface. This minimally invasive technique reduces postoperative pain, allows thorough joint evaluation, and is widely accepted as the surgical treatment of choice for canine elbow dysplasia.

200761.long_answer: Ischiopatellar dysplasia (small-patella syndrome) is caused by TBX4 mutations and affects bones derived from the hind-limb bud. In addition to hypoplastic or absent patellae, mid-foot involvement is characteristic: the navicular bone frequently shows delayed ossification, marked hypoplasia or complete absence. This selective navicular deficiency is a well-described radiological hallmark of the disorder.

162206.long_answer: Haemophilia A is caused by mutations in the F8 gene that lower or eliminate coagulation-factor VIII activity. Factor VIII functions in the intrinsic coagulation cascade within the circulating blood, and its absence leads to defective clot formation. Thus the primary organ/system affected by this genetic deficiency is the blood (haematologic system), producing the characteristic bleeding tendency of the disorder.

303768.long_answer: Smoking or inhaling cocaine fumes (especially crack cocaine) is a well-documented precipitant of acute eosinophilic pneumonia. The irritant combustion products and drug itself injure the alveolar epithelium, triggering release of Th2-type cytokines (IL-5, eotaxin) and massive pulmonary eosinophil recruitment, leading to the characteristic febrile, hypoxic presentation and eosinophil-rich infiltrates on bronchoalveolar lavage or lung biopsy.

369881.long_answer: Relapsing polychondritis can be accompanied by livedo reticularis, a cutaneous vascular phenomenon that produces a lace-like, purplish (reticular) mottling of the skin. This pattern results from impaired blood flow in the dermal vessels and is commonly seen in systemic autoimmune or vasculitic disorders, including relapsing polychondritis.

194465.long_answer: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome is a congenital over-growth disorder characterized by features such as macroglossia, organomegaly and hemihyperplasia. Children with this imprinting disorder have a markedly increased risk of embryonal tumors, especially Wilms tumor and hepatoblastoma, making routine abdominal ultrasound surveillance standard care in the first years of life.

963635.long_answer: A hydatidiform mole (molar pregnancy) is a gestational trophoblastic disease characterized by abnormal proliferation of trophoblastic tissue. The trophoblasts secrete very high amounts of beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG), often far exceeding levels seen in normal pregnancy. These markedly elevated β-hCG concentrations stimulate maternal estrogen and thyroid pathways, provoking severe nausea and vomiting—clinically termed hyperemesis gravidarum. Thus, the disease most classically linked to high β-hCG levels and intense gestational nausea is the hydatidiform mole.

726301.long_answer: During limb development, BMP-4, a TGF-β family member produced in the apical ectodermal ridge and interdigital mesenchyme, activates caspase-dependent programmed cell death in the interdigital tissue. This apoptosis removes the webbing between the digits, allowing separate fingers and toes to form; blocking BMP-4 signaling prevents this cell death and results in syndactyly.

150309.long_answer: In adults, a normal absolute neutrophil count spans roughly 1.5–8.0 × 10⁹ cells per litre (1,500–8,000 cells/µL). Counts below 1.5 × 10⁹ cells/L define neutropenia; therefore 1.5 × 10⁹ cells/L (≈1,500 cells/µL) is accepted as the lower limit of the reference range.

655660.long_answer: Guanfacine is an antihypertensive drug that functions as an α-2A adrenergic receptor agonist. Beyond lowering blood pressure, its presynaptic α-2A activation enhances prefrontal cortical regulation of attention and impulse control. Because of this mechanism, an extended-release formulation of guanfacine (Intuniv) is FDA-approved and widely used as a non-stimulant treatment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).

371215.long_answer: Over 85–90 % of osteogenesis imperfecta (all classical types I–IV) are caused by dominant pathogenic variants in the collagen type I genes COL1A1 and COL1A2, which encode the α1(I) and α2(I) chains of type I collagen. Defective or reduced type I collagen disturbs bone matrix formation and strength, producing the characteristic brittle-bone phenotype. Therefore, these two genes are the ones most commonly linked to osteogenesis imperfecta.

241260.long_answer: An intravenous pyelogram (IVP) is performed by injecting radiopaque contrast medium into a vein; the contrast is filtered by the kidneys and outlines the renal collecting systems, ureters, and bladder on sequential X-ray images. This contrast-enhanced imaging specifically highlights the urinary tract anatomy and function, making it a standard diagnostic study in evaluating malformations such as cloacal exstrophy.

246346.long_answer: The CD70 gene (TNFSF7) encodes the CD70 ligand that binds directly to the costimulatory receptor CD27. Biallelic CD70 deficiency is a recognized cause of Epstein-Barr virus–driven primary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Thus, among genes linked to primary HLH, CD70 is the one whose product physiologically interacts with the protein CD27.

924872.short_answer: Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders
924872.long_answer: Dissociative disorders are classified in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), the authoritative diagnostic handbook produced and periodically revised by the American Psychiatric Association. The DSM provides standardized criteria and coding for mental health conditions, including dissociative identity disorder, dissociative amnesia, and depersonalization/derealization disorder.

509758.long_answer: Noonan syndrome exemplifies locus heterogeneity, where pathogenic variants in several different genes (e.g., PTPN11, SOS1, RAF1, KRAS, NRAS, etc.) all produce the same clinical disorder. Thus, a single phenotype arises from mutations at multiple distinct genetic loci.

204800.long_answer: Helen Singer Kaplan emphasized that performance anxiety—persistent worry about one’s sexual adequacy and self-monitoring during intercourse—activates sympathetic arousal and distracts attention from erotic stimuli. This anxiety can inhibit the parasympathetic vasocongestive responses required for vaginal lubrication and genital swelling, thereby precipitating or maintaining female sexual arousal disorder.

213204.long_answer: Transient neonatal diabetes mellitus (TNDM) is most commonly caused by overexpression of the imprinted gene PLAGL1 (also called ZAC) located at chromosome 6q24. Paternal uniparental disomy, paternal duplication, or loss of maternal methylation at this locus increases PLAGL1 expression, leading to the transient diabetic phenotype in newborns.

475263.long_answer: Mutations in the DNAH11 gene, which encodes an outer-dynein-arm heavy chain, impair the motility of nodal (embryonic) cilia. During early embryogenesis these cilia generate the left-ward fluid flow that establishes left–right body asymmetry. Loss-of-function DNAH11 variants therefore cause primary ciliary dyskinesia accompanied by laterality defects such as situs inversus, illustrating their critical role in nodal cilia function.

497457.long_answer: Women who carry deleterious BRCA1 mutations are advised to undergo risk-reducing (prophylactic) bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy—surgical removal of both ovaries and fallopian tubes—after completion of childbearing, typically by age 35–40. This intervention eliminates most of the ovarian and fallopian-tube epithelium where high-grade serous carcinomas originate, lowering ovarian cancer incidence by roughly 80–90% and improving overall survival in this high-risk population.

748697.long_answer: Gómez–López-Hernández syndrome is characterized by the cerebellar malformation rhombencephalosynapsis. High-resolution fetal magnetic resonance imaging can depict this mid-hind-brain anomaly in utero, making fetal MRI the imaging technique capable of establishing the diagnosis prenatally.

657821.long_answer: In Lesch–Nyhan syndrome the loss of HGPRT blocks the purine-salvage pathway, so guanine cannot be recycled to GMP and then to GTP. The resulting cerebral deficiency of GTP (a guanine nucleotide) impairs tetrahydrobiopterin and dopamine synthesis in the basal ganglia, which is believed to underlie the characteristic neurological and behavioral abnormalities of the disorder.

555707.long_answer: Burning mouth syndrome (BMS) is a chronic condition in which patients experience a persistent burning or scalding sensation—often on the tongue, lips, palate, or entire oral mucosa—despite normal clinical examination and laboratory findings. Because no local or systemic medical cause can be identified, it is classified as an idiopathic orofacial pain disorder.

712165.short_answer: In the lateral cervical region near the nerve ring
712165.long_answer: Deirids are a pair of small cuticular sensory papillae found in Secernentea nematodes on the lateral lines of the neck (cervical area), typically at or just posterior to the level of the oesophageal nerve ring.

587449.long_answer: In Caplan's syndrome, the rheumatoid arthritis component is managed with disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs). These agents—such as methotrexate, sulfasalazine, hydroxychloroquine, or biologic DMARDs—slow the underlying autoimmune inflammation, limit joint destruction, and improve long-term function, while the pulmonary nodules usually require no specific therapy.

654251.long_answer: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are commonly prescribed for hypochondriasis (now termed illness-anxiety disorder). By blocking the serotonin transporter, they prevent reuptake of serotonin into presynaptic neurons, thereby raising extracellular serotonin levels in the brain and alleviating anxiety-related symptoms.

925769.long_answer: The very first clinical report of human uniparental disomy (Spence et al., 1988) described a child with cystic fibrosis who had inherited two maternal copies of chromosome 7 (maternal isodisomy 7). This case established chromosome 7 as the chromosome involved in the first documented instance of uniparental disomy causing human disease.

115052.long_answer: Trimethadione is a well-established teratogen. Maternal use during early pregnancy produces the fetal trimethadione syndrome, whose hallmark craniofacial defect is a cleft palate (often with or without cleft lip), caused by disruption of palatal shelf fusion in the first trimester.

289214.long_answer: Ligneous conjunctivitis occurs in people with congenital plasminogen (type I) deficiency. Because plasmin is required to lyse fibrin and remodel extracellular matrix, lack of plasminogen prevents normal fibrinolysis during tissue repair, leading to fibrin-rich ‘woody’ pseudomembranes and markedly impaired wound healing on the conjunctiva and other mucous membranes.

346546.long_answer: The condition is called estrogen insensitivity (or estrogen resistance) syndrome. It is an extremely rare disorder caused by inactivating mutations in the ESR1 gene that render estrogen receptors non-functional, so tissues cannot respond to circulating estrogens. This receptor failure underlies the intersex/sexual-development abnormalities seen in affected individuals.

152367.long_answer: In scleroderma renal crisis, vascular injury in the kidney stimulates juxtaglomerular cells to release the enzyme renin. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, initiating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system cascade that drives severe vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and malignant hypertension characteristic of the crisis.

806445.long_answer: DiGeorge (22q11.2 deletion) syndrome commonly results from haploinsufficiency of the TBX1 gene. TBX1 encodes a T-box transcription factor that directs patterning and morphogenesis of the pharyngeal arches and their derivatives—including the thymus, parathyroids, and great cardiac vessels—explaining the characteristic craniofacial, cardiac, and immunologic defects seen in the syndrome.

142051.long_answer: Type I cryoglobulinemia is classically linked to B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders. Among the leukemias, chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is the one most consistently associated because the malignant B-cells secrete a monoclonal immunoglobulin that precipitates in the cold, forming cryoglobulins.

381356.long_answer: The TP63 gene, which encodes the p63 transcription factor and whose mutations cause Hay–Wells (ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate) syndrome, is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 3 at band 3q28.

800842.long_answer: Polysplenia syndrome, a form of heterotaxy, is defined by the presence of multiple small accessory spleens rather than a single normal spleen. It results from disturbed left–right body patterning, a developmental process that depends on motile embryonic cilia. Defects in ciliary structure or function (primary ciliary dyskinesia) therefore predispose to laterality errors such as polysplenia, making the two conditions frequently associated.

357284.long_answer: Carpenter syndrome (acrocephalopolysyndactyly type II) is an autosomal-recessive craniosynostosis syndrome caused by mutations in RAB23 or MEGF8. Its cardinal features include craniosynostosis, pre- and post-axial polysyndactyly/syndactyly, early-onset obesity, and proportionate short stature, fitting the clinical picture described.

381281.long_answer: James B. Pollack, the noted NASA planetary scientist who studied the atmospheres of Mars, Venus and Titan, was afflicted with esophageal achalasia—a rare motility disorder in which degeneration of Auerbach’s plexus prevents relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter. The resultant dysphagia and aspiration contributed to the respiratory complications that led to his death in 1994.

855553.long_answer: In untreated typhoid fever the heart rate is often slower than would be expected for the degree of fever—a phenomenon called relative bradycardia (Faget sign). This pulse-temperature dissociation is a well-described clinical finding in typhoid, attributed to Salmonella Typhi endotoxin effects on the cardiac conduction system and autonomic regulation.

224421.long_answer: Hereditary mucoepithelial dysplasia is an autosomal-dominant ectodermal disorder that primarily affects the skin, hair, nails, and mucous membranes; management centers on monitoring and treating these cutaneous and mucosal manifestations. Consequently, dermatologists—specialists in diseases of the skin and its appendages—are the medical professionals most directly involved in the ongoing care of patients with this condition.

660977.long_answer: When the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor is stimulated, it couples to the Gs heterotrimeric G protein. The G-protein’s alpha subunit (Gαs) exchanges GDP for GTP, dissociates from the βγ subunits, and directly activates membrane adenylyl cyclase, leading to increased intracellular cyclic AMP and downstream signaling.

680777.long_answer: Fechtner syndrome is an Alport-related MYH9 disorder that, in addition to nephritis, sensorineural deafness, cataracts and leukocyte inclusions, is distinguished by a reduced platelet count—i.e., thrombocytopenia (often manifesting as macrothrombocytopenia).

556572.long_answer: Cyclophosphamide is an alkylating chemotherapeutic agent included in standard mantle cell lymphoma regimens such as R-CHOP and VR-CAP. Its hepatic metabolism produces the urotoxic metabolite acrolein, which can damage the bladder epithelium and lead to hemorrhagic cystitis, a characteristic dose-limiting adverse effect that is often prevented with vigorous hydration and MESNA.

645377.long_answer: Congenital absence (aplasia) of the gluteal muscles occurring in association with spina bifida occulta has been reported mainly in affected siblings born to unaffected parents, a pattern characteristic of autosomal-recessive inheritance. No sex bias or parent-to-child transmission has been documented, further supporting an autosomal recessive mode of transmission.

229156.long_answer: Adie (tonic) pupils respond to topical cholinergic miotics; dilute pilocarpine eye drops stimulate the denervated sphincter muscle, constricting the pupil and improving accommodation, thus treating the pupillary symptoms of Adie syndrome.

798258.long_answer: The most prevalent form of congenital disorder of glycosylation, CDG type Ia caused by phosphomannomutase-2 (PMM2) deficiency, typically manifests with neurological features dominated by cerebellar involvement; patients characteristically develop truncal and limb ataxia along with hypotonia and developmental delay. Thus, PMM2-CDG is the subtype most commonly associated with ataxia.

941870.long_answer: Ataxia-telangiectasia (ATM gene mutation) is the most frequently encountered inherited disorder that presents with both cerebellar ataxia and extrapyramidal choreiform movements. The progressive cerebellar degeneration produces ataxia, while basal-ganglia involvement gives rise to chorea/athetosis, making it a characteristic and relatively common inherited cause of the combined symptom pattern.

410383.long_answer: Fanconi anemia is an inherited chromosomal-instability syndrome that markedly increases the risk of malignancies (especially acute myeloid leukemia and solid tumors). Among its characteristic congenital anomalies are radial-ray defects, including hypoplastic radius, absent thumbs, and congenital radioulnar synostosis, making Fanconi anemia the tumor-predisposition syndrome classically associated with radioulnar synostosis.

831025.long_answer: EEC (Ectrodactyly-Ectodermal Dysplasia-Cleft) syndrome is a well-described autosomal-dominant disorder in which affected individuals can show complete or partial absence of the tibia together with orofacial clefts, most often cleft lip and/or cleft palate. The syndrome’s core triad is limb malformations (classically split hand/foot or other long-bone defects such as tibial aplasia), ectodermal dysplasia features, and cleft lip/palate, making it the canonical condition linking absent tibia with a cleft lip.

777423.long_answer: Hodgkin lymphoma is diagnosed pathologically by finding Reed–Sternberg cells—large, often binucleate or multinucleate B-cell–derived cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli—in an appropriate reactive inflammatory background on lymph node biopsy. Their presence is considered pathognomonic for the disease.

368148.long_answer: Ethanol metabolism raises the cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, driving pyruvate toward lactate. If the enzyme pyruvate dehydrogenase is deficient (as can occur in thiamine-dependent alcoholics or in genetic PDH complex defects), pyruvate cannot enter the tricarboxylic acid cycle, accumulates, and is further reduced to lactate, producing marked lactic acidosis during ethanol poisoning.

563726.long_answer: In punctate inner choroiditis, disruption of Bruch’s membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium frequently triggers growth of abnormal choroidal blood vessels—choroidal neovascularization (CNV). This sight-threatening complication is also well documented in other white dot syndromes such as multifocal choroiditis and presumed ocular histoplasmosis, making CNV the shared and most common serious sequela.

509772.long_answer: Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome is a hereditary neurodegenerative disorder whose core triad includes cerebellar ataxia. Because the prominent, progressive neurological manifestation is cerebellar dysfunction, patients are most commonly evaluated and followed by a neurologist, with additional subspecialty input (endocrinology for hypogonadism and ophthalmology for retinal dystrophy) as needed.

364573.long_answer: GPC1 (glypican-1) has been identified by genome-wide association studies as a susceptibility gene for biliary atresia. Glypican-1 is a cell-surface heparan-sulfate proteoglycan that modulates Hedgehog ligand presentation and signalling, and it also participates in the control of inflammatory responses. Thus, GPC1 links biliary atresia risk with regulation of inflammation and Hedgehog pathway activity.

321314.long_answer: Osgood–Schlatter disease is produced by repetitive traction of the patellar tendon where the quadriceps attach to the tibial tubercle. Conditioning programmes that focus on strengthening the quadriceps femoris (especially the vastus medialis) improve knee-extensor control and reduce the relative tensile load on the apophysis, thereby helping to lessen pain and facilitate recovery.

463096.long_answer: Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis targets the smallest veins in the skin—the postcapillary venules. Immune-complex deposition occurs predominantly in these vessels, leading to neutrophilic inflammation and vessel wall necrosis that produce the characteristic palpable purpura.

266924.long_answer: Cystine stones arise in patients with cystinuria, a hereditary defect in renal re-absorption of the dibasic amino acids. Poorly soluble cystine (the oxidized dimer of cysteine) precipitates in urine, leading to recurrent kidney stones. Thus, the amino acid cystine is directly linked to an increased risk of nephrolithiasis through formation of characteristic cystine calculi.

385853.long_answer: Edwards syndrome, also called trisomy 18, is caused by the presence of an extra (third) copy of chromosome 18. The chromosomal imbalance leads to multiple congenital anomalies; a hallmark prenatal finding is severe intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR).

586277.long_answer: Primary ovarian insufficiency can be a late consequence of mumps virus infection. The paramyxovirus that causes mumps can produce oophoritis (inflammation of the ovaries), and in some women this inflammatory damage results in loss of follicular reserve and premature cessation of ovarian function, leading to primary ovarian insufficiency.

581781.long_answer: Primary biliary cholangitis (formerly primary biliary cirrhosis) is the autoimmune liver disease characteristically accompanied by non-caseating granulomas within portal tracts. These granulomatous lesions reflect the immune-mediated destruction of small intrahepatic bile ducts that defines the disease.

580747.long_answer: After Diphyllobothrium eggs reach fresh water they hatch into a ciliated, free-swimming larva called the coracidium. This coracidium is physiologically adapted to an external aquatic environment, whereas the adult worm lives attached to the mucosa of the definitive host’s small intestine. Thus the coracidium stage is the life-cycle phase adapted to a markedly different environment from that of the adult form.

235765.long_answer: In congenital muscular dystrophy, infants and children often develop severe joint contractures and progressive scoliosis. Orthopaedic procedures such as tendon-release or spinal fusion are therefore frequently undertaken to correct these deformities, lessen pain, and enhance mobility, thereby improving overall quality of life.

378533.long_answer: In intermediate uveitis the chronic inflammation and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier often lead to cystoid macular edema (CME). Persistent CME can destroy photoreceptors and cause irreversible macular scarring, making it one of the main causes of permanent vision loss in these patients.

676060.long_answer: Congenital hypoprothrombinemia results from pathogenic variants in the coagulation factor II (F2) gene. Cytogenetic mapping places the F2 gene on the short arm of chromosome 11 (band 11p11-q12), making chromosome 11 the chromosomal location implicated in this condition.

387562.long_answer: Only about one-third of people who show a positive local contracture after an intramuscular halothane injection are confirmed to be malignant-hyperthermia-susceptible when retested with the standard in-vitro caffeine/halothane contracture test; studies place the positive predictive value at roughly 35 %, highlighting the test’s limited reliability for diagnosing MH susceptibility.

134281.long_answer: Trichostasis spinulosa is a follicular disorder of the skin and hair shafts. Diagnosis relies on clinical examination and dermatoscopic or histologic evaluation of the pilosebaceous unit, and management may include topical keratolytics or laser therapy. These evaluations and treatments fall squarely within the expertise of a dermatologist—a physician specially trained in disorders of the skin, hair, and nails—making a dermatologist the appropriate specialist to diagnose and treat trichostasis spinulosa.

595214.long_answer: Nyctalopia (night blindness) is a hallmark of retinitis pigmentosa because rod photoreceptors, which mediate dim-light vision, degenerate first. In the cone-rod type of congenital amaurosis with congenital hypertrichosis, rod dysfunction is likewise present early, so affected individuals also experience profound difficulty seeing in low-light conditions. Therefore, night blindness is a common symptom shared by both disorders.

847519.long_answer: Generalized vulvodynia—also called dysesthetic vulvodynia—is characterized by diffuse, spontaneous vulvar pain described as burning, stinging, or electric-shock sensations. These neuropathic, neuralgia-like symptoms distinguish it from localized or provoked forms of vulvodynia.

464731.long_answer: Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma is a genetic disorder characterized by generalized scaling and erythroderma of the skin from birth. Because it primarily affects the skin’s structure and function, its diagnosis, genetic counseling, and long-term management fall under the expertise of dermatology, the medical specialty dedicated to disorders of the skin, hair, and nails.

901432.long_answer: Among the local anesthetics, prilocaine is well known for producing clinically significant methemoglobinemia. Prilocaine is metabolized to o-toluidine, an oxidizing agent that converts the ferrous iron (Fe2+) in hemoglobin to the ferric form (Fe3+), generating methemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen. High doses or topical/IV regional use of prilocaine have repeatedly produced this complication in clinical reports and are specifically cautioned against for this reason.

817686.long_answer: Individuals with histrionic personality disorder typically have adequate social skills but deploy them primarily to attract attention and approval. Their interactions are often dramatic, rapidly shifting, and shallow, which can make relationships superficial and less authentic despite apparent sociability.

882675.long_answer: In 2010, Peru’s Ministry of Health and the World Health Organization reported an outbreak of plague caused by Yersinia pestis in the La Libertad Region. Pneumonic cases were specifically documented in the Chocope District of Ascope Province, leading to a health emergency declaration for that province.

761482.long_answer: Shapiro syndrome classically presents with recurrent episodes of spontaneous hypothermia (marked falls in core body temperature). Hypothermia is likewise the primary factor that limits the duration a person can safely swim in cold water, because prolonged exposure causes a dangerous drop in body temperature. Thus, hypothermia is both a hallmark symptom of Shapiro syndrome and the major physiological limitation during cold-water swimming.

513140.long_answer: Hirschsprung’s disease is almost always confined to the rectum-sigmoid region, but in rare ‘long-segment’ or ‘total colonic aganglionosis’ variants the aganglionic segment extends proximally through the whole colon and can reach the terminal ileum of the small intestine. Thus, in these uncommon cases the terminal ileum is the intestinal segment that becomes involved.

679459.short_answer: Male hemizygosity for the X chromosome
679459.long_answer: Males possess only one X chromosome (are hemizygous); if that single X carries a dominant pathogenic mutation, every cell expresses the defective gene with no normal allele to counterbalance it. Females have two X chromosomes, so a normal copy on the second X and mosaicism from random X-inactivation typically dampen the mutation’s impact, making the condition less severe and less often lethal in females.

767709.long_answer: Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular tumors of the central nervous system that characteristically arise in the cerebellum, brainstem, or spinal cord and occur with increased frequency in patients with Von Hippel–Lindau (VHL) syndrome due to germ-line VHL gene mutations.

528441.long_answer: Tyrosinemia type II is an inherited inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of tyrosine aminotransferase. Diagnosis requires biochemical and molecular genetic testing, and treatment involves specialized dietary management under metabolic protocols. These activities are routinely performed by physicians trained in medical genetics (often called metabolic geneticists), the specialty that manages hereditary metabolic disorders.

517329.long_answer: Langerhans cell histiocytosis lesions contain proliferating Langerhans-type dendritic cells admixed with large numbers of eosinophils; the abundance of this granulocyte led to the historical term “eosinophilic granuloma.” Thus, eosinophils are the granulocytes characteristically involved in the formation of LCH lesions.

938234.long_answer: Social anxiety disorder (social phobia) is most effectively and safely treated first-line with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT). High-quality trials and guidelines (e.g., NICE, APA) show that individual CBT using exposure, cognitive restructuring, and social-skills training produces durable remission and outperforms placebos and many pharmacologic agents, making it the recommended initial intervention.

265050.long_answer: Dextrocardia with situs ambiguus (heterotaxy) is a congenital malposition of the thoracic and abdominal organs that is typically managed by pediatric cardiologists and cardiothoracic or general pediatric surgeons, because the major surgical issues involve complex intracardiac repairs, great-vessel rerouting, and occasionally abdominal organ malrotation or splenic anomalies. Otolaryngology–head and neck (ENT) surgeons specialize in diseases of the ear, nose, throat, and related head-and-neck structures; they do not operate on the heart, great vessels, or abdominal viscera. Therefore, an ENT surgeon would not ordinarily be part of the surgical team treating dextrocardia with situs ambiguus unless there were an unrelated ear-, nose-, or airway-specific problem. Consequently, the statement that an ENT surgeon would be involved in the surgical treatment of dextrocardia situs ambiguus is not supported by standard medical practice.

424351.long_answer: The German pharmaceutical company Bayer synthesized suramin (originally called “Bayer 205”) in 1916; this drug proved to be the first reliably effective and safe therapy for human African trypanosomiasis (sleeping sickness), replacing the highly toxic arsenical atoxyl that had been used previously.

701080.long_answer: Serum amylase is a digestive enzyme produced mainly by the pancreas (and salivary glands). When pancreatic tissue is injured or inflamed—such as in acute pancreatitis—cellular contents leak into the bloodstream, raising circulating amylase levels. Because amylase is released whenever these tissues are damaged, an elevated serum amylase concentration is a recognized biochemical indicator of tissue damage and is routinely used in the diagnosis and monitoring of pancreatitis.

345224.long_answer: Parakeratosis refers to abnormal keratinization in which pyknotic nuclei are retained within the cells of the stratum corneum. This histological change is a characteristic feature of several papulosquamous dermatoses and can be seen in lesions associated with lichen planus.

901674.long_answer: Reactive attachment disorder (RAD) is grouped with trauma- and stressor-related disorders in DSM-5 because its core pathology arises from early severe neglect or abuse. Neurobiological studies show that children with RAD exhibit alterations in stress-response systems—blunted or dysregulated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity, abnormal cortisol rhythms, and limbic (amygdala/hippocampal) changes—patterns that closely mirror findings in post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Hence PTSD is often cited as having a similar neurobiological basis to RAD.

543745.long_answer: SATB2 (Special AT-rich sequence-binding protein 2) is located at chromosome 2q33.1. Haplo-insufficiency or mutation of SATB2 disrupts craniofacial development, giving rise to cleft lip and/or cleft palate. 2q32-q33 microdeletions that remove SATB2 were first described in patients diagnosed with acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis, establishing this gene as the molecular link between the dysostosis and the clefting phenotype.

230540.long_answer: Intravenous labetalol, a combined α- and β-adrenergic blocker, is recommended for rapid blood-pressure reduction in hypertensive emergencies such as hypertensive encephalopathy. It effectively lowers systemic vascular resistance without markedly decreasing uteroplacental blood flow and has an established safety profile in pregnancy, making it a preferred agent for pregnant women with this condition.

997523.long_answer: Canavan’s disease is a leukodystrophy caused by ASPA deficiency that leads to accumulation of N-acetylaspartate and spongy degeneration of the cerebral white matter, damaging the myelin that normally insulates nerve fibers.

802136.long_answer: Traumatic telecanthus arises when the medial canthal ligament loses its normal bony attachment. The ligament is anchored to the anterior lacrimal crest, which is part of the frontal process of the maxilla. Fracture or displacement of this portion of the maxilla (as in naso-orbito-ethmoidal injuries) allows the ligament and medial eyelids to splay laterally, producing the increased intercanthal distance characteristic of traumatic telecanthus.

127657.long_answer: Members of the genus Neisseria are gram-negative diplococci; Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the agent of gonorrhea, while its close relative Neisseria meningitidis is a leading cause of bacterial meningitis. Thus the Neisseria genus encompasses organisms capable of causing both diseases.

269225.long_answer: The current standard clinical classification of Pfeiffer syndrome into types I (classic), II (with cloverleaf skull) and III (severe without cloverleaf skull) was proposed and published by the craniofacial geneticist Michael Cohen Jr. in the early 1990s; his scheme remains the most widely accepted framework for describing the syndrome’s clinical variability.

734463.long_answer: In fulminant or necrotizing pyelonephritis where the renal tissue is extensively destroyed and infection cannot be controlled by antibiotics or drainage, surgical removal of the affected kidney (nephrectomy) may be required to eliminate the source of sepsis and preserve overall health.

164056.long_answer: Experimental and clinical studies show that the underlying dura mater directs osteogenic signaling at cranial sutures; abnormalities in its signaling can trigger premature osteoblastic activity and fusion, making the dura mater the meningeal layer implicated in craniosynostosis.

394301.long_answer: Idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease is characterized by systemic inflammation, widespread lymph-node involvement, and enlargement of reticuloendothelial organs. One of the most frequent organ manifestations is splenic enlargement (splenomegaly), reported in more than half of iMCD patients and incorporated as a minor diagnostic criterion in current consensus guidelines.

555519.long_answer: Fowler’s syndrome, a cause of urinary retention in young women due to abnormal urethral sphincter activity, shows a strong association with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in women of reproductive age, characterized by hyperandrogenism, ovulatory dysfunction, and polycystic ovarian morphology. Studies report a high prevalence of PCOS among women diagnosed with Fowler’s syndrome, linking the two conditions clinically.

338919.long_answer: Transient erythroblastopenia of childhood (TEC) typically appears several weeks after a self-limited febrile illness. Most studies implicate a preceding viral infection—parvovirus B19, enteroviruses, adenovirus, EBV, and others—as the stimulus that transiently suppresses erythroid precursors. Thus, a nonspecific viral infection is considered the usual trigger for TEC.

207216.long_answer: A loading dose is an initial, larger-than-maintenance dose administered to rapidly raise the plasma concentration of a drug to the therapeutic range. In conditions such as pheochromocytoma, where prompt blockade of excess catecholamine effects is crucial, a loading dose accelerates attainment of effective drug levels before subsequent maintenance dosing.

786134.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain is often obtained to exclude structural or neurological lesions (tumors, strokes, demyelination, frontal-temporal abnormalities) that can mimic or precipitate manic episodes, thereby helping to rule out secondary causes of mania in patients presumed to have Bipolar I disorder.

596738.long_answer: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia results from inactivating germ-line mutations in the calcium-sensing receptor (CASR) gene. The defective receptor perceives serum calcium as low, shifting the set-point for parathyroid hormone secretion and renal calcium reabsorption, producing lifelong mild hypercalcaemia with relative hypocalciuria.

137870.long_answer: Epidemiological studies during the 2015–2016 outbreaks in Brazil and other countries showed a sharp rise in infants born with microcephaly that correlated with maternal infection by Zika virus during pregnancy. Virological and pathological investigations demonstrated that Zika virus crosses the placenta, infects fetal neural progenitor cells, and disrupts neurodevelopment, establishing a causal link between Zika virus infection and congenital microcephaly.

523915.long_answer: WAGR syndrome results from micro-deletions at chromosome 11p13 that encompass the PAX6 gene. Loss of one copy of PAX6 not only causes the aniridia seen in WAGR but also disrupts brain development, leading to neurological manifestations such as intellectual disability, epilepsy, and structural brain malformations. Thus, deletion of PAX6 on chromosome 11 links WAGR syndrome with neurological conditions.

375564.long_answer: Atypical lipomatous tumors (well-differentiated liposarcomas) almost uniformly show high-level amplification of the MDM2 oncogene, which resides on chromosome 12q15. Detection of MDM2 amplification by FISH or PCR is a standard diagnostic marker distinguishing these tumors from benign lipomas.

701480.long_answer: Reactive arthritis—also known as Reiter syndrome—is an autoimmune spondyloarthropathy that typically presents with the classic triad of arthritis, urethritis, and conjunctivitis. The autoimmune inflammation is triggered by a preceding gastrointestinal or genitourinary infection, and ocular involvement commonly manifests as conjunctivitis.

149167.long_answer: Macrophagic myofasciitis (MMF) is a specific histopathological lesion seen in muscle biopsies, characterized by dense aggregates of PAS-positive macrophages that contain aluminum hydroxide adjuvant crystals within their cytoplasm. The diagnosis is supported by special stains (e.g., aluminon), energy-dispersive X-ray microanalysis, or electron microscopy demonstrating aluminum—not by detection of potassium iodide. Potassium iodide plays no role in the pathologic identification or confirmation of MMF. Therefore, the statement that MMF is confirmed by the presence of potassium iodide is incorrect.

351164.long_answer: The Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) gene encodes the SHH morphogen that is secreted by the zone of polarizing activity in the developing limb bud. If the DNA sequence of the SHH gene itself is mutated or deleted, transcription of the gene is reduced or the mRNA/protein produced is defective, leading to decreased SHH protein levels and consequent disturbances in limb patterning along the anterior-posterior axis.

586806.long_answer: Cronkhite–Canada syndrome has no firmly established causative agent; current evidence indicates an idiopathic origin, with autoimmune mechanisms only suspected but unproven.

460912.long_answer: A Wright-Giemsa–stained peripheral blood smear allows direct microscopic examination of red cells, where the DNA remnants known as Howell-Jolly bodies appear as dark, round inclusions. In hereditary spherocytosis, hyposplenism or postsplenectomy reduces splenic clearance of these inclusions, so the smear is the standard test that reveals Howell-Jolly bodies.

500988.long_answer: Efficacy of the mRNA therapy for methylmalonic acidemia is being investigated in an interventional Phase 1/2 clinical trial in affected patients, where dosing, safety, pharmacodynamics and therapeutic benefit (e.g., reductions in methylmalonic acid levels) are systematically measured.

431355.long_answer: Chronic therapy for hypoparathyroidism relies on high-dose oral calcium and active vitamin D. Because parathyroid hormone is absent, the kidneys cannot efficiently reabsorb calcium; the excess filtered calcium leads to persistent hypercalciuria. Over years, this promotes calcium deposition within the renal parenchyma, causing nephrocalcinosis, a recognized long-term complication of conventional hypoparathyroidism treatment.

999594.long_answer: Fucosidosis is caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme α-L-fucosidase. Without this enzyme, fucose-containing oligosaccharide side-chains cannot be removed and degraded, leading to the intralysosomal build-up of fucose-rich glycoproteins (and related glycolipids). Thus, the principal macromolecules that accumulate in tissues and body fluids in fucosidosis are glycoproteins.

453032.long_answer: Doxorubicin intercalates DNA and poisons topoisomerase II, creating double-strand breaks that activate ATM/ATR kinases. This rapidly stabilises and activates p53, leading to a characteristic transcriptional programme: up-regulation of DNA-damage-response, cell-cycle-arrest and apoptotic genes (e.g., CDKN1A/p21, GADD45, BAX) and concurrent repression of many proliferation-associated transcripts. Thus, the net effect on the cellular transcriptome is a p53-dependent shift toward damage-response and death pathways while suppressing genes needed for growth and division.

402833.long_answer: Gorlin syndrome (also called nevoid basal-cell carcinoma syndrome) has been historically described in the pathology literature as “cystic hamartoma of the lung and kidney,” reflecting the multiple hamartomatous cysts that can develop in both organs alongside the better-known skin and jaw manifestations caused by germ-line PTCH1 mutations.

840401.long_answer: The most prevalent type of colour-blindness is red-green (specifically deuteranomaly/deuteranopia), which arises from mutations or unequal recombination affecting the medium-wavelength (green-sensitive) opsin gene OPN1MW located at Xq28 on the X chromosome. Defects in OPN1MW disrupt normal green-cone photopigment function, producing the characteristic red-green vision deficiency that is most common in the population.

681804.long_answer: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune neuromuscular disorder in which antibodies target acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. This impairs synaptic transmission, producing fluctuating skeletal-muscle weakness. Bulbar muscles that control swallowing and speech are commonly affected, so patients frequently experience dysphagia and difficulty chewing, especially after prolonged activity.

956835.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix glycoprotein fibrillin-1. Defective fibrillin-1 disrupts microfibril formation, leading to the characteristic skeletal, ocular (lens dislocation), and cardiovascular (aortic root dilatation) manifestations of the syndrome.

116175.long_answer: Mutations in the AIRE (Autoimmune Regulator) gene lead to autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1, historically known as Whitaker syndrome. Loss-of-function variants in AIRE impair central T-cell tolerance, resulting in multiorgan autoimmunity (chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, adrenal insufficiency, etc.). Hence, the disease beginning with “W” tied to AIRE mutations is Whitaker syndrome.

347130.long_answer: Hodgkin lymphoma arises from malignant transformation of germinal-center B lymphocytes; the characteristic Reed–Sternberg cells that define the disease are clonally derived from these B cells.

975454.long_answer: Blau syndrome is an autosomal-dominant granulomatous disease produced by gain-of-function mutations in the NOD2 (also known as CARD15) gene. This gene resides at chromosomal band 16q12, so pathogenic NOD2 variants on chromosome 16 are responsible for the disorder.

489641.long_answer: Real-time prenatal ultrasonography can directly visualize amniotic (constriction) bands encircling fetal limbs or digits and the resulting distal edema or deformities, thereby confirming constriction ring syndrome in utero.

248285.long_answer: In the punctate form of palmoplantar keratoderma, the lesions present as numerous discrete hyperkeratotic papules scattered over the palms and soles. This distinguishes it from the diffuse and focal forms, which show continuous thickening or localized plaques rather than individual papules.

961878.long_answer: The definitive way to diagnose and confirm oral lichen planus is to take an incisional mucosal biopsy of the affected area and examine the tissue histopathologically; the characteristic band-like lymphocytic infiltrate and basal cell degeneration seen microscopically establish the diagnosis.

286253.long_answer: Andersen’s disease (glycogen storage disease type IV) leads to abnormal glycogen deposition in the liver, progressing to hepatomegaly, cirrhosis, and liver failure. The medical specialty focused on diagnosing and managing liver disorders—hepatology (a branch of gastroenterology)—is therefore the primary specialty involved in treating these hepatic complications.

990396.long_answer: Lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia results from loss-of-function mutations in the STAR gene, which encodes the steroidogenic acute regulatory protein that transports cholesterol into mitochondria for steroid biosynthesis. The STAR gene is mapped to chromosome 8p11.2, and its disruption abolishes adrenal and gonadal steroid production, producing the classic lipoid CAH phenotype.

558607.long_answer: Banti’s syndrome—chronic congestive (hypersplenic) portal hypertension with massive splenomegaly—classically arises when the splenic vein becomes obstructed or thrombosed. Blockage of this vein impedes venous outflow from the spleen, producing sustained splenic congestion, portal-hypertensive changes, cytopenias and the clinical picture described by Banti.

580060.long_answer: Aniridia is a congenital disorder characterized by partial or complete absence of the iris and associated ocular abnormalities such as glaucoma, cataract, and foveal hypoplasia. Management of these eye‐specific problems falls under the expertise of ophthalmologists, the physicians who diagnose and treat diseases of the eye. Therefore, the relevant medical specialty is ophthalmology.

392582.long_answer: The cerebral aqueduct connects the third and fourth ventricles; if it becomes occluded after a traumatic brain injury, cerebrospinal fluid can no longer pass downstream. This causes CSF to accumulate in the lateral and third ventricles, enlarging them and raising intracranial pressure—a pattern characteristic of non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus.

618556.long_answer: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited (codominant) disorder in which misfolded α1-antitrypsin accumulates in hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum. The resulting chronic hepatitis and cirrhosis markedly raise the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma, making this genetic disease a well-established predisposing factor for HCC.

285691.long_answer: Andersen’s disease, the classic glycogen storage disease type IV, is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the GBE1 gene, which encodes the glycogen-branching enzyme. The same GBE1 mutations have been documented in families presenting with congenital arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (fetal akinesia deformation sequence), showing that defects in this single gene can lead to both Andersen’s disease and a form of arthrogryposis.

391158.long_answer: Phakomatosis pigmentovascularis is a rare congenital neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by the simultaneous presence of vascular malformations (capillary malformations) and pigmentary skin lesions (nevus flammeus with dermal melanocytosis). As a member of the phakomatoses, it involves developmental anomalies of tissues derived from the neuroectoderm, linking skin findings with potential ocular or neurologic manifestations.

316394.long_answer: Tietze syndrome is an inflammatory disorder of the costal cartilage that, like costochondritis, causes sharp chest wall pain. However, it is distinguished by visible or palpable swelling at the affected costochondral junctions, a feature typically absent in costochondritis. Because the pain locations and character are similar, the two conditions are frequently confused clinically, but the presence of localized swelling points to Tietze syndrome.

497916.long_answer: During ventricular fibrillation the ventricles quiver instead of pumping, so cardiac output and cerebral blood flow fall to near zero. Neurons tolerate only a few minutes without oxygen; after about 3–5 minutes of this global cerebral hypoxia-ischemia, neuronal death becomes permanent, producing irreversible brain damage.

252716.long_answer: The Scottish ophthalmologist Charles Howard Usher systematically studied families in which retinitis pigmentosa occurred together with congenital deafness and, in a 1914 report, established this combination as a single inherited disorder. His work defined the condition now called Usher syndrome—retinitis pigmentosa linked with deafness.

720988.long_answer: Hypoparathyroidism leads to hypocalcaemia, which increases neuromuscular excitability and can cause tetany of the laryngeal muscles. This may precipitate laryngospasm, producing stridor and acute airway obstruction, a recognised respiratory complication of the disorder.

305415.long_answer: Isotretinoin markedly reduces sebaceous gland activity, causing mucocutaneous dryness. More than 90 % of patients develop cheilitis—dry, inflamed, and sometimes fissured lips—as a characteristic and very common adverse effect.

383873.long_answer: Robinow syndrome can arise from mutations in several genes; the autosomal-recessive form is most often due to mutations in the ROR2 gene. ROR2 (receptor tyrosine kinase-like orphan receptor 2) is located on chromosome 9q22, making it the Robinow-associated gene situated on chromosome 9.

268128.long_answer: Among malignancies linked to ionizing radiation, leukemia (particularly acute myeloid and acute lymphoblastic forms) shows the strongest, well-documented association. High-dose radiation can damage hematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow, induce DNA double-strand breaks, and generate chromosomal translocations (e.g., t(15;17), t(9;22)), leading to malignant clonal expansion and the development of leukemia. Epidemiological evidence from atomic-bomb survivors, radiotherapy patients, and nuclear-industry accidents consistently demonstrates a markedly increased leukemia incidence after substantial ionizing radiation exposure.

285752.long_answer: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is a relentlessly progressive interstitial lung disease; numerous cohort studies show a median survival (and thus average life expectancy) of roughly three to five years from the time of diagnosis, making its prognosis comparable to many malignant cancers.

606030.long_answer: Lichen myxedematosus (scleromyxedema) is a primary cutaneous mucinosis characterized by papular skin lesions and dermal mucin deposition. Diagnosis and management of this skin-limited or systemic disorder are handled by dermatologists; thus, the relevant medical specialty is dermatology.

935591.long_answer: Calluses are thickened areas of stratum corneum. Keratolytic therapy employs agents such as salicylic acid or urea that break down keratin in this outer layer, softening the hyperkeratotic tissue so it loosens and sloughs off, thereby reducing the callus.

162283.long_answer: Dental remains of the South African australopithecine Paranthropus robustus consistently exhibit generalized, symmetrically distributed pitting and thinning of the enamel on many teeth. The uniform, bilateral pattern across the entire dentition matches the diagnostic presentation of the hereditary enamel defect amelogenesis imperfecta, leading paleo-anthropologists to conclude that this extinct hominid species suffered from that condition.

185895.long_answer: During gastrulation, cells leaving the primitive streak must undergo an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) to become the loose embryonic mesenchyme that will give rise to mesodermal tissues. Fibroblast-growth-factor (FGF) signals—particularly FGF8 acting through FGFR1 and the downstream MAPK/ERK cascade—are required for this process. FGF signaling suppresses E-cadherin expression, promotes cell migration, and enables the epiblast cells to delaminate and adopt a mesenchymal phenotype. Loss or inhibition of FGF signaling blocks EMT and mesenchyme formation, underscoring its essential role in embryonic mesenchyme development.

196864.long_answer: Acromesomelic dysplasia of the Grebe and Hunter-Thompson types is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the GDF5 (growth differentiation factor 5) gene. GDF5 encodes a bone morphogenetic protein crucial for chondrogenesis; it directs proliferation and differentiation of growth-plate chondrocytes and the formation of cartilage and joints. When GDF5 is mutated, normal cartilage development is impaired, resulting in the severe limb-shortening characteristic of acromesomelic dysplasia.

334546.long_answer: BMPR2 (bone morphogenetic protein receptor type 2) is the most commonly mutated gene in heritable pulmonary arterial hypertension. It encodes a receptor for bone morphogenetic proteins, key regulators of osteoblast differentiation and overall bone formation and resorption, linking the gene directly to bone metabolism.

393391.long_answer: Both Blue cone monochromacy (BCM) and X-linked cone dystrophy have been repeatedly linked to the same missense change in the X-chromosomal cone opsin genes, a substitution of cysteine with arginine at position 203 (C203R, p.Cys203Arg) in the OPN1LW/OPN1MW opsins. This single point mutation disrupts proper folding and trafficking of the L- and M-cone photopigments, leading to absent or progressively dysfunctional red/green cones—producing the clinical pictures of BCM and cone dystrophy, respectively.

508800.long_answer: SATB2 (Special AT-rich Sequence-Binding Protein 2) encodes a chromatin-organizing transcription factor that recruits histone-modifying enzymes, thereby influencing epigenetic regulation of gene expression during craniofacial development. Pathogenic variants or altered expression of SATB2 have been repeatedly linked to abnormal palatogenesis, leading to cleft lip and/or cleft palate in both syndromic and nonsyndromic cases.

498928.long_answer: Compression of spinal nerves or their roots leads to damage and dysfunction of those nerve roots, producing a neuropathy known as radiculopathy. In radiculopathy, mechanical pressure or inflammation at the spinal nerve root impairs sensory and/or motor function in the corresponding dermatome or myotome, distinguishing it from peripheral mononeuropathies or polyneuropathies.

226349.long_answer: Venous compliance reflects how easily veins expand to store blood. When compliance is high, veins accommodate more blood at a given pressure, so less blood is propelled back to the right atrium, lowering venous return. Conversely, when compliance falls (e.g., via venoconstriction), veins become stiffer, their volume decreases, central venous pressure rises, and a larger fraction of blood is returned to the heart. Thus, venous return changes inversely with venous compliance.

560302.long_answer: Myhre syndrome is caused by heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the SMAD4 gene, a key intracellular mediator of TGF-β signalling. Independent pathogenic variants in this same gene have also been reported in families with autosomal-dominant keratosis pilaris atrophicans, a recognized subtype of keratosis pilaris. Thus, SMAD4 is the common genetic link between Myhre syndrome and that specific form of keratosis pilaris.

845609.long_answer: N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase (the lysosomal enzyme encoded by the GALNS gene) catalyzes the hydrolysis of the 6-sulfate group from N-acetyl-D-galactosamine-6-sulfate residues that occur in certain glycosaminoglycans, chiefly keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate. Removal of this sulfate group is an essential step in the lysosomal degradation (breakdown) pathway of these molecules. When the enzyme is deficient, as in Morquio A (mucopolysaccharidosis IVA), undegraded keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate accumulate within cells. Therefore, by carrying out this desulfation reaction, N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase indeed promotes the normal breakdown of chondroitin sulfate.

795803.long_answer: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism accompanied by anosmia characterizes Kallmann syndrome. The classical and best-established genetic cause of this syndrome is loss-of-function mutations in the KAL1 (now termed ANOS1) gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein anosmin-1 required for migration of olfactory and GnRH neurons. Disruption of KAL1/ANOS1 impairs olfactory bulb development, producing anosmia, and prevents GnRH neurons from reaching the hypothalamus, leading to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

102990.long_answer: Carbamazepine, a sodium-channel–blocking anticonvulsant used for focal and generalized tonic-clonic seizures, is contraindicated in absence (petit mal) epilepsy because it can increase thalamocortical burst firing and has been repeatedly shown to precipitate or worsen absence seizures in both clinical studies and practice guidelines.

323701.long_answer: TNF receptor associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) is an autosomal-dominant autoinflammatory disorder caused by pathogenic mutations in the TNFRSF1A gene, which encodes the type 1 tumor necrosis factor receptor (TNF-R1). These mutations impair normal TNF-R1 folding and signaling, leading to recurrent fever episodes and systemic inflammation characteristic of TRAPS.

367865.long_answer: Cushing syndrome is characterized by chronic excess glucocorticoids, producing central (truncal) obesity and violaceous abdominal striae. Cortisol also exerts mineralocorticoid-like actions and increases vascular responsiveness to catecholamines, leading to secondary hypertension.

633786.long_answer: An activating mutation in the parathyroid hormone 1 receptor gene (PTH1R), most often the R150C variant, has been documented in patients with both Metachondromatosis and Ollier disease. This gain-of-function change alters PTH/PTHrP signalling in growth-plate cartilage, promoting the formation of multiple enchondromas and osteochondromas that characterize these disorders.

220570.long_answer: Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is a granulomatous disorder marked by recurrent episodes of facial (VII cranial nerve) paralysis, often accompanied by orofacial edema and fissured tongue. It is part of the spectrum of orofacial granulomatosis and can occur in association with other granulomatous diseases such as Crohn’s disease or sarcoidosis.

885575.long_answer: Achondrogenesis type 1B is an autosomal-recessive, lethal chondrodysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC26A2 gene (also known as DTDST). SLC26A2 encodes a sulfate transporter that is essential for proper sulfation of cartilage proteoglycans; defective sulfate transport disrupts cartilage matrix formation, leading to the severe skeletal abnormalities characteristic of achondrogenesis type 1B.

436635.long_answer: Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is an autoimmune blistering disorder of the skin and mucous membranes. Diagnosis relies on dermatologic evaluation, skin biopsy with immunofluorescence, and serologic testing, and treatment typically involves topical or systemic immunosuppressive therapies overseen by dermatologists. Therefore, the specialty most directly responsible for diagnosing and managing EBA is Dermatology.

559340.long_answer: In hyperprolactinemic women, elevated prolactin suppresses hypothalamic GnRH release, lowering LH and FSH secretion. The resulting hypoestrogenism reduces bone mineral density through increased bone resorption and decreased formation, leading to osteoporosis.

829681.long_answer: Brazilian hemorrhagic fever is caused by the Sabiá arenavirus, a highly contagious viral hemorrhagic fever. Management requires expertise in diagnosing, treating, and containing severe viral infections, which falls under the purview of infectious disease specialists, who coordinate antiviral therapy, isolation precautions, and public-health measures.

447110.long_answer: Because the patients are children, the specialty that focuses on the diagnosis and management of health problems in this age group is Pediatrics. Pediatricians are trained to evaluate and treat sleep-related disorders in children, including those precipitated by substances such as caffeine.

673700.long_answer: Drugs that block angiogenesis—most commonly anti-VEGF angiogenesis inhibitors such as bevacizumab—suppress the action of vascular endothelial growth factor, thereby preventing new blood-vessel formation. This same mechanism is used to treat choroidal neovascularization in presumed ocular histoplasmosis syndrome and to restrict tumor blood supply in several cancers.

829207.long_answer: Heterozygous truncating mutations in the SRCAP (SNF2-related CREBBP Activator Protein) gene have been identified in individuals diagnosed with Nasodigitoacoustic (Keipert) syndrome. These loss-of-function variants disrupt SRCAP’s role as a chromatin-remodelling co-activator of CREBBP, leading to the characteristic triad of a broad nasal tip (naso-), brachydactyly/syndactyly (digito-) and sensorineural hearing loss (acoustic). The detection of the same SRCAP mutations in both classic Floating-Harbor syndrome and patients labelled as Nasodigitoacoustic syndrome has established SRCAP haploinsufficiency as the causal mechanism for this condition.

623273.long_answer: Phenylketonuria is most commonly caused by mutations in the PAH gene, which encodes phenylalanine hydroxylase. Loss-of-function variants in PAH impair conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, leading to toxic phenylalanine accumulation. If untreated, this neurotoxicity results in severe cognitive impairment and other mental disorders.

727387.long_answer: Several dysmorphology reviews note that proximal femoral focal deficiency (PFFD) represents the lower-limb manifestation of, and is probably identical to, the femur-fibula-ulna (FFU) syndrome/complex. Both conditions show congenital absence or severe hypoplasia of the proximal femur, often accompanied by fibular and, variably, ulnar deficiencies, suggesting they are part of the same malformation spectrum rather than separate entities.

472202.long_answer: People with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) commonly experience recurrent, vivid nightmares that replay traumatic events. These persistent distressing dreams can lead to an intense fear of dreaming itself—oneirophobia—because the person dreads reliving the trauma each time they sleep.

487479.long_answer: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy is most often caused by mutations in NDP, FZD4, LRP5 or TSPAN12, all of which encode components of the canonical Wnt (Norrin-FZD4-LRP5) signaling cascade. This Wnt/β-catenin pathway is essential for normal eye morphogenesis and for guiding retinal vascular development; disruption of its signaling leads to the abnormal, incomplete blood vessel growth that characterizes FEVR.

295643.long_answer: Ectodermal dysplasia is a group of inherited disorders in which tissues derived from the embryonic ectoderm—most notably hair, teeth, nails, and sweat glands—develop abnormally. Mutations in genes such as EDA, EDAR, or EDARADD disrupt signaling pathways (e.g., ectodysplasin-NF-κB) that guide ectodermal organ formation, leading to sparse or absent hair (hypotrichosis), missing or cone-shaped teeth, dystrophic nails, and reduced or absent sweat glands (hypohidrosis or anhidrosis).

762035.long_answer: The vast majority of classic homocystinuria cases result from a deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase (CBS), which catalyzes the conversion of homocysteine to cystathionine in the trans-sulfuration pathway. Loss of CBS activity leads to accumulation of homocysteine and its metabolites, producing the characteristic vascular, ocular, skeletal, and neurodevelopmental manifestations of homocystinuria.

780261.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the SOX10 gene, which encodes a transcription factor essential for neural-crest development, are a recognized cause of Waardenburg syndrome type 2E. Because SOX10 is also required for proper maturation of glial cells and neural circuitry, loss-of-function mutations can lead to additional neurodevelopmental abnormalities, and several patients with SOX10 mutations have presented with autism-like behavioral and cognitive symptoms alongside the characteristic pigmentary changes and sensorineural deafness of Waardenburg syndrome.

627573.long_answer: Mutations in the SPG7 gene (encoding the mitochondrial protein paraplegin) are a well-established cause of autosomal-recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia type 7. Numerous clinical and genetic studies have shown that the same SPG7 mutations frequently produce cerebellar ataxia—either isolated or combined with spasticity—demonstrating that this single gene is involved in both hereditary spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia.

589966.long_answer: A cranial computed tomography (CT) scan rapidly visualizes brain structures and clearly delineates the ventricular system; enlargement of the ventricles on CT indicates cerebrospinal fluid accumulation, making it the standard imaging test for diagnosing hydrocephalus.

364201.long_answer: Case reports and small clinical observations indicate that the atypical antipsychotic quetiapine can markedly reduce the visual distortions, after-images, and ‘trailing’ phenomena seen in Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder (HPPD). Improvement is thought to stem from quetiapine’s antagonism of 5-HT2A receptors (implicated in psychedelic-induced visual symptoms) together with its relatively low, transient dopamine-D2 occupancy, making it better tolerated than other antipsychotics that often exacerbate HPPD. Thus, quetiapine has emerged as the antipsychotic showing the most promise for treating HPPD-related visual disturbances.

532371.long_answer: When prostaglandin E1 is infused for prolonged periods to keep the ductus arteriosus open, neonates can develop periostitis—subperiosteal new-bone formation and cortical hyperostosis of the long bones. This bone reaction appears after days to weeks of continuous therapy and regresses once the prostaglandin is discontinued, making it a recognized adverse effect of long-term use.

907940.long_answer: For vein of Galen aneurysmal malformations, the current standard of care is endovascular embolization, in which a microcatheter is navigated into the feeding vessels and occlusive materials (e.g., liquid adhesive, coils, or Onyx) are deliberately delivered to create an intravascular embolus. This targeted occlusion reduces the arteriovenous shunt, alleviates high-flow cardiac load, and preserves surrounding brain tissue, making it the preferred treatment over open surgery or conservative management.

565660.long_answer: Asfotase alfa is a recombinant form of tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase used as enzyme-replacement therapy. It is FDA- and EMA-approved for perinatal/infantile-onset and juvenile-onset hypophosphatasia, where it supplements the deficient alkaline phosphatase activity, reduces accumulation of inorganic pyrophosphate, and thereby promotes normal bone mineralization.

924729.long_answer: Current psychiatric consensus (e.g., DSM-5) places selective mutism within the anxiety-disorder spectrum because the vast majority of affected children fulfill criteria for social anxiety disorder. Selective mutism is therefore regarded as an early-onset or more severe variant of social anxiety disorder, not a separate, unrelated condition.

124145.long_answer: The hallmarks of Spondylocamptodactyly syndrome are (1) congenital or early-onset camptodactyly—fixed flexion deformity of the fingers—and (2) progressive vertebral dysplasia producing kyphosis/kyphoscoliosis. These two skeletal abnormalities are consistently present and are used clinically to recognise the syndrome.

897136.long_answer: Amusia is a neurological disorder in which individuals cannot perceive or recognize musical tones, melodies, or rhythms, even though their peripheral hearing, language skills, and general intellectual abilities are normal. The condition can be congenital or acquired after brain damage, but in all cases the hallmark is a specific deficit in music perception or production without broader auditory impairment.

152555.long_answer: Cyclosporiasis is caused by the coccidian protozoan Cyclospora cayetanensis. Its spherical oocysts in stool become variably acid-fast and appear pink-red when a modified Ziehl-Neelsen (modified acid-fast) stain is applied, allowing definitive microscopic identification of the pathogen.

259000.long_answer: According to Rachman’s three-pathway theory and subsequent dental‐anxiety research, most people acquire dental fear after experiencing a painful or traumatic dental visit themselves; this direct personal experience establishes a conditioned association between dental treatment and pain/distress. Therefore, the classical (direct) conditioning pathway is the commonest route through which dental fear develops.

740707.long_answer: Multicentric carpotarsal osteolysis syndrome frequently evolves into a focal-segmental glomerulosclerosis–type nephropathy. Case reports show that treatment with the calcineurin-inhibitor immunosuppressant cyclosporine A reduced proteinuria and helped stabilise renal function in affected patients, so this drug is recommended when nephropathy develops.

429779.long_answer: Hemolytic anemia causes accelerated destruction of red blood cells, generating excess unconjugated bilirubin that produces hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice. The increased clearance of damaged RBCs in the reticulo-endothelial system, especially the spleen, leads to splenic hypertrophy and clinically evident splenomegaly.

410165.long_answer: In β-thalassemia, deficient β-globin synthesis causes the body to compensate by increasing production of the δ-globin chains that form Hemoglobin A₂ (α₂δ₂). As a result, patients show a persistently elevated Hb A₂ fraction (typically >3.5% of total hemoglobin), which is the classic laboratory hallmark used in screening and diagnosing β-thalassemia trait and disease.

939335.long_answer: Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is a hereditary polyposis and cancer-predisposition disorder caused by germline loss-of-function mutations in the STK11 gene (also called LKB1) on chromosome 19p13.3. STK11 encodes a serine/threonine kinase that acts as a tumor-suppressor by regulating cellular polarity and AMPK signaling; its inactivation leads to the hamartomatous polyps and increased malignancy risk characteristic of the syndrome.

649161.long_answer: In men with type 1 diabetes, chronic hyperglycaemia often damages the autonomic nerves that supply the penile tissues. This diabetic autonomic neuropathy impairs the neuro-vascular signals required to initiate and maintain an erection, making it one of the most frequent biologic causes of erectile dysfunction in this population.

501155.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the FREM1 gene (FRAS1-related extracellular matrix protein 1) cause the syndrome known as “bifid nose, renal agenesis, and anorectal malformations” (BNAR). Patients with FREM1 mutations characteristically present with a midline bifid nose together with anorectal anomalies (e.g., imperforate anus) and renal defects (such as unilateral or bilateral renal agenesis), establishing FREM1 as the causal gene for this triad of abnormalities.

276560.long_answer: Curry–Jones syndrome is caused by a recurrent post-zygotic missense mutation in the SMO gene (Smoothened, a Hedgehog-signaling receptor). Mosaic activation of SMO (e.g., p.Leu412Phe) drives the characteristic craniofacial, limb, and cutaneous abnormalities observed in this syndrome.
