347155.long_answer: The most severe form of von Willebrand disease is Type 3, which results from virtually complete absence of von Willebrand factor. Type 3 VWD is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner: affected individuals carry pathogenic variants in both alleles of the VWF gene, while heterozygous carriers are typically asymptomatic or only mildly affected.

821618.long_answer: The constellation of type II diabetes mellitus accompanied by clinical signs of androgen excess (such as hirsutism and virilization) is called Achard–Thiers syndrome. It is named after the French physicians Émile Achard and Joseph Thiers, who first described the condition in 1921.

131350.long_answer: Aromatase excess syndrome is caused by gain-of-function genomic rearrangements (duplications, inversions or promoter fusions) that increase expression of the CYP19A1 gene on chromosome 15q21.2, which encodes the aromatase enzyme. Overexpression of CYP19A1 elevates estrogen synthesis, producing the clinical features of the syndrome such as gynecomastia and advanced bone age.

250427.long_answer: In industrialized countries, stringent screening of blood products has largely removed transfusion-related risk. Today, the great majority of new hepatitis C infections arise from percutaneous exposure to contaminated blood when people share needles, syringes, or other injection equipment—i.e., injection drug use is the dominant transmission route.

106829.long_answer: Yes. The most widely used laboratory method for confirming schistosomiasis is microscopic detection of Schistosoma eggs in excreta. Eggs of Schistosoma mansoni, S. japonicum and related intestinal species are sought in stool samples (e.g., Kato-Katz thick smear), while eggs of Schistosoma haematobium are typically detected in urine (e.g., urine filtration or sedimentation techniques). These parasitological examinations remain the diagnostic gold standard in endemic areas, and positive findings in either stool or urine definitively establish infection.

971532.long_answer: In many hospitalized alcohol-dependent patients, portal hypertension from alcoholic liver disease produces splenomegaly. The enlarged spleen sequesters and prematurely destroys circulating platelets (hypersplenism), leading to a reduced platelet count—thrombocytopenia.

471835.long_answer: Diamond-Blackfan anemia (DBA) is a congenital hypoplastic anemia in which erythroid precursors in the bone marrow are markedly reduced, leading to pure red-cell aplasia. Besides hematologic manifestations, children with DBA commonly show growth retardation; several studies and case reports document true growth hormone deficiency in a subset of these patients. Thus, DBA is the congenital disorder of red cell precursor deficiency that can also present with growth hormone deficiency.

841320.long_answer: In the 5q- syndrome, deletion of the chromosome segment 5q33 removes one copy of the ribosomal protein gene RPS14. Haploinsufficiency of RPS14 impairs ribosome biogenesis in erythroid precursors, activates p53-mediated apoptosis, and thereby produces the characteristic macrocytic anemia seen in this deletion syndrome.

741522.long_answer: Under the U.S. Orphan Drug Act a condition is classified as a rare disease when it affects fewer than 200,000 people nationwide. Arachnoiditis—including adhesive arachnoiditis—is listed by the National Institutes of Health’s Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center (GARD) and by the National Organization for Rare Disorders (NORD) as a rare disorder. Epidemiologic estimates place its prevalence well below the 200,000-person threshold, and authoritative sources such as the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke describe it as a “rare” condition. Therefore, within the United States arachnoiditis is officially regarded as a rare disease.

327155.long_answer: Saal Greenstein syndrome has been associated with episodes of hydrocephalus, a disorder in which cerebrospinal fluid accumulates within the brain’s ventricles, causing their expansion and raising intracranial pressure.

538712.long_answer: In newborns and infants with Down syndrome, somatic mutations in the GATA1 gene (producing the truncated “GATA1-short” protein) drive transient abnormal myelopoiesis and Down-syndrome–associated acute megakaryoblastic leukemia. The altered GATA1 impairs normal megakaryocyte differentiation and leads to excessive proliferation of platelet precursor (megakaryocytic) cells.

495861.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis is confirmed when bilateral sacroiliitis is seen on imaging. The standard diagnostic technique is a plain anteroposterior X-ray of the pelvis (sacroiliac joints), which visualises joint-space narrowing, sclerosis, and erosions characteristic of sacroiliitis.

168974.long_answer: Cutaneous small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis usually resolves spontaneously, but lesions persisting beyond about 3–4 weeks are commonly treated with colchicine. Colchicine inhibits microtubule-dependent neutrophil chemotaxis and degranulation, reducing the immune-complex–driven inflammation in the small dermal vessels and hastening clearance of the rash.

723033.long_answer: Sugarman syndrome is another name for familial juvenile hyperuricaemic nephropathy, a kidney disorder most often caused by pathogenic variants in the UMOD gene (and less commonly REN or MUC1). Reported families show vertical transmission with affected individuals in successive generations and equal involvement of males and females, establishing an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

169556.long_answer: Linezolid, an oxazolidinone antibiotic used for serious Gram-positive infections (e.g., MRSA, VRE), is a well-documented cause of black hairy tongue. The drug alters normal oral flora and promotes keratin accumulation on the filiform papillae, leading to the characteristic dark, hairy appearance of the tongue. This adverse effect is listed in the FDA label and multiple clinical reports.

206551.long_answer: Excess vitamin A activates osteoclasts and suppresses osteoblast function, accelerating bone turnover and thereby increasing the rate of bone resorption.

471048.long_answer: In oral squamous cell carcinoma, the depth of invasion (tumor depth) is one of the strongest independent predictors of outcome. As the tumor extends more deeply into underlying tissues, the likelihood of occult cervical lymph-node metastasis, local recurrence, and reduced disease-specific or overall survival rises markedly. Consequently, depth of invasion is now incorporated into the AJCC/UICC staging system and guides decisions on elective neck dissection and adjuvant therapy.

813733.long_answer: Olfactory Reference Syndrome is viewed as an obsessive-compulsive–spectrum disorder. The first-line pharmacologic treatment mirrors OCD management, with selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors—such as fluoxetine, sertraline, paroxetine, or fluvoxamine—consistently shown to reduce the intrusive odor preoccupation and associated anxiety. Thus, SSRIs are the drug class most commonly prescribed for ORS.

513209.long_answer: The PKD1 gene, whose mutations are responsible for the majority of autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease cases, is located on the short arm of chromosome 16 (region 16p13.3).

107678.long_answer: In some individuals with WAGR syndrome the chromosomal deletion extends telomeric to PAX6 and removes one copy of the BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor) gene. Haploinsufficiency of BDNF disrupts central appetite-regulating pathways, producing marked hyperphagia and early-onset obesity, hence the designation “WAGRO” (WAGR-obesity) when BDNF is deleted.

413038.long_answer: The great majority of idiopathic acute anterior uveitis—the most common form of autoimmune uveitis—is strongly associated with the class I major histocompatibility complex antigen HLA-B27. Approximately one-half to two-thirds of patients with this uveitis carry the HLA-B27 allele, and its presence markedly increases the risk of developing recurrent autoimmune ocular inflammation as well as related spondyloarthropathies.

909539.long_answer: Risk variants (G1 and G2) of the APOL1 gene, located on chromosome 22q13, are strongly associated with ‘hypertensive’ nephropathy—kidney failure historically attributed to hypertension, particularly in individuals of African ancestry. These APOL1 variants increase susceptibility to progressive glomerulosclerosis and ESRD independent of blood-pressure level, explaining much of the excess risk previously ascribed to hypertensive nephropathy.

869067.long_answer: Comparative genomic and DNA–DNA hybridization studies of the Bacillus cereus group demonstrated that strains classified as Bacillus weihenstephanensis are genetically indistinguishable from Bacillus mycoides. On this basis, taxonomists concluded that B. weihenstephanensis is not a separate species but a heterotypic synonym of Bacillus mycoides.

888845.long_answer: Rud syndrome—a rare constellation of congenital ichthyosis, hypogonadism, short stature and intellectual disability—has been variably associated with ocular findings. Several case reports describe retinal degeneration typical of retinitis pigmentosa, but other documented patients lack any retinal changes. Because this pigmentary retinopathy is present in only a subset of reported cases, retinitis pigmentosa is considered an inconsistently reported manifestation of Rud syndrome.

936795.long_answer: Both presbyopia, the age-related loss of accommodation, and eye strain (asthenopia) commonly present with headaches—typically frontal or temporal pain that appears after prolonged near-vision tasks—because excessive or ineffective accommodative effort fatigues the ciliary and extra-ocular muscles.

556333.long_answer: The osteon, or Haversian system, is the basic functional unit of compact bone. Each osteon consists of concentric lamellae of mineralized matrix surrounding a central (Haversian) canal that houses blood vessels and nerves. During craniofacial bone healing and regeneration, new osteons are laid down by osteoblasts, remodeling the bone and restoring its mechanical strength and vascular supply, making the osteon critical to successful craniofacial regeneration.

230167.long_answer: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in the FOXC2 transcription-factor gene cause the autosomal-dominant disorder called lymphedema–distichiasis syndrome. A hallmark of the condition is distichiasis—a second row of eyelashes—together with primary lymphatic dysfunction that produces chronic swelling of the limbs (lymphedema), typically beginning in adolescence. The FOXC2 gene’s role in lymphatic valve and eyelid development explains these characteristic clinical features.

155216.long_answer: Mutations in the PHEX gene, located on the X chromosome (Xp22.1), cause X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets. Because the pathogenic allele on one X chromosome is sufficient to produce disease in both males (hemizygous) and heterozygous females, the trait follows an X-linked dominant pattern of inheritance.

836578.long_answer: Caroli disease is a congenital disorder characterized by segmental cystic dilatation of the intra-hepatic bile ducts. It represents a ductal-plate malformation that often coexists with congenital hepatic fibrosis (the combination is termed Caroli syndrome) and is frequently seen in patients who have autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease. Thus, Caroli disease is the liver condition associated with both congenital hepatic fibrosis and polycystic kidney disease.

460029.long_answer: Yes. Inborn errors of metabolism are hereditary disorders caused by pathogenic variants in genes encoding metabolic enzymes or transporters. Modern clinical practice guidelines recommend genetic testing—ranging from single-gene analysis to multigene panels, whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing—as a key tool for confirming a biochemical diagnosis, guiding treatment, and enabling family counseling. Licensed physicians can order these tests through certified clinical laboratories and interpret the results in the context of the patient’s clinical and biochemical findings. Thus, performing (i.e., ordering, overseeing, and utilizing) genetic testing for suspected inborn errors of metabolism is a standard component of medical care.

967331.long_answer: Hereditary pyropoikilocytosis (HPP) results when an individual inherits two deleterious alleles—often involving α- or β-spectrin mutations—leading to severe membrane instability of red blood cells. Because disease expression requires biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) mutations, HPP follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

933892.long_answer: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (an X-linked combined immunodeficiency caused by mutations in the WAS gene) is classically marked by the triad of eczema, thrombocytopenia with small platelets, and bleeding manifestations such as bloody diarrhea. Lymphocytes from affected patients show abnormally low 5′-nucleotidase activity, a laboratory clue that helps distinguish this disorder from other immunodeficiencies.

605705.long_answer: Rüdiger originally described the EEC (Ectrodactyly–Ectodermal-dysplasia–Cleft lip/palate) syndrome. This condition is characterized by limb split-hand/foot malformations, ectodermal dysplasia features and an orofacial cleft, most frequently a cleft palate. Hence, the cleft-palate-containing syndrome associated with Rüdiger syndrome is EEC syndrome.

312460.long_answer: Craniofrontonasal dysplasia is caused by pathogenic variants in the EFNB1 gene. Definitive prenatal confirmation therefore requires molecular analysis of fetal DNA obtained through invasive sampling procedures. Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) in the first trimester or amniocentesis in the second trimester provides fetal cells that can be tested for the EFNB1 mutation known in the family, thereby confirming the diagnosis before birth.

130884.long_answer: The majority of otherwise unexplained cases of short stature accompanied by late onset of pubertal development are due to Constitutional Growth Delay, a benign variant in which children grow at a normal velocity but follow a delayed growth curve, entering puberty and achieving final adult height later than their peers without underlying endocrine or genetic pathology.

262584.long_answer: Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa is an inherited blistering disorder caused by defects in type VII collagen that make the skin extremely fragile. Because the manifestations are primarily cutaneous—recurrent blisters, erosions, scarring, and chronic wounds—the specialty most directly responsible for diagnosis, ongoing management, and coordination of wound care is dermatology.

844984.long_answer: The electrocardiographic finding considered virtually pathognomonic for digoxin toxicity is paroxysmal atrial tachycardia accompanied by second-degree (usually 2:1) atrioventricular block. Digoxin increases atrial automaticity while simultaneously enhancing vagal tone at the AV node; this unique combination produces a rapid atrial rhythm that is intermittently blocked at the AV node, yielding the characteristic pattern on ECG.

204955.long_answer: Wallis–Zieff–Goldblatt syndrome is a rare skeletal dysplasia in which growth deficiency predominantly affects the middle segments of the limbs (forearms and lower legs). This pattern of disproportionate limb shortening is classified as mesomelic, so the syndrome produces mesomelic short stature.

514205.long_answer: In AIDS dysmorphic syndrome, enlargement or abnormal firmness of lymph nodes—termed lymphadenopathy—is frequently observed. This reflects chronic immune activation and viral infection of lymphoid tissues, making lymphadenopathy a characteristic clinical finding in affected individuals.

833248.long_answer: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH) is mediated by Donath–Landsteiner IgG auto-antibodies that cause complement-dependent hemolysis. The chronic form was classically linked to tertiary syphilis, whereas the acute, self-limited form occurs mainly in children after certain viral illnesses. Among these, measles virus infection is the prototypical and most frequently cited precipitating infection in the literature, making measles virus the virus classically associated with the acute form of PCH.

696557.long_answer: For aggressive non-Hodgkin lymphomas, especially diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, clinicians use the International Prognostic Index (IPI). The IPI combines five readily measured clinical factors—age, serum LDH, performance status, Ann Arbor stage, and number of extranodal sites—to stratify patients into risk groups and predict overall survival and treatment outcome.

895290.long_answer: Acute intermittent porphyria is an autosomal-dominant porphyrin metabolism disorder caused by deficient porphobilinogen deaminase. The enzymatic block leads to accumulation of porphobilinogen and other porphyrin precursors that precipitate acute neurovisceral attacks, characterized by severe abdominal pain, autonomic instability, and dramatic neurological crises such as motor neuropathy, seizures, and psychiatric symptoms.

354297.long_answer: Yes. NYU Grossman School of Medicine (part of NYU Langone Health) operates the Dysautonomia Center, which includes the Familial Dysautonomia Treatment & Research Center. Founded more than four decades ago, this multidisciplinary program—directed by faculty such as Dr. Horacio Kaufmann—provides comprehensive clinical care, genetic counseling, and research specifically for patients with familial dysautonomia (Riley–Day syndrome). It is one of the world’s principal referral and treatment centers for this rare hereditary autonomic neuropathy, confirming that NYU Grossman School of Medicine does indeed have a dedicated treatment center for familial dysautonomia.

221811.long_answer: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency results from pathogenic variants in the CYP21A2 gene. CYP21A2, located in the HLA class III region on chromosome 6p21.3, encodes the cytochrome P450 21-hydroxylase enzyme required for cortisol and aldosterone synthesis. Loss-of-function mutations disrupt steroidogenesis, leading to the classic and non-classic forms of CAH.

120945.long_answer: Brunner syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MAOA gene, which normally degrades monoamines. The resulting MAOA deficiency prevents normal breakdown of serotonin, leading to markedly elevated serotonin levels; this excess serotonin is a hallmark biochemical feature of the disorder and is linked to the impulsive aggression and other neurobehavioral symptoms seen in affected individuals.

948210.long_answer: In histidine catabolism, urocanase (urocanate hydratase) converts urocanic acid to 4-imidazolone-5-propionic acid. When urocanase is deficient, this step is blocked, causing urocanic acid to accumulate and be excreted in excess in the urine (urocanic aciduria).

505441.long_answer: The Ponseti method is a serial casting technique specifically designed for correcting congenital clubfoot (talipes equinovarus). Clubfoot is a common foot deformity seen in infants with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, and numerous clinical studies confirm that Ponseti casting followed by bracing effectively corrects the equinus, cavus, adductus, and varus components of the deformity in this population.

239359.long_answer: Kabuki syndrome—also called Kabuki make-up syndrome—is a congenital disorder whose hallmark facial features include long palpebral fissures with eversion of the lateral third of the lower eyelid and frequent upper-eyelid ptosis. A consistent systemic manifestation is mild-to-moderate intellectual disability. The combination of ptosis and cognitive impairment, together with post-natal growth retardation and skeletal anomalies, forms the classic clinical picture of Kabuki syndrome, which is most often caused by pathogenic variants in the KMT2D or KDM6A genes.

882254.long_answer: Glycogen storage diseases predominantly involve the liver, the body’s central organ for glycogen metabolism. Hepatocytes synthesize glycogen after meals (glycogenesis) and break it down during fasting (glycogenolysis); defects in these pathways lead to hepatic enlargement, hypoglycemia, and other features characteristic of glycogen storage disorders.

247667.long_answer: Placental site nodules are benign residual foci of intermediate trophoblast that most commonly arise in the endocervical canal; thus, the uterine cervix is the part of the female reproductive system that can be affected in this form of gestational trophoblastic disease.

508196.long_answer: Because skeletal muscle glycogenolysis is blocked in McArdle disease, contracting muscle must obtain ATP by adenylate kinase (2 ADP → ATP + AMP). The excess AMP is then deaminated by myoadenylate deaminase, producing inosine-5′-monophosphate (IMP) and releasing free ammonia. This AMP-to-IMP deamination constitutes the key step of the purine nucleotide cycle, making this pathway the principal source of the exercise-induced ammonia seen in individuals with McArdle disease.

560688.long_answer: The BK polyomavirus possesses a circular double-stranded DNA genome of roughly 5,100 base pairs, commonly described as about 5 kilobases in length.

224520.long_answer: The optic nerve (cranial nerve II) carries the axons of retinal ganglion cells, conveying visual signals from the retina through the optic chiasm and optic tracts to central visual relay nuclei in the brain, making it the cranial nerve responsible for transmitting visual information.

238028.long_answer: Camurati-Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia) is most often caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the TGFB1 gene, which encodes transforming growth factor-β1. Excessive TGFB1 signaling leads to hyperostosis of the diaphyses; the resulting thickened cortical bone can compress adjacent neurovascular structures, producing nerve damage such as cranial nerve palsies or peripheral neuropathies.

562488.long_answer: Type III galactosemia results from UDP-galactose-4-epimerase deficiency, which blocks normal galactose metabolism. Accumulated galactose and its toxic metabolite galactitol damage the liver, leading to jaundice. Eliminating dietary sources of galactose—primarily lactose-containing milk and dairy—prevents substrate buildup, thereby averting hepatic injury and jaundice. Hence, a strict galactose-free (lactose-free) diet is the recommended management.

890874.long_answer: Runs of premature ventricular contractions can degenerate into ventricular tachycardia. In ventricular tachycardia the ventricles beat rapidly and ineffectively, causing a sudden drop in cardiac output and cerebral perfusion, which often produces hypotension and syncope.

254985.long_answer: Heyde’s syndrome describes the well-established association in which severe aortic stenosis causes high-shear fragmentation of von Willebrand factor multimers, leading to an acquired type 2A von Willebrand disease and resultant bleeding from intestinal angiodysplasias. Thus, the coexistence of aortic stenosis and gastrointestinal bleeding is recognized clinically as Heyde’s syndrome.

996777.long_answer: Tokophobia is a specific phobic anxiety disorder characterized by an intense, pathological fear of pregnancy and childbirth. In affected women, this fear can become so overwhelming that they request an elective cesarean section to avoid labor, despite the absence of obstetric indications. Tokophobia is recognized in psychiatric and obstetric literature as a clinically significant condition that can arise in pregnancy, often requiring psychological support or counseling.

550671.long_answer: A localized abnormal-cell phenomenon in the pancreas corresponds to carcinoma in situ, which in the TNM system is classified as Tis (tumor in situ), with no regional lymph-node involvement (N0) and no distant metastasis (M0).

885619.long_answer: Klumpke's paralysis is produced by injury to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, which is formed by the ventral rami of the eighth cervical (C8) and first thoracic (T1) spinal nerves; damage to C8-T1 roots causes the characteristic intrinsic hand muscle weakness and claw hand deformity.

138255.long_answer: About 70 % of Charcot–Marie–Tooth cases (type 1A) are caused by a duplication of the PMP22 gene on chromosome 17p11.2, and a further 10–15 % (type 1B) result from mutations in the MPZ gene on chromosome 1q22. These two chromosomes therefore account for the majority of mutation-related CMT cases reported.

759666.long_answer: Both thyroid hormone resistance and primary goitre typically present with an enlarged thyroid gland—clinically termed goitre. In thyroid hormone resistance, impaired feedback keeps TSH relatively high, stimulating thyroid hyperplasia; in goitre, the gland is by definition enlarged. Thus thyroid enlargement (goitre) is the shared symptom.

663679.long_answer: Superficial thrombophlebitis of the subcutaneous veins of the breast or anterior chest wall is called Mondor's disease, first described in 1939 by the French surgeon Henri Mondor.

249642.long_answer: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) involves washing the distal airways and alveoli via a bronchoscope and analyzing the recovered fluid. In hypersensitivity pneumonitis, BAL typically shows a marked lymphocytic alveolitis, providing direct evidence of active inflammatory processes in the lung parenchyma. Therefore, BAL is a useful diagnostic procedure to detect and quantify pulmonary inflammation in patients suspected of having hypersensitivity pneumonitis.

144590.long_answer: Stratton-Parker syndrome belongs to the short-rib polydactyly group of lethal osteochondrodysplasias. A defining skeletal hallmark of these disorders, including the Stratton-Parker subtype, is the presence of post-axial polydactyly—extra fingers and/or toes accompanying the markedly shortened ribs and limbs.

787932.long_answer: The classic prenatal and neonatal “double-bubble” sign—two adjacent fluid-filled bubbles representing the stomach and proximal duodenum—is characteristic of duodenal atresia. Epidemiologic studies show that this congenital intestinal obstruction occurs in roughly 20–40% of infants with trisomy 21, making duodenal atresia a well-established malformation associated with Down syndrome.

704845.long_answer: Organophosphate insecticides (e.g., malathion, naled, temephos) are widely used agricultural pesticides and are also applied in mosquito-control programs. By inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, they rapidly kill larval and adult mosquitoes, thereby lowering vector populations and cutting the transmission of arboviruses such as dengue, Zika, chikungunya and West Nile virus.

161330.long_answer: When conventional ventilation, surfactant, and inhaled nitric oxide fail to oxygenate a newborn with severe pulmonary hypoplasia, the definitive rescue therapy is extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). ECMO temporarily bypasses the underdeveloped lungs, oxygenating and removing CO₂ from the blood extracorporeally, giving the infant time for pulmonary and cardiorespiratory stabilization; thus, it is considered the last-resort treatment in these critical cases.

501010.long_answer: Both spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) selectively degenerate the lower motor neurons located in the anterior (ventral) horn of the spinal cord. Loss of these anterior-horn motor neurons leads to progressive muscle weakness and atrophy characteristic of these motor neuron diseases.

606250.long_answer: Acitretin, the active metabolite of etretinate prescribed for severe psoriasis, is eliminated slowly from the body; pharmacokinetic studies show an average terminal elimination half-life of about 49 hours (commonly reported range ~33–96 hours).

450216.long_answer: Distal arthrogryposis (particularly type 1) is most often caused by pathogenic variants in the TPM2 gene, which encodes β-tropomyosin of fast-twitch skeletal muscle. TPM2 is situated at the chromosomal locus 9p13.2; mutations at this defined position disrupt thin-filament regulation during muscle contraction and lead to the congenital limb contractures that characterise distal arthrogryposis.

532613.long_answer: In the United States, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis is commonly called “Lou Gehrig’s disease,” a name derived from the famed New York Yankees baseball player Lou Gehrig, who was diagnosed with ALS in 1939 and publicized the illness, leading to the eponymous designation.

980366.long_answer: Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited hemolytic anemia caused by defects in red-cell membrane proteins. Because it is a disorder of the blood, patients are typically evaluated and managed by hematologists, the medical specialists who diagnose and treat diseases of the blood and hemopoietic organs, including congenital hemolytic anemias.

833851.long_answer: Screwdriver-shaped (conical) incisors are a typical dental feature of tricho-dento-osseous syndrome. This syndrome results from pathogenic mutations in the DLX3 (distal-less homeobox 3) gene on chromosome 17q21. DLX3 loss-of-function alters epithelial-mesenchymal signaling during tooth morphogenesis, leading to enamel hypoplasia and the characteristic tapering, screwdriver-like shape of the incisors.

869919.long_answer: Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a common cause of so-called “atypical” or walking pneumonia and characteristically lacks a peptidoglycan cell wall. Instead, its plasma membrane contains sterols, rendering it intrinsically resistant to β-lactam antibiotics and giving rise to its pleomorphic, cell-wall-deficient morphology.

992935.long_answer: Perrault syndrome is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by sensorineural deafness together with bilateral ovarian agenesis/ovarian dysgenesis in phenotypic 46,XX females, leading to primary amenorrhoea and infertility. Hence it is the syndrome classically associated with bilateral absence of functional ovaries.

722314.long_answer: Excess maternal thyroid hormone (hyperthyroidism) accelerates fetal bone maturation, promoting premature fusion of the metopic suture; this early synostosis produces the triangular forehead characteristic of trigonocephaly.

217957.long_answer: Martinican pit vipers (Bothrops lanceolatus) commonly prey on small mammals such as rats and mice. These rodents are well-recognized reservoirs for numerous zoonotic pathogens (e.g., Leptospira, Hantaviruses, and Yersinia pestis), making them noteworthy in both ecological and public-health contexts.

141199.long_answer: Choroid plexus papillomas over-produce cerebrospinal fluid, leading to hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure; the most frequent clinical manifestation of this pressure increase is persistent headache.

121695.long_answer: Testosterone is converted into the potent estrogen estradiol through the enzymatic process called aromatization, catalyzed by the cytochrome P450 enzyme aromatase (CYP19A1). In postmenopausal women, peripheral aromatization of androgens in adipose and other tissues becomes the primary source of estrogens, and the resulting estradiol can drive the growth of hormone-receptor–positive breast cancer.

917548.long_answer: During colonisation of the human nasopharyngeal mucosa, Neisseria meningitidis is first met by polymorphonuclear neutrophils. These innate immune phagocytes migrate into the mucosal epithelium and attempt to engulf the bacteria; meningococcal capsule, LOS and other factors help the pathogen resist neutrophil-mediated killing.

294534.long_answer: After incision and curettage of a chalazion, the discomfort is usually mild; routine practice is to advise an oral non-antiplatelet analgesic. Acetaminophen (paracetamol) is recommended because it provides adequate postoperative pain control without increasing bleeding risk, unlike aspirin or other NSAIDs.

980563.long_answer: The phenomenon of an unfounded or exaggerated fear of chemicals is termed chemophobia. The purposeful, laboratory-based carrying out of chemical reactions to create desired compounds is known as chemical synthesis.

425689.long_answer: Both oncocytomas and so-called eosinophilic (Warthin) tumours are composed of oncocytes—large, granular, mitochondria-rich epithelial cells with intensely eosinophilic (oxyphilic) cytoplasm. Thus the cell type common to the two lesions is the oncocyte.

814105.long_answer: WAGR syndrome is a contiguous-gene deletion on chromosome 11p13 involving PAX6 and WT1. Its cardinal clinical tetrad is Wilms tumor predisposition, congenital aniridia (absence of the iris), genitourinary anomalies, and mental/psychomotor retardation. The combination of missing irises and psychomotor delay therefore points to WAGR syndrome.

547354.long_answer: Linear porokeratosis is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the mevalonate-kinase gene (MVK). The very same MVK mutations that create the porokeratotic clone have repeatedly been identified in squamous-cell carcinomas that arise within these lesions, showing a direct genetic link between MVK mutation and cutaneous SCC development.

470334.long_answer: Reactive (post-prandial) hypoglycaemia is usually managed first with non-pharmacologic measures. Clinical guidelines and endocrinology texts consistently recommend dietary modification as the cornerstone of therapy. Patients are advised to:  • eat small, frequent meals (every 3–4 h) rather than large single meals;  • emphasise complex carbohydrates with high fibre, adequate protein and healthy fats;  • avoid or limit rapidly absorbable/simple sugars, especially on an empty stomach;  • include protein and/or fat with carbohydrate to slow gastric emptying and glucose absorption;  • limit alcohol and caffeine that can precipitate swings in glucose;  • consider bedtime snacks if nocturnal symptoms occur.  These measures reduce the rapid glucose peaks that trigger exaggerated insulin release and subsequent hypoglycaemia. Pharmacologic therapy is rarely required unless dietary measures fail. Therefore, according to established medical practice, recommending dietary changes for patients with reactive hypoglycaemia is standard and evidence-based.

607371.long_answer: Xanthine oxidase is the enzyme that normally converts hypoxanthine to xanthine and subsequently converts xanthine to uric acid. In hereditary or acquired xanthine oxidase deficiency (classically seen in the inborn error of metabolism called xanthinuria), this enzymatic step is blocked. Because xanthine can no longer be efficiently oxidized to uric acid, both hypoxanthine and, more prominently, xanthine accumulate in blood and urine. Clinically, this leads to markedly low serum and urinary uric-acid levels and the formation of xanthine stones in the urinary tract. Therefore, a deficiency of xanthine oxidase does indeed cause a build-up of xanthine in the body.

227205.long_answer: Familial male-limited precocious puberty is caused by activating mutations in the LHCGR gene that are transmitted on an autosome. A single mutant allele is sufficient for the trait to be expressed, but clinical manifestations are limited to males; therefore, the disorder shows an autosomal dominant pattern with sex-limited (male-only) expression.

698828.long_answer: Both essential thrombocythemia and anemia frequently present with fatigue. In anemia, reduced hemoglobin diminishes oxygen delivery to tissues, leading to tiredness and low energy. In essential thrombocythemia, chronic inflammation and altered blood flow from markedly elevated platelet counts likewise produce systemic fatigue. Thus, fatigue is a well-recognized symptom that the two conditions share.

744640.long_answer: X-linked dilated cardiomyopathy classically results from mutations in the DMD gene that encodes the sarcolemmal protein dystrophin; because the gene is located on the X chromosome, the trait shows X-linked inheritance, with affected males and carrier females.

230950.long_answer: With vertical transmission, a pathogen’s spread is tied to the host’s ability to survive, reproduce, and pass the infection to offspring. If the pathogen severely harms or kills the parent, it sharply lowers its own chance of reaching the next generation. Natural selection therefore favors strains that keep the host healthy enough to reproduce, leading to evolution toward lower virulence in vertically transmitted infections.

902056.long_answer: Alport syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the genes encoding the type IV collagen α-chains of the glomerular basement membrane. Molecular testing most often detects mutations in COL4A5 (X-linked form) and, less commonly, in COL4A3 or COL4A4 (autosomal recessive or dominant forms). Identifying a disease-causing variant in any of these three genes confirms the diagnosis and guides inheritance counseling.

823233.long_answer: Decompression sickness ("the bends" or Caisson disease) is treated primarily with hyperbaric oxygen therapy, which involves placing the patient in a pressurized chamber to recompress them and accelerate inert-gas elimination. Physicians trained in the specialty of Hyperbaric Medicine (often termed Undersea and Hyperbaric Medicine) are specifically qualified to manage these cases, making this the medical specialty most likely to treat decompression sickness.

762880.long_answer: Prophylaxis of hypokalemic periodic paralysis commonly involves carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide). These drugs induce a mild metabolic acidosis and modify ionic fluxes in skeletal muscle fibers, thereby reducing the frequency and severity of paralytic attacks.

882660.long_answer: Humans acquire dracunculiasis by drinking water that contains copepods (water fleas) harboring the infective third-stage (L3) larvae of Dracunculus medinensis. These L3 larvae are released in the stomach, penetrate the intestinal wall, and begin their migration and maturation, initiating infection.

275400.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant mutations in the CAV3 gene, which encodes the muscle membrane protein caveolin-3, often present as isolated or asymptomatic hyper-CK-aemia. Affected individuals show chronically elevated serum creatine kinase despite minimal or absent clinical muscle weakness, because the altered caveolin-3 disrupts sarcolemmal membrane stability, allowing leakage of intracellular CK into the blood.

466754.long_answer: In hereditary angioedema, swelling of the gastrointestinal mucosa produces acute abdominal pain; this painful intestinal edema commonly provokes nausea and can culminate in vomiting during an attack.

660788.long_answer: Optic-nerve complications of Behçet’s disease are ocular manifestations that require detailed eye examination, visual-field testing, and imaging of the optic disc; these evaluations and the initiation of anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive therapy are carried out by an ophthalmologist (often a neuro-ophthalmology subspecialist), the specialist trained to diagnose and treat diseases of the eye and optic nerve.

779587.long_answer: Congenital afibrinogenemia is characterized by an absence of fibrinogen (coagulation factor I). During normal hemostasis, the serine protease thrombin (activated factor II, or factor IIa) cleaves fibrinogen to release fibrinopeptides A and B, thereby converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin, its active clot-forming form. Thus, thrombin is the enzyme that activates the protein lacking in individuals with congenital afibrinogenemia.

945198.long_answer: The most common form of congenital cicatricial alopecia is Marie-Unna hereditary hypotrichosis. This disorder is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the U2HR regulatory region of the hairless (HR) gene, which resides on chromosome 8p21-22; therefore, chromosome 8 is the chromosomal location classically associated with this congenital scarring alopecia.

174905.long_answer: Tachycardia is defined as a resting heart rate greater than 100 beats per minute. Excess catecholamines (epinephrine and norepinephrine) stimulate β-adrenergic receptors in the sinoatrial node, increasing its firing rate and producing the rapid heartbeat characteristic of tachycardia.

468117.long_answer: Cone dystrophy primarily damages macular cone photoreceptors, producing loss of central retinal function. Perimetric testing therefore most often shows a central scotoma—a localized defect in the visual field corresponding to the macula—making it the characteristic visual field abnormality in these patients.

647622.long_answer: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2B (MEN 2B) is a RET-mutated syndrome that classically presents with a marfanoid body habitus. Because of its underlying connective-tissue abnormality, patients frequently develop axial skeletal deformities, including kyphosis and scoliosis, in addition to hallmark features such as mucosal neuromas, medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

513544.long_answer: Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease is the prototypical form of hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy (HMSN), a group of inherited peripheral nerve disorders. In HMSN, genetic mutations impair myelin or axonal proteins in peripheral nerves, producing the progressive motor weakness and sensory loss characteristic of Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease.

446686.long_answer: Familial hypobetalipoproteinemia is an inherited disorder—most often caused by truncating mutations in the APOB gene—that produces marked hypolipoproteinemia (very low LDL-cholesterol and apoB levels). The same biochemical picture can also occur secondarily in severe malnutrition or cachectic ‘wasting’ states, so wasting can produce a form of hypobetalipoproteinemia that mimics the genetic disease.

355928.long_answer: Crohn's disease is a form of inflammatory bowel disease that affects the gastrointestinal tract; its diagnosis, medical management, and endoscopic monitoring are handled chiefly by the medical specialty of gastroenterology.

591543.long_answer: Benign familial neonatal seizures segregate with a pericentric inversion of chromosome 20, cytogenetically designated inv(20)(p11q13). The inversion acts as a marker for the disease locus on 20q13 where the KCNQ2 gene that underlies most cases of this benign neonatal epilepsy is located.

360702.long_answer: Herpetophobia is classified as a specific phobia. The evidence-based, first-line behavioral treatment for specific phobias is systematic desensitization (graduated exposure therapy), in which the patient is gradually and repeatedly exposed to reptile-related stimuli while practicing relaxation techniques, leading to extinction of the fear response.

252233.long_answer: In blue diaper syndrome, malabsorption of tryptophan leads to excess production of indole in the gut; the liver converts indole to indoxyl-sulfate (indican), which is excreted in the urine. When the urine in the infant’s diaper is exposed to air, indican is oxidized to the blue dye indigo, producing the characteristic bluish discoloration.

990712.long_answer: An acquired deficiency of prekallikrein can occur in nephrotic syndrome because the damaged glomerular filtration barrier allows excessive urinary loss of plasma proteins, including the contact-system protein prekallikrein (Fletcher factor). The continual loss of this protein in the urine lowers its circulating level, producing the observed deficiency.

916189.long_answer: Septo-optic dysplasia frequently includes hypopituitarism, leading to deficiencies of growth hormone, cortisol, thyroid hormone and others. Management of these endocrine deficits requires hormone replacement therapy and ongoing monitoring, tasks that fall within the expertise of a pediatric endocrinologist.

715387.long_answer: Guidelines from the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the American Academy of Pediatrics state that if a rapid antigen detection test (RADT) for Group A Streptococcus is negative in a child or adolescent with suspected streptococcal pharyngitis, a conventional throat culture of a tonsillopharyngeal swab should be performed. Throat culture provides higher sensitivity (≈95%) than RADT and is the reference standard for confirming or excluding Group A streptococcal infection.

355512.long_answer: The form of spondyloenchondrodysplasia with immune dysregulation is most often linked to a homozygous ACP5 point mutation (c.136C>T) that replaces arginine with tryptophan at residue 46 of tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (p.Arg46Trp). This missense change eliminates TRAP activity, leading to the skeletal dysplasia and immune abnormalities characteristic of the disorder.

334784.long_answer: In Sigmund Freud’s famous 1909 case study of the five-year-old boy known as “Little Hans,” the central clinical focus was the child’s intense, persistent fear of horses. Freud interpreted this equinophobia as a manifestation of underlying Oedipal and castration anxieties, using the case to support his psychoanalytic theory of psychosexual development.

336164.long_answer: Iron overload in congenital dyserythropoietic anemia is managed with iron-chelation therapy. Deferoxamine binds excess ferric iron and promotes its urinary and biliary excretion, thereby lowering body iron stores and preventing organ damage. It is the standard chelator historically recommended for CDA patients who accumulate iron from ineffective erythropoiesis and transfusions.

521730.short_answer: Ferdinand-Jean Darier and James Clarke White
521730.long_answer: Darier’s disease, also called Darier-White disease or keratosis follicularis, was independently described in 1889 by the French dermatologist Ferdinand-Jean Darier and soon after by the American dermatologist James Clarke White. Because both physicians characterized the same inherited keratinization disorder, their surnames are attached to the condition.

140983.long_answer: Surgical removal of congenital cataracts is performed by an ophthalmologist—a physician specialized in ophthalmology who is trained to diagnose and surgically treat disorders of the eye, including congenital lens opacities seen in cataract-ataxia-deafness syndrome.

469645.long_answer: When Gorham-Stout disease extends to the ribs or thoracic vertebrae, the abnormal lymphatic proliferation can disrupt the thoracic duct and pleural lymphatics, allowing chyle to leak into the pleural space. The resulting chylothorax leads to massive pleural effusions, respiratory failure, and is the principal life-threatening complication of chest involvement in Gorham’s disease.

954008.long_answer: An electroencephalogram records the brain’s electrical activity through scalp electrodes, allowing clinicians to visualize abnormal discharges such as focal or generalized slowing, periodic complexes, or epileptiform spikes that commonly occur in encephalitis. Because encephalitic inflammation disrupts normal neuronal firing patterns, EEG is routinely employed to detect and monitor these pathological electrical changes.

876787.long_answer: In lipoid (lipid) pneumonia the alveoli become packed with lipid-laden (foamy) macrophages. Fusion of these lipid-filled macrophages produces Touton giant cells—multinucleated cells with a ring of nuclei surrounding a central lipid-rich cytoplasm—which are characteristic of lesions rich in neutral fat and cholesterol.

448273.long_answer: Möbius syndrome is characterized by congenital hypoplasia or absence of the abducens (VI) and facial (VII) cranial nerve nuclei/nerve fibers. This underdevelopment causes the hallmark findings of impaired lateral eye movement and bilateral facial paralysis seen in affected individuals.

401636.long_answer: Because myotonic dystrophy produces distal leg weakness and foot-drop, clinicians commonly prescribe an ankle-foot orthosis (AFO). The rigid or hinged brace supports the ankle in neutral position, prevents excessive plantar-flexion, and stabilizes gait, reducing the energy cost of walking and lowering fall risk in patients with this neuromuscular disorder.

260765.long_answer: Distal trisomy 10q (duplication of the distal segment of chromosome 10q) is a well-described chromosomal duplication syndrome. Reported individuals show multiple congenital anomalies, growth and developmental delay, characteristic craniofacial features, and abnormal muscle tone—most commonly neonatal hypotonia that may later be followed by hypertonia or spasticity. Normal or “typical” muscle tone is not a defining or characteristic finding in this condition. Hence the statement that distal trisomy 10q is characterized by typical (i.e., normal) muscle tone is not consistent with the established clinical description of the syndrome.

687429.long_answer: Dandy–Walker malformation (also called Dandy–Walker syndrome) is a congenital brain malformation characterized by hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle. It is a recognized feature of Marden–Walker syndrome and is frequently accompanied by agenesis or hypogenesis of the corpus callosum, linking all three conditions.

516422.long_answer: In surgical correction of foot drop caused by distal myopathy, the tendon of the tibialis posterior muscle is detached, routed through the interosseous membrane, and attached to the dorsum of the foot. Once transferred, tibialis posterior can contract to dorsiflex the ankle, effectively substituting for the weakened or absent tibialis anterior muscle.

625772.long_answer: Cat-scratch disease is an infectious lymphadenitis produced by the Gram-negative, intracellular bacterium Bartonella henselae, which is transmitted to humans mainly through scratches or bites from cats harboring this pathogen.

922359.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the NTRK1 gene cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy type IV). Affected individuals are typically homozygous or compound-heterozygous for loss-of-function mutations, while each parent is an asymptomatic carrier, demonstrating the classic autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

359602.long_answer: Serotonin, released mainly from enterochromaffin cells in the gut wall, activates receptors on enteric neurons to stimulate smooth-muscle contraction and coordinate colonic motility patterns, thereby regulating colonic motor activity.

843814.long_answer: Kabuki syndrome, also known as Niikawa-Kuroki syndrome, was first described in 1981 in Japanese patients and families. The multisystem disorder is marked by characteristic facial features, growth delay, intellectual disability, skeletal anomalies, and genitourinary malformations; hypospadias is one of its common urogenital manifestations. Pathogenic variants in KMT2D or, less frequently, KDM6A underlie most cases.

916782.long_answer: Selective immunoglobulin A (IgA) deficiency is strongly associated with celiac disease: up to 10–15 % of IgA-deficient individuals develop this autoimmune enteropathy, compared with ≈1 % in the general population. The lack of mucosal IgA alters gut immune tolerance, facilitating an autoimmune response to gluten, making celiac disease significantly more common in these patients.

729402.long_answer: Midodrine, prescribed for symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, is administered as an inactive prodrug that is rapidly converted in vivo to the active metabolite desglymidodrine, an α1-adrenergic agonist responsible for its blood-pressure-raising effect.

136288.long_answer: Selamectin is an avermectin applied as a monthly ‘spot-on’ solution (e.g., Revolution) that is licensed and widely used to eliminate Sarcoptes scabiei infestations in dogs; the drug is absorbed transdermally after topical application and kills the mites systemically.

440786.long_answer: Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic with proven activity against Toxoplasma gondii. It is commonly employed as an alternative to the standard pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine regimen for ocular toxoplasmosis, particularly in patients who cannot tolerate sulfonamides. Oral or intravitreal clindamycin, often combined with pyrimethamine or used alone intravitreally, achieves therapeutic intraocular concentrations and has been shown in clinical studies to control active retinochoroiditis effectively.

516263.long_answer: Elosulfase alfa, marketed as Vimizim, is a recombinant form of the missing enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase. It received FDA approval in 2014 as an enzyme-replacement therapy specifically for patients with Morquio syndrome Type A (mucopolysaccharidosis IVA), addressing the underlying enzyme deficiency that leads to glycosaminoglycan accumulation.

800188.long_answer: Persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) is classified as a mood disorder. Diagnosis, pharmacologic management (e.g., SSRIs, SNRIs), and coordination of psychotherapy for mood disorders fall within the domain of psychiatry, the medical specialty dedicated to treating mental illnesses. Therefore, psychiatrists are the specialists most likely to manage patients with persistent depressive disorder.

792640.long_answer: X-linked dominant protoporphyria is produced by gain-of-function (hyperactive) mutations in the erythroid-specific aminolevulinate synthase 2 gene (ALAS2) located on the X chromosome. The mutant ALAS2 enzyme increases heme precursor synthesis, leading to excess protoporphyrin IX accumulation and the characteristic photosensitive phenotype.

964424.long_answer: In chronic mountain sickness, sustained hypoxia causes pulmonary vasoconstriction, producing chronic pulmonary hypertension. Persistently elevated pressure overloads the right ventricle, leading to right-sided ventricular hypertrophy and eventual failure—a condition termed cor pulmonale.

398531.long_answer: Hurler syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type I) is an autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by complete deficiency of the enzyme α-L-iduronidase. Lack of this enzyme leads to accumulation of dermatan and heparan sulfate, producing coarse facies, corneal clouding, hepatosplenomegaly, developmental delay, and characteristic umbilical or inguinal hernias, making it the lysosomal disease classically associated with hernias.

983973.long_answer: Granuloma annulare is characterized histologically by palisading aggregates of dermal epithelioid histiocytes (dermal dendrocytes). These histiocytic cells strongly express transglutaminase Factor XIIIa. Immunohistochemical staining for Factor XIIIa is therefore the standard method used to highlight and examine the dermal epithelioid histiocytes in granuloma annulare, aiding in both identification and differential diagnosis from other granulomatous conditions.

857641.long_answer: Medical historians have suggested that Tiny Tim’s small stature, bone deformities, muscle weakness, need for a crutch, and potentially fatal but reversible course are most consistent with type I (distal) renal tubular acidosis. This disorder causes chronic metabolic acidosis, leading to rickets-like skeletal changes and growth failure; with appropriate alkali therapy—plausibly affordable after Scrooge’s transformation—his condition could have improved, fitting Dickens’ narrative that Tim survives once the family’s finances improve.

915519.short_answer: Factitious disorder imposed on another; diagnosis
915519.long_answer: When a caregiver deliberately fabricates or induces illness in someone under their care, the psychiatric condition is called Factitious Disorder Imposed on Another (historically termed Munchausen syndrome by proxy). The systematic medical procedure used to identify the illness or condition that best explains a patient’s signs and symptoms is known as diagnosis.

252199.long_answer: The condition described is Meigs syndrome; ascites and pleural effusion disappear once the benign ovarian mass (usually a fibroma) is surgically excised, making operative removal of the ovarian tumor the definitive treatment.

626124.long_answer: Jancar syndrome is one of the eponymous names for the ectrodactyly–mental retardation (EMR) syndrome. The hallmark skeletal anomaly in this disorder is ectrodactyly (split-hand/foot malformation or “lobster-claw” deformity), in which central digits are absent and the hand or foot appears cleft. This distinctive limb defect is consistently reported in affected individuals and is considered characteristic of the syndrome.

553160.long_answer: Chondrosarcoma is the malignant cartilage-forming tumor that characteristically infiltrates surrounding bone and soft tissues and can metastasize—most often to the lungs—distinguishing it from benign cartilage tumors, which remain localized.

672176.long_answer: Tibialis posterior, a deep posterior-compartment muscle of the leg, is innervated by the tibial nerve. It functions as the principal dynamic stabiliser of the lower leg and foot, supporting the medial longitudinal arch and controlling pronation during gait, thereby providing key stability to the lower limb.

482940.long_answer: Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant that is also used as a mood-stabilizing agent in bipolar disorder. A well-documented, though uncommon, hematologic adverse effect of carbamazepine therapy is agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia), thought to result from immune-mediated or direct toxic suppression of granulocyte precursors. Consequently, periodic blood count monitoring is recommended in patients receiving carbamazepine.

123812.long_answer: In the United States the majority of limb amputations are performed because of dysvascular disease—peripheral arterial occlusive disease, most often associated with diabetes mellitus. This peripheral vascular disease accounts for more amputations than trauma, tumors, infections, or congenital abnormalities, making it the single most common cause of amputation in the U.S.

668290.long_answer: Weight-based stigma functions as a persistent psychosocial stressor. Repeated exposure to teasing, discrimination, and social rejection activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, elevating cortisol and sympathetic tone. This chronic stress promotes visceral fat deposition, insulin resistance, systemic inflammation, hypertension, and dyslipidemia, while also discouraging healthcare seeking and physical activity. Consequently, the stress pathway triggered by obesity stigma directly amplifies the metabolic and cardiovascular risks already linked to excess adiposity.

687043.long_answer: Real-time prenatal ultrasonography (including high-resolution or 3-D ultrasound) can visualize amniotic bands encircling a fetal limb and the resulting distal edema or deformity, allowing definitive confirmation of constriction ring (amniotic band) syndrome while the pregnancy is still ongoing.

994905.long_answer: After gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Turner syndrome), the next most frequent reason a girl fails to menstruate despite reaching the age threshold is Müllerian agenesis, also called Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. In this condition the Müllerian ducts do not develop, so the uterus and upper vagina are absent, yet ovarian function and secondary sexual characteristics are normal, leading to primary amenorrhea. Multiple epidemiologic reviews list it as the second-most common etiology of primary amenorrhea, accounting for roughly 15–20 % of cases.

568795.long_answer: Neuroblastoma cells express the norepinephrine transporter of sympathetic-derived tissue. This allows them to actively take up norepinephrine (and its radiolabeled analogue ¹²³I- or ¹³¹I-MIBG), a property exploited in diagnostic scintigraphy and staging of neuroblastoma.

755645.long_answer: Tunga penetrans (the jigger flea) burrows into the skin, leading to local inflammation and subsequent peeling or sloughing off of the superficial epidermis. This shedding of dead keratinized cells is medically termed desquamation, the characteristic skin condition associated with tungiasis.

988792.long_answer: Wyburn-Mason syndrome (Bonnet-Dechaume-Blanc syndrome) is a rare neuro-oculo-cutaneous disorder characterized by large arteriovenous malformations of the retina, midbrain and diencephalon. These intracranial AVMs frequently lie in the midline and drain into, or compress, the deep venous system, thereby directly or indirectly involving the Great Cerebral Vein of Galen and its outflow into the straight sinus.

152477.long_answer: In complete penoscrotal transposition the scrotum lies cephalad, and the penis is displaced posterior-inferiorly so that it emerges from the perineum, behind/below the scrotal sacs.

216155.long_answer: In WAGR syndrome, the characteristic ocular defect is aniridia—the partial or complete absence of the iris. Lack of iris tissue disrupts normal light regulation and is commonly accompanied by foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, cataract, and glaucoma, all of which can significantly reduce visual acuity. Thus, aniridia is the eye condition in WAGR syndrome that leads to decreased vision.

717203.long_answer: In low-light (scotopic) conditions the retina relies mainly on rod photoreceptors, which are relatively insensitive to long-wavelength red light; this spectral sensitivity shift toward blue-green, called the Purkinje shift, makes red objects appear much darker. People with Stargardt disease lose central cone function and depend even more on rod-mediated vision in dim illumination, so the Purkinje shift further impairs their ability to detect red objects.

707473.long_answer: Otodental syndrome is most often produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions involving the FGF3 gene on chromosome 11q13. FGF3 encodes fibroblast growth factor 3, a signaling protein required for normal inner-ear morphogenesis; its haplo-insufficiency impairs cochlear development and results in the characteristic sensorineural hearing loss seen in otodental syndrome.

980432.long_answer: Brad Carter—an American guitarist and actor—was diagnosed with essential tremor and later underwent deep-brain stimulation surgery. He recorded a public-service announcement describing how the neurological disorder affected his ability to play music and how treatment helped, thereby raising awareness about living with essential tremor.

549068.long_answer: Azumolene is a water-soluble analogue of dantrolene that has been investigated experimentally for malignant hyperthermia. Studies in susceptible animal models and isolated muscle preparations show that azumolene inhibits excessive calcium release from the ryanodine receptor with potency comparable to dantrolene, thereby preventing or reversing the hypermetabolic crisis characteristic of malignant hyperthermia.

741613.long_answer: Holt-Oram syndrome (the “heart-hand” syndrome) is caused by pathogenic variants in the TBX5 gene. Patients typically show hand anomalies such as clinodactyly of the 5th finger together with congenital fusion (coalition) of the carpal bones in the wrist. These limb findings accompany the cardiac septal defects that characterize the condition, making Holt-Oram the classic syndrome combining clinodactyly with carpal bone fusion.

466271.long_answer: Berk–Tabatznik syndrome denotes the bradycardia–tachycardia (sick-sinus) pattern in which episodes of supraventricular tachycardia alternate with marked sinus bradycardia or pauses. Because it arises from dysfunction of the heart’s conduction system and produces abnormal heart rhythms, it is classified as a cardiac arrhythmia.

807736.long_answer: Hyperimmunoglobulin E syndrome (Job’s syndrome) is characterized by markedly elevated serum IgE levels and defective neutrophil chemotaxis. This immune defect predisposes patients to recurrent ‘cold’ skin and pulmonary abscesses that are classically caused by the gram-positive coccal bacterium Staphylococcus aureus.

446228.long_answer: Vaginismus (now classified under genito-pelvic pain/penetration disorder in DSM-5) is understood to arise from an interaction of psychological and physical factors. Established clinical literature and consensus guidelines list several pre-disposing or precipitating factors, including:  • Anxiety disorders or high trait anxiety/fear of pain and penetration.  • Prior pelvic or genital injury (e.g., childbirth trauma, episiotomy, accidents) that conditions the individual to expect pain.  • Prior pelvic or gynecologic surgery (e.g., hymenectomy, vaginal or vulvar procedures) that can create pain memories or physical sensitivity.  These factors are repeatedly cited in gynecology and sexual-medicine texts and in reviews by the International Society for the Study of Women’s Sexual Health (ISSWSH) as contributors to both primary and secondary vaginismus. Therefore, anxiety disorders, prior injury, and prior surgery are indeed considered recognized risk factors for developing vaginismus.

825672.long_answer: Mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1, are the well-established genetic cause of Marfan syndrome. Distinct heterozygous missense mutations in the same gene—especially those altering residues near the RGD integrin-binding motif—have also been shown to cause Stiff skin syndrome. Thus, pathogenic variants in FBN1 are implicated in both disorders.

707408.long_answer: Polymyalgia rheumatica is highly sensitive to glucocorticoids; guidelines recommend starting with a low daily dose of an oral corticosteroid, typically prednisone 10–20 mg. This rapidly relieves the characteristic proximal muscle pain and stiffness and confirms the diagnosis, after which the dose is tapered based on clinical response and inflammatory markers.

584867.long_answer: Metoclopramide is a dopamine-D2 receptor antagonist frequently prescribed as a pro-kinetic agent for gastro-oesophageal reflux and heartburn. By blocking hypothalamic D2 receptors it lifts dopamine’s normal inhibitory control over pituitary lactotrophs, leading to increased prolactin secretion. Consequently, metoclopramide is a well-documented cause of drug-induced hyperprolactinemia.

775312.long_answer: Onychocryptosis, commonly called an ingrown toenail, occurs overwhelmingly on the hallux (great toe). The great toe endures the highest mechanical pressure from footwear and gait, making its nail plate most prone to penetrating the periungual skin, so it is cited as the digit most frequently affected in clinical series.

557082.long_answer: Rickettsia are obligate intracellular bacteria that cause infections such as Rocky Mountain spotted fever and epidemic typhus. Diagnosis, selection of appropriate antimicrobials (e.g., doxycycline), and management of systemic complications fall under the expertise of physicians trained in the medical specialty of infectious disease, making this specialty the one most involved in treating rickettsial illnesses.

482384.long_answer: Epidemiological and clinical studies of personality–disorder comorbidity consistently show that avoidant personality disorder co-occurs at very high rates with both paranoid personality disorder (cluster A) and obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (cluster C). Correlation matrices from large samples (e.g., Torgersen et al., 2001; Pulay et al., 2009) demonstrate strong comorbidity coefficients between avoidant PD and paranoid PD, and similarly between avoidant PD and OCPD, making avoidant personality disorder the disorder most characteristically shared with both of these conditions.

178129.long_answer: Echocardiography—particularly transesophageal echocardiography (TEE)—is essential for diagnosing infective endocarditis because it directly visualizes valvular vegetations, abscesses, and prosthetic-valve involvement, findings that constitute a major Duke diagnostic criterion.

907966.long_answer: Patients with Gustavson syndrome frequently experience acute otitis media—recurrent middle-ear infections that typically arise during or shortly after viral upper-respiratory tract infections. This symptom is repeatedly described in the clinical literature on the X-linked Gustavson (hypotonic facies–seizures) syndrome, making acute otitis media a characteristic and common manifestation.

102818.long_answer: 1p36 deletion syndrome is confirmed by demonstrating loss of the subtelomeric region of chromosome 1p using fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) probes (or equivalent chromosomal microarray). FISH directly visualizes the absence of the 1p36 signal, providing definitive molecular cytogenetic evidence of the deletion.

245251.long_answer: The HMGCL gene encodes mitochondrial 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase, which crystallographic and biochemical studies have shown assembles into a homotetramer—four identical subunits arranged as a dimer of dimers. This quaternary structure is required for its catalytic cleavage of HMG-CoA in ketogenesis and leucine degradation.

880573.long_answer: Oligodactyly is a congenital limb malformation characterized by the presence of fewer than the normal five digits on a hand or foot. It arises from disruptions in early limb bud development, often due to genetic mutations or vascular insults, leading to the absence or failure of formation of one or more fingers or toes.

522806.long_answer: Confirmation of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy can be obtained by performing a nerve biopsy—most commonly a sural nerve biopsy—which allows histopathological examination of the peripheral nerve tissue for segmental demyelination, remyelination, and inflammatory infiltrates characteristic of CIDP.

725119.long_answer: Chronic myelogenous (myeloid) leukemia typically shows marked basophilia—an abnormally high number of basophils in the peripheral blood. While many myeloid lineage cells are elevated, persistent elevation of basophils is characteristic and helps distinguish CML from other leukocytoses.

243349.long_answer: In acute angle-closure glaucoma the iris becomes ischemic and the pupil often becomes mid-dilated and fails to constrict when light is shone into either eye. Checking the pupillary light reflex therefore reveals a fixed (non-reactive), mid-dilated pupil, a classic and common sign of an acute attack.

887559.long_answer: Historical chronicles of the Western Han state that the celebrated cavalry general Huo Qubing (died 117 BCE) suddenly fell ill after returning from a northern campaign and succumbed to a rapidly fatal ‘epidemic pestilence’ (瘟疫). Modern historians identify this description with bubonic plague, making Huo Qubing the first documented Han-dynasty figure recorded as dying from plague contamination.

417924.long_answer: Al-Gazali-Donnai-Mueller syndrome is a severe variant of frontonasal dysplasia characterized by midline facial clefts and dermoid or encephalocele tracts that can communicate between the nasal cavity and the cranial cavity. Because these tracts provide a direct pathway for bacteria to reach the central nervous system, bacterial meningitis is a well-documented and potentially life-threatening complication of the disorder.

653819.long_answer: Thalidomide is a powerful human teratogen; exposure during pregnancy can cause severe congenital malformations such as limb reduction defects. Therefore, when thalidomide is used to treat HIV-associated ulcers or wasting, the major risk is the potential induction of serious birth defects if a patient becomes pregnant, necessitating stringent contraception and pregnancy-prevention measures.

375782.long_answer: Mepolizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that targets interleukin-5 (IL-5). By blocking IL-5 signaling, it reduces eosinophil development and survival, thereby lowering the pathogenic eosinophil count characteristic of hypereosinophilic syndrome. Clinical trials demonstrated its efficacy and safety, leading to regulatory approval specifically for the treatment of hypereosinophilic syndrome in patients who do not respond adequately to conventional therapy.

596528.long_answer: Onychophosis is a hyperkeratotic thickening that develops in the nail folds—most commonly of the toes—leading to pain and difficulty with footwear. Because it is a disorder of the toenails and surrounding skin, diagnosis and definitive care (debridement, pressure‐relief, footwear advice) are routinely provided by podiatrists, the medical specialists dedicated to conditions of the foot and toenails.

340477.long_answer: The FRAXD locus corresponds to the folate-sensitive rare fragile site fra(X)(q27.3)D. Cytogenetic and sequence mapping place this gene at band q27.3 of the human X chromosome; hence FRAXD is located on chromosome X.

279660.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene, which encodes fibrillin-1. Defective fibrillin weakens elastic fibers throughout the body, including the lung pleura, predisposing patients to apical blebs and an elevated incidence of spontaneous pneumothorax.

200331.long_answer: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) most commonly arises when the X chromosomes fail to separate properly during meiosis I or II in either the mother’s oogenesis or the father’s spermatogenesis. This meiotic nondisjunction produces a gamete with an extra X chromosome; when it is fertilized by a normal gamete, the resulting zygote carries the XXY karyotype characteristic of Klinefelter syndrome.

925133.long_answer: Hyperkalemic periodic paralysis is most commonly caused by mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the α-subunit of the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav1.4). Pathogenic variants in SCN4A disrupt sodium channel inactivation, leading to sustained depolarization of muscle fibers and episodic weakness triggered by elevated serum potassium.

373740.long_answer: Petrolatum, commonly called petroleum jelly, is a widely used ingredient in skin-care creams and ointments. It forms an occlusive barrier on the epidermis that prevents transepidermal water loss, making it a first-line moisturizer for xeroderma (abnormally dry skin). Its barrier and emollient properties also protect minor wounds and promote healing, explaining its common recommendation for both skin protection and repair.

642198.long_answer: Aedes aegypti is the primary mosquito vector that transmits dengue virus to humans. Its day-biting behavior, preference for human blood, and ability to breed in urban water containers make it the chief driver of dengue fever outbreaks worldwide.

686852.long_answer: OMIM identifies mutations in the MUT gene, which encodes the enzyme methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, as the cause of the classic ‘mut’ type (mut0/mut–) methylmalonic acidemia. This mutational class accounts for the majority of methylmalonic acidemia cases, making MUT the gene most commonly responsible for the disorder.

115087.long_answer: In his 1st-century AD medical encyclopedia De Medicina, the Roman encyclopaedist Aulus Cornelius Celsus advised patients with nyctalopia (night blindness) to eat liver—an organ later found to be exceptionally rich in vitamin A, the nutrient whose deficiency causes the disorder.

956593.long_answer: In the television series “Zoey’s Extraordinary Playlist,” Zoey’s father, Mitch Clarke, is depicted as living with progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). The storyline shows the characteristic neurological decline of PSP—loss of voluntary eye movement, motor impairment, speech and swallowing difficulties—highlighting the disease’s progressive neurodegenerative nature.

904173.long_answer: Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) is a rapid heart rhythm that originates in tissue located at or just above the atrioventricular (AV) node. In SVT, ectopic pacemaker cells or re-entrant circuits near the AV node fire repeatedly and much faster than the normal sino-atrial pacemaker, driving the heart rate well above normal limits.

513893.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked chloride channel gene CLCN5 are the classic cause of Dent’s disease (Dent disease type 1). Loss-of-function of CLCN5 impairs proximal-tubule endocytosis, leading to phosphaturia as well as low-molecular-weight proteinuria and hypercalciuria. The resulting chronic renal phosphate wasting can produce the skeletal picture of hypophosphatemic rickets, so CLCN5 mutations are recognised as a genetic cause of both Dent’s disease and hypophosphatemic rickets.

314498.long_answer: Carbamazepine is an anticonvulsant that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, thereby reducing repetitive neuronal firing. By dampening peripheral nerve hyperexcitability in neuromyotonia (Isaacs’ syndrome), it lessens the continuous muscle fiber activity responsible for spasms, stiffness, and neuropathic pain, and is therefore commonly used as first-line symptomatic therapy for this disorder.

651370.long_answer: In Crigler–Najjar syndrome, unconjugated bilirubin can rise to neurotoxic levels. When this hyperbilirubinemia becomes severe and must be lowered rapidly, an exchange transfusion is employed to remove bilirubin-laden blood and replace it with donor blood, thereby quickly reducing serum bilirubin concentrations and preventing kernicterus.

473346.long_answer: Patients with Hyperimmunoglobulin E (Job) syndrome are prone to recurrent cutaneous and pulmonary infections caused mainly by Staphylococcus aureus. Continuous or intermittent prophylaxis with the antistaphylococcal antibiotic trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the standard first-line measure to prevent these infections, as it provides reliable activity against S. aureus and has demonstrated reduction in infection frequency in this patient population.

656843.long_answer: Abrupt cessation of chronic heavy alcohol use produces Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome, in which CNS hyper-excitability from down-regulated GABAergic and up-regulated glutamatergic signaling can precipitate generalized tonic-clonic seizures. These withdrawal-induced seizures may merge into prolonged, recurrent seizures without recovery of consciousness—i.e., status epilepticus.

598302.long_answer: Infants born with gastroschisis frequently develop necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) because their exposed, inflamed intestines have impaired perfusion and motility, predisposing them to ischemia and bacterial translocation. Preterm infants likewise have immature intestinal barriers and altered gut perfusion, making NEC one of their most feared gastrointestinal complications. Thus, NEC is a shared and well-recognized complication in both populations.

878720.long_answer: High-resolution ultrasound can non-invasively visualize the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, allowing assessment of its cross-sectional area, echogenicity, and swelling. These sonographic findings correlate with carpal tunnel syndrome, making ultrasound a widely accepted imaging tool for its diagnosis.

251720.long_answer: Celiac disease (gluten-sensitive enteropathy) is an autoimmune condition triggered by gluten that leads to IgA autoantibody production. The same IgA-mediated immunity underlies two extra-intestinal manifestations: dermatitis herpetiformis, a pruritic vesicular rash pathognomonic for celiac disease, and Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA vasculitis), in which IgA immune-complex deposition produces palpable purpura. Thus, celiac disease is the autoimmune disorder epidemiologically and mechanistically linked to both Henoch–Schönlein purpura and dermatitis herpetiformis.

326956.long_answer: Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type II corresponds to spinocerebellar ataxia type 7, a disorder caused by CAG-repeat expansion in the ATXN7 gene. Mutant ATXN7 protein leads to neurodegeneration that affects both the cerebellum and the retina, producing the characteristic combination of progressive ataxia and pigmentary retinal degeneration.
