The same ADH-potentiating effect can lead to excessive water reabsorption, dilutional hyponatremia, and the clinical picture of syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH).

766608.long_answer: Freeman-Sheldon syndrome (also called whistling-face or distal arthrogryposis type 2A) is defined by craniofacial anomalies such as microstomia, pursed lips and mid-face hypoplasia together with malformations of the extremities, notably severe contractures, camptodactyly and club-foot. Because these limb deformities arise from congenital distal arthrogryposis, the condition is classed among musculoskeletal abnormalities, fulfilling the association described in the question.

392515.long_answer: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma characteristically produces painless peripheral lymphadenopathy, and the inguinal (groin) lymph nodes are among the nodal groups most often enlarged. In contrast, Hodgkin lymphoma more typically involves cervical or mediastinal nodes. Therefore, swollen lymph nodes in the groin are most commonly associated with Non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

306214.long_answer: Ankylosing spondylitis, a strongly HLA-B27–linked genetic spondyloarthropathy, carries a markedly increased risk of acute anterior uveitis; up to one-third of patients experience recurrent uveitic episodes due to the same immune-mediated inflammation that drives the axial arthritis.

687433.long_answer: Crome syndrome is a rare congenital-genetic disorder that presents in infancy with findings such as microcephaly, severe growth retardation, retinal degeneration and other developmental abnormalities. Because the condition is evident from birth or early childhood and requires coordinated evaluation of growth, development, vision and hearing, its diagnosis and longitudinal care are classically overseen by a pediatric specialist (often together with pediatric geneticists and other subspecialists). Thus, the medical specialty most likely to handle both diagnosis and management is Pediatrics.

390541.long_answer: In the WHO Classification of Tumours of Soft Tissue and Bone, the World Health Organization designates fibromatosis (also called desmoid-type fibromatosis) as an “intermediate (locally aggressive)” soft-tissue tumor, reflecting its tendency for local invasion without metastatic potential.

147084.long_answer: Autosomal recessive Robinow syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the ROR2 gene, which encodes the receptor tyrosine kinase–like orphan receptor 2 involved in WNT signaling and skeletal development.

898054.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is almost always caused by pathogenic mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1. FBN1 is located on chromosome 15q21, and defective fibrillin-1 disrupts microfibril formation in connective tissue, producing the skeletal, ocular, and cardiovascular manifestations characteristic of Marfan syndrome.

865304.long_answer: The superior thyroid artery is the first anterior branch of the external carotid artery. It descends anterior to the neck structures to reach and vascularise the superior poles of the thyroid gland, providing its primary arterial supply in conjunction with the inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk.

227614.long_answer: Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy) is a genetic epilepsy most often caused by de-novo loss-of-function mutations in the SCN1A sodium-channel gene. The disorder characteristically starts in the first year of life with prolonged febrile seizures, making it a well-recognized genetic condition associated with febrile seizures.

816972.long_answer: Lyngstadaas syndrome is included in the U.S. National Institutes of Health (NIH) Office of Rare Diseases (ORD) database, which designates it as a rare disease within its Genetic and Rare Diseases (GARD) information resources.

542435.long_answer: Ischiopatellar dysplasia (small-patella syndrome) is an autosomal-dominant skeletal disorder caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the TBX4 gene, which is located on chromosome 17q23.1–q23.2. Mutations in TBX4, a T-box transcription factor essential for limb and pelvic development, underlie the characteristic absent or hypoplastic patellae and pelvic anomalies seen in this condition.

533501.long_answer: In diabetes, especially during diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperglycaemia and acidosis impair neutrophil chemotaxis and phagocytosis while releasing free iron into serum; this combination both weakens innate immune defense and provides nutrients that stimulate Mucorales growth, making diabetics far more susceptible to mucormycosis.

163413.long_answer: Pancreatoblastoma usually grows to a considerable size before detection and its mass effect or ductal obstruction commonly produces marked upper-abdominal/epigastric pain. This pain is the symptom reported most often in published series and is the chief complaint that typically brings patients to the emergency room for evaluation.

906605.long_answer: Amblyomma americanum (the lone star tick) transmits Ehrlichia chaffeensis, the cause of human monocytic ehrlichiosis. The established first-line therapy for this bacterial infection is doxycycline, which rapidly clears the intracellular Ehrlichia and improves outcomes when started promptly.

447902.long_answer: Pachygyria is a neuronal-migration disorder that causes thickened cerebral gyri, developmental delay, and often refractory epilepsy. Assessment of brain malformations, seizure management, and neurodevelopmental follow-up fall within the expertise of pediatric neurologists, making pediatric neurology the specialty most commonly responsible for treating children with pachygyria.

956114.long_answer: In Hirayama disease, dynamic magnetic resonance imaging of the cervical spine obtained in neck flexion shows anterior displacement of the posterior dura and engorged epidural veins compressing the spinal cord. This characteristic appearance on cervical flexion MRI confirms the diagnosis.

789738.long_answer: CHIME syndrome (Coloboma, Heart defects, Ichthyosiform dermatosis, Mental retardation, and Ear anomalies) has been conclusively linked to loss-of-function mutations in the PIGL gene, which encodes an enzyme required for early steps of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis. Pathogenic PIGL variants disrupt GPI-anchor formation, leading to the multisystem manifestations characteristic of CHIME syndrome.

554803.long_answer: An illusion is the misinterpretation of a real external stimulus (e.g., mistaking a coat on a chair for a person). Because an actual sensory input is present, the distortion is less severe than a true hallucination, in which perception occurs without any stimulus. Therefore, psychiatry classifies an illusion as a mild form of hallucination and lists it under perceptual disturbances.

295529.long_answer: X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets (caused by PHEX gene mutations) is an inherited disorder that increases fibroblast growth factor 23, producing excessive renal phosphate wasting. The resulting chronic hypophosphatemia impairs bone mineralization, leading to vitamin D-resistant rickets and osteomalacia.

187348.long_answer: The paraglottic space is a fat-filled potential space that lies lateral to the laryngeal ventricle, between the mucosa and the thyroid cartilage. Because it contains loose connective tissue and lymphatics, laryngeal carcinomas—especially supraglottic and trans-glottic tumours—readily extend into this space and can then spread beyond the larynx into the neck.

375452.long_answer: After bilateral adrenalectomy, loss of cortisol feedback can allow an ACTH-secreting pituitary tumor to enlarge (Nelson’s syndrome). The excess ACTH is processed to melanocyte-stimulating peptides, producing diffuse skin and mucosal hyperpigmentation, which—together with visual field defects from the expanding tumor—is a classic clinical clue to Nelson’s syndrome.

377558.long_answer: Scoliosis is a musculoskeletal deformity of the spine; in children it is evaluated and managed by orthopedic surgeons who have additional training in pediatric musculoskeletal disorders. These pediatric orthopedic surgeons are experts in growth-related spinal curvature, bracing strategies, and corrective spine surgery, making them the specialists who treat scoliosis in children.

618391.long_answer: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 is caused by mutations in the ABCB11 gene, which encodes the bile salt export pump (BSEP) located on the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes. Defective ABCB11 impairs biliary secretion of bile acids, leading to cholestasis characteristic of this disorder.

469359.long_answer: In levo-transposition of the great arteries (congenitally corrected TGA), there is atrioventricular and ventriculo-arterial discordance. The morphologic right ventricle is connected to the systemic outflow tract, so it ejects oxygenated blood into the aorta, which then delivers it to the body.

442305.long_answer: Acute megakaryoblastic leukemia is characterized by uncontrolled growth of malignant megakaryoblasts, the precursors of megakaryocytes. Megakaryocytes normally fragment their cytoplasm to generate platelets (thrombocytes). Thus, the cell fragments whose production is linked to the excessive proliferation of megakaryoblasts in this leukemia are platelets.

542393.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis results from biallelic pathogenic mutations in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. Because the disease manifests only when both alleles are defective, it follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern: carriers with one mutant allele are typically asymptomatic, and children of two carriers have a 25 % chance of being affected, a 50 % chance of being carriers, and a 25 % chance of being unaffected.

120024.long_answer: In a newborn with agenesis of a pulmonary artery, surgeons can establish blood flow to the affected lung by creating a systemic-to-pulmonary arterial shunt. The standard operation is the (modified) Blalock-Taussig shunt, which anastomoses the subclavian or innominate artery to the intrapulmonary artery with a small Gore-Tex tube. This redirects systemic blood into the absent-artery lung, relieves hypoxaemia, promotes pulmonary arterial growth and reduces pulmonary hypertension, making it an accepted initial surgical treatment for neonatal pulmonary artery agenesis.

674093.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the transcription factor FOXJ1 disrupt the formation and motility of ependymal motile cilia that propel cerebrospinal fluid. The resulting ciliary dysfunction impairs CSF flow and clearance, leading to congenital or early-onset hydrocephalus. Thus, FOXJ1 is the key genetic factor linking defective cilia to the development of hydrocephalus.

824174.long_answer: Hashimoto’s encephalopathy, also called steroid-responsive encephalopathy associated with autoimmune thyroiditis, is a rare neurological disorder that occurs in patients with autoimmune (Hashimoto’s) thyroiditis. It can manifest with fluctuating cognitive impairment, seizures, myoclonus, and neuropsychiatric symptoms, including acute psychosis. High serum antithyroid antibodies and a typically favorable response to corticosteroids support the diagnosis.

950147.long_answer: Schwartz–Jampel syndrome (SJS) type 1, the osteochondrodysplasia characterized by myotonia and skeletal anomalies, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HSPG2 gene. HSPG2 encodes perlecan, a heparan-sulfate proteoglycan essential for cartilage and neuromuscular junction integrity; pathogenic HSPG2 variants disrupt perlecan’s function, leading to the skeletal dysplasia and myotonic features typical of SJS.

449193.long_answer: IκB kinase-α (IKKα, encoded by the CHUK gene) functions as a tumour-suppressor in epidermal keratinocytes. Experimental deletion of IKKα in mouse skin or marked reduction of its expression in human epidermis blocks normal keratinocyte differentiation, causes hyper-proliferation and markedly increases susceptibility to malignant transformation. Accordingly, loss or severe down-regulation of IKKα is frequently detected in cutaneous squamous-cell carcinomas, indicating that its absence is a key step in the progression of normal keratinocytes to malignant cSCC.

125312.long_answer: A VIP-secreting tumour (VIPoma) characteristically produces WDHA syndrome—Watery Diarrhea, Hypokalemia, and Achlorhydria. The resulting severe hypokalemia often manifests as lethargy, linking this syndrome directly to the symptom mentioned.

981881.long_answer: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes accumulation of deoxyadenosine and dATP, which are toxic to developing lymphocytes. The ensuing severe combined immunodeficiency prevents normal T-cell maturation, resulting in a markedly hypoplastic or virtually absent thymus—the lymphoid organ where T cells normally develop.

999389.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the GREB1L gene have been identified in families where some carriers present with Müllerian agenesis (MRKH syndrome) while others have different genitourinary anomalies or are unaffected, demonstrating marked variable expressivity. GREB1L encodes a transcriptional co-activator important for embryonic development of the reproductive and urinary tracts, and its mutations show incomplete penetrance and diverse phenotypic outcomes characteristic of variable expressivity.

340322.long_answer: Pathogenic mutations in the Bestrophin-1 (BEST1) chloride channel cause the protein to misfold and become retained within the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) instead of being trafficked to the basolateral plasma membrane of retinal pigment epithelium cells. This ER retention/mislocalization disrupts BEST1 function and underlies several retinal degenerative diseases such as Best vitelliform macular dystrophy.

857134.long_answer: Trisomy 9 is usually detected before birth through procedures such as high-resolution fetal ultrasound, chorionic villus sampling, or amniocentesis. These investigations are routinely ordered and interpreted by maternal-fetal medicine (perinatology) specialists, the obstetrics subspecialty focused on high-risk pregnancies and prenatal genetic diagnosis; hence they are the physicians most likely to make a prenatal diagnosis of trisomy 9.

181513.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15. A single mutated copy of FBN1 is sufficient to produce the phenotype, and affected individuals have a 50% chance of passing the mutation to each offspring, fulfilling the criteria for autosomal-dominant inheritance.

673629.long_answer: Fatigue is one of the most frequently reported somatic complaints in somatic symptom disorder, where patients experience distressing tiredness without an identifiable medical cause. The same symptom can arise in myasthenia gravis, an autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction that produces activity-induced muscle weakness and a characteristic sense of fatigue that improves with rest.

194215.long_answer: The human PNPLA2 gene, which encodes adipose triglyceride lipase and whose mutations cause neutral lipid storage disease with myopathy, is mapped to chromosome 11 (cytogenetic band 11p15.5).

229093.long_answer: Loss-of-function of the X-linked vesicle-trafficking gene RAB39B, whether by pathogenic point mutation or Xq28 micro-deletion, produces a syndromic disorder characterized by intellectual disability and childhood epilepsy; affected males typically go on to develop early-onset parkinsonism. Hence, alteration or deletion of RAB39B is the genetic lesion that causes epilepsy in the early-onset parkinsonism-intellectual disability syndrome.

175999.long_answer: Pain in nail–patella syndrome usually arises from joint dysplasia and early osteoarthritis; first-line pharmacologic management is with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which reduce inflammation and provide analgesia for musculoskeletal pain.

783344.long_answer: Apparent mineralocorticoid excess results from deficient activity of the renal enzyme 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2, which normally converts active cortisol to inactive cortisone. When this enzyme is reduced, cortisol accumulates and overstimulates mineralocorticoid receptors, producing sodium retention, hypertension, and the characteristic suppression of renin release.

874508.long_answer: Camera-trap studies in Mizoram’s Dampa Tiger Reserve have estimated densities of around five clouded leopards (Neofelis nebulosa) per 100 km², a figure that ranks among the highest recorded anywhere in South or South-East Asia. Consequently, Dampa is recognised for harbouring one of the region’s most substantial clouded leopard populations.

120510.long_answer: Kabuki syndrome is a genetic disorder (most often from pathogenic variants in KMT2D or KDM6A) that presents with conductive hearing loss caused by middle-ear malformations, eyelid ptosis as part of its characteristic facial gestalt, and a spectrum of skeletal anomalies including vertebral defects, brachydactyly, and hip dislocation.

483968.long_answer: Hemangioblastomas are highly vascular, well-circumscribed tumors that can usually be removed en bloc. Complete surgical resection is therefore the standard first-line therapy; adjuvant radiosurgery or observation is reserved for unresectable or residual lesions.

721908.long_answer: Persistent truncus arteriosus is frequently observed in 22q11.2-deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome and in animal models lacking the transcription factor TBX1. TBX1 belongs to the T-box (TBX) gene family, whose members direct cardiac outflow-tract septation by controlling neural-crest cell migration and second heart-field development. Disruption of this gene family, particularly TBX1, therefore leads to failure of truncal septation and the congenital defect known as persistent truncus arteriosus.

909919.long_answer: In Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome, atrial fibrillation can conduct rapidly to the ventricles via the accessory pathway. Definitive treatment is achieved by radiofrequency catheter ablation, which targets and eliminates the accessory conduction pathway, thereby preventing both pre-excitation and AF-related rapid ventricular responses.

769614.long_answer: The Orphanet rare-disease database entry for “Galactorrhea-hyperprolactinemia” (ORPHA:3103) enumerates pregnancy as a recognized physiological/medical cause of the condition, alongside other etiologies such as pituitary adenoma, hypothyroidism and drug-induced hyperprolactinemia. Thus, Orphanet explicitly lists pregnancy as a possible cause of galactorrhea with hyperprolactinemia.

140316.long_answer: Most cases of congenital lactic acidosis accompanied by intellectual disability are due to loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked PDHA1 gene, which encodes the E1-α subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex. Defective PDHA1 blocks the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, forcing excess pyruvate to be reduced to lactate, thereby causing severe neonatal lactic acidosis. Energy failure in the developing brain leads to neurodevelopmental delay and long-term intellectual disability.

142862.long_answer: Apert syndrome (acrocephalosyndactyly) is a congenital disorder caused mainly by activating mutations in the FGFR2 gene. It leads to premature fusion of cranial sutures, producing characteristic mid-face abnormalities, and to complex syndactyly that impairs normal formation of the fingers and toes—thereby affecting both facial features and digits.

671671.long_answer: Genome-wide association studies have shown that the IL6R locus on chromosome 1q21.3, which encodes the interleukin-6 receptor, confers susceptibility to both Takayasu’s arteritis and atherosclerotic disease. Variants such as rs2228145 (Asp358Ala) modulate IL-6 signalling, influencing vascular inflammation in Takayasu’s arteritis and systemic inflammation that promotes or protects from atherosclerosis, linking this single chromosomal region to both conditions.

925717.long_answer: Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), a human gamma-herpesvirus that establishes latent infection in B lymphocytes, is detected in the Reed-Sternberg tumor cells of a substantial proportion of Hodgkin lymphoma cases. Epidemiological and molecular studies show that prior EBV infection increases the risk of developing Hodgkin lymphoma, making EBV the virus most clearly associated with this malignancy.

112582.long_answer: Agoraphobia is an anxiety disorder marked by intense fear or avoidance of situations—such as public places, crowds, or traveling—where escape might be difficult or help unavailable if panic-like symptoms occur. Epidemiological studies consistently show high comorbidity between agoraphobia (with or without panic attacks) and substance use disorders, as individuals often turn to alcohol or drugs to cope with the distressing anxiety, fulfilling the criteria stated in the question.

239399.long_answer: Extensive epidemiological data, clinical studies, and public-health guidance agree that people with diabetes (both type 1 and type 2) have a markedly higher likelihood of developing severe manifestations of COVID-19 compared with non-diabetic individuals of the same age. Large cohort studies from China, Europe, and the United States show that diabetes roughly doubles the risk of hospitalisation, admission to intensive-care units, and death. Meta-analyses published in peer-reviewed journals report pooled odds ratios for severe disease or mortality in the range of 1.5–3.0 after adjusting for age and other comorbidities. Mechanistically, chronic hyperglycaemia can impair innate and adaptive immune responses, promote a pro-inflammatory state, and is frequently accompanied by cardiovascular, renal, and obesity-related comorbidities, all of which compound COVID-19 severity. Consequently, authoritative bodies such as the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the World Health Organization (WHO), and the International Diabetes Federation list diabetes as a high-risk condition for severe COVID-19. Therefore, the statement is supported by the established scientific consensus.

986180.long_answer: Onychomatricoma, a benign tumor of the nail matrix that produces xanthonychia (yellow nail discoloration) and can resemble an acral fibrokeratoma, is treated definitively by complete surgical excision of the lesion, which removes the proliferating matrix filaments and prevents recurrence.

556519.long_answer: Trichinella spiralis is a nematode parasite commonly called the “pork worm” because humans usually acquire it by eating under-cooked pork containing encysted larvae. After ingestion, larvae are released, mature in the intestine, and their newborn larvae disseminate hematogenously; during this migration they can invade the pulmonary parenchyma, provoking marked peripheral eosinophilia and the characteristic eosinophilic pneumonia seen in early trichinellosis.

937489.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is characterized by intellectual disability and distinctive physical features including brachydactyly (short fingers). Individuals with Down syndrome have a markedly increased incidence of congenital heart disease—particularly atrioventricular septal defects and ventricular or atrial septal defects—making it the genetic disorder classically linked to both short fingers and heightened risk of heart malformations.

722138.long_answer: Lung cancers can trigger disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), a paraneoplastic coagulopathy in which tumor-derived pro-coagulant factors activate the clotting cascade systemically. This results in the formation of microthrombi throughout the vasculature, consuming platelets and clotting factors and paradoxically leading to both widespread thrombosis and bleeding.

606075.long_answer: Freiberg disease is an osteochondrosis (avascular necrosis) of a metatarsal head, producing fore-foot pain and structural collapse of bone. Disorders of bones and joints of the foot are typically managed by orthopedic surgeons, especially those specializing in foot and ankle, making orthopedic surgery the specialty most commonly responsible for treating Freiberg disease.

359069.long_answer: POEMS syndrome frequently presents with pleural effusion, the abnormal accumulation of fluid in the pleural cavity surrounding the lungs. This effusion contributes to dyspnea and is part of the extravascular volume overload manifestations commonly observed in the disorder.

452853.long_answer: Among the recognized subtypes of acromesomelic dysplasia (Maroteaux, Hunter-Thompson, Grebe, etc.), the Grebe type is distinctive for segmentation defects of the carpal and tarsal bones that lead to congenital fusion (carpal and tarsal coalition). Radiographs classically show coalesced or block-like carpal bones, making carpal coalition a hallmark of the Grebe variety.

820082.long_answer: In September 2015 the U.S. FDA granted approval to uridine triacetate (brand name Xuriden) as the first specific therapy for hereditary orotic aciduria. Uridine triacetate is an orally-bioavailable prodrug of uridine that bypasses the deficiency of the enzyme UMP synthase, replenishing pyrimidine nucleotides, normalizing hematologic parameters and reducing urinary orotate accumulation in affected patients.

425889.long_answer: Heterozygous missense mutations in the MYH3 gene, which encodes the embryonic myosin heavy-chain 3, are a well-established cause of distal arthrogryposis syndromes. These disorders present with congenital joint contractures (arthrogryposis) and histologically abnormal skeletal muscle tissue. The pathogenic mechanism is a missense (gain-of-function) alteration in MYH3 that disrupts normal sarcomere function, leading to the characteristic contractures and myopathic changes.

162387.long_answer: Dalal et al. (2010) described a child with the characteristic features of Primrose syndrome who, from birth, had thyroid hormone deficiency fulfilling criteria for congenital hypothyroidism. This co-occurrence highlighted endocrine involvement as part of the phenotypic spectrum of Primrose syndrome.

552407.long_answer: Keutel syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by abnormal cartilage calcification, brachytelephalangy, and distinctive facial abnormalities. The condition is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MGP gene (Matrix Gla Protein), which normally inhibits ectopic calcification. Disruption of MGP leads to the craniofacial and skeletal features observed in Keutel syndrome, linking this gene directly to the facial abnormalities characteristic of the disease.

860587.long_answer: Klippel–Trénaunay syndrome is now recognized as part of the PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS). Somatic activating mutations in the PIK3CA gene, which encodes the p110α catalytic subunit of phosphatidylinositol-3-kinase, hyperactivate the PI3K–AKT–mTOR signaling pathway and drive the combined vascular malformations and tissue overgrowth characteristic of the syndrome.

515102.long_answer: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a group of inherited connective-tissue disorders in which mutations in collagen genes or in collagen-processing enzymes lead to structurally abnormal collagen fibers. The defective collagen weakens the dermal matrix, resulting in markedly increased skin elasticity (hyperextensible, fragile skin) and joint hypermobility.

272223.long_answer: The classical autosomal-dominant form of hyper-IgE syndrome is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the STAT3 gene, which encodes the transcription factor Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3. Defective STAT3 signaling impairs Th17 cell differentiation and cytokine responses, leading to recurrent staphylococcal infections, eczema, skeletal abnormalities, and markedly elevated serum IgE – the hallmarks of hyperimmunoglobulin E syndrome.

295106.long_answer: Noonan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant developmental disorder caused most often by mutations in RAS–MAPK pathway genes (e.g., PTPN11). It produces characteristic facial features (hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures, low-set ears) together with multiple skeletal abnormalities such as short stature, pectus deformities and the typical increased carrying angle of the elbows known as cubitus valgus. The presence of cubitus valgus is therefore a well-described component of the skeletal phenotype in Noonan syndrome.

785511.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the IRF6 gene, which encodes the transcription factor Interferon Regulatory Factor 6, disrupt epithelial and craniofacial development. Such mutations are the primary cause of Van der Woude syndrome and account for a significant proportion of nonsyndromic cleft lip and cleft palate, firmly establishing IRF6 mutation as a key genetic driver of these malformations.

816299.long_answer: St. Helena familial genu valgum was first identified in an extended family living on Saint Helena Island in the South Atlantic Ocean; the disorder takes its name from this isolated island where the initial kindred with the severe hereditary knock-knee deformity was described.

621789.long_answer: In hyperammonemia, excess ammonia increases extracellular glutamate and augments nitric-oxide production, leading to excessive stimulation of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors on neurons. Overactivation of these ionotropic glutamate receptors triggers calcium influx, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and excitotoxic neuronal damage, making NMDA receptor overactivation a key mechanism in ammonia-induced brain injury.

414467.long_answer: Avascular necrosis (osteonecrosis) occurs when the blood supply to a region of bone is interrupted. The resulting ischemia causes death of the bone tissue (osseous tissue) in the epiphysis, weakening the structural integrity of the bone, producing joint pain, and eventually leading to subchondral collapse and secondary arthritis.

278189.long_answer: Phenytoin, a classic antiepileptic drug, commonly produces nystagmus as a dose-related adverse effect; this ocular oscillation is the same symptom that appears in benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.

931993.long_answer: Mutations in the CAPN3 gene, which encodes the muscle-specific protease calpain-3, are responsible for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A (LGMD2A). LGMD2A accounts for the largest proportion of LGMD cases worldwide—reported in many cohorts to represent 20–40 % of all LGMD patients—making CAPN3 mutation the most frequent genetic cause of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy globally.

403680.long_answer: Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) syndrome is a disorder of the corneal endothelium and iris that can lead to secondary angle-closure glaucoma and corneal edema. Diagnosis and management—including slit-lamp examination, gonioscopy, intraocular pressure control, laser or surgical glaucoma procedures, and possible corneal transplantation—are carried out by ophthalmologists, the medical specialists trained to treat diseases of the eye.

459597.long_answer: A bile duct hamartoma is classically referred to as a Von Meyenburg complex, an eponym honoring the Swiss pathologist Hanns von Meyenburg who first described these benign malformative lesions of intrahepatic bile ducts.

722431.long_answer: Excess parathyroid hormone in hyperparathyroidism stimulates osteoclast-mediated bone resorption, progressively producing osteoporosis, and raises serum calcium and phosphate excretion, promoting nephrolithiasis and nephrocalcinosis. The resulting calcific injury can progress to chronic kidney disease, so hyperparathyroidism is a single condition that can lead to both osteoporosis and chronic kidney disease.

675601.long_answer: In systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, an uncommon but potentially life-threatening complication is macrophage activation syndrome (MAS). MAS represents a form of secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis triggered by excessive activation of T-lymphocytes and macrophages, leading to high fever, cytopenias, liver dysfunction, coagulopathy, and markedly elevated ferritin levels. Prompt recognition and immunosuppressive treatment are critical because MAS carries a high mortality if untreated.

317935.long_answer: Cold abscesses are collections of pus that lack the heat, redness and acute inflammatory reaction typical of ordinary abscesses. They are classically produced in tuberculosis, where infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis elicits a granulomatous rather than an acute neutrophilic response; necrotic material therefore accumulates quietly, giving rise to a ‘cold’ abscess without marked inflammation.

412386.long_answer: Bathophobia, meaning an irrational fear of depths, is a lexicographic term rather than a formal diagnostic category; its definition is given in standard English and medical dictionaries (e.g., Merriam-Webster, Dorland’s). Thus, you would locate the definition in a dictionary.

546235.long_answer: Deficiency of linoleic acid, the principal omega-6 essential fatty acid, disrupts epidermal barrier lipid synthesis and eicosanoid production. This produces a scaly, erythematous dermatitis that closely mimics the rash observed in zinc or biotin deficiency.

820626.long_answer: Randomized controlled trials have demonstrated that selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs—e.g., paroxetine, fluvoxamine, sertraline) can reduce the urges and behaviors of problem gambling, while SSRIs are also an established first-line pharmacologic treatment for major depressive disorder. Their efficacy in both conditions is thought to stem from modulation of central serotonergic pathways implicated in impulse control and mood regulation.

609153.long_answer: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is one of the most common congenital viral infections and is well-documented to cause long-term neurologic and neurodevelopmental sequelae. Epidemiologic studies and clinical follow-up of infants with congenital CMV consistently list cognitive and motor developmental delay/intellectual disability among its major complications, alongside sensorineural hearing loss, microcephaly, seizures, and vision impairment. Therefore, developmental disability is a recognized and established potential complication of congenital CMV infection.

630490.long_answer: The Norwood procedure is the standard staged surgical palliation for hypoplastic left heart syndrome that develops after severe fetal aortic stenosis. In Stage I, surgeons create a systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (e.g., modified Blalock–Taussig or Sano shunt) to supply pulmonary blood flow. In Stage II (bidirectional Glenn/hemi-Fontan), that initial shunt is removed and superior vena caval blood is redirected to the pulmonary arteries. Thus the operation explicitly involves first creating and later removing shunts to manage the circulation in infants with HLHS secondary to fetal aortic stenosis.

332786.long_answer: Familial cases of Pentalogy of Cantrell have shown an X-linked pattern of inheritance. Linkage studies mapped the responsible region to the X-chromosomal locus Xq25–q26.1, implicating genes within this interval in the pathogenesis of the characteristic midline thoraco-abdominal and cardiac defects.

322256.long_answer: Van der Woude syndrome is the commonest syndromic form of orofacial clefting. It typically presents with cleft lip with or without cleft palate, and its mildest manifestation can be a sub-mucous cleft or a bifid uvula. Thus, the combination of a cleft lip and a bifid uvula is characteristic of Van der Woude syndrome.

107428.long_answer: Iridodonesis—the trembling or vibration of the iris during eye movement—occurs when the iris loses the stabilising support normally provided by the crystalline lens. In dogs, this loss of support most commonly results from lens luxation (complete or partial displacement of the lens), allowing the iris to wobble freely with ocular motion.

443609.long_answer: Acute tubular necrosis damages the renal tubules within the kidney. The kidney’s fundamental structural and functional unit is the nephron, which comprises the glomerulus and its associated tubule segments and is responsible for filtration, reabsorption, and secretion. Injury to tubular epithelial cells of the nephron underlies the pathophysiology of acute tubular necrosis.

517260.long_answer: X-linked Juvenile Retinoschisis is an inherited disorder that causes splitting of the retinal layers and progressive visual loss; evaluation and management require expertise in retinal imaging, electrophysiology, and potential surgical or low-vision interventions, all of which fall under the domain of ophthalmology (often a pediatric or retinal subspecialist).

854121.long_answer: In the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM-5), several previously distinct pervasive developmental disorders—including childhood disintegrative disorder and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified—were consolidated under the single diagnostic category ‘Autism spectrum disorder’. This change reflected evidence that these conditions share common symptom domains (social-communication deficits and restricted, repetitive behaviors) and differ mainly in severity rather than in qualitative features.

745093.long_answer: Microscopic polyangiitis is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis strongly associated with perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA). The antigen most frequently targeted by these p-ANCAs is the neutrophil enzyme myeloperoxidase. Therefore, the antibody characteristically present in patients with microscopic polyangiitis is the anti-myeloperoxidase (MPO) ANCA.

346903.long_answer: If achalasia is not treated during the mid-stage, the chronically stagnant food and saliva cause longstanding mucosal irritation and inflammation. Over years this markedly increases the risk of malignant transformation of the esophageal epithelium, most often resulting in squamous-cell esophageal carcinoma, a life-threatening complication documented to be 10–30 times more common in untreated achalasia than in the general population.

330552.long_answer: Management of PHACE syndrome is multidisciplinary; when mental health issues such as anxiety, depression, or behavioral disorders arise, the medical specialty that evaluates and treats these conditions is psychiatry.

456914.long_answer: Arakawa's syndrome II (also known as the hyper-ornithinaemia, hyper-ammonaemia, homocitrullinuria or HHH syndrome) results from biallelic pathogenic variants in the SLC25A15 gene that encodes the mitochondrial ornithine transporter-1. Because the disorder manifests only when both copies of the gene are defective and carrier parents are typically unaffected, it follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

511972.long_answer: Wildervanck syndrome, also called cervico-oculo-acoustic syndrome, includes congenital sensorineural deafness as a core feature together with Duane retraction syndrome and Klippel-Feil cervical vertebral fusion. Because accurate diagnosis and management hinge on detailed assessment of the auditory system and provision of interventions such as audiologic testing, hearing aids, or cochlear implantation, the specialty most centrally involved is otolaryngology (ear, nose, and throat). ENT physicians are trained to evaluate and treat inner-ear malformations and related cranial-nerve anomalies, making them the primary specialists for this syndrome.

781874.long_answer: Omenn syndrome often presents with chronic diarrhea caused by intestinal inflammation and infections resulting from the underlying immunodeficiency. Chronic diarrhea is likewise a well-recognized driver of childhood malnutrition worldwide because persistent fluid and nutrient losses impair growth and nutrient absorption.

258100.long_answer: Heterozygous (autosomal-dominant) mutations in the PAX6 gene are a well-established cause of Peters’ Anomaly type 2 and other anterior segment dysgeneses, making PAX6 the classic dominantly inherited gene linked to this disorder.

648379.long_answer: Activating germ-line mutations in the ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase) proto-oncogene can arise at the moment of fertilisation, so the mutation is present in every cell of the embryo. Such de-novo (or inherited) germline ALK mutations are a well-established pre-disposing factor for the development of neuroblastoma.

312876.long_answer: Pheochromocytomas are catecholamine-secreting tumors of the adrenal medulla. Excess release of epinephrine and norepinephrine produces episodic or sustained, potentially life-threatening hypertension that often presents with classic symptoms such as severe headaches, palpitations, and sweating.

698673.long_answer: Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome (SGBS) is an overgrowth/obesity condition caused by loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked glypican-3 (GPC3) gene. Because the gene is on the X chromosome, the disorder follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern: hemizygous males are affected, whereas carrier females are usually asymptomatic or only mildly affected. A characteristic clinical feature is excessive growth with progressive childhood obesity, alongside coarse facial features, macroglossia and organomegaly, fitting the description of an obesity-associated genetic disorder inherited as X-linked recessive.

112266.long_answer: Radiation-induced cerebral cavernous malformations are a documented late complication of cranial irradiation. Multiple clinical series have shown that patients treated with high-dose proton beam therapy for brain or skull-base tumors can develop de-novo CCMs years later. The particle radiation damages endothelial cells and small cerebral vessels, leading to capillary telangiectasia that evolve into cavernous malformations. Therefore, proton beam radiation therapy is a recognized cause of CCMs.

918691.long_answer: Autosomal-dominant hypertension with brachydactyly (Bilginturan syndrome) is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the PDE3A gene, which encodes phosphodiesterase-3A. PDE3A is expressed in vascular smooth muscle and cardiac tissue, where it regulates cyclic AMP signalling and thus vascular tone and cardiac contractility. Hyperactive PDE3A variants accelerate cAMP degradation, increasing peripheral vascular resistance and producing the severe, early-onset hypertension that characterises the syndrome alongside brachydactyly.

621379.long_answer: TAR (thrombocytopenia-absent radius) syndrome is characterized by severe congenital thrombocytopenia that predisposes patients to bleeding; management centers on monitoring platelet counts and providing platelet transfusions or other blood-related therapies. These aspects fall squarely within the expertise of hematologists (typically pediatric hematologists), who are therefore the specialists most commonly responsible for treating patients with TAR syndrome.

608868.long_answer: Spasticity in infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy is treated symptomatically. The muscle relaxant baclofen, a GABA-B receptor agonist that acts at the spinal cord to inhibit excitatory neurotransmission, is commonly prescribed to reduce the heightened muscle tone and spasms seen in these patients.

151288.long_answer: Jacksonian (simple partial motor) seizures originate in a discrete area of the motor cortex and produce repetitive, rhythmic jerking of the affected muscle groups. This repeated jerking is the clinical manifestation of clonic muscle contractions, which may progressively ‘march’ from one region to adjacent ones (the Jacksonian march).

858339.long_answer: The fovea centralis, a small depression at the center of the macula lutea, contains the highest density of cone photoreceptors and no rods. This dense packing of cones with minimal neural convergence provides maximal spatial resolution and color discrimination, making the fovea centralis responsible for sharp, high-resolution vision in bright (photopic) light required for tasks such as reading.

740442.long_answer: In a cerebral arteriovenous malformation, the direct abnormal tangle where arterial blood passes into veins without an intervening capillary bed is called the nidus. This nidus comprises dysplastic vessels that create the pathological arteriovenous shunt characteristic of an AVM.

373101.long_answer: In July 2022, two paediatric cases of toxin-producing Corynebacterium diphtheriae were reported in northern New South Wales, prompting NSW Health to declare a diphtheria outbreak—the first locally acquired cases in the state in many decades.

102954.long_answer: Chlorhexidine gluconate is a bis-biguanide antiseptic incorporated in prescription and some over-the-counter mouthwashes. Owing to its high substantivity, it binds to oral tissues and is slowly released, providing broad-spectrum antibacterial activity that suppresses dental plaque biofilm—the primary etiologic factor in gingivitis. Numerous controlled clinical trials and systematic reviews show that daily rinsing with 0.12–0.2 % chlorhexidine mouthwash significantly reduces plaque accumulation and gingival inflammation compared with placebo or essential-oil rinses, making it the most consistently effective anti-gingivitis ingredient in commercial mouthwashes.

925646.long_answer: Essential fructosuria results from deficiency of hepatic ketohexokinase (KHK). Molecular mapping studies have placed the human KHK gene at cytogenetic band 2p23, establishing that the gene responsible for this benign metabolic trait resides on chromosome 2.

159442.long_answer: The commonest cause of virilisation and ambiguous external genitalia in otherwise 46,XX (genotypically normal female) infants is classic congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency. This enzymatic defect results from pathogenic mutations in the CYP21A2 gene, leading to excess adrenal androgen production that masculinises the external genitalia in utero.

907623.long_answer: In bacterial vaginosis, the hallmark clinical feature is a thin gray-white vaginal discharge that emits a characteristic fishy or amine odor, particularly after sexual intercourse or when potassium hydroxide is applied (the “whiff test”). Unlike vulvovaginal candidiasis, pruritus (itching) is usually absent, making the malodorous discharge the primary and most common symptom.

510791.long_answer: Patients with pyruvate kinase deficiency often require chronic red-cell transfusions for hemolytic anemia. Each unit of transfused blood contains about 200–250 mg of elemental iron, and the body has no active mechanism to excrete excess iron. Over time, the cumulative iron load from repeated transfusions can exceed storage capacity, leading to systemic iron deposition (transfusional hemosiderosis/hemochromatosis) that may damage the liver, heart, and endocrine organs.

380819.long_answer: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs in the tracheo-oesophageal groove immediately behind the thyroid gland. As a thyroid carcinoma enlarges it can breach the thyroid capsule and grow straight into adjacent tissues; the nerve is one of the first structures encountered. Consequently, thyroid cancers frequently infiltrate the recurrent laryngeal nerve directly, leading to vocal-cord paralysis without requiring lymphatic or blood-borne spread.

509688.long_answer: Wernicke encephalopathy is classically caused by a deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1), which impairs cerebral energy metabolism. Crohn’s disease, through small-intestinal inflammation, resection, or malabsorption, can likewise lead to inadequate thiamine uptake. Thus, thiamine deficiency is the common nutritional deficit associated with both conditions.

939905.long_answer: Cytosine residues in DNA can spontaneously lose their amino group—a deamination reaction that converts cytosine to uracil (and 5-methyl-cytosine to thymine). If the resulting U•G or T•G mismatches are not repaired, they become C→T transition mutations. Defects in DNA repair pathways seen in progeroid syndromes (e.g., Werner, Cockayne) allow these deamination-induced lesions to accumulate, contributing to the mutational load characteristic of premature‐aging disorders.

513557.long_answer: Hoyeraal–Hreidarsson syndrome is a severe variant of dyskeratosis congenita caused by mutations in telomere-maintenance genes (e.g., DKC1, TERT, RTEL1). A hallmark of the disease is critically short telomeres in somatic cells, far below the age-matched normal range, leading to bone-marrow failure, immunodeficiency and other clinical features.

432741.long_answer: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is routinely employed to visualize and quantify cerebellar structures. High-resolution T1- and T2-weighted MRI can reveal cerebellar cortical and vermian atrophy, pontine atrophy, and other posterior-fossa structural changes characteristic of autosomal dominant (spinocerebellar) cerebellar ataxias, making it the imaging modality of choice for detecting such abnormalities.

610153.long_answer: The amygdala is a medial-temporal lobe nucleus that receives convergent inputs from the sensory thalamus and cortical sensory areas, allowing it to integrate and evaluate sensory information. Functional imaging consistently shows hyper-activation of the amygdala in people with generalized anxiety disorder, reflecting its central role in generating and regulating fear and anxiety responses. Because it both processes sensory input and orchestrates emotional reactions, the amygdala is the structure implicated in sensory processing as well as in the pathophysiology of anxiety disorders.

360272.long_answer: Familial male-limited precocious puberty (testotoxicosis) is driven by excess testicular steroid production that is independent of gonadotropin control. Therapy therefore focuses on blocking the peripheral action of these steroids. Antiandrogen drugs (e.g., spironolactone, flutamide, bicalutamide) antagonise the androgen receptor, thereby preventing the biological effects of the androgens produced by gonadal steroidogenesis and slowing or reversing the precocious pubertal changes.

407075.long_answer: The British microbiologist Derek Baxby, a virologist at the University of Liverpool, analysed and published data on zoonotic orthopoxvirus infections and documented 12 confirmed human cases of cowpox that occurred in England between 1965 and 1976, highlighting transmission from domestic animals (especially cats) to humans.

685823.long_answer: Naegleria fowleri, a free-living thermophilic amoeba, can invade the nasal mucosa during exposure to contaminated warm freshwater. It migrates along the olfactory nerve through the cribriform plate into the brain, where it produces a rapidly progressive and often fatal infection called primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM).

465124.long_answer: The male infertility seen in Young’s syndrome is caused by obstructive azoospermia of the epididymis; investigation and treatment of such genitourinary tract obstructions are undertaken by urologists (andrology within urology). Therefore, the appropriate specialty for managing the reduced male fertility is Urology.

527063.long_answer: Thiazide-type diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone) are widely prescribed antihypertensive agents. A well-documented metabolic adverse effect of this drug class is elevation of serum total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, thereby producing hyperlipidemia in some patients.

596159.long_answer: During pregnancy, anticoagulation for women with mechanical (prosthetic) heart valves is achieved with low-molecular-weight heparin (e.g., enoxaparin) because heparin does not cross the placenta, avoids warfarin-associated teratogenicity, and provides effective prophylaxis against valve thrombosis and deep vein thrombosis.

763626.long_answer: Hypobetalipoproteinemia is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the APOB gene, which encodes apolipoprotein B. Apolipoprotein B-100 is the obligatory structural protein of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles; it wraps around the LDL lipid core and is required for their assembly, secretion, and receptor binding. Thus, the same protein—apolipoprotein B—is directly implicated in both the genetic disorder hypobetalipoproteinemia and the structural integrity of LDL particles.

902219.long_answer: Prolactin is synthesized and secreted by lactotroph cells of the anterior pituitary gland. Elevated prolactin levels can disrupt the normal balance between estrogens and androgens, leading to relative estrogen excess and stimulation of breast tissue in males, thereby contributing to the development of gynecomastia.

634635.long_answer: The Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator (CFTR) gene is situated on the long arm (q arm) of human chromosome 7, specifically at cytogenetic band 7q31.2. Mutations in this gene disrupt chloride ion transport across epithelial membranes, leading to the multisystem manifestations characteristic of cystic fibrosis.

719816.long_answer: Spirurida nematodes, like all nematodes, have no heart or blood vessels and therefore lack a true blood-vascular network. Transport of nutrients and gases occurs by diffusion through the pseudocoelomic fluid, so they do not possess a closed circulatory system.

946964.long_answer: Treacher Collins syndrome is most commonly caused by mutations in the TCOF1 gene, which encodes the nucleolar protein treacle. Genetic mapping and sequencing studies place TCOF1 on the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q32-q33). Pathogenic variants in this chromosomal locus disrupt ribosomal biogenesis during craniofacial development, leading to the characteristic features of Treacher Collins syndrome.

575542.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type I is caused by pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene, which encodes neurofibromin. Neurofibromin functions as a GTPase-activating protein (GAP) that negatively regulates the RAS signaling pathway by accelerating the conversion of active RAS-GTP to inactive RAS-GDP. Loss of NF1 activity therefore leads to increased RAS pathway signaling, driving the clinical manifestations of the disorder.

958259.long_answer: Digoxin toxicity often produces a combination of increased atrial automaticity and enhanced vagal inhibition of the AV node. This yields a rapid paroxysmal atrial tachycardia that is partially conducted, typically with a 2:1 or higher AV block. The pattern—atrial tachycardia with AV block—is considered the classic, most characteristic arrhythmia seen in digoxin intoxication.

792325.long_answer: In a subset of patients, chronic lymphocytic leukemia undergoes ‘Richter transformation,’ in which the CLL clone acquires additional genetic lesions (e.g., MYC activation, TP53 loss) and converts into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). DLBCL is a high-grade, rapidly proliferating lymphoma that is clinically much more aggressive than indolent CLL.

688760.long_answer: Maple syrup urine disease (MSUD) is an autosomal-recessive inborn error of metabolism in which mutations in the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex genes (BCKDHA, BCKDHB, DBT) block the catabolism of the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine and valine. Their corresponding keto-acids accumulate, producing a toxic buildup of organic acids that leads to metabolic acidosis and the characteristic maple-syrup odor of urine.

640331.long_answer: In ring chromosome 20 (r(20)) syndrome the epileptic phenotype is linked to disturbance of genes in the distal long-arm subtelomeric segment of chromosome 20. Molecular studies repeatedly implicate the 20q13.3 region, which contains epilepsy-related genes such as KCNQ2 and CHRNA4. Altered dosage or epigenetic silencing of this 20q13.3 segment in the ring chromosome is therefore considered the chief chromosomal region associated with the characteristic epilepsy seen in r(20) syndrome.

201812.long_answer: Marfan syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, commonly features ectopia lentis—superior-temporal subluxation of the crystalline lens—due to weakened zonular fibers in the eye.

974604.long_answer: In autoimmune hemolytic anemia, auto-IgG or IgM antibodies bind antigens on the patient’s own red blood cell surface; this antibody coating triggers complement activation and/or Fc-mediated phagocytosis, a classic antibody-mediated (Type II) hypersensitivity reaction that destroys the red cells.

153777.long_answer: Polymorphous low-grade adenocarcinoma is included in the World Health Organization classification as a malignant epithelial neoplasm of the salivary glands (a salivary gland carcinoma). It arises most often in minor salivary glands and, despite its generally indolent behavior, is histopathologically and clinically categorized as a malignant salivary gland tumor.

457938.long_answer: At least one well-documented case report describes a woman with a 48,XXXX (tetrasomy X) karyotype who developed systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). This observation supports the known association between excess X-chromosome dosage and increased risk of autoimmune disorders such as SLE, which is more common in females and in individuals carrying additional X chromosomes (e.g., Klinefelter 47,XXY males).

702960.long_answer: Thin basement membrane disease is defined by diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane, a change that is only visible at ultrastructural level. Performing electron microscopy on a renal (kidney) biopsy allows direct measurement of basement-membrane thickness and therefore distinguishes thin basement membrane disease from other causes of glomerular hematuria such as IgA nephropathy or Alport syndrome, which show normal or thickened/laminated membranes, respectively.

403942.long_answer: The non-photosensitive (non–DNA-repair‐deficient) form of trichothiodystrophy is most often caused by biallelic mutations in the TTDN1 gene (also called C7orf11). Unlike the photosensitive forms linked to NER genes such as ERCC2/XPD, ERCC3/XPB, and GTF2H5, TTDN1 mutations do not impair nucleotide-excision repair, so patients lack abnormal UV sensitivity while still exhibiting the characteristic brittle, sulfur-deficient hair and developmental features of trichothiodystrophy.

890618.long_answer: Langer–Giedion syndrome, also called trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type II, is a form of ectodermal dysplasia produced by a contiguous-gene deletion on chromosome 8q24. This microdeletion removes both the TRPS1 gene and neighboring genes such as EXT1, leading to sparse scalp hair, nail and skin changes typical of ectodermal dysplasia together with characteristic facial features and multiple exostoses.

471236.long_answer: Cayler cardiofacial syndrome presents with asymmetric crying facies caused by depressor-anguli-oris hypoplasia together with congenital heart defects (e.g., ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot). Because the major morbidity and need for intervention arise from these cardiac malformations, the specialty that routinely diagnoses, evaluates (echocardiography, genetic work-up) and treats such congenital heart disease is pediatric cardiology.

435440.long_answer: Basilar invagination (also called basilar impression or cranial settling) is a craniovertebral junction anomaly in which the floor of the skull (the basiocciput) is drawn upward, allowing the odontoid process and superior portion of the C2 vertebra to migrate into the foramen magnum. This upward displacement can compress neural structures and is the classic condition described as invagination of the skull base with superior migration of C2.

795931.long_answer: Current WHO, ILCOR, and Neonatal Resuscitation Program (NRP) guidelines advise initiating positive-pressure ventilation with room air (≈21 % O₂) rather than 100 % oxygen for term or near-term newborns suffering perinatal asphyxia. Clinical trials have shown that bag-and-mask ventilation with room air achieves equivalent or better restoration of spontaneous breathing, reduces oxidative injury, and lowers mortality compared with pure oxygen; supplemental oxygen is added only if the infant fails to improve.

159611.long_answer: After a surgically created arteriovenous fistula matures, the low-resistance venous outflow causes a large rise in arterial inflow. Doppler studies show the brachial artery flow increases from roughly 50–100 mL/min at baseline to about 0.6 L per minute (≈600 mL/min), a value accepted clinically as the minimum adequate flow for a functioning haemodialysis fistula.

828178.long_answer: Post-polio syndrome is a late neurologic complication of poliomyelitis that manifests with new muscle weakness, fatigue, and pain decades after the initial infection. Diagnosis requires exclusion of other neurologic conditions and electrophysiologic evaluation of lower-motor-neuron function, tasks that fall within the expertise of a neurologist. Management likewise relies on neurologic assessment of motor units and coordination with rehabilitation strategies, so the medical specialty primarily responsible is Neurology.

678971.long_answer: Aicardi–Goutières syndrome is an inherited encephalopathy that presents in infancy with cerebral calcifications, chronic neuro-inflammation, developmental delay, spasticity, and seizures. Because it primarily affects the central nervous system in children, diagnosis and ongoing care are typically directed by a pediatric neurologist, the medical specialty focused on neurologic disorders in childhood.

431388.long_answer: Guillain–Barré syndrome is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy managed primarily by neurologists, who use disease-modifying therapies such as intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange to halt immune attack on peripheral nerves.

622248.long_answer:
Current epidemiological and neuropathological data do not place cerebral microinfarcts as the “fourth most important” independent cause of dementia. The major recognized aetiologies of chronic degenerative dementia in the population are, in rough order of prevalence: (1) Alzheimer’s disease, (2) vascular dementia (principally from larger-territory infarcts and diffuse small-vessel disease, which may include microinfarcts but does not treat them as a separate category), (3) dementia with Lewy bodies/Parkinson’s disease dementia, and (4) frontotemporal lobar degeneration.  

Microinfarcts are exceedingly common in the aged brain and are now understood to contribute to the overall burden of vascular cognitive impairment, often in combination with Alzheimer pathology (“mixed dementia”). Some autopsy studies show that the presence of microinfarcts adds substantially to the risk of dementia, in some analyses ranking second only to Alzheimer pathology in their statistical contribution. However, that contribution is considered part of the broader category of vascular dementia rather than a distinct, fourth-place cause after Alzheimer’s disease. Hence, the assertion that microinfarcts are the fourth most important cause of dementia after Alzheimer’s disease is not supported by prevailing consensus.

769650.long_answer: Spastic diplegia is a cerebral palsy subtype in which spasticity predominantly involves the lower limbs. The legs (lower extremities) are essential for weight-bearing and postural balance, so involvement of these muscles leads to the characteristic gait and stability problems seen in spastic diplegia.

177525.long_answer: Mutations in the homeobox gene MSX1 are a well-established cause of hypodontia/anodontia, and the same gene is recurrently implicated in nonsyndromic cleft lip with or without cleft palate. Thus, MSX1 links both tooth agenesis and cleft lip-palate phenotypes.

994292.long_answer: Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is mainly spread by the fecal-oral route through contaminated water or food. While it usually causes a self-limited acute hepatitis in the general population, infection during pregnancy—especially in the third trimester—can lead to fulminant hepatic failure with markedly increased maternal and fetal mortality, distinguishing it from other viral hepatitides.

638861.long_answer: X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the IL2RG gene, which encodes the common γ-chain of several interleukin receptors. Sequencing (mutation analysis) of the IL2RG gene in genomic DNA directly identifies these variants and therefore provides a definitive genetic diagnosis of X-SCID.

978283.long_answer: Meningiomas frequently contain psammoma bodies—concentric, lamellated calcific spherules that form within whorled clusters of tumor cells and are a classic microscopic hallmark of these tumors.

232168.long_answer: Aerobic exercise—such as brisk walking, jogging, cycling or swimming—raises heart and respiratory rates for sustained periods. This improves cardiovascular fitness, lowers blood pressure and LDL-cholesterol, enhances endothelial function, and increases insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake in skeletal muscle. These physiological adaptations reduce atherosclerotic risk and help maintain normal blood glucose levels, thereby decreasing the likelihood of developing heart disease and Type 2 diabetes.

616508.long_answer: Prince Randian, billed as “The Human Torso,” was born without arms or legs. This complete absence of all four limbs is the defining feature of the congenital disorder known as tetra-amelia syndrome, a rare condition most often linked to mutations affecting the WNT3 signaling pathway during embryonic limb development.

335959.long_answer: On April 27, 2017 the U.S. FDA approved cerliponase alfa (brand name Brineura), an intraventricular enzyme-replacement therapy that supplies the deficient tripeptidyl-peptidase 1 (TPP1) enzyme in patients with late-infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis type 2 (Jansky–Bielschowsky disease).

172058.long_answer: Oculocerebrocutaneous (Delleman) syndrome frequently involves midline cerebral malformations, with partial or complete agenesis of the corpus callosum being one of the most consistently reported findings on neuro-imaging. This structure’s absence or hypoplasia contributes to the neurological manifestations seen in affected individuals.

370625.long_answer: Type I cryoglobulinemia consists of a single (monoclonal) immunoglobulin that is typically produced in disorders such as monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). MGUS is a clinically recognized premalignant (precancerous) plasma-cell condition that can progress to multiple myeloma or other lymphoproliferative malignancies. Therefore, the type of cryoglobulinemia linked to a precancerous condition is Type I.

879458.long_answer: Filippi syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by growth retardation, microcephaly, intellectual disability and syndactyly. Exome-sequencing studies have shown that affected individuals carry biallelic frameshift (loss-of-function) mutations in the CKAP2L gene (Cytoskeleton-Associated Protein 2-Like). CKAP2L encodes a mitotic spindle–associated protein; truncating frameshift variants impair proper spindle organization during neurodevelopment, providing the causal mechanism for Filippi syndrome. Hence, frameshift mutations in CKAP2L are responsible for the disease.

338459.long_answer: Most myocardial infarctions occur when atherosclerotic plaques in the coronary arteries rupture or erode, triggering platelet aggregation and thrombus formation that abruptly occludes blood flow. Thus, the underlying blood-vessel disorder responsible for the majority of myocardial infarctions is coronary atherosclerosis.

117137.long_answer: Studies of panic disorder consistently show dysregulation of the brain’s serotonergic system—e.g., altered 5-HT receptor binding and benefit from selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors. Independent research on personality disorders (especially borderline and antisocial types) also implicates low or unstable serotonin activity in impulsivity and affective instability. Thus, irregular serotonin neurotransmission links panic disorder and several personality disorders.

244936.long_answer: Barbiturates are sedative-hypnotic drugs that were historically prescribed for insomnia. Prolonged, daily use can lead to tolerance and physical dependence, and chronic intoxication is well documented to produce persistent cognitive deficits—memory loss, confusion and disorientation—described clinically as an organic brain syndrome.

773867.long_answer: Dermato-osteolysis, Kirghizian type causes progressive osteolysis of the carpal, tarsal and other bones in childhood, leading to deformity, instability and functional impairment. Treatment centers on musculoskeletal monitoring, bracing and corrective or stabilizing surgery—interventions that fall squarely within the expertise of pediatric orthopedic surgeons. Therefore, pediatric orthopedics is the specialty most likely to direct management of the disease’s symptoms in children.

531097.long_answer: Nonoxynol-9, the most common surfactant compound in spermicidal foams, gels, and films, has been studied in epidemiologic cohorts and randomized trials; these data show no significant increase or decrease in the incidence of bacterial vaginosis among users compared with non-users. Therefore, exposure to Nonoxynol-9 does not alter a woman’s risk of developing bacterial vaginosis.

782939.long_answer: Hereditary multiple osteochondromas (also called hereditary multiple exostoses) characteristically produce osteocartilaginous outgrowths at the metaphyses of long bones. In the forearm, both long bones—the radius and the ulna—can develop these osteochondromas, leading to ulnar shortening, radial bowing, and potential deformity or functional impairment.

468451.long_answer: Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune sequela of group A streptococcal pharyngitis in which antibodies formed against streptococcal M-protein cross-react with cardiac tissue (molecular mimicry). The resulting pancarditis produces chronic inflammation and scarring of the heart valves—particularly the mitral and aortic valves—leading to rheumatic valvular heart disease.

859910.long_answer: Keloid scars are commonly treated with the 585–595 nm pulsed dye laser (PDL). This vascular‐selective laser targets hemoglobin within the abundant microvasculature of keloids, producing selective photothermolysis that decreases blood supply, down-regulates fibroblast activity, and leads to gradual flattening and softening of the scar while also reducing redness and pruritus.

607336.long_answer: Metaphyseal chondrodysplasia Schmid type is characterized by abnormalities in the metaphyses—the flared, actively growing zones just below the growth plate of long bones. Mutations in the COL10A1 gene disrupt type X collagen in hypertrophic chondrocytes, and the resulting cartilage and bone matrix defects are most pronounced in the metaphyseal regions, leading to the typical widening and irregularity seen on radiographs.

865125.long_answer: Following liver injury hepatic stellate cells become activated, transform into myofibroblast-like cells and are the main source of type I/III collagen and other extracellular matrix components. Their sustained collagen deposition and matrix remodeling drive hepatic fibrosis, the pathological process that culminates in cirrhosis.

439395.long_answer: Strabismus—misalignment of the eyes, often presenting as esotropia or exotropia—is frequently observed in children with cerebral palsy. Neuromotor impairment of the extra-ocular muscles and their central control pathways makes ocular alignment unstable, so up to 40–60 % of cerebral palsy patients develop strabismus, far above the prevalence in the general pediatric population.

197744.long_answer: Chronic psychological or physiological stress persistently stimulates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, keeping cortisol and catecholamine levels chronically elevated. Prolonged cortisol exposure drives visceral fat accumulation, promotes insulin resistance, increases hepatic gluconeogenesis, raises blood pressure through mineralocorticoid effects, and alters lipid metabolism. Together these cortisol-mediated changes—central obesity, hyperglycaemia, hypertension, and dyslipidaemia—constitute the core abnormalities that define metabolic syndrome.

910555.long_answer: Conversion disorder (functional neurological symptom disorder) can indeed present with motor phenomena such as functional dystonia, so an association with dystonia is accepted. However, by definition the symptoms in conversion disorder are not consciously produced or feigned; intentional production of illness is characteristic of factitious disorder or malingering, not conversion disorder. Therefore, conversion disorder is not considered to be associated with feigning illness. Because the statement claims an association with both dystonia and feigning illness, it is not fully correct.

677483.long_answer: Excess intake of vitamin A or its analogues (e.g., isotretinoin) can raise intracranial pressure, producing idiopathic intracranial hypertension (also called pseudotumor cerebri). Elevated intracranial pressure leads to bilateral optic disc swelling (papilledema) and associated visual symptoms.

584795.long_answer: In high-grade lymphomas, rapid destruction of malignant cells can trigger tumor lysis syndrome. The sudden release of intracellular potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids causes hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hypocalcemia and other metabolic derangements. These electrolyte imbalances can precipitate fatal cardiac arrhythmias, making tumor lysis syndrome a life-threatening complication that may lead to sudden cardiac death.

446189.long_answer: Grady Stiles Jr., popularly known as “Lobster Boy,” was born with ectrodactyly, a congenital limb malformation in which one or more of the central digits of the hands or feet fail to develop. The resulting cleft gives the limbs a split-hand/split-foot appearance. Ectrodactyly is often inherited in an autosomal-dominant pattern and can involve genes such as TP63 that direct limb bud formation; the deficiency or complete absence of the central rays is its defining feature.

278988.long_answer: Noonan syndrome is a RAS-MAPK–pathway developmental disorder characterized by distinctive facial features, most notably down-slanting palpebral fissures, together with multiple skeletal anomalies such as pectus excavatum/carinatum, cubitus valgus and short stature. These hallmark findings make Noonan syndrome the classically recognized syndrome that links downslanting palpebral fissures with skeletal abnormalities.

555736.long_answer: A congenital cleft of the soft palate disrupts the muscular sling (e.g., the levator veli palatini), preventing the soft palate from sealing against the posterior pharyngeal wall. This structural defect results in velopharyngeal inadequacy, allowing air to escape through the nose during speech and causing hypernasality.

253727.long_answer: Mutations in the metabolic enzyme isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1 or IDH2) are recurrently found in chondrosarcoma and in several leukemias, especially acute myeloid leukemia. These neomorphic IDH mutations produce the oncometabolite 2-hydroxyglutarate, which drives epigenetic dysregulation and contributes to tumorigenesis in both malignancies.

385329.long_answer: Fryns-Aftimos syndrome is produced by mosaic tetrasomy of the short arm of chromosome 12 (12p), most often due to an extra isochromosome 12p. Hence, the clinical picture is directly linked to abnormalities of human chromosome 12.

279243.long_answer: Maculopathy is any pathological condition that specifically involves the macula lutea—the small, central, yellow-pigmented area of the retina responsible for high-acuity and color vision.

738542.long_answer: When fluoride is consumed chronically at concentrations higher than those used for community water fluoridation (~0.7–1 ppm), it disrupts normal enamel mineralization in developing teeth. This results in hypomineralized, opaque, and sometimes mottled enamel—a condition termed dental fluorosis.

236749.long_answer: RAB39B encodes a small Rab-family GTPase located on Xq28. Rab proteins orchestrate budding, movement and fusion of membrane vesicles, thereby controlling the trafficking of proteins and lipids between the endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi, endosomes and the plasma membrane. Pathogenic loss-of-function mutations in RAB39B disrupt this vesicular trafficking and have been repeatedly documented in families with X-linked intellectual disability, confirming its role in both intracellular transport and the cognitive disorder.

794727.long_answer: Mutations in the SPAST gene (also known as SPG4 or spastin) are the single most frequent cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia. They account for roughly 40 % of autosomal-dominant HSP and about 25 % of all HSP cases across inheritance patterns, making SPAST the gene responsible for approximately one-quarter of hereditary spastic paraplegia overall.

679651.long_answer: Apert syndrome is caused by specific missense mutations (most commonly Ser252Trp or Pro253Arg) in the FGFR2 gene, which encodes fibroblast growth factor receptor 2. These gain-of-function mutations dysregulate FGFR2 signaling during craniofacial and limb development, leading to premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) and syndactyly.

356233.long_answer: The TYR gene encodes tyrosinase, the rate-limiting enzyme in melanin biosynthesis. Pathogenic variants on both alleles—often as compound heterozygous mutations—abolish or markedly reduce tyrosinase activity, leading to the autosomal-recessive disorder oculocutaneous albinism type 1 (OCA1), characterized by hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and eyes and visual abnormalities.

799378.long_answer: Mustelidae is the mammalian family that encompasses weasels, otters, wolverines, ferrets, and related carnivores. Members of this family are known definitive hosts for several Diphyllobothrium species, whose life cycles involve piscivorous mammals such as mustelids becoming infected when they consume fish containing plerocercoid larvae.

115658.long_answer: 14-3-3 proteins are abundant neuronal adaptor proteins whose presence in cerebrospinal fluid is a clinical marker of neurotoxicity (e.g., prion diseases). They also regulate apoptosis by binding the phosphorylated form of the pro-apoptotic protein BAD, keeping BAD sequestered in the cytosol and thereby modulating cell death signalling.

118010.long_answer: Multiple occurrences of Crane–Heise syndrome have been reported in siblings born to unaffected parents, with no vertical transmission. This sib-clustering pattern with unaffected carriers is characteristic of autosomal recessive inheritance, so the syndrome is thought to represent an autosomal recessive genetic disorder.

155675.long_answer: Among the mucopolysaccharidoses, type II—Hunter syndrome—is classically associated with a high prevalence of obstructive sleep apnea. Glycosaminoglycan accumulation in the upper airway leads to adenotonsillar hypertrophy, macroglossia and airway narrowing, predisposing patients with MPS II to obstructive sleep apnea.

891775.long_answer: Aromatase deficiency (caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CYP19A1 gene) leads to markedly reduced or absent conversion of androgens to estrogens. In both humans and animal models, the lack of estrogen results in metabolic disturbances that include insulin resistance and the compensatory development of hyperinsulinemia. Clinical reports of aromatase-deficient males and females describe elevated fasting insulin levels, impaired glucose tolerance, and, in some cases, progression to type 2 diabetes. Estrogen replacement in affected patients or in aromatase-knockout mice normalizes insulin sensitivity and lowers insulin concentrations, confirming a causal link.
