Therefore, hyperinsulinemia is an established metabolic manifestation associated with aromatase deficiency.

548949.long_answer: Berdon syndrome, also called megacystis-microcolon-intestinal hypoperistalsis syndrome, is classically inherited in an autosomal recessive manner: affected children have pathogenic variants in both copies of a visceral smooth-muscle gene (e.g., MYH11, LMOD1, MYL9), received one from each heterozygous carrier parent. This recessive transmission pattern is the form most consistently reported in the medical literature for the disorder.

807097.long_answer: Baló's concentric sclerosis generally lacks the polyspecific intrathecal antibody response to measles, rubella and varicella-zoster viruses (the MRZ-reaction) that is characteristic of typical multiple sclerosis. Hence, the MRZ-reaction is usually negative in Baló's concentric sclerosis.

239070.long_answer: In ICD-10, Disinhibited Attachment Disorder is coded as F94.2 within the group “Disorders of social functioning with onset specific to childhood and adolescence” (F94). The official exclusion note for this F94 category states that cases meeting criteria for pervasive developmental disorders (F84.–)—i.e., autism spectrum disorders—must not be classified here. Thus, pervasive developmental disorders are specifically excluded from the category that contains Disinhibited Attachment Disorder.

503149.long_answer: Linezolid, an oxazolidinone antibiotic, is FDA-approved and widely used in the United States for infections caused by vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE). It inhibits bacterial protein synthesis by binding the 50S ribosomal subunit, providing bacteriostatic activity against VRE and serving as a first-line therapeutic option in clinical practice.

682949.long_answer: Staphylococcus aureus food-borne illness is caused by ingestion of pre-formed, heat-stable staphylococcal enterotoxins, most commonly enterotoxin A. This superantigenic toxin survives cooking, is rapidly absorbed in the gut, and triggers massive cytokine release from T cells and intestinal mast cells, producing abrupt gastrointestinal symptoms including intense abdominal cramping, profuse watery diarrhea, and vomiting within a few hours of food consumption.

328855.long_answer: The convoluted scalp disorder was first described in 1837, but it was the German dermatologist Paul Gerson Unna who, in 1907, introduced and formalized the name “cutis verticis gyrata,” referring to the scalp skin (cutis) of the vertex that is thrown into brain-like gyri.

220760.long_answer: Phytophotodermatitis occurs after skin contact with plants that contain furocoumarins (psoralens). These molecules absorb UVA light and become highly reactive, producing free-radical damage in epidermal cells; this phototoxic action is what makes furocoumarins the key photosensitizers responsible for the condition.

975262.long_answer: In infective endocarditis, friable valve lesions called vegetations form; they consist of a mesh of platelets and fibrin that traps bacterial microcolonies and contains only sparse inflammatory cells.

681061.long_answer: During atrial fibrillation, irregularly long-short R–R cycles can cause rate-dependent bundle-branch aberration, producing wide QRS complexes known as Ashman phenomenon. This aberrant conduction can also appear in patients with Wolff–Parkinson–White syndrome experiencing atrial fibrillation, leading to intermittent wide-complex beats that mimic other tachyarrhythmias.

442976.long_answer: According to internationally accepted hematology criteria (e.g., the International Council for Standardization in Haematology), polycythemia in adult men is diagnosed when the hematocrit reaches or exceeds 52 %. This cutoff reflects a red-cell mass more than 25 % above predicted normal and reliably distinguishes true erythrocytosis from normal physiologic variation.

315630.long_answer: Calluses on the foot are most frequently produced on the plantar surface—the sole—because this weight-bearing region is subjected to repeated pressure and friction during standing and walking, prompting hyperkeratosis of the epidermis.

121724.long_answer: Aniridia in humans is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PAX6 gene. PAX6 encodes a paired box/homeodomain transcription factor that governs eye formation; its nucleotide and protein sequences are highly conserved from zebrafish to humans. Disruption of this single gene impairs ocular development, leading to the characteristic absence of the iris seen in aniridia patients.

845502.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked gene L1CAM cause the SPG1 form of hereditary spastic paraplegia. The L1 cell-adhesion molecule encoded by L1CAM is a key axon-guidance receptor; it partners with neuropilin-1 to transmit class-3 semaphorin (e.g., Sema3A) signals that steer growing corticospinal and other axons. This well-documented interaction and guidance role link L1CAM directly to both hereditary spastic paraplegia and neuropilin-1–dependent axon pathfinding.

897662.long_answer: In cerebellar hypoplasia—particularly the pontocerebellar hypoplasia syndromes—the pons is characteristically under-developed along with the cerebellum. MRI and neuropathologic studies consistently show pontine hypoplasia, linking this specific brainstem region to cerebellar hypoplasia.

662111.long_answer: Screwdriver- or peg-shaped incisors are a characteristic dental anomaly in hypohidrotic/anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. This condition is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the EDA gene (ectodysplasin A) on chromosome Xq12–q13, which disrupt epithelial–mesenchymal signaling during tooth morphogenesis and results in conical, tapered (screwdriver-shaped) incisors.

117918.long_answer: The autosomal-dominant hereditary form of spasmodic torticollis (idiopathic cervical dystonia) has been mapped to the DYT7 locus on chromosome 18p11.3. Linkage studies in affected families demonstrated co-segregation of the disease with markers on the short arm of chromosome 18, establishing this chromosomal region as the primary genetic association.

938139.long_answer: Pretibial myxedema, also called thyroid dermopathy, is a rare extrathyroidal manifestation of Graves' disease characterized by marked mucopolysaccharide deposition in the dermis of the lower legs. This leads to non-pitting edema and thickened, hyperpigmented skin that can resemble the massive lymphedematous swelling seen in elephantiasis, making misdiagnosis possible.

232935.long_answer: The filamentous fungal genus Cephalosporium (now classified within Acremonium) has been documented to provoke hypersensitivity pneumonitis in exposed workers and patients. In 1945, Sardinian scientist Giuseppe Brotzu isolated Cephalosporium acremonium from sewage outflow and discovered that it produced cephalosporin C, the β-lactam compound that became the progenitor of the cephalosporin class of antibiotics. Thus, the same genus is linked both to hypersensitivity lung disease and to the origin of cephalosporin antimicrobials.

543824.long_answer: In idiopathic aplastic anemia, autoreactive cytotoxic T-cells secrete IFN-γ and other cytokines that up-regulate the death receptor Fas (encoded by the FAS gene, also called CD95) on hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. Engagement of Fas by Fas ligand on T-cells triggers caspase-mediated apoptosis, leading to immune-mediated destruction of the bone-marrow compartment. Thus, the FAS gene is centrally involved in the pathogenic immune attack responsible for aplastic anemia.

980537.long_answer: Hydrolethalus syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HYLS1 centrosomal protein, which is essential for assembling primary cilia. Failure to form functional primary cilia disrupts Hedgehog and other cilia-dependent signalling pathways during embryogenesis, leading to the characteristic severe developmental defects of the syndrome. Thus, dysfunction of the primary cilium is the proximate cellular cause of Hydrolethalus syndrome phenotypes.

824146.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the FLNB gene cause the lethal skeletal disorder known as boomerang dysplasia. Radiographically, the most characteristic finding is that each femur is grossly malformed and bowed into the shape of a boomerang, giving the condition its name. Thus, the femur is the bone that exhibits the distinctive “boomerang” malformation in FLNB-related disease.

266951.long_answer: Canvaxin is an allogeneic, polyvalent whole-cell melanoma vaccine derived from three human melanoma cell lines. Early-phase and some phase III trials reported improved immune responses and a trend toward longer survival in patients with stage III/IV melanoma, indicating that this skin cancer showed the most notable though ultimately limited success with Canvaxin.

884829.long_answer: Inherited forms of distal (type I) renal tubular acidosis that arise in the collecting-duct intercalated cells are most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding key acid–base transport proteins: ATP6V1B1 (B1 subunit) and ATP6V0A4 (a4 subunit) of the vacuolar H⁺-ATPase, and SLC4A1 (anion exchanger 1/AE1).  Defects in these proteins impair proton secretion or bicarbonate reclamation in the cortical collecting duct, producing the characteristic acidosis, alkaline urine and related sequelae of distal RTA.

348053.long_answer: Palovarotene, a selective retinoic-acid-receptor-γ agonist marketed as Sohonos, is the first therapy approved (in Canada) for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva and had previously been granted orphan drug designation by both the U.S. FDA and the European Medicines Agency because of the disease’s extreme rarity.

890011.long_answer: After bilateral oophorectomy the normal physiologic response is loss of ovarian estrogen-inhibin feedback, leading to very high serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) concentrations (typically >40–50 IU/L, in the post-menopausal range). When functioning ovarian tissue is unintentionally left behind (ovarian remnant syndrome, ORS), that tissue can continue to secrete estradiol and inhibin and will partially suppress pituitary FSH release. Consequently, patients with ORS often show FSH values that are lower than expected for a surgically menopausal woman and may even fall into the pre-menopausal range. For this reason, measurement of FSH (usually together with estradiol) is recommended in the diagnostic work-up of suspected ORS: an unexpectedly low or normal FSH level raises suspicion for residual, hormone-producing ovarian tissue, whereas a consistently high FSH level makes ORS much less likely. Imaging and/or laparoscopic exploration are still needed for definitive localisation, but FSH is a useful biochemical indicator. Therefore, FSH can indeed indicate the presence of ovarian remnant syndrome after oophorectomy.

414820.long_answer: The German physiologist and chemist Felix Hoppe-Seyler gave the first documented description of porphyria in 1871, when he isolated the red-purple pigment (haematoporphyrin) from the urine of an affected patient. His observation of this characteristic pigment and the accompanying clinical features laid the foundation for recognising porphyria as a distinct metabolic disease of the haem biosynthetic pathway.

907365.long_answer: Infective endocarditis is an infection of the heart valves and endocardial surface. Because it primarily involves cardiac structures and often requires expertise in valvular disease, hemodynamics, and possible surgical referral, patients are most commonly managed under the care of cardiologists, with additional input from infectious-disease specialists as needed.

699338.long_answer: Acromegaly is caused by excessive secretion of growth hormone, almost always due to a functional adenoma of the anterior pituitary gland. Pierre Marie first described the syndrome, linking its characteristic skeletal overgrowth and soft-tissue enlargement to this hyperactive pituitary source.

928204.long_answer: Population studies have shown that inadequate iodine intake during pregnancy—the result of low environmental iodine levels in food and water—raises the incidence of congenital hypothyroidism in newborns. Iodine is essential for fetal thyroid hormone synthesis, and deficiency impairs thyroid development and hormone production, leading to statistically higher rates of congenital hypothyroidism in affected regions.

269357.long_answer: Parsonage–Turner syndrome (neuralgic amyotrophy) most frequently affects branches of the upper brachial plexus, with the suprascapular nerve being the nerve most commonly involved. The suprascapular nerve arises from the C5-C6 roots and provides motor innervation to the supraspinatus (and infraspinatus) muscles; therefore it both characterizes the typical neuropathy seen in Parsonage–Turner syndrome and is responsible for activating the supraspinatus muscle.

280765.long_answer: In medical terminology, the term "ptosis" (from the Greek for 'falling') denotes the abnormal downward displacement or drooping of a body part or organ, such as eyelid ptosis or uterine ptosis. It is the standard term used in anatomy and clinical practice to describe this condition.

857826.long_answer: Classic X-linked lymphoproliferative disease (XLP, also called XLP1) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SH2D1A gene, which encodes the SLAM-associated protein (SAP). Defective SAP disrupts signaling through SLAM family receptors on T, NK, and NKT cells, leading to uncontrolled immune activation—classically after Epstein-Barr virus infection—and the clinical manifestations of XLP.

418079.long_answer: If phenytoin is infused too rapidly intravenously (>50 mg/min in adults), the drug and its solvent (propylene glycol) can depress myocardial conduction and contractility, precipitating severe hypotension and life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias such as bradycardia, heart block, ventricular tachycardia, or cardiac arrest.

143728.long_answer: Pipecolic acidemia (primary hyperpipecolic acidemia), caused by deficiency of the peroxisomal enzyme pipecolic acid oxidase involved in lysine catabolism, is transmitted as an autosomal recessive disorder—both copies of the gene must be mutated for the condition to manifest.

225740.long_answer: Pinta is caused by Treponema carateum, a member of the genus Treponema. Treponemes are slender, helically coiled bacteria—classified morphologically as spirochetes—giving them a characteristic spiral (corkscrew) shape.

646481.long_answer: Needle electromyography is the standard diagnostic test for distal myopathies. By recording motor-unit potentials from the laryngeal and pharyngeal muscles, EMG reveals the small-amplitude, short-duration, polyphasic potentials that are characteristic of a primary myopathic process, allowing objective assessment of vocal-cord and pharyngeal involvement in distal myopathy.

289383.long_answer: Mutations in the AAAS gene, which encodes the nuclear-pore protein ALADIN, cause Triple A syndrome (also called Allgrove syndrome). This autosomal-recessive disorder is typified by achalasia, alacrima, and adrenal insufficiency; the cortisol deficiency from adrenal failure frequently presents with unexplained, recurrent hypoglycemia.

569056.long_answer: Streptococcus pneumoniae (the pneumococcus) is an encapsulated Gram-positive diplococcus that accounts for most cases of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection because splenectomized patients lose the spleen’s ability to clear opsonized encapsulated bacteria. The same organism is also the leading cause of community-acquired bacterial pneumonia worldwide, producing lobar pneumonia and other invasive pneumococcal diseases.

899786.long_answer: The first in-vivo CRISPR human trial (EDIT-101) for Leber congenital amaurosis type 10 focused on excising the pathogenic intronic mutation (c.2991+1655A>G) in the CEP290 gene, whose defects are a well-established cause of this form of Leber congenital amaurosis.

240929.long_answer: In drug-induced liver injury, rising serum bilirubin signals impaired hepatic conjugation and excretion of bilirubin; its accumulation in blood and tissues produces the yellow discoloration known clinically as jaundice, a marker of significant hepatocellular or cholestatic damage and increased risk of liver failure.

474413.long_answer: Sturge–Weber syndrome is almost always caused by a post-zygotic, somatic activating missense mutation in the GNAQ gene (classically c.548G>A, p.Arg183Gln). The mutation hyperactivates the Gαq signaling pathway, driving abnormal capillary–venous malformation in skin, leptomeninges and eye that characterizes the syndrome.

545803.long_answer: Several studies have detected herpes simplex virus (HSV) DNA in the corneal endothelium or aqueous humour of patients with iridocorneal endothelial (ICE) syndrome. This finding led to the hypothesis that a prior HSV infection of the corneal endothelium can trigger aberrant proliferation and migration of endothelial-like cells into the anterior chamber angle and over the iris surface, producing the characteristic abnormal endothelialization seen in ICE syndrome.

723532.long_answer: The IL2RG gene encodes the common γ-chain shared by several interleukin receptors (IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, IL-21) that are essential for thymic maturation signals. A loss-of-function mutation in IL2RG disrupts these cytokine pathways, blocking normal development of T lymphocytes (and secondarily NK cells), so patients with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency lack functional T cells while B-cell numbers are relatively preserved but ineffective.

947000.long_answer: Septo-optic dysplasia is a congenital malformation characterized by optic nerve hypoplasia, midline brain defects and possible pituitary dysfunction. Because the optic nerves are under-developed, visual input to the ocular motor system is abnormal, frequently leading to sensory nystagmus—an involuntary oscillation of the eyes. Thus, this condition links optic nerve hypoplasia with involuntary eye movement.

531642.long_answer: Cyprus, an island nation in the eastern Mediterranean, has one of the world’s highest carrier frequencies for β-thalassemia (≈13–15 % of the population are heterozygotes). This high prevalence led Cyprus to pioneer nationwide screening and prenatal prevention programs for the disorder.

492722.long_answer: Denys–Drash syndrome classically results from missense mutations in the Wilms-tumor suppressor gene WT1 on chromosome 11p13, which disrupt the zinc-finger DNA-binding domain. The same WT1 gene—when altered by different pathogenic variants such as splice-site changes—is also a recognized cause of 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis (e.g., Frasier/Swyer phenotypes). Thus, WT1 mutations underlie both Denys–Drash syndrome and 46,XY gonadal dysgenesis.

795082.long_answer: Patients with Sturge-Weber syndrome frequently harbor a diffuse choroidal hemangioma. Topical prostaglandin-F2α analogues such as latanoprost can augment choroidal blood flow and vascular permeability, predisposing the hemangioma to exudation or serous retinal detachment. Therefore, the presence of a diffuse choroidal hemangioma is considered a contraindication to prescribing latanoprost in these patients.

240431.long_answer: The suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus receives direct retinal input via the retino-hypothalamic tract, allowing it to sense environmental light—an essential element of visual information. This same nucleus serves as the body’s master circadian clock, generating and synchronizing daily rhythms of physiology and behavior. Because it both processes light signals from the visual system and orchestrates circadian timing, the SCN is the brain region that links visual processing with regulation of circadian rhythms.

343259.long_answer: Howel–Evans syndrome (tylosis with oesophageal cancer) is produced by germ-line mutations in the RHBDF2 gene, which was mapped to the tylosis oesophageal cancer (TOC) locus at 17q25.1. Thus the disease-causing gene is located on chromosome 17.

864341.long_answer: Osteochondromas characteristically harbor loss-of-function mutations in the EXT1 (exostosin-1) gene, resulting in absent or markedly reduced EXT1 expression in the tumor. Trevor disease (dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica) lacks these EXT1 alterations and shows preserved EXT1 expression. Hence, analysis of the EXT1 gene (or its protein expression) is routinely used to distinguish Trevor disease from osteochondroma.

157398.long_answer: Children born with congenital rubella syndrome have a markedly increased risk of developing autism later in childhood—epidemiologic studies show 7–13 % of CRS survivors meet criteria for autism spectrum disorder, reflecting rubella’s disruptive effects on fetal brain development.

558700.long_answer: In thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) patients already have profound thrombocytopenia, so adding an antiplatelet agent such as aspirin, which irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase and impairs aggregation, markedly heightens the risk of serious bleeding. Therefore aspirin is avoided until the platelet count has safely recovered.

878013.long_answer: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2D (LGMD2D) is a sarcoglycanopathy produced by pathogenic mutations in the SGCA gene, which encodes the alpha-sarcoglycan subunit of the dystrophin–glycoprotein complex in skeletal muscle.

847393.long_answer: Tethered cord syndrome is frequently reported in patients with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, a hereditary connective-tissue disorder characterized by defects in collagen synthesis that lead to joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility. The abnormal connective-tissue elasticity can allow excessive elongation and fixation of the spinal cord and its filum terminale, predisposing individuals with Ehlers–Danlos syndrome to develop tethered cord pathology.

242778.long_answer: Dejerine–Sottas disease, the severe early-onset demyelinating neuropathy classified as Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 3, involves mutations in myelin-related genes such as PMP22, MPZ or EGR2. Because the disorder demyelinates not only peripheral nerves but also cranial nerves, the vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerve can be affected, leading to moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss in many patients.

549359.long_answer: Ethmoidal polyps originate from the mucosa of the ethmoidal air cells, which drain into and protrude through the middle nasal meatus; therefore, these polyps characteristically arise in the middle meatus region.

160377.long_answer: A recurrent duplication of the X-chromosomal segment Xq28 that includes the MECP2 gene—commonly termed MECP2 duplication—is a well-established cause of X-linked intellectual disability. Males with this copy-number gain typically present with severe cognitive impairment, hypotonia, seizures and recurrent infections, defining the MECP2 duplication (Xq28 microduplication) syndrome.

834630.long_answer: Cortés-Lacassie syndrome is a rare congenital neurodevelopmental disorder whose neurological hallmark is the early appearance of epileptic infantile spasms (the seizure pattern that characterizes West syndrome). Affected infants develop flexor or extensor spasms in clusters during the first months of life, reflecting the severe encephalopathy that accompanies the syndrome.

613462.long_answer: Gaucher’s disease commonly leads to hepatomegaly because Gaucher cells accumulate in the liver. The liver is the body’s main site for detoxifying blood-borne substances and for synthesizing plasma proteins such as albumin and clotting factors, making it the organ that fits both criteria.

824765.long_answer: People with diabetes mellitus frequently have elevated blood and tissue glucose levels and impaired neutrophil function, conditions that favor overgrowth of Candida species. As a result, they are significantly more prone to develop candidiasis—yeast infections of the mouth (oral thrush), genital tract, or skin—making this the most common fungal infection associated with diabetes.

861165.long_answer: Anisakiasis is the human nematode infection acquired by eating raw or inadequately cooked fish or squid that contain third-stage larvae of Anisakis species. After ingestion, the larvae can penetrate the gastric or intestinal wall, producing acute gastrointestinal symptoms. Diagnosis is confirmed by recovering the larva endoscopically or by biochemical and immunological methods (e.g., ELISA, immunoblot, PCR) that identify Anisakis antigens or DNA, linking the infection specifically to consumption of contaminated seafood.

970775.long_answer: The Pap (Papanicolaou) test examines cervical cells for characteristic abnormalities—such as koilocytosis and dysplasia—that are induced by infection with human papillomavirus (HPV), a common sexually transmitted infection. Detection of these HPV-related cytologic changes allows early identification of HPV infection and prevention of cervical cancer.

525373.long_answer: When a fetus is suspected of being large for gestational age, clinicians perform an obstetric ultrasound to obtain biometric measurements (e.g., abdominal circumference, head circumference, femur length). These data are entered into validated formulas to estimate fetal weight non-invasively, making ultrasound the standard prenatal diagnostic method for this purpose.

459622.long_answer: Reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) can directly detect SARS-CoV RNA in respiratory, stool or blood samples. A positive RT-PCR result provides laboratory confirmation of infection and upgrades a suspect case to a probable/confirmed SARS case even when chest X-ray findings are negative.

312186.long_answer: The first medically documented case of hypertrichosis involved Petrus Gonsalvus, born on Tenerife in 1537 and described by Renaissance naturalists such as Ulisse Aldrovandi. His lanugo-type hair growth over the entire body was recorded and illustrated at European courts during the mid-to-late 16th century, making this Renaissance period the earliest verifiable report of the disorder.

938379.long_answer: The PAX3 gene, located on chromosome 2q35-q36, encodes a paired-box transcription factor critical for neural-crest-derived craniofacial and limb development. Heterozygous pathogenic variants in PAX3 have been reported in families with acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis, producing the characteristic combination of frontonasal malformation and distal limb anomalies. The same gene is well known to cause Waardenburg and craniofacial-deafness-hand syndromes, where cleft lip and/or cleft palate are recurrent findings. Thus PAX3 satisfies both features mentioned in the question: involvement in acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis and the ability to produce cleft lip/palate, and it is situated on chromosome 2.

548915.long_answer: Qazi–Markouizos syndrome is the same clinical entity that geneticists now call CATSHL syndrome (Camptodactyly-Tall Stature-Hearing Loss syndrome). It is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in the FGFR3 gene and is characterized by congenital camptodactyly, excessive linear growth, spinal curvature, and sensorineural hearing impairment. Because the original family was reported by Qazi and Markouizos, the disorder carries their names as an alternative eponym.

715641.long_answer: Cor pulmonale—right-sided heart failure secondary to chronic pulmonary hypertension—can arise from both emphysema and the broader spectrum of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In these disorders, persistent airway obstruction and destruction of alveolar capillary beds elevate pulmonary arterial pressures. The sustained pressure overload forces the right ventricle to hypertrophy and eventually fail, producing cor pulmonale as a common and serious complication.

242559.long_answer: X-linked thrombocytopenia is the mild allelic variant of Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome and results from loss-of-function mutations in the WAS gene, which encodes the Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS) protein involved in actin cytoskeleton organization of hematopoietic cells.

968406.long_answer: Roussy–Lévy syndrome and Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease type 1A share pathogenic alterations in the PMP22 (peripheral myelin protein 22) gene. Duplication or other mutations of PMP22 disrupt myelin integrity in peripheral nerves, producing the demyelinating neuropathy characteristic of both disorders.

303385.long_answer: Tetrasomy X is defined by the presence of four X chromosomes (48,XXXX). Clinical findings alone are not specific, so confirmation requires cytogenetic examination: a standard G-banded karyotype (chromosome analysis of peripheral blood lymphocytes) that visually demonstrates the 48,XXXX complement.

985964.long_answer: Pure black-piedra hairs infected by Piedraia hortae do not fluoresce. If the affected hairs show fluorescence (typically a faint green-yellow glow) under a Wood’s lamp, this is taken as evidence that bacteria have secondarily colonised the hair shaft, because the porphyrins produced by these bacteria are what fluoresce.

249228.long_answer: Cranial CT studies in patients with Pallister–Killian syndrome repeatedly show multiple small, punctate (‘spot’) calcifications localised to the basal ganglia (especially the globus pallidus/putamen region). These basal-ganglia calcifications are considered a characteristic, though not universal, neuroradiological feature of the syndrome.

711914.long_answer: Alagille syndrome is primarily a cholestatic liver disease caused by developmental paucity of intra-hepatic bile ducts and related JAG1/NOTCH2 mutations. Because its main manifestations involve chronic liver dysfunction, a hepatologist (often a pediatric hepatologist/gastroenterologist) is the specialist who evaluates liver enzymes, orders confirmatory genetic testing and liver biopsy, and manages complications such as pruritus, fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, and potential need for liver transplantation. Thus, the medical specialty responsible for diagnosing and treating Alagille syndrome is hepatology.

699268.long_answer: Both chronic bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) are strongly linked to long-term inhalation of tobacco smoke. Cigarette smoking induces persistent airway inflammation, mucus hypersecretion, and loss of elastic recoil, which drive the pathogenesis of chronic bronchitis and the airflow limitation characteristic of COPD. Consequently, smoking is recognized as the leading modifiable risk factor for developing both conditions.

240845.long_answer: Because the heart and great vessels are mirror-imaged in dextrocardia situs inversus, implanting a normally oriented donor heart requires complex rerouting and reconstruction of the aorta, pulmonary artery, and caval veins. This anatomical mismatch makes the great-vessel anastomoses the principal technical challenge during transplantation.

702847.long_answer: Western equine encephalitis can leave infants and children with permanent neurologic and developmental deficits after the acute infection. The ongoing evaluation and management of these serious post-encephalitic sequelae (e.g., cognitive impairment, motor dysfunction, seizures) fall under the scope of pediatrics, the medical specialty dedicated to the health care of infants, children, and adolescents.

301369.long_answer: Guidelines from the American Academy of Pediatrics state that neither continuous nor intermittent antiepileptic (anticonvulsant) therapy—such as phenobarbital, valproate, or diazepam—should be used after a simple febrile seizure. These drugs only modestly lower recurrence risk but carry significant adverse-effect profiles; therefore, routine anticonvulsant prophylaxis is not recommended to prevent further simple febrile seizures in children.

715332.long_answer: Werner syndrome is an autosomal-recessive progeroid disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WRN helicase gene. A hallmark of the condition is accelerated aging, and affected individuals typically develop degenerative joint disease—including symptomatic osteoarthritis of large joints—in their 20s–30s, decades earlier than the general population.

462663.long_answer: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an inherited platelet function disorder caused by qualitative or quantitative defects in the platelet membrane glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3). Because this receptor is essential for fibrinogen-mediated platelet aggregation, affected individuals have impaired clot formation and present with mucocutaneous bleeding manifestations, including epistaxis, easy bruising, and notably heavy menstrual bleeding (menorrhagia) in women.

303591.long_answer: Genetic studies have shown that many patients with paramyotonia congenita in northern Germany carry the same SCN4A founder mutation (e.g., p.T1313M). This single ancestral mutation arose in the Schleswig-Holstein region, leading to a markedly higher local prevalence of the disease compared with other areas.

743186.long_answer: Controlled studies in infants and young boys with the sex-chromosome aneuploidy 49,XXXXY have demonstrated that a brief course of early androgen (testosterone) therapy leads to significant gains in gross and fine motor coordination, expressive language, and non-verbal cognitive (IQ) scores when compared with untreated peers. The improvement is attributed to replacing the androgen deficiency characteristic of this syndrome during a critical period of neurodevelopment.

169793.long_answer: Auscultation is the diagnostic technique that relies on listening to internal body sounds with a stethoscope. In suspected renal artery stenosis, clinicians auscultate the abdomen and flanks for a systolic-diastolic bruit produced by turbulent blood flow through a narrowed renal artery, providing a non-invasive clinical clue to the presence of the stenosis.

100359.long_answer: Dermatitis herpetiformis is an autoimmune blistering skin disease in which IgA antibodies directed against epidermal transglutaminase deposit in the dermal papillae, producing intensely pruritic grouped vesicles and blisters, especially on extensor surfaces. It is the classic cutaneous manifestation of gluten-sensitive enteropathy and is strongly associated with coeliac disease; both conditions improve on a strict gluten-free diet.

529012.long_answer: Pentoxifylline, a methylxanthine phosphodiesterase inhibitor, is routinely prescribed in oral submucous fibrosis because it improves micro-circulation, inhibits fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition, and enhances collagenase activity. These anti-fibrotic actions have been shown clinically to increase maximal mouth opening, thereby ameliorating the functional limitation characteristic of the disease.

953160.long_answer: Humans are trichromats; their color vision relies on three distinct cone photoreceptor types in the retina—S-cones (short-wavelength, blue), M-cones (medium-wavelength, green), and L-cones (long-wavelength, red). The combined responses of these three cone classes enable full-color perception, a system termed trichromatic vision.

585776.long_answer: For severe, rapidly progressive systemic scleroderma (systemic sclerosis), high-dose immunoablation followed by reinfusion of the patient’s own hematopoietic stem cells—a procedure called autologous hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation (HSCT)—is employed. Randomized trials such as ASTIS and SCOT have shown that autologous HSCT can improve skin fibrosis, lung function, and overall survival by ‘resetting’ the aberrant immune response driving the disease.

798582.long_answer: Polyarteritis nodosa is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis affecting medium-sized arteries. Disorders of systemic vasculitis are most often diagnosed and treated by rheumatologists, the specialists in autoimmune and inflammatory connective-tissue diseases. Hence, management of polyarteritis nodosa is typically overseen by a rheumatologist, who coordinates immunosuppressive therapy and monitors organ involvement.

670909.long_answer: In malakoplakia, the characteristic Michaelis–Gutmann bodies are intracytoplasmic, partially calcified inclusions found within large foamy macrophages known as Von Hansemann cells. These defective macrophages accumulate undigested bacterial remnants, leading to the pathognomonic appearance of Michaelis–Gutmann bodies on microscopy.

426346.long_answer: Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome is a rare FGFR2-related craniosynostosis disorder distinguished by premature cranial suture fusion and cerebriform skin folds (cutis gyrata). Patients frequently develop acanthosis nigricans, making this syndrome the established genetic condition that links craniosynostosis, cutis gyrata, and acanthosis nigricans.

542981.long_answer: Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) leads to deficient aldosterone and cortisol production, causing hyponatremia and volume depletion. Patients commonly develop hypergeusia (heightened taste perception) specifically for salt and manifest intense cravings for salty foods as a compensatory response to their low sodium state, making Addison disease classically associated with both features.

289226.long_answer: Muscle atrophy is the condition in which skeletal-muscle fibers shrink in cross-sectional area because protein breakdown exceeds synthesis, typically during disuse, immobilization, or aging. Regular exercise—especially resistance and weight-bearing training—reactivates anabolic signaling pathways (e.g., mTOR), stimulates protein synthesis, and thereby prevents or reverses the loss of muscle-cell size characteristic of muscle atrophy.

714008.long_answer: Precocious puberty in McCune–Albright syndrome is gonadotropin-independent and driven by excess ovarian estrogen production. The current standard treatment is the third-generation aromatase inhibitor letrozole, which blocks conversion of androgens to estrogens, lowers circulating estradiol, slows bone-age advancement, and reduces episodes of vaginal bleeding. Clinical studies and guidelines now recommend letrozole as first-line therapy for this form of peripheral precocious puberty.

942683.long_answer: In medical terminology, ptosis denotes the sagging or abnormal downward displacement of an organ or body part from its normal anatomical position. The suffix “-ptosis” (from the Greek πτῶσις, meaning “falling”) is used in terms such as blepharoptosis (drooping eyelid), gastroptosis (downward‐displaced stomach), and visceroptosis (sagging abdominal viscera), all illustrating this pathologic descent.

469604.long_answer: Mutations in the SLC2A1 gene, which encodes the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT-1, cause GLUT-1 deficiency syndrome. Impaired GLUT-1 transport limits glucose entry into the developing brain, frequently leading to congenital or early-onset microcephaly along with seizures and developmental delay. Thus, SLC2A1 links defective glucose transport with the microcephaly phenotype.

634414.long_answer: In Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis, chronic anterior uveitis (also called iridocyclitis) is a well-recognized extra-articular manifestation. Persistent inflammation of the iris and ciliary body can damage the lens and promote posterior synechiae, ultimately leading to cataract formation if adequate ophthalmologic treatment is not instituted.

907759.long_answer: Cardiospondylocarpofacial syndrome is produced by heterozygous mutations in the MAP3K7 gene, which encodes the kinase TAK1 involved in TGF-β/BMP signaling. These same MAP3K7 variants are documented to cause cranio-skeletal manifestations that include supernumerary teeth (hyperdontia), linking the mutation both to CSCFS and to dental anomalies.

978316.long_answer: The majority of organic acidemias are caused by loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding metabolic enzymes. Disease manifests only when both alleles are defective, so affected individuals are typically homozygous or compound heterozygous, while heterozygous carriers remain asymptomatic. This classic pattern corresponds to autosomal recessive inheritance.

685761.long_answer: Neutral Lipid Storage Disease is marked by the cytoplasmic accumulation of triglyceride-filled lipid droplets in circulating white blood cells (leukocytes), a finding known as Jordans’ anomaly and used diagnostically for the disorder.

478670.long_answer: Fifth disease (erythema infectiosum) is caused by human parvovirus B19. Demonstrating virus-specific IgM antibodies in the patient’s serum by a serologic assay (e.g., ELISA) confirms an acute or recent parvovirus B19 infection, thereby verifying the diagnosis of fifth disease.

345165.long_answer: Strümpell-Lorrain disease is the eponymous name for hereditary spastic paraplegia. The first detailed description of this inherited spastic gait disorder was published in 1893 by the German neurologist Adolf von Strümpell, for which he is credited with its identification; Maurice Lorrain later provided an independent report, giving rise to the combined eponym.

355819.long_answer: Calcium-pyrophosphate deposition disease (pseudogout) frequently occurs in joints already affected by osteoarthritis and is also a recognized complication of Paget’s disease of bone, where increased bone turnover favors CPP crystal formation. Thus, pseudogout is associated with both Paget’s disease of bone and osteoarthritis.

321706.long_answer: Renovascular hypertension is driven by increased renin-angiotensin-aldosterone activity from reduced renal perfusion. An ACE inhibitor (e.g., captopril, enalapril) blocks conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, decreasing vasoconstriction and aldosterone-mediated sodium retention, thus lowering blood pressure. ACE inhibitors are therefore commonly prescribed for medical management of renovascular hypertension, with monitoring of renal function and serum potassium.

937319.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome is an autosomal-dominant craniosynostosis disorder caused mainly by FGFR2 mutations. Premature fusion of the cranial sutures alters orbital anatomy, leading to ocular problems; strabismus (often a large-angle V-pattern) is reported in a majority of affected children. Thus, this genetic craniosynostosis syndrome is well known to present with strabismus in addition to skull and facial abnormalities.

121715.long_answer: Systemic primary carnitine deficiency impairs the carnitine-dependent shuttle that moves long-chain fatty acids into the mitochondrial matrix for β-oxidation. Because mitochondria cannot oxidize these fatty acids, energy production in heart, skeletal muscle and liver is compromised, producing the characteristic hypoketotic hypoglycemia, cardiomyopathy and myopathy. Thus, mitochondrial dysfunction underlies the clinical manifestations of the disorder.

565643.long_answer: Congenital varicella syndrome can be definitively confirmed prenatally by performing polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing on amniotic fluid obtained via amniocentesis; detection of varicella-zoster virus DNA in the fluid establishes fetal infection.

238319.long_answer: Post-natal Vitamin A supplementation (e.g., 5 000 IU intramuscularly three times weekly) is given to extremely low-birth-weight, premature infants with or at risk for bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Vitamin A is essential for normal lung epithelial growth and alveolar development; supplementing deficient pre-term infants improves pulmonary mechanics and gas exchange, thereby lessening the severity of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and improving overall lung function.

675932.long_answer: The retina can become inflamed during posterior uveitis (retinitis) and is the structure from which the vitreous gel separates in a posterior vitreous detachment. Thus, it is the ocular tissue common to both conditions.

743508.long_answer: Hypersexual behaviour in Klüver–Bucy syndrome is often controlled pharmacologically with the steroidal anti-androgen cyproterone acetate. By blocking androgen receptors and suppressing testosterone production, cyproterone acetate lowers libido and reduces inappropriate sexual drive that characterises the syndrome.

681467.long_answer: Chondrodystrophy (classically referring to achondroplasia/chondrodystrophic dwarfism) is produced by gain-of-function mutations in the FGFR3 gene and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner—one mutant allele is sufficient to produce the phenotype, although many cases arise from new (de novo) mutations.

721338.long_answer: Ollier disease (multiple enchondromatosis) is characterized by numerous benign cartilaginous tumors within bones, leading to limb deformities, pathologic fractures, and growth disturbances. Diagnosis, monitoring, and surgical management of these skeletal lesions fall under the expertise of orthopedic specialists, often in collaboration with orthopedic oncologists for tumor surveillance.

248891.long_answer: The aggressive, juvenile-onset form of laryngeal papillomatosis associated with HPV-11 often spreads beyond the larynx; among lower-airway sites, the trachea is the one most frequently involved, preceding extension to bronchi or lung parenchyma.

352232.long_answer: SARS-CoV-2 infection has been linked to Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy in which peripheral nerve demyelination causes rapidly progressive, often ascending muscle weakness, gait difficulty, and loss of reflexes. Numerous case reports and series have documented GBS emerging days to weeks after COVID-19 onset, consistent with the post-infectious autoimmune mechanism classically seen with this disorder.

606169.long_answer: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued ‘Make Listening Safe’ guidelines noting that more than a billion adolescents and young adults risk noise-induced hearing loss, and therefore advises them to limit the volume and duration of exposure to loud sounds from personal audio devices, concerts and other recreational settings.

627832.long_answer: Epidermolysis bullosa simplex Ogna type is an autosomal-dominant form of EBS caused by missense mutations in the PLEC gene, which encodes the cytolinker protein plectin. Defective plectin weakens the keratin–intermediate filament anchorage at hemidesmosomes, leading to skin fragility and the blistering phenotype characteristic of the Ogna variant.

848967.long_answer: High cellular S-adenosyl methionine binds allosterically to cystathionine β-synthase (CBS), increasing CBS activity and shunting homocysteine into the trans-sulfuration pathway (conversion to cystathionine and then cysteine). This regulation prevents homocysteine accumulation when methionine/SAM levels are elevated.

407565.long_answer: Mulibrey nanism results from loss-of-function mutations in the TRIM37 gene, which has been mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 17 at cytogenetic band 17q22–q23.

572792.long_answer: In ZAP70-deficient individuals the T-cell receptor is still expressed on the cell surface, but because the ZAP-70 tyrosine kinase is absent or non-functional the phosphorylation cascade normally triggered after TCR engagement cannot proceed. Consequently, antigen recognition by the TCR does not generate the intracellular signals required for thymic positive selection of CD8⁺ T cells or for peripheral T-cell activation and cytokine production, leading to a profound defect in cell-mediated immune responses.

488988.long_answer: Noggin is a secreted protein produced by the primitive node, notochord and adjacent mesoderm. It binds directly to bone morphogenetic proteins (especially BMP-4), blocking their interaction with BMP receptors. By antagonizing BMP signaling in the overlying ectoderm, Noggin removes the epidermal-inducing influence of BMPs, allowing that ectoderm to differentiate into neuroectoderm and form the neural plate during neurulation.

265985.long_answer: Analgesic medications—such as acetaminophen or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen—reduce pain by inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes and lowering prostaglandin levels, thereby relieving the headache, muscle aches, and sore throat commonly experienced during a cold.

810555.long_answer: Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited hemolytic anemia caused by red-cell membrane protein defects. Diagnosis relies on specialized hematologic tests—peripheral blood smear, osmotic fragility or EMA binding assays, and interpretation of anemia and hemolysis parameters—all of which are routinely performed and interpreted by hematologists. Therefore, a hematologist (the hematology specialty) is the professional most likely to establish the diagnosis.

729042.long_answer: Historians and medical researchers have suggested that King George III’s recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, dark-colored urine, and severe neuropsychiatric disturbances match the clinical picture of porphyria—a hereditary defect in heme biosynthesis that causes intermittent accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors. Genetic analyses of collateral royal descendants have identified mutations consistent with variegate porphyria, supporting the hypothesis that this autosomal-dominant porphyric disorder underlay the king’s celebrated ‘madness.’

749146.long_answer: The D-xylose test assesses carbohydrate absorption by measuring the amount of orally administered D-xylose that appears in the urine over a set period. In small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, bacteria metabolize the D-xylose before it can be absorbed, so urinary excretion falls. A low urinary D-xylose level therefore indicates malabsorption related to SIBO.

916902.long_answer: Junctional epidermolysis bullosa results from mutations in genes (LAMA3, LAMB3, LAMC2) that encode laminin-332, formerly called laminin-5. Laminin-332 is a major anchoring-filament glycoprotein of the basement membrane zone; its loss weakens adhesion at the lamina lucida, producing the characteristic blistering of junctional EB.

760512.long_answer: In conditions such as rhabdomyolysis or malignant hyperthermia, an abnormal rise in intracellular Ca²⁺ in skeletal muscle fibers activates proteases and phospholipases that damage the sarcolemma. This membrane disruption allows myoglobin to leak out of the muscle cell into the bloodstream and urine, producing myoglobinuria.

535762.long_answer: In light chain deposition disease (LCDD), monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains accumulate linearly along renal basement membranes, with the earliest, most intense, and diagnostic deposits occurring in the tubular (particularly distal tubular) basement membranes. These deposits later extend to glomerular and vascular walls, but the primary and hallmark renal site is the tubular basement membrane.

653451.long_answer: Osteosarcoma typically shows highly pleomorphic malignant osteoblasts whose cells and nuclei vary greatly in size, shape and staining. This marked cellular and nuclear pleomorphism is a sign of anaplasia, a hallmark of cancer progression that indicates loss of normal differentiation and aggressive malignant potential.

873251.long_answer: Idiopathic CD4+ lymphocytopenia is defined by an unexplained, persistent depletion of CD4-positive T lymphocytes. It is the CD4+ T helper cell subset—responsible for coordinating adaptive immune responses—that is selectively and markedly reduced, while other lymphocyte populations such as CD8+ cytotoxic T cells or B cells are usually preserved.

601976.long_answer: Propionic acidemia is caused by a deficiency of the mitochondrial enzyme propionyl-CoA carboxylase. Without this biotin-dependent enzyme, propionyl-CoA cannot be converted to methylmalonyl-CoA, leading to a buildup of propionyl-CoA and its metabolite propionic acid. The excess propionic acid enters the bloodstream, producing severe metabolic acidosis and other clinical features of the disorder.

293279.long_answer: Genitopatellar syndrome is caused by de novo truncating mutations in the KAT6B gene, which encodes the lysine acetyltransferase 6B histone-acetylating enzyme. Loss-of-function of this acetyltransferase disrupts chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation during development, leading to the characteristic skeletal, genital, and neurodevelopmental anomalies of the syndrome.

125035.long_answer: Sensenbrenner syndrome (cranioectodermal dysplasia) is a ciliopathy caused by pathogenic variants in several intraflagellar transport (IFT) genes. The IFT43 gene, located on chromosome 14q24.3, encodes a component of the IFT-A complex essential for retrograde ciliary transport. Loss-of-function mutations in IFT43 are a well-established cause of Sensenbrenner syndrome, and affected individuals commonly present with microcephaly in addition to the characteristic skeletal, craniofacial and ectodermal anomalies. Thus, IFT43 is the chromosome-14 gene whose disruption leads to Sensenbrenner syndrome and associated microcephaly.

957074.long_answer: Juvenile nephronophthisis is a hereditary tubulointerstitial kidney disease whose cardinal clinical features are polyuria, polydipsia, secondary enuresis, growth retardation, anemia, and progressive loss of renal concentrating ability leading to chronic kidney failure. Because the primary pathology involves the renal tubules and interstitium rather than the glomeruli, the urine sediment is typically ‘bland’; significant hematuria or proteinuria is uncommon and, when present, tends to be only microscopic and incidental. Therefore, hematuria is not considered a common symptom of juvenile nephronophthisis.

257994.long_answer: Schizophreniform disorder is classified and diagnosed according to criteria listed in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (currently the DSM-5). This manual is authored and published by the American Psychiatric Association, which is the authoritative organization responsible for its development and updates.

441242.long_answer: In Desmin-related myofibrillar myopathy, mutant or mis-folded desmin and associated proteins accumulate as cytoplasmic aggregates, disrupting the myofibrillar network. This stress activates the intrinsic (mitochondrial) caspase pathway, and affected muscle fibres show TUNEL-positive nuclei and cleaved caspase-3/-9, hallmarks of programmed cell death. Thus the predominant form of cell death in this disorder is apoptosis.

851909.long_answer: The common MTHFR (methylenetetrahydro­folate reductase) C677T polymorphism lowers enzymatic conversion of 5,10-methylene-THF to 5-methyl-THF, slowing remethylation of homocysteine to methionine and causing moderate hyperhomocysteinemia. Supplementation with folic acid (vitamin B9) increases circulating folate pools and 5-methyl-THF availability, thereby restoring remethylation capacity and reliably lowering plasma homocysteine levels in individuals with this MTHFR deficiency.

666808.long_answer: Hwabyeong (also written hwa-byung, literally “anger illness”) is a Korean culture-bound syndrome marked by chronic, suppressed anger that manifests as somatic and emotional symptoms such as chest pressure, heat sensations, palpitations, and anxiety–depression. It was still being clinically described and treated in South Korea into the mid-2000s, illustrating its persistence as a culturally specific disorder well after many other folk illnesses had declined.

666432.long_answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative rod that frequently causes peritonitis, particularly in patients undergoing peritoneal dialysis, and is widely recognized as an opportunistic pathogen that exploits weakened host defenses in individuals with burns, cancer, neutropenia, cystic fibrosis, or other forms of immune compromise.

974285.long_answer: Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) is an autoimmune connective-tissue disease characterized by progressive fibrosis that causes hardening and tightening of the skin and can also affect internal organs. Pulmonary involvement, including interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension, may lead to pleural inflammation and fluid accumulation, making pleural effusion a recognized complication of systemic sclerosis.

919684.long_answer: Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome is part of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS) caused by gain-of-function mutations in NLRP3 that drive overproduction of interleukin-1β. Daily subcutaneous anakinra, a recombinant interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, blocks IL-1 signalling and reliably abolishes the fever, urticarial rash and arthralgia of FCAS, making it the standard targeted therapy for this disorder.

793624.long_answer: FRAS1 (Fraser extracellular matrix complex subunit 1) is one of the principal genes mutated in Fraser syndrome. Loss-of-function variants in FRAS1 disrupt basement-membrane integrity during embryogenesis, producing the typical Fraser features (cryptophthalmos, syndactyly, renal malformations) and, in a significant subset of affected fetuses, atypical or ambiguous genitalia. Because these genital anomalies are classified clinically as disorders of sex development (intersex), FRAS1 is a gene that links Fraser syndrome with intersex development.

827603.long_answer: Crohn disease, especially when the terminal ileum is inflamed or resected, impairs bile-salt reabsorption. Loss of bile salts reduces the solubilization of cholesterol in bile, leading to supersaturation and precipitation of cholesterol or mixed gallstones. Consequently, patients with Crohn disease have a markedly higher incidence of gallstone formation than the general population.

777192.long_answer: In Potter sequence, chronic oligohydramnios prevents normal lung expansion in utero, resulting in markedly underdeveloped lungs (pulmonary hypoplasia). At birth these infants cannot achieve adequate gas exchange, leading to severe respiratory failure, which is the most frequent cause of neonatal death.

162571.long_answer: Multiple carboxylase deficiency is an inherited defect (most often biotinidase or holocarboxylase-synthetase deficiency) that inactivates all biotin-dependent carboxylation enzymes. Loss of pyruvate, propionyl-CoA, and acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity disrupts energy and organic-acid metabolism, producing metabolic acidosis, seizures, dermatitis, and pronounced hypotonia in infants.

395074.long_answer: Banki syndrome is characterised radiologically by congenitally slender shafts of the long bones; the diaphysis (the shaft portion) shows marked thinning while the metaphyses and epiphyses remain relatively normal. Thus, the thin part of the long bone in Banki syndrome is the diaphysis.

900911.long_answer: In leukemia, malignant leukocyte proliferation crowds the bone marrow, suppressing normal megakaryocyte and platelet production. The resulting thrombocytopenia (markedly reduced platelet count) disrupts the blood-clotting cascade and predisposes patients to easy bruising, mucosal bleeding, and hemorrhage, making it a major clotting-related complication of the disease.

263156.long_answer: Genome-wide association studies have shown that variants in the HERC2 gene—particularly the rs12913832 allele that regulates the neighboring OCA2 pigment gene—are linked to increased risk of alcohol dependence. The very same variant is the principal determinant of blue versus brown eye color, making HERC2 a genetic factor common to both alcohol dependence susceptibility and eye-color determination.

626213.long_answer: Mondini dysplasia is a congenital malformation in which the cochlea fails to develop its normal 2½ turns and instead shows an incomplete, 1½-turn partition. This abnormal cochlear development is the hallmark of the Mondini deformity and underlies the sensorineural hearing loss seen in affected individuals.

683303.long_answer: Hemifacial microsomia involves maldevelopment of the external ear canal, middle-ear ossicles, and surrounding temporal bone structures. These anatomic anomalies impede sound conduction to the inner ear, making conductive hearing loss the characteristic form of auditory impairment seen in this condition.

767854.long_answer: Bipolar II disorder is linked to dysregulation of the catecholaminergic system, notably altered norepinephrine signaling—elevated activity during hypomanic states and relative deficiency during depressive episodes—indicating that norepinephrine dysfunction is central to its pathophysiology.

162788.long_answer: The lower (cardiac) esophageal sphincter lies at the distal, or inferior/caudal, end of the esophagus, marking the point where the esophagus joins the stomach. Thus, in anatomical terminology its position relative to the rest of the esophagus is described as distal.

766138.long_answer: Hypermethioninemia is an inherited inborn error of methionine metabolism caused by mutations in genes such as MAT1A or GNMT. Because its diagnosis relies on genetic testing and its management requires counseling about hereditary transmission and metabolic treatment plans typical for genetic metabolic disorders, the condition falls under the expertise of the medical genetics specialty.

201263.long_answer: Immunohistochemical staining for p40—the ΔNp63 isoform of the p63 transcription factor—is currently the most sensitive and highly specific marker for squamous differentiation. Because p40 is expressed in normal stratified squamous epithelium and is retained in malignant transformation, its strong nuclear positivity is used in surgical pathology to confirm the diagnosis of squamous-cell carcinoma and to distinguish it from adenocarcinoma or other non-squamous tumors.

178760.long_answer: The Lennox–Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) Foundation is a U.S.-based 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization headquartered in New York, United States, where it coordinates education, advocacy, and research support for this severe epilepsy syndrome.

456169.long_answer: The COCH gene, situated on human chromosome 14q11–q13, encodes the inner-ear protein cochlin. Pathogenic variants in COCH produce the DFNA9 form of autosomal-dominant, progressive, nonsyndromic sensorineural deafness (often with vestibular dysfunction). Thus COCH is the chromosome-14 gene classically associated with nonsyndromic deafness.

917404.long_answer: Among Australian paediatric populations, transient and chronic tic disorders (including Tourette syndrome) are the most prevalent movement disorders. Community-based studies consistently show tics affecting up to 10–20 % of school-aged children at some stage, far exceeding the prevalence of other childhood movement disorders such as dystonia, chorea or cerebral palsy. Their characteristic brief, stereotyped, involuntary movements or vocalisations make them readily recognisable and account for the majority of movement-disorder presentations to Australian paediatric neurology services.

314709.long_answer: Binswanger's disease (subcortical leukoencephalopathy) is classically linked to long-standing, poorly controlled hypertension, which causes small-vessel arteriosclerosis and chronic cerebral ischemia leading to diffuse white-matter damage.

952072.long_answer: Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) is an autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disorder produced by loss-of-function mutations in the PANK2 gene, which encodes the mitochondrial isoform of pantothenate kinase—the rate-limiting enzyme of coenzyme A biosynthesis. Defective PANK2 activity disrupts CoA metabolism, leading to iron accumulation and progressive basal ganglia degeneration characteristic of PKAN.

802215.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the WISP3 gene lead to progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia. The disorder manifests only when an individual inherits two non-functional WISP3 alleles—one from each carrier parent—demonstrating an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

992924.long_answer: Systemic corticosteroids (glucocorticoids) dampen innate and adaptive immunity by inhibiting neutrophil migration, macrophage activation, and cytokine production. This immunosuppression reduces the host’s ability to contain invasive bacterial pathogens, thereby increasing the risk of rapidly progressive soft-tissue infections such as necrotizing fasciitis.

269128.long_answer: Bullous pemphigoid is an autoimmune blistering skin disease in which IgG autoantibodies against hemidesmosomal proteins (BP180 and BP230) disrupt the dermal-epidermal junction. The resulting cleavage occurs below the epidermis, producing tense subepidermal blisters and widespread erythematous or urticarial lesions on the skin.

911235.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in COL4A1, which encodes the α1 chain of type IV collagen in cerebral vessel basement membranes, cause fragile small vessels that bleed in utero. The resulting intracranial hemorrhage can cavitate into porencephalic cysts, and survivors typically present with congenital or early-onset hemiparesis due to the unilateral brain injury. Thus, COL4A1 mutations are the well-established genetic cause linking porencephaly with hemiparesis.

757364.long_answer: Inherited pathogenic variants in the tumor-suppressor genes BRCA1 and BRCA2 greatly elevate lifetime breast-cancer risk—often to 50–80%—because loss of their DNA-repair (homologous recombination) function leads to genomic instability and malignant transformation of breast epithelial cells.

936708.long_answer: Brunner syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the monoamine oxidase A (MAOA) gene on the X chromosome. The defective MAOA enzyme fails to degrade serotonin, dopamine and norepinephrine properly, leading to elevated neurotransmitter levels that manifest clinically as impulsive and aggressive behavior characteristic of the syndrome.

291076.long_answer: Leri-Weill dyschondrosteosis is an autosomal-dominant skeletal dysplasia produced by haplo-insufficiency of the SHOX gene. The hallmark clinical feature is mesomelic dwarfism—marked shortening of the middle limb segments (radius/ulna and tibia/fibula)—often accompanied by Madelung deformity of the wrist. Because this condition specifically causes mesomelic limb shortening within the spectrum of genetic skeletal dysplasias, it is the classic disorder associated with mesomelic dwarfism.

359378.long_answer: Post-partum (puerperal) infections occur far more frequently after cesarean delivery than after vaginal birth; the uterine incision, devascularized tissue, and foreign bodies introduced during the operation create an optimal environment for bacterial contamination and growth. Consequently, cesarean delivery is recognized as the single most important and well-documented risk factor for postpartum infectious morbidity.

312281.long_answer: Aqueductal stenosis blocks cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) flow between the third and fourth ventricles, leading to obstructive hydrocephalus. A ventriculoperitoneal shunt is surgically placed to divert excess CSF from the cerebral ventricles to the peritoneal cavity, relieving intracranial pressure and preventing further ventricular enlargement.

221180.long_answer: In the salt-wasting form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, deficient aldosterone production leads to hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. Management therefore requires replacement of mineralocorticoid activity. The standard drug used is fludrocortisone, a potent synthetic analogue of aldosterone, which promotes renal sodium retention and potassium excretion, correcting the electrolyte imbalance in patients with salt-wasting CAH, including the rare variant caused by 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) deficiency.

451271.long_answer: Diltiazem, a benzothiazepine calcium-channel blocker, is commonly prescribed (often 240–480 mg/day) to reduce cutaneous calcium deposition in calcinosis cutis, especially the dystrophic form seen in systemic sclerosis and dermatomyositis.

269763.long_answer: Acrorenal mandibular syndrome is characterized by limb malformations that include absence (aplasia) or severe hypoplasia of the fibula—the long bone situated lateral to the tibia in the lower leg.

238297.long_answer: Neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies of Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy consistently demonstrate structural and functional abnormalities in the supplementary motor area (SMA), a medial frontal-lobe region that plans and initiates voluntary movement. Altered SMA activity within thalamo-cortical motor circuits is thought to help generate the characteristic myoclonic jerks of the disorder, linking this motor-control area directly to JME pathophysiology.

187627.long_answer: A virus-specific IgM antibody-capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (MAC-ELISA) detects newly produced IgM antibodies in serum or cerebrospinal fluid. Because IgM appears only after recent infection and there are no cross-reacting vaccines for most arboviruses, a positive MAC-ELISA result is accepted as definitive evidence of an arboviral infection.

419335.long_answer: Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is a developmental disorder that results from prenatal exposure to alcohol. Alcohol teratogenicity disrupts neurodevelopment, leading to brain structural abnormalities and functional deficits. Children with FAS commonly show impaired fine motor skills, poor hand–eye coordination, and difficulties with tasks requiring precise motor control due to damage in cerebellar and cortical motor pathways.

925706.long_answer: Beginning in the 18th century, naval surgeons such as James Lind showed that juices from lemons and later West Indian limes cured and prevented scurvy because they supply vitamin C (ascorbic acid), which is lacking in the diet of sailors on long voyages. Lemon or lime juice therefore became a standard anti-scurvy ration in many navies, giving British sailors the nickname “limeys.”

736446.long_answer: In patients with megaureter, the ureter is surgically re-implanted into the bladder through a new submucosal tunnel (ureteroneocystostomy). This antireflux reimplantation creates a length-to-diameter ratio that functions as a flap valve, preventing vesicoureteral reflux while allowing unobstructed urine drainage.

630221.long_answer: Andrew Ross Sorkin, the New York Times financial columnist and DealBook founder, was born with an ocular coloboma, a congenital defect that leaves a key-hole–shaped gap in structures such as the iris and makes his left pupil appear unusually large and elongated.

802889.long_answer: Mismatch repair cancer syndrome, more commonly referred to as constitutional mismatch repair deficiency (CMMRD), is caused by biallelic germ-line mutations in one of the DNA mismatch-repair genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2). Fewer than a few hundred families have been reported worldwide, and its estimated prevalence is well below 1 per 1,000,000 in the general population. It is listed in rare-disease catalogs such as Orphanet (Orpha number 180989) and the U.S. Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center. Therefore, by internationally accepted epidemiologic criteria and official designations, mismatch repair cancer syndrome is indeed considered a rare disease.

599273.long_answer: West Nile virus translates its genome as a single polyprotein that must be processed to yield the individual viral proteins. This processing is carried out by the virus-encoded NS3 serine protease (which functions with its cofactor NS2B). The NS3 protease recognizes specific cleavage sites in the polyprotein and catalyzes their hydrolysis, thereby releasing the separate structural and non-structural proteins required for viral replication.

298495.long_answer: Right-atrial enlargement raises venous pressure, often producing peripheral edema—visible swelling of the ankles, legs, or abdomen. Swelling (tumor) is also one of the cardinal signs of inflammation, the body’s primary anti-infection defense mechanism. Thus, edema/swelling is a symptom common to both conditions.

118956.long_answer: The presence of duplicated, opposable triphalangeal thumbs indicates a disturbance in anterior–posterior limb-bud patterning. This phenotype is classically produced by mutations that up-regulate or mis-express Sonic Hedgehog (SHH)—often via point mutations in its ZPA enhancer—resulting in pre-axial polydactyly and conversion of the thumb into a three-phalanged digit. Thus, finding duplicated triphalangeal thumbs on physical examination strongly implicates an SHH gene mutation.

383891.long_answer: The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) updated its Clinical Practice Guidelines to state that active surveillance (watch-and-wait) rather than immediate surgical resection should be the preferred initial approach for most desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis) tumors, reserving surgery for progressive or symptomatic disease. Thus, the NCCN no longer recommends surgery as the first-line treatment.

140177.long_answer: Leukemias are malignancies that arise from blood-forming (hematopoietic) tissues in the bone marrow. Myeloid leukemia specifically involves the uncontrolled proliferation of cells of the myeloid lineage (e.g., granulocytes, monocytes, their precursors). Because it originates in and primarily affects the blood and bone marrow, it is classified within the broader category of hematologic (blood) diseases and disorders. This classification is universally accepted in hematology and oncology textbooks and by organizations such as the World Health Organization and the National Cancer Institute.

473145.long_answer: Endotracheal intubation often requires forceful, wide mouth opening maintained for several minutes while a laryngoscope and tube are placed. This sustained stretching of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ) and its ligaments can produce capsular strain or subtle subluxation, leading to post-operative temporomandibular joint dysfunction in some patients.

518647.long_answer: Encephaloceles are structural defects of the skull that expose brain tissue; definitive management is neurosurgical. The protruding sac is excised and the dura and skull defect are closed, often with cranial reconstruction, to protect the brain and prevent infection or CSF leakage. No medical therapy can correct the defect, so timely surgical repair is the primary treatment.

826630.long_answer: Basophils are a type of circulating granulocyte that contain cytoplasmic granules rich in histamine. When activated during immune responses such as infections or allergic reactions, basophils degranulate and release histamine, which increases capillary permeability and promotes vasodilation, facilitating the movement of immune cells and plasma proteins into affected tissues.

182412.long_answer: The mediastinum is the central compartment of the thoracic cavity that houses vital structures including the heart, esophagus, trachea, and major blood vessels. Because it contains numerous lymph nodes and thymic tissue, it is a common site for both Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphomas to arise or spread, often presenting as a mediastinal mass.

579743.long_answer: Children with germ-line RB1 mutations who develop retinoblastoma are at particular risk for a primitive neuroectodermal tumor arising in the pineal gland, called a pineoblastoma. This pineal PNET together with ocular retinoblastoma constitutes the classic ‘trilateral retinoblastoma’ association.

320415.long_answer: Administration of synthetic androgens (e.g., oxymetholone, danazol) can transiently stimulate erythropoiesis and myelopoiesis in Fanconi anemia, raising red cell, neutrophil, and platelet counts and thus partially compensating for bone-marrow failure until definitive treatment such as hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is undertaken.

779776.long_answer: Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6), particularly the HHV-6B variant, is well documented to reactivate after hematopoietic stem-cell or solid-organ transplantation and can invade the central nervous system, leading to post-transplant limbic encephalitis characterized by memory loss, seizures, and MRI abnormalities of the temporal lobes.

496487.long_answer: Newborn screening programs quantify free carnitine (C0) in dried-blood-spot samples by acylcarnitine profiling with tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS). A markedly low C0 level detected by this MS/MS technique is the standard method for identifying systemic primary carnitine deficiency in newborns.

717411.long_answer: In DSM-5 the old diagnosis of conversion disorder was moved from the somatoform group and renamed functional neurological symptom disorder. This category covers neurologic-appearing symptoms—such as tremor, weakness, abnormal gait or other movement problems—that lack an identifiable organic cause, reflecting current clinical understanding of these functional movement disorders.

247687.long_answer: The only confirmed X-linked subtype of Fanconi anemia is complementation group B. This form arises from loss-of-function mutations in the FANCB gene, which is located on the X chromosome at Xp22. Mutations in FANCB disrupt the Fanconi anemia DNA-repair pathway, producing the characteristic chromosomal instability and clinical features of X-linked Fanconi anemia.

544392.long_answer: Elevated blood uric-acid levels (hyperuricaemia) can precipitate monosodium urate crystal deposition, producing gout. Epidemiologic and clinical studies list gout as a systemic disorder frequently associated with degenerative (calcific) aortic stenosis, making gout the condition linked to both aortic stenosis and high serum urate.

363296.long_answer: The disorder was first reported in a multi-generation pedigree living near the town of Upington, which lies in South Africa’s Northern Cape Province; hence the condition was named “Upington disease.”

295599.long_answer: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia (type III hyperlipoproteinemia) is typically caused by homozygosity for the APOE ε2 (ApoE2) variant, a missense mutation in the APOE gene (Arg158→Cys). The altered apolipoprotein E has markedly reduced affinity for the LDL receptor, leading to accumulation of remnant (β-VLDL/IDL) particles rich in cholesterol. This remnant accumulation promotes accelerated atherosclerosis, so the APOE E2 mutation confers the increased atherosclerotic risk seen in affected individuals.

800151.long_answer: Both types of hyperprolinemia (type I due to PRODH deficiency and type II due to ALDH4A1 deficiency) are transmitted in an autosomal-recessive fashion, meaning affected individuals inherit two pathogenic alleles—one from each carrier parent.

177946.long_answer: When both copies of the same homologous chromosome are inherited from a single heterozygous carrier parent (uniparental isodisomy), the child becomes homozygous for any recessive pathogenic variant present on that chromosome. This homozygosity can unmask rare autosomal-recessive disorders that would not appear if one normal allele were received from the other parent.

714068.long_answer: Vagabond's disease is a chronic dermatosis caused by long-standing infestation with the body louse Pediculus humanus corporis. It occurs mainly in individuals with nutritional deficiency and poor personal hygiene, leading to widespread pruritus, excoriations, and diffuse, dirty-brown skin pigmentation.

406891.long_answer: Whooping cough (pertussis) classically progresses through catarrhal, paroxysmal, and convalescent stages. In the convalescent stage the violent coughing wanes and the patient appears to recover, yet Bordetella pertussis organisms can still be present in the respiratory tract, so the individual may remain infectious for several weeks.

295842.long_answer: Alopecia areata is an autoimmune disorder that produces sudden, painless loss of scalp hair. Abrupt diffuse shedding is also a classic manifestation of heavy-metal intoxications such as thallium or arsenic poisoning, so patients with alopecia areata have on occasion been erroneously suspected of being poisoned.
