Recognition of the characteristic exclamation-mark hairs and non-scarred smooth scalp helps differentiate alopecia areata from toxic (poisoning-related) alopecia.

639671.long_answer: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs, including aspirin) inhibit cyclo-oxygenase enzymes, decreasing protective gastric prostaglandins and impairing platelet aggregation. This combination both predisposes the gastro-oesophageal mucosa to injury and hampers haemostasis, making NSAID use a well-established risk factor for upper gastrointestinal bleeding from Mallory-Weiss tears.

787973.long_answer: Sub-acute sclerosing panencephalitis produces pyramidal-tract damage, so patients develop increased muscle tone (hypertonia). Spasticity itself is defined as velocity-dependent hypertonia due to upper-motor-neuron lesions. Therefore, increased muscle tone (hypertonia) is a symptom seen in both conditions.

734252.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the modality of choice for multiple system atrophy; it sensitively depicts pontocerebellar atrophy, showing reduced volume of the cerebellum and pons and characteristic signs such as the “hot-cross-bun” pontine signal.

458719.long_answer: Lithium accumulates in principal cells of the renal collecting duct, entering via the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). There it disrupts vasopressin (ADH) signaling and down-regulates aquaporin-2 water channels, impairing water reabsorption and producing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

923758.long_answer: ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia mutated) is the serine/threonine-kinase gene whose loss-of-function mutations are the primary cause of classic ataxia–telangiectasia. The ATM protein also interacts directly with aprataxin and other single-strand break–repair factors; disruption of this ATM-centred repair pathway is integral to the pathogenesis of ataxia–ocular apraxia-1. Thus ATM is the common gene functionally linked to both disorders.

236850.long_answer: Birdshot chorioretinopathy is an autoimmune posterior uveitis that is commonly managed with immunosuppression; systemic or peri-ocular corticosteroids are first-line agents because they dampen T-cell–mediated inflammation. Corticosteroids (glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids) are endogenous steroid hormones synthesized in the adrenal cortex of vertebrates, and the same class of molecules is formulated as drugs such as prednisone, prednisolone, or triamcinolone for clinical use.

922123.long_answer: A lack of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) impairs myelin synthesis in peripheral nerves, producing demyelination and axonal degeneration. Clinically this manifests as symmetric distal paresthesias, numbness, and loss of proprioception—hallmarks of peripheral neuropathy. Correction of the B12 deficiency often halts or reverses these neurologic deficits.

682809.long_answer: Mutations in the LIG4 gene (encoding DNA ligase IV) lead to Ligase IV syndrome, a rare DNA-repair disorder characterized by severe microcephaly, growth retardation, immunodeficiency, and radiosensitivity.

246638.long_answer: Woodhouse–Sakati syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by pathogenic mutations in the DCAF17 gene (formerly C2orf37). Molecular diagnosis relies on sequence analysis and dosage/duplication studies of DCAF17, because both point mutations and larger exonic duplications or deletions in this gene can be detected with gene duplication analysis.

112466.long_answer: Definitive confirmation of berylliosis (chronic beryllium disease) is obtained by an open lung biopsy, which provides a surgical sample of lung parenchyma that can be examined histologically for the characteristic non-caseating granulomas produced by beryllium exposure.

218245.long_answer: Glutathione-synthetase deficiency causes recurrent 5-oxoproline accumulation and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The acidosis is corrected acutely and chronically by administering sodium bicarbonate, which buffers excess acid and restores normal blood pH.

378548.long_answer: Meningococcal septicemia (meningococcemia) progresses rapidly to septic shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation and multiorgan failure; even with prompt antibiotics and intensive care the case-fatality rate is about 10–40 %, and many survivors sustain major sequelae such as limb loss or neurologic deficits. Hence the overall prognosis is considered poor.

264134.long_answer: Maple syrup urine disease is an autosomal-recessive defect of the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex. Inability to catabolize the branched-chain amino acids leucine, isoleucine, and valine leads to accumulation of their ketoacids, producing severe ketoacidosis along with the characteristic sweet-smelling urine.

133342.long_answer: In PCOS, the hypothalamic GnRH pulse generator fires at an abnormally rapid rate. This high-frequency GnRH secretion drives the pituitary to release disproportionately more luteinising hormone (LH) than follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Excess LH stimulates ovarian theca cells to overproduce androgens, while relatively low FSH fails to support normal follicular maturation. The resulting hyperandrogenism and arrested follicles underpin the cyst formation, anovulation and other core features of polycystic ovary syndrome.

922144.long_answer: The gene for the enzyme 5′-methylthioadenosine phosphorylase (MTAP) is located on chromosome 9p21. When an isochromosome 9p produces tetrasomy 9p, four copies of the MTAP gene are present, leading to a markedly increased MTAP enzymatic activity in blood or cultured cells. Quantifying this elevated MTAP activity therefore serves as a biochemical marker for confirming tetrasomy 9p.

988272.long_answer: Osteoma cutis is characterized by ectopic bone formation within the skin and subcutaneous tissue. Because it is a primary cutaneous disorder, initial evaluation, diagnosis (e.g., skin biopsy), and management are overseen by physicians trained in diseases of the skin—namely dermatologists (often pediatric dermatologists in newborns). Therefore, the specialty most likely to treat a newborn with osteoma cutis is Dermatology.

709278.long_answer: DNAH5 (dynein axonemal heavy chain 5) is one of the most frequently mutated genes in primary ciliary dyskinesia, where loss-of-function variants impair the outer dynein arm and ciliary motility. Transcriptomic and functional studies of nasal mucosa in allergic rhinitis have shown that DNAH5 expression is modulated during allergen-induced inflammation and participates in the epithelial inflammatory response, linking the gene to both primary ciliary dyskinesia and the pathophysiology of allergic rhinitis.

515811.long_answer: Excessive production of androgens in females can lead to virilization, a condition in which typically male secondary sexual characteristics—such as deepening of the voice, increased muscle mass, hirsutism, and clitoral enlargement—develop in a woman.

767594.long_answer: In XX gonadal dysgenesis the streak gonads produce virtually no sex steroids, so estrogen-dependent breast development is absent. Pubic and axillary hair, however, still appear because the adrenal cortex continues to secrete the weak androgen dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA, and its sulfate DHEAS). DHEA is converted peripherally to more potent androgens (testosterone, DHT) that act on hair follicles, making DHEA the hormone chiefly responsible for pubic hair development in these patients.

582943.long_answer: Molluscum contagiosum produces characteristic 2–5 mm dome-shaped, pink or flesh-colored papules that possess a central depression or dimple. Dermatologically, such small raised lesions with a central pit are termed “umbilicated papules,” which are pathognomonic for this poxvirus infection.

615395.short_answer: Preservation of the alveolar basal lamina
615395.long_answer: In cryptogenic organizing pneumonia the epithelial basal lamina is largely preserved after the initial lung injury. This intact basement-membrane scaffold prevents collapse and obliteration of the alveolar walls and permits granulation tissue to remain confined to airspaces, enabling reversible repair rather than permanent interstitial fibrosis.

292697.long_answer: Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) is well known to produce autonomic nervous system dysfunction—orthostatic hypotension, constipation, urinary and sweating abnormalities—because α-synuclein pathology involves brain-stem autonomic nuclei and peripheral autonomic ganglia. Dysautonomia is therefore a recognised clinical feature included in consensus diagnostic criteria for DLB, distinguishing it from Alzheimer’s disease and other dementias.

703637.long_answer: Arakawa’s syndrome II is grouped with the inborn errors of amino-acid metabolism (aminoacidopathies). It represents a defect in a pathway that degrades specific amino acids, so it is classified as an amino acid metabolic disorder rather than an organic acidemia, carbohydrate disorder, or lipid/storage disease.

128090.long_answer: Kounis syndrome presents as an acute coronary syndrome—angina or myocardial infarction—triggered by an allergic reaction. Because its hallmark is coronary artery spasm or thrombosis requiring evaluation with ECG, cardiac biomarkers, and often coronary angiography, the specialty that routinely diagnoses and manages such acute coronary events is cardiology; cardiologists are therefore the clinicians most likely to recognize and treat Kounis syndrome.

569989.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the VPS13B (also known as COH1) gene cause Cohen syndrome, an autosomal-recessive neurodevelopmental disorder. A proportion of individuals with Cohen syndrome experience epileptic seizures, linking the disorder to seizure susceptibility through defects in VPS13B.

201042.long_answer: Congenital rubella syndrome arises when a non-immune pregnant woman contracts rubella. Immunization with the live-attenuated rubella vaccine, routinely administered as part of the combined measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine, induces long-lasting immunity that prevents maternal rubella infection and thereby protects the fetus from congenital rubella syndrome.

923861.long_answer: In collagenous colitis, subepithelial collagen thickening is suspected on routine H&E sections, but confirmation requires a special histochemical technique. Masson trichrome stain selectively binds collagen fibres, coloring them bright blue-green and clearly delineating the collagen layer between colonic glands, thereby confirming the diagnosis.

733954.long_answer: Most Turbellaria flatworms possess both male and female reproductive organs in the same individual, making them simultaneous hermaphrodites (monoecious). This allows any two adults to cross-fertilize, a common reproductive strategy in this class.

786504.long_answer: The autosomal-dominant form of centronuclear myopathy is most commonly caused by mutations in the DNM2 (dynamin-2) gene, which is located on chromosome 19 (region 19p13). Hence, chromosome 19 is the chromosome associated with the autosomal dominant variant of this myopathy.

708783.long_answer: Endosalpingiosis consists of ectopic glands lined by fallopian-tube-type epithelium. These epithelial cells retain the same 9+2 microtubule ‘motile cilia’ (kinocilia) that normally propel the ovum within the tubal lumen. The presence of these motile cilia identifies the tissue as salpingotic and underlies its growth outside the fallopian tubes in endosalpingiosis.

461462.long_answer: The cytochrome bc1 complex (Complex III of the respiratory chain) contains a cytochrome b subunit that carries two b-type protoheme IX groups (designated heme bL and heme bH). These b-type hemes are the characteristic heme species present in the bc1 complex and participate in electron transfer between ubiquinol and cytochrome c.

700204.long_answer: The MYOC (myocilin) gene is classically associated with juvenile-onset and adult primary open-angle glaucoma, not with primary congenital glaucoma (PCG). PCG, which presents at birth or within the first three years of life, is most commonly caused by pathogenic variants in genes such as CYP1B1, LTBP2, TEK, ANGPT1, and FOXC1. While an isolated case report may occasionally describe very early glaucoma in a child carrying a MYOC variant, large genetic studies, clinical reviews, and authoritative databases (e.g., OMIM, GeneReviews, ClinGen) consistently show no established causal relationship between MYOC mutations and primary congenital glaucoma. Therefore, according to current scientific consensus, MYOC mutations are not linked to primary congenital glaucoma.

110825.long_answer: Gum arabic (acacia gum) is the dried exudate of Acacia species and is widely employed in both foods and pharmaceutical preparations as a stabilising and emulsifying agent. Inhalation of the fine gum powder can lead to IgE-mediated sensitisation; numerous case reports have documented occupational rhinitis and asthma in workers handling or manufacturing gum arabic. Thus, gum arabic is the natural emulsifier-gum known to cause occupational asthma in gum-manufacturing personnel.

637196.long_answer: When the ureter becomes abnormally dilated (a megaureter or hydroureter), placement of a ureteral stent—typically a double-J stent—creates an internal drainage channel that bypasses the obstructed or atonic segment. The stent allows urine to flow freely from the kidney to the bladder, relieves back-pressure, and gradually reduces the dilation of the ureter.

892903.long_answer: Mepolizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody that targets interleukin-5 (IL-5), a key cytokine driving eosinophil growth and survival. By neutralizing IL-5, mepolizumab markedly lowers blood and tissue eosinophil counts, reducing the organ damage characteristic of hypereosinophilic syndrome. Clinical trials demonstrated steroid-sparing efficacy and symptom control, leading to its FDA approval for treating hypereosinophilic syndrome without the FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion.

872766.long_answer: During ascent, expanding air can rupture alveoli; gas then enters the pulmonary veins and is carried into the systemic arterial circulation. This arterial gas embolism is a well-recognized, potentially fatal complication of pulmonary barotrauma in scuba divers, leading to neurologic deficits, cardiovascular collapse, or stroke-like events.

968541.long_answer: Historically, congenital lymphatic malformations were referred to as “cystic hygromas.” Modern ISSVA classifications recognize that these lesions are developmental malformations rather than true tumors, and current literature therefore abandons the term cystic hygroma in favor of “lymphatic malformation.”

312129.long_answer: Jarcho-Levin syndrome is a form of spondylocostal/spondylothoracic dysostosis characterized by congenital malformations of the vertebrae and ribs that produce severe spinal curvature and thoracic deformity. Management focuses on correcting or stabilizing these skeletal abnormalities—often with procedures such as VEPTR implantation or spinal fusion—tasks that fall within the expertise of orthopedic surgeons, especially those specializing in pediatric spine disorders.

131248.long_answer: Biallelic (often compound-heterozygous) loss-of-function variants in the CNNM4 gene disrupt the magnesium transporter essential for both retinal photoreceptors and enamel-forming ameloblasts. This causes Jalili syndrome, a recessive disorder characterized by the combination of cone-rod dystrophy and amelogenesis imperfecta.

525704.long_answer: In mucopolysaccharidoses, accumulation of glycosaminoglycans and skeletal malformations (such as odontoid hypoplasia and vertebral canal narrowing) can compress the spinal cord. Progressive cord compression damages descending motor pathways, and the major neurological consequence is loss of motor function in the lower limbs—clinically presenting as paraplegia.

195909.long_answer: Type I hypersensitivity (immediate allergy) is driven by IgE antibodies bound to surface FcεRI receptors on mast cells. Upon re-exposure to the allergen, cross-linking of these IgE molecules triggers mast cell degranulation, releasing histamine and other mediators that produce the characteristic allergic reactions such as urticaria, bronchoconstriction, and anaphylaxis.

390297.long_answer: Glycerin, also known as glycerol, is a humectant that attracts and retains water in the stratum corneum, making it an effective moisturizer frequently recommended for psoriatic skin care. Because of its excellent safety profile and skin-hydrating properties, glycerin is likewise a ubiquitous ingredient in baby lotions and a wide range of cosmetic products.

580599.long_answer: Restless legs syndrome (RLS) disrupts nocturnal sleep and can produce excessive daytime sleepiness or hypersomnia. A well-established etiological factor for RLS is iron deficiency—low serum or CNS iron/ferritin levels increase RLS risk and treating the iron deficit often alleviates symptoms. Hence, RLS is both associated with hypersomnia and can be caused by iron deficiency.

889115.long_answer: Elevated plasma levels of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol are strongly and independently correlated with the initiation and progression of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. LDL particles infiltrate the arterial intima, undergo oxidative modification, and trigger inflammatory processes that lead to plaque formation, making LDL the key lipoprotein risk factor for atherosclerosis.

462115.long_answer: Collagenous colitis is a form of microscopic colitis that typically responds to budesonide, antidiarrheals, or bile-acid sequestrants. For patients whose disease is refractory or intolerant to these agents, immunosuppressants and biologic anti-TNF therapies have been used. Multiple case reports and small case series, as well as both the American Gastroenterological Association (2016) and European Microscopic Colitis Group guidelines (2021), list infliximab as a therapeutic option for severe, steroid-refractory microscopic colitis, including collagenous colitis. Although the evidence base is limited and its use is off-label, infliximab has been documented to induce clinical and histologic remission in such patients. Therefore, it is scientifically accurate to say that infliximab can be used to treat collagenous colitis in selected, refractory cases.

174838.long_answer: Chorionic villus sampling (CVS) obtains fetal trophoblast tissue early in pregnancy, providing DNA that can be analyzed for pathogenic mutations in genes such as LIS1 or DCX. Molecular testing of this CVS-derived fetal DNA allows definitive prenatal diagnosis of lissencephaly-causing genetic mutations.

284076.long_answer: Branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome is most frequently caused by pathogenic variants in the EYA1 gene. EYA1 encodes a transcriptional co-activator essential for ear and kidney development. The EYA1 gene is located on human chromosome 8q13.3, and heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in EYA1 account for the majority of BOR syndrome cases.

616645.long_answer: During cardiac embryogenesis, the endocardial cushions form the atrioventricular septum and contribute to the lower (primum) portion of the atrial septum, the membranous part of the ventricular septum, and the atrioventricular valves. Maldevelopment of these cushions leads to atrioventricular septal defects that present as combined atrial and ventricular septal defects in congenital heart disease.

561535.long_answer: Gunther disease (congenital erythropoietic porphyria) causes extreme photosensitivity because accumulated porphyrins in the skin are activated by ultraviolet and visible light. Sunscreens that rely on the physical blocker zinc oxide form an opaque layer that reflects and scatters a broad spectrum of UV radiation (UVA and UVB) and part of the visible range, thereby reducing the phototoxic reactions characteristic of the disease. Consequently, zinc oxide–containing sunscreens are recommended to help protect patients with Gunther disease from UV light exposure.

663330.long_answer: Papulopustular rosacea is the clinical subtype in which inflammatory, edematous papules and pustules develop on a background of central facial erythema. These lesions distinguish it from the erythematotelangiectatic form (mainly flushing and telangiectasias) and from other subtypes such as phymatous or ocular rosacea.

550846.long_answer: Both dysexecutive syndrome and the various forms of dementia characteristically include memory impairment—particularly problems with working or recent (short-term) memory—as a core cognitive deficit. In dysexecutive syndrome this stems from disrupted frontal-lobe circuitry essential for working-memory maintenance and retrieval strategies, while in dementia (e.g., Alzheimer’s disease) progressive cortical and hippocampal degeneration compromises the encoding and recall of new information. Thus, impaired memory is a shared, well-documented symptom in both conditions.

529790.long_answer: Barth syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in the TAZ (tafazzin) gene, classically presents with a severe form of cardiomyopathy. The most frequent cardiac manifestation is dilated cardiomyopathy—often with features of left-ventricular non-compaction—leading to ventricular dilation, impaired systolic function, and heart failure in affected males.

277960.long_answer: People with diabetes mellitus frequently develop candidiasis (infections by Candida species, e.g., oral thrush or vulvovaginal yeast infections). Hyperglycaemia and glycosuria provide an ideal growth medium for Candida, and diabetes-related immune dysfunction (impaired neutrophil and cytokine responses) further increases susceptibility, making candidiasis the most common fungal infection seen in this population.

379103.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome is a syndromic craniosynostosis caused by FGFR2 mutations. Premature fusion of the cranial sutures produces mid-face hypoplasia and a narrow nasopharyngeal airway; this airway restriction frequently causes obstructive sleep apnea in affected children.

559437.long_answer: Schamberg’s disease (a pigmented purpuric dermatosis) is often asymptomatic, but when itching occurs it is routinely managed with topical corticosteroid creams or ointments. The local anti-inflammatory effect of corticosteroids diminishes dermal inflammation and therefore relieves the pruritus associated with the condition.

727325.long_answer: Mutations in the SPAST gene (also called SPG4), which encodes the microtubule-severing protein spastin, are the single most common cause of hereditary spastic paraplegia and account for roughly 25 % of all inherited spastic paraplegia cases.

769307.long_answer: Acute pancreatitis—an inflammatory condition of the pancreas—is classically associated with sudden, severe epigastric pain that often radiates to the back and is accompanied by nausea and persistent vomiting. The inflammation leads to release of pancreatic enzymes and local irritation, which stimulates the vomiting center via visceral afferent pathways, making vomiting a prominent symptom.

852122.long_answer: Esotropia is a form of strabismus (inward deviation of one or both eyes). Diagnosis, optical correction, amblyopia therapy, and possible strabismus surgery are managed by ophthalmologists—particularly pediatric ophthalmologists—making ophthalmology the specialty that typically treats a child with esotropia.

818978.long_answer: Mowat–Wilson syndrome is classically caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the ZEB2 (also called SIP1) gene. Defective ZEB2 disrupts neural-crest-derived enteric ganglia development, predisposing affected infants to Hirschsprung disease and related gastrointestinal dysmotility, which clinically presents as severe constipation.

987874.long_answer: Patients with ankylosing spondylitis characteristically show elevated serum levels of Immunoglobulin A. Numerous studies have demonstrated that IgA concentrations correlate with disease activity and inflammation in AS, reflecting heightened mucosal and systemic immune responses typical of this spondyloarthropathy.

498756.long_answer: Patients with polycystic kidney disease commonly develop renin-angiotensin–mediated hypertension; current nephrology guidelines recommend an angiotensin-converting-enzyme (ACE) inhibitor as first-line therapy because RAAS blockade lowers blood pressure, reduces proteinuria, and may slow cyst-related decline in renal function.

805824.long_answer: In 2002 the State of California enacted legislation that prohibits the prescription and sale of pharmaceutical lindane products, thereby banning its use for the treatment of scabies (and head-lice) because of concerns over neurotoxicity in patients and persistent contamination of water supplies.

668624.long_answer: In cases of tricyclic antidepressant overdose, activated charcoal is typically delivered through nasogastric intubation; a tube is passed from the nostril into the stomach, allowing rapid gastric administration of the charcoal to adsorb the drug and limit systemic absorption.

305802.long_answer: Phenytoin, a hydantoin-class antiepileptic drug, is teratogenic when taken during pregnancy. In utero exposure disrupts embryonic folate metabolism and oxidative stress pathways, producing the characteristic craniofacial, limb, and growth defects collectively termed fetal hydantoin syndrome.

808576.long_answer: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP) is an opportunistic lung infection caused by the yeast-like fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii. It occurs predominantly in individuals with impaired cellular immunity—such as patients with advanced HIV/AIDS, those on prolonged corticosteroid therapy, or organ-transplant recipients—because their weakened immune defenses allow this normally harmless organism to proliferate in the alveoli, leading to diffuse interstitial pneumonia.

591650.long_answer: Acrokeratoelastoidosis is typically resistant to topical keratolytics and systemic retinoids, but multiple case reports and small series have shown marked flattening of the palmar and plantar papules after psoralen-UVA (PUVA) photochemotherapy. Consequently, PUVA has been cited in the dermatologic literature as the most consistently effective treatment for this condition.

284260.long_answer: In primary myelofibrosis, the neoplastic megakaryocytes release profibrotic cytokines (e.g., PDGF, TGF-β) that stimulate non-neoplastic stromal fibroblasts in the marrow. These fibroblasts are the cells that synthesize and secrete the extracellular matrix proteins collagen (type I) and reticulin (type III), leading to the characteristic marrow fibrosis.

813404.long_answer: Prospective cohort studies and randomized trials (e.g., the PREDIMED study) show that a Mediterranean diet—rich in vegetables, fruits, whole-grain cereals, legumes, nuts, olive oil, and fish, with limited red/processed meat and refined sugars—improves insulin sensitivity, reduces systemic inflammation, and is associated with a 20–30 % lower incidence of type 2 diabetes compared with low-fat or Western diets.

811818.long_answer: Myodesopsia is the ophthalmic term for perceiving vitreous 'floaters'—mobile opacities within the vitreous humour that cast shadows on the retina—causing moving spots or threads in the patient’s visual field.

402982.long_answer: Glossophobia, the intense fear of speaking in front of others, is clinically categorized as a performance-only presentation of social anxiety disorder (also called social phobia). Social anxiety disorder involves marked fear of social or performance situations where one might be judged, making public-speaking anxiety one of its most common and well-documented manifestations.

969999.long_answer: Rosenthal–Kloepfer syndrome is an historical name for florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (multiple cementoma), a benign fibro-osseous condition that affects the jaws. Evaluation, monitoring and any necessary surgical management of these jaw lesions are carried out by specialists in oral and maxillofacial surgery (dentistry), the discipline responsible for diseases and deformities of the facial bones and oral cavity.

300450.long_answer: GM1 gangliosidoses are rare, inherited lysosomal storage disorders caused by mutations in the GLB1 gene, so their diagnosis relies on genetic testing and enzymatic assays, and management centers on genetic counselling, metabolic monitoring, and coordination of supportive therapies. These activities fall primarily within the remit of the medical genetics (clinical/biochemical genetics) specialty, which is specifically trained to evaluate, diagnose, and guide treatment for inborn errors of metabolism such as GM1 gangliosidosis.

117707.long_answer: In familial lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) deficiency, defective esterification of plasma cholesterol alters red-cell membrane lipid composition, producing fragile target cells and stomatocytes. This leads to increased destruction of erythrocytes and manifests clinically as a mild to moderate hemolytic anemia.

115743.long_answer: Ollier disease (multiple enchondromatosis) is frequently caused by post-zygotic somatic mutations in the isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1) gene. Patients who carry these mosaic IDH1 mutations not only develop multiple enchondromas but also have a markedly increased risk of developing intracranial gliomas, typically low-grade gliomas that harbor the same IDH1 (most often R132H) mutation. Thus, the presence of an IDH1 mutation is the molecular alteration linked to the higher incidence of cranial gliomas in Ollier disease.

716179.long_answer: A clinical prediction rule that weighs features such as resistant hypertension, abdominal bruit and rise in creatinine with ACE-inhibitors can be followed by captopril renography (ACE-inhibitor renal scintigraphy). This nuclear medicine scan compares renal perfusion and excretory curves before and after captopril; a fall in function or delayed tracer wash-out after the ACE inhibitor indicates haemodynamically significant renal artery stenosis, allowing the presence of the stenosis to be confirmed non-invasively.

276923.long_answer: Population‐based studies indicate that reactive attachment disorder (RAD) is rare in the general child population, with epidemiological surveys in school-age cohorts finding DSM-defined RAD in roughly 1 %–2 % of children. Higher rates are observed only in high-risk groups such as maltreated or foster-care populations, but in the community the prevalence remains around one to two percent.

130588.long_answer: Chronic toluene inhalation produces selective neurotoxicity in the cerebellum, especially loss of Purkinje cells, leading to cerebellar atrophy and the characteristic motor ataxia seen in long-term abusers.

852311.long_answer: Ectrodactyly (split-hand/foot malformation) is an autosomal-dominant genetic disorder in which the central rays of the hand or foot fail to develop, leaving a cleft and functional peripheral digits. Because the remaining digits retain full sensation and proprioception, many individuals find that this natural, sensate grasp is more useful than an insensate prosthetic device, and therefore choose to keep their limb in its native form rather than use prosthetics.

798619.long_answer: Hemoglobin C disease produces chronic, low-grade hemolysis; the increased red-cell turnover raises the body’s demand for folate. Daily supplementation with folic acid (vitamin B9) prevents folate deficiency, supports erythropoiesis, and thereby helps lessen the anemia associated with hemoglobin C disease.

706701.long_answer: Pregabalin is an α2δ-subunit calcium-channel modulator approved for the treatment of painful peripheral neuropathies (e.g., diabetic neuropathy, post-herpetic neuralgia). By dampening central neuronal excitability it can produce central nervous system depression, so commonly reported adverse effects include dizziness, somnolence, and clinically significant fatigue.

363581.long_answer: In the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10), hepatorenal syndrome—a functional renal failure occurring in advanced liver disease—is specifically coded as K76.7 under the chapter for Diseases of the Digestive System (K70–K77).

522090.long_answer: Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis (Sweet syndrome) characteristically responds within 24–48 hours to oral systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone, which rapidly suppress the neutrophilic inflammation. Because of this prompt, reliable clinical improvement and extensive supporting evidence, systemic corticosteroid therapy is universally regarded as the gold-standard treatment for Sweet syndrome.

674865.long_answer: A meta-analysis of randomized trials comparing large-volume paracentesis with other interventions for refractory ascites (e.g., Salerno et al., Ann Intern Med 2007) showed that placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) achieved significantly higher rates of complete or partial resolution of ascites than repeated paracentesis. By creating a low-resistance channel between the portal and hepatic veins, TIPS lowers portal venous pressure and thereby reduces the formation and accumulation of ascitic fluid, making it more effective at removing (and preventing recurrence of) ascites than paracentesis alone.

177009.long_answer: In individuals with short-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (SCAD) deficiency, metabolic stressors such as fasting or a febrile viral illness can precipitate energy demand that exceeds impaired fatty-acid oxidation capacity, thereby triggering clinical symptoms.

188114.long_answer: In patients with untreated or poorly controlled hyperthyroidism, an intercurrent stress such as a systemic infection can precipitate a thyroid storm (thyrotoxic crisis). This acute exaggeration of thyrotoxic symptoms is life-threatening, characterized by hyperpyrexia, tachyarrhythmias, heart failure, and altered mental status, and requires emergent treatment.

139363.long_answer: External orthotic leg braces are commonly prescribed for Becker muscular dystrophy. By spanning the hips, knees, and ankles, the braces support the legs and pelvis, helping to stabilize weak muscles, maintain proper alignment, and make walking easier, thereby reducing fatigue and other symptoms associated with the disease.

144693.long_answer: Bronchogenic cysts are congenital malformations derived from the primitive foregut; their walls recapitulate normal bronchial wall components. Histologically they show ciliated pseudostratified columnar (respiratory) epithelium, cartilage, mucous glands, and bundles of smooth muscle— the same smooth muscle that forms the muscular layer of bronchi. No skeletal or cardiac muscle is present in these cysts.

147680.long_answer: In brachydactyly, surgically realigning or lengthening the shortened phalanges with an osteotomy can improve finger alignment and joint function. By cutting and repositioning (and sometimes gradually distracting) the bone, the procedure restores more normal length or orientation, thereby enhancing grasp and dexterity.

190127.long_answer: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is a very rare autosomal-recessive lysosomal storage disorder; epidemiologic studies in Europe and North America consistently place its birth incidence at roughly one affected infant per 40 000 live births (ranging in different surveys from 1:40 000 to 1:100 000). Thus, in the general population the accepted incidence is about 1 in 40 000.

583694.long_answer: Although most cases of Goldenhar syndrome (oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum) occur sporadically, the families in which multiple first-degree relatives are affected can be accounted for by an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with reduced penetrance and variable expressivity. This pattern permits transmission from an affected parent to offspring in successive generations while explaining the wide phenotypic variability and occasional skipping of generations observed in reported familial clusters.

385631.long_answer: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection of the eye produces classic dendritic (branching, fern-like) epithelial ulcers on the cornea. These linear lesions with terminal bulbs are pathognomonic for HSV keratitis, reflecting viral replication in corneal epithelial cells and associated inflammatory response.

847439.long_answer: Pfam is the widely used Protein families database that organizes proteins into families and domains defined by hidden-Markov-model profiles. It contains dedicated entries for cytochrome c oxidase subunits (e.g., COX1, COX2, COX3), providing alignments, HMMs and functional annotations, so it is the appropriate resource for finding information on those protein families.

823703.long_answer: Mutations in the PC gene impair the mitochondrial enzyme pyruvate carboxylase, whose normal role is to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate. Loss of this activity blocks anaplerotic entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle, causing accumulation of pyruvate that is instead reduced to lactate, producing severe lactic acidosis. Thus, deficiency of mitochondrial pyruvate carboxylase underlies the described clinical phenotype.

452908.long_answer: Langer mesomelic dysplasia results from homozygous or compound heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SHOX (short stature homeobox) gene. SHOX resides in the pseudoautosomal region 1 (PAR1) shared by the short arms of the X and Y chromosomes (Xp22.33/Yp11.32). Because it escapes X-inactivation and is present on both sex chromosomes, biallelic disruption of SHOX leads to the severe limb-shortening skeletal dysplasia characteristic of Langer mesomelic dysplasia.

365959.long_answer: Pseudomembranous colitis is the classic endoscopic and pathologic manifestation of infection by Clostridium (Clostridioides) difficile. Toxins produced by C. difficile damage the colonic mucosa, leading to necrosis and the formation of yellow-white fibrinous plaques—pseudomembranes—on the mucosal surface. Hence, C. difficile-associated colitis is commonly termed pseudomembranous colitis.

187672.long_answer: The triad of intestinal aganglionosis (Hirschsprung’s disease), hypoplastic or absent nails, and subtle facial dysmorphism corresponds to the microdeletion-8q24 disorder that is widely known as Feingold syndrome type 2. This autosomal dominant condition extends the classical Feingold phenotype to include Hirschsprung disease and nail hypoplasia, distinguishing it from type 1 that is caused by MYCN mutations.

215930.long_answer: Chorea-acanthocytosis is caused by biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) loss-of-function mutations in the VPS13A gene (encoding chorein). Because two pathogenic alleles are required for disease expression, the disorder follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, with carrier parents typically being asymptomatic.

416761.long_answer: In Metaphyseal dysostosis-intellectual disability-conductive deafness syndrome, the skeletal abnormality specifically involves the metaphyses—the widened, growth-plate–adjacent regions—of the long bones. These metaphyseal areas show abnormal modeling and radiographic irregularities characteristic of the disorder.

698966.long_answer: Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome causes bilateral adrenal hemorrhage that destroys the adrenal cortex, leading to acute and often permanent deficiency of cortisol (and frequently aldosterone). Survivors therefore may require lifelong corticosteroid replacement therapy—typically hydrocortisone (with or without fludrocortisone)—to compensate for the loss of endogenous adrenal hormones.

324134.long_answer: Goldenhar syndrome (oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum) results from abnormal development of the first and second pharyngeal (branchial) arches, which give rise to facial bones, mandible, external ear structures, and related tissues affected in this disorder.

747817.long_answer: Serum B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) – a cardiac hormone released from ventricular myocardium when it is stretched or failing – rises markedly in heart-failure states. Measuring BNP (or its inactive fragment NT-proBNP) is therefore routinely used to help confirm the diagnosis of peripartum cardiomyopathy, distinguishing it from non-cardiac causes of dyspnoea in late pregnancy or the early postpartum period.

151922.long_answer: Astaxanthin is a red-orange carotenoid pigment synthesized by certain microalgae (e.g., Haematococcus pluvialis). When these algae are consumed along the food chain, the astaxanthin accumulates in animals such as shrimp, krill, salmon, and flamingos, giving them their characteristic pink or reddish coloration. Because of its antioxidant properties, astaxanthin is also extracted and marketed as a human dietary supplement.

106128.long_answer: Uniparental disomy most commonly originates when homologous chromosomes fail to segregate properly during meiosis I or II—a process called meiotic nondisjunction. This error creates a gamete that carries two copies of the same chromosome (or none). After fertilization, mechanisms such as trisomy rescue can leave the embryo with both chromosomes coming from one parent, producing uniparental disomy.

180429.long_answer: Untreated or incompletely treated acute tonsillitis caused by Group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus can trigger an immune reaction in which circulating immune complexes deposit in the renal glomeruli, leading to inflammation and complement activation. This process produces post-streptococcal (acute) glomerulonephritis, typically appearing 1–3 weeks after the throat infection and characterised by haematuria, proteinuria, oedema and hypertension.

829891.long_answer: Chronic multifocal Langerhans cell histiocytosis is definitively diagnosed by histologic and immunophenotypic examination of affected tissue; therefore, a biopsy of an involved lesion (typically a bone lesion) is performed to confirm the disease.

628961.long_answer: Myoclonus-dystonia (DYT11) is most often caused by mutations in the SGCE gene, which encodes epsilon-sarcoglycan. Epsilon-sarcoglycan is a transmembrane glycoprotein component of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex on the cell membrane. Pathogenic loss or dysfunction of this membrane protein alters cell-signalling in neurons, producing the characteristic myoclonic and dystonic movements.

536999.long_answer: A cardiac myxoma is classified as a benign neoplasm arising from mesenchymal (connective-tissue) cells in the endocardium. It is the most common primary benign tumor of the adult heart, distinguished from malignant sarcomas by its non-invasive, slow-growing behavior and lack of metastatic potential.

456454.long_answer: Brachydactyly type D (characterized by shortened thumbs) has been linked to pathogenic variants in the homeobox gene HOXD13. HOXD13 resides within the HOXD gene cluster on chromosome 2q31.1, and its dosage‐sensitive role in limb patterning explains the digital shortening seen in this condition.

676966.long_answer: A tracheoesophageal fistula is a congenital malformation in which an aberrant passage forms between the esophagus and the trachea, allowing air to enter the gastrointestinal tract and gastric contents to enter the airway. This abnormal communication reflects faulty separation of the foregut into tracheal and esophageal tubes during embryogenesis.

279203.long_answer: Yes. Beginning in the mid-1980s several peer-reviewed medical journal articles argued that Joseph Merrick (the "Elephant Man") most likely had Proteus syndrome rather than the earlier diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1.  The first widely cited paper was J.R. Tibbles and M.M. Cohen Jr., “The Proteus syndrome: the Elephant Man diagnosed,” published in 1986 in The British Medical Journal (later expanded in the American Journal of Medical Genetics).  Subsequent reviews and case analyses in journals such as the Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, Clinical Genetics, and the American Journal of Medical Genetics have reiterated or supported that proposal.  Thus, medical journals have indeed proposed Proteus syndrome as the condition that afflicted Joseph Merrick.

533795.long_answer: Epidemiological studies have shown that people employed in pottery or ceramic production have a higher incidence of lung cancer. Pottery workers inhale large amounts of respirable crystalline silica (from clay and glazes) and, in some plants, radon-emitting materials and metallic pigments. Chronic silica dust exposure causes silicosis and persistent pulmonary inflammation, both established pathways that increase lung-cancer risk, explaining the excess cases observed in this occupation.

416985.long_answer: Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) is brain injury caused by perinatal asphyxia. Newborns who experience HIE frequently develop persistent hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia; this perinatal-stress–induced form of hypoglycaemia is classified among the causes of congenital hyperinsulinism.

137912.long_answer: In autoimmune hemolytic anemia, autoantibodies (often IgG) bind to red blood cells. These antibody-coated RBCs are recognized by Fc-receptors on splenic macrophages of the mononuclear phagocyte system, which then engulf and destroy the cells. Thus, splenic macrophages are the principal immune cells responsible for the phagocytosis of red blood cells in this condition.

828462.long_answer: After a focal or generalized seizure, some patients experience a transient post-ictal neurological deficit—classically a focal weakness of a limb, one side of the body, or less commonly generalized flaccidity. This reversible deficit is known as Todd’s paralysis (Todd’s paresis, postictal paralysis), and typically lasts minutes to hours before full strength returns.

838281.long_answer: Dysosteosclerosis can result from loss-of-function mutations in TNFRSF11A, the gene encoding the RANK receptor. TNFRSF11A is situated on chromosome 18q21.33, and pathogenic variants impair RANK-mediated osteoclast differentiation, leading to the characteristic sclerosing bone changes of dysosteosclerosis.

425837.long_answer: Among spontaneous abortions, the single most frequent chromosomal abnormality detected is trisomy 16. Cytogenetic analyses of first-trimester miscarriages consistently show that this autosomal trisomy accounts for the largest proportion of chromosomally abnormal conceptions, making it the leading chromosomal cause of miscarriage.

703717.long_answer: Viljoen–Kallis–Voges syndrome has been described in multiple affected siblings born to the same unaffected parents, with equal involvement of both sexes and no transmission through successive generations. This familial pattern led the original investigators to conclude that the disorder most likely follows an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

359140.long_answer: Children with Aarskog–Scott syndrome commonly present with proportionate short stature. Clinical reports and practice guidelines indicate that administering recombinant human growth hormone can stimulate linear growth and improve final height in these patients, making growth hormone therapy the standard treatment aimed specifically at their short stature.

995786.long_answer: HIV-associated vacuolar myelopathy is a spinal cord disorder seen in advanced HIV infection. Degeneration of the lateral and posterior columns produces progressive spastic weakness of the legs and gait disturbance, mimicking paraplegia or spastic paraparesis.

765490.long_answer: Brain CT scanning is the preferred imaging technique for diagnosing neurocysticercosis when calcified cysticerci are present, because CT is highly sensitive to intracranial calcifications and clearly delineates the small calcified cysts characteristic of the infection.

801505.long_answer: Visna-maedi virus is a member of the Lentivirus genus in the Retroviridae family, making it a lentivirus—a type of retrovirus that causes slow, progressive infections such as ovine progressive pneumonia in sheep.

416430.long_answer: Population-based epidemiological studies from Europe, North America, and Asia consistently report point prevalences for myasthenia gravis in the range of about 12–25 cases per 100 000 inhabitants. The value most frequently cited in reviews and textbooks is roughly 20 per 100 000 people, equivalent to about 1 affected individual in every 5 000 of the general population.

277233.long_answer: Macroglobulinemia, particularly Waldenström macroglobulinemia, is a malignant disorder of B-cell lymphoplasmacytic origin that causes excess IgM (a macroglobulin) in the blood. Because it is a hematologic malignancy involving abnormal blood cells and immunoglobulins, diagnosis and management—including plasmapheresis, chemotherapy, and targeted agents—are handled by specialists in hematology (often combined with medical oncology).

497877.long_answer: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is most often produced by pathogenic variants in the PKD1 gene, which is located on chromosome 16 at the 16p13-p12 region. Mutation of PKD1 leads to formation of numerous renal cysts, progressive enlargement of the kidneys, and ultimately impaired kidney function and renal failure.

786477.long_answer: In pernicious anemia, auto-antibodies attack the stomach’s parietal cells, which reside in the gastric mucosa. Destruction of this mucosal tissue eliminates intrinsic-factor production, preventing vitamin B12 absorption and leading to the characteristic megaloblastic anemia.

278468.long_answer: Several case reports describe girls with Aicardi syndrome who developed choroid plexus papillomas within the lateral ventricles. This benign neuro-epithelial tumor of the choroid plexus is thus considered the tumor type most often reported in association with the syndrome.

940951.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is a chromosomal disorder characterized by brachydactyly—abnormally short fingers and toes—and about half of affected infants are born with congenital heart defects such as atrioventricular septal or ventricular septal defects.

177623.long_answer: Hydrogen cyanide (HCN) is a highly toxic, rapidly acting cellular asphyxiant. When inhaled, HCN binds to the ferric ion in cytochrome-c oxidase (complex IV) of the mitochondrial electron-transport chain, blocking oxidative phosphorylation and preventing cells from utilizing oxygen. The brainstem respiratory centers are extremely sensitive to this acute tissue hypoxia. Within seconds to minutes of significant exposure, victims can develop dyspnea, loss of consciousness, seizures, and apnea (temporary or complete cessation of breathing). If exposure continues or is severe, this apnea progresses to sustained respiratory arrest and death. Thus, according to toxicology texts and clinical reports, inhalation of hydrogen cyanide can indeed cause a temporary cessation of breathing.

246059.long_answer: In Klinefelter syndrome, the extra X chromosome causes primary testicular failure. Impaired Sertoli and Leydig cell function lowers testosterone output, removing negative feedback on the pituitary, so FSH and LH rise. The combination of low sex steroids with high gonadotropins defines hypergonadotropic (primary) hypogonadism.

348648.long_answer: Endometriosis can implant on the urinary tract, most commonly on the urinary bladder. The bladder’s primary physiological role is to act as a hollow muscular organ that collects and stores urine before micturition, making it the organ both affected by endometriotic lesions and responsible for urine storage.

208599.long_answer: Fucosidosis is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by an inherited deficiency of the lysosomal hydrolase alpha-L-fucosidase. Lack of this enzyme prevents the normal degradation of fucose-containing glycoproteins and glycolipids, leading to pathological accumulation of fucose moieties in tissues and body fluids.

259908.long_answer: Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FXN gene located on chromosome 9q13. A well-recognized musculoskeletal complication of this chromosome 9–linked disease is progressive scoliosis, which develops in a majority of affected patients during childhood or adolescence.

203025.long_answer: Oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD) is classically caused by heterozygous pathogenic mutations in the GJA1 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin 43. These GJA1 mutations disrupt intercellular communication during limb development, leading to syndactyly that typifies the disorder.

305369.long_answer: Donnai–Barrow syndrome is autosomal-recessive. If a meiotic error leads to uniparental disomy—specifically isodisomy for chromosome 2 carrying the LRP2 mutation—the child can inherit two identical mutant alleles from a single carrier parent and none from the other parent, producing the disease without biparental inheritance.

563459.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PYCR1 gene have been documented in individuals diagnosed with De Barsy syndrome, and the same mutations define autosomal-recessive cutis laxa type 2B. PYCR1 encodes mitochondrial pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase 1, a key enzyme in proline biosynthesis; its deficiency disrupts connective-tissue integrity, producing the skin laxity and progeroid features characteristic of both disorders.

123839.long_answer: Koro is classified as a culture-bound anxiety disorder in the DSM and ICD systems. Evaluation, diagnosis, and management—including reassurance, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and anxiolytic or antidepressant medication when needed—are carried out by psychiatrists and other mental-health professionals. Therefore the relevant medical specialty is Psychiatry.

867870.long_answer: Classical homocystinuria is most frequently caused by inherited deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase (CBS), which normally converts homocysteine to cystathionine in the trans-sulfuration pathway. Loss of CBS activity leads to accumulation of homocysteine and methionine in blood and urine and accounts for the great majority of homocystinuria cases reported worldwide.

512744.long_answer: Low-dose methotrexate is an established first-line systemic therapy for lymphomatoid papulosis because it suppresses the aberrant proliferation of CD30-positive T cells. The same antimetabolite drug is widely used as a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) to control inflammation and slow disease progression in rheumatoid arthritis, making methotrexate a treatment common to both conditions.

491816.long_answer: Mutations in the TBX22 gene, which encodes a T-box transcription factor, are a well-established cause of X-linked cleft palate with or without ankyloglossia. Multiple peer-reviewed studies available in PubMed describe how loss-of-function or missense variants in TBX22 disrupt palate development, leading to isolated or syndromic cleft palate in affected individuals.

567771.long_answer: In alopecia areata, the immune attack on hair follicles is often accompanied by involvement of the nail matrix, producing regular, finely punctate depressions in the nail plate known as nail pitting. This is the most characteristic and commonly reported nail change in patients with alopecia areata.

461766.long_answer: Infantile hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors that typically appear within the first weeks of life, occur in about 4–5% of infants, and grow rapidly before slowly involuting over several years. They are distinguished from congenital vascular malformations because they arise postnatally, are not present fully formed at birth, and therefore are not classified as birth defects.

547164.long_answer: In severe croup, epinephrine (usually as racemic epinephrine) is delivered by aerosol through a nebulizer, which converts the liquid medication into a mist that can be inhaled directly into the upper airway to rapidly relieve airway obstruction.

692612.long_answer: African iron overload has been linked to the Q248H missense mutation in the ferroportin gene (SLC40A1). This variant reduces the normal hepcidin-mediated inhibition of ferroportin, promoting excess intestinal iron absorption. Studies in African and African-American cohorts show that carriers of Q248H who develop type 2 diabetes frequently display elevated serum ferritin and hepatic iron, indicating the same mutation can affect individuals with diabetes as well.

146316.long_answer: The CLN3 gene, situated on chromosome 16p12, encodes a lysosomal membrane protein; pathogenic mutations in CLN3 are the classic cause of juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (Batten disease). Thus, among NCL-associated genes, CLN3 is the one located on chromosome 16.

826886.long_answer: Schwartz–Jampel syndrome involves continuous myotonic muscle activity and myopathic changes; the resulting muscle-fiber leakage commonly leads to a moderate rise of the muscle enzyme creatine kinase (CK) in the bloodstream.

800917.long_answer: A sternal cleft results from failed midline fusion of the sternum; the definitive and universally accepted management is early surgical repair, usually primary closure of the defect (sometimes with grafts or mesh) to protect intrathoracic organs and restore chest wall stability.

857979.long_answer: More than half of Japanese patients with Sotos syndrome carry a recurrent ~1.9–2.2 Mb microdeletion at chromosome 5q35 that removes the entire NSD1 gene. Loss of this region (and hence NSD1 haplo-insufficiency) is the documented cause in over 50 % of cases in Japan, whereas point mutations within NSD1 predominate in Western populations.

269409.long_answer: The CYLD tumor-suppressor gene, mutations of which cause CYLD cutaneous syndrome (Brooke-Spiegler syndrome and related disorders), is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 16 (16q12-q13).

777702.long_answer: Creatine is normally produced when guanidinoacetate is methyl-ated by guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT). The methyl donor in this reaction is S-adenosyl-methionine, which is formed from the essential amino acid methionine. Thus, methionine is the essential amino acid directly involved in the blocked methyl-transfer step of creatine synthesis in individuals with GAMT deficiency.

309052.long_answer: 3-Methylglutaconic aciduria type III (also known as DCMA syndrome caused by biallelic DNAJC19 mutations) shows a founder effect in the Hutterite colonies of southern Alberta, Canada, where the carrier frequency is about 1 in 12, resulting in the highest concentration of affected individuals in the country.

196118.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the PLCG2 gene (encoding phospholipase C-γ2) produce the syndrome known as PLAID/APLAID, characterized by cold-induced urticaria together with humoral immunodeficiency and other immune dysregulation features. Thus, PLCG2 mutations link cold urticaria and immunodeficiency in the same patients.

516965.long_answer: Secondary cold agglutinin disease most frequently follows respiratory infection with Mycoplasma pneumoniae. This atypical bacterium stimulates production of high-titer IgM cold agglutinins, usually directed against the ‘I’ antigen on red cells, leading to complement-mediated hemolysis. Consequently, M. pneumoniae pneumonia is recognized as the commonest bacterial precipitant of secondary cold agglutinin disease.

287743.long_answer: Paragangliomas are typically treated by complete surgical removal of the tumor. Because these neuroendocrine tumors are often well-circumscribed and can cause catecholamine excess or local mass effects, surgical resection offers definitive therapy, symptom control, and the best chance for cure or long-term disease-free survival.

101278.long_answer: Brachydactyly is usually just a cosmetic variation, but when the shortened phalanges limit grasping or other hand functions, orthopedic/hand surgeons may perform reconstructive surgery—such as bone-lengthening osteotomies or grafts—to restore proper finger length and improve functional range of motion.

598908.long_answer: Stroke, specifically an ischemic stroke, occurs when cerebral blood flow is cut off or greatly reduced (ischemia), depriving brain tissue of oxygen and glucose. Within minutes, neurons begin to malfunction and die, leading to neurological deficits. Thus, stroke is the classic brain condition that directly results from ischemia.

102931.long_answer: Chondrosarcoma is the malignant form of a cartilage-forming tumor. Unlike benign chondromas, chondrosarcomas infiltrate surrounding bone and soft tissue and possess the capacity to metastasize, most commonly to the lungs, making them locally aggressive and systemically dangerous.

246740.long_answer: The FBN1 gene, encoding the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1 whose mutations cause Marfan syndrome, is mapped to chromosome 15, specifically the 15q21.1 region.

497832.long_answer: Mast cells express the high-affinity IgE receptor FcεRI on their surface. The α-chain of FcεRI specifically recognizes and binds the Fc (constant) region of IgE antibodies, allowing mast cells to become sensitized and to degranulate upon subsequent antigen-mediated cross-linking of bound IgE.

573404.long_answer: The SETBP1 gene encodes the SET-binding protein 1. Recurrent somatic missense mutations in SETBP1 are characteristic of several myeloid neoplasms, especially atypical chronic myeloid leukemia (aCML), where they promote leukemic transformation. Independently, de novo germline SETBP1 mutations that cluster in the same protein region cause the congenital disorder Schinzel-Giedion syndrome, establishing a shared genetic basis between these two conditions.

801311.long_answer: Both asbestosis and interstitial lung disease commonly present with progressive shortness of breath (dyspnea). In these fibrotic lung disorders, scarring of the alveolar–interstitial tissue stiffens the lungs and impairs gas exchange, leading patients to experience increasing breathlessness, especially during exertion.

942306.long_answer: Trisomy 22 is a numerical chromosomal abnormality in which there are three copies of autosome 22 instead of the normal two, classifying it as an autosomal trisomy.

391648.long_answer: Familial exudative vitreoretinopathy causes abnormal, leaky retinal vessels. Plasma rich in lipids and proteins seeps from these telangiectatic vessels, accumulating within or beneath the retina as yellow-white lipoproteinaceous exudative fluid.

792409.long_answer: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis—a chronic, autosomal-dominant disorder marked by progressive gingival overgrowth—has been linked to loss-of-function mutations in the SOS1 gene (Son of Sevenless 1). Variants such as the c.3047C>T nonsense mutation in SOS1 disrupt RAS–MAPK signalling in gingival fibroblasts, driving the lifelong fibrotic enlargement of the gums.

251353.long_answer: Fasciola jacksoni is a liver fluke species whose definitive host is the Asian elephant (Elephas maximus). Numerous veterinary reports from India and Sri Lanka document hepatic fascioliasis caused by F. jacksoni in captive and wild Asian elephants, establishing this species as the characteristic host for the parasite.

471054.long_answer: Menarche is the medical term for the first menstrual period, marking the onset of female reproductive capability. In Turner syndrome, gonadal dysgenesis leads to estrogen deficiency and ovarian failure, so most affected individuals do not experience menarche (primary amenorrhea).

300982.long_answer: Supervised physical therapy—particularly range-of-motion and strengthening exercises guided by a physiotherapist—reduces limb stiffness, enhances joint mobility, and promotes lymphatic flow, thereby improving range of motion in patients with lymphedema.

116391.long_answer: The modified Gomori trichrome stain selectively colours skeletal-muscle fibres, highlighting abnormalities such as “ragged-red” fibres that are characteristic of mitochondrial and other myopathies; therefore, this trichrome dye is routinely used to identify muscle-fiber pathology when diagnosing myopathy.

201561.long_answer: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), named after French neurologists Georges Guillain and Jean-Alexandre Barré, is an acute autoimmune polyradiculoneuropathy in which antibodies and immune cells mistakenly attack the myelin and/or axons of peripheral nerves. It typically follows respiratory or gastrointestinal infections (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, influenza) and, more rarely, can be precipitated by vaccinations. The resulting demyelination causes rapid-onset muscle weakness and sensory disturbances.

385015.long_answer: The pancreas contains acinar tissue that secretes digestive enzymes into ducts (exocrine function) and islets of Langerhans that release hormones such as insulin directly into the bloodstream (endocrine function), so it is classified as a heterocrine gland—one that has both exocrine and endocrine secretions.

390828.long_answer: Among the two characteristic translocations of alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma—t(2;13)(q35;q14) producing the PAX3-FOXO1 fusion and t(1;13)(p36;q14) producing the PAX7-FOXO1 fusion—the t(2;13)(q35;q14) variant is consistently linked to higher metastatic potential and lower overall survival, thus conferring a poorer prognosis.

645310.long_answer: Persistent allergic (IgE-mediated) rhinitis produces long-standing eosinophilic inflammation and edema of the nasal mucosa; over time this chronic inflammatory process promotes mucosal overgrowth, leading to the development of nasal polyps.

308785.long_answer: Reports of Zeichi-Ceide syndrome involve multiple affected siblings born to consanguineous, unaffected parents, a pattern that fits an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance—two carrier parents each pass on a mutant allele, producing the disorder in homozygous offspring.

100681.long_answer: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy (FNA) involves inserting a thin, hollow needle into the breast lump to withdraw a small sample of cells, which are then examined cytologically for malignant characteristics. Because it directly collects cells from the suspicious mass, FNA provides definitive pathological evidence to confirm or rule out breast cancer.

339050.long_answer: The vast majority of hereditary hemochromatosis cases, particularly in populations of Northern European descent, are caused by homozygosity for the C282Y missense mutation in the HFE gene on chromosome 6. Because over 80–90 % of affected individuals carry this specific mutation, molecular testing for C282Y in HFE is the primary and most widely used genetic assay in the diagnostic work-up for hereditary hemochromatosis.

732928.long_answer: Pain in torticollis arises from acute spasm and inflammation of the cervical muscles; first-line relief is provided by non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which decrease prostaglandin-mediated inflammation and provide analgesia, thereby reducing both pain and muscle soreness.

440904.long_answer: Fowler's syndrome is a rare disorder of the urethral sphincter characterized by failure of sphincter relaxation and consequent chronic urinary retention in young women. Clinical studies have shown a strong association between Fowler's syndrome and polycystic ovary syndrome, making it the classical syndrome linked to PCOS that produces urinary retention.

511744.long_answer: Beyond the inherited Factor V Leiden mutation, acquired resistance to activated protein C is most often produced by antiphospholipid antibodies. In antiphospholipid syndrome, lupus-anticoagulant and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies interfere with the protein C anticoagulant pathway, producing an acquired form of activated protein C resistance and a heightened risk of thrombosis.

695033.long_answer: Pythium insidiosum is an aquatic oomycete that infects mammals and occasionally humans, producing a severe granulomatous disease known as pythiosis. The organism’s hyphae invade tissue, provoking eosinophilic inflammation and vascular or cutaneous lesions, which is why the condition is universally referred to as pythiosis in veterinary and medical literature.

452476.long_answer: Börjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome is caused by pathogenic mutations in the PHF6 gene located on the X chromosome (Xq26.3). Because the defective gene is on the X chromosome, the disorder is transmitted in an X-linked recessive manner: affected males show the full clinical picture, while heterozygous females are usually asymptomatic or only mildly affected.

997135.long_answer: Grover’s disease, or transient acantholytic dermatosis, which Ralph Wier Grover first described in 1970, is characterized chiefly by sudden-onset, severely itchy (pruritic) papules and vesicles on the trunk; the predominant and most troublesome symptom is intense pruritus.

986384.long_answer: When Alice in Wonderland syndrome arises secondary to epileptic activity, the underlying seizures are managed with antiepileptic (anticonvulsant) medications—such as carbamazepine, valproate, or other seizure-control agents. By stabilizing neuronal firing and preventing epileptic discharges in the temporal-occipital cortex, these drugs can eliminate the perceptual distortions characteristic of the syndrome.

114901.long_answer: Apert syndrome is almost always caused by de novo missense mutations in the FGFR2 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 2) gene—most often the Ser252Trp or Pro253Arg substitutions. These gain-of-function mutations alter FGFR2 signaling, leading to premature craniosutural fusion and the characteristic craniofacial and limb abnormalities of Apert syndrome.

597347.long_answer: The vast majority of chronic bronchitis cases are attributable to long-term cigarette smoking, whose inhaled toxins provoke persistent airway irritation, mucous gland hypertrophy, and chronic inflammation, leading to the characteristic productive cough that defines the disease.

781212.long_answer: Floortime, formally known as the DIR/Floortime model, was created by child psychiatrist Dr. Stanley I. Greenspan. Greenspan designed the approach to foster emotional and developmental growth in young children by engaging them at their current developmental level and building ‘circles of communication.’ This technique is now widely applied to conditions involving attachment and social-emotional difficulties, including reactive attachment disorder.

501777.long_answer: Digoxin toxicity is well-known to precipitate a variety of supraventricular and ventricular arrhythmias. A characteristic manifestation is an accelerated junctional rhythm or junctional tachycardia (sometimes historically called the “digitalis rhythm”). The drug’s action of increasing intracellular calcium and enhancing automaticity of the atrioventricular (junctional) tissue, together with increased vagal tone, creates conditions that favor a junctional focus taking over the heart rate. Consequently, the appearance of a junctional tachycardia on the ECG is considered a classic sign of digoxin (digitalis) toxicity according to standard cardiology and pharmacology references.

815104.long_answer: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is an autosomal-dominant cancer-predisposition disorder caused by inherited germ-line mutations in the TP53 tumor-suppressor gene. Loss of normal p53 function impairs DNA-damage checkpoints and apoptosis, so affected individuals accumulate additional mutations more readily and develop a broad spectrum of malignancies (breast cancer, sarcomas, brain tumors, leukemias, etc.) at markedly elevated frequencies and at young ages. Thus this genetic disorder exemplifies the increased cancer risk that results from inherited genetic defects.

926301.long_answer: Xanthelasma palpebrarum consists of cholesterol-laden deposits in eyelid skin; their presence is strongly associated with elevated serum lipids (hypercholesterolemia/hypertriglyceridemia). Thus, xanthelasma often serves as a visible dermatologic marker indicating underlying hyperlipidemia.

311587.long_answer: At high altitude the fall in inspired PO₂ disturbs oxygen homeostasis. The body undergoes acclimatization: peripheral chemoreceptors drive hyperventilation, kidneys dump bicarbonate to offset respiratory alkalosis, hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF-1α) up-regulates erythropoietin leading to increased red-cell mass, and 2,3-BPG rises to unload O₂ to tissues. Together these coordinated adjustments restore arterial O₂ content and pH, re-establishing systemic homeostasis despite the hypoxic environment.

206204.long_answer: The oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III) arises from paired oculomotor nuclei located in the midbrain, specifically in the ventral periaqueductal gray at the level of the superior colliculus. Therefore, lesions of the midbrain can damage these nuclei and produce oculomotor nerve palsy.

179974.long_answer: Familial studies of primary palmar (focal) hyperhidrosis have mapped a susceptibility locus to the long arm of chromosome 14 (14q11.2-q13). This linkage indicates that genetic variants on chromosome 14 underlie the inherited form of excessive palmar sweating.

584570.long_answer: Patients with Marfanoid habitus can develop conductive hearing loss because lax connective tissue and recurrent otitis media may weaken or scar the tympanic membrane and ossicular chain. Damage or inefficient vibration of the tympanic membrane impairs sound transmission into the middle ear, so hearing loss is a recognized symptom attributable to tympanic-membrane pathology in these individuals.

232616.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder produced by pathogenic variants in the FBN1 gene on chromosome 15, which encodes fibrillin-1. The abnormal connective tissue weakens the aortic root and cardiac valves, often causing cardiovascular manifestations such as aortic dilation, valve prolapse, and resultant heart palpitations.

244992.long_answer: Essential pentosuria is a benign hereditary metabolic disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme L-xylulose reductase in the uronic acid pathway. Because L-xylulose cannot be efficiently reduced to xylitol, it accumulates and is excreted in the urine, leading to the characteristic finding of large amounts of L-xylulose in urine.

491772.long_answer: The German physiologist-neurologist Hugo Karl Liepmann (1863–1925) first defined and analyzed ideomotor apraxia, showing that damage to the dominant parietofrontal network disrupts the translation of an idea of movement into its motor execution. His classic studies laid the foundation for the modern understanding and classification of apraxic disorders.

764545.long_answer: In the early 1980s, British dermatologist Professor Christopher E. M. Griffiths proposed the now-standard classification of pityriasis rubra pilaris into six clinical types (classical adult, atypical adult, classical juvenile, circumscribed juvenile, atypical juvenile, and later the HIV-associated form). His work provided a systematic framework that is still used to guide diagnosis and management of the disorder.

856979.long_answer: Babesiosis is a tick-borne parasitic infection caused by Babesia species; management requires recognizing the pathogen, ordering specialized blood smears/PCR, and prescribing specific antimicrobials such as atovaquone-azithromycin or clindamycin-quinine. These diagnostic tests and treatment regimens fall within the expertise of an infectious diseases specialist, the medical specialty that routinely evaluates and treats parasitic and other systemic infections.

276083.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome most commonly results from missense mutations in FGFR2 that replace critical cysteine residues (e.g., Cys342 or Cys278). Loss or alteration of these cysteine residues disrupts disulfide-bond formation in the receptor’s extracellular domain, leading to constitutive FGFR2 signaling and the craniosynostosis characteristic of Crouzon syndrome.

557793.long_answer: The Apolipoprotein L1 (APOL1) gene lies on chromosome 22q12.3. Two coding risk variants—G1 (S342G/I384M) and G2 (ΔN388/Y389)—are strongly associated with hypertension-attributed nephropathy and progression to end-stage renal disease, especially in people of African ancestry. Clinical and epidemiologic studies have also shown that carriers of these APOL1 risk alleles have a higher incidence of severe pruritus (itching), particularly in chronic kidney disease and haemodialysis settings, linking the same gene variants to both hypertensive nephropathy and itching.

378104.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the NLRP3 gene (also called CIAS1 or cryopyrin) are a well-established cause of the cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) spectrum, which includes Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome, and Neonatal-Onset Multisystem Inflammatory Disease/Chronic Infantile Neurologic Cutaneous and Articular syndrome. These conditions are prototypical hereditary periodic fever (autoinflammatory) syndromes characterized by recurrent episodes of fever, rash, and systemic inflammation. This relationship is documented in numerous genetic and clinical studies and is part of current medical consensus. Hence, NLRP3 mutations do cause periodic fever syndromes.

583122.long_answer: Late congenital syphilis classically causes interstitial keratitis—a chronic, immune-mediated inflammation of the corneal stroma that produces corneal vascularization and subsequent scarring, leading to visual impairment. This ocular manifestation is part of Hutchinson’s triad (interstitial keratitis, sensorineural deafness, and Hutchinson teeth) seen in late congenital syphilis.

144656.long_answer: In mycosis fungoides—the most common form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma—patients typically present with erythematous patches or plaques, but the symptom they report most often is intense itching. Multiple clinical studies and dermatologic reviews cite pruritus as the predominant, most frequently mentioned complaint, occurring in a large proportion of cases and often prompting patients to seek medical attention.

313043.long_answer: The disorder is X-linked sideroblastic anemia with ataxia (XLSA/A). It was first reported by May et al. in 1997 in a single two-generation Mexican family in which only six hemizygous males were affected. All showed microcytic sideroblastic anemia accompanied by a mild, progressive cerebellar ataxia. The condition is caused by a missense mutation in the X-chromosomal ABCB7 gene, and no additional families have been documented, making these six males the only described cases.

320815.long_answer: People with coeliac disease frequently develop Hashimoto's thyroiditis—an autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland—because both conditions share predisposing HLA-DQ2/DQ8 alleles and similar loss-of-tolerance mechanisms. Epidemiological studies show the prevalence of Hashimoto’s in coeliac patients is several-fold higher than in the general population, making it the autoimmune thyroid disease most commonly associated with coeliac disease.

577761.long_answer: Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionic megacolon) is characterized by developmental absence of enteric ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses—the ‘tendinous plexus layer’ referred to. Without these neural plexuses, coordinated peristalsis in the affected segment fails, causing functional obstruction that manifests clinically as severe, chronic constipation and abdominal distension.

654735.long_answer: Herpesviruses possess a nucleocapsid with icosahedral symmetry (T=16), built from 162 capsomeres. This icosahedral capsid is surrounded by the tegument layer and the viral envelope, but the core structural geometry of the capsid itself is distinctly icosahedral.

540191.long_answer: Hyperkeratosis is a pathologic thickening of the stratum corneum.
