Vitamin A deficiency impairs normal keratinocyte differentiation, leading to excessive keratin accumulation (follicular hyperkeratosis). Mechanical irritation from repeated friction or pressure similarly stimulates keratinocyte proliferation and cornification, producing callus-type hyperkeratosis in the affected skin.

483822.long_answer: Turner syndrome (45,X or its variants) is definitively identified in utero by obtaining fetal cells through amniocentesis (or earlier by chorionic villus sampling) and performing karyotype or chromosomal microarray analysis. Demonstration of a monosomy X cell line confirms the diagnosis during pregnancy.

135666.long_answer: Shapiro syndrome (episodic spontaneous hypothermia with or without agenesis of the corpus callosum) is characterized by a failure of central thermoregulation. Thermoregulatory control in humans is governed mainly by the anterior pre-optic region of the hypothalamus, and neuroimaging as well as pathophysiological studies of Shapiro syndrome consistently implicate dysfunction of this hypothalamic thermoregulatory center as the cause of the profound hypothermia and hyperhidrosis attacks.

131444.long_answer: Within ovarian follicles, follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) binds to FSH receptors expressed on granulosa cells. These cells are responsible for converting androgens to estrogens and supporting oocyte maturation. When there is FSH insensitivity—such as from loss-of-function mutations in the FSH receptor—the granulosa cells cannot respond to circulating FSH, disrupting follicular growth and estrogen production. Therefore, granulosa cells are the cell type specifically affected by FSH insensitivity in ovarian follicles.

393975.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular microfibril protein fibrillin-1, are the established cause of acromicric dysplasia. The identical cluster of FBN1 missense variants (particularly within the TB5 domain) has also been documented in patients described clinically as having short-limb disproportionate short stature. Thus, pathogenic FBN1 mutations underlie both acromicric dysplasia and the short-limb disproportionate short-stature phenotype.

861785.long_answer: The SERPINA1 gene, which encodes alpha-1 antitrypsin and whose mutations cause alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, is located on the long arm of chromosome 14 (region 14q32.13).

913976.long_answer: Polysplenia syndrome is a heterotaxy (left-isomerism) disorder characterized by the presence of multiple small accessory spleens. It frequently coexists with other laterality defects such as dextrocardia, malpositioned abdominal organs, and can include hepatobiliary anomalies like biliary atresia. The combination of these findings firmly points to polysplenia syndrome as the underlying congenital condition.

546644.long_answer: When a microbe is passed vertically—i.e., from parent to offspring—its survival becomes tied to the host’s reproductive success. Natural selection therefore favors strains that do not harm, and often benefit, the host. Over evolutionary time this alignment of fitness interests drives a transition from parasitism toward a mutually beneficial symbiosis (mutualism), as seen in many insect endosymbionts and the ancestral origin of mitochondria.

965565.long_answer: Pathogenic germ-line variants in the BRCA2 gene markedly increase a man’s lifetime risk of developing prostate cancer. BRCA2 encodes a key protein in the homologous-recombination pathway of DNA damage repair; loss-of-function mutations impair double-strand break repair, promoting genomic instability and cancer development.

195859.long_answer: Encephalitis lethargica (von Economo’s encephalitis) was the epidemic viral encephalitis that swept the world in the early 20th century. Survivors frequently developed a delayed parkinsonian syndrome—termed post-encephalitic parkinsonism—characterized by rigidity, bradykinesia, and tremor. Thus, encephalitis lethargica is the classic neurological disorder that causes post-encephalitic parkinsonism.

923039.long_answer: Dental floss is routinely recommended in addition to tooth-brushing because it removes plaque and food debris from the interdental spaces that bristles cannot reach. Regular interdental cleaning with floss reduces bacterial biofilm accumulation, thereby lowering gingival inflammation and the risk of progression to periodontal disease.

237212.long_answer: In gastric (stomach) cancer staging, the TNM system uses the number of metastatic regional lymph nodes (N0, N1, N2, N3) to classify disease spread. The presence and count of positive lymph nodes directly determine the N category, which in turn up- or down-stages the overall stage and is a major prognostic indicator.

156429.long_answer: Trisomy X is characterized by the presence of an extra X chromosome in each somatic cell, yielding a total of 47 chromosomes instead of the normal 46. The standard karyotype notation for this sex-chromosome aneuploidy is 47,XXX.

292237.long_answer: The aqueous, bicarbonate-rich pancreatic fluid is produced by the epithelial cells lining the pancreatic ducts. Malignant transformation of these duct-secreting cells gives rise to pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the commonest form of pancreatic cancer.

129349.long_answer: Kurt Fearnley was born with sacral agenesis—also called caudal regression syndrome—a congenital malformation in which parts of the sacrum and lower spine fail to form properly. This developmental defect causes severe impairment of lower-limb growth and function, explaining why Fearnley uses a wheelchair and competes in Paralympic events.

322393.long_answer: The human RET proto-oncogene, implicated in familial and sporadic papillary thyroid carcinoma as well as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2, is mapped to band q11.2 on the long arm of chromosome 10.

952812.long_answer: Conservative management of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome typically starts with physical therapy and pain control. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as ibuprofen or naproxen are routinely prescribed because they reduce inflammation of surrounding soft tissues and provide analgesia, thereby alleviating the arm and shoulder pain characteristic of the syndrome.

901751.long_answer: Kearns–Sayre syndrome is caused by a sporadic, large-scale deletion within mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), typically a single deletion of 1.3–10 kb (classically the 4,977-bp deletion). This loss of mtDNA segments impairs oxidative phosphorylation in affected tissues, producing the characteristic multisystem manifestations of the syndrome.

304785.long_answer: Down syndrome is a congenital chromosomal disorder identified at birth or in early infancy. Comprehensive care—including monitoring of growth, development, congenital heart defects, thyroid function, and hearing/vision—is coordinated from childhood onward. These responsibilities fall primarily to pediatricians, making Pediatrics the specialty most commonly responsible for treating and managing patients with Down syndrome.

999652.long_answer: Marfan syndrome is an autosomal-dominant connective-tissue disorder caused mainly by mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1. Affected individuals characteristically have a tall, thin (marfanoid) habitus with long limbs and fingers, and up to two-thirds develop scoliosis or other spinal curvatures due to weakened connective tissue in the vertebral column.

950110.long_answer: When severe aortic stenosis in the fetus threatens to arrest left-ventricular growth and evolve into hypoplastic left heart syndrome, the established intervention is ultrasound-guided fetal balloon aortic valvuloplasty. In this procedure a needle and guidewire are advanced through the maternal abdomen and fetal chest into the left ventricle; a balloon catheter is then inflated across the stenotic aortic valve to relieve the obstruction, promote antegrade flow, and allow the left heart structures to continue developing, thereby reducing progression to hypoplastic left heart syndrome.

492484.long_answer: Oculodentodigital dysplasia (ODDD) is classically caused by heterozygous mutations in the GJA1 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-43. These mutations disrupt intercellular communication, producing the characteristic ocular, digital and dental anomalies. The defective enamel and dentin formed in ODDD patients make teeth highly susceptible to dental caries, so GJA1 mutations are directly linked to both the syndrome and the increased incidence of caries.

242737.long_answer: Gastrocutaneous (Gardner) syndrome features numerous adenomatous polyps throughout the gastrointestinal tract in addition to cutaneous lesions. Because the dominant, life-threatening component is the gastrointestinal polyposis with a very high risk of colorectal carcinoma, patients are primarily managed and treated by gastroenterologists (often with colorectal surgical support) who perform endoscopic surveillance and prophylactic colectomy when needed.

964120.long_answer: Klüver–Bucy syndrome often arises after bilateral lesions of the medial temporal lobes. One condition capable of producing such damage is meningoencephalitis—the simultaneous inflammation of the meninges (meningitis) and brain parenchyma (encephalitis). Viral meningoencephalitis, particularly due to herpes simplex virus, can destroy temporal-lobe structures like the amygdala and hippocampus, precipitating the characteristic behavioural changes of Klüver–Bucy syndrome.

447302.long_answer: Tamoxifen, a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM), is commonly used in the medical management of desmoid tumors because it binds to and blocks estrogen receptors, reducing estrogen-driven cellular proliferation in these tumors.

390453.long_answer: High-resolution abdominal ultrasonography is the standard imaging technique for detecting intramural or intraluminal masses in the gallbladder. Smooth-muscle tumours such as leiomyomas produce a well-defined, homogeneously echogenic or hypoechoic mass that can be visualised on ultrasound, allowing non-invasive identification and differentiation from other gallbladder lesions.

905940.long_answer: The first enzyme-replacement drug for Gaucher’s disease (recombinant glucocerebrosidase, marketed as Cerezyme) is manufactured in cultured Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells. These hamster cells are engineered to produce the human enzyme, which is purified and administered to patients to replace the deficient lysosomal glucocerebrosidase characteristic of Gaucher’s disease.

683293.long_answer: Primary myelofibrosis is characterized by bone-marrow fibrosis that drives extramedullary hematopoiesis, most prominently in the spleen. This results in marked splenic enlargement—splenomegaly—which is the classic organ enlargement associated with the disease and is present in the great majority of patients.

687192.long_answer: Walking pneumonia—most often caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae—is an atypical form of pneumonia whose symptom complex commonly includes low-grade fever, persistent dry cough, fatigue, and characteristic night sweats. The systemic, slowly progressive infection provokes autonomic dysregulation and cytokine release that lead to intermittent sweating episodes during sleep, distinguishing it clinically from many other pneumonias.

761104.long_answer: BMPR2 (bone morphogenetic protein receptor type II) is the principal gene mutated in heritable and idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. It encodes a receptor for BMP ligands that regulate bone morphogenesis and remodeling, directly linking the gene to bone metabolism as well as vascular function.

635906.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the homeobox gene OTX2 are a recognised cause of septo-optic dysplasia. Because OTX2 is a master transcription factor for early eye field specification, the same mutations frequently produce severe bilateral ocular malformations—most notably anophthalmia or microphthalmia—together with the optic nerve hypoplasia and pituitary abnormalities that characterise septo-optic dysplasia.

251535.long_answer: Hereditary fructose intolerance is caused by pathogenic variants in the aldolase-B (ALDOB) gene. Definitive confirmation is obtained by molecular genetic testing that identifies these ALDOB mutations, eliminating the need for risky fructose challenge tests or liver biopsy enzyme assays.

329504.long_answer: When a double-outlet right ventricle presents with physiology of transposition of the great arteries (Taussig-Bing type), definitive repair is achieved with an arterial switch (Jatene) procedure, usually combined with an intraventricular tunnel to route left-ventricular blood to the neo-aorta. This restores normal ventriculo-arterial connections and separates the systemic and pulmonary circulations.

704411.long_answer: De Barsy syndrome (autosomal-recessive progeroid cutis laxa) has been associated with loss-of-function mutations in the ALDH18A1 gene, which encodes Δ¹-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase. Disruption of ALDH18A1 impairs proline biosynthesis, adversely affecting collagen and elastin maturation and leading to the characteristic skin laxity, progeroid appearance, and systemic findings of the syndrome.

631897.long_answer: Generalized Arterial Calcification of Infancy (GACI) is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in ENPP1, the enzyme that generates inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi) from extracellular ATP. PPi is a small inorganic phosphate dimer that potently inhibits hydroxyapatite crystal nucleation and growth, thereby preventing extracellular matrix calcification. When PPi levels fall because ENPP1 is defective, calcification of arterial walls and other tissues occurs, making inorganic pyrophosphate the key physiological inhibitor whose deficiency underlies GACI.

430036.long_answer: Spondylolisthesis is the anterior (or posterior) slippage of one vertebra relative to the one below it. The displacement can narrow neural foramina or the spinal canal, compressing exiting nerve roots and producing radicular (nerve root) pain. When the slip is progressive or causes instability and neurological symptoms that do not respond to conservative treatment, surgical stabilization with spinal fusion is commonly performed to prevent further slippage and relieve nerve compression.

340244.long_answer: A congenital genetic defect in the brush-border disaccharidase lactase prevents hydrolysis of lactose in the small intestine. The undigested lactose osmotically draws water into the lumen and is fermented by colonic bacteria, producing gas, bloating, abdominal pain, and osmotic diarrhea—clinical features collectively termed lactose intolerance.

478898.long_answer: Galactorrhea accompanied by hyperprolactinemia is most often produced by a prolactinoma—a lactotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary that secretes excess prolactin. The elevated prolactin levels stimulate milk production (galactorrhea) even in non-lactating individuals.

918443.long_answer: Short rib–polydactyly syndrome is an autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia caused by mutations in genes that disrupt ciliogenesis. Because it is a congenital, heritable disorder requiring genetic diagnosis, carrier testing, prenatal counselling and coordination of multidisciplinary management, the specialty responsible is medical genetics.

922563.long_answer: Systemic corticosteroids such as prednisone are frequently prescribed to control the inflammatory and eosinophilic components of Kimura’s disease. Prolonged or high-dose glucocorticoid therapy raises circulating cortisol-like activity, producing classic iatrogenic (exogenous) Cushing’s syndrome with features such as moon face, central obesity, and skin thinning.

332552.long_answer: Intramuscular injection of botulinum toxin type A (e.g., onabotulinumtoxinA) is the main pharmacologic therapy for many forms of focal dystonia. Although it is FDA-approved for cervical dystonia and blepharospasm, clinicians routinely use it off-label for other focal dystonias such as writer’s cramp, musician’s hand dystonia, oromandibular and laryngeal dystonia. The toxin blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, weakening overactive muscles and reducing the involuntary postures characteristic of these disorders.

121489.long_answer: Fibrous dysplasia arises from a post-zygotic activating mutation in the GNAS gene, which encodes the stimulatory G-protein α-subunit (Gsα). The mutation causes constitutive cAMP signaling in osteogenic precursors, leading to replacement of normal bone with fibrous tissue—hallmark of the disease and of related McCune-Albright syndrome.

597793.long_answer: Long-term benzodiazepine use can lead to dependence and inter-dose withdrawal that provokes panic-like symptoms. To avoid these feelings, some patients begin to fear and avoid places where escape or help might be hard to obtain, fulfilling DSM criteria for agoraphobia—an anxiety disorder characterized by marked fear of situations such as crowds, bridges, or leaving home alone.

170655.long_answer: Short-limb skeletal dysplasia with severe combined immunodeficiency (e.g., cartilage-hair hypoplasia caused by biallelic RMRP mutations) is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner: affected individuals have pathogenic variants on both alleles, while heterozygous parents are clinically unaffected carriers.

402024.long_answer: Adopting an anti-inflammatory eating pattern (e.g., Mediterranean-style, rich in omega-3 fatty acids, fruits, vegetables, whole grains and low in refined sugar and saturated fat) lowers systemic levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6 and improves gut-microbiota balance. By dampening the autoimmune-driven inflammation that damages lacrimal and salivary glands, this dietary approach can reduce ocular and oral dryness, arthralgia and fatigue, thereby relieving the overall severity of Sjögren’s disease symptoms.

228823.long_answer: Most Erdheim–Chester disease lesions carry the somatic BRAF V600E point mutation, an activating change in the BRAF gene that substitutes valine with glutamic acid at codon 600. This alteration constitutively activates the MAPK/ERK signaling pathway and is detected in roughly 50–70% of patients, guiding the use of BRAF inhibitors as targeted therapy.

623138.long_answer: In dystrophy, the degeneration of tissue is mainly the result of faulty or inadequate nutrition of the cells—i.e., a metabolic disturbance that deprives the tissue of the substances it needs to maintain normal structure and function. This defective nutrition leads to progressive cellular damage and degeneration characteristic of dystrophic changes.

741812.long_answer: Chronic liver cirrhosis can lead to several characteristic nail findings. Hypoalbuminemia from impaired hepatic protein synthesis produces paired white transverse bands known as Muehrcke’s lines. Altered nail-bed vascularity and connective-tissue changes give the nails a white, ‘ground-glass’ appearance with a distal brown band, termed Terry’s nails. Cirrhosis is also a recognized cause of digital clubbing, likely through hepatopulmonary and vascular mechanisms. Thus, liver cirrhosis is the single condition classically associated with the triad of Muehrcke’s lines, Terry’s nails, and nail clubbing.

206979.long_answer: Coffin–Lowry syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the X-linked RPS6KA3 gene (encoding the RSK2 kinase). Mutations in RPS6KA3 not only produce the characteristic neuro-skeletal phenotype of the syndrome but have also been documented in patients who developed dilated cardiomyopathy progressing to heart failure, linking RPS6KA3 mutations to cardiac decompensation in CLS.

461487.long_answer: The RECQL4 gene, mutations of which cause Rothmund–Thomson syndrome, is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 8 (region 8q24.3).

630229.long_answer: Waardenburg syndrome is a genetic disorder characterized by congenital sensorineural hearing loss together with pigmentary abnormalities, most notably poliosis (a white forelock or patches of depigmented hair). Mutations in genes involved in neural crest and melanocyte development (e.g., PAX3, MITF, SOX10, EDNRB/EDN3) underlie the syndrome, leading to both auditory defects and hair/skin depigmentation.

680172.long_answer: Firm, subcutaneous rheumatoid nodules are a classic extra-articular manifestation of rheumatoid arthritis; they appear on pressure points such as the elbows, fingers, or Achilles region and represent areas of granulomatous inflammation associated with the disease.

444094.long_answer: Oxytocin is synthesized by neurons in the paraventricular and supra-optic nuclei of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It promotes milk ejection (let-down reflex) and fosters maternal bonding. Damage or disease of the hypothalamus can impair oxytocin production or release, disrupting both lactation and bonding behaviors.

349017.long_answer: Say–Meyer syndrome is classified among the X-linked intellectual-developmental disorders (OMIM: MRXSM). Reported families show affected males who inherit the pathogenic locus through carrier mothers, while heterozygous females are largely unaffected or only mildly affected—an inheritance pattern that is characteristic of X-linked recessive transmission.

979645.long_answer: St. Helena familial genu valgum is a hereditary bone-alignment deformity (knock-knees) that affects the growth and angulation of the lower limbs. Evaluation of limb alignment, imaging, growth-plate assessment, and corrective interventions such as osteotomy or guided growth are all within the scope of orthopedic surgeons, particularly pediatric orthopedists. Therefore, the orthopedic specialty is responsible for diagnosing and treating this condition.

696655.long_answer: For every patient who presents to the hospital with new-onset ascites, guidelines recommend performing a diagnostic paracentesis on admission. Sampling and analyzing the ascitic fluid (cell count with differential, culture, albumin, total protein, etc.) is essential to detect spontaneous bacterial peritonitis or other etiologies and to guide immediate management.

325515.long_answer: Hecht–Scott syndrome, also known as femoral hypoplasia–unusual facies (femoral–facial) syndrome, is characterized by marked hypoplasia or absence of the femurs, whereas other long bones are largely unaffected. Therefore, the femur is the bone primarily affected in this disorder.

641866.long_answer: Lachiewicz–Sibley syndrome is an eponym for benign familial hematuria (thin-basement-membrane nephropathy), a hereditary collagen IV defect that thins the glomerular basement membrane. The disorder manifests as persistent microscopic hematuria arising from the renal glomeruli, so the organ primarily affected is the kidney.

212322.long_answer: Patients who experience spontaneous bouts of hypothermia accompanied by profuse sweating—as seen in Shapiro syndrome or spontaneous periodic hypothermia–hyperhidrosis—often present with low body temperature, tachycardia, diaphoresis and altered sensorium. These signs closely mimic the systemic inflammatory response seen in severe infection, so they are frequently misdiagnosed as sepsis before the true neurogenic thermoregulatory disorder is recognized.

357449.long_answer: Cystic hygroma is typically identified in utero by high-resolution prenatal ultrasonography, which visualizes the characteristic multilocular, fluid-filled lymphatic cysts—often seen as increased nuchal translucency or a neck mass—during routine first- or second-trimester obstetric scans.

477384.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the LMNA gene (coding for lamin A/C) produce an aggressive form of familial dilated cardiomyopathy that is distinguished by early-onset ventricular arrhythmias and rapid progression to end-stage heart failure. Because of these malignant electrical and mechanical complications, LMNA-positive patients show a markedly high rate of implantable defibrillator therapy and ultimately cardiac transplantation, features that substantially diminish quality of life.

668663.long_answer: Al-Gazali-Donnai-Mueller syndrome is the same disorder that was later termed facio-oculo-acoustico-renal (FOAR) syndrome, also known as Donnai-Barrow syndrome. It is an autosomal-recessive condition caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the LRP2 gene and is characterized by distinctive facial features, ocular anomalies (severe myopia, retinal degeneration), sensorineural deafness, and renal tubular proteinuria, often with agenesis of the corpus callosum and diaphragmatic hernia. Thus, the accepted alternate name for Al-Gazali-Donnai-Mueller syndrome is facio-oculo-acoustico-renal syndrome.

522379.long_answer: Intramuscular injections of botulinum toxin (e.g., onabotulinumtoxinA) are a standard therapy for treating focal spasticity in patients with hemiparesis. The neurotoxin selectively blocks presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, producing temporary chemodenervation of overactive muscles and thereby reducing hypertonia and improving functional movement.

540114.long_answer: Nephronophthisis is an autosomal-recessive cystic kidney disease in which mutations of NPHP (cilia-related) genes cause progressive tubulointerstitial damage. Because the same genes are expressed in cerebellar and ocular motor pathways, some affected patients develop the cerebellar vermis hypoplasia/​Joubert spectrum, manifesting oculomotor apraxia along with ataxia and abnormal breathing. Thus, nephronophthisis is the genetic kidney disorder that can be accompanied by oculomotor apraxia.

221173.long_answer: In the 2022 International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) syndrome classification, Early Myoclonic Encephalopathy (EME) is grouped among the neonatal-onset developmental and epileptic encephalopathies (DEEs). These syndromes are characterized by early-life onset of intractable seizures accompanied by severe impairment of cerebral development, reflecting both developmental and epileptic contributions to the encephalopathy.

222451.long_answer: Focal cortical dysplasia is a malformation of cortical development that arises from disordered neuronal proliferation and migration during fetal life. Because the dysplastic cortex generates frequent epileptogenic discharges that are poorly responsive to antiseizure medications, it is recognized as the single most common pathological substrate underlying medically intractable (drug-resistant) epilepsy in children.

176287.long_answer: Among the genes known to cause Galloway–Mowat syndrome (GAMOS), the only one located on the X-chromosome is LAGE3 (L antigen family member 3). Because LAGE3 mutations are inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, heterozygous females are typically unaffected carriers who can transmit the pathogenic allele to their children—sons may be affected and daughters may become carriers. Thus, LAGE3 is the gene that can be passed on specifically by female carriers in GAMOS.

456289.long_answer: Undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma lacks obvious line-age-specific features on routine light microscopy. To determine whether the tumor cells express markers of any particular differentiation (e.g., cytokeratin, desmin, S-100, CD34, vimentin), pathologists apply immunohistochemistry—antibody-based staining of tissue sections—which is the standard technique for examining and classifying these undifferentiated tumor cells.

381608.long_answer: Infantile Refsum disease belongs to the Zellweger spectrum of peroxisomal biogenesis disorders caused by biallelic (two-allele) loss-of-function mutations in PEX genes. Because disease manifests only when both copies of the gene are defective and carriers are asymptomatic, the condition follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

326394.long_answer: Danazol is an attenuated androgen given prophylactically in hereditary angioedema to raise C1-esterase inhibitor levels. Because it retains androgenic activity, patients—especially females—may experience masculinizing adverse effects such as hirsutism, acne, voice deepening, and menstrual disturbances.

383242.long_answer: In Long QT syndrome, delayed ventricular repolarization sets up early after-depolarizations that precipitate the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia known as torsades de pointes. On ECG this arrhythmia shows a characteristic ‘twisting’ sinusoidal wave of QRS complexes around the baseline, making torsades de pointes the wave pattern classically associated with Long QT–related arrhythmias.

349532.long_answer: Albinism in kangaroos is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TYR gene, which encodes the enzyme tyrosinase. Tyrosinase catalyzes the first committed steps of melanin biosynthesis; when the TYR gene is defective, melanocytes cannot produce melanin, resulting in the characteristic white hair and red eyes seen in albino kangaroos.

395900.long_answer: Mutations in the CYP7B1 gene cause hereditary spastic paraplegia type 5 (SPG5). CYP7B1 encodes oxysterol-7α-hydroxylase, a key enzyme of the alternative bile-acid pathway that converts oxysterols such as 25-hydroxycholesterol and 27-hydroxycholesterol into bile-acid intermediates. This enzymatic step is essential for maintaining cholesterol catabolism and systemic cholesterol homeostasis, linking CYP7B1 directly to both hereditary spastic paraplegia and cholesterol regulation.

306263.long_answer: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner. Males possess only one X chromosome, so when they carry a pathogenic variant in the responsible gene (e.g., BCOR), they have just a single copy of that allele and are therefore hemizygous for the mutation.

883843.long_answer: Inhalation or aspiration of oil-based substances (e.g., mineral oil, petroleum jelly, oil-based nasal drops) introduces lipids into the airways and alveoli. These exogenous fats are taken up by alveolar macrophages, triggering an inflammatory response that produces the characteristic lipid-laden macrophages and radiographic infiltrates of lipoid pneumonia.

363814.long_answer: Mucha–Habermann disease (pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta) presents with crops of small erythematous-to-violaceous papules that acquire overlying scale and may become necrotic, forming a papulosquamous eruption. This papulosquamous skin abnormality—papules with scale that heal with varioliform scarring—is the characteristic cutaneous feature of the disease.

957505.long_answer: Borborygmus refers to the loud, gurgling or rumbling noises produced by movement of gas and fluid in the intestines. MNGIE (mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalomyopathy) patients frequently report this symptom, which is clinically described as stomach or bowel rumbling.

663335.long_answer: Barakat syndrome, also called HDR (hypoparathyroidism-deafness-renal dysplasia) syndrome, is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the GATA3 gene. GATA3 encodes a zinc-finger transcription factor essential for embryonic development of the parathyroids, inner ear, and kidneys; disruption of this gene explains the triad of hypoparathyroidism, sensorineural deafness, and renal anomalies characteristic of Barakat syndrome.

320254.long_answer: Clomipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant with strong serotonin-reuptake-inhibiting and anti-obsessional properties, has been reported in case series as beneficial for patients with the somatic subtype of delusional disorder (e.g., monosymptomatic hypochondriacal psychosis, olfactory reference syndrome). These observations led to the recommendation of clomipramine as a pharmacologic option for this specific delusional presentation.

774561.long_answer: Digoxin inhibits the cardiac Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, secondarily raising intracellular Ca²⁺ levels. The extra Ca²⁺ binds more readily to the contractile regulatory protein troponin C in cardiac myocytes, enhancing actin–myosin interaction and thereby increasing myocardial contractility.

532446.long_answer: A comprehensive skeletal survey using conventional X-ray imaging is the standard method for detecting the characteristic long-bone slenderness, tall vertebral bodies, and other skeletal dysplasia features seen in 3-M syndrome, allowing confirmation of the disorder’s skeletal abnormalities.

927154.long_answer: Mutations and common variants in the IRF6 (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6) gene are a well-established cause of Van der Woude and related syndromes that feature cleft lip and/or cleft palate, and genome-wide association studies have repeatedly shown IRF6 variants to be the strongest genetic risk factor for isolated, nonsyndromic orofacial clefts. IRF6 encodes a transcription factor essential for epithelial differentiation during craniofacial development, so disruption of its function directly predisposes to the formation of cleft lip and cleft palate.

358365.long_answer: Lipoid pneumonia is a distinct type of pneumonia in which lipids—often cholesterol or cholesterol-rich oils—accumulate within the alveoli. The presence of these fats provokes a foreign-body inflammatory reaction, leading to consolidation and respiratory symptoms. It can arise exogenously (inhalation or aspiration of cholesterol-containing oils) or endogenously (cholesterol released from tissue breakdown), making cholesterol a well-recognized cause of this specific pneumonia.

612857.long_answer: Following intestinal resection for short-bowel syndrome, parts of the remaining jejunum or ileum can become bypassed or dilated, leading to stasis and heavy bacterial overgrowth. This postoperative bacterial overgrowth produces malabsorption, steatorrhoea and vitamin-B12 deficiency – the clinical picture known as blind loop (small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth) syndrome.

531763.long_answer: Impetigo is a superficial bacterial infection of the skin most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes. Because it is a cutaneous disorder, the medical specialist who routinely diagnoses and manages skin infections and other dermatologic conditions is a dermatologist. Dermatologists are trained to recognize the characteristic honey-colored crusts of impetigo, order or interpret necessary cultures if indicated, and prescribe appropriate topical or systemic antibiotics, making them the specialists most likely to handle its diagnosis and treatment.

290413.long_answer: Osteopetrosis (especially the infantile malignant form) is a congenital disorder in which defective osteoclast-mediated bone resorption produces markedly sclerotic, abnormally dense bones. The excessive bone fragility, marrow failure, and associated complications commonly lead to severe morbidity and early death.

584260.long_answer: Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) is a form of neonatal brain injury characterized by ischemic-hypoxic damage and softening of the white matter adjacent to the lateral ventricles. It is most frequently seen in premature infants and is strongly linked to later neurodevelopmental disorders such as spastic cerebral palsy. The hallmark lesion is focal necrosis and gliosis in the periventricular white matter, making PVL the classic disorder associated with white-matter damage near the brain’s ventricles in infants.

627811.long_answer: The standard treatment for pseudomyxoma peritonei is extensive cytoreductive surgery, often including peritonectomy procedures, aimed at removing all visible mucinous tumor deposits. This surgery is typically followed intra-operatively by heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) to eradicate microscopic disease, but the key surgical component is the cytoreductive resection itself.

458844.long_answer: Septo-optic dysplasia involves malformations of midline brain structures and the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. The pituitary impairment most often affects the somatotroph cells, so growth hormone production is reduced; growth hormone deficiency is therefore the most prevalent endocrine abnormality seen in patients with this disorder.

541711.long_answer: Baclofen, a selective GABA-B receptor agonist, is the standard pharmacologic agent used to reduce spasticity that accompanies upper-motor-neuron lesions such as post-stroke hemiparesis. By enhancing inhibitory GABAergic transmission in the spinal cord, it decreases tonic stretch reflexes and skeletal-muscle tone, thereby alleviating spasticity in hemiparetic patients.

731603.long_answer: Punctate inner choroiditis is an inflammatory disorder of the choroid and retina. Evaluation and management—including fundus examination, optical coherence tomography, fluorescein angiography, and treatment with corticosteroids or immunomodulatory agents—are performed by ophthalmologists, typically retina subspecialists. Therefore, the medical specialty most involved is ophthalmology.

648898.long_answer: Van der Woude syndrome is most commonly produced by heterozygous mutations in the IRF6 gene (Interferon Regulatory Factor 6). Many IRF6 mutations create truncated or missense proteins that act in a dominant-negative fashion, disrupting normal IRF6 transcription-factor activity and thereby interfering with the function of the remaining wild-type allele in affected individuals.

635747.long_answer: Pegvisomant is a growth-hormone receptor antagonist that binds to hepatic GH receptors and blocks their activation, thereby suppressing hepatic production of insulin-like growth factor I (IGF-I). Clinical reports have shown that pegvisomant can normalize elevated IGF-I concentrations in patients with GH excess, and it has therefore been identified as a potential medical therapy for childhood gigantism when surgery or somatostatin analogues are insufficient.

220888.long_answer: Heterotopic ossification—the pathological formation of mature bone within peri-articular soft tissues—is a well-recognized complication after total hip arthroplasty and can likewise develop following traumatic hip dislocation, because both procedures involve substantial local tissue trauma that triggers aberrant osteogenic signaling.

434454.long_answer: Because their skin barrier is severely disrupted and covered with fragile blistering lesions, neonates with Epidermolytic ichthyosis are highly susceptible to invasion by bacteria, which can rapidly enter the bloodstream and lead to life-threatening systemic infection (neonatal sepsis).

632046.long_answer: Infants with Laron syndrome commonly develop recurrent hypoglycemic episodes because of their profound growth-hormone resistance and low IGF-1 levels. These hypoglycemic events frequently precipitate seizures, making seizures a well-documented clinical feature of Laron syndrome and a classic neurologic manifestation of hypoglycemia.

190375.long_answer: Hereditary multiple exostoses (multiple osteochondromas) is classically produced by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the exostosin-1 gene (EXT1). Deficiency of this Golgi membrane glycosyl-transferase impairs heparan-sulfate chain elongation and is classified among the congenital disorders of glycosylation as EXT1-CDG (formerly CDG type IIj). Hence, EXT1-CDG is the CDG subtype associated with hereditary multiple exostoses.

297594.long_answer: Streptozocin is an alkylating chemotherapy agent of the nitrosourea class that is FDA-approved specifically for metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine (islet-cell) tumors. It is preferentially taken up by pancreatic endocrine cells and induces DNA alkylation, leading to tumor cell death, making it a standard cytotoxic option for pNET treatment.

229274.long_answer: Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the MCT8 (SLC16A2) transporter, which is responsible for shuttling the thyroid hormone triiodothyronine (T3) into neurons. Without efficient T3 uptake, developing nerve cells cannot receive the thyroid-hormone signal required for proper brain growth and myelination, leading to the characteristic severe neurodevelopmental deficits of the disorder.

656183.long_answer: Diverticulitis is an inflammatory complication of diverticulosis. When a colonic diverticulum becomes obstructed and infected, inflammation compromises the local blood supply; if not treated, this can progress to ischemia, full-thickness bowel wall necrosis, and perforation.

298340.long_answer: The hereditary (autosomal-dominant) form of triphalangeal thumb maps to chromosome 7q36. Duplications or point mutations in the ZPA regulatory sequence (ZRS) within the LMBR1 gene on 7q36 disrupt Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling during limb development, producing a thumb with three phalanges.

693378.long_answer: Mefloquine, quinacrine, and chloroquine are antimalarial drugs that can cross the blood–brain barrier; when taken in excessive doses they injure neuronal and glial cells, producing a diffuse brain dysfunction classified as toxic encephalopathy. This drug-induced encephalopathy is commonly evaluated in the field of neuropsychiatry, the discipline that integrates neurology and psychiatry to assess how chemical insults to the brain generate both neurological and psychiatric symptoms.

551750.long_answer: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a functional gastrointestinal disorder characterized by recurrent crampy abdominal pain accompanied by bloating, often related to altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both). Visceral hypersensitivity and disordered gut motility lead to gas retention and bowel spasms, producing the typical combination of cramping pain and abdominal distension.

703292.long_answer: Gestational trophoblastic disease originates from the trophoblastic cells of the blastocyst (cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast). These cells normally form the placenta, but abnormal proliferation of trophoblasts produces the spectrum of tumors and neoplastic lesions classified as gestational trophoblastic disease, including hydatidiform mole and choriocarcinoma.

999601.long_answer: Breast milk contains relatively little total protein and therefore much lower amounts of the cationic amino acids lysine, arginine and ornithine whose intestinal and renal transport is defective in lysinuric protein intolerance. The small amino-acid load does not overwhelm the impaired y+LAT-1 transporter, so metabolic disturbances (hyperammonemia, failure to thrive, etc.) do not develop until the infant is weaned to higher-protein formulas or solid foods.

886874.long_answer: Oculocerebrocutaneous (Delleman) syndrome is classically linked to developmental malformations of the midbrain-hindbrain region, such as cerebellar vermis agenesis, brainstem dysplasia, and other posterior fossa anomalies. These midbrain-hindbrain defects constitute the characteristic central nervous system component of the syndrome alongside its ocular and cutaneous features.

305817.long_answer: A standard chest radiograph (chest X-ray) is routinely obtained in suspected acute respiratory distress syndrome and shows bilateral, diffuse alveolar infiltrates that signify fluid accumulation (pulmonary edema) in the lungs, helping confirm the diagnosis of ARDS.

716155.long_answer: Xanthinuria results from a deficiency of xanthine oxidase (also known as xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidoreductase), the enzyme that normally oxidizes hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid in purine catabolism. When this enzyme is absent or inactive, xanthine cannot be further converted to uric acid, leading to its accumulation and increased excretion in the urine.

130573.long_answer: In dogs with sarcoptic mange, gentle scratching of the ear margin (pinna) typically elicits an involuntary rhythmic hind-leg scratching motion (pedal response). This is called the pinnal-pedal reflex; a positive response is highly suggestive of mange and is commonly used by veterinarians as a quick diagnostic aid.

766430.long_answer: The cochlear (auditory) nerve is the branch of cranial nerve VIII that carries the electrical impulses generated by cochlear hair cells to the auditory centers of the brain. In presbycusis—age-related sensorineural hearing loss—degeneration and loss of these cochlear nerve fibers contribute to the progressive decline in hearing, underscoring its central role in both signal transmission and the pathology of the disorder.

180472.long_answer: Brachydactyly type A3, also termed brachymesophalangy V, is defined by shortening and wedge-shaping of the middle phalanx of the little finger. This structural change causes the distal phalanx of the fifth digit to curve toward the radial and volar (palmar) sides, producing the characteristic radial-volar clinodactyly described in the question.

474216.long_answer: Achondroplasia is the most prevalent skeletal dysplasia, responsible for roughly 70 % of all dwarfism cases. Caused by gain-of-function mutations in the FGFR3 gene, it leads to disproportionate short stature characterized by shortened limbs with relative preservation of trunk length. Medical and advocacy groups—such as Little People of America and other dwarfism organizations—identify achondroplasia as the prototypical and most common form of dwarfism.

299671.long_answer: The widely accepted amyloid-cascade model holds that Alzheimer’s disease is initiated by abnormal proteolytic processing of amyloid precursor protein, leading to extracellular buildup of insoluble β-amyloid (Aβ) peptides that aggregate into plaques. This Aβ accumulation triggers tau hyper-phosphorylation, synaptic loss, neuroinflammation, and progressive neuronal degeneration, making β-amyloid deposition the primary pathogenic driver identified for Alzheimer’s disease.

746759.long_answer: If phenytoin is infused too rapidly (exceeding about 50 mg/min in adults), the propylene-glycol–containing formulation can cause marked hypotension and severe disturbances of cardiac conduction, leading to life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias and possible cardiac arrest.

921947.long_answer: Homocystinuria, an autosomal-recessive cystathionine-β-synthase deficiency, produces a marfanoid habitus with long, thin fingers (arachnodactyly). The disorder leads to accumulation of homocystine/homocysteine that is excreted in large amounts in urine; a simple urine cyanide-nitroprusside screening test detects the excess homocystine, allowing laboratory confirmation of the diagnosis.

852253.long_answer: Contact dermatitis is an inflammatory skin disorder caused by irritants or allergens; its diagnosis (often via patch testing) and management of severe cases fall under the expertise of dermatologists, the physicians specialized in diseases of the skin.

453133.long_answer: An aberrant right subclavian artery (arteria lusoria) is a rare congenital anomaly of the aortic arch in which the right subclavian artery originates distally and courses posterior to the oesophagus and trachea. Its abnormal retro-oesophageal path can exert extrinsic compression on these mediastinal structures, producing symptoms such as dysphagia and atypical chest pain. Thus, chest pain arising from compressive effects of this anomalous vessel is a recognized, though uncommon, clinical presentation.

886151.long_answer: Amelogenesis imperfecta is an inherited disorder that affects the formation and quality of tooth enamel. Management consists of dental interventions such as protective restorations, crowns, veneers, and, in children, preventive and restorative care—all procedures carried out by dental specialists (e.g., pediatric dentists or prosthodontists). Consequently, patients with amelogenesis imperfecta are most commonly treated within the field of dentistry.

582745.long_answer: For most solid malignant neoplasms (cancers), complete surgical excision of the tumor with adequate margins is the cornerstone and first-line ('primary') treatment, as it offers the best chance for cure or local control before adjuvant modalities such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy are considered.

329082.long_answer: Idoxuridine is a halogenated thymidine analogue first synthesized and developed for antiviral use by William H. Prusoff. Applied topically to the eye, it inhibits herpes simplex virus DNA replication and became the first approved antiviral drug, specifically indicated for treating herpes simplex keratitis.

564950.long_answer: Veralipride is a dopamine-antagonist benzamide that was marketed in several countries to relieve vasomotor menopausal symptoms (e.g., hot flashes). By chronically blocking dopamine D2 receptors it markedly raises prolactin levels; the resulting hyperprolactinaemia suppresses gonadotropin secretion and oestrogen production, producing amenorrhoea, galactorrhoea and clinical hypogonadism in women. Because of these endocrine effects and additional neurological adverse events, veralipride was withdrawn from the market.

438162.long_answer: Pulmonary capillary hemangiomatosis causes diffuse, irreversible proliferation of capillaries within the lung parenchyma, leading to severe pulmonary hypertension and respiratory failure. Pharmacologic vasodilators or anticoagulation provide little benefit and can precipitate fatal pulmonary edema. Because the pathologic process is confined to the lungs, replacing the diseased lungs is the only curative option; thus, bilateral lung transplantation is regarded as the sole definitive treatment for this disorder.

338944.long_answer: Sprengel's deformity, a congenital elevation of the scapula, is clinically suspected from the high-riding, rotated scapula. Standard plain X-ray films of the shoulder girdle/cervical spine demonstrate the elevated, hypoplastic scapula and any associated omovertebral bone, thereby objectively confirming the clinical diagnosis.

239970.long_answer: Brain imaging in Cockayne syndrome characteristically shows intracranial calcifications concentrated in the basal ganglia (especially the putamen and caudate nuclei). These deposits are a well-documented radiologic hallmark of the disorder, reflecting neurodegenerative changes linked to the underlying DNA-repair defect.

149436.long_answer: A mutation in the LDLR (low-density lipoprotein receptor) gene on chromosome 19q13 disrupts LDL receptor function, reducing hepatic clearance of LDL particles from the bloodstream. The resulting accumulation of LDL cholesterol produces familial hypercholesterolemia, a classic form of hyperlipidemia.

439695.long_answer: The classic and most prevalent form of hereditary elliptocytosis is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner: a single pathogenic allele in genes encoding red-cell membrane proteins (most often α- or β-spectrin) is sufficient for the phenotype, and affected individuals typically have an affected parent and a 50% transmission risk to offspring.

135558.long_answer: In VACTERL association, congenital vertebral segmentation anomalies such as hemivertebrae or fused vertebrae are common. As the spine grows, these asymmetric defects can lead to progressive lateral curvature, so affected children are at increased risk of developing scoliosis during childhood or adolescence.

228992.long_answer: The Horne-Östberg Morningness–Eveningness Questionnaire is widely used in sleep-medicine research and clinical practice to characterize an individual’s circadian phase preference. By scoring whether a person is a ‘morning type’ or ‘evening type’, it helps identify the delayed circadian phase typical of Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder, making it an appropriate tool for assessing the circadian rhythm in these patients.

277003.long_answer: Schilder’s disease, also termed diffuse myelinoclastic sclerosis, is an acquired inflammatory demyelinating disorder considered a variant of multiple sclerosis. Its hallmark is large, bilateral cerebral white-matter plaques that resemble the symmetric involvement seen in hereditary leukodystrophies; hence neuropathology classifications list it as a “leukodystrophy-like” demyelinating disease.

909896.long_answer: Ackerman syndrome is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by gingival fibromatosis, facial and dental anomalies, and ocular involvement. One well-documented ocular manifestation is early-onset (juvenile) glaucoma, in which elevated intra-ocular pressure leads to buphthalmos and optic-nerve damage. Thus, juvenile glaucoma is a recognized eye condition that can accompany Ackerman syndrome.

697006.long_answer: The axial twist theory proposes that, during early vertebrate development, the anterior head region undergoes a left-right rotational (twisting) process relative to the trunk, establishing the normal contralateral and asymmetric organization of the cerebral hemispheres. Failure or aberration of this twist disrupts midline formation and hemispheric separation; the theory therefore interprets holoprosencephaly—where the forebrain fails to cleave—as the most extreme outcome of disturbed brain asymmetry generated by the axial twist.

208110.long_answer: Nemaline myopathy can weaken the bulbar and oropharyngeal muscles, leading to dysarthria and dysphagia. A speech-language pathologist (also called a speech and language therapist) is the specialist trained to evaluate and treat speech and swallowing problems, providing exercises, compensatory strategies, and feeding recommendations to maintain safe swallowing and effective communication in these patients.

635124.long_answer: Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) therapy for pernicious or severe vitamin B12–deficiency anemia is routinely administered by intramuscular injection, allowing direct replenishment of body stores when intestinal absorption is impaired.

534577.long_answer: Esophageal manometry (standard or high-resolution) directly measures lower esophageal sphincter pressure and its relaxation during swallowing, allowing precise assessment of motor function in children with achalasia-microcephaly syndrome.

765432.long_answer: In aplasia cutis congenita-intestinal lymphangiectasia syndrome the congenital intestinal lymphangiectasia causes massive loss of serum proteins into the gut (protein-losing enteropathy). The ensuing profound hypoalbuminemia, edema, malnutrition, and immune compromise lead to life-threatening complications, and affected infants typically die from this protein-losing enteropathy.

619829.long_answer: Kyasanur Forest disease virus is most sensitively diagnosed by a real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assay that amplifies a conserved region of the viral NS-5 gene, allowing rapid and specific detection of the infection in clinical specimens.

632904.long_answer: Dermatology is the medical specialty devoted to the study, diagnosis, and treatment of disorders of the skin, hair, and nails, including conditions such as eczema, psoriasis, acne, and skin cancers.

265225.long_answer: Tofacitinib, an oral Janus-kinase (JAK-1/3) inhibitor, has produced complete or near-complete hair regrowth in many patients with alopecia universalis by suppressing the γ-chain cytokine signals that drive the autoimmune attack on hair follicles. The same JAK-dependent cytokines (IL-4, IL-13, IL-31, IL-22, IFN-γ) are central to the type-2/Th1 inflammation of atopic dermatitis, and both systemic and topical tofacitinib have demonstrated significant reductions in eczema severity in clinical studies. Therefore, tofacitinib is a treatment effective in both alopecia universalis and atopic dermatitis.

885743.long_answer: Freeman–Sheldon syndrome is a congenital myopathy; the same MYH3-related muscle weakness that produces facial and limb contractures also affects the intercostal and accessory respiratory muscles.  Because their cough is weak and chest expansion is restricted, patients clear airway secretions poorly, so viral or bacterial upper-respiratory infections linger and take longer to resolve.

585166.long_answer: Listeria monocytogenes infection (listeriosis) often manifests in pregnant women as an influenza-like illness with fever, myalgia, and malaise. The bacterium can cross the placenta or contaminate the birth canal, allowing transmission to the neonate during delivery, where it may cause severe neonatal sepsis or meningitis.

666163.long_answer: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) shows the highest and most consistent comorbidity with major depressive disorder; epidemiologic and clinical studies report lifetime co-occurrence rates exceeding 50–80 %. Shared affective dysregulation, impulsivity, and serotonergic deficits help explain why depressive episodes frequently arise in individuals with BPD.

643115.long_answer: Fucosidosis results from biallelic pathogenic variants in the FUCA1 gene encoding α-L-fucosidase. Because disease manifests only when both copies of the gene are defective, it follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern: affected individuals inherit one mutated allele from each carrier parent, males and females are equally affected, and the risk of recurrence in siblings is 25%.

361281.long_answer: Across Europe and Asia, the single most common form of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is LGMD2A/LGMDR1, caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the CAPN3 (calpain-3) gene. This disorder is transmitted only when an affected individual inherits one mutated CAPN3 allele from each heterozygous carrier parent, defining an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

396788.long_answer: After an acute spinal cord injury, loss of sympathetic tone can produce neurogenic shock with profound hypotension. Intravenous vasopressor drugs (e.g., norepinephrine, phenylephrine, dopamine) are administered to cause peripheral vasoconstriction, raise systemic vascular resistance, and keep the mean arterial pressure high enough to perfuse the spinal cord and other organs. Therefore, vasopressors are the medication class used to maintain blood pressure in these patients.

596741.long_answer: Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens (CBAVD) is regarded as a genital variant of cystic fibrosis. Over 75 % of men with this condition carry pathogenic mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, which encodes an epithelial chloride channel. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) has extensively investigated CFTR mutations because they underlie both classic cystic fibrosis and isolated CBAVD, confirming CFTR mutation as the principal genetic cause of congenital absence of the vas deferens.

547852.long_answer: Pathogenic alterations in the mitochondrial genome—such as point mutations or deletions in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA)—impair genes that encode components of oxidative-phosphorylation complexes. These mtDNA mutations disrupt ATP production and are responsible for classic mitochondrial disorders (e.g., MELAS, LHON), which show maternal inheritance and tissue energy failure.

553762.long_answer: The vascular birthmark colloquially called a “stork bite” is medically classified as a nevus simplex, a benign capillary malformation that commonly appears on the nape of the neck, eyelids, or glabella in newborns and typically fades with time.

923987.long_answer: The R77C (c.229C>T) missense mutation occurs in the SGCA gene encoding α-sarcoglycan. This variant disrupts α-sarcoglycan folding and integration into the sarcoglycan complex, leading to limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2D—the disease classically termed α-sarcoglycanopathy.

719596.long_answer: In low-risk essential thrombocythemia, daily low-dose aspirin is recommended because it irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclo-oxygenase-1, suppressing thromboxane A₂ production and thereby decreasing platelet aggregation and the likelihood of arterial or venous thrombotic events.

825100.long_answer: Members of the Herpesviridae family—especially cytomegalovirus (CMV) and herpes simplex virus (HSV)—are well-documented causes of neonatal (congenital or perinatal) hepatitis. These enveloped DNA viruses can cross the placenta or be transmitted during delivery, infect the neonatal liver, and produce jaundice, hepatomegaly, and elevated transaminases characteristic of neonatal hepatitis.

994643.long_answer: Protein–energy malnutrition lowers available amino acids and energy substrates, disrupts testosterone and gonadotropin production, and increases oxidative stress in the testes. These changes impair flagellar structure and mitochondrial ATP generation in spermatozoa, leading to decreased progressive movement—i.e., reduced sperm motility (asthenozoospermia).

667600.long_answer: In 3-Hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency, accumulated organic acids from impaired ketogenesis and leucine catabolism enter the blood, titrating bicarbonate and widening the anion gap. A widened (high) anion gap therefore signals metabolic acidosis due to this organic acidemia.

424328.long_answer: In primary ciliary dyskinesia the motile cilia of the airway epithelium beat ineffectively, so mucus, bacteria, and particulates are not propelled out of the respiratory tract. The resulting loss of mucociliary clearance leads to persistent colonisation of the airways and, therefore, to chronic and recurrent infections of the nose, sinuses, bronchi, and lungs (e.g., sinusitis, otitis media, bronchiectasis).

991904.long_answer: Under WHO’s current yaws (Treponema pallidum pertenue) eradication strategy, the only countries in the WHO South-East Asia Region that still report endemic transmission are Indonesia and Timor-Leste; consequently, these two nations are the specific Southeast Asian targets for yaws eradication campaigns such as the 2012 ‘Morges Strategy’ that uses mass azithromycin treatment and surveillance to interrupt transmission.

183662.long_answer: Deep vein thrombosis often produces aching or cramping pain in the affected limb because the clot obstructs venous blood flow and raises venous pressure. Similar leg pain can also arise from poor circulation (e.g., peripheral arterial disease) or from nerve damage (neuropathy), making it a symptom common to all three conditions.

453669.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the FRMD7 gene, located on Xq26 of the X chromosome, are a well-established cause of X-linked infantile (congenital) nystagmus. FRMD7 encodes a FERM-domain–containing protein important for neuronal development of ocular motor control, and its disruption leads specifically to the nystagmus phenotype.

758001.long_answer: Christiaan Eijkman showed that the peripheral neuropathy known as beriberi results from a dietary deficiency—specifically the absence of the anti-beriberi factor later identified as vitamin B₁ (thiamine) found in rice husks. This demonstration that a nutrient lack, rather than infection, caused the disease earned him the 1929 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

145738.short_answer: To enlarge the atrial septal opening
145738.long_answer: Balloon (atrial) septostomy is performed to rip open or widen the foramen ovale/atrial septal defect so that oxygen-rich pulmonary venous blood can mix with systemic venous blood. This temporary increase in inter-atrial mixing raises systemic oxygen saturation and stabilizes cyanotic infants with defects such as transposition of the great arteries until definitive surgical repair can be done.

376705.long_answer: Malouf syndrome is a rare genetic condition originally described by Malouf et al. in 1979. The cardinal features include dilated cardiomyopathy together with hyper-gonadotropic hypogonadism caused by primary gonadal failure. Affected females typically have streak ovaries/ovarian dysgenesis, and affected males may have testicular atrophy—both forms representing gonadal dysgenesis. Therefore, gonadal dysgenesis is a defining component of Malouf syndrome, and the two conditions are indeed linked.

662292.long_answer: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by deficiency of 7-dehydrocholesterol reductase, the final enzyme in the cholesterol biosynthetic pathway. The block in cholesterol synthesis leads to accumulation of 7-dehydrocholesterol and reduced cholesterol levels. Clinically, patients can show multiple congenital anomalies, developmental delay, and, owing to lipid accumulation and impaired hepatic function, may develop hepatomegaly or hepatosplenomegaly.

982950.long_answer: Turner syndrome (classically 45,X monosomy) is characterized by streak or absent ovaries—i.e., gonadal agenesis—which leads to primary ovarian failure and estrogen deficiency. The absent/under-developed gonads result in hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, making Turner syndrome a well-recognized condition featuring both gonadal agenesis and hypogonadism.

334488.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ITGA8 gene, which encodes the integrin-α8 subunit, have been shown to cause bilateral renal agenesis. The absence of both kidneys leads to severe oligohydramnios, producing the characteristic features of Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, limb and facial anomalies). Thus, ITGA8 mutations are a documented genetic cause of Potter sequence secondary to bilateral renal agenesis.

650284.long_answer: Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon (a form of congenital ptosis) is frequently accompanied by unilateral amblyopia. The amblyopia often arises when the affected eye has significant anisometropia—unequal refractive error between the two eyes—which causes chronic image blur and cortical suppression of that eye, leading to reduced visual acuity.

967431.long_answer: Because IgE-mediated tree-nut allergy can provoke severe reactions and no curative therapy exists, standard clinical guidance is lifelong, strict avoidance of all tree nuts and products that may contain them, with vigilant label reading to prevent accidental exposure.

131126.long_answer: Scurvy, also termed Barlow disease in infants, results from vitamin C deficiency. The consequent defective collagen synthesis leads to periosteal reactions, subperiosteal hemorrhage, and bone swelling that can closely resemble the radiographic and clinical findings of infantile cortical hyperostosis (Caffey disease), making scurvy a key diagnostic mimic.

804090.long_answer: Frontonasal dysplasia (median cleft face syndrome) is a congenital malformation complex characterized by craniofacial anomalies such as severe ocular hypertelorism, broad nasal root, and midline facial clefting. Because the midline defect often extends through the anterior skull base, affected infants can present with an associated fronto-ethmoidal meningo-encephalocele. This well-established association makes frontonasal dysplasia the classic syndrome linking craniofacial anomalies with encephaloceles.

369581.long_answer: Treponema pallidum, the causative agent of syphilis, remains exquisitely sensitive to penicillin. Current CDC and WHO guidelines designate a single intramuscular dose of long-acting benzathine penicillin G as the first-line treatment for early syphilis (and appropriately dosed courses for later stages), because its sustained serum levels effectively eradicate the spirochete.

807181.long_answer: Patients with Fitzsimmons–Guilbert syndrome characteristically present with a prominent chest wall deformity described as pectus carinatum (‘pigeon chest’). This protrusion of the sternum is one of the diagnostic skeletal features reported alongside short stature, microcephaly, brachydactyly and intellectual disability in the original clinical descriptions that define the syndrome.

381070.long_answer: The cause of Hallermann–Streiff syndrome remains unknown, but isolated case reports have identified de-novo heterozygous variants in the GJA1 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-43, in individuals diagnosed with this syndrome. Although these findings suggest a possible link, no clinical genetic test is yet available and the association has not been definitively established.

252607.long_answer: Sleep-related eating disorder (SRED) is a parasomnia in which individuals partially arouse from sleep and consume food or non-nutritive, even toxic, substances without full awareness. Episodes typically occur in the first half of the night, and sufferers often have no memory of the event on awakening.

612737.long_answer: In infantile myofibromatosis, the activating PDGFRB mutation Asn666Lys (N666K) lies in the kinase domain’s activation loop. This substitution locks PDGFR-β in an active conformation that imatinib, which binds only to the inactive (DFG-out) state, cannot effectively inhibit, rendering the tumor cells resistant to the drug.

623339.long_answer: Acute kidney injury resulting from obstruction of urine outflow is a post-renal problem that requires relief of the blockage (e.g., catheterization, stent placement, stone or prostate surgery). These diagnostic and interventional procedures fall under the scope of the urology specialty, which manages structural disorders of the urinary tract.

331319.long_answer: Familial renal amyloidosis belongs to the group of hereditary systemic amyloidoses caused by mutations in circulating plasma proteins (e.g., fibrinogen Aα-chain, apolipoprotein A-I). These disorders are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, meaning a single mutant allele inherited from one affected parent is sufficient to cause disease.

330628.long_answer: Blepharophimosis syndrome (blepharophimosis–ptosis–epicanthus inversus syndrome, BPES) is usually caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the FOXL2 gene. These mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, showing high penetrance but variable expressivity in affected families.

725412.long_answer: In vitamin B₁₂–dependent metabolism, methylmalonyl-CoA is converted to succinyl-CoA. When B₁₂ is lacking, this reaction slows and methylmalonic acid accumulates in blood and urine. Therefore, elevated methylmalonic acid is a sensitive and fairly specific biochemical marker of vitamin B₁₂ deficiency, often rising before overt hematologic or neurologic signs appear.

894114.long_answer: After a myocardial infarction, the body rapidly mobilises a large reservoir of monocytes stored in the spleen. These splenic monocytes are released into the bloodstream, migrate to the injured myocardium, and differentiate into macrophages and dendritic cells that clear necrotic debris, modulate inflammation, and facilitate tissue repair. This spleen-derived monocyte contribution is a well-established mechanism in post-infarct cardiac healing.

921376.long_answer: Gray matter heterotopia is a malformation in which islands or nodules of cortical gray matter are ectopically located within the cerebral white matter. It is frequently reported on MRI in patients who have optic nerve hypoplasia and other midline brain developmental anomalies.

653448.long_answer: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors block the formation of angiotensin II, the principal stimulant of aldosterone secretion by the adrenal zona glomerulosa. Reduced angiotensin II levels lead to markedly decreased aldosterone synthesis, so chronic ACE-inhibitor therapy can produce drug-induced hypoaldosteronism, often evidenced by hyperkalaemia and a mild metabolic acidosis.

383169.long_answer: Both aminolevulinic acid dehydratase deficiency porphyria and tyrosinemia type I involve functional inhibition of the enzyme aminolevulinic acid dehydratase (ALAD, also called porphobilinogen synthase). In ALAD-deficiency porphyria the enzyme is genetically deficient, while in tyrosinemia type I the metabolite succinylacetone—accumulated because of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase deficiency—directly inhibits ALAD. Thus ALAD inhibition is the biochemical feature common to both disorders.

642291.long_answer: Current evidence indicates that in-utero (vertical) transmission of SARS-CoV-2 can occur, although it appears to be uncommon. Several well-documented case reports and cohort studies have shown: (1) detection of SARS-CoV-2 RNA or infectious virus in placental tissue, amniotic fluid, umbilical-cord blood, and neonatal nasopharyngeal swabs obtained immediately after birth; (2) histopathologic placental findings consistent with viral infection; and (3) neonates with SARS-CoV-2-specific IgM antibodies, which cannot cross the placenta and therefore imply fetal synthesis after intra-uterine exposure. Large systematic reviews from the World Health Organization, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and peer-reviewed meta-analyses conclude that while the absolute risk is low (generally <5% of pregnancies in infected mothers), true intra-uterine transmission is biologically plausible and has been confirmed. Thus, the established consensus is that vertical transmission is possible but rare.

936250.long_answer: Autoimmune-mediated congenital heart block arises when maternal anti-Ro/SSA or anti-La/SSB antibodies injure the fetal atrioventricular node. The only drug shown to cross the placenta in therapeutic concentrations and used in attempts to halt or reverse early (first- or second-degree) block is the fluorinated glucocorticoid dexamethasone (typically 4 mg orally per day to the mother). Because dexamethasone is not extensively metabolized by placental 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, it reaches the fetus, dampening the antibody-induced inflammatory response and fibrosis. Hence, dexamethasone is the steroid drug employed in management of autoimmune congenital heart block.

500048.long_answer: The Pediatric Crohn’s Disease Activity Index (PCDAI) includes the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) as a laboratory parameter. ESR is a widely used blood test that rises with systemic inflammation, and its value is incorporated into the PCDAI scoring system to quantify inflammatory activity in children with Crohn’s disease.

829751.long_answer: In mitral valve prolapse, global left-ventricular systolic function is typically maintained; therefore the ejection fraction is usually normal (or even slightly elevated) despite the valvular abnormality.

366875.long_answer: Folliculitis decalvans is classified as a neutrophilic scarring alopecia; biopsy typically shows a dense perifollicular infiltrate of polymorphonuclear leukocytes. This neutrophil-dominated innate immune response drives the pustular inflammation and follicular destruction characteristic of the disease.

794759.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in COL4A1, the gene encoding the α1-chain of type IV collagen, weaken vascular basement membranes. Prenatal or perinatal cerebral hemorrhages caused by this defect often heal as cystic cavities, producing congenital or familial porencephaly. Affected newborns classically present with neurological deficits that include generalized hypotonia, linking a COL4A1 mutation to the combined findings of porencephaly and hypotonia.

483394.long_answer: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia involves structural under-development of the cerebellum and brainstem; high-resolution brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is the preferred modality because it provides superior soft-tissue contrast and detailed visualization of posterior fossa structures compared with CT or ultrasound, enabling accurate assessment of cerebellar and pontine hypoplasia.

265039.long_answer: Ogilvie syndrome (acute colonic pseudo-obstruction) is thought to arise from an imbalance in autonomic control of the colon. Loss or inhibition of sacral parasympathetic outflow—or relative sympathetic over-activity—diminishes colonic peristalsis, leading to massive dilatation in the absence of a mechanical obstruction. Thus, dysfunction of the autonomic nervous system is central to the regulation of colonic motor activity in this condition.

408399.long_answer: Donnai–Barrow syndrome (also called facio-oculo-acoustico-renal syndrome) is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by diaphragmatic hernia, ocular anomalies, sensorineural hearing loss, developmental delay, and low-molecular-weight proteinuria. Multiple genetic studies, including the original linkage and positional-cloning work in 2007, have shown that biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the LRP2 gene, which encodes the multi-ligand endocytic receptor megalin, are the causal defect. Subsequent case reports and functional analyses have confirmed that pathogenic variants in LRP2 disrupt megalin’s role in renal and developmental pathways, producing the Donnai-Barrow phenotype. Therefore, LRP2 is directly and conclusively associated with Donnai–Barrow syndrome.

838516.long_answer: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration is an autoimmune paraneoplastic neurological syndrome in which antibodies generated against a systemic tumor (e.g., ovarian, breast, lung cancers) cross-react with neuronal antigens, leading to selective loss of Purkinje cells and other neurons within the cerebellum. The resulting cerebellar inflammation and neuronal death cause the hallmark subacute cerebellar ataxia, confirming that the cerebellum is the principal region of the nervous system affected.

549218.long_answer: Global Burden of Disease studies consistently show that malaria accounts for by far the greatest number of disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) lost among all parasitic diseases—tens of millions annually—owing to its high incidence, severe morbidity and substantial mortality, particularly in young children in sub-Saharan Africa.

144374.long_answer: In acromesomelic dysplasia of the Hunter-Thompson type, radiographs characteristically show marked brachydactyly with absent or severely hypoplastic middle (second) phalanges of the fingers and toes. This hypoplasia of the second phalanges distinguishes the Hunter-Thompson variety from other acromesomelic dysplasia subtypes such as the Maroteaux or Grebe types.

541308.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the OXCT1 gene, which encodes mitochondrial succinyl-CoA:3-ketoacid CoA transferase (SCOT), block the first step of ketone-body degradation. When SCOT activity is absent or markedly reduced, tissues cannot convert acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA, so acetoacetate accumulates in the bloodstream and is excreted in the urine, producing persistent ketonemia and ketonuria with markedly elevated acetoacetate levels.

857899.long_answer: Adenosquamous carcinoma is an uncommon variant of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Large clinicopathologic series and the WHO tumor classification agree that it represents only about 1 – 4 % of all exocrine pancreatic cancers.

162908.long_answer: Pigeon toe (in-toeing) in children is an orthopedic alignment issue of the lower limbs or feet. Evaluation and management—ranging from physical examination and gait analysis to corrective casting, bracing, or surgery when necessary—are performed by pediatric orthopedic specialists, the branch of orthopedics focused on musculoskeletal disorders in children.

714298.long_answer: Synechia refers to adhesions within the eye—most commonly between the iris and either the lens (posterior synechia) or the cornea (anterior synechia). Evaluation, medical management (e.g., mydriatics, anti-inflammatory therapy), and surgical correction when necessary all fall under the expertise of an ophthalmologist. Therefore, the medical specialty that treats ocular synechiae is ophthalmology.

190745.long_answer: In the diagnostic work-up of a patient who presents with psychotic symptoms, clinicians routinely perform a panel of blood tests precisely to rule out or confirm medical conditions that can mimic or trigger psychosis. Standard investigations include complete blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate levels, inflammatory markers, serology for infections such as HIV or syphilis, and sometimes autoimmune or paraneoplastic antibody panels. Abnormalities in any of these tests can reveal metabolic disturbances, endocrine disorders, nutritional deficiencies, infections, or systemic autoimmune processes that may be responsible for the psychotic presentation.
