When results are normal, many of these potential organic causes are effectively excluded, guiding the clinician toward a primary psychiatric disorder. Therefore, blood investigations are an established and evidence-based means of excluding numerous potential medical causes of psychosis.

746551.long_answer: Constriction ring syndrome—also called amniotic band syndrome—occurs in utero when fibrous amniotic bands encircle parts of the fetus, producing constriction rings, limb deformities, or amputations present at birth. Because these anomalies originate during fetal development, constriction ring syndrome is classified as a congenital malformation, i.e., a birth defect.

665209.long_answer: In amniotic band syndrome, rupture of the amnion releases fibrous strands that wrap around developing fetal limbs or digits. These constricting bands impede blood flow and growth, leading to deep constriction rings, distal swelling, and, in severe cases, intrauterine (congenital) amputations of the affected extremities.

295844.long_answer: The MYO7A gene, whose mutations cause Usher syndrome type 1B, is mapped to the long arm (q) of chromosome 11 at band 11q13.5. This chromosomal localization is well established through linkage and sequencing studies of affected families.

838527.long_answer: Jacobsen syndrome (11q deletion disorder) frequently involves neurodevelopmental impairments; studies show that roughly half of affected individuals meet diagnostic criteria for autism spectrum disorder (ASD), making ASD one of the most common neurological/behavioral conditions associated with this chromosomal deletion.

564639.long_answer: The Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), established in 1945, works jointly with the World Health Organization (WHO) through the FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius Commission to develop internationally harmonized food standards, guidelines, and codes of practice that protect consumer health and facilitate fair trade.

896442.long_answer: Erythroblastopenia is the hallmark of pure red cell aplasia (PRCA), a hematologic disorder in which erythroblasts are selectively absent or severely reduced in the bone marrow, leading to a marked decrease in circulating red blood cells while white blood cells and platelets remain normal. PRCA therefore presents clinically as a severe normocytic-normochromic anemia caused by failure of red cell production.

451326.long_answer: Infection of an upper-jaw tooth can spread to, and obstruct, the contiguous maxillary sinus. Obstruction prevents normal drainage and aeration, leading to inflammation of the sinus lining—clinically termed maxillary sinusitis.

469698.long_answer: Deficiency of muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase), as seen in McArdle disease, blocks the release of glucose-1-phosphate from muscle glycogen. Without this substrate, the glycolytic pathway cannot generate ATP during strenuous exercise. The resulting energy failure in skeletal muscle produces painful cramps, fatigue and muscle pain during heavy exertion.

757138.long_answer: Otodental syndrome (globodontia with ocular and auditory anomalies) has been shown to result from heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions involving the fibroblast growth factor 3 (FGF3) gene on chromosome 11q13. FGF3 is essential for proper development of both the inner ear and the dentition; its disruption therefore produces the characteristic combination of globodontia and congenital sensorineural hearing loss observed in affected individuals.

130454.long_answer: Hemoglobin’s primary role is to bind oxygen molecules in the lungs, carry them through the bloodstream, and release the oxygen to body tissues where it is needed for cellular respiration. Its iron-containing heme groups reversibly bind O₂, enabling efficient pickup in high-oxygen environments (lungs) and release in low-oxygen environments (peripheral tissues).

720424.long_answer: Nager syndrome (Nager acrofacial dysostosis) features pre-axial limb defects, most characteristically hypoplasia or complete absence of the radial bones of the forearms. This radial-ray deficiency is a core diagnostic finding and often accompanies thumb aplasia or hypoplasia.

730669.long_answer: Hearing loss related to Paget’s disease of bone results from bony overgrowth and deformity of the skull that impairs the structures of the middle and inner ear. Disorders of the ear and auditory system are managed by an otolaryngologist—also known as an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialist—who diagnoses and treats conductive or sensorineural hearing loss, including that secondary to skeletal diseases like Paget’s.

833933.long_answer: Endothelial dysfunction in pulmonary arterial hypertension reduces production of nitric oxide from L-arginine, blunting the NO–soluble guanylate cyclase–cGMP pathway. Loss of this vasodilatory, anti-proliferative signalling promotes pulmonary vasoconstriction and vascular-smooth-muscle hyperplasia, driving the development of pulmonary arterial hypertension.

151704.long_answer: Epidemiological studies have shown that mothers who smoke cigarettes during early pregnancy have a higher likelihood of giving birth to infants with limb-bud anomalies, including both pre-axial and post-axial polydactyly. Toxins in tobacco smoke can disturb key morphogen pathways (e.g., Sonic Hedgehog signaling) during limb development, and meta-analyses report a statistically significant increase (odds ratio ≈1.3–1.5) in polydactyly among newborns of smoking mothers compared with nonsmokers.

913547.long_answer: Coenzyme Q10 (ubiquinone) is frequently recommended as a dietary supplement for patients with mitochondrial diseases because it is an essential electron carrier in the mitochondrial respiratory chain. Supplementation can help bypass or lessen deficiencies in endogenous CoQ10 biosynthesis, improve electron transport efficiency, and enhance ATP production, which together may alleviate energy‐deficit symptoms characteristic of many mitochondrial disorders.

242912.long_answer: Plasmodium falciparum is a mosquito-borne protozoan parasite that can cross the placenta or infect the mother peripartum, leading to congenital or neonatal malaria. It is transmitted by Anopheles mosquitoes and is well documented as a cause of malaria in newborns.

525985.long_answer: For patients whose non-small-cell lung cancer is confined and operable, the standard primary treatment is surgical resection (typically lobectomy or pneumonectomy), because removing the tumor offers the highest likelihood of cure and superior survival compared with other modalities.

455584.long_answer: Glomus jugulare tumors are highly vascular paragangliomas that arise in the region of the jugular bulb. Because of their rich arterial supply and close proximity to the middle and inner ear structures, blood flow within the tumor transmits a rhythmic sound that patients perceive as pulsatile tinnitus.

358275.long_answer: Numerous epidemiological and interventional studies have shown that children who spend more hours outdoors have a significantly lower risk of developing or progressing in myopia (nearsightedness). Bright outdoor light is thought to stimulate retinal dopamine release, which slows axial elongation of the eyeball—the key anatomical change that causes myopia. Thus, time spent outdoors during childhood is an important environmental factor influencing this very common refractive eye disorder.

214404.long_answer: This EBV-associated extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (nasal type) commonly involves the nasal cavity and hard palate. Its angiocentric, angio-destructive growth produces extensive tissue necrosis that can manifest clinically as painful ulcerations or even perforation of the palate, a classic presentation of this lymphoma subtype.

287884.long_answer: Cornelia de Lange syndrome is a multisystem developmental disorder in which upper-limb skeletal anomalies such as radioulnar synostosis are common. Core clinical features also include marked prenatal-onset growth deficiency leading to short stature, microcephaly, progressive scoliosis, and moderate-to-severe intellectual disability. This constellation of findings matches all of the manifestations listed in the question, making Cornelia de Lange syndrome the established diagnosis.

778044.long_answer: To address the neurological manifestations of Hunter syndrome, clinical trials are delivering the enzyme idursulfase directly into the cerebrospinal fluid via intrathecal infusion. This intrathecal administration bypasses the blood–brain barrier, allowing the enzyme to reach the central nervous system and is being tested specifically to halt or slow cognitive decline in affected patients.

187184.long_answer: Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations or deletions in the X-linked GPC3 (glypican-3) gene. Disruption of GPC3 alters growth-factor signaling during embryogenesis, producing the severe over-growth and fluid accumulation that can manifest prenatally as hydrops fetalis.

824284.long_answer: In hereditary angioedema, laryngeal swelling can rapidly obstruct the upper airway. The recommended emergency measure is early endotracheal intubation to secure and protect the airway; if intubation fails, a surgical airway (e.g., cricothyrotomy or tracheostomy) is performed. Prompt airway control is lifesaving while specific therapy (C1-inhibitor concentrate, icatibant, etc.) takes effect.

856625.long_answer: Group A β-hemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis often produces tiny hemorrhagic spots—petechiae—on the soft palate. These palatal petechiae result from capillary rupture triggered by streptococcal exotoxins and are a classic, relatively specific physical-examination clue pointing toward streptococcal infection rather than viral causes.

841482.long_answer: Scotopic vision is the form of sight generated solely by rod photoreceptors. Rods are highly sensitive to low-light levels but do not convey color information; therefore scotopic vision is monochromatic. In achromatopsia, cone function is absent or severely impaired, so affected individuals rely almost entirely on rod-mediated scotopic vision for both day and night vision, leading to total color blindness and reduced visual acuity.

604592.long_answer: Game-Friedman-Paradice syndrome is one of the hereditary gingival-overgrowth syndromes; its cardinal feature is massive, benign fibrous enlargement of the gingiva (gingival fibromatosis), often beginning in childhood and unassociated with drug use or systemic disease.

235408.long_answer: Parvovirus B19’s multifunctional non-structural protein NS1 specifically recognizes and binds DNA motifs located upstream of the viral p6 promoter. Through this direct binding, NS1 acts as a transcriptional trans-activator, modulating initiation from the p6 promoter and thereby controlling early gene expression necessary for viral replication.

988973.long_answer: Alport syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in collagen IV genes (COL4A3, COL4A4, COL4A5), damages the basement membranes of the cochlea as well as the kidney glomeruli. This leads to bilateral, progressive sensorineural hearing loss rather than conductive or mixed loss, typically beginning in late childhood or adolescence.

485776.long_answer: A benign insulinoma is confined to the pancreas, whereas a metastatic (malignant) insulinoma has spread beyond the pancreas—most often to regional lymph nodes or the liver—demonstrating true metastasis and thus malignant behavior.

545555.long_answer: Behçet disease is a systemic vasculitis that characteristically produces recurrent, painful ulcers on oral and genital mucous membranes and causes ocular inflammation, including uveitis and posterior segment involvement such as chorioretinitis.

265042.long_answer: In acquired dysfibrinogenemia, abnormal fibrinogen molecules arise most often secondary to liver disease. Because the liver is the sole site of fibrinogen synthesis and post-translational modification, hepatic disorders (e.g., cirrhosis, hepatitis) can produce structurally altered fibrinogen that impairs clot formation, leading to the acquired form of dysfibrinogenemia.

738457.long_answer: Maternal overweight or obesity before or during early pregnancy is consistently associated with an elevated incidence of congenital heart defects in the offspring. Large population-based studies show a dose-response pattern: compared with normal-weight women, being overweight raises the odds of CHDs by roughly 10–30 %, and maternal obesity raises it by 30–60 % or more. Proposed mechanisms include maternal hyperglycaemia and insulin resistance, chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and impaired folate metabolism, all of which can disrupt cardiac morphogenesis during the first trimester.

579374.long_answer: Toxoplasmosis is an infectious disease produced by the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii. This unicellular organism is a pathogenic agent that infects warm-blooded animals, including humans. Therefore, toxoplasmosis is indeed caused by a pathogen.

605339.long_answer: Light chain deposition disease (LCDD) most often arises in patients who have a small B-cell/plasma-cell clone producing monoclonal light chains; the common underlying disorder is monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS). MGUS is a benign-appearing plasma cell dyscrasia that can remain stable for years but carries an annual risk of about 1% of transforming into overt multiple myeloma or another malignant plasma-cell neoplasm. Thus, MGUS is the plasma cell disorder classically linked to LCDD and recognized as a precursor state that may progress to multiple myeloma.

129009.long_answer: A widely used approach for relieving the intractable flank pain of Loin Pain Hematuria Syndrome is renal autotransplantation, in which the affected kidney is surgically removed and re-implanted in the pelvis. The procedure denervates the kidney and alters its blood supply, leading to sustained pain relief in a substantial proportion of LPHS patients when conservative analgesic therapy has failed.

834207.long_answer: Classic forms of brachydactyly (types A–E) are usually caused by heterozygous mutations in genes such as IHH, ROR2, and HOXD13. These mutations are expressed when only one copy of the altered gene is present, so the trait is passed from an affected parent to offspring with a 50 % risk each pregnancy, demonstrating an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

534055.long_answer: Primary hyperaldosteronism (also called Conn syndrome when due to an adrenal adenoma) is characterized by autonomous overproduction of the mineralocorticoid aldosterone by the adrenal cortex. While it can produce hypertension, hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis, many patients are initially asymptomatic, making it a classic example of an endocrine disorder that may go unnoticed despite excess aldosterone secretion.

632783.long_answer: Retinitis pigmentosa is characterized by progressive degeneration of rod and cone photoreceptors. The gold-standard test for detecting and monitoring this functional loss is full-field electroretinography (ERG), which records the retina’s electrical responses to flashes of light. In RP the ERG amplitudes progressively diminish and eventually become undetectable, providing an objective, sensitive measure of photoreceptor dysfunction before funduscopic changes are advanced.

945253.long_answer: PFAPA (Periodic Fever, Aphthous Stomatitis, Pharyngitis, and Cervical Adenitis) is classified among the autoinflammatory periodic fever syndromes. These disorders are routinely diagnosed and managed in pediatric rheumatology clinics, where specialists have expertise in recurrent fever disorders, immune dysregulation, and related treatment strategies such as corticosteroid bursts or tonsillectomy. Therefore, children with PFAPA are most commonly treated by pediatric rheumatologists.

293626.long_answer: Hypertelorism refers to an abnormally increased interpupillary and interorbital distance (wide-set eyes). In Apert syndrome, premature fusion of cranial sutures impairs normal skull and midfacial growth, producing midface dysplasia; the same aberrant craniofacial development frequently results in hypertelorism, making the two features commonly associated in this condition.

955957.long_answer: Mutations in the homeobox transcription factor gene MSX1 disrupt the epithelial-mesenchymal interactions needed for odontogenesis and nail formation. Pathogenic variants in MSX1 are a well-established cause of isolated hypodontia (selective tooth agenesis) and also produce the autosomal-dominant Tooth-and-Nail (Witkop) syndrome, which combines hypodontia with nail dysplasia. Thus, MSX1 is the gene common to both hypodontia and Witkop syndrome.

103150.long_answer: Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome type 1 is classically caused by loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked gene GPC3 (glypican-3). Because glypican-3 regulates Hedgehog and other morphogen signalling pathways that pattern the limbs, GPC3 mutations not only produce the overgrowth phenotype of Simpson–Golabi–Behmel syndrome but can also manifest with congenital anomalies such as postaxial polydactyly.

722918.long_answer: Mondini dysplasia is a congenital malformation of the inner ear in which the cochlea is incompletely partitioned (roughly 1.5 turns instead of the normal 2.5). Because the defect involves the cochlea and other membranous labyrinth structures, it primarily disrupts the sensory (hair-cell/neural) mechanisms of hearing, leading classically to sensorineural hearing loss. Mixed or progressive losses can occur, but the characteristic and most commonly cited form is congenital sensorineural hearing loss.

747480.long_answer: Vestibular schwannomas typically harbor loss-of-function mutations in the NF2 (neurofibromin-2/merlin) gene. NF2 loss activates the mTOR signaling pathway, and everolimus—an mTOR inhibitor—is being evaluated to suppress growth of these NF2-mutant tumors.

956755.long_answer: In severe (advanced) hepatic encephalopathy the electro-encephalogram shows marked slowing, with the background rhythm dominated by high-amplitude generalized delta-frequency activity, indicating widespread cortical dysfunction characteristic of the later stages of the disorder.

276076.long_answer: Cutaneous larva migrans occurs when infective larvae of animal hookworms—most commonly Ancylostoma braziliense and Ancylostoma caninum—penetrate human skin. These hookworm species belong to the family Ancylostomatidae, whose members are unable to complete their life-cycle in humans but can migrate within the epidermis, producing the characteristic serpiginous lesions.

341801.long_answer: Acquired hypoprothrombinemia can occur in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) when patients develop antiphospholipid-type autoantibodies (often termed lupus anticoagulant) that target prothrombin (coagulation factor II). These anti-prothrombin antibodies accelerate clearance of prothrombin, producing marked factor II deficiency and bleeding—known as the lupus-anticoagulant hypoprothrombinemia syndrome. Thus, SLE is the autoimmune disease classically linked to autoantibody-mediated acquired hypoprothrombinemia.

262730.long_answer: In kidney (renal) transplant recipients, episodes of viremia with Human herpesvirus 6 (HHV-6) often precede and promote the reactivation of latent cytomegalovirus (CMV). HHV-6 immediate-early gene products can trans-activate CMV promoters and the virus impairs CMV-specific T-cell responses, making CMV reactivation and disease more likely in these patients.

486446.long_answer: Kindler syndrome is an autosomal-recessive genodermatosis caused by loss-of-function mutations in the FERMT1 (also known as KIND1) gene, which encodes the focal-adhesion protein kindlin-1 that is essential for integrin activation and dermal-epidermal adhesion.

632214.long_answer: In the United Kingdom, Daubenton’s bat (Myotis daubentonii) has repeatedly been found infected with European Bat Lyssavirus type 2, a rabies-like virus. Surveillance and the 2002 human fatality linked to this species established it as the primary UK bat host for rabies-related lyssaviruses.

354969.long_answer: Trisomy 18, also called Edwards syndrome, is a chromosomal disorder caused by the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 18. Characteristic craniofacial findings include hypertelorism (abnormally wide‐spaced eyes), micrognathia, low-set ears, and cleft lip/palate. The additional chromosome disrupts normal embryonic development, leading to these distinctive facial anomalies along with multiple systemic malformations.

951243.long_answer: During the 1970s and 1980s, the term “nesidioblastosis” was commonly used as a synonym for congenital hyperinsulinism. Nesidioblastosis describes diffuse or focal proliferation of pancreatic β-cells (islet cell hyperplasia), leading to persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycaemia in neonates and infants. Although modern classification now prefers the umbrella term congenital hyperinsulinism, the historical term nesidioblastosis referred to the same disease process.

291650.long_answer: Individuals with 3-M syndrome can have jaw-size discrepancies and malocclusion; an orthodontist is the dental specialist who evaluates and corrects such alignment and bite problems, helping manage the syndrome’s dental manifestations.

311084.long_answer: Copper is the third most abundant essential trace metal in the human body, after iron and zinc. While small amounts are vital for the activity of enzymes such as cytochrome-c oxidase and superoxide dismutase, excess copper can accumulate in tissues, generating reactive oxygen species and leading to hepatic, neurologic, and renal toxicity (as seen in conditions like Wilson’s disease or from high-dose supplementation).

530694.long_answer: Lithium carbonate is a prototypical mood-stabilizing drug that is first-line therapy for Bipolar I disorder, preventing manic and depressive relapses. Clinical reports and small series also demonstrate that lithium markedly reduces the frequency and severity of hypersomnia episodes in Kleine–Levin syndrome, making it one of the few medications effective in both conditions.

359985.long_answer: The National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NINDS), part of the U.S. National Institutes of Health, is the federal biomedical research organization that funds and conducts studies on neurological and lysosomal storage disorders such as sialidosis.

243857.long_answer: Heterophoria (latent strabismus) is identified with tests such as the cover-uncover test, Maddox rod, and prism assessments, and its management may require prisms, vision therapy, or, rarely, surgery. All of these diagnostic procedures and treatments fall within the scope of an ophthalmologist—a medically trained eye specialist qualified to detect and manage binocular-vision disorders.

793411.long_answer: In both dogs and cats, congenital valvular dysplasia most frequently involves the atrioventricular valves—the tricuspid valve on the right side of the heart and the mitral valve on the left. Tricuspid valve dysplasia is particularly common in certain dog breeds such as Labrador Retrievers, while mitral valve dysplasia is also reported in several breeds and in cats. Dysplastic changes in these valves lead to malformed leaflets, chordae, or papillary muscles, resulting in regurgitation and characteristic murmurs detected in young animals.

837576.long_answer: Scleredema (scleredema adultorum of Buschke) classically develops after an acute upper-respiratory infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, the group A β-hemolytic streptococcus. Numerous case series document the temporal association between streptococcal pharyngitis and the abrupt onset of the woody skin induration characteristic of scleredema.

932992.long_answer: Hemochromatosis type 4B causes systemic iron overload with especially heavy deposition in the liver, leading to hepatic fibrosis, cirrhosis, and risk of hepatocellular carcinoma. Monitoring liver injury, staging fibrosis, instituting surveillance for malignancy, and coordinating iron-removal therapy are core tasks of a hepatologist, making hepatology the specialty most directly involved in managing the major complications of this disorder.

164179.long_answer: HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders are formally confirmed with standardized neuropsychological testing, which evaluates performance across multiple cognitive domains. According to the Frascati diagnostic criteria, documenting impairment on a formal neuropsychological battery (along with functional assessment) is required to establish the presence and severity of HAND, whereas imaging or routine laboratory studies are only supportive or exclusionary.

344497.long_answer: Mutations in the SQSTM1 gene, which encodes the autophagy-adaptor protein p62/sequestosome-1, are well established as a frequent cause of Paget’s disease of bone and have also been identified in familial and sporadic amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Defective p62 impairs ubiquitin-mediated protein turnover and autophagy, pathogenic mechanisms shared by both disorders, making SQSTM1 mutation a common genetic link between ALS and Paget’s disease.

272620.long_answer: Iridocorneal Endothelial (ICE) syndrome is an ocular disorder that affects the corneal endothelium, iris, and anterior chamber angle, often leading to corneal edema and secondary glaucoma. Diagnosis, monitoring, and management—including slit-lamp examination, gonioscopy, intraocular pressure control, and possible surgical intervention—fall within the expertise of ophthalmologists (particularly cornea or glaucoma subspecialists). Therefore, the medical specialty that treats ICE syndrome is Ophthalmology.

558725.long_answer: Viral pleurisy (inflammation of the pleural membranes) is most frequently associated with infection by Coxsackievirus B, an enterovirus in the Picornaviridae family. Numerous studies and clinical reviews identify Coxsackie B as the leading viral agent in cases of idiopathic or uncomplicated pleurisy, often presenting with sharp pleuritic chest pain and sometimes termed Bornholm disease or epidemic pleurodynia.

168904.long_answer: Zika virus crosses the placenta, infects and replicates preferentially in fetal cortical neural progenitor cells (radial glia/neural stem cells). Viral infection triggers cell-cycle arrest, apoptosis and reduced neurogenesis, depleting the progenitor pool needed for brain growth, which culminates in the severe reduction of cranial size characteristic of microcephaly.

189263.long_answer: In Fanconi syndrome the proximal renal tubule loses phosphate, bicarbonate and other solutes. Phosphate wasting causes defective bone mineralization; in growing children this presents as rickets (while adults develop osteomalacia). Therefore, rickets is a well-recognized and common complication of Fanconi syndrome in children.

259755.long_answer: In acromesomelic dysplasia, mutations that disrupt natriuretic-peptide signaling impair the cartilage of the epiphyseal (physeal) growth plates found at the ends of long bones. Damage to these growth plates hinders normal endochondral ossification, producing the characteristic abnormal bone growth and limb shortening seen in the disorder.

322623.long_answer: Patients with Turner syndrome (45,X karyotype) have streak, dysgenetic gonads. This gonadal dysgenesis markedly increases the risk of malignant germ-cell tumors, particularly dysgerminoma, compared with women who have normal ovaries.

332990.long_answer: A frequent ocular manifestation of Jacobsen syndrome is strabismus, a misalignment of the eyes (commonly “crossed eyes”). Clinical surveys report that roughly half of affected individuals exhibit strabismus, making it one of the most common eye-related problems associated with the 11q deletion characteristic of Jacobsen syndrome.

731662.long_answer: Activating mutations in the KCNJ11 gene, which encodes the Kir6.2 subunit of the pancreatic ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel, are a well-established cause of permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus. These same KCNJ11 mutations can also disrupt neuronal KATP channel function, leading to neurodevelopmental problems such as developmental delay, epilepsy, and the full DEND (Developmental delay, Epilepsy, and Neonatal Diabetes) syndrome, thereby increasing the risk of developmental disabilities in affected infants.

656615.long_answer: Mumps meningitis is diagnosed by detecting mumps virus (viral RNA or virus-specific IgM) in cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture, because CSF directly reflects infection and inflammation of the meninges.

788627.long_answer: Among the typical clinical manifestations of swine influenza (e.g., fever, cough, sore throat), patients frequently report malaise—a nonspecific sensation of discomfort, uneasiness, or general ‘not feeling well.’ Because malaise reflects the systemic inflammatory response that accompanies influenza infection, it is consistently listed in medical literature as a common symptom of swine-origin H1N1 and other influenza viruses.

822958.long_answer: Nonoxynol-9, the non-ionic surfactant used as the active spermicide in many contraceptive foams, gels, films and condoms, can provoke hypersensitivity reactions; contact allergy to this agent leads to vulvovaginal irritation and allergic vaginitis in susceptible women.

477897.long_answer: In Bowlby’s framework, children with an anxious-ambivalent (insecure-resistant) attachment become markedly distressed when the caregiver leaves and remain clingy, fearful, and hard to soothe even after reunion. This exaggerated, prolonged separation distress parallels the core clinical features of separation anxiety disorder, making the anxious-ambivalent attachment style the closest analogue.

620792.long_answer: The MYH7 gene encodes the β-myosin heavy chain, a principal structural protein that forms the thick filaments of the cardiac‐muscle sarcomere. Pathogenic variants in MYH7 alter sarcomeric architecture and contractility, and are a well-established cause of left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and related LVH phenotypes.

450081.long_answer: Intestinal lymphangiectasia causes leakage of intestinal lymph into the gut lumen. Because lymph is rich in lymphocytes, especially T-cell lymphocytes, their continuous loss leads to marked lymphopenia. Thus, the white blood cells lost in greatest quantity are lymphocytes.

363643.long_answer: Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune form of megaloblastic anemia in which patients produce autoantibodies against intrinsic factor (and parietal cell antigens). These antibodies block or destroy intrinsic factor, preventing vitamin B12 absorption in the ileum and leading to B12 deficiency and anemia.

675333.long_answer: Magnetic resonance imaging of the internal auditory canals with gadolinium contrast is the test of choice because its superior soft-tissue resolution and enhancement patterns can detect vestibular schwannomas as small as 2–3 mm, delineate their extent along the VIII cranial nerve and cerebellopontine angle, and avoids ionizing radiation—features that CT or other modalities cannot match.

292898.long_answer: Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome is mucopolysaccharidosis type VI, which results from a hereditary deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase B (also called N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase). Lack of this enzyme blocks degradation of dermatan sulfate and related glycosaminoglycans, leading to their accumulation in tissues. The resultant storage in soft tissues such as the tongue produces the characteristic macroglossia seen in affected individuals.

518196.long_answer: When people with a specific phobia are exposed to the feared object or situation, they commonly develop autonomic arousal that produces shortness of breath or a smothering sensation. This identical complaint—shortness of breath—is the cardinal manifestation of dyspnea, which is medically defined as the subjective experience of breathing discomfort. Therefore, shortness of breath is a shared physical symptom of both specific phobia and dyspnea.

714812.long_answer: When osteoporosis occurs in the paediatric age-group—typically in pre-pubertal or early adolescent patients—it is termed juvenile osteoporosis (often specified as juvenile idiopathic osteoporosis). This condition is characterized by low bone mass and increased fracture risk in otherwise healthy children or adolescents, distinguishing it from the post-menopausal or senile forms seen in adults.

712885.long_answer: Congenital cataracts-facial dysmorphism-neuropathy (CCFDN) syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by CTDP1 mutations. A defining triad is bilateral congenital cataracts, gradual sensorineural hearing loss, and a progressive demyelinating peripheral neuropathy; affected individuals often show facial dysmorphism and mild developmental delay as well. These features make CCFDN the prototypic genetic condition that combines congenital cataracts and progressive deafness with peripheral neuropathy.

286646.long_answer: Cortical neurons are born in the ventricular (germinal) zone lining the cerebral ventricles. In normal development they migrate radially from this periventricular region to the cortical plate. When this migration from the ventricular germinal zone is arrested or disordered, the cortex fails to form normal gyri and sulci, producing the ‘smooth brain’ appearance characteristic of lissencephaly.

700611.long_answer: Calsequestrin 2 (encoded by the CASQ2 gene) is the main calcium-binding/buffering protein inside the cardiac sarcoplasmic reticulum. Loss-of-function or missense mutations in CASQ2 disrupt SR calcium storage and release, producing adrenergically driven ventricular arrhythmias characteristic of catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT type 2). Thus the same protein links SR calcium buffering with the inherited arrhythmia syndrome.

126891.long_answer: Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa is almost always caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The recommended therapy is a prolonged course of an antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone, most commonly ciprofloxacin, which achieves high bone and cartilage penetration and is active against Pseudomonas species.

440065.long_answer: In males with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, exogenous testosterone is given in gradually increasing doses to mimic normal pubertal androgen levels. Testosterone directly stimulates the epiphyseal growth plates, triggering the pubertal growth spurt, while simultaneously enlarging the penis, scrotum, and other androgen-dependent tissues and promoting development of secondary sexual characteristics (voice deepening, muscle mass, body hair). Thus, testosterone replacement therapy both advances skeletal maturation via the epiphyseal plate and improves genital and pubertal development.

603174.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the FLG2 gene, which encodes filaggrin-2, cause the ‘ichthyotic’ form of peeling skin syndrome. Because filaggrin-2 is essential for cornified-envelope formation and stratum-corneum hydration, its absence produces generalized superficial skin peeling and pronounced xerosis (dry, scaly skin). Thus, an FLG2 defect links peeling skin syndrome with clinical dryness of the skin.

651366.long_answer: Rhizomelic dwarfism is defined by disproportionate shortening of the proximal limb segments—the humeri and femora—relative to the middle and distal segments. This pattern of limb involvement distinguishes it from mesomelic (middle‐segment) and acromelic (distal‐segment) forms of dwarfism.

535877.long_answer: In tertiary (third-stage) syphilis, chronic endarteritis of the vasa vasorum leads to syphilitic aortitis. The resulting weakening of the aortic wall predisposes patients to formation of thoracic aortic aneurysms, a hallmark cardiovascular complication of late syphilis.

679678.long_answer: In catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT), adrenergic stimulation causes intracellular Ca²⁺ overload, producing delayed afterdepolarizations (DADs). These DAD-triggered beats give rise to the characteristic arrhythmia of CPVT—bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, in which the QRS axis alternates beat-to-beat.

169299.long_answer: AIDS-related lymphoma can infiltrate and enlarge both the liver and spleen. The simultaneous abnormal enlargement of these two organs is called hepatosplenomegaly, and it is a recognized clinical sign that may accompany this lymphoma.

467010.long_answer: The retina is the light-sensitive, visual-perception layer lining the back of the eye. At the point where the optic nerve fibers converge and exit the eye—the optic disc—there are no photoreceptors, producing the physiological blind spot. Thus, the retina is the ocular structure that both enables vision and contains the blind spot created by the optic nerve’s departure.

628376.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MYH3 gene, which encodes the embryonic myosin heavy-chain, are a well-established cause of multiple forms of distal arthrogryposis (e.g., Freeman-Sheldon syndrome/DA2A and Sheldon-Hall syndrome/DA2B). These mutations disrupt sarcomeric myosin function during fetal muscle development, leading to congenital contractures of the distal joints characteristic of distal arthrogryposis.

550779.long_answer: Kabuki syndrome (Kabuki make-up syndrome) is a congenital genetic disorder whose classic skeletal findings include fifth-finger clinodactyly and characteristic cranial shape abnormalities such as trigono- or brachycephaly (‘trigonobrachycephaly’). The syndrome, usually caused by pathogenic variants in KMT2D or KDM6A, presents with distinctive facial features, post-natal growth deficiency, intellectual disability, and the skeletal anomalies noted above, making Kabuki syndrome the well-established condition that fits the described features.

631868.long_answer: Wiedemann–Rautenstrauch (neonatal-progeroid) syndrome has been traced to pathogenic variants in POLR3A, the gene encoding the largest catalytic subunit of RNA polymerase III. Patients with POLR3A mutations typically show congenital progeroid features together with relative or absolute macrocephaly, linking the same POLR3A defect to both the syndrome and the enlarged head size.

635715.long_answer: Fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) is the prototypical and most frequently encountered arterial dysplasia. It is a non-atherosclerotic, non-inflammatory disease in which abnormal growth of smooth-muscle and fibrous tissue within the arterial wall produces the classic ‘string-of-beads’ appearance, leading to arterial stenosis, aneurysm, or dissection—most commonly in the renal and carotid arteries.

925961.long_answer: Loss of genetic material from the short arm of chromosome 3 (3p-) produces 3p deletion syndrome, a contiguous-gene disorder characterized by growth retardation, distinctive facial features and, importantly, moderate to severe intellectual disability due to haplo-insufficiency of multiple genes on 3p.

453014.long_answer: Abdominal aortic aneurysms are dilatations of the abdominal aorta that carry a risk of life-threatening rupture. Definitive management requires either open surgical repair or endovascular stent-graft placement, procedures that are planned and performed by vascular surgeons. Therefore, the medical specialty most commonly responsible for treating patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm is vascular surgery.

908758.long_answer: In a documented case of Satoyoshi syndrome, circulating auto-antibodies were found against the enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD, particularly the 65-kDa isoform). Detection of anti-GAD antibodies supports an autoimmune mechanism for the muscle spasms and other features of the syndrome, paralleling their role in other neurologic autoimmune disorders such as stiff-person syndrome.

546853.long_answer: Telangiectasia refers to clusters of abnormally dilated capillaries and venules visible in the skin or mucosa. These small, superficial blood vessels can appear anywhere on the body and are frequently noted around joints such as the knee, where repetitive trauma or venous pressure favors their development. The condition is characterized by fine red or purple lines or webs (so-called “spider veins”) that are the hallmark of dilated dermal capillaries.

802573.long_answer: The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that marks key regulatory proteins—most notably securin and mitotic cyclins—for proteasomal degradation at the end of metaphase. Destruction of securin releases the protease separase, which then cleaves cohesin rings and allows sister chromatids to separate, initiating anaphase. By ensuring that securin and cyclins are removed only when all chromosomes are properly attached to the spindle, the APC/C safeguards accurate chromosome segregation and thereby prevents chromosome nondisjunction.

996646.short_answer: Quantitative urinary free sialic acid analysis
996646.long_answer: Infantile free sialic acid storage disease is confirmed by demonstrating markedly elevated levels of free (unconjugated) sialic acid in the patient’s urine. Quantitative analysis—typically performed by high-performance liquid chromatography or mass spectrometry—shows concentrations far above the normal range, establishing the diagnosis.

937537.long_answer: During maggot (larval) therapy, blow-fly larvae digest and absorb dead or decaying tissue rather than living tissue. They secrete proteolytic enzymes that liquefy the necrotic material outside their bodies and then ingest the breakdown products, a mode of heterotrophic feeding known as saprophytic (saprotrophic) nutrition. This saprophagy is what enables the maggots to debride and clean necrotic wounds.

347371.long_answer: Köhler disease is a childhood osteochondrosis characterized by avascular necrosis of the tarsal navicular bone in the foot, leading to pain and limping until re-ossification occurs.

372106.long_answer: Karyotypic analysis of placental cells obtained by chorionic villus sampling (CVS) can reveal an extra copy of chromosome 9. Because CVS is performed early in pregnancy and detects chromosomal complements in trophoblastic tissue, a finding of trisomy 9 (often mosaic) in the villi raises suspicion and therefore suggests the presence of trisomy 9 in the fetus, prompting confirmatory testing such as amniocentesis.

112314.long_answer: Pemphigus vulgaris is an autoimmune blistering disorder that shows increased prevalence among Ashkenazi Jews. The disease is characterized by IgG autoantibodies directed against the desmosomal cadherin desmoglein-3 (and often desmoglein-1), leading to loss of keratinocyte cohesion (acantholysis) and formation of flaccid mucocutaneous bullae.

174801.long_answer: Pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE) is overwhelmingly caused by pathogenic variants in the ATP-binding cassette sub-family C member 6 (ABCC6, formerly MRP6) gene on chromosome 16p13.1. More than 300 distinct ABCC6 mutations—missense, nonsense, splice-site, small insertions/deletions, and large rearrangements—have been catalogued in the literature and are indexed in PubMed reports. No other gene shows the same consistent, causal relationship with classic PXE, making ABCC6 the definitive gene whose mutations are documented for this disease in the PubMed database.

153389.long_answer: Yersinia pseudotuberculosis is a zoonotic Gram-negative bacterium that, after ingestion, invades Peyer’s patches and mesenteric lymph nodes. The resulting inflammation of these lymph nodes produces mesenteric adenitis (lymphadenitis), a well-recognized clinical syndrome in humans that can mimic acute appendicitis.

270483.long_answer: In anaplastic (undifferentiated) thyroid carcinoma the regional cervical lymph nodes are usually not enlarged or clinically involved; therefore the absence of palpable cervical lymphadenopathy is characteristic and helps distinguish it from papillary or medullary thyroid cancers, which commonly show nodal metastases.

620292.long_answer: The persistent, excessive and irrational fear of dreams is termed oneirophobia. Classified clinically as a type of specific phobia, individuals with oneirophobia experience marked anxiety or panic at the prospect of dreaming and may avoid sleep to prevent dreams, leading to distress and functional impairment.

343018.long_answer: Brachydactyly type D (short distal phalanx of the thumb) has been linked to mutations or copy-number changes in the HOXD13 gene. HOXD13, a homeobox transcription factor critical for patterning of the distal limb, is located on chromosome 2q31. Disrupted HOXD13 function alters digit morphogenesis, producing the characteristic thumb shortening seen in brachydactyly type D.

856287.long_answer: Angel-shaped phalango-epiphyseal dysplasia is an autosomal-recessive skeletal dysplasia caused by loss-of-function mutations in the XYLT1 gene, which encodes xylosyltransferase-1, the enzyme that initiates glycosaminoglycan chain formation on proteoglycans. Defective XYLT1 activity disturbs cartilage matrix synthesis, producing the characteristic angel-shaped middle phalanges and other skeletal changes seen in this disorder.

898337.long_answer: Revesz syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the TINF2 gene, a shelterin-complex component essential for telomere maintenance. The TINF2 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 14q12 on chromosome 14, making chromosome 14 the chromosomal location associated with Revesz syndrome.

603399.long_answer: In multiple myeloma, excess free κ or λ immunoglobulin light chains (Bence-Jones proteins) are filtered by the glomerulus and precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein in the distal nephron. The resulting obstructing casts and accompanying tubulointerstitial inflammation—termed light-chain (Bence-Jones) cast nephropathy—are the leading mechanism of acute and chronic kidney failure in myeloma patients.

793618.long_answer: Cousin–Walbraum–Cegarra syndrome is a very rare Mendelian disorder; pinpointing the underlying pathogenic variant in the responsible gene allows a definitive diagnosis. Whole exome sequencing, a next-generation sequencing technology that reads all protein-coding regions of the genome, can detect that causal mutation and is therefore the appropriate tool for diagnosing the syndrome by uncovering its genetic cause.

139293.long_answer: Erythema nodosum is an acute inflammatory disorder of the subcutaneous fat that presents with tender, erythematous nodules on the shins and other extensor surfaces. Because it is primarily a cutaneous manifestation, patients are most commonly evaluated and managed by dermatologists, who diagnose the condition clinically and address underlying triggers and supportive treatment.

432120.long_answer: In hereditary motor and sensory neuropathies (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease), weakness and impaired muscle control result from degeneration of the large-diameter, heavily myelinated A-alpha motor fibers (and their homologous large sensory fibers). Loss of these fast-conducting, myelinated axons disrupts efficient activation of skeletal muscle, producing the characteristic motor deficits.

311511.long_answer: Isovaleric acidemia (isovaleric aciduria) is an inborn error of leucine metabolism caused by deficiency of isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase. Accumulation of isovaleric acid and related metabolites produces the characteristic ‘sweaty-feet’ odor and precipitates acute metabolic crises with vomiting, lethargy, and metabolic acidosis.

420942.long_answer: Cutis laxa is a disorder of skin and elastic connective tissue that presents with loose, pendulous, inelastic skin folds. As a primary skin disease, its evaluation (clinical examination, skin biopsy, genetic testing) and management (symptom control, monitoring for systemic involvement, referral to other specialists when needed) are chiefly carried out within the field of dermatology.

508117.long_answer: Beals syndrome, formally called congenital contractural arachnodactyly, is produced by pathogenic variants in the FBN2 gene.  Affected individuals can develop dilation and aneurysms of the ascending aorta, similar to Marfan-type disorders, and almost all show congenital joint contractures – most characteristically camptodactyly (permanent flexion of the fingers).  Thus this single genetic condition links aortic aneurysm formation with camptodactyly.

502355.long_answer: Parkes Weber syndrome presents with cutaneous manifestations such as extensive capillary malformations (port-wine stains) and other vascular skin lesions. The medical specialist trained to diagnose and treat disorders of the skin, hair and nails—including vascular birthmarks—is a dermatologist, who therefore commonly manages the skin symptoms of this syndrome.

275162.long_answer: Orofaciodigital syndrome is an inherited disorder involving multiple congenital anomalies of the face, oral cavity, and digits. Because it results from pathogenic genetic variants and requires genetic testing for confirmation, risk assessment for relatives, and counseling, its diagnosis and ongoing management fall under the domain of the medical genetics specialty.

166670.long_answer: In familial chylomicronemia (type I hyperlipoproteinemia), massive accumulation of chylomicrons leads to triglyceride-laden macrophages sequestering in reticulo-endothelial tissues. This lipid deposition often produces splenomegaly, so the spleen can become visibly enlarged in patients with this severe hypertriglyceridemia.

997479.long_answer: Ivermectin is the first-line anthelmintic for Strongyloides stercoralis infection and is specifically recommended in patients who may become immunosuppressed—such as those with acute radiation syndrome—to prevent or treat the potentially fatal Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome. Its high efficacy and safety profile make it the drug of choice in this setting.

895337.long_answer: Azathioprine is a purine-analog immunosuppressant widely used as a steroid-sparing agent for myasthenia gravis. By inhibiting de-novo purine synthesis it suppresses T- and B-lymphocyte proliferation, improving neuromuscular transmission in MG. Long-term azathioprine therapy is well documented to raise the incidence of certain malignancies—particularly lymphomas and non-melanoma skin cancers—because its metabolites cause DNA damage and impair immune surveillance against tumor cells.

620776.long_answer: Agenesis of the corpus callosum is classified as a congenital malformation of the brain—a neurodevelopmental defect present at birth that results from abnormal formation of the corpus callosum during embryogenesis.

489862.long_answer: Miosis refers to an abnormal constriction of the pupil, an ocular sign that can impair vision and often signals eye disease or systemic neurologic issues. Evaluation and management of pupillary abnormalities, including the use of pharmacologic agents (e.g., anticholinergics) or surgical intervention if needed, are within the scope of ophthalmology—the medical specialty dedicated to diagnosing and treating disorders of the eye and its adnexa.

741086.long_answer: A computed tomography (CT) scan allows precise cross-sectional imaging of the lower-limb bones, letting clinicians calculate femoral anteversion and tibial torsion angles. These numerical torsion measurements are used to grade how severe an in-toeing (pigeon-toe) deformity is, making CT the standard imaging modality for quantifying its severity.

773118.long_answer: Zion Clark was born with caudal regression syndrome, a rare congenital disorder in which the lower (caudal) segments of the spine and associated structures fail to develop properly during early embryogenesis. This incomplete formation of the sacrum and lumbar vertebrae can lead to severe malformations of the pelvis, lower limbs, and lower organs; in Clark’s case, it resulted in the complete absence of functional legs.

794070.long_answer: The muscle that produces abduction of the fifth toe is the abductor digiti minimi. This intrinsic foot muscle is supplied by the lateral plantar nerve, a terminal branch of the tibial nerve. Consequently, the lateral plantar nerve provides the motor innervation required for abducting the fifth toe.

176009.long_answer: Deletion of chromosome 22q11.2 (DiGeorge/velocardiofacial syndrome) causes thymic hypoplasia and impaired T-cell–mediated immunity. Individuals with this immune dysfunction have a markedly elevated lifetime risk of developing schizophrenia or schizo-affective disorders, making 22q11.2 deletion syndrome the best-established genetic condition linking immune deficits to schizophrenia.

965932.long_answer: In the renal corpuscle, blood plasma is forced through the fenestrated glomerular capillaries into Bowman’s capsule by hydrostatic pressure. This process, called glomerular filtration, produces the initial filtrate that contains water and small solutes—including glucose—while excluding large proteins and cells.

290997.long_answer: A defining histologic feature of angiolipoma is the presence of fibrin microthrombi occluding many of its small capillary-sized vessels. These eosinophilic plugs consist of fibrin, the protein generated when thrombin cleaves fibrinogen, making them a unique morphologic hallmark of this tumor.

899614.long_answer: Gray matter heterotopia arises when neurons that are generated in the periventricular germinal zone fail to complete their normal migration to the cerebral cortex during fetal development. The malformation therefore specifically involves (and reflects disordered formation of) the cerebral cortex.

377120.long_answer: The Alcoholic Beverage Labeling Act of 1988 amended the Federal Alcohol Administration Act to mandate that all alcoholic beverage containers sold in the United States display a government health warning. The required label warns that consumption of alcohol during pregnancy can cause birth defects, thereby informing consumers of the risk of fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.

136445.long_answer: In Renal dysplasia-limb defects (RDL) syndrome, the elbow anomaly is a synostosis between the distal humerus and the proximal radius—termed radiohumeral fusion (humeroradial synostosis). The forearm bone that participates in this fusion is the radius.

221355.long_answer: Chronic hepatitis C infection is a recognised extra-hepatic cause of insulin resistance and new-onset type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is also one of the systemic diseases most often linked to chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), with numerous reports describing CIDP as a neurological manifestation of hepatitis C. Thus, hepatitis C both predisposes to type 2 diabetes and is associated with CIDP.

125197.long_answer: In the United States nitrous oxide is considered a drug under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. When it is supplied or promoted for human inhalation—such as for recreational ‘whippet’ use—the product becomes an unapproved, misbranded drug. The federal agency that enforces this statute and therefore regulates the distribution and use of nitrous oxide for recreational purposes is the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA); nitrous oxide is not scheduled by the DEA, so primary federal oversight falls to the FDA.

409768.long_answer: Parvovirus B19 transiently halts erythropoiesis by infecting and lysing erythroid precursor cells in the bone marrow. Because patients with sickle cell disease already have a shortened red-cell lifespan, this brief cessation of red-cell production precipitates a profound, rapid fall in hemoglobin known as an aplastic crisis, making Parvovirus B19 infection a well-recognized cause of severe anemia in these patients.

747637.long_answer: Left ventricular wall thickness is most accurately and routinely quantified with transthoracic echocardiography, an ultrasound-based imaging technique that provides real-time cross-sectional views of the heart and allows direct measurement of myocardial thickness in patients with left ventricular hypertrophy.

232465.long_answer: In the Spanish type of heart-hand syndrome the affected individuals were born to unaffected parents and several sibs were involved, often in consanguineous families. The equal sex distribution and vertical non-transmission point to a recessive mode of inheritance, so the syndrome is considered to follow an autosomal recessive pattern.

773068.long_answer: Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is classically known as Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome, named after the physicians who first characterized the triad of sparse hair, missing or cone-shaped teeth, and reduced or absent sweating that define this inherited ectodermal disorder.

185514.long_answer: Cytomegaloviruses place short upstream open reading frames in the 5′-untranslated regions of several viral mRNAs. Scanning ribosomes initiate at these uORFs during the initiation step of eukaryotic translation, which reduces or delays re-initiation at the downstream main start codon. This uORF-mediated control lets the virus modulate the efficiency and timing of translation of its proteins, thereby regulating viral gene expression during infection.

163238.long_answer: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias (such as sustained ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation) can occur. Current cardiology guidelines recommend implanting an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) in patients who develop these dangerous irregular heartbeats or are at high risk for them. The ICD continuously monitors cardiac rhythm and automatically delivers pacing or a shock to terminate the arrhythmia, thereby preventing sudden cardiac death.

457920.long_answer: Mounier-Kuhn syndrome, also called congenital tracheobronchomegaly, is a rare congenital disorder in which the trachea and main bronchi are markedly dilated due to atrophy or absence of elastic and smooth-muscle fibers in their walls. The resulting abnormally enlarged airways impair mucociliary clearance, predisposing patients to frequent, recurrent lower respiratory tract infections and bronchiectasis.

251459.long_answer: Persistent or troublesome eyelid myokymia is commonly treated with local injections of botulinum toxin type A. The toxin blocks presynaptic release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, temporarily weakening the orbicularis oculi muscle and abolishing the involuntary twitching for several months.

734698.long_answer: Beare-Stevenson cutis gyrata syndrome is an autosomal dominant FGFR2-related craniosynostosis disorder distinguished by premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) and thick, furrowed scalp skin (cutis gyrata). Reported patients frequently have associated airway anomalies, including choanal atresia or stenosis, making this syndrome the well-known genetic cause that links all three features.

776978.long_answer: The uterus arises from the paired paramesonephric, also called Müllerian, ducts during embryogenesis. These ducts fuse in the midline to form the uterine corpus, cervix, fallopian tubes, and upper vagina. Because malignant mixed Müllerian tumors originate in tissues derived from this Müllerian system, the paramesonephric ducts are the developmental source of the uterus in which such tumors can occur.

275614.long_answer: Fibromuscular dysplasia most often affects the renal arteries, producing renovascular hypertension and possible loss of renal function. Evaluation and management of these renal-artery lesions—including blood-pressure control, renal function monitoring, and decisions about angioplasty—are typically overseen by a nephrologist, the medical specialist in kidney and renovascular diseases.

572645.long_answer: Both dysexecutive syndrome, which reflects frontal-lobe executive dysfunction, and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder frequently co-occur with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Frontal-striatal circuit abnormalities that underlie executive deficits predispose individuals with either condition to the inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity that define ADHD, making it a well-documented shared comorbidity.

414931.long_answer: Color Doppler ultrasound is an ultrasonographic technique that superimposes color-coded velocity information on standard gray-scale images, allowing real-time visualization of vascularity. By detecting and mapping blood flow within and around an ovarian cyst, it helps differentiate benign from potentially malignant lesions and assess cyst perfusion.

244671.long_answer: Rothmund–Thomson syndrome type II is most commonly caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the RECQL4 helicase gene. Because RECQL4 is essential for DNA replication and repair in rapidly dividing cells, its deficiency can impair germ-cell development, and multiple RTS patients with RECQL4 mutations have been reported to develop primary gonadal failure and consequent hypogonadism. Thus, the RECQL4 mutation links both Rothmund–Thomson syndrome and hypogonadism.

505487.long_answer: Fraser syndrome (cryptophthalmos-syndactyly) is classically produced by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in genes such as FRAS1, FREM2 and GRIP1. Because two pathogenic alleles—one inherited from each carrier parent—are required for the phenotype to appear, the condition follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

412017.long_answer: The idiopathic condition known as Burning Mouth Syndrome (BMS) is defined by a chronic, persistent burning or scalding sensation of the tongue, lips, palate, or entire oral mucosa in the absence of any clinically identifiable oral lesion or systemic cause. Because no local or systemic pathology can be found to explain the pain, BMS is classified as an idiopathic (primary) or neuropathic pain disorder.

745266.long_answer: Dental fusion occurs when two adjacent tooth germs unite during development, producing a single, enlarged tooth with a deep developmental groove at the line of union. This groove tends to trap plaque and food debris, making the fused tooth significantly more susceptible to dental caries (cavities).

172125.long_answer: The disease referred to is myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which the World Health Organization has placed in the neurological chapter of the International Classification of Diseases since 1969. The cardinal, hallmark symptom that defines ME/CFS is post-exertional malaise: a characteristic worsening of fatigue, pain, cognitive dysfunction and other symptoms after even minor physical or mental exertion, often with delayed onset and prolonged recovery. This symptom is required in current diagnostic criteria and is considered pathognomonic for the condition.

723803.long_answer: Glycogen-storage disease type IV (Andersen disease) results from absence of the glycogen branching enzyme (amylo-α-1,4→α-1,6-transglucosidase). Lack of this enzyme yields very poorly branched glycogen that accumulates in the liver, skeletal muscle, and heart. The branching enzyme participates solely in glycogen synthesis and has no role in the hepatic or renal hydroxylations that activate vitamin D; therefore its deficiency is unrelated to vitamin D metabolism.

234062.long_answer: Cutaneous small-vessel vasculitis is diagnosed histologically by a pattern of leukocytoclastic vasculitis, characterized by neutrophilic infiltration of post-capillary venules with nuclear dust (leukocytoclasia), fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall, and extravasated red cells. This histologic picture is the defining finding for cutaneous small-vessel (immune-complex) vasculitis.

351641.long_answer: Pulmonic stenosis is most often a congenital narrowing of the pulmonary valve or right ventricular outflow tract. Evaluation and management—including echocardiography, catheter-based balloon valvuloplasty, and coordination of surgical repair—are performed by specialists in pediatric cardiology, the branch of cardiology dedicated to heart disorders in children.

868083.long_answer: Diseases characterized by absence or dysfunction of motile respiratory cilia, such as primary ciliary dyskinesia/Kartagener syndrome, are classically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, requiring biallelic pathogenic variants in genes encoding axonemal proteins (e.g., DNAI1, DNAH5).

752527.long_answer: Because the narrowed pulmonary valve limits right-ventricular outflow, persistence of the ductus arteriosus creates an alternative channel from the aorta into the pulmonary artery distal to the obstruction. Left-to-right flow through this patent ductus arteriosus supplies additional blood to the lungs, partially compensating for the reduced pulmonary perfusion caused by pulmonic stenosis.

791962.long_answer: Exercise-induced anaphylaxis is a well-described clinical disorder in which vigorous physical activity triggers an anaphylactic reaction. Major medical references (e.g., UpToDate, World Allergy Organization guidelines, the Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center, Orphanet) list it as a distinct condition, and these alphabetical disease indexes place it under the letter “E” because the name begins with “exercise-induced.” Therefore, it is indeed considered a disease entity that appears in lists of disorders starting with the letter “E.”

143027.long_answer: The only pharmacologic agent with regulatory approval specifically for pulmonary hypertension secondary to interstitial lung disease (PH-ILD) is inhaled treprostinil, a prostacyclin analogue shown in clinical trials (e.g., INCREASE study) to improve 6-minute walk distance and reduce NT-proBNP in adults with PH-ILD.

468883.long_answer: A frequent neurological manifestation of tetrasomy 18p is recurrent epileptic seizures. Clinical reviews of individuals with the isochromosome 18p consistently report epilepsy as one of the most common nervous-system symptoms, reflecting the chromosomal imbalance’s impact on brain excitability and development.

238471.long_answer: Distal arthrogryposis is most often produced by heterozygous missense mutations in genes that encode skeletal-muscle contractile proteins (e.g., MYH3, TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2). These single–nucleotide substitutions change a critical amino-acid residue, disrupting sarcomere function and leading to the characteristic distal joint contractures.

697053.long_answer: Bordetella pertussis is the Gram-negative coccobacillus classically responsible for whooping cough (pertussis). In addition to producing the characteristic paroxysmal cough, B. pertussis can invade the lower respiratory tract, leading to bronchopneumonia or lobar bacterial pneumonia, particularly in infants and unvaccinated individuals.

532689.long_answer: High-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) provides detailed cross-sectional images of lung parenchyma, allowing detection and serial comparison of nodules, reticulation, and fibrotic changes characteristic of pneumoconiosis. Because it is more sensitive than standard chest radiography, HRCT is routinely used to track disease progression over time.

194167.long_answer: Mutations in the L1CAM gene cause the X-linked form of hereditary spastic paraplegia designated SPG1. The same gene is responsible for several other X-linked neurodevelopmental syndromes collectively termed the L1-syndrome spectrum, which includes MASA syndrome, X-linked hydrocephalus, and agenesis of the corpus callosum. Thus, L1CAM is the gene shared between hereditary spastic paraplegia and multiple other X-linked disorders.

590765.long_answer: During withdrawal from chronic cannabis use (Cannabis use disorder), patients commonly experience marked irritability, anger or aggression together with vivid, unpleasant dreams and nightmares. These features are part of the DSM-5 diagnostic criteria for cannabis withdrawal, distinguishing it from withdrawal syndromes of other substances.

217455.long_answer: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted approval for tamoxifen to be used as a chemopreventive agent to lower the incidence of breast cancer in women at elevated risk, a category that explicitly includes carriers of BRCA2 pathogenic mutations. This approval is based on large clinical trials (e.g., NSABP P-1) demonstrating that tamoxifen’s selective estrogen-receptor modulation can cut breast-cancer risk by roughly 40–50 % in these high-risk populations.

359423.long_answer: The Safe-in-Sound Excellence in Hearing Loss Prevention Award, created by NIOSH and partner organizations, honors companies and institutions that have implemented exemplary programs to prevent noise-induced hearing loss—one of the leading causes of acquired hearing impairment.

963318.long_answer: Paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration most classically accompanies ovarian carcinoma. Auto-antibodies such as anti-Yo (PCA-1) generated against the tumor cross-react with Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, leading to rapid-onset ataxia and cerebellar dysfunction despite the cancer often being clinically silent.

500560.long_answer: In the manga and anime series “One Week Friends,” the heroine Kaori Fujimiya exhibits classic anterograde amnesia: each Monday her brain fails to consolidate new episodic memories of friends made the previous week, while older long-term memories and procedural knowledge remain intact. This inability to form and retain new personal memories after a specific point is the hallmark of anterograde amnesia.

850437.long_answer: Cushing syndrome is the clinical state produced by chronically elevated cortisol levels. Excess glucocorticoids promote abnormal redistribution of adipose tissue—central obesity with thinning of limb and gluteal fat—often described as centripetal lipodystrophy. Thus, the cortisol-driven Cushing syndrome can manifest both hypercortisolism and lipodystrophy.

762201.long_answer: Hydrolethalus syndrome (also called Salonen-Herva syndrome) is an autosomal-recessive, perinatally lethal disorder whose cardinal findings include marked intra-uterine growth delay, severe hydrocephaly, and pulmonary (lung) hypoplasia, together with craniofacial anomalies and post-axial polydactyly. The combination of growth retardation, massive hydrocephalus and under-developed lungs is characteristic and diagnostic for this syndrome.

235359.long_answer: X-linked myotubular myopathy is caused by pathogenic variants in the MTM1 gene on the X chromosome. Females are typically asymptomatic carriers because random X-chromosome inactivation leaves enough cells expressing the normal allele. If X-inactivation is markedly skewed so that the X chromosome bearing the normal MTM1 allele is preferentially silenced, most cells express the mutant allele, leading a heterozygous female to manifest the full disease phenotype.

633222.long_answer: Acral peeling skin syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TGM5 gene, which encodes epidermal transglutaminase-5. Defective TG-5 impairs cross-linking of structural proteins in the cornified envelope, making the stratum corneum fragile and leading to characteristic peeling of acral (palms and soles) skin.

997726.long_answer: Glucagonoma often occurs as part of the Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 syndrome. This syndrome results from germ-line loss-of-function mutations in the MEN1 gene on chromosome 11q13, which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein menin. Individuals carrying MEN1 mutations have a substantially increased risk of developing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, including glucagonoma.

737786.long_answer: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction in which antibodies target postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors. The reduced number of functional receptors causes transmission failure that becomes more pronounced with repeated stimulation, so patients develop fatigable muscle weakness that appears or worsens after exercise and improves with rest.

459022.long_answer: The medical term for inward-turning eyes is “esotropia,” derived from the Greek prefix “eso-,” meaning “within” or “inward,” and the Greek noun “tropē/-tropia,” meaning “turn” or “turning.” Thus, the word literally denotes an inward turn of the eye.

315531.long_answer: Phenobarbital is a long-acting barbiturate (elimination half-life ≈ 2–5 days) routinely used in detoxification protocols for barbiturate dependence. Its prolonged action provides stable plasma levels, allowing clinicians to substitute it for the shorter-acting abused barbiturate and then taper the dose gradually, thereby preventing withdrawal seizures and other abstinence symptoms.

227952.long_answer: Waldmann disease (primary intestinal lymphangiectasia) is characterized by marked dilatation of the intestinal lymphatic vessels, most prominently in the mucosa and submucosa of the jejunum, leading to protein-losing enteropathy.

136446.long_answer: Epidemiological studies of candidemia and invasive candidiasis consistently show that Candida albicans accounts for the largest proportion of bloodstream and deep-seated systemic Candida infections worldwide. Although non-albicans species such as C. glabrata, C. parapsilosis, and C. tropicalis have increased in certain settings, C. albicans remains the predominant pathogen in most patient populations and is therefore considered responsible for the majority of systemic Candida infections.

158114.long_answer: Deafness-vitiligo-achalasia syndrome is produced by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations (e.g., in the neural-crest transcription factor SOX10). Because a single mutant allele is sufficient to cause the phenotype, the condition is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion, although penetrance can be variable.

542584.long_answer: Andersen’s Disease (glycogen storage disease type IV) is caused by autosomal-recessive mutations in the GBE1 gene, which encodes the glycogen-branching enzyme. Deficiency of this enzyme leads to accumulation of abnormally structured glycogen in hepatocytes, driving progressive hepatic fibrosis and culminating in cirrhosis.

230484.long_answer: Anal atresia (imperforate anus/anorectal malformation) is a defining component of VACTERL association and is also one element of the Currarino triad, making it the birth defect most characteristically shared by both conditions.

382207.long_answer: Kerion is a severe inflammatory form of tinea capitis that arises when a dermatophyte (fungal) infection invades the hair follicle, provoking a marked immune response with boggy swelling, pustules, and crusting.

256900.long_answer: Stickler syndrome commonly causes sensorineural hearing loss because the collagen defects affect structures of the middle and inner ear. Assessment of the degree of loss, ongoing monitoring, and fitting of hearing aids are best handled by an audiologist—a clinician specialized in diagnosing and managing hearing problems.

420343.long_answer: In the Gell-Coombs classification, type III hypersensitivity reactions are driven by immune complexes—aggregates of antigen bound to IgG or IgM antibodies—that deposit in tissues or vessel walls. Complement activation and recruitment of neutrophils at these sites produce inflammation and tissue damage, exemplified by serum sickness, Arthus reaction, and some forms of vasculitis.

294106.long_answer: Tarsal tunnel syndrome often worsens when excessive foot pronation or fallen arches increase pressure on the posterior tibial nerve. Custom orthotic shoe inserts (foot orthoses) support the medial arch, correct abnormal biomechanics, and redistribute plantar pressures, thereby reducing nerve compression within the tarsal tunnel and relieving pain and paresthesias.

118287.long_answer: Cat eye syndrome is produced by a partial trisomy/tetrasomy of the proximal 22q11 region created by a supernumerary marker chromosome. Within this duplicated segment lies the gene CECR2 (Cat-Eye-Syndrome Chromosome Region, candidate 2) on chromosome 22q11.21. Because CECR2 dosage is increased in the marker chromosome and its disruption in animal models reproduces key CES features such as ocular coloboma, it is considered the principal gene associated with Cat eye syndrome.

691979.long_answer: Chronic Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia often results from mutations in the TWNK gene, which encodes the Twinkle mitochondrial DNA helicase. Twinkle is a key component of the mitochondrial replisome, unwinding mtDNA strands so that polymerase γ can synthesize new DNA. Pathogenic TWNK mutations impair mtDNA replication and maintenance, leading to multiple mtDNA deletions that characterize CPEO.

316277.long_answer: Fibrin is the insoluble protein that forms the meshwork of a blood clot. It is generated when the enzyme thrombin cleaves circulating fibrinogen into fibrin monomers that polymerise into strands. In Haemophilia B, deficiency of clotting factor IX disrupts the cascade that normally produces thrombin, so adequate fibrin cannot be produced. Restoring the cascade (e.g., with factor IX concentrates) is aimed at enabling thrombin-mediated conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin, making fibrin the critical end product for effective clotting in these patients.

433884.long_answer: In achondroplasia, defective endochondral bone growth narrows the skull base, especially the foramen magnum. This stenosis can compress the cervicomedullary junction, leading to brain-stem dysfunction, central apnea and even sudden death, making it one of the most serious complications in affected children.

780606.long_answer: People with spina bifida are frequently exposed to latex-containing medical devices from infancy (e.g., during repeated surgeries and catheterizations), predisposing them to IgE-mediated sensitization. Consequently, they carry a markedly increased risk of intra-operative latex allergy, which can manifest as severe anaphylactic reactions during surgery.

746066.long_answer: Influenza A virus belongs to the Orthomyxoviridae family and contains eight separate segments of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA. This segmented, antisense RNA genome must be transcribed by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase into positive-sense mRNA before host ribosomes can translate viral proteins.

639358.long_answer: In iodine-sufficient, developed countries, chronic autoimmune destruction of the thyroid—known as Hashimoto (autoimmune) thyroiditis—is the leading cause of primary hypothyroidism. Lymphocytic infiltration with anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies gradually destroys thyroid tissue, reducing hormone production and making it the most common etiology in these settings.

503498.long_answer: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy (APMPPE) can be associated with cerebral vasculitis, an inflammatory vasculopathy of the central nervous system. This vascular inflammation may compromise cerebral blood flow, leading to neurological complications such as headaches, focal neurological deficits, or ischemic strokes, making cerebral vasculitis the key neurological condition linked to APMPPE.

596649.long_answer: Russell-Silver syndrome (Silver-Russell syndrome) is a genetic growth disorder marked by prenatal and post-natal proportionate short stature. A characteristic physical sign is fifth-finger clinodactyly produced by hypoplasia of the middle phalanx. A significant number of affected children also show delayed speech and language development, distinguishing the syndrome from disproportional skeletal dysplasias. These core features establish Russell-Silver syndrome as the condition fitting the description.
