It is characterized by hypoplasia of the zygomatic (cheek) bones and mandible, and about one-third of affected individuals also have a cleft palate, making it the classic genetic condition that presents with both cheek–jaw underdevelopment and cleft palate.

584258.long_answer: Fanconi anemia is an inherited bone-marrow failure syndrome caused by mutations in the FANCA/FANCC and related genes that impair the DNA inter-strand cross-link repair pathway. The resulting genomic instability affects rapidly dividing germ-cells, producing hypogonadism, diminished spermatogenesis or premature ovarian failure, and thus a high rate of infertility in affected males and females.

900536.long_answer: Mycosis fungoides, the most common cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, is staged with the tumor–node–metastasis–blood (TNMB) classification endorsed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer and the International Society for Cutaneous Lymphomas. This system evaluates extent of skin lesions (T), lymph-node involvement (N), visceral metastasis (M) and the presence of malignant T cells in peripheral blood (B) to assign an overall stage.

709258.long_answer: Guillain–Barré syndrome is confirmed by performing electromyography with nerve conduction studies, which measure the speed and pattern of electrical impulses along peripheral nerves; the characteristic finding of slowed conduction or conduction block supports the diagnosis.

615753.long_answer: In this case, both copies of the chromosome 2 segment containing the LRP2 gene were inherited from the same parent (isodisomy), a phenomenon called uniparental disomy. This made the child homozygous for the parent’s pathogenic LRP2 mutation and produced Donnai–Barrow syndrome even though the other parent carried no mutation.

941359.long_answer: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy (digital clubbing with periostitis of long bones) occurs as a paraneoplastic syndrome in lung cancers. Among the histologic subtypes, non-small-cell tumors—particularly peripheral lung adenocarcinoma—account for the majority of cases, making adenocarcinoma the type most commonly linked to hypertrophic osteoarthropathy.

853679.long_answer: Pituitary dwarfism results from deficient secretion of growth hormone by the anterior pituitary gland—a primary endocrine disorder—leading to proportionate but markedly reduced stature.

383551.long_answer: Mutations in the CAPN3 gene, which encodes the muscle-specific calcium-dependent protease calpain-3, cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A (LGMD2A, also called calpainopathy). This autosomal-recessive muscular dystrophy is characterized by progressive weakness and wasting of the shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles and is the well-established clinical consequence of CAPN3 loss-of-function variants worldwide, including in Eurasian populations.

165635.long_answer: In the acquired form of C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency, patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) can develop IgG autoantibodies that bind to and neutralize the C1 esterase inhibitor protein. This antibody-mediated inactivation lowers functional C1-INH levels, leading to complement activation and episodes of angio-edema characteristic of acquired angio-edema associated with SLE.

793023.long_answer: High-risk types of human papillomavirus (especially HPV-16 and HPV-18) are the established causal agents of virtually all cervical cancers and are also frequently detected in HPV-positive oropharyngeal and oral squamous cell carcinomas, making the virus etiologically linked to both oral and cervical cancers.

721202.long_answer: Saito–Kuba–Tsuruta syndrome is a lethal congenital contracture/fetal akinesia sequence. Affected infants are born with severe pulmonary hypoplasia and extremely weak respiratory muscles; they are unable to establish adequate ventilation after birth. Consequently, death invariably occurs from respiratory failure within the perinatal period.

294521.long_answer: After heart-lung transplantation, the most frequent chronic rejection complication is bronchiolitis obliterans (also called bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome), in which inflammation and fibrotic scarring progressively narrow and obliterate the terminal bronchioles—the smallest airways—leading to irreversible airflow obstruction.

923674.long_answer: Lennox–Gastaut syndrome is characterized by multiple seizure types, but tonic seizures are the most prevalent, affecting the great majority of patients. These seizures typically consist of brief, generalized muscle stiffening and are especially common during periods of non-REM (slow-wave) sleep, where they may cluster or occur repetitively. Their high frequency in this sleep stage and overall predominance make tonic seizures the hallmark seizure type of Lennox–Gastaut syndrome.

862066.long_answer: Naxos syndrome—characterized by arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, palmoplantar keratoderma, and woolly hair—is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the plakoglobin gene (JUP). Plakoglobin is a desmosomal protein essential for cell-to-cell adhesion in skin and cardiac tissue; its mutation disrupts desmosomal integrity, leading to the hair shaft abnormalities (woolly hair) and associated cutaneous and cardiac manifestations typical of the syndrome.

290357.long_answer: In normal anatomy the stomach lies in the left upper quadrant, just medial to the spleen. In patients with situs ambiguus (heterotaxy), the stomach bubble is frequently displaced to an atypical side or location; this abnormal position is one of the standard imaging clues used to recognise the disorder. Therefore, malposition of the stomach is a common and easily observed indicator of situs ambiguus.

134422.long_answer: Cortical (central) achromatopsia occurs when the colour-processing centre in the ventral occipital cortex—specifically area V4 located on the lingual and posterior fusiform gyri—is damaged. Lesions of the lingual gyrus therefore abolish colour perception even though the eyes and optic nerves remain intact.

532044.long_answer: Certain atypical variants of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) are mediated by IgG4-class autoantibodies that target paranodal cell-adhesion proteins such as neurofascin-155 or contactin-1. These IgG4 autoantibodies drive the autoimmune response and underlie the distinct clinical and therapeutic features of these CIDP subtypes.

794853.long_answer: Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE) is an autoimmune form of cutaneous lupus in which lymphocyte-mediated inflammation targets the skin and hair follicles. When DLE lesions develop on the scalp they produce erythematous, inflamed plaques that destroy follicular units, leading to permanent cicatricial (scarring) alopecia. Thus, this autoimmune disease is a well-recognized cause of hair loss accompanied by scarring and marked inflammation.

510223.long_answer: Short-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (SCAD) deficiency is an autosomal recessive fatty-acid oxidation disorder produced by pathogenic variants in the ACADS gene, which encodes the mitochondrial enzyme short-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase. Mutations in ACADS impair the β-oxidation of short-chain fatty acids, leading to accumulation of butyrylcarnitine and ethylmalonic acid that characterize the clinical condition.

947559.long_answer: In chronic graft-versus-host disease, donor T-cells attack host squamous epithelium, and in the oral cavity this produces a lichenoid mucositis that clinically and histologically resembles lichen planus—white reticular or plaque-like striae with areas of atrophy and ulceration—representing the characteristic tissue damage of chronic GVHD in the mouth.

956338.long_answer: In reproductive-age women the vaginal pH is acidic (≈4.0–4.5) because estrogen supports lactobacilli that produce lactic acid. After menopause, estrogen withdrawal diminishes lactobacilli, so the environment becomes less acidic; in atrophic vaginitis the pH typically rises to about 6–7 (i.e., ≥5). This elevated pH is a characteristic finding used clinically to confirm postmenopausal atrophic change.

214057.long_answer: Aphalangy-syndactyly-microcephaly syndrome (OMIM 102510) has been described in multiple affected siblings born to phenotypically normal, often consanguineous parents. The equal occurrence in males and females and the absence of vertical transmission indicate an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

330222.long_answer: Both Hodgkin and most non-Hodgkin lymphomas typically present with painless enlargement of the cervical (often including the supraclavicular) lymph nodes, making this nodal group the one most commonly affected at initial diagnosis.

524082.long_answer: Penicillamine is a thiol-containing copper-chelating drug widely used as first-line therapy for Wilson’s disease. Case reports have documented development of the characteristic triad of yellow nails, lymphedema and pleural effusions in patients receiving penicillamine, linking the medication to yellow nail syndrome. Thus, penicillamine is both associated with yellow nail syndrome and routinely employed to treat Wilson’s disease.

192369.long_answer: Systemic lupus erythematosus shows its strongest and most reproducible genetic link to particular class II major-histocompatibility-complex alleles—specifically the HLA-DR2 (e.g., DRB1*1501) and HLA-DR3 (e.g., DRB1*0301) haplotypes. Individuals carrying these alleles have a several-fold higher risk of developing lupus, reflecting altered presentation of self-nuclear antigens to CD4⁺ T cells and consequent loss of immune tolerance. While many other loci contribute to risk, DR2 and DR3 remain the variants most commonly cited in clinical and immunology literature as being associated with lupus erythematosus.

720087.long_answer: In January 2008, researchers reported that loss-of-function mutations in the PCNT gene, which encodes the centrosomal protein pericentrin, are responsible for microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (a form of primordial dwarfism). PCNT mutations disrupt centrosome organisation and mitotic spindle assembly, leading to markedly reduced cell proliferation and the extreme intra-uterine and postnatal growth restriction characteristic of primordial dwarfism.

615568.long_answer: Fabry disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the GLA gene, which markedly reduce the activity of the lysosomal enzyme alpha-galactosidase A. Deficiency of this enzyme prevents normal degradation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3), allowing its accumulation in cardiomyocytes, vascular endothelium and conduction tissue. The resulting glycosphingolipid buildup produces left-ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmias and other cardiac complications characteristic of Fabry disease.

198896.long_answer: Lesions in the dominant (usually left) angular gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule characteristically produce Gerstmann syndrome, whose core features include agraphia (inability to write) and finger agnosia (inability to recognize or name fingers). Therefore, the angular gyrus is the brain region linked to both deficits.

800599.long_answer: Köhler disease is an osteochondrosis characterized by avascular necrosis of the tarsal navicular bone in children, leading to mid-foot pain and swelling until the bone re-vascularizes and remodels.

172973.long_answer: Persistent Müllerian duct syndrome results when anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH) signalling is lost. Autosomal-recessive mutations in either the AMH gene itself or in its type II receptor gene (AMHR2) prevent production or action of AMH produced by fetal Sertoli cells. Without functional AMH, the embryonic Müllerian ducts do not regress, so a uterus and fallopian tubes are retained in otherwise 46,XY males, producing the characteristic PMDS phenotype.

195606.long_answer: Legionella pneumophila infection presents primarily as Legionnaires' disease, an atypical form of pneumonia. Because the bacteria cause inflammatory damage to alveolar tissues, patients can develop pulmonary infiltrates that occasionally bleed, leading to hemoptysis (coughing up blood). This symptom is well documented in severe cases of Legionnaires' disease.

637086.long_answer: High plasma homocysteine is rapidly converted intracellularly to S-adenosyl-homocysteine (SAH). SAH is a potent competitive inhibitor of DNA methyltransferases; its accumulation reduces the S-adenosyl-methionine : SAH ratio, causing global DNA hypomethylation. Hypomethylation alters expression of vascular‐protective genes (e.g., eNOS) and increases pro-atherogenic, pro-inflammatory gene expression, thereby promoting endothelial dysfunction, smooth-muscle proliferation, and atherogenesis that culminate in cardiovascular disease.

649386.long_answer: Sugarman syndrome is the eponym used for the congenital disorder caused by formation of a ring chromosome derived from human chromosome 15. The ring configuration results in deletion of terminal segments of chromosome 15 and produces the characteristic clinical picture of growth retardation, craniofacial anomalies and developmental delay that define the syndrome.

213735.long_answer: Boudhina-Yedes-Khiari syndrome is a hereditary neuro-ophthalmologic disorder that has been reported exclusively in consanguineous families; linkage analyses and pedigree studies show affected individuals only when both parents are carriers, establishing an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

718938.long_answer: Chronic, long-term ingestion of excessive fluoride overwhelms normal mineral metabolism and leads to fluorosis. Depending on age and dose, this manifests as enamel hypomineralization (dental fluorosis) or progressive bone changes (skeletal fluorosis), both of which are well-documented consequences of sustained high fluoride exposure.

881063.long_answer: Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy is caused by heterozygous inactivating mutations in the GNAS gene, whose expression is regulated by parent-of-origin–specific methylation marks. Because only the maternal allele is active in key endocrine tissues, a mutation inherited from the mother produces the full phenotype with hormone resistance (pseudohypoparathyroidism Ia), whereas the same mutation from the father yields the skeletal features alone (pseudo-pseudohypoparathyroidism). This parent-of-origin effect is the classic example of genomic imprinting.

231765.long_answer: In choroideremia, loss-of-function mutations in the CHM gene lead to deficiency of Rab escort protein-1. This disrupts vesicular trafficking in retinal cells, causing gradual atrophy of the choroid, the retinal pigment epithelium, and overlying photoreceptors. The ensuing progressive degeneration of these chorioretinal tissues is the direct, primary reason patients lose night vision, peripheral vision, and eventually central vision.

669868.long_answer: Although Pneumocystis jirovecii most often causes pneumonia, in immunocompromised patients it can disseminate; the spleen is a well-recognized extrapulmonary site, where nodular or calcified lesions due to pneumocystosis are frequently documented.

275933.long_answer: Hereditary multiple exostoses (HME) is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in EXT1 or EXT2, enzymes required for heparan-sulfate biosynthesis. In a published mouse model that mimics the human condition (Ext1+/– mice), researchers demonstrated reduced brain heparan sulfate, impaired formation of excitatory synapses, and a constellation of behavioural abnormalities: diminished social interaction, lack of preference for social novelty, reduced ultrasonic vocalisations and increased stereotyped/repetitive activities. These findings were interpreted as an autism-like phenotype in the mice. On the basis of those results, the authors suggested that children who carry EXT1/EXT2 mutations and present with HME could potentially exhibit similar autism-like social difficulties. Hence, according to the cited mouse-model study, autism-like social problems may indeed be observed in children with hereditary multiple exostoses.

182976.long_answer: Leucoraja naevus, commonly called the cuckoo ray, is a skate species. Skates are grouped within the order Rajiformes, and Leucoraja is classified in the family Rajidae—the principal family that comprises most skate species.

977500.long_answer: Sclerosing mesenteritis is an uncommon disorder in which the adipose tissue of the intestinal mesentery undergoes chronic, nonspecific inflammation followed by fat necrosis and progressive fibrosis. This fibro-inflammatory process can produce a thickened, scarred mesentery visible on imaging and responsible for abdominal pain or obstructive symptoms, fitting the description of a condition that affects the mesentery with both inflammation and fibrosis.

401260.long_answer: Treacher Collins syndrome (mandibulofacial dysostosis) is a congenital craniofacial defect characterized by maldevelopment of the first and second pharyngeal arches. Typical features include hypoplastic or absent external and middle ear structures (microtia, atresia of the auditory canal), leading to conductive hearing loss and visibly incomplete development of the ear.

998668.long_answer: Treacher Collins syndrome (also called mandibulofacial dysostosis) is an autosomal-dominant genetic disorder caused most often by pathogenic variants in the TCOF1 gene (or, less commonly, POLR1D/POLR1C). The mutation disrupts neural-crest cell development derived from the first and second pharyngeal arches, leading to underdevelopment of the zygomatic complex, mandible, ears, and lower eyelids. As a result, affected individuals show striking, characteristic malformations of the head and face—including downward-slanting palpebral fissures, hypoplastic cheek and jaw bones, ear anomalies, and cleft palate—making it the prototypical genetic disorder defined by distinctive craniofacial abnormalities.

770919.long_answer: Methylmalonic acidemias are diagnosed by demonstrating excessive methylmalonic acid in body fluids. Routine metabolic screening labs use gas chromatography coupled with mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to separate urinary organic acids and detect the characteristic mass fragments of methylmalonic acid, allowing accurate quantification of the elevated metabolite.

479293.long_answer: Hypogammaglobulinemia causes a deficiency of serum immunoglobulins, leaving patients unable to opsonize and clear encapsulated bacteria such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae. These pathogens commonly infect the mucosa-lined air-containing spaces of the upper respiratory tract, especially the middle ear cavity, leading to recurrent or chronic otitis media that is classically noted in patients with antibody deficiencies.

608581.long_answer: Tuber cinereum hamartomas are hypothalamic lesions capable of autonomously producing hypothalamic releasing factors. When they secrete corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), this drives pituitary corticotrophs to release excessive adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), leading to ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism (Cushing’s disease). Thus, CRH from the hamartoma is the hormone responsible for the excessive ACTH production.

513775.long_answer: Diffuse nonepidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (the classic Unna-Thost type) is produced by heterozygous mutations in the keratin 1 (KRT1) gene. Altered KRT1 disrupts the keratin intermediate-filament network in palmoplantar epidermis, leading to hyperkeratosis without the histological epidermolysis seen with KRT9 mutations, thus giving the nonepidermolytic phenotype.

450504.long_answer: The syndromic form of chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis seen in Majeed syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LPIN2 gene, which encodes the lipid-metabolizing enzyme lipin-2. Patients with biallelic LPIN2 mutations develop the triad of CRMO, congenital dyserythropoietic anemia, and neutrophilic dermatosis, establishing LPIN2 as the gene definitively linked to this syndromic presentation.

547287.long_answer: Pentasomy X is characterized by the constitutional chromosome complement 49,XXXXX. Performing a standard cytogenetic karyotype (G-banded chromosome analysis) on peripheral blood lymphocytes allows direct visualization and counting of the five X chromosomes, thereby definitively confirming the diagnosis.

212603.long_answer: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, also known as pseudotumor cerebri, elevates intracranial pressure without a mass lesion. The raised pressure can stretch the long intracranial course of the abducens (sixth cranial) nerve along the clivus, producing a sixth nerve palsy that manifests as horizontal diplopia.

608181.long_answer: HACNS1 (Human-Accelerated Conserved Non-coding Sequence 1) is a limb-development enhancer that acquired a cluster of human-specific mutations. Experimental work shows these changes increase its activity in the embryonic forelimb, a shift proposed to have helped shape the fully opposable human thumb. Because the enhancer’s altered function depends on many coordinated nucleotide substitutions, investigators describe its structure as being as fragile and finely balanced as "a house of cards."

961412.long_answer: Hereditary mucoepithelial dysplasia is an autosomal-dominant disorder in which epithelial cells show markedly reduced intercellular adhesion. Ultrastructural studies demonstrate absent or malformed desmosomes and poorly organized tonofilaments, indicating that faulty desmosome formation is the primary cellular defect responsible for the disease’s mucosal and cutaneous manifestations.

917939.long_answer: Thin basement membrane disease (benign familial hematuria) has been linked to heterozygous mutations in the COL4A4 gene, which encodes the α4 chain of type IV collagen; such defects impair the type IV collagen network of the glomerular basement membrane, leading to its uniform thinning and persistent microscopic haematuria observed in affected families.

801827.long_answer: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) provides high-resolution cross-sectional images of the retina, allowing visualization of the small schisis cavities and microcystic changes characteristic of X-linked Juvenile Retinoschisis. It is therefore the preferred tool to detect the tiny retinal cysts produced by this disorder.

117679.long_answer: In Marcus Gunn jaw-winking phenomenon (a congenital ptosis with synkinetic eyelid elevation), the drooping lid or associated strabismus/anisometropia can block or blur visual input during early development. This sensory deprivation frequently leads to amblyopia—permanently decreased visual acuity in the affected eye—unless it is detected and treated early.

928868.long_answer: Dermatochalasis (baggy, redundant eyelid skin) is a hallmark of the autosomal-dominant gelsolin (AGel) amyloidosis known as familial amyloidosis, Finnish type (Meretoja syndrome). Mutant gelsolin deposits as amyloid in skin and other tissues, leading to characteristic cutis laxa and eyelid drooping alongside lattice corneal dystrophy and cranial neuropathy.

389523.long_answer: Elejalde syndrome (neuroectodermal melanolysosomal disorder) is caused by pathogenic mutations in the MYO5A gene, which encodes the motor protein myosin-Va responsible for intracellular melanosome transport. Loss-of-function variants in MYO5A disrupt melanin distribution and neuronal vesicle trafficking, producing the characteristic pigmentary dilution and severe neurologic manifestations of Elejalde syndrome.

114671.long_answer: Seckel syndrome, also called ‘bird-headed dwarfism,’ is classically characterized by pronounced intra-uterine and post-natal growth retardation (producing marked short stature) together with craniofacial anomalies that include a prominent beak-like nose, microcephaly, and a striking micrognathia. The coexistence of severe short stature and micrognathia makes Seckel syndrome the well-recognized disorder fitting the description.

644153.long_answer: Classic galactosemia often presents with lethargy—a marked lack of energy and decreased responsiveness—because toxic metabolites of galactose impair hepatic and cerebral energy metabolism. The same feeling of sluggishness or tiredness (lethargy) is frequently experienced by otherwise healthy individuals after too little sleep or excessive physical exertion, making it a symptom common to both situations.

750925.long_answer: Loose anagen syndrome is usually diagnosed on the basis of clinical findings (easily extractable hair in young children) combined with a hair-pull test and light-microscopic examination of the plucked anagen hairs, which show the characteristic ruffled cuticle and absent inner and outer root sheaths. A scalp biopsy is rarely required and is not considered necessary for routine diagnosis; it is reserved only for atypical cases when another hair-loss disorder must be ruled out. Therefore, a biopsy is not necessary for diagnosing loose anagen syndrome.

884746.long_answer: Fechtner syndrome is an MYH9-related disorder characterized by renal disease, sensorineural deafness, cataracts, and a hematologic finding of macro-thrombocytopenia. This blood abnormality is defined by a reduced platelet count (thrombocytopenia) often accompanied by enlarged platelets, and is a hallmark feature of the syndrome.

691845.long_answer: Aplasia cutis congenita is a recognised cutaneous sign of Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, which results from a terminal deletion of the short arm of chromosome 4 (4p-). Numerous case series document scalp ACC as part of the clinical spectrum of this 4p deletion, establishing the chromosomal loss of 4p as the deletion linked to this dermatological manifestation.

949618.long_answer: In laryngeal papillomatosis, papillomas can narrow the airway, producing dyspnea—felt by patients as shortness of breath. This symptom is not unique to the disorder; it is likewise a hallmark of other respiratory illnesses such as asthma and pneumonia, making it a common but nonspecific clinical feature.

922181.long_answer: Eczema herpeticum (Kaposi varicelliform eruption) is most frequently triggered by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1); epidemiologic studies show HSV-1 accounts for the vast majority of cases, whereas HSV-2 is a much less common cause.

154762.long_answer: Occipital horn syndrome (formerly Ehlers-Danlos type IX) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the ATP7A copper-transport gene. A hallmark of the condition is generalized cutis laxa together with characteristic skeletal abnormalities such as occipital horns, joint laxity, and bony exostoses, fitting the description in the question.

710939.long_answer: Pancreas divisum is most accurately demonstrated by imaging studies that delineate the pancreatic ductal anatomy. Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) has traditionally served as the gold-standard, directly opacifying the dorsal and ventral ducts and showing their separate drainage. Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), especially with secretin stimulation, is now widely used because it is non-invasive yet provides high-resolution images of the pancreatic ductal system and reliably depicts the failure of ductal fusion characteristic of pancreas divisum.

397700.long_answer: Howel–Evans syndrome (tylosis with oesophageal cancer) is caused by germ-line mutations in the RHBDF2 gene, which encodes the inactive rhomboid protein iRhom2. The same RHBDF2 mutations identified in affected families have been reported in individuals who also presented with congenital pulmonary stenosis, suggesting that altered iRhom2-mediated EGFR-ligand signalling can contribute to maldevelopment of the pulmonary valve in addition to producing the characteristic palmoplantar keratoderma and oesophageal cancer susceptibility seen in Howel–Evans syndrome.

876989.long_answer: The World Health Organization reported that health authorities in Equatorial Guinea confirmed an outbreak of Marburg virus disease in mid-February 2023, marking the country’s first recorded occurrence of the filovirus infection.

692974.long_answer: Mutations in the GJB6 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-30, are the classical cause of Clouston’s hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED2). The same gene is implicated in certain forms of palmoplantar keratoderma, where connexin-30 defects disturb epidermal gap-junction communication and lead to hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles.

785378.long_answer: Cushing’s syndrome results from chronic excess cortisol. An adrenocortical (adrenal cortex) adenoma that autonomously secretes cortisol can independently raise blood cortisol levels, producing the characteristic manifestations of Cushing’s syndrome.

682052.long_answer: After a spinal cord injury the descending autonomic pathways that normally modulate sympathetic outflow may be disrupted.  The result can be a chronic sympathetic over-activity in the preserved segments, producing persistently increased eccrine sweat-gland stimulation.  This leads to permanent, excessive sweating—clinically termed hyperhidrosis—in the areas whose sympathetic supply remains intact.

198776.long_answer: Shwachman–Diamond syndrome is most commonly caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the SBDS gene. SBDS (Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome gene) resides on the long arm of chromosome 7 at band q11. It encodes a protein critical for ribosome biogenesis and mitotic spindle stabilization, and its deficiency leads to the characteristic exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, bone-marrow failure, and skeletal abnormalities seen in the disorder.

155988.long_answer: Lattice corneal dystrophy type II (Meretoja syndrome) results from a gelsolin mutation that produces systemic amyloid deposition. The amyloid accumulates in cranial nerves, especially the seventh (facial) nerve, leading to a progressive bilateral facial nerve palsy, a well-recognized neurological manifestation of this corneal dystrophy.

724958.long_answer: Although the precise cause of most scoliosis cases is termed ‘idiopathic,’ multiple family and twin studies show a clear hereditary component, and several susceptibility genes (e.g., CHD7, LBX1, PAX1) have been linked to curve development. These observations support the consensus that genetic factors play a central role in the onset and progression of scoliosis.

354832.long_answer: Iridogoniodysgenesis, dominant type (anterior-segment dysgenesis with early-onset glaucoma) is caused by heterozygous mutations or dosage alterations in the FOXC1 gene on chromosome 6p25. FOXC1 encodes the forkhead box C1 transcription factor that controls neural-crest–derived tissue development in the eye; when mutated, it impairs formation of the iris stroma and trabecular meshwork, leading to the characteristic glaucoma phenotype.

263482.long_answer: Acute myeloblastic leukemia without maturation (FAB subtype M1) arises from the granulocytic (myeloid) lineage and consists almost entirely of myeloblasts with little or no maturation into neutrophils. Importantly, no monocytic component is present; monocytic white blood cells are not involved in this leukemia subtype, distinguishing it from subtypes M4 (myelomonocytic) and M5 (monocytic).

230362.long_answer: In Mary Webb’s novel ‘Precious Bane’, the protagonist Prudence (“Prue”) Sarn is born with a congenital cleft lip—referred to in the book as a ‘hare-lip’. This physical difference shapes her experiences and relationships throughout the story, making her the character specifically identified with a cleft lip.

845920.long_answer: Alopecia totalis is a severe form of alopecia areata characterized by complete loss of hair on the scalp, while body hair elsewhere is typically spared.

557376.long_answer: In Schamberg's disease, leaky dermal capillaries allow red blood cells to escape into the skin; their hemoglobin breaks down to hemosiderin, whose brown-rust pigment gives the lesions their characteristic rust-colored appearance.

215248.long_answer: Ankyloblepharon is the condition in which fibrous bands develop between the opposing lid margins, leading to partial or complete fusion of the upper and lower eyelids. These adhesions can be congenital or acquired after inflammation, trauma, or burns, and may restrict eyelid opening and normal ocular function.

794752.long_answer: Juvenile nephronophthisis, an autosomal-recessive cystic kidney disease, commonly presents with normochromic-normocytic anemia long before advanced renal failure. Reduced erythropoietin production by the damaged renal tubules leads to the blood disorder, making anemia a characteristic systemic symptom of the disease.

106665.long_answer: Jean Chrétien, who served as Canada’s 20th Prime Minister from 1993 to 2003, contracted Bell’s palsy in childhood. The acute, idiopathic paralysis of the facial nerve left him with a lifelong partial facial weakness and the characteristic asymmetrical smile that remained visible throughout his political career.

332656.long_answer: Mutations in the FBN1 gene, which encodes the extracellular matrix protein fibrillin-1, are known to cause several connective-tissue disorders. Specific pathogenic variants in FBN1 have been documented in patients with Stiff skin syndrome, characterized by rock-hard skin and joint contractures, and in the autosomal-dominant form of Weill–Marchesani syndrome, marked by short stature, brachydactyly, and ocular anomalies. Thus, FBN1 is the gene causally linked to both conditions.

575148.long_answer: In classical medical terminology, the study of disease is called “pathologia,” the Latinised form of the Greek roots pathos (suffering or disease) and-logia (study). This term underlies the modern English word “pathology,” denoting the discipline that investigates the causes, mechanisms and effects of diseases.

471427.long_answer: In gluconeogenesis, oxaloacetate is first formed from pyruvate, then it is decarboxylated and phosphorylated to yield phosphoenolpyruvate. The enzyme responsible for this decarboxylation step is phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK), which uses GTP (or ATP in some organisms) to remove CO₂ from oxaloacetate while transferring a phosphate, producing phosphoenolpyruvate.

176716.long_answer: Cushing’s disease is specifically caused by a corticotroph (ACTH-producing) pituitary adenoma. The tumor releases excess adrenocorticotropic hormone, which overstimulates the adrenal cortex to produce cortisol, leading to the clinical features of Cushing’s disease.

415997.long_answer: Vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical vocal fold motion) involves inappropriate closure of the vocal cords during inspiration, producing episodic shortness of breath, wheeze-like noises, and throat tightness. Because these attacks mimic asthma but do not improve with bronchodilators and show normal spirometry outside episodes, the condition is frequently misdiagnosed as asthma.

149269.long_answer: Persistent fatigue is one of the most frequently reported systemic symptoms in autoimmune disorders such as systemic lupus erythematosus and rheumatoid arthritis, where chronic inflammation and cytokine release impair energy metabolism. The same profound tiredness can arise in HIV/AIDS patients because opportunistic infections (e.g., cytomegalovirus, Mycobacterium avium complex) and the associated immune activation place high metabolic demands on the body, leading to marked fatigue. Therefore, fatigue is a shared, well-recognized symptom in both settings.

897250.long_answer: In children with severe spina bifida, marked spinal instability or scoliosis can develop. To stabilise and straighten the vertebral column, surgeons may perform a spinal fusion, permanently joining two or more vertebrae with bone grafts and metal rods/screws. This orthopaedic procedure reduces deformity, protects the spinal cord, and prevents further neurological compromise, making it the accepted surgical option for the most severe cases.

289281.long_answer: The corpus callosum is the principal commissural fiber bundle that physically connects the left and right cerebral hemispheres. A hallmark neuroanatomical abnormality in septo-optic dysplasia is hypoplasia or agenesis of this structure, reflecting impaired midline brain development.

786420.long_answer: Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency is an inherited fatty-acid-oxidation disorder in which the enzyme needed to break down medium-chain fatty acids is absent. Because these fats cannot be converted into acetyl-CoA for energy, they accumulate in the liver, especially during fasting or illness, leading to fatty infiltration and hepatomegaly.

700743.long_answer: In diabetic nephropathy, chronic hyperglycemia induces non-enzymatic glycation and accumulation of extracellular matrix proteins, leading to diffuse and nodular thickening specifically of the glomerular basement membrane in the renal glomerulus. This alteration impairs the filtration barrier and is a hallmark histopathologic change of the disease.

729238.long_answer: Lysosomal acid lipase deficiency (both Wolman disease and cholesterol-ester storage disease) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LIPA gene, which encodes lysosomal acid lipase. Without functional LIPA, the enzyme cannot hydrolyze cholesteryl esters and triglycerides within lysosomes, leading to their pathological accumulation in cells and tissues.

828468.long_answer: Congenital infection with human cytomegalovirus (CMV) can cross the placenta during pregnancy and disrupt fetal brain development, frequently resulting in microcephaly as well as other neurodevelopmental defects such as sensorineural hearing loss and intracranial calcifications.

800731.long_answer: Neisseria meningitidis is protected by a polysaccharide capsule. The spleen is the main site where IgM-opsonized, complement-coated encapsulated organisms are filtered and phagocytosed. Without a spleen, these opsonizing antibodies, complement activation, and splenic macrophage functions are markedly reduced, so encapsulated pathogens like N. meningitidis are not efficiently cleared, leading to a greatly increased risk of invasive infection.

530897.long_answer: Because hypochondroplasia can cause short pedicles and narrowing of the spinal canal, affected patients who develop symptomatic spinal stenosis are typically treated with a decompressive laminectomy. Removing the lamina relieves pressure on the spinal cord and nerve roots and is the standard surgical intervention for stenosis in this skeletal dysplasia.

444930.long_answer: During the late follicular phase, FSH acts on granulosa cells of the dominant follicle. This stimulation triggers transcription of the luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor (LHCGR) gene, leading to a marked increase in LH receptor numbers. The newly expressed LH receptors allow the granulosa cells to respond to the mid-cycle LH surge, an essential step for final oocyte maturation and ovulation. Hence, FSH is the hormone required for up-regulating the LH/CG receptor in preparation for ovulation.

228594.long_answer: Bevacizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody that binds vascular endothelial growth factor-A (VEGF-A), is employed as an adjuvant treatment for recurrent respiratory papillomatosis. By inhibiting VEGF-mediated angiogenesis within papillomatous lesions, intralesional or systemic bevacizumab can reduce lesion vascularity and growth, thereby decreasing the frequency of surgical debulking in patients with this HPV-driven airway disease.

607456.long_answer: Wandering spleen is usually identified first with abdominal ultrasonography, which shows absence of the spleen in its normal position and a mobile splenic mass elsewhere. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) is then used to confirm the diagnosis, delineating the ectopic spleen, its vascular pedicle, and any associated torsion or infarction.

179838.long_answer: Sorsby's fundus dystrophy is classically caused by heterozygous mutations in the TIMP3 gene, which encodes tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinases-3 on chromosome 22q12.3. These gain-of-function or misfolding mutations in TIMP3 are transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion, producing the characteristic macular degeneration seen in the disorder.

700922.long_answer: In reported cases of Cryptorchidism-arachnodactyly-intellectual disability syndrome, an orofacial cleft—most often a cleft palate—recurred alongside the core findings of undescended testes, long slender fingers, and developmental delay. Because this palatal cleft appears in multiple affected individuals, it is considered a common accompanying birth defect in the syndrome.

943610.long_answer: Women with antisocial or conduct-related traits are more likely both to smoke during pregnancy and to transmit genetic and environmental risks for conduct disorder to their children, making maternal antisocial behavior a key confounding variable in the observed association.

172606.long_answer: When blood flow is restored to an ischemic tissue, the sudden influx of oxygen and inflammatory cells generates large amounts of reactive oxygen species, calcium overload, and complement activation. These events disrupt cell membranes and mitochondria, causing uncontrolled loss of ion homeostasis and swelling—hallmarks of necrotic cell death. Thus, the tissue damage observed in reperfusion injury is chiefly mediated by necrosis (although some apoptosis can also occur).

818378.long_answer: The first documented case of Fasciola hepatica resistance to triclabendazole was reported in Australia, with Overend and Bowen’s 1995 Veterinary Record paper describing treatment failure on a Victorian sheep farm. Subsequent studies in other countries followed, but this Australian report is accepted as the earliest evidence of triclabendazole-resistant F. hepatica.

693509.long_answer: The Norwood procedure is the first stage in the surgical palliation of hypoplastic left heart syndrome and is usually carried out within the first few days of life. It reconstructs the aorta and establishes a reliable source of systemic blood flow while creating a shunt to provide pulmonary circulation, allowing the right ventricle to assume the role of the systemic ventricle until later staged operations (Glenn and Fontan) can be performed.

700974.long_answer: Idiopathic hypertryptophanemia is a rare metabolic disorder characterized by markedly elevated plasma tryptophan and neuro-developmental impairment. A distinctive feature repeatedly described in affected patients is repetitive, self-injurious poking or pressing of the eyes (the oculodigital sign). This abnormal eye-directed behavior is considered a characteristic clinical clue to the condition.

178706.long_answer: Activating missense mutations in the GNAS gene – classically involving codon 201 of the Gsα-subunit – constitute the hallmark molecular lesion in fibrous dysplasia and have likewise been detected in cherubism-type gnathic giant-cell/fibro-osseous lesions. Thus, alteration of GNAS provides the common genetic link between these two fibro-osseous disorders.

460974.long_answer: Mutations in the IGHMBP2 gene cause the neuromuscular disorder spinal muscular atrophy with respiratory distress type 1 (SMARD1). Research groups have shown that delivering a functional IGHMBP2 cDNA with adeno-associated virus (AAV9) vectors rescues motor neurons and prolongs survival in animal models, and early clinical trials are now pursuing this AAV-mediated gene replacement approach. Thus, the therapy under investigation is gene therapy aimed at restoring normal IGHMBP2 function.

232649.long_answer: Multiple sulfatase deficiency results from a lack of active sulfatase enzymes, which normally reside in lysosomes and degrade sulfated lipids and glycosaminoglycans. When lysosomal sulfatases are inactive, these substrates accumulate, so the key organelle whose dysfunction underlies the buildup of lipids and mucopolysaccharides is the lysosome.

818886.long_answer: Factor VIII replacement for Haemophilia A is delivered directly into a vein. Because the clotting protein is large and would be digested if taken orally, it must enter the bloodstream intact; therefore, both prophylactic and on-demand treatments use intravenous infusion (often through a peripheral vein or implanted venous access device) as the standard route of administration.

440497.long_answer: Isoniazid inactivates pyridoxal-5′-phosphate, the active form of vitamin B6, producing a functional vitamin B6 deficiency that manifests as sensory peripheral neuropathy. Administering pyridoxine (vitamin B6) restores pyridoxal phosphate levels and reliably prevents or alleviates the neuropathy induced by isoniazid treatment.

269690.long_answer: Children and adults with dysgraphia often struggle with writing tasks, which can lead to repeated frustration and fear of failure. Over time this stress frequently evolves into anxiety—especially school- or performance-related anxiety—making it one of the most common emotional problems observed alongside dysgraphia.

273164.long_answer: Antithrombin circulates as two glycoforms: the common α-antithrombin and the high-heparin-affinity β-antithrombin. β-Antithrombin lacks one N-glycan, giving it a 5- to 10-fold higher affinity for heparin and heparan-sulfate chains that become exposed or released at sites of tissue injury. This allows β-antithrombin to localise rapidly to the damaged vascular surface and to inactivate thrombin and factor Xa more efficiently than the α-form. Consequently, β-antithrombin is considered the principal isoform for limiting thrombogenic events that arise after tissue injury.

492403.long_answer: Glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD) is an X-linked metabolic disorder produced by mutations or deletions in the glycerol kinase (GK) gene on Xp21. Loss of GK activity blocks phosphorylation of glycerol to glycerol-3-phosphate, leading to hyperglycerolaemia, episodes of hypoglycaemia, and neuromuscular features such as neonatal or infantile hypotonia. Thus, the genetic defect in the glycerol kinase gene directly causes the hypotonia-associated disorder known as glycerol kinase deficiency.

132196.long_answer: Conditions characterized by absent or immotile cilia in the respiratory epithelium, such as primary ciliary dyskinesia (including Kartagener syndrome), are classically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern: both alleles of an associated gene (e.g., DNAI1, DNAH5) must be mutated to abolish functional cilia, and parents are typically asymptomatic carriers.

347793.long_answer: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2D is classically caused by dominant missense mutations in the GARS1 gene, which encodes glycyl-tRNA synthetase. These GARS1 mutations produce a toxic gain-of-function that preferentially injures peripheral motor and sensory axons. The resulting axonal degeneration often manifests clinically as neuropathic pain, making GARS1 mutation the established genetic cause linking CMT2D to pain symptoms.

196753.long_answer: In cats infected with Sporothrix spp., the purulent exudate that drains from cutaneous nodules and ulcers can be collected and examined cytologically. Smears of this exudative fluid typically reveal large numbers of characteristic cigar-shaped yeast cells within macrophages, making the draining lesion exudate the fluid of choice for rapid cytological diagnosis of feline sporotrichosis.

591018.long_answer: Trigger finger is most commonly diagnosed through a focused physical (clinical) examination in which the clinician palpates the flexor tendon sheath, observes catching or locking of the affected digit, and feels the characteristic tender nodule at the A1 pulley. Imaging is usually unnecessary because these clinical findings alone reliably establish the diagnosis.

931765.long_answer: Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) is an inherited retinal dystrophy that typically presents in the first months of life with nystagmus, poor pupillary responses, and markedly reduced or absent electroretinogram signals. Mutations in any of more than 20 genes (e.g., RPE65, CEP290) disrupt photoreceptor or retinal pigment epithelium function, producing severe, progressive vision loss that often culminates in childhood blindness. Because symptoms manifest in infancy and vision loss is a principal feature, LCA fits the description of a genetic disorder with infancy-onset symptoms that can lead to vision loss.

233511.long_answer: Paget’s disease of bone is most often linked to mutations in the SQSTM1 gene, which encodes the p62 protein. While SQSTM1 mutations account for a significant proportion of familial and some sporadic cases in people of European ancestry, genetic surveys show that such mutations are rare among individuals of Asian descent, making them much less common in these populations.

704793.long_answer: Carney complex is most commonly caused by inactivating germ-line mutations in the PRKAR1A gene located on chromosome 17q22-24. Loss of PRKAR1A disrupts the regulatory subunit type 1α of cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA), leading to constitutive PKA activation that drives the endocrine and cardiac myxoma manifestations characteristic of Carney complex.

136855.long_answer: Bannayan–Riley–Ruvalcaba syndrome is part of the PTEN-hamartoma tumor syndrome spectrum. Germline loss-of-function mutations in the PTEN tumor-suppressor gene on chromosome 10q23 lead to hyperactivation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, producing the characteristic features of BRRS such as macrocephaly, hamartomatous intestinal polyps, lipomas, and pigmented penile macules.

774810.long_answer: Gougerot–Blum syndrome is a pigmented purpuric dermatosis, a chronic inflammatory disorder that affects the skin. Diagnosis, management, and research of such cutaneous diseases fall under the medical specialty of dermatology, the branch of medicine devoted to conditions of the skin, hair, and nails.

177998.long_answer: In dogs, osteochondritis dissecans produces cartilage flaps and joint inflammation that, over time, progress to degenerative joint disease. This chronic degeneration of articular cartilage and underlying bone is clinically recognized as osteoarthritis, a long-term condition particularly seen in large and rapidly growing breeds affected by OCD.

445904.long_answer: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the CPS1 gene; because disease manifests only when both alleles are defective, it follows an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

458792.long_answer: Loa loa infection is routinely diagnosed by identifying its sheathed microfilariae in peripheral blood. Thick or thin blood smears stained with Giemsa allow visualization of the characteristic microfilariae with nuclei extending to the tail tip, making Giemsa staining the standard technique for laboratory confirmation of Loa loa filariasis.

839031.long_answer: Alpha-N-acetyl neuraminidase is the lysosomal sialidase that removes terminal sialic acid (N-acetyl-neuraminic acid) residues from glycoproteins and oligosaccharides. When this enzyme is deficient (sialidosis), the sialic-acid–containing oligosaccharides cannot be degraded and therefore accumulate within lysosomes of neurons and other cells.

411999.long_answer: Maternal use of cocaine—commonly smoked as crack cocaine—is a well-established risk factor for placental abruption. The potent sympathomimetic action of cocaine causes intense vasoconstriction of uterine and placental vessels, leading to placental ischemia and premature separation (abruption) of the placenta.

174323.long_answer: Bronchogenic cysts arise from abnormal budding of the ventral foregut and tracheobronchial tree during the early embryonic period, specifically between the 3rd and 7th weeks of gestation, when the respiratory diverticulum is forming.

160231.long_answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a gram-negative opportunistic pathogen that often causes hospital-acquired infections such as ventilator-associated pneumonia, bloodstream infections, and complicated urinary tract or wound infections. Management typically requires selection of appropriate anti-pseudomonal antibiotics, assessment of resistance patterns, and coordination of infection-control measures—tasks that fall within the expertise of an infectious disease specialist.

237573.long_answer: Organic acidemias cause accumulation of toxic organic acids that readily cross the blood–brain barrier, producing metabolic acidosis, hyperammonemia and energy deficiency in neural tissue. These disturbances manifest as encephalopathy, seizures and developmental delay, making the central nervous system the organ system most frequently and prominently affected.

792085.long_answer: Glycine encephalopathy – more commonly called non-ketotic hyperglycinemia (NKH) – is an autosomal-recessive defect of the glycine-cleavage system and therefore belongs to the group of inborn errors of amino-acid metabolism (aminoacidopathies). Population studies performed in the 1970s-1990s in Finland, Canada and several European countries estimated its birth prevalence at roughly 1 : 55 000-110 000. On the basis of these data it has routinely been cited, in textbooks and review articles, as the fourth most frequent congenital amino-acid disorder, ranking after phenylketonuria (PKU), maple-syrup-urine disease (MSUD) and homocystinuria. Consequently, describing “the fourth most common congenital disorder of amino-acid metabolism” as glycine encephalopathy is consistent with the established medical literature.

174094.long_answer: Congenital iodine deficiency syndrome (cretinism) often damages the developing auditory pathway and laryngeal function, leading to sensorineural deafness together with an inability to develop speech—termed deaf-mutism. This classic symptom impairs the child’s capacity to communicate without spoken words and is one of the most frequently described clinical features of the disorder.

852562.long_answer: Binswanger’s disease is a subcortical leukoencephalopathy caused by chronic small-vessel ischemic changes in the brain’s white matter. Because its pathogenesis is cerebrovascular (arteriosclerosis, hypertension), it is classified as a form of vascular dementia rather than an Alzheimer-type or other neurodegenerative dementia.

491956.long_answer: Kallmann syndrome is a congenital form of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in which failure of embryonic migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory bulbs leads to two hallmark findings: complete or severe loss of smell (anosmia) and markedly reduced or absent development of secondary sexual hair, often described clinically as alopecia. The concurrence of alopecia with anosmia is therefore characteristic of Kallmann syndrome.

142301.long_answer: A brachiocephalic arteriovenous fistula is fashioned by connecting the brachial artery to the cephalic vein at the ante-cubital fossa. The resultant arterial pressure increases flow up the cephalic vein and, via the median-cubital crossover, into the basilic venous system. Thus both the cephalic vein (proximal arm) and the basilic vein receive the augmented blood flow that characterises this fistula.

233611.long_answer: Esophoria is a latent tendency for the eyes to drift inward when fusion is disrupted. A classic ocular-muscle imbalance producing this condition is convergence excess, where the medial rectus (convergence) activity is relatively over-strong—or divergence amplitudes are insufficient—compared with the lateral rectus (divergence) system. This imbalance shifts the resting ocular alignment toward an inward position, giving rise to esophoria.

123950.long_answer: A contrast barium swallow (esophagram) can outline the esophageal lumen and mucosal irregularities; it often reveals masses, strictures, or filling defects caused by esophageal carcinoma when an upper-GI endoscope cannot pass or has missed the lesion, making it the next diagnostic step if endoscopy is unsuccessful.

213043.long_answer: Excessive sweating keeps the axillary folds warm and moist, conditions that allow Candida albicans to overgrow and produce an erythematous, macerated rash known as candidal intertrigo. Endocrine disorders that impair immunity and raise tissue glucose, such as Cushing’s syndrome, are well-recognized predisposing factors for this cutaneous Candida infection.

672713.long_answer: Propionic acidemia results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PCCA or PCCB genes encoding the two subunits of propionyl-CoA carboxylase. Because disease manifests only when both copies of the gene are defective and carriers are asymptomatic, the disorder follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

854162.long_answer: The most frequently diagnosed muscle-specific glycogen storage disease is McArdle disease (GSD type V). It results from autosomal-recessive mutations in the PYGM gene, which encodes the skeletal-muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase). Loss of PYGM activity blocks glycogen breakdown in muscle, leading to exercise intolerance, cramps, and myoglobinuria—hallmark features that make GSD V the commonest myopathic glycogen storage disorder.

343847.long_answer: I-123 (iodine-123) is a gamma-emitting radioisotope used almost exclusively for diagnostic nuclear-medicine imaging studies, particularly of the thyroid. It delivers radiation to the body and has no pharmacologic or biological action that mitigates radiation injury or removes radioactive contaminants. In cases of radiation exposure or internal contamination with radioactive iodine, the recommended countermeasure is administration of non-radioactive potassium iodide (stable iodine), which saturates the thyroid and blocks uptake of the radioactive isotope. Other decorporation agents (e.g., Prussian blue, Ca- or Zn-DTPA) are used for different radionuclides. Giving I-123 to a patient who has radiation poisoning would add additional radiation dose and provide no therapeutic benefit. Therefore, I-123 is not a useful treatment for radiation poisoning.

661421.long_answer: In the few families reported with Katz syndrome, the affected children are born to clinically normal parents, recurrence is seen among siblings, and both males and females are affected in equal numbers. The absence of vertical (parent-to-child) transmission together with sibling clustering is characteristic of an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance, indicating that two mutated copies of the responsible gene are required for the syndrome to manifest.

282727.long_answer: Blood-injection-injury phobia is typically treated with cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), which combines cognitive restructuring to correct distorted catastrophic thoughts about blood with graduated exposure and behavioral techniques (e.g., applied tension). CBT has strong empirical support for reducing fear and avoidance in specific phobias, making it the standard intervention for blood phobia.

997727.long_answer: In Alzheimer disease, progressive cortical neurodegeneration eventually involves motor-controlling cortical and subcortical networks. In this advanced (late) stage, patients often develop generalized myoclonus—brief, shock-like muscle jerks—alongside other late manifestations such as seizures. Thus, myoclonus is a recognized late-stage clinical feature of Alzheimer disease.

927687.long_answer: Research on learning disabilities shows that the persistent writing difficulties characteristic of dysgraphia often lead to repeated academic failures and negative feedback. These experiences lower individuals’ confidence in their ability to perform writing-related tasks, generalizing to broader academic and personal domains. Consequently, dysgraphia is consistently associated with diminished self-efficacy—the belief in one’s capability to organize and execute actions required for desired outcomes.

460991.long_answer: Hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) is the standard cytoreductive drug for essential thrombocythemia. It inhibits the enzyme ribonucleotide reductase, preventing conversion of ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides, thereby blocking DNA synthesis and reducing excessive platelet production.

894357.long_answer: A complete blood count (CBC) is the standard laboratory test that quantitatively measures circulating blood cells, including platelets. In Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura, the CBC reveals an isolated low platelet count, which is essential for confirming the diagnosis and excluding other cytopenias.

711193.long_answer: The International Classification of Diseases (ICD) is maintained and published by the World Health Organization (WHO). Dercum's disease (also called adiposis dolorosa) is listed in the ICD—currently under code E88.2 in ICD-10—reflecting the WHO's formal recognition of the disorder.

771949.long_answer: Choroid plexus papillomas are benign intraventricular tumors that commonly cause obstructive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. The accepted, curative treatment for symptomatic lesions is complete surgical excision (total resection), which simultaneously removes the tumor and alleviates CSF obstruction, providing long-term control without the need for adjuvant therapy.

748591.long_answer: Congenital or acquired factor VII deficiency can be treated with a prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC). PCC preparations provide not only factor VII but also the other vitamin-K-dependent clotting factors (II, IX and X), thereby correcting the deficiency while supplying additional coagulation proteins needed for haemostasis.

855797.long_answer: Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign smooth-muscle tumors of the uterus. They commonly cause menorrhagia—excessive or prolonged menstrual bleeding—which can result in anemia and disrupt the normal uterine environment. By distorting the uterine cavity or impairing endometrial receptivity, fibroids can interfere with implantation and embryo development, making them a well-recognized cause of infertility.

639902.long_answer: Lymphoma is a malignant disorder of the lymphatic and hematopoietic systems, so its evaluation and management fall under the subspecialty of Hematology (often combined with Oncology). Hematologists are trained to perform diagnostic procedures such as lymph node biopsy interpretation, staging with blood and marrow studies, and to administer systemic therapies like chemotherapy, monoclonal antibodies, and hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation for lymphoma patients.

766060.long_answer: The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) quantifies how much plasma the kidneys filter per minute and therefore directly reflects overall renal excretory capacity. As GFR declines, nitrogenous and other uremic toxins accumulate, so the level of GFR is the accepted standard for staging chronic kidney disease and gauging the severity of uremia.

193351.long_answer: Oculofaciocardiodental (OFCD) syndrome is produced by pathogenic variants in the BCOR gene. BCOR encodes the BCL-6 corepressor, a transcriptional coregulatory protein essential for normal ocular, facial, cardiac and dental development; loss-of-function mutations in BCOR underlie the characteristic anomalies seen in OFCD.

324263.long_answer: Mutations in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the α-subunit of the skeletal-muscle voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV1.4), disrupt normal sodium influx in muscle fibres. The persistent or aberrant Na+ entry forces the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (sodium-potassium pump) to work harder to re-establish ionic gradients, linking SCN4A mutations to pump-dependent membrane excitability disorders such as hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis and paramyotonia congenita.

299673.long_answer: Organic brain syndrome is classically divided into two principal clinical categories: delirium, representing an acute, fluctuating confusional state, and dementia, representing a chronic, progressive loss of cognitive functions. This acute-versus-chronic distinction underlies the standard psychiatric classification of organic mental disorders.

921363.long_answer: Homozygous or compound-heterozygous mutations in the GOSR2 gene (encoding Golgi SNAP-receptor complex member 2) are a recognized cause of progressive myoclonus epilepsy type 6. A hallmark of this disorder is the co-occurrence of cerebellar ataxia, reflecting GOSR2’s role in neuronal vesicle trafficking; loss-of-function disrupts cerebellar Purkinje cell function, producing gait and limb ataxia alongside the myoclonus and generalized seizures characteristic of progressive myoclonus epilepsy.

921664.long_answer: Mutations in the DYT1 gene cause a defect in the ATP-binding chaperone protein TorsinA. This defective TorsinA is the established cause of early-onset generalized torsion dystonia and can also present as focal dystonias such as writer’s cramp.

433799.long_answer: Enchondromatosis is characterized by the development of multiple intramedullary cartilage tumors (enchondromas) within the bones; this condition is classically known as Ollier disease. The term 'Ollier disease' is widely used in orthopedic and oncologic literature as the synonymous designation for enchondromatosis.

203965.long_answer: The spleen contains marginal-zone macrophages and IgM-producing B cells that opsonize and clear encapsulated bacteria (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae type b, Neisseria meningitidis). After splenectomy this immune function is lost, so these organisms are not efficiently removed from the bloodstream, leading to a markedly increased risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI).

918551.long_answer: Vitamin B2, also known as riboflavin, is converted to the flavin cofactors FMN and FAD that shuttle electrons in many oxidation–reduction (redox) reactions. FAD is the required cofactor for methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR); in riboflavin-responsive forms of homocystinuria, high-dose riboflavin enhances residual MTHFR activity and lowers homocysteine/homocystine levels, making riboflavin an established therapeutic vitamin for this disorder.

843304.long_answer: Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsy is a neuro‐degenerative condition characterized by lower-motor-neuron weakness and epileptic myoclonic seizures. Diagnosis, seizure control, and management of neuromuscular degeneration fall primarily under the expertise of neurologists (often pediatric or neuromuscular subspecialists), making Neurology the specialty most involved in caring for these patients.

166375.long_answer: Xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) is an autosomal-recessive disorder in which mutations in nucleotide-excision-repair genes (e.g., XPA–XPG) sharply reduce the cell’s ability to remove UV-induced thymine dimers, making patients extremely sensitive to sunlight. One well-recognized consequence of severe or repeated sunburn in the general population is malignant melanoma, a pigment-cell skin cancer whose risk rises markedly after intense intermittent UV exposure. Thus, XP is the DNA-repair defect, and melanoma is a common skin condition that can follow severe sunburn.

488968.long_answer: Deletion of all four α-globin genes (α-thalassemia major) produces severe fetal anemia. The profound anemia forces the fetal heart to pump a much larger volume of blood to maintain oxygen delivery, leading to high-output cardiac failure and generalized edema—manifesting as hydrops fetalis.

166397.long_answer: In multiple myeloma the malignant plasma cells secrete a monoclonal immunoglobulin (M-protein). When the patient’s serum is subjected to protein electrophoresis, this abnormal antibody migrates as a sharp, discrete band—an “M-spike.” Therefore, serum protein electrophoresis is the standard laboratory technique used to detect and quantify these abnormal antibody proteins and is a key component of multiple myeloma diagnosis.

626884.long_answer: In trigonocephaly the metopic (frontal) suture fuses prematurely, forcing the two halves of the frontal bone to close early. Because the frontal bone forms the anterior part of the skull—commonly called the forehead—the abnormal fusion produces the characteristic triangular-shaped front of the head. Thus, the anatomical structure occupying the front of the head in a child with trigonocephaly is the frontal bone.

319137.long_answer: Erythema nodosum is a panniculitis characterized by tender, red nodules—typically on the shins—whose occurrence is classically linked to a diverse set of conditions. It is well-documented as a hypersensitivity reaction in patients with Hodgkin’s disease (Hodgkin lymphoma) and also arises in certain infections, including typhoid fever caused by Salmonella enterica serotype Typhi. Hence, erythema nodosum is the condition associated with both Hodgkin’s disease and S. Typhi infection.

991090.long_answer: In congenital lactic acidosis, especially in disorders such as pyruvate-dehydrogenase or other mitochondrial defects, a high-fat, very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet is sometimes prescribed. By shifting energy metabolism away from glycolysis toward fatty-acid β-oxidation and ketone utilization, it decreases pyruvate accumulation and subsequent lactate formation, thereby helping to mitigate chronic lactic acidosis in some patients.

504083.long_answer: Neisseria meningitidis possesses a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane rich in lipooligosaccharide, so it does not retain the crystal-violet dye during Gram staining and instead takes up the counter-stain. This staining behavior classifies it as a Gram-negative bacterium (more specifically, a Gram-negative diplococcus).

479198.long_answer: Topical 5-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) is used to treat skin lesions in patients with Epidermodysplasia verruciformis. ALA is a pro-photosensitiser that cells convert to protoporphyrin IX; when exposed to specific light wavelengths it produces reactive oxygen species that destroy abnormal cells. The same light-activated mechanism underlies its established use in photodynamic therapy for several cancers and precancerous skin conditions.

999441.long_answer: Many patients with primary hyperparathyroidism are asymptomatic; the disorder is frequently discovered only when serum calcium is checked as part of an osteoporosis evaluation. The unexpectedly elevated calcium level (hypercalcemia) prompts further testing, leading to the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism.

922497.long_answer: When antithrombotic therapy fails or is contraindicated, placing an endovascular stent across the dissected segment of the carotid artery re-apposes the intimal flap, restores luminal patency, prevents thrombus formation and thereby lowers the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke.

651772.long_answer: Erythrokeratodermia with ataxia is a hereditary neuro-cutaneous syndrome in which progressive cerebellar ataxia (a neurologic disorder) is the principal disabling feature, while the erythrokeratodermic skin plaques are secondary manifestations. Because the core clinical problem involves cerebellar dysfunction and coordination impairment, patients are most appropriately evaluated and managed by a neurologist; dermatologic care is adjunctive.

299193.long_answer: Acute mediastinitis resulting from an esophageal perforation requires urgent operative management—primary repair of the esophageal tear, mediastinal drainage and debridement—procedures that are performed by thoracic surgeons. Consequently, the specialty of thoracic surgery is directly involved in treating this life-threatening condition.

867040.long_answer: Microdeletions in the AZF (Azoospermia Factor) region of the Y chromosome frequently remove the DAZ (Deleted in Azoospermia) gene cluster. DAZ encodes RNA-binding proteins expressed exclusively in germ cells and is essential for the development and maturation of spermatozoa; loss of DAZ disrupts spermatogenesis and is a common genetic cause of male infertility.

560352.long_answer: Tetracycline is a broad-spectrum antibiotic that has historically been used in long courses to treat Whipple’s disease. It binds to the 30S ribosomal subunit of bacteria, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA attachment and thereby inhibiting protein synthesis, which suppresses growth of Tropheryma whipplei, the causative organism.

304163.long_answer: Betulin is a triterpene that constitutes the major active component of birch bark extract. Formulated as the topical gel Oleogel-S10 (Filsuvez), betulin promotes re-epithelialisation and has been studied and used clinically as a treatment to accelerate wound healing in patients with epidermolysis bullosa.

509464.long_answer: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders are caused by maternal consumption of ethanol during pregnancy. Alcohol freely crosses the placenta and interferes with neural crest migration and ocular morphogenesis, leading to eye defects such as microphthalmia, optic nerve hypoplasia, retinal dysplasia, strabismus, and reduced visual acuity.

937738.short_answer: Posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe
937738.long_answer: Intralobar (intrapulmonary) sequestrations overwhelmingly arise in the lower lobes, and roughly two-thirds are found in the left lung. The classic and most frequent site is the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe, where an isolated portion of lung parenchyma receives systemic arterial blood rather than the normal pulmonary arterial supply.

969494.long_answer: The yolk sac tumor (also called an endodermal-sinus tumor) is a malignant germ-cell neoplasm whose cells recapitulate yolk-sac differentiation and characteristically produce and secrete alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), making elevated AFP a key diagnostic marker for this malignancy.

138133.long_answer: Schimke syndrome, also called Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia, is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the SMARCAL1 gene. Because disease manifests only when both alleles are mutated, the condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, with unaffected carrier parents each contributing one defective allele to an affected child.

212165.long_answer: May-Hegglin anomaly is a rare inherited platelet disorder characterized by thrombocytopenia, giant platelets and Döhle-like inclusions in granulocytes. Because it affects blood cell morphology and platelet number/function, diagnosis and management (e.g., bleeding risk assessment, transfusion planning, genetic counseling) fall within the expertise of a hematologist; therefore, the medical specialty involved is Hematology.

896867.long_answer: Alopecia totalis is considered an autoimmune disorder in which the immune system—especially cytotoxic T-cells—mistakenly targets and attacks hair follicle structures, leading to complete loss of scalp hair. This classification is supported by the presence of perifollicular lymphocytic infiltrates, association with other autoimmune conditions, and responsiveness to immunomodulatory therapies.

359026.long_answer: Basal-cell carcinomas commonly harbor loss-of-function mutations in the PTCH1 gene, a tumor-suppressor that encodes the Hedgehog receptor Patched-1. PTCH1 is located on chromosome 9q22.3, and its inactivation drives constitutive Hedgehog pathway signaling, promoting the development of sporadic basal-cell carcinomas as well as the nevoid basal-cell carcinoma (Gorlin) syndrome.

374362.long_answer: Children and adults with Aicardi syndrome frequently have severe oral-motor and swallowing problems that make it hard to take in enough nutrition by mouth. A surgically placed gastrostomy tube (G-tube) allows liquid nutrition to be delivered directly into the stomach, bypassing oral feeding difficulties and reducing the risk of aspiration, so it is commonly recommended for nutritional support in this condition.

947697.long_answer: Mutations in the ERCC2 gene, which encodes the XPD helicase subunit of the TFIIH complex, can cause classic xeroderma pigmentosum (XP-D) as well as the combined XP/Cockayne syndrome phenotype. Defective ERCC2 impairs nucleotide-excision repair and transcription-coupled repair, explaining its involvement in both disorders.

134714.long_answer: Kwashiorkor is a severe form of protein-energy malnutrition in children that develops when dietary protein is inadequate despite adequate caloric intake. Deficient apolipoprotein synthesis in the liver impairs export of triglycerides, producing fatty liver (hepatic steatosis) and hepatomegaly, hallmark features of the condition.

165971.long_answer: Mitochondrial neurogastrointestinal encephalopathy (MNGIE) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TYMP gene, which encodes the enzyme thymidine phosphorylase. Deficient thymidine phosphorylase activity prevents normal degradation of thymidine and deoxyuridine, leading to systemic accumulation of these nucleosides that damages mitochondrial DNA and produces the characteristic clinical features of MNGIE.

486177.long_answer: The condition described—multiple pigmented, verrucous papules on the penile shaft—corresponds to Bowenoid papulosis, which is etiologically linked to infection with high-risk types of Human papillomavirus (especially HPV-16, but also types 18, 31, and 33). HPV DNA is regularly identified in these lesions, establishing the virus as the associated pathogen.

415891.long_answer: Bethlem myopathy has no disease-modifying or curative drug; management relies on supportive symptomatic therapy—primarily physiotherapy, stretching, orthopedic interventions, and respiratory support—to preserve mobility and manage contractures and other complications.

631021.long_answer: Blue Rubber Bleb Nevus Syndrome is characterized by multiple venous malformations, most abundantly in the gastrointestinal tract. Recurrent or massive bleeding from these gut lesions leads to chronic anemia and, in severe episodes, fatal exsanguination. Consequently, uncontrolled gastrointestinal hemorrhage is the leading cause of death in affected patients.

993163.long_answer: Thrombocytopenia is a disorder characterized by abnormally low platelet counts in the blood. Assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of platelet, red-cell, and white-cell abnormalities fall under hematology—the branch of medicine that studies blood, blood-forming organs, and blood disorders.

831466.long_answer: In cor triatriatum, the abnormal fibro-muscular membrane that divides the atrium is usually perforated by one or more small openings. These openings are referred to as “fenestrations,” a term commonly used in cardiology and pathology to denote small, window-like perforations in a membrane or septum.

932371.long_answer: Staphylococcus epidermidis, a common skin commensal, binds to Toll-like receptor-2 (TLR2) on epidermal keratinocytes. This interaction triggers expression of cytokines and antimicrobial peptides such as β-defensins, thereby modulating both innate and adaptive immune responses in the skin.

203858.long_answer: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy arises when chronically high blood-glucose damages peripheral nerves; the hyperglycaemia is a direct result of inadequate or ineffective secretion of the pancreatic hormone insulin. For this reason, clinicians routinely include a serum insulin (or C-peptide) determination—alongside glucose/HbA1c—in the laboratory work-up to confirm that the neuropathy is secondary to diabetes and impaired insulin regulation.

711161.long_answer: Gaucher disease is a lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of the enzyme β-glucocerebrosidase. The accumulated substrate (glucocerebroside) leads to massive hepatosplenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia and bone crises. Standard treatment is enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant β-glucocerebrosidase (e.g., imiglucerase, velaglucerase), which reduces organomegaly and improves hematologic and skeletal manifestations.
