This chromosomal aneuploidy produces multiple congenital anomalies, one of which is micrognathia (an abnormally small mandible). The defining cytogenetic feature is complete or mosaic trisomy of chromosome 9, distinguishing it from other trisomies such as Patau (trisomy 13) or Edwards (trisomy 18).

406328.long_answer: Abciximab is a chimeric monoclonal antibody Fab fragment that binds with high affinity to the platelet glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) receptor. By occupying this receptor, it prevents fibrinogen (and von Willebrand factor) from binding, thereby blocking the final common pathway of platelet aggregation and exerting its antiplatelet effect.

477236.long_answer: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is the most prevalent leukemia among adults in Western countries. Population-based data (e.g., SEER 2012-2018) show a 5-year relative survival rate of roughly 85 %, reflecting the generally indolent nature of CLL and advances in targeted therapies.

487909.long_answer: Because there is no definitive curative therapy for Gorham-Stout (Gorham’s) disease, management focuses on controlling pain, preventing complications, and maintaining function. Therefore, treatment is primarily supportive care, with interventions such as analgesics, physical therapy, and other symptom-directed measures.

321257.long_answer: X-linked recessive chondrodysplasia punctata (CDPX1) is caused by deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase E. Coumarin-derivative anticoagulants such as warfarin are known to inhibit arylsulfatase E activity; when taken during pregnancy they can produce the same skeletal phenotype (warfarin embryopathy) characterised by stippled epiphyses and nasal hypoplasia.  Thus, warfarin is the medication that can inhibit the enzyme associated with CDPX1.

270870.long_answer: Definitive diagnosis of microvillus inclusion disease requires visualization of characteristic intracellular microvillus inclusions within enterocytes. These inclusions are only resolvable at the ultrastructural level, so a transmission electron microscope is employed to examine intestinal-biopsy specimens and confirm the presence of the diagnostic microvillus inclusions.

921716.long_answer: Acute posterior multifocal placoid pigment epitheliopathy often presents with photopsia—brief flashes of light perceived by the patient. Photopsia is likewise a classic warning sign of retinal detachment, caused by mechanical stimulation of the retina as it separates. Therefore, the overlapping symptom between these two ocular conditions is photopsia.

942613.long_answer: Transforming growth factor-β1 (TGF-β1) is consistently found in high levels within Peyronie’s disease plaques and is regarded as the principal profibrotic cytokine driving the disorder. TGF-β1 promotes fibroblast activation, extracellular matrix deposition, and collagen cross-linking, making it a central mediator of fibrosis in multiple tissues and the most prominently overexpressed cytokine in Peyronie’s disease.

994399.long_answer: The American Psychiatric Association’s revised third edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-III-R, published in 1987) was the first to list the “blood-injury-injection” subtype of simple (specific) phobia. This designation formally recognized fear of needles and injections—‘needle phobia’—as an official specific phobia.

960198.long_answer: Edwards syndrome (trisomy 18) is a rare chromosomal disorder in which affected infants typically have characteristic low-set, posteriorly rotated ears and a high incidence of congenital heart disease (e.g., ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus). These features are part of the well-described clinical constellation resulting from the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 18.

464840.long_answer: Hereditary hemochromatosis is an autosomal-recessive disorder (often due to HFE mutations) in which excessive intestinal iron absorption leads to systemic iron overload. Iron deposition in the anterior pituitary and in the gonads disrupts gonadotropin secretion and steroidogenesis, frequently resulting in secondary hypogonadism.

893341.long_answer: The microphthalmia-associated transcription factor (MITF) is normally expressed in retinal pigment epithelium cells, where it controls genes required for melanogenesis and early eye morphogenesis. Experimental loss or mutation of MITF abolishes its expression in the RPE, disrupting normal ocular development and producing markedly small eyes—i.e., microphthalmia—in both animal models and affected humans.

366087.long_answer: Within the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, the α (alpha) cells synthesize and secrete the peptide hormone glucagon, which raises blood glucose levels by promoting hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

598261.long_answer: A short postoperative course of the NSAID indomethacin (e.g., 25 mg three times daily for several weeks) is routinely recommended after total hip arthroplasty because it inhibits prostaglandin-mediated osteogenic activity, thereby markedly reducing the incidence of heterotopic ossification around the hip joint.

490633.long_answer: The classical LIS1 gene, whose official symbol is PAFAH1B1, is mapped to chromosome 17p13.3. Deletions or pathogenic variants in PAFAH1B1 (LIS1) are a well-established cause of type-1 (classical) lissencephaly and Miller-Dieker lissencephaly syndrome. No portion of this gene resides on chromosome 2; chromosome 2 harbors other loci that can cause cortical malformations (e.g., RELN on 2q24 for lissencephaly with cerebellar hypoplasia), but not LIS1. Therefore, stating that the LIS1 gene is located on chromosome 2 is incorrect.

372763.long_answer: British table-tennis player Will Bayley, who won Paralympic gold in the men’s singles Class 7 event at the 2016 Rio Games, was born with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita—a congenital condition characterized by joint contractures and muscle weakness.

935567.long_answer: Isoniazid therapy can produce peripheral neuropathy manifested as numbness, because the drug forms a complex with pyridoxal-5′-phosphate and increases urinary loss of pyridoxine. Supplementing with Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) restores pyridoxine levels, prevents or reverses the neuropathy, and is routinely co-prescribed with isoniazid for this reason.

629202.long_answer: Mutations in the TGM1 gene, which encodes epidermal transglutaminase-1, are a well-established cause of autosomal recessive congenital ichthyoses. Pathogenic TGM1 variants have been documented in patients presenting clinically as lamellar ichthyosis as well as in those with congenital (non-bullous) ichthyosiform erythroderma, linking this single gene to both disorders.

329141.long_answer: Excess thyroid hormone in hyperthyroidism stimulates osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and shortens the bone-remodeling cycle. The resulting high bone turnover leads to net loss of bone mineral density, making hyperthyroidism a well-recognized endocrine cause of secondary osteoporosis.

583607.long_answer: Classic galactosemia—caused by deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridyltransferase—leads to accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol after lactose ingestion. Toxic build-up damages the liver, kidneys and brain, producing vomiting, jaundice and, if untreated, marked failure to thrive in the newborn. Eliminating galactose/lactose from the diet prevents the growth failure and other life-threatening complications.

962198.long_answer: Karel Frederik Wenckebach described the progressive prolongation of AV nodal conduction culminating in a dropped ventricular beat—now called the Wenckebach phenomenon (also termed Mobitz type I or Luciani-Wenckebach second-degree AV block).

137167.long_answer: The Glu6Val point mutation in the β-globin chain produces hemoglobin S in red blood cells. Individuals carrying one HbS allele (sickle-cell trait) are significantly protected against severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria because the altered hemoglobin impairs parasite growth and enhances immune clearance of infected erythrocytes.

370816.long_answer: Epidemiological data show that the leading causes of traumatic spinal cord injury worldwide are motor-vehicle crashes, falls (particularly in the elderly and in construction settings), acts of violence (gunshot or stab wounds), and sports/recreational mishaps such as diving accidents. All of these mechanisms occur largely outside the body and can be significantly reduced through well-established preventive measures—seat-belt and helmet use, traffic-safety enforcement, environmental modifications to prevent falls, workplace safety regulations, firearm-injury prevention strategies, and sports safety guidelines. Because the majority of spinal cord injuries arise from these external, modifiable events rather than from unavoidable internal disease processes, the most common causes are considered preventable by public-health authorities (e.g., WHO, CDC, National Spinal Cord Injury Statistical Center).

382194.long_answer: Corticobasal degeneration is characterized pathologically and on MRI by marked, unilateral-predominant loss of gray matter in the parietal cortex (often extending to adjacent posterior frontal areas). This asymmetric parietal atrophy corresponds to the lateralized motor and cortical sensory deficits that typify the disorder.

616583.long_answer: Osteochondritis (commonly osteochondritis dissecans/osteochondrosis) disrupts normal cartilage and subchondral bone in developing joints such as the shoulder, elbow, stifle, and hock. The resulting pain, inflammation, and joint incongruity frequently manifest clinically as lameness, one of the most common orthopedic conditions observed in dogs.

266309.long_answer: Pogosta disease is caused by Sindbis virus, an alphavirus that circulates between passerine birds and mosquitoes. In Finland and other parts of northern Europe the virus is mainly transmitted to humans by mosquitoes of the genus Culex (especially Culex torrentium/Culex pipiens), making Culex mosquitoes the principal vector for Pogosta disease.

644070.long_answer: Juvenile primary lateral sclerosis is a rare upper-motor-neuron form of motor neuron disease. Diagnosis, monitoring of spasticity and weakness, and coordination of symptomatic therapies are managed by a neurologist—often one with neuromuscular or pediatric-neurology expertise—making neurology the primary medical specialty involved in its treatment.

151887.long_answer: Henoch–Schönlein purpura (IgA-mediated small-vessel vasculitis) frequently involves the kidneys; IgA immune-complex deposition in glomerular mesangium produces an IgA nephropathy–like picture that can manifest as hematuric or nephritic syndrome.

377695.long_answer: Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome) commonly presents with widened cranial sutures and a markedly large or late-closing anterior fontanelle. The extra chromosome 21 alters bone and connective-tissue development, delaying membranous ossification of the skull; this characteristic finding is routinely listed among the dysmorphic features used to clinically recognize the genetic disorder.

564848.long_answer: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome predisposes patients to recurrent bacterial, particularly Staphylococcus aureus, infections of the skin and lungs. Because no curative therapy exists, the cornerstone of management is continuous or prophylactic antibiotic therapy—most commonly agents such as trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole—to prevent and control these infections.

561941.long_answer: Spondylodiscitis denotes concurrent inflammation or infection of the vertebral bodies (spondylitis) and the adjacent intervertebral disc space (discitis). It is the accepted medical term when both structures are involved.

463737.long_answer: When hypokalemia co-exists with metabolic acidosis, the preferred supplement is potassium bicarbonate because it supplies potassium while its bicarbonate anion directly counteracts the acidotic state, helping to restore both serum potassium and systemic acid-base balance.

488981.long_answer: Patients with alkaptonuria frequently accumulate homogentisic acid in bile, which polymerizes and precipitates, leading to pigmented gallstones. Thus, the development of gallbladder stones (cholelithiasis) is a well-recognized complication of the disorder.

264748.long_answer: In allergic contact dermatitis, cutaneous lymphatic vessels carry hapten-loaded Langerhans cells/dendritic cells and soluble allergen from the epidermis to the regional (draining) lymph nodes. Within these lymph nodes the dendritic cells present processed antigen to naïve T-lymphocytes, initiating their activation, clonal expansion, and differentiation into allergen-specific effector and memory T cells. This priming step in the draining lymph nodes is essential for generating the delayed-type (type IV) hypersensitivity response that manifests clinically as allergic contact dermatitis.

370340.long_answer: Andersen-Tawil syndrome is an autosomal dominant KCNJ2 channelopathy whose clinical triad includes frequent ventricular extrasystoles and bidirectional ventricular tachycardia causing syncopal episodes, episodic muscle weakness, and characteristic dysmorphic features such as a low anterior hairline, micrognathia, and short stature. This combination of cardiac arrhythmia with a low anterior hairline makes Andersen-Tawil syndrome the established genetic disorder fitting the description.

820134.long_answer: Mal de Meleda, an autosomal-recessive palmoplantar keratoderma, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLURP1 gene (Secreted Ly6/U-PAR-related protein 1) located on chromosome 8q24.3. Pathogenic variants in SLURP1 impair epidermal homeostasis and lead to the characteristic diffuse thickening of the palms and soles observed in this disorder.

507759.long_answer: A galactocele is a closed retention cyst filled only with breast milk. Human milk inside the obstructed duct remains sterile and contains bacteriostatic factors (e.g., lactoferrin, lysozyme, secretory IgA). Because bacteria neither enter nor thrive in this medium, galactoceles very rarely become infected.

677064.long_answer: In Infantile Refsum disease defective peroxisomal biogenesis impairs lipid metabolism needed for Schwann-cell myelin formation, producing marked hypomyelination of peripheral nerves; nerve conduction studies show slow velocities and pathology reveals thin or absent myelin sheaths in the peripheral nervous system.

660335.long_answer: Patients with MPI-CDG (mannose-phosphate isomerase congenital disorder of glycosylation) frequently experience chronic diarrhea due to intestinal involvement and protein-losing enteropathy. Diarrhea leads to excessive fluid loss from the gastrointestinal tract, making it a well-recognized cause of dehydration in affected individuals.

707592.long_answer: LQT3 results from gain-of-function mutations in the cardiac sodium channel gene SCN5A, producing a persistent late Na⁺ current and prolonging repolarisation. The class IB anti-arrhythmic mexiletine selectively blocks this late sodium current, thereby shortening the QT interval and reducing arrhythmic risk. Consequently, mexiletine is the medication specifically employed to treat the LQT3 subtype of Romano–Ward syndrome.

163959.long_answer: Oral lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory, immune-mediated disorder that specifically involves the stratified squamous epithelium lining the mouth—tongue, buccal mucosa, gingiva, and other intra-oral surfaces—rather than skin or other organs.

772640.long_answer: Posterior urethral valves create an obstructing membrane in the posterior urethra of male infants. The gold-standard test is a voiding (micturating) cystourethrogram, which fills the bladder with contrast and images the urethra during voiding. This study reveals the characteristic dilated posterior urethra and valve leaflets, definitively diagnosing posterior urethral valve disorder in newborn boys.

537973.long_answer: Familial isolated vitamin E deficiency is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the TTPA gene, which encodes the α-tocopherol transfer protein. Because disease manifests only when both alleles are altered and carriers are asymptomatic, it follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.

274761.long_answer: In one reported Primrose syndrome case, cytogenetic analysis revealed an interstitial microdeletion at chromosome 3q13.3. This segment includes the ZBTB20 locus, now known to be the critical gene whose haploinsufficiency or de novo point mutation causes Primrose syndrome, thereby linking the 3q13.3 deletion with the disorder.

593297.long_answer: In primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) cortisol production is lost, removing the negative feedback on the pituitary. This drives markedly increased secretion of adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). Addison’s disease is therefore an endocrine dysfunction linked to acanthosis nigricans that is specifically characterized by elevated ACTH levels.

702485.long_answer: Alveolar capillary dysplasia with misalignment of pulmonary veins (ACDMPV) is most often caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or microdeletions involving the transcription factor gene FOXF1. The FOXF1 gene is situated at cytogenetic band 16q24.1 on human chromosome 16, so the pathogenic variants responsible for this disorder map to chromosome 16.

177572.long_answer: Mevalonate kinase deficiency manifests clinically as Hyper-IgD Syndrome. A distinguishing laboratory feature of this condition is persistently elevated serum levels of immunoglobulin D (IgD), often exceeding 100 IU/mL, making IgD elevation a characteristic biomarker for the disorder.

966023.long_answer: Selenium sulfide is routinely formulated as 1-2.5 % medicated shampoo to eradicate the fungal infection (Piedraia hortae) responsible for black piedra. Animal studies have shown that chronic exposure to selenium sulfide produces hepatocellular carcinomas in mice and rats, leading regulatory agencies (e.g., IARC, OSHA) to classify it as a potential human carcinogen. Thus, the same compound used therapeutically for black piedra carries a recognized carcinogenic hazard.

686225.long_answer: Estrogen-containing combined oral contraceptive pills markedly raise the risk of thrombo-embolic events. In people who already have migraine with aura—a condition that independently increases ischemic stroke risk—the added estrogen further elevates cerebrovascular risk. Therefore, combined oral contraceptives (those with both estrogen and progestin) are considered contraindicated in this population.

131821.long_answer: Population-based analyses of German statutory health-insurance claims data show that systemic scleroderma (systemic sclerosis) affects roughly 23–25 individuals per 100 000 residents, equivalent to about 1 case in every 4 000 people in Germany.

496449.long_answer: MacDermot-Winter syndrome is an extremely rare, X-linked intellectual-developmental disorder that has been described in only a small number of families worldwide. Fewer than a dozen affected males have been documented in the medical literature, and no population-based incidence or prevalence data exist because cases are so scarce. Consequently, it is considered an ultra-rare condition and is not common among live births.

493674.long_answer: Telangiectasia represents a persistent, focal dilation of small superficial blood vessels—most commonly the capillaries (and sometimes adjacent venules). When these capillaries become widened and tortuous, they appear as fine red ‘spider-like’ lines on skin or mucous membranes, which is the hallmark of telangiectasia.

882257.long_answer: Diffusion-tensor MRI studies have shown reduced fractional anisotropy and other diffusion changes in multiple cerebral white-matter tracts (e.g., posterior corona radiata, superior longitudinal fasciculus) in children diagnosed with sensory processing disorder, indicating that the microstructure of white matter—not gray matter—is abnormally altered in this condition.

244025.long_answer: Larsen syndrome is classified as a connective tissue disorder: mutations in the FLNB gene disrupt filamin-B, a cytoskeletal protein critical for the integrity of connective tissues, leading to joint dislocations, skeletal abnormalities, and characteristic facial features.

710865.long_answer: Loss of the mitochondrial enzyme malonyl-CoA decarboxylase (MCD) blocks conversion of malonyl-CoA to acetyl-CoA. The excess malonyl-CoA is hydrolyzed to malonic acid, producing marked malonic aciduria. Malonic acid is a potent inhibitor of succinate dehydrogenase (complex II) and, together with malonyl-CoA–mediated inhibition of carnitine palmitoyl-transferase I, interferes with β-oxidation and electron-transport activity, thereby compromising oxidative phosphorylation and cellular ATP generation.

360733.long_answer: During fasting, patients with glycogen storage disease type VI break down increased amounts of purine nucleotides, leading to hyperuricemia. The excess uric acid can crystallize in joints, producing gout—a painful inflammatory arthritis that is a recognized complication of this disorder.

969514.long_answer: Hypoparathyroidism is a well-known secondary cause of bilateral basal ganglia and other intracranial calcifications. Chronic deficiency of parathyroid hormone leads to hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia, promoting calcium-phosphate deposition in brain tissues; on neuroimaging this pattern is virtually indistinguishable from the calcifications seen in Primary Familial Brain Calcification (Fahr disease).

834008.long_answer: Reports of femoral-facial (femoral hypoplasia–unusual facies) syndrome consistently list maternal exposure to ionizing radiation—such as diagnostic or therapeutic X-rays—during early pregnancy as a recognized teratogenic risk factor. The DNA-damaging effects of ionizing radiation on the developing embryo can disturb limb-bud and craniofacial morphogenesis, contributing to the anomalies that characterize facial femoral syndrome.

622199.long_answer: Pyruvate kinase deficiency is an inherited red-blood-cell enzyme defect that produces chronic hemolytic anemia. Diagnosis, monitoring of hemoglobin levels, management with transfusions, splenectomy, or emerging enzyme-activating drugs all fall under the expertise of hematologists, the specialists who treat blood disorders.

230145.long_answer: Acute appendicitis typically starts when the appendiceal lumen—the hollow interior passage of the vermiform appendix—is obstructed by a fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia, or other material. Obstruction of this lumen causes mucus accumulation, increased intraluminal pressure, ischemia, bacterial overgrowth, and ultimately inflammation of the appendix.

276728.long_answer: In Langerhans cell histiocytosis, an MRI of the head can simultaneously show the three components of the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad: lytic skull lesions, orbital/orbital apex involvement producing exophthalmos, and hypothalamic-pituitary stalk infiltration responsible for central diabetes insipidus. Because MRI provides high-resolution soft-tissue contrast as well as bone detail with appropriate sequences, it is the preferred imaging technique to detect this classic triad.

961067.long_answer: Both mercury poisoning and long-term exposure to environmental noise have been shown to raise systemic arterial blood pressure. Mercury can induce oxidative stress and autonomic dysfunction, promoting vasoconstriction and leading to hypertension. Chronic noise activates the sympathetic–adrenal system and the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, similarly causing sustained elevations in blood pressure. Thus, the cardiovascular condition common to both exposures is hypertension (high blood pressure).

534026.long_answer: Bothrops lanceolatus is the binomial name of the Martinique lancehead. In the Linnaean hierarchy a two-part (genus + specific epithet) Latin name designates the species level; therefore Bothrops lanceolatus occupies the taxonomic rank of species.

530453.long_answer: Body lice (Pediculus humanus corporis) transmit the bacterium Bartonella quintana. This infection, known as trench fever, is frequently reported in modern urban homeless populations where body-louse infestation is common. The lice become infected by feeding on an infected person’s blood and pass the bacteria to others through their feces, which enter the skin via scratching; outbreaks of trench fever have been documented repeatedly among homeless individuals worldwide.

745627.long_answer: Pemphigus foliaceus is mediated by pathogenic IgG autoantibodies, with the IgG4 subclass being the dominant and most pathogenic isotype. After synthesis in the rough endoplasmic reticulum, IgG4 molecules are conveyed to and selectively sorted in the Golgi apparatus—specifically the trans-Golgi network—before being packaged into secretory vesicles for extracellular release. These secreted IgG4 autoantibodies then bind desmoglein-1 on keratinocytes, driving the autoimmune blistering characteristic of the disease.

182995.long_answer: Valproic acid (sodium valproate) is the first-line broad-spectrum antiepileptic drug for myoclonic seizures in generalized epilepsies, such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. It raises brain GABA levels, stabilizes neuronal firing, and is consistently recommended in treatment guidelines for controlling myoclonic jerks.

505083.long_answer: An interval of more than 48 months from the antecedent pregnancy places a placental site trophoblastic tumor in a high-risk category. International Society for the Study of Trophoblastic Diseases and FIGO guidelines advise treating such high-risk or metastatic PSTT with the multi-agent, platinum–etoposide-based regimen EMA/EP (etoposide-methotrexate-actinomycin D / etoposide-cisplatin), because single-agent regimens are inadequate for this relatively chemoresistant tumor.

990158.long_answer: Polydactyly is a congenital genetic disorder in which mutations affecting limb patterning genes (such as SHH or GLI3) lead to the development of supernumerary digits, resulting in more than the usual five fingers (or toes) on a hand or foot.

878160.long_answer: The human leukocyte antigen HLA-B27 allele is present in about 90 % of patients with ankylosing spondylitis, making it a characteristic genetic marker for this spondyloarthropathy. In contrast, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) shows no association with HLA-B27, distinguishing the two conditions genetically and pathogenetically.

934735.long_answer: Hyperopia, also called farsightedness, is a refractive error in which near objects appear blurry while distant objects remain clearer. Although genetic factors are most common, systemic conditions such as diabetes mellitus can alter the eye’s refractive state by changing lens shape or thickness and thereby precipitate or exacerbate hyperopia.

923349.long_answer: Dubin–Johnson syndrome causes lifelong, fluctuating conjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to impaired hepatic secretion of conjugated bilirubin, but it does not damage the liver or other organs. Affected individuals remain asymptomatic aside from mild jaundice and have a normal life expectancy, so the overall prognosis is considered benign.

289974.long_answer: Hypermobility spectrum disorder belongs to the group of heritable connective tissue disorders, the same category that includes conditions such as the various types of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. These disorders are characterized by genetically based abnormalities in collagen or related extracellular-matrix components that lead to systemic manifestations like joint hypermobility, skin findings, and tissue fragility.

602625.long_answer: Congenital self-healing reticulohistiocytosis is a benign variant of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The disorder is characterized by clonal proliferation and activation of epidermal antigen-presenting Langerhans cells (CD1a⁺, langerin⁺ dendritic cells), which leads to the transient cutaneous lesions that spontaneously regress. Thus, the primary immune system component activated is the population of Langerhans cells.

312005.long_answer: Cirrhosis—especially alcoholic liver cirrhosis—is a chronic liver disease in which fibrosis and regenerative nodules distort hepatic architecture. This increases intrahepatic vascular resistance, making cirrhosis the most common cause of portal hypertension and a well-known long-term complication of chronic alcohol abuse.

706053.long_answer: In Conan Doyle’s story Holmes discovers that Godfrey Emsworth was not a leper but had ichthyosis—a non-contagious ‘pseudo-leprosy’ in which the skin becomes thickened, dry and scaly, giving a blanched, white appearance that can be mistaken for Hansen’s disease. This benign dermatological condition explains Emsworth’s pallor without the dangers associated with true leprosy.

361224.long_answer: Hookworm larvae hatch in soil contaminated with human feces and penetrate bare skin, usually through the feet. Consistently wearing shoes or other protective footwear creates a physical barrier between skin and contaminated soil, interrupting the parasite’s transmission cycle and markedly reducing new infections in areas lacking adequate sanitation.

638938.long_answer: Larsen syndrome is produced by pathogenic variants in the FLNB gene, which encodes filamin-B, a cytoskeletal protein essential for the structure and function of connective tissue—particularly cartilage and the supporting tissues around joints. The defect therefore primarily compromises connective tissue, leading to the characteristic multiple joint dislocations, craniofacial anomalies, and other skeletal abnormalities seen in the syndrome.

645153.long_answer: Gemcitabine is a nucleoside analogue chemotherapy agent that is routinely combined with cisplatin (the GC regimen) as first-line treatment for advanced or metastatic transitional cell (urothelial) carcinoma. Clinical trials showed that gemcitabine-cisplatin provides response rates and overall survival comparable to older MVAC regimens but with significantly less toxicity, so guidelines list gemcitabine plus cisplatin as a standard option for this disease setting.

634456.long_answer: In fatty liver disease—particularly non-alcoholic fatty liver disease—most hepatic triglyceride originates from free fatty acids released by white adipose tissue. Insulin-resistant, inflamed adipose tissue undergoes heightened lipolysis, flooding the liver with fatty acids that are re-esterified and stored, leading to hepatic steatosis. Thus, dysfunctional adipose tissue is a primary upstream driver of fat accumulation in the liver.

207138.long_answer: Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) occurs when hepatic activity of the enzyme-protein uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) is reduced. UROD normally converts uroporphyrinogen III to coproporphyrinogen III in the heme-biosynthetic pathway. Its deficiency leads to hepatic and cutaneous accumulation of uroporphyrins, producing the blistering photosensitivity typical of PCT. Because UROD is a liver-synthesised protein whose normal function is also needed for proper secretion of retinol-binding complexes, its deficiency disrupts both heme formation and systemic retinol (vitamin A) transport, linking the enzyme defect to the clinical and biochemical features seen in PCT.

705908.long_answer: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is an autosomal-recessive inborn error of metabolism caused by deficiency of the enzyme phenylalanine hydroxylase. Toxic accumulation of phenylalanine in the brain begins soon after birth and classically produces early neurologic signs, including irritability, seizures, and coarse or fine tremors in infants. Prompt dietary restriction of phenylalanine prevents these tremor manifestations, underscoring the genetic basis of the disorder.

509563.long_answer: In annular pancreas a ring of pancreatic tissue encircles and narrows the second part of the duodenum. The constriction is usually proximal to the entry point of the common bile and pancreatic ducts, so the major duodenal papilla—also called the ampulla of Vater—lies just distal (below) the site of obstruction.

557735.long_answer: Oculocutaneous albinism type I is caused by pathogenic variants in the TYR gene; therefore, molecular genetic testing that sequences the TYR gene’s coding regions (and, if necessary, deletion/duplication analysis) is performed to establish the diagnosis.

212681.long_answer: The Anaplasma species that affect ruminants, dogs, and horses is Anaplasma phagocytophilum; it multiplies within the cytoplasmic vacuoles of neutrophilic granulocytes. This tropism for neutrophils (rather than red blood cells or monocytes) underlies tick-borne fever in cattle and sheep, canine granulocytic anaplasmosis, and equine granulocytic anaplasmosis.

919389.long_answer: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a 22q11.2 microdeletion on chromosome 22. The deletion disrupts genes critical for development of the pharyngeal arches, leading to craniofacial anomalies, cleft palate and recurrent otitis media, which together predispose to conductive and sometimes sensorineural hearing loss.

842703.long_answer: Bloom syndrome is an autosomal-recessive chromosomal-instability disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the BLM helicase gene. The defective DNA-repair helicase leads to excessive chromosomal breakage and markedly elevated sister-chromatid exchange, producing genome instability. Because of this instability, affected individuals have a greatly increased lifetime risk of many malignancies, including leukemias, lymphomas and solid tumours.

817696.long_answer: The prototypical Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker (GSS) mutation is a proline-to-leucine substitution at codon 102 of the prion protein gene (PRNP P102L). This mutation causes the inherited prion disease characterized by early cerebellar degeneration, which manifests clinically as gait ataxia and dysarthria.

753935.long_answer: In infantile Pompe disease, excessive glycogen deposition in the myocardium causes generalized cardiac enlargement. A standard postero-anterior chest X-ray is routinely used to visualise the cardiac silhouette, and an enlarged heart shadow on this radiograph is the classic, first-line means of detecting cardiomegaly in these patients.

656624.long_answer: The original description of Combarros–Calleja–Leno syndrome involved several affected siblings born to clinically unaffected, non-consanguineous parents, with both males and females showing the same phenotype and no evidence of vertical (parent-to-child) transmission. This pattern—multiple affected children of unaffected parents, equal sex distribution, and absence of male-to-male transmission—best fits an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.

753721.long_answer: Porocarcinomas characteristically harbor recurrent gene fusions involving YAP1 (e.g., YAP1-MAML2 or YAP1-NUTM1). These fusions drive strong nuclear accumulation of the Hippo-pathway transcription co-activator YAP1, and immunohistochemical detection of YAP1 has proven highly sensitive and specific for both eccrine poroma and its malignant counterpart, porocarcinoma. Consequently, the YAP1 protein family is now routinely used as a diagnostic marker to identify porocarcinoma.

734930.long_answer: When a glioma infiltrates or compresses the optic nerve, it disrupts transmission of visual signals from the eye to the brain, leading to loss or reduction of vision (visual acuity/field defects). Thus, affected patients commonly experience vision loss.

336585.long_answer: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is classified among the obsessive-compulsive and related disorders. Patients are preoccupied with imagined or slight defects in appearance, experience intrusive thoughts about these perceived flaws, and engage in repetitive or compulsive behaviors—such as mirror checking, excessive grooming, or camouflaging—to hide or fix them.

979614.long_answer: Aspirin and related non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs irreversibly acetylate the enzyme cyclooxygenase (also called prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase, COX-1/COX-2). By blocking COX, the conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandin H₂—the precursor of all prostaglandins—is prevented. This reduction in prostaglandin production, particularly of PGD₂, is why low-dose aspirin is often given with niacin therapy for hyperlipidemia to lessen prostaglandin-mediated flushing.

319365.long_answer: Pilocytic astrocytoma is usually confirmed radiologically with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MRI provides high-resolution, multiplanar views of the brain, and with gadolinium contrast it characteristically shows a well-circumscribed, often cystic mass with an enhancing mural nodule—findings that are diagnostic for pilocytic astrocytoma and guide surgical planning.

202247.long_answer: Tuberous sclerosis complex, an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in TSC1 or TSC2, classically presents with a triad of (1) intellectual disability, (2) epilepsy/seizures, and (3) characteristic facial angiofibromas (formerly called adenoma sebaceum) that clinicians often mistake for acne or psoriatic skin lesions. The combination of neurological impairment and psoriasiform cutaneous findings makes tuberous sclerosis the recognized genetic syndrome described.

693571.long_answer: In Victor Hugo’s 1869 novel “The Man Who Laughs” (French: “L’Homme qui rit”), he introduces the Comprachicos, a band of child-traders who surgically mutilate and disfigure children—most notably giving the protagonist, Gwynplaine, a permanent grotesque grin. This portrayal of deliberate child deformity is the archetypal depiction of such practices in Hugo’s works and parallels any brief allusion to similar horrors elsewhere, including in The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.

390141.long_answer: Both human parainfluenza viruses (types 1–4) and the mumps virus are enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA viruses classified in the family Paramyxoviridae. This family groups several genera—including Respirovirus (HPIV-1 and ‑3) and Orthorubulavirus (mumps virus and HPIV-2,-4)—based on shared genomic organization, replication strategy, and structural proteins.

896651.long_answer: In isolated hypermethioninemia, elevated blood methionine is usually due to pathogenic variants in the MAT1A gene, which encodes methionine adenosyl-transferase, or in the GNMT gene, which encodes glycine N-methyltransferase. Both enzymes catalyze the first steps of methionine catabolism; when either gene is mutated, the corresponding enzyme activity drops, methionine is not efficiently broken down, and the amino acid accumulates.

649891.long_answer: Troyer syndrome (a complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia, classified as SPG20) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SPG20 gene, which encodes the protein spartin. Pathogenic variants in SPG20 lead to the characteristic combination of lower-limb spasticity, distal muscle weakness, dysarthria, short stature, and other features that define Troyer syndrome.

980287.long_answer: Bloom syndrome is an autosomal-recessive genodermatosis that presents with multiple café-au-lait patches, photosensitive telangiectatic erythema and proportionate short stature. The disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the BLM gene, which encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase necessary for genomic stability.

849584.long_answer: Hereditary Factor X deficiency results from mutations in the F10 gene, which encodes coagulation factor X. The F10 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 13q34 on human chromosome 13, so all known congenital Factor X deficiencies trace to this chromosomal location.

406975.long_answer: Jarcho-Levin syndrome (classically the spondylothoracic/spondylocostal dysostosis spectrum) is most often caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in genes such as DLL3, MESP2, LFNG, or HES7. These pathogenic variants are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, meaning an affected individual carries two mutated alleles—one from each carrier parent.

271678.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the WNT3 gene disrupt the Wnt signaling pathway that triggers limb bud initiation during early embryogenesis. This leads to tetra-amelia syndrome, a congenital disorder marked by complete absence of all four limbs and severe malformations of facial, cranial, urogenital, pulmonary and other structures.

880195.long_answer: The main genetic risk factor for progressive supranuclear palsy is the H1 haplotype/variant of the MAPT gene, which is located on chromosome 17q21. MAPT encodes the microtubule-associated protein tau; abnormal tau accumulation disrupts mitochondrial transport and dynamics, contributing to mitochondrial dysfunction observed in PSP and other tauopathies. Hence, chromosome 17 carries the variant linked to PSP and implicated in mitochondrial impairment.

242126.long_answer: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a genetic disorder in which infants lack the adrenal-cortical enzyme 21-hydroxylase (or, more rarely, another steroidogenic enzyme). This enzyme deficiency impairs cortisol and often aldosterone synthesis, causing adrenal crisis, salt-wasting, failure to thrive, and potentially life-threatening complications in newborns.

364431.long_answer: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (an inherited disorder beginning with the letter “N”) is caused by pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene. Molecular mapping and sequencing studies have established that NF1 resides on chromosome 17, band 17q11.2. Mutations at this locus disrupt production of neurofibromin and produce the characteristic features of the disease.

187031.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the SGCE gene (encoding ε-sarcoglycan, locus DYT11) are the established cause of the autosomal-dominant myoclonus-dystonia syndrome. A cardinal feature of this syndrome is dystonia—typically affecting the neck or upper body—accompanied by action myoclonus, and symptoms often improve with alcohol. Thus, SGCE mutation is a well-known genetic cause of a syndrome in which dystonia is a key symptom.

116212.long_answer: The constellation of obstructive azoospermia with chronic sinusitis and bronchiectasis was first recorded in a 1972 report by British urologist Dr. Donald Young, whose observations led to the eponym 'Young’s syndrome'.

620685.long_answer: The Martinican pit viper (Bothrops lanceolatus) belongs to the pit-viper subfamily Crotalinae. This subfamily was formally erected in 1811 by the German naturalist and herpetologist Nicolaus Michael Oppel, whose classification work first separated pit vipers (crotalines) from other vipers. Hence, Oppel is the scientist who established the subfamily that includes the Martinican pit viper.

800447.long_answer: The hereditary prion disease Gerstmann–Sträussler–Scheinker syndrome (GSS) carries the eponym of Josef Gerstmann—the same neurologist whose name designates Gerstmann syndrome, a tetrad (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation) produced by a lesion in the dominant angular gyrus of the parietal lobe. Thus the prion disease and the angular-gyrus lesion syndrome share the name 'Gerstmann.'

580093.long_answer: Mutations in the COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein) gene are responsible for pseudoachondroplasia, a skeletal dysplasia that presents with disproportionate short stature, deformities of the hips and knees, and marked ligamentous laxity. Defective COMP disrupts cartilage extracellular matrix organization, leading to abnormal endochondral bone growth and the characteristic clinical features.

928865.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked androgen receptor (AR) gene cause Testicular Feminization Syndrome, also called complete androgen insensitivity. This disorder is listed under the letter “T” and affects individuals with an XY karyotype, so it primarily manifests in genetic males.

365205.long_answer: Several chromatin-regulating genes on the X chromosome that cause X-linked intellectual disability—such as PHF6 (Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome), PHF8 (Siderius type XLID) and KDM5C/JARID1C—encode proteins containing a Plant Homeodomain (PHD) finger. Recurring pathogenic variants in this zinc-binding PHD finger domain highlight it as a characteristic structural motif associated with genes involved in X-linked intellectual disability.

682308.long_answer: Methionine synthase (also called 5-methyltetrahydrofolate-homocysteine methyltransferase) catalyzes the remethylation of homocysteine to regenerate methionine, using 5-methyltetrahydrofolate as the methyl donor and vitamin B₁₂ as a cofactor. Impairment of this enzyme’s activity prevents efficient conversion of homocysteine, leading to its elevation in blood (hyperhomocysteinemia).

680441.long_answer: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia type 1 (AOA1) is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the APTX gene, which encodes the DNA-repair enzyme aprataxin. Aprataxin processes single-strand DNA breaks by hydrolysing 5′-adenylated ends, thereby removing obstructive termini and restoring ligatable 5′-phosphate groups. Defects in this end-cleaning step impair DNA strand-break repair in neurons, leading to the characteristic cerebellar ataxia and oculomotor apraxia seen in AOA1.

301792.long_answer: Progressive pseudorheumatoid dysplasia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WISP3 (CCN6) gene, which maps cytogenetically to 6q22–q23 on human chromosome 6.

239297.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the OFD1 gene, which encodes a centrosomal–basal body protein essential for primary cilium formation, produce Oro-facio-digital syndrome type 1. This ciliopathy is classically defined by malformations of the face (hypertelorism, wide nasal bridge), the oral cavity (cleft palate, lobulated tongue), and the digits (polydactyly, brachydactyly), establishing OFD1 mutation as the causal genetic defect.

144522.long_answer: Smith–Fineman–Myers syndrome is an X-linked intellectual-disability disorder. Molecular studies have shown that it is caused by pathogenic mutations in the GDI1 gene, which encodes Rab GDP-dissociation inhibitor-α. Loss-of-function GDI1 variants disrupt Rab-mediated vesicle trafficking in neurons and are consistently associated with the syndrome’s core features, including severe language delay.

940145.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked OFD1 gene cause oral-facial-digital syndrome type I, a disorder whose core features include congenital heart malformations, tongue (lingual) hamartomas, and digital anomalies such as postaxial polydactyly. Loss-of-function variants in OFD1 disrupt ciliary function during development, producing the characteristic combination of oral, facial, cardiac, and limb defects seen in the syndrome.

570138.long_answer: Mutations in the TJP2 gene, which encodes tight junction protein 2 (ZO-2) that organizes epithelial and endothelial intercellular junctions, are a recognized cause of progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC type 4).

341016.long_answer: Idiopathic pulmonary hemosiderosis presents with recurrent alveolar‐capillary bleeding and intra-alveolar iron deposition that impair oxygen transport. The cornerstone of management is prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy (e.g., oral prednisone), which suppresses pulmonary inflammation, reduces hemorrhage, and improves gas exchange.

185070.long_answer: Carnosinemia results from deficiency of the enzyme carnosinase (CNDP1-encoded), whose normal three-dimensional fold is that of a zinc-dependent metallo-exopeptidase. The protein’s active site contains a catalytic Zn2+ ion characteristic of zinc metalloproteases; loss or absence of this metalloprotease leads to accumulation of carnosine in blood and urine, producing carnosinemia.

308078.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator) gene, which is located on the long arm of chromosome 7 (7q31.2). There is no recognized linkage of the primary cystic-fibrosis-causing gene to chromosome 8. Therefore, the statement that the gene primarily associated with cystic fibrosis is located on chromosome 8 is incorrect.

512464.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SLC6A20 gene, which encodes the brush-border Na⁺/Cl⁻-dependent imino-acid transporter (IMINO) of the renal proximal tubule, cause iminoglycinuria. This transporter is chiefly responsible for reabsorbing glycine, proline and hydroxyproline; when SLC6A20 is mutated, these amino acids are not reclaimed efficiently and are excreted in the urine, producing the characteristic disorder.

144648.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the LHCGR (luteinizing hormone/chorionic-gonadotropin receptor) gene abolish receptor signaling, making the gonads unresponsive to luteinizing hormone. This LH insensitivity produces Leydig cell hypoplasia, a disorder of sex development characterized by undervirilization of 46,XY individuals and absent pubertal testosterone rise.

699435.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the LRP5 gene cause osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome, a disorder marked by congenital or very early-onset blindness due to retinal dysgenesis and by severe juvenile osteoporosis with frequent fractures. Loss of LRP5 impairs Wnt signaling that is critical for retinal vascular development and bone mass acquisition, explaining the combination of visual loss and pronounced skeletal fragility.

512596.long_answer: Hajdu–Cheney syndrome is caused by truncating mutations in exon 34 of the NOTCH2 gene that delete the protein’s C-terminal PEST sequence—a proline-, glutamic acid-, serine- and threonine-rich degradation motif. Loss of this PEST domain prevents normal ubiquitin-mediated turnover of NOTCH2, prolonging its signaling activity and producing the clinical features of the syndrome.

544740.long_answer: The F5 gene encodes coagulation Factor V, a plasma glycoprotein essential for thrombin generation. This protein is synthesized mainly by hepatocytes—the parenchymal cells of the liver—before being secreted into the bloodstream where it participates in the coagulation cascade.

967463.long_answer: Family studies of polycystic ovary syndrome show vertical transmission of the trait through successive generations, affecting both female and male relatives, consistent with an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance with variable penetrance.

871880.long_answer: The F2 gene encodes coagulation factor II, commonly called prothrombin. During the blood-clotting cascade, prothrombin is proteolytically cleaved by the prothrombinase complex to produce the active serine protease thrombin.

940561.long_answer: The NF2 gene encodes the tumor-suppressor protein merlin, which normally binds to and inhibits the serine/threonine kinase p21-activated kinase 1 (PAK1) within the Rac/Cdc42 signaling pathway. Loss-of-function mutations in NF2 abolish merlin’s inhibitory effect, allowing PAK1 to become constitutively active and drive aberrant proliferation and survival of Schwann and meningeal cells characteristic of Neurofibromatosis type II.

262533.long_answer: Meckel-Gruber syndrome is classified as a ciliopathy. Mutations in genes such as MKS1, TMEM67, and CEP290 compromise assembly and function of the primary cilium (the microtubule-based organelle projecting from most vertebrate cells). Loss of proper ciliary structure impairs critical protein signaling pathways during embryogenesis, producing the characteristic malformations of Meckel-Gruber syndrome. Thus, the organelle whose malfunction in protein-related assembly and trafficking leads directly to the disease is the primary cilium.

112797.long_answer: Mutations in the ABCB11 gene, which encodes the bile salt export pump (BSEP), cause progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 (PFIC2). BSEP deficiency leads to severe cholestasis, rapid progression to cirrhosis, and a markedly increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma that can present in infancy or early childhood.

211285.long_answer: The syndrome characterized by progressive memory impairment and global cognitive decline was first described in 1906 by the German neurologist Alois Alzheimer, who reported the clinical course and post-mortem neuropathology (amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles) of his patient Auguste Deter; this condition was later named Alzheimer’s disease in his honor.

471868.long_answer: The hair disease characterized by beaded (moniliform) hair shafts and patchy alopecia is monilethrix. It is classically caused by missense mutations in the type II hair-keratin genes KRT81 (hHb1), KRT83 (hHb3), and KRT86 (hHb6). Defects in these keratin proteins weaken the hair cortex, leading to the periodic constrictions that give hair a beaded appearance and result in fragility and alopecia.

496069.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations or 17p11.2 deletions that disrupt the RAI1 gene cause Smith–Magenis syndrome, a disorder whose core features include moderate intellectual disability, early-onset obesity, and characteristic dysmorphic facial appearance (broad square face, brachycephaly, midface retrusion). Haploinsufficiency of RAI1 is therefore the established molecular basis of this syndrome.

721311.long_answer: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme β-hexosaminidase A causes Tay-Sachs disease. In this GM2 gangliosidosis, storage of ganglioside within neurons leads to progressive neurodegeneration, hypotonia, a ‘cherry-red’ macular spot, and characteristically enlarged head size (macrocephaly/megalencephaly) in affected infants. Thus macrocephaly is a recognised clinical feature directly linked to β-hexosaminidase A deficiency.

218432.long_answer: Mutations in the intraflagellar transport gene IFT57 (also known as C19orf56/HIPPI) cause cranio-ectodermal dysplasia, the clinical entity originally described as Sensenbrenner syndrome. The IFT57 locus is situated on chromosome 19 (19q13), which is the same chromosome that contains the primary microcephaly gene WDR62. Thus, IFT57 is the Sensenbrenner-associated gene located on the same chromosome as WDR62.

367268.long_answer: Galloway–Mowat syndrome (GAMOS) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder. The X-linked form of the disease, designated GAMOS2, is caused by pathogenic variants in the LAGE3 gene (L antigen family member 3) located on chromosome Xp11.23. LAGE3 encodes one of the members of the LAGE (L-antigen) protein family and functions as a subunit of the KEOPS complex involved in tRNA modification. Because the disease-causing gene itself is LAGE3, it is, by definition, a member of the LAGE3/L-antigen gene family. Therefore, the gene associated with X-linked Galloway–Mowat syndrome does indeed belong to the LAGE3 family.

893516.long_answer: Huntington’s disease results from an expanded CAG-repeat mutation in the HTT (huntingtin) gene. This gene, which directs synthesis of the huntingtin protein, is located at cytogenetic band 4p16.3 on chromosome 4; the pathogenic expansion here leads to the neurodegenerative features of the disorder.

235793.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SOST gene, which encodes the Wnt-signalling inhibitor sclerostin, cause sclerosteosis. This high-bone-mass disorder presents with marked cranial sclerosis and consequent macrocephaly due to excessive bone formation in the skull.

105199.long_answer: Williams–Beuren syndrome is caused by a hemizygous micro-deletion at chromosome 7q11.23 that removes the ELN (elastin) gene. Loss of elastin disrupts arterial wall integrity and classically produces supravalvular aortic stenosis, making the ELN gene deletion the genetic mutation associated with this aortic-stenosis-containing condition.

684037.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the MITF (microphthalmia-associated transcription factor) gene disrupt melanocyte development. This causes Waardenburg syndrome type 2/Tietz spectrum, characterised clinically by patchy areas of hypo- and hyperpigmented skin, ocular anomalies such as microcornea, and severe congenital sensorineural hearing loss.

700677.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the X-linked gene ZIC3 are a well-established cause of heterotaxy (situs ambiguus). In carrier mothers, each pregnancy has a 50 % chance of transmitting the mutation, and affected fetuses frequently develop right-isomerism with congenital heart disease and absence or severe hypoplasia of the spleen (asplenia). Thus, a ZIC3 mutation confers the noted 50 % risk of a condition that often results in asplenia.

279219.long_answer: Antithrombin (historically called antithrombin III) is a serine-protease inhibitor that neutralizes thrombin and several other coagulation factors. The protein is encoded by the SERPINC1 gene (Serpin Peptidase Inhibitor, Clade C, Member 1), located on chromosome 1q23-q25. SERPINC1 is the official HGNC gene symbol recognized in human genetics and clinical diagnostics.

441649.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PCNT gene, which encodes the centrosomal protein pericentrin, cause microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (a form of primordial dwarfism). Affected fetuses show profound intra-uterine growth restriction and remain extremely small throughout life, making this PCNT mutation a well-established genetic cause of dwarfism characterized by unusually small size even before birth.

809290.long_answer: Red–green colour vision deficiency (protanopia/protanomaly) is most commonly produced by mutations, deletions or unequal recombination in the X-linked OPN1LW gene, which encodes the long-wavelength-sensitive (red) cone opsin. Loss or alteration of this opsin impairs discrimination between red and green light, giving rise to the characteristic condition.

240775.long_answer: Species in the genus Toxicodendron—such as poison ivy, poison oak, and poison sumac—contain the oleoresin urushiol. Upon skin contact, urushiol acts as a potent sensitizer, triggering a type IV delayed-hypersensitivity reaction that manifests as allergic contact dermatitis.

558116.long_answer: Classic homocystinuria most commonly results from deficiency of the enzyme cystathionine β-synthase (CBS). CBS normally converts homocysteine plus serine into cystathionine, leading ultimately to the production of cysteine—the sulfur-containing amino acid capable of forming disulfide bonds. When CBS is absent or defective, homocysteine accumulates and cysteine levels fall, linking the disorder to the amino acid known for disulfide bond formation.

967977.long_answer: Corneal-cerebellar syndrome is classically defined by the triad of bilateral corneal dystrophy, progressive cerebellar ataxia, and intellectual disability (mental retardation). Reports of affected sibships describe normal early milestones followed by cognitive delay and permanent intellectual impairment. In contrast, spastic ataxia-corneal dystrophy syndrome is characterized chiefly by spastic paraplegia, ataxia, and corneal dystrophy, with cognitive function generally preserved. Therefore, the syndrome that causes intellectual disability is corneal-cerebellar syndrome.

526977.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the NTRK1 gene, which encodes the high-affinity nerve growth factor receptor TrkA, cause congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (HSAN type IV). Because TrkA signaling is essential for the development and survival of nociceptive and thermosensitive neurons, NTRK1 mutations lead to a complete inability to perceive pain and temperature.

417242.long_answer: Glomerulopathy with fibronectin deposits (fibronectin glomerulopathy) is an autosomal-dominant renal disease in which glomeruli are markedly enlarged owing to massive deposits located in the mesangium and along the subendothelial aspect of the capillary walls. Pathogenic heterozygous mutations in the FN1 gene, which encodes fibronectin 1, have been repeatedly identified in affected families, establishing FN1 as the causative gene for this rare form of glomerulopathy.

419885.long_answer: Mutations in the MCOLN1 gene, which encodes the lysosomal TRPML1 non-selective cation channel, cause mucolipidosis type IV—a well-characterized lysosomal storage disorder. Loss of TRPML1 channel activity disrupts lysosomal ion homeostasis and trafficking, leading to the accumulation of undigested macromolecules characteristic of this disease.

652819.long_answer: Mutations in the COL1A1 gene, which encodes the pro-α1 chain of type I collagen, disrupt normal collagen synthesis and structure. Defective type I collagen weakens the bone matrix, leading to osteogenesis imperfecta—a disorder marked by fragile bones and a markedly increased propensity for fractures.

625245.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the X-linked BCOR (BCL6 corepressor) gene cause Lenz microphthalmia syndrome. This disorder is classically defined by severe eye defects such as microphthalmia or anophthalmia and by skeletal malformations affecting the digits and limbs, establishing BCOR as the gene responsible for this eye-and-limb anomaly syndrome.

655000.long_answer: The most frequent genetic alteration in meningiomas is mutation or loss of the NF2 tumor-suppressor gene (located on chromosome 22q), whose product merlin is expressed in the meningeal (dura-mater–lining) cells from which these tumors arise.

282992.long_answer: Tricho-rhino-phalangeal syndrome type 1 is caused by pathogenic variants in the TRPS1 gene. Cytogenetic mapping places TRPS1 at 8q24 (approximately 8q23.3-q24.1), so the responsible gene resides on human chromosome 8.

141433.long_answer: More than 90 % of adults with systemic mastocytosis carry the activating point mutation D816V in the KIT proto-oncogene (c-KIT). This Asp→Val substitution in exon 17 constitutively activates the KIT tyrosine-kinase receptor, driving clonal mast-cell proliferation and the diverse systemic symptoms, including mediator-related manifestations such as myalgia.

292006.long_answer: A smooth cerebral cortex (lissencephaly) is classically caused by mutations or deletions in the LIS1 gene, formally known as PAFAH1B1, located on chromosome 17p13.3; loss of LIS1 disrupts neuronal migration during cortical development, producing the characteristic ‘smooth brain’ appearance.

217582.long_answer: Pathogenic loss-of-function mutations in the FANCA gene cause Fanconi anaemia, a hereditary bone-marrow failure syndrome. Defective FANCA impairs the Fanconi DNA-repair pathway, leading to progressive pancytopenia: thrombocytopenia results in easy bruising, while erythrocyte deficiency produces anaemia and fatigue.

669696.long_answer: Elevated circulating T3 and T4 with unsuppressed or even elevated TSH characterizes thyroid hormone resistance. Over 80 % of patients have heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the THRB gene, which encodes the β-isoform of the thyroid hormone receptor. The mutant receptor impairs negative feedback at the pituitary and hypothalamus, so TSH secretion is not suppressed despite high thyroid hormone levels.

982342.long_answer: Phenylketonuria (PKU) is caused by mutations in the phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 12 (region 12q23.2). Defective PAH activity on this chromosome leads to elevated phenylalanine levels characteristic of PKU.

933019.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the NFKB2 gene, which encodes the p100/p52 subunit of the non-canonical NF-κB pathway, produce the disorder known as DAVID syndrome. Patients present with adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)–dependent adrenal insufficiency together with common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), reflecting impaired pituitary ACTH production and defective B-cell maturation due to disrupted NF-κB signaling.

117181.long_answer: Activating mutations in the KCNJ11 gene, which encodes the Kir6.2 subunit of the pancreatic ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel, cause permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus. Sulfonylurea drugs close the over-active KATP channels, restoring insulin secretion, so patients with KCNJ11-related diabetes can often switch from insulin injections to oral sulfonylurea therapy.

306143.long_answer: Börjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome is an X-linked disorder produced by pathogenic variants in the PHF6 gene. Affected males typically present with moderate-to-severe intellectual disability, progressive (often truncal) obesity, and hypogonadism that leads to gynecomastia, along with characteristic facial features. Thus, mutation of PHF6 is the recognized genetic cause of the syndrome characterized by intellectual disability, obesity, and gynecomastia.

654418.long_answer: Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis and the related condition infantile systemic hyalinosis are allelic, autosomal-recessive disorders marked by multiple skin and gingival nodules, hyaline deposition in tissues, osteolytic bone lesions, and progressive joint contractures. Both diseases are produced by loss-of-function mutations in the ANTXR2 gene (also known as CMG2), which encodes the anthrax toxin receptor 2 involved in extracellular-matrix homeostasis.

799486.long_answer: In Chédiak–Higashi syndrome, a defect in the LYST gene disrupts microtubule-dependent trafficking of lysosomal granules. Because lysosomes cannot effectively fuse with phagosomes, phagolysosome formation is impaired, preventing release of degradative enzymes and thereby blocking the dissolution and killing of ingested bacteria.

624001.long_answer: Cherubism—the disorder named for the cherubic, chubby-cheeked faces of Renaissance putti—is caused by gain-of-function mutations in the SH3BP2 gene on chromosome 4p16.3. Mutant SH3BP2 hyper-activates osteoclast signaling, producing bilateral fibro-osseous expansion of the mandible and maxilla that leads to the characteristic facial disfigurement.

741809.long_answer: Marinesco–Sjögren syndrome is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SIL1 gene, which resides on the long arm of human chromosome 5 (cytogenetic location 5q31.2). Therefore, the gene associated with this syndrome is located on chromosome 5.

137805.long_answer: Thanatophoric dysplasia, a lethal skeletal dysplasia marked by extremely short limbs, redundant skin folds, narrow thorax, and often a clover-leaf skull, is caused by specific activating mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene. These gain-of-function FGFR3 mutations disrupt endochondral bone growth, producing the characteristic severe phenotype.

456710.long_answer: Thomas H. Weller, who shared the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, successfully isolated the varicella-zoster virus—the agent of shingles (and chickenpox)—in cell culture in the early 1950s, providing material critical for later diagnostic and vaccine developments.

826852.long_answer: Multiple hamartomas of the tongue are characteristic of Oral-Facial-Digital syndrome type 1, an X-linked dominant condition. Pathogenic variants in the OFD1 gene (also called CXORF5) on chromosome Xp22 cause this syndrome; therefore, mutation of OFD1 is the genetic defect associated with tongue hamartomas in this disorder.

740084.long_answer: Farber disease (Farber lipogranulomatosis) is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the ASAH1 gene, which encodes acid ceramidase. The same ASAH1 mutations can also lead to spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME), a disorder characterized by myoclonic seizures. Thus, ASAH1 is the gene linked to both Farber disease and a seizure-associated condition.

698755.long_answer: All-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) is a pharmacologic form of vitamin A that binds and activates the retinoic acid receptor-α (RARA). ATRA is used both to replace vitamin A in states of deficiency and, at higher doses, to treat acute promyelocytic leukemia by targeting the PML-RARA fusion protein. Therefore, the vitamin deficiency treated with the same agent that targets RARA is vitamin A deficiency.

558793.long_answer: Mutations in the androgen receptor (AR) gene cause androgen-insensitivity syndrome. Because defective AR signaling prevents normal response to fetal and pubertal androgens, affected 46,XY individuals often have incompletely virilized external genitalia and testes that fail to descend, leading to cryptorchidism (undescended testicles).

199937.long_answer: Mutations in the FLG gene, which encodes the epidermal protein filaggrin, disrupt skin barrier formation. Loss-of-function FLG variants lead to ichthyosis vulgaris, a condition marked by scaly, thick, and excessively dry skin due to impaired keratin aggregation and reduced natural moisturizing factors.

936547.long_answer: Epidemiological studies consistently show that Restless Legs Syndrome affects only about 1–2 % of adults in East Asian countries, whereas U.S. population–based surveys report prevalences of roughly 5–10 %. Thus, East Asia has the markedly lower prevalence.

404103.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the THAP1 gene (designated DYT6 dystonia) frequently produce an adult-onset cranio-cervical dystonia in which involuntary eyelid closure—blepharospasm—is one of the characteristic manifestations.

283404.long_answer: Mutations in the MTTP (microsomal triglyceride transfer protein) gene cause abetalipoproteinemia. In this disorder the absence of apo-B–containing lipoproteins alters red-cell membrane lipid composition, producing the characteristic spiculated red blood cells known as acanthocytes.

299529.long_answer: Duplications involving the cytogenetic band Xp11.2 occur on the short arm of the X chromosome and are a recognized cause of certain forms of X-linked intellectual disability (XLID). These rearrangements affect genes located on the X chromosome (e.g., IL1RAPL1, NDP, PHF8, etc.). The Y chromosome is not involved in these duplications: it neither carries homologous sequence at Xp11.2 nor participates in the pathogenic copy-number gains underlying XLID. Therefore, the Y chromosome is not associated with duplications at Xp11.2 that cause X-linked intellectual disability.

775607.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive, non-photosensitive trichothiodystrophy (TTD) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the MPLKIP gene, also known as TTDN1/C7orf11. Defects in MPLKIP disrupt its interaction with the mitotic kinase PLK1, leading to the brittle sulfur-deficient hair and developmental abnormalities characteristic of this non-photosensitive TTD subtype.

554949.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene (type II collagen) cause Stickler syndrome type 1. Stickler syndrome is characterised by severe ocular problems, including high myopia and a high lifetime risk of retinal detachment that can lead to permanent vision loss, and it frequently presents with cranio-facial anomalies such as cleft palate or complete cleft lip-palate (often as part of the Pierre-Robin sequence). Thus, a COL2A1 mutation links the potential for vision-threatening eye disease with cleft lip and palate formation.

343944.long_answer: The gene underlying Alström syndrome, ALMS1, was mapped and cloned through a collaborative effort between investigators at The Jackson Laboratory (Bar Harbor, Maine) and scientists at the University of Exeter in the United Kingdom. This partnership successfully isolated ALMS1, establishing its mutations as the cause of the multisystem disorder.

720434.long_answer: The G6PD gene encodes glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase; mutations in this gene cause G6PD deficiency, the most common enzymatic red-blood-cell disorder worldwide. Thousands of PubMed citations describe the molecular genetics, biochemical mechanisms, and clinical consequences of G6PD deficiency, making G6PD the well-established gene responsible for this deficiency.

797702.long_answer: Ritalin lung is a form of pulmonary talcosis and emphysema that arose in people who crushed and injected Ritalin tablets. At the time these cases were reported (1970s-1980s), Ritalin (methylphenidate) was produced and marketed by the pharmaceutical company Ciba-Geigy; thus Ciba-Geigy was the manufacturer of the drug linked to this condition.

151310.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PCNT gene, which encodes the centrosomal protein pericentrin, cause microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II—a form of primordial dwarfism in which affected individuals are profoundly, proportionately small, leading to the popular nickname 'Thumbelina' stature. Defective pericentrin impairs centrosome organization and mitotic spindle formation, reducing overall cell proliferation and thus body size.

389155.long_answer: Dent disease, an X-linked proximal tubulopathy that produces the full biochemical picture of Fanconi syndrome, is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the CLCN5 gene encoding the renal chloride/proton exchanger ClC-5. The resulting generalized proximal-tubular reabsorptive defect—glycosuria, phosphaturia, amino-aciduria, bicarbonate loss, etc.—is why Dent disease is regarded as an inherited cause of Fanconi syndrome.

471240.long_answer: Angelman syndrome is most commonly produced by loss-of-function of the maternally inherited UBE3A gene on chromosome 15q11-q13. A cardinal manifestation of this disorder is epilepsy; seizures are typically treated with anti-seizure drugs such as carbamazepine, phenobarbital and clobazam, making UBE3A mutation the genetic cause underlying the syndrome managed by these medications.

128761.long_answer: Renal cell carcinoma spreads hematogenously, and the pulmonary vasculature is usually the first capillary bed encountered after the renal veins drain into the inferior vena cava. Consequently, the lungs are the most frequent site of kidney-cancer metastases, observed in roughly 50–60 % of patients with secondary spread.

744918.long_answer: Mutations or dosage changes in the Sonic hedgehog (SHH) gene are well-known to produce a spectrum of abnormalities in early embryogenesis. Loss-of-function variants cause holoprosencephaly by impairing midline fore-brain cleavage, whereas gain or ectopic expression can lead to pre-axial polydactyly. Because SHH also directs early eye-field separation, the same mutations frequently result in ocular defects such as coloboma or microphthalmia. Thus SHH is the gene whose disruption underlies the syndrome combining holoprosencephaly, polydactyly and eye involvement.

270401.long_answer: Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is an autosomal-dominant syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in the APC gene that produces hundreds of adenomatous colonic polyps beginning in childhood. Children with FAP have a markedly elevated risk of developing hepatoblastoma, a primary malignant liver tumour that arises disproportionately in the right hepatic lobe. Thus, the early-onset colonic polyp syndrome that is classically linked to a liver cancer favoring the right lobe is FAP.

609092.long_answer: Thalidomide exposure in utero can cause phocomelia, an extreme limb-reduction defect. The inherited (genetic) form of this same limb malformation is Roberts syndrome, also called pseudothalidomide syndrome. Roberts syndrome is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the ESCO2 gene, which is located on chromosome 8p21.1. Thus, chromosome 8 is the chromosomal locus linked to the genetic form of the condition that thalidomide can produce teratogenically.

852722.long_answer: Several leukemia-predisposition genes, most notably RUNX1 (also called AML1), reside on human chromosome 21. Germ-line mutations in RUNX1 or having an extra copy of chromosome 21, as occurs in Down syndrome (trisomy 21), markedly elevate the likelihood of developing acute myeloid leukemia, demonstrating that chromosome 21 carries genes whose alteration increases AML risk.

289734.long_answer: The disease originally described by Jacques Jean Lhermitte (Lhermitte–Duclos disease) is linked to germ-line mutations in the PTEN tumor-suppressor gene, which is located on chromosome 10q23. Loss-of-function PTEN mutations underlie the cerebellar dysplastic gangliocytoma characteristic of this condition and its association with Cowden syndrome.

488953.long_answer: Androgen Insensitivity Syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the androgen receptor (AR) gene located on the X chromosome (locus Xq11-q12). Because males have only one X chromosome, a single mutated AR allele causes the disease in 46,XY individuals, while heterozygous 46,XX females are typically asymptomatic carriers. This pattern defines the disorder as X-linked recessive inheritance.

939937.long_answer: Pseudocowpox is caused by the Pseudocowpox virus, which is classified within the genus Parapoxvirus of the Poxviridae family. Parapoxviruses are large, enveloped DNA viruses that infect ruminants and can produce zoonotic dermal lesions in humans, fitting the established taxonomy for pseudocowpox.

392284.long_answer: Mitochondrial myopathies are characterized by abnormal aggregates of mitochondria that collect just beneath the plasma membrane of muscle fibres, producing the classic "ragged-red" appearance on histological stains. The plasma membrane of a muscle cell is called the sarcolemma, making it the membrane structure directly involved in these diseases.

232937.long_answer: Pathogenic gain-of-function variants in the CHN1 gene, which encodes the Rac-GTPase–activating protein α2-chimerin, are a well-established cause of Duane retraction syndrome (a congenital cranial dysinnervation disorder). A hallmark of this disorder is impaired abduction—an inability of the eye to move outward—due to aberrant innervation of the lateral rectus muscle. Multiple independent CHN1 missense variants have been shown to hyperactivate α2-chimerin, disrupt normal oculomotor axon guidance, and produce the characteristic congenital limitation of outward eye movement.

215213.long_answer: In multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis, infiltration of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis—part of the endocrine system—damages the posterior pituitary, reduces antidiuretic hormone secretion, and frequently produces central diabetes insipidus.

535998.long_answer: Mutations in TSEN54 cause several subtypes of pontocerebellar hypoplasia (most notably PCH type 2). TSEN54 encodes the 54-kDa subunit of the heterotetrameric tRNA-splicing endonuclease complex, the enzyme that cleaves introns from precursor tRNAs during their maturation. Thus, TSEN54 links pontocerebellar hypoplasia to defective tRNA splicing.

930948.long_answer: GAPO syndrome (Growth Retardation, Alopecia, Pseudoanodontia, Optic Atrophy) is produced by homozygous or compound-heterozygous loss-of-function mutations—including whole-gene deletions—in the ANTXR1 gene, which encodes anthrax toxin receptor 1/TEM8. Absence of functional ANTXR1 disrupts extracellular-matrix homeostasis, leading to the characteristic growth failure, sparse hair, delayed/absent teeth, and progressive optic atrophy seen in this rare disorder.

989461.long_answer: The autosomal-recessive disorder acrodermatitis enteropathica, characterized by impaired zinc absorption through the intestinal epithelium and resulting skin lesions, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC39A4 gene (ZIP4) located on chromosome 8q24.3. SLC39A4 encodes a zinc transporter critical for zinc uptake; its mutation disrupts systemic zinc homeostasis, leading to the disease phenotype.

141438.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the RET proto-oncogene disrupt signaling between glial cell-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) and the ureteric bud, preventing its outgrowth from the Wolffian duct.
