922375.long_answer: Mutations in any of the genes encoding components of the glycine cleavage system (e.g., GLDC, AMT, GCSH) cause non-ketotic hyperglycinemia. Affected individuals inherit two pathogenic alleles—one from each carrier parent—demonstrating classic autosomal recessive inheritance.

804007.long_answer: The most common form of Batten disease is the juvenile form (juvenile neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinosis, or CLN3 disease). This form is caused by pathogenic variants in the CLN3 gene. The CLN3 gene is located on chromosome 16 (specifically 16p12.1), not on chromosome 20. Therefore, chromosome 20 does not contain the gene responsible for the most common form of Batten disease.

220375.long_answer: Variegate porphyria is caused by mutations in the PPOX gene, which encodes the enzyme protoporphyrinogen oxidase. The human PPOX gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 1 (cytogenetic band 1q22). Defects in this chromosome-1 gene reduce enzyme activity, leading to the biochemical accumulation of porphyrin precursors characteristic of variegate porphyria.

759393.long_answer: Acute kidney injury can arise from post-renal obstruction produced by severe urinary retention. Passing a urethral (Foley) catheter—bladder catheterization—rapidly decompresses the over-distended bladder, re-establishes urine flow, and thereby relieves the obstruction that is compromising renal function.

659488.long_answer: Molybdenum cofactor is required for the function of xanthine oxidase (also called xanthine dehydrogenase). When the cofactor is missing, the enzyme is completely inactive. Xanthine oxidase normally catalyzes the final steps of purine degradation—converting hypoxanthine → xanthine and xanthine → uric acid—so loss of its activity is the reason purine catabolism and uric-acid homeostasis are disturbed in molybdenum cofactor deficiency.

711214.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the MAN2B1 gene, which is mapped to chromosome 19p13.1-p13.2, cause the lysosomal storage disorder alpha-mannosidosis. Individuals with alpha-mannosidosis develop progressive skeletal-muscle involvement that often produces proximal muscle weakness and a characteristic waddling (myopathic) gait, linking the mutation in MAN2B1 to the described clinical picture.

103221.long_answer: The first gene shown to cause Adams–Oliver syndrome is ARHGAP31, which is located at cytogenetic band 3q13.31 on human chromosome 3; pathogenic mutations in ARHGAP31 lead to the characteristic scalp and limb defects of the disorder.

384152.long_answer: Sengers syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the AGK gene (acylglycerol kinase, mitochondrial). AGK encodes the mitochondrial lipid kinase acylglycerol kinase, which phosphorylates mono- and diacylglycerols to lysophosphatidic and phosphatidic acids—key intermediates in cardiolipin biosynthesis. Disrupted cardiolipin metabolism impairs mitochondrial energy production and leads to cardiomyopathy, linking AGK to cardiovascular disease and establishing it as the gene responsible for Sengers syndrome.

391734.long_answer: The first recognized outbreak of rickettsialpox was documented in 1946 among residents of the Kew Gardens neighborhood in the borough of Queens, New York City. Epidemiologic investigation by Dr. Robert Huebner traced the febrile, vesicular illness to mites (Liponyssoides sanguineus) carried by house mice in apartment buildings there, establishing Kew Gardens as the locus of the initial rickettsialpox outbreak.

413877.long_answer: Hereditary myopathy with exercise intolerance (a mitochondrial myopathy presenting as lifelong exercise intolerance) is caused by mutations in the ISCU gene, which lies on chromosome 12q24. ISCU encodes the scaffold protein needed for iron–sulfur-cluster assembly in mitochondrial respiratory-chain enzymes; defective ISCU impairs complexes I, II and III, producing the characteristic exercise-intolerant myopathy.

802575.long_answer: Börjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the PHF6 gene located on the X chromosome. Because males are hemizygous for the X chromosome, a single mutated PHF6 allele produces the full clinical picture, while heterozygous females are typically unaffected or only mildly affected depending on X-inactivation. This pattern of transmission is therefore classified as X-linked recessive.

640842.long_answer: Stocco dos Santos syndrome is the original description of camptodactyly-arthropathy-coxa vara-pericarditis (CACP) syndrome. The disorder results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PRG4 (lubricin) gene, which was mapped to the chromosomal locus 1q25–q31. Hence, the camptodactyly seen in Stocco dos Santos syndrome is linked to the 1q25–q31 region of chromosome 1.

170805.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the AK2 gene (adenylate kinase 2) produce reticular dysgenesis, the most severe form of severe combined immunodeficiency. AK2 deficiency blocks both myeloid and lymphoid hematopoiesis, leading to agranulocytosis and lymphopenia, and also disrupts inner-ear development, resulting in congenital sensorineural deafness.

856726.long_answer: The X-linked form of congenital zonular (lamellar) cataract accompanied by nystagmus is produced by pathogenic variants in the NDP gene on Xp11.3, which encodes the signaling protein norrin. Mutations in NDP explain both the ocular phenotype and the X-linked pattern of inheritance observed in affected families.

153170.long_answer: Familial multiple intestinal atresia results from recessive mutations in the TTC7A gene (tetratricopeptide repeat domain 7A). TTC7A is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 2 at band 2p16.3, establishing chromosome 2 as the chromosomal location of the disease-causing gene.

643945.long_answer: Absence of fingerprints-congenital milia syndrome (also called adermatoglyphia) is caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the skin-specific isoform of the SMARCAD1 gene. SMARCAD1 is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 4 (4q22.3). Thus, the responsible gene resides on chromosome 4.

358053.long_answer: Gunther disease (congenital erythropoietic porphyria) is caused by autosomal-recessive mutations in the UROS gene, which encodes uroporphyrinogen III synthase. The UROS gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 10 (10q25.2-q26.3), making chromosome 10 the chromosomal location responsible for this disorder.

308266.long_answer: The USH2A gene is mutated in Usher syndrome type II. It encodes the trans-membrane protein usherin, which is essential for the proper development and long-term maintenance of stereocilia in inner-ear hair cells and of photoreceptor cells in the retina. Loss-of-function variants in USH2A disrupt these structures, leading to the characteristic hearing impairment and progressive retinitis pigmentosa seen in the disorder.

316826.long_answer: Worth syndrome (endosteal hyperostosis) results from mutations in the LRP5 gene. LRP5 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 11 (region 11q13), so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 11.

408729.long_answer: Isolated microphthalmia type 1 (MCOP1) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the homeobox transcription factor gene VSX2 (also known as CHX10). The VSX2/CHX10 gene is mapped to the 14q24.3 cytogenetic band, placing it on human chromosome 14.

733016.long_answer: The common juvenile form of Batten disease (juvenile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis) is caused by pathogenic variants in the CLN3 gene. The human CLN3 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 16p12.1 on chromosome 16, making this chromosome the locus for the gene underlying the most prevalent form of Batten disease.

905268.long_answer: Mutations in the RPE65 gene, which is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (band 1p31), are a well-established cause of Leber congenital amaurosis. This chromosomal location was determined through linkage and positional cloning studies, and the gene’s role has been confirmed by successful gene-replacement therapies that restore vision in affected individuals.

966824.long_answer: The Wilms tumor protein is encoded by the WT1 gene, which is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 11 (11p13). This chromosomal location was identified through linkage and cytogenetic studies of patients with Wilms tumor and related syndromes, firmly establishing chromosome 11 as the site of the WT1 gene.

841452.long_answer: Fetal (prenatal) ultrasound can visualize characteristic skeletal abnormalities—such as bowing, fractures, and cortical thickening—caused by autosomal-dominant COL1A1 pathogenic variants (e.g., in osteogenesis imperfecta or Caffey disease). Therefore, prenatal ultrasonography is the key diagnostic tool used to identify affected pregnancies.

578179.long_answer: Pseudoachondroplasia is an autosomal-dominant skeletal dysplasia produced by pathogenic variants in the COMP (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein) gene. The COMP gene is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 19 (region 19p13.1-p12), so chromosome 19 is the chromosomal location responsible for the disorder.

158815.long_answer: WAGR syndrome results from a contiguous-gene deletion at band 11p13 on chromosome 11 that removes or disrupts the WT1 and PAX6 genes. Loss of these genes produces the characteristic features—Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary anomalies, and intellectual disability—linking the disorder specifically to chromosome 11.

699070.long_answer: Most cases of Alagille syndrome result from pathogenic variants or deletions in the JAG1 gene, which is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 20 (band 20p12). Mutations in this chromosome-20-encoded gene disrupt JAG1–NOTCH signaling, leading to the characteristic multisystem features of Alagille syndrome.

569226.long_answer: Kenji Bandō wrote the story that became the Japanese film and novel “Taiyō no Uta” (Midnight Sun), in which the male protagonist falls in love with Kaoru Amane, a girl suffering from xeroderma pigmentosum—a DNA-repair disorder that makes exposure to ultraviolet light potentially lethal. The plot revolves around her need to avoid sunlight and the romance that develops in spite of this medical condition.

853682.long_answer: The gene C4orf26 (Chromosome 4 open reading frame 26), whose loss-of-function mutations cause Kohlschütter–Tönz syndrome, is physically located on human chromosome 4 (band 4q21). Hence chromosome 4 harbors this disease-associated gene.

674071.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in KIF11 (kinesin family member 11) are known to cause the syndrome of microcephaly with or without chorioretinopathy, lymphedema, and mental retardation (MCLMR). A characteristic neuroimaging finding in affected patients is microlissencephaly—a markedly reduced brain size with a simplified or nearly smooth cortical pattern—together with congenital peripheral lymphedema. Thus, a pathogenic KIF11 mutation is the established genetic cause of this rare form of microlissencephaly accompanied by congenital lymphedema.

665042.long_answer: Heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the PTPN11 gene (coding for the SHP-2 tyrosine-phosphatase) are the most frequent cause of Noonan syndrome, a condition whose cardinal clinical features include proportionate short stature and characteristic craniofacial dysmorphisms such as a broad forehead, hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures and low-set ears.

646579.long_answer: The major Alzheimer’s disease susceptibility gene is APOE (apolipoprotein E). The ε4 allele of APOE markedly increases the risk of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease, and this gene is located on chromosome 19q13.2. Hence, chromosome 19 harbors the principal genetic locus most strongly linked to Alzheimer’s susceptibility in the general population.

898063.long_answer: The glypican-1 gene (GPC1), whose variation has been implicated in susceptibility to biliary atresia, is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q37).

926968.long_answer: Mutations in the FOXC2 gene, which encodes a forkhead-box transcription factor, cause lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome. A hallmark of this condition is distichiasis—a congenital double row of eyelashes—making FOXC2 the gene most clearly associated with this clinical feature.

850980.long_answer: Macroglossia seen in α-mannosidosis is caused by deficiency of lysosomal α-mannosidase encoded by the MAN2B1 gene. MAN2B1 is located on chromosome 19 (region 19p13–q13); therefore, chromosome 19 contains the gene responsible for this mannosidosis-related form of macroglossia.

688450.long_answer: A gain-of-function mutation in the FGFR3 gene (most commonly the p.G380R substitution) underlies achondroplasia, the prototypic skeletal dysplasia characterized by rhizomelic shortening of the long bones—including marked shortening of the femur—due to impaired endochondral ossification at the growth plates.

885314.long_answer: Lafora disease (progressive myoclonic epilepsy type 2) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in two genes: EPM2A, which encodes the dual-specificity phosphatase laforin, and NHLRC1 (also called EPM2B), which encodes the E3 ubiquitin-ligase malin. Defects in either gene disrupt glycogen metabolism, leading to accumulation of insoluble polyglucosan (Lafora) bodies in neurons and other tissues, producing the characteristic neurodegeneration and myoclonic seizures of Lafora disease.

198944.long_answer: Gliosarcoma, a rare variant of glioblastoma containing both glial and sarcomatous components, is documented to metastasize extracranially (e.g., to lung, liver, bone) more often than other cerebral gliomas. The sarcomatous element is believed to confer greater vascular invasiveness, which underlies its higher propensity for systemic spread compared with typical gliomas confined largely to the central nervous system.

272987.long_answer: The gene most commonly implicated in hereditary spastic paraplegia that alters endoplasmic reticulum morphology is ATL1 (atlastin-1, SPG3A). ATL1 encodes a dynamin-like GTPase that mediates homotypic fusion of ER tubules; mutations disturb ER network structure and cause the early-onset, autosomal-dominant form of HSP. The ATL1 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 14 (region 14q22.1), so chromosome 14 carries this disease-linked locus.

559118.long_answer: The nuclear-encoded gene COX20 (also known as FAM36A) produces the COX20 protein, an inner-mitochondrial-membrane assembly factor essential for the biogenesis and stabilization of cytochrome c oxidase subunit II (COX2). The human COX20 gene is located on Chromosome 1 (band 1q44), so Chromosome 1 contains the gene responsible for this function.

944483.long_answer: The autosomal-dominant, hereditary form of macular dystrophy known as Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy / malattia Leventinese is produced by a missense mutation (classically p.R345W) in the EFEMP1 gene, which encodes the extracellular-matrix protein fibulin-3. Mutant EFEMP1 accumulates beneath the retinal pigment epithelium, forming drusen that progress to macular dystrophy.

333057.long_answer: Mutations in the NTRK1 gene, which encodes the high-affinity receptor (TrkA) for nerve growth factor (NGF), cause Hereditary Sensory and Autonomic Neuropathy type IV (congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis). Loss-of-function variants impair NGF signaling required for survival and differentiation of sensory and autonomic neurons, leading to the characteristic neuropathy.

651510.long_answer: Familial Mediterranean fever is caused by mutations in the MEFV gene, which encodes the inflammation-regulating protein pyrin. The MEFV gene is situated on the short arm of human chromosome 16 (16p13.3); defects here lead to the recurrent peritoneal inflammation characteristic of the disease.

382650.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the IRF6 gene cause Van der Woude syndrome, an autosomal-dominant disorder whose cardinal features include cleft lip and/or cleft palate (malformations of the palate) and lower-lip pits. IRF6 encodes a transcription factor essential for epithelial differentiation during craniofacial development; when mutated, it disrupts palatogenesis, producing the characteristic palatal anomalies seen in the syndrome.

743228.long_answer: Swiss ophthalmologist Adolphe Franceschetti was the first to describe the constellation of optic-nerve coloboma (papillary dysplasia) and renal malformations that later became known as Papillorenal or renal-coloboma syndrome. Molecular studies have since shown that many patients with this syndrome carry heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the transcription-factor gene PAX2, confirming the genetic basis of the disorder he originally delineated.

767984.long_answer: Tuberous sclerosis complex arises from mutations in either the TSC1 or TSC2 genes. Mutations in TSC2, located on human chromosome 16p13.3, are consistently associated with a more severe clinical phenotype than mutations in TSC1 on chromosome 9. Hence, chromosome 16 harbors the gene whose defects produce the more severe form of tuberous sclerosis.

273648.long_answer: Fumarase (fumarate hydratase) deficiency results from pathogenic variants in the FH gene. The FH gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 1q42.1 on human chromosome 1, so chromosome 1 is the chromosomal location responsible for the disorder.

475488.long_answer:
Primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) is most frequently caused by pathogenic variants in genes such as CYP1B1, LTBP2, TEK, FOXC1, and PITX2. By contrast, the only gene that has been conclusively linked, by numerous independent studies, to Peters-plus syndrome is B3GLCT (formerly B3GALTL), an autosomal-recessive glycosyltransferase gene. Pathogenic B3GLCT variants produce the full Peters-plus phenotype (Peters anomaly with short stature, brachydactyly, developmental delay, craniofacial anomalies, etc.).

No peer-reviewed reports or databases (e.g., OMIM, ClinVar, HGMD) document B3GLCT mutations causing isolated primary congenital glaucoma, nor do genes classically mutated in PCG (CYP1B1, LTBP2, TEK, FOXC1, PITX2, MYOC) produce Peters-plus syndrome. Therefore, according to established genetic evidence, there is currently no mutation known to be shared between primary congenital glaucoma and Peters-plus syndrome.

290619.long_answer: Hereditary haemochromatosis, an iron-overload disorder that can disturb thermoregulation, is most commonly caused by mutations in the HFE gene. The HFE gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 6 (6p21.3-p22). Consequently, chromosome 6 carries the gene responsible for this iron-related thermoregulatory condition.

704823.long_answer: In primary hyperparathyroidism, excess parathyroid hormone causes hypercalcemia and marked hypercalciuria. The high urinary calcium fosters the formation of calcium-containing renal calculi (nephrolithiasis). Recurrent or large kidney stones can obstruct the urinary tract, cause infection, and progressively damage renal parenchyma, ultimately leading to chronic kidney disease and renal failure. Thus, nephrolithiasis is a common and clinically significant complication of primary hyperparathyroidism that can progress to kidney failure if untreated.

668547.long_answer: In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, one possible pancreatic tumor is a glucagonoma. This tumor arises from pancreatic alpha cells, which normally secrete the hormone glucagon. Excess glucagon stimulates hepatic gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis, opposing insulin action and producing marked hyperglycemia. Therefore, the alpha cell is the pancreatic cell type whose hormone secretion can lead to hyperglycemia in MEN 1 patients.

832671.long_answer: Juvenile Neuronal Ceroid Lipofuscinosis (Batten disease, JNCL) is caused by mutations in the CLN3 gene. The CLN3 gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 16p12.1 on human chromosome 16, establishing chromosome 16 as the chromosomal location responsible for JNCL.

196149.long_answer: Erythrokeratodermia variabilis is caused by mutations in connexin genes (e.g., GJB3/Connexin-31 and GJB4/Connexin-30.3) that encode gap-junction proteins highly expressed in epidermal keratinocytes. The defective connexins impair intercellular communication among these keratinocytes, leading to the characteristic transient erythema and hyperkeratotic plaques of the disease.

615171.long_answer: Northern epilepsy syndrome (also known as Finnish progressive epilepsy with mental retardation or EPMR) is produced by recessive mutations in the CLN8 gene, which is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 8 (region 8p23.3).

152431.long_answer: Beta thalassemia results from mutations in the beta-globin (HBB) gene, which is located on the short arm of chromosome 11 (region 11p15.5). Alterations in this gene disrupt β-globin chain production, leading to the characteristic imbalance of globin chains that underlies the clinical manifestations of beta thalassemia.

176253.long_answer: NCSTN (nicastrin), PSEN1 (presenilin-1), and PSENEN (PEN-2) encode core components of the γ-secretase complex. Loss-of-function mutations in any of these subunits impair γ-secretase activity, disrupt Notch signaling in follicular epithelium, and are a well-established genetic cause of familial hidradenitis suppurativa.

432386.long_answer: The reported Primrose syndrome patient had congenital cryptorchidism (an undescended testis), a well-established risk factor that predisposes germ cells to malignant transformation and thus likely contributed to the development of his testicular tumor.

640712.long_answer: Hypochondroplasia is caused by activating mutations in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 3) gene, which regulates bone growth during embryonic development. FGFR3 is localized to the short arm of human chromosome 4 (4p16.3); therefore, chromosome 4 harbors the gene whose alteration leads to hypochondroplasia.

572079.long_answer: Canavan disease, a leukodystrophy that characteristically presents with megalencephaly (macrocephaly), is caused by pathogenic variants in the ASPA gene located on human chromosome 17 (17p13.2). Mutations here impair aspartoacylase activity, leading to spongiform white-matter degeneration and the clinical picture of macrocephaly-associated leukodystrophy.

929142.long_answer: ATR-16 (α-thalassemia/mental-retardation) syndrome is produced by large deletions on chromosome 16p13.3 that remove the α-globin gene cluster. The critical genes lost for the haematological phenotype are the two closely linked α-globin genes, HBA1 and HBA2; their absence abolishes α-globin synthesis, producing the α-thalassemia component of the syndrome.

395418.long_answer: Spastic paraplegia type 11 (SPG11) results from pathogenic variants in the SPG11 gene (encoding the protein spatacsin). Cytogenetic mapping places SPG11 on the long arm of human chromosome 15 (15q21.1), establishing chromosome 15 as the locus responsible for this hereditary spastic paraplegia subtype.

227531.long_answer: Craniometaphyseal dysplasia exists in two genetic forms. The autosomal-dominant form is linked to ANKH on chromosome 5 and is generally milder. The autosomal-recessive form is clinically much more severe, often causing extreme skull bone overgrowth with optic-canal narrowing and consequent visual impairment. Linkage studies have mapped this recessive, severe form to the locus on chromosome 6q21–q22.

161779.long_answer: A Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews analysis concluded that conjunctival autograft surgery was significantly less likely to show pterygium recurrence at 6 months than amniotic membrane transplantation, highlighting lower risk ratios for recurrence in the autograft group.

508819.long_answer: Adult-onset autosomal dominant leukodystrophy (ADLD), a disorder marked by progressive central nervous system demyelination together with prominent autonomic failure (e.g., orthostatic hypotension, bladder and bowel dysfunction), is produced by a genomic duplication of the LMNB1 gene. The duplicated LMNB1 allele leads to over-expression of the nuclear envelope protein lamin-B1, which disrupts myelin gene regulation, resulting in the characteristic demyelination and autonomic dysfunction.

708802.long_answer: Niemann–Pick disease type C is caused in the great majority of cases by mutations in the NPC1 gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 18 (band 18q11.2). Defects in NPC1 disrupt intracellular cholesterol trafficking, leading to the characteristic lipid accumulation seen in the disorder.

606905.short_answer: Mutations in GALNT3, FGF23, and KL (Klotho)
606905.long_answer: The peri-articular, tumor-like form of calcinosis cutis—known as tumoral calcinosis and also encountered as a complication in patients on chronic renal dialysis—has been linked to loss-of-function mutations in three phosphate-regulating genes: GALNT3, FGF23, and KL (Klotho). These mutations disrupt the FGF23-mediated pathway that maintains phosphate homeostasis, leading to hyperphosphatemia and massive calcium-phosphate deposition around joints.

328554.long_answer: Schinzel–Giedion syndrome is caused by de-novo pathogenic variants in the SETBP1 gene, which is located on the long arm of chromosome 18 (18q12.3). Because SETBP1 resides on an autosome, it is not present on either human sex chromosome (X or Y).

957103.long_answer: The Fragile X mental-retardation 1 (FMR1) gene that causes X-linked intellectual disability resides on the X chromosome, while the huntingtin (HTT) gene responsible for Huntington’s disease is located on chromosome 4 (locus 4p16.3).

308837.long_answer: Spastic paraplegia autosomal dominant type 42 (SPG42) is caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC33A1 gene, which encodes the acetyl-CoA transporter 1. The SLC33A1 gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 3 at band q25.33; therefore, the gene responsible for SPG42 resides on chromosome 3.

154679.long_answer: The ABO gene, located at 9q34 on human chromosome 9, encodes the glycosyl-transferases that determine ABO blood groups. Individuals with blood group O (a result of a specific ABO allele) show markedly reduced Plasmodium falciparum rosetting of infected erythrocytes, diminishing microvascular obstruction and thereby lowering the risk of severe malaria. Hence, the chromosomal location relevant to this rosetting-reducing gene is chromosome 9.

598235.long_answer: The Old Kingdom governor Harkhuf, whose tomb inscription records several expeditions to Nubia, famously returned with a living pygmy (dwarf) for Pharaoh Pepi II. His autobiography at Qubbet el-Hawa describes the mission and the king’s delight, making Harkhuf the official historically linked to bringing a pygmy—stature sometimes associated with microcephaly—from Nubia to Egypt.

484402.long_answer: Loss of the copper-dependent enzyme tyrosinase stops the conversion of tyrosine to DOPA-melanin, producing oculocutaneous albinism. Without melanin, the skin lacks pigment, so underlying blood vessels give it a pink-reddish tint and the skin becomes extremely sensitive to sunlight and other cutaneous insults.

148155.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the OSGEP gene, which encodes the catalytic subunit of the KEOPS complex responsible for N6-threonyl-carbamoylation (t6A) of adenosine-37 in ANN-type tRNAs, have been repeatedly identified in patients with Galloway–Mowat syndrome. Loss-of-function mutations impair t6A modification, leading to the neuro-renal manifestations characteristic of this disorder.

342587.long_answer: Meleda disease (autosomal-recessive palmoplantar keratoderma) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the SLURP1 gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 8 (region 8q24). Hence, the responsible gene resides on chromosome 8.

607762.long_answer: Choriocarcinoma is a highly vascular malignant trophoblastic tumor that aggressively invades uterine tissue and blood vessels. This invasion frequently produces profuse vaginal bleeding, which can be severe enough to cause significant blood loss and resultant hypovolemia.

636201.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the transcription-factor gene SALL1 cause Townes-Brocks syndrome, whose core features include external ear anomalies such as pre-auricular pits or tags and a high frequency of renal malformations. Unlike branchio-oto-renal (BOR) syndrome, clinically significant hearing loss is typically absent or mild, so the presence of preauricular pits with renal disease but no hearing impairment points to a pathogenic SALL1 mutation.

855971.long_answer: Acyl-CoA oxidase deficiency (also called pseudoneonatal adrenoleukodystrophy) is caused by pathogenic variants in the ACOX1 gene, which encodes peroxisomal straight-chain acyl-CoA oxidase 1—the first enzyme of the peroxisomal β-oxidation pathway. Loss of ACOX1 activity blocks degradation of very-long-chain fatty acids, leading to their pathological accumulation.

936449.long_answer: Among patients with inflammatory bowel disease, a very common extraintestinal complication is iron-deficiency anemia. Chronic intestinal bleeding and impaired iron absorption lead to iron depletion, resulting in reduced hemoglobin synthesis and anemia, which manifests outside the gastrointestinal tract.

284452.long_answer: László Seitelberger, a Hungarian-born neurologist and neuropathologist, was one of the first investigators to describe and analyse infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy (later linked to PLA2G6 mutations). In the early literature this childhood neurodegenerative disorder was frequently mistaken for a form of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis because both conditions show intracellular autofluorescent storage material. Seitelberger’s clinicopathological studies were pivotal in recognising it as a distinct disease, separating it from the NCLs.

574969.long_answer: The inherited form of triphalangeal thumb maps to the 7q36 region of chromosome 7. Mutations or duplications in the ZRS regulatory element within the LMBR1 gene on this chromosome alter Sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling during limb development, producing a thumb with three phalanges that often necessitates corrective plastic surgery.

887116.long_answer: Fabry disease, an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder that can manifest as coronary vasospasm and variant (Prinzmetal) angina, is caused by pathogenic mutations in the GLA gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme α-galactosidase A. Loss-of-function mutations in GLA lead to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in vascular smooth-muscle and endothelial cells, predisposing affected patients to the vasospastic chest pain characteristic of variant angina.

933413.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the NOG gene, which encodes the bone morphogenetic protein antagonist noggin, cause disorders such as stapes ankylosis with broad thumbs and toes/multiple synostosis syndrome. These conditions present with congenital, non-progressive conductive hearing loss due to stapes fixation together with characteristic skeletal deformities (digital broadening, joint fusions, other bone abnormalities).

815179.long_answer: According to the case reports catalogued in the dysmorphology and OMIM literature, the combination of congenital distichiasis with structural congenital heart defects and mixed peripheral vascular malformations has been documented in only two individual patients. No additional patients or families have been reported since those original descriptions, making the total number of published cases two.

716696.long_answer: Tangier disease results from loss-of-function mutations in the ATP-binding cassette transporter A1 (ABCA1) gene. The ABCA1 gene resides on chromosome 9q31; defects in this transporter impair cholesterol efflux from cells, leading to the markedly low HDL levels characteristic of Tangier disease.

531165.long_answer: Myxoid liposarcomas are commonly driven by the t(12;16)(q13;p11) translocation that fuses the FUS gene on chromosome 16p11 with the DDIT3 gene on chromosome 12q13. Thus, the FUS gene resides on chromosome 16.

394032.long_answer: Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita often involves severe, rigid deformities of the feet; congenital talipes equinovarus (clubfoot) occurs in the majority of affected infants and is therefore regarded as a common birth defect associated with arthrogryposis.

825091.long_answer: After a traumatic brain injury, excessive glutamatergic signalling can cause hyperactivity of neurons—particularly excitatory cortical and hippocampal pyramidal cells. This sustained neuronal overexcitation produces abnormal synchronous firing and network hyperexcitability, a well-established mechanism that can progress to post-traumatic epilepsy.

205244.long_answer: Pendred syndrome, in which children typically progress to profound sensorineural hearing loss by about 10 years of age, is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the SLC26A4 gene (encoding the anion transporter pendrin).

738222.long_answer: The human GIF gene encodes gastric intrinsic factor, the glycoprotein that binds vitamin B12 (cobalamin) in the duodenum and carries it to the ileum for absorption. Crystal structures of intrinsic factor–B12 complexes have been solved and deposited in the Protein Data Bank, confirming the gene-to-protein relationship.

301586.long_answer: Mutations in the SRD5A2 gene, which encodes the type-2 5-α-reductase enzyme that converts testosterone to the more potent androgen dihydrotestosterone (DHT), cause 5-α-reductase deficiency. Affected 46,XY individuals are under-virilized at birth and may present with predominantly female external genitalia, a condition that older literature labeled “male pseudohermaphroditism.” Thus, loss-of-function mutations in SRD5A2 underlie the disorder historically referred to by that term.

526495.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the TUBA1A gene, located on chromosome 12q13, disrupt α-tubulin function and neuronal microtubule dynamics. This impairs neuronal migration during cortical development and produces the tubulinopathy form of lissencephaly (often called LIS3). Hence, TUBA1A mutations on chromosome 12 are a well-established genetic cause of lissencephaly.

972964.long_answer: The key negative regulator of prolactin release is dopamine acting through the pituitary D2 dopamine receptor. The gene encoding this receptor (DRD2), which governs dopamine-mediated inhibition of prolactin secretion, is located on human chromosome 11 (band 11q22-q23).

144569.long_answer: Abdallat–Davis–Farrage syndrome has been documented in siblings born to non-affected, consanguineous parents, with males and females equally affected. This segregation pattern—affected children of healthy carrier parents and no vertical transmission—establishes that the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.

232679.long_answer: The spleen normally resides high in the left upper quadrant of the abdomen, tucked beneath the left hemidiaphragm and protected by the 9th–11th ribs. In Felty’s syndrome—characterized by rheumatoid arthritis, neutropenia, and splenomegaly—the organ enlarges in this same left upper quadrant location.

654919.long_answer: Mutations in the OTC (ornithine transcarbamylase) gene disrupt the urea cycle enzyme ornithine transcarbamylase, preventing efficient conversion of ammonia to urea. This enzymatic block causes toxic accumulation of ammonia in the bloodstream, the hallmark of the most common inherited urea-cycle disorder, ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency.

743047.long_answer: Fryns-Aftimos syndrome is caused by a single pathogenic variant present in only one of the two ACTB alleles. Reported patients harbor de-novo or dominantly inherited heterozygous mutations in ACTB; no homozygous or compound-heterozygous cases have been documented. Hence, the disease-causing ACTB mutation is heterozygous.

208919.long_answer: Sporadic inclusion body myositis is an acquired, inflammatory myopathy (with endomysial T-cell infiltrates), whereas hereditary inclusion body myopathies are genetically inherited, non-inflammatory muscle disorders; the key distinction is the presence of immune-mediated inflammation in IBM versus purely genetic (inherited) causation in hIBM.

183487.long_answer: Mutations in the CAPN3 gene, located at 15q15 on human chromosome 15, cause limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2A (LGMD2A). CAPN3 encodes the skeletal-muscle–specific protease calpain-3, and loss-of-function variants impair muscle fiber maintenance, producing the characteristic proximal muscle weakness of this LGMD subtype. Hence, the critical LGMD-linked gene resides on chromosome 15.

215780.long_answer: Conditions that impair fat absorption—such as cholestatic liver disease, cystic fibrosis, or biliary atresia—can lead to vitamin E deficiency. Lack of vitamin E allows oxidative damage to long-axon neurons and posterior column pathways, frequently manifesting as peripheral neuropathy (loss of vibration/position sense, distal weakness, paresthesias). Thus, peripheral neuropathy is a well-recognized neurological complication of vitamin E deficiency arising from these malabsorptive disorders.

850246.long_answer: Mutations in the OAT gene, which encodes ornithine aminotransferase, cause gyrate atrophy of the choroid and retina. Loss of this enzyme blocks normal ornithine metabolism, producing marked hyper-ornithinemia in blood and leading to progressive retinal degeneration that culminates in blindness.

888513.long_answer: The first and most widely cited autosomal-dominant locus for hereditary spastic paraplegia (SPG3A/ATL1) was mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 14 (14q22-q24). Mutations in this chromosome-14 gene are a well-established cause of classical hereditary spastic paraplegia, confirming that the responsible gene is located on chromosome 14.

374634.long_answer: Jackson–Weiss syndrome is produced by pathogenic variants of the FGFR2 (fibroblast growth factor receptor 2) gene. FGFR2 is mapped to band q26 on human chromosome 10 (10q26). Thus, chromosome 10 is the chromosome that harbors the causative gene for this craniosynostosis syndrome affecting the occipital bone.

693067.long_answer: The PEX6 gene, whose pathogenic variants cause Heimler syndrome (a mild peroxisome-biogenesis disorder), is mapped to human chromosome 6 (cytogenetic band 6p21). Mutations in this chromosome-6 gene impair the PEX6 ATPase needed for peroxisomal protein import, leading to the clinical features of Heimler syndrome.

364083.long_answer: Gain-of-function mutations in the HRAS gene, located on chromosome 11p15.5, cause Costello syndrome. This Rasopathy presents with characteristic facial features, cardiac defects, growth delay, and moderate to severe intellectual disability, making HRAS mutation a well-established genetic cause of a disorder that includes intellectual disability.

418886.long_answer: The TYR gene, which encodes the enzyme tyrosinase, has been repeatedly identified in genetic studies of vitiligo. Tyrosinase is a key catalytic enzyme in the melanin-biosynthetic pathway within melanocytes and is not an immune-system protein. Variants of TYR alter melanin production and also serve as autoantigenic targets in vitiligo, explaining the gene’s association with the disease while its primary biological role remains melanin synthesis.

550680.long_answer: Gilbert syndrome is caused by mutations in the UGT1A1 gene, which is mapped to human chromosome 2 (band 2q37). The gene encoding serum albumin (ALB) resides on human chromosome 4 (band 4q13). Thus, the Gilbert-syndrome gene is on chromosome 2, whereas the albumin gene is on chromosome 4.

343857.long_answer: Focal palmoplantar and gingival keratosis is a hereditary palmoplantar keratoderma. The disorder is characterized by well-circumscribed hyperkeratotic plaques (callosities) confined to sites of pressure on the palms and soles and by a whitish or verrucous hyperkeratosis of the attached gingiva and, occasionally, other oral mucosa. It does not manifest as round or oval, thin plaques distributed mainly on the trunk. Truncal macules or plaques are not part of the clinical picture that defines this entity. Therefore the statement describing trunk-predominant, discrete patches or thin plaques is inconsistent with the established clinical presentation of focal palmoplantar and gingival keratosis.

901462.long_answer: Apert syndrome—classed among first-branchial-arch (mandibular) disorders—results from activating mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor-2 (FGFR2) gene. FGFR2 is located on chromosome 10q25-q26, and the altered receptor disturbs neural-crest/mesenchymal signalling during development of first arch derivatives, producing the characteristic craniofacial malformations.

315093.long_answer: In patients with emphysema, chronic destruction of alveolar tissue causes hypoxic vasoconstriction and loss of pulmonary capillaries, raising pulmonary arterial pressure. This comorbid pulmonary hypertension increases right-ventricular afterload and frequently progresses to cor pulmonale, a form of right-sided heart failure.

333067.long_answer: The human UMPS gene encodes the bifunctional enzyme orotate phosphoribosyl-transferase/orotidine-5′-phosphate decarboxylase, which catalyzes the final two reactions that generate uridine monophosphate (UMP) in de novo pyrimidine biosynthesis. Cytogenetic and sequence mapping place the UMPS gene on chromosome 3 (region 3q13-q21).

675134.long_answer: Pascual-Castroviejo syndrome type 1 is the X-linked form of the blepharophimosis–intellectual-disability (Ohdo) spectrum and is caused by pathogenic variants in the MED12 gene. MED12 is situated on the long arm of the human X chromosome (region Xq13), so the gene responsible for this syndrome is carried on the X chromosome.

930823.long_answer: Heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the ABCC9 gene, which encodes the SUR2 regulatory subunit of ATP-sensitive potassium channels, cause Cantú syndrome. One of the hallmark clinical features of Cantú syndrome is congenital generalized hypertrichosis that is especially pronounced on the eyebrows and eyelashes.

732984.long_answer: The myeloperoxidase (MPO) gene—which, when deficient, alters the crosstalk between neutrophils and dendritic cells in lymph nodes—is situated on chromosome 17 (band 17q23.1).

736934.long_answer: Inhalation of cotton (and other vegetable-fiber) dust by textile workers produces byssinosis, an occupational pneumonitis. With continued exposure the airway inflammation and obstruction characteristic of byssinosis can progress to chronic bronchitis and ultimately emphysema.

997806.long_answer: Because 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type II is needed to convert Δ5 precursors to the Δ4 steroid androstenedione, its absence blocks the testicular pathway that produces testosterone. Genetic (46,XY) males with 3β-HSD congenital adrenal hyperplasia therefore have markedly reduced testosterone levels, leading to undervirilization, cryptorchidism and later impaired spermatogenesis—key aspects of compromised testicular function.

268698.long_answer: The HEXA gene, located on human chromosome 15 (15q23-q24), encodes the α-subunit of β-hexosaminidase A. Pathogenic mutations in HEXA lead to Tay-Sachs disease, a lysosomal storage disorder characterized by GM2 ganglioside accumulation and severe degeneration of the central nervous system.

946282.long_answer: Hereditary neurocutaneous angioma (Von Hippel–Lindau disease) can produce hemangioblastomas within the spinal cord. Expansion or hemorrhage of these vascular tumors compresses the descending corticospinal tracts, and this may result in paraplegia—loss of motor function in both lower limbs—which is a well-documented neurological complication of the disorder.

422417.long_answer: A common missense mutation (e.g., C677T) in the methylenetetrahydrofolate-reductase (MTHFR) gene disrupts folate metabolism and raises homocysteine levels during early embryogenesis. Impaired folate availability hampers closure of the cranial neural tube, producing severe defects such as anencephaly, in which the fetus develops little or no functional brain tissue.

182507.long_answer: Mitral valve prolapse that results from defects in primary cilia has been linked to pathogenic variants in the DZIP1 gene, which encodes a protein required for ciliogenesis in valve cells. The DZIP1 gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 13 (13q32), making chromosome 13 the chromosome that carries the gene responsible for this cilia-related form of mitral valve prolapse.

856805.long_answer: In Pashayan (blepharo-naso-facial) syndrome, the combination of blepharophimosis, telecanthus, a broad flat nasal bridge and reduced facial expression makes the face appear rigid and expressionless; clinicians therefore describe it as having a ‘mask-like’ appearance, comparing the facies to a mask.

548263.long_answer: Cystic fibrosis is caused by mutations in the CFTR gene, which is located on the long arm (region 7q31.2) of chromosome 7. Defects in this chloride channel gene disrupt epithelial ion transport, leading to the characteristic pulmonary and pancreatic manifestations of the disease.

302219.long_answer: A deficiency of the enzyme dihydropteridine reductase (DHPR) impairs regeneration of the cofactor tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), which is required for phenylalanine hydroxylase activity. This causes hyperphenylalaninemia, but, unlike classic phenylketonuria, it also blocks BH4-dependent synthesis of the neurotransmitters dopamine and serotonin. The resulting neurotransmitter deficiency produces progressive neurologic deterioration, seizures, and developmental delay despite dietary phenylalanine restriction.

302877.long_answer: Familial multiple intestinal atresia is most often caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TTC7A gene (Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 7A). TTC7A is mapped to cytogenetic band 2p16.2, locating the disease-causing gene on human chromosome 2.

469755.long_answer: A variant form of benign familial infantile epilepsy, often combined with paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia, is caused by mutations in the PRRT2 gene (proline-rich transmembrane protein 2) located on chromosome 16p11.2. Pathogenic PRRT2 variants disrupt synaptic regulation, leading to the characteristic self-limited infantile seizures observed in this epilepsy variant.

424632.long_answer: PEHO syndrome (Progressive Encephalopathy with Edema, Hypsarrhythmia, and Optic atrophy) belongs to the Finnish disease heritage and is caused by biallelic mutations in the ZNHIT3 gene. A Finnish founder variant, c.92C>T (p.Ser31Leu), in ZNHIT3 disrupts the zinc-finger HIT-type protein it encodes, leading to the characteristic neurodevelopmental deterioration, infantile spasms, edema, and optic atrophy seen in PEHO syndrome.

153457.long_answer: A heterozygous mutation in the TUBB4A gene (the DYT4 dystonia locus) has been identified in families with the extremely rare “whispering” form of spasmodic dysphonia. This mutation in the β-tubulin 4A protein disrupts microtubule function, producing a focal laryngeal dystonia that presents clinically as spasmodic dysphonia.

782268.long_answer: Familial chordoma susceptibility is linked to duplication or variants of the T (TBXT, brachyury) gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 6 at 6q27. Hence, chromosome 6 harbors the gene associated with inherited risk for chordoma.

757774.long_answer: Rabson–Mendenhall syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the INSR gene, which encodes the insulin receptor and underlies the syndrome’s profound insulin resistance. The INSR gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 19 (19p13.2), so chromosome 19 is the chromosome that carries the causative gene.

743475.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the MITF (microphthalmia-associated transcription factor) gene impair melanocyte differentiation. The resulting deficiency of melanin causes generalized albinism of skin, intermittent dark (black) hair locks, and congenital sensorineural deafness—clinical features classically seen in Tietz/Waardenburg type 2 albinism-deafness syndrome.

412939.long_answer: Petrus J. Waardenburg formally delineated the condition later termed Waardenburg syndrome type 1 in his 1951 paper entitled “A new syndrome combining developmental anomalies of the eyelids, eyebrows and nose root with pigmentary defects of the iris and head hair and with congenital deafness,” published in the American Journal of Human Genetics. This inaugural description established the clinical entity and its characteristic features, making that journal the first venue in which the syndrome was described.

930895.long_answer: Germ-line mutations in the NF1 gene (coding for neurofibromin) cause neurofibromatosis type 1. A common early sign of NF1 is infantile horizontal nystagmus produced by optic-pathway involvement, and the same mutation predisposes patients to optic pathway gliomas—a low-grade brain tumor. Thus, the NF1 gene mutation links nystagmus with a specific type of brain tumor.

564199.long_answer: Familial multiple intestinal atresia is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TTC7A gene (tetratricopeptide repeat domain 7A). The TTC7A locus is situated at 2p16 on human chromosome 2; therefore, the pathogenic mutation resides on chromosome 2.

863836.long_answer: The glycogen storage disease involving the liver isoform of phosphorylase b kinase is caused by mutations in the PHKA2 gene, which encodes the α-subunit specific to the hepatic isoform of this enzyme. PHKA2 is located on the short arm of the X chromosome (Xp22). Thus, the relevant gene—and the disease it causes—maps to the X chromosome.

318381.long_answer: Iron is required for hemoglobin synthesis; when iron stores are insufficient, hemoglobin production falls, causing iron-deficiency anemia. Severe anemia reduces the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity, leading to tissue hypoxia, cardiac strain, heart failure, and, if uncorrected, death.

185000.long_answer: Inherited chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis can be caused by loss-of-function mutations in IL-17F, the Th17-derived cytokine critical for mucocutaneous antifungal defense. The human IL17F gene is located at cytogenetic band 6p12 on chromosome 6; thus chromosome 6 contains the gene encoding the cytokine affected in this disorder.

175221.long_answer: Friedreich ataxia is produced by a GAA trinucleotide repeat expansion in the frataxin (FXN) gene on chromosome 9. Loss of frataxin impairs mitochondrial iron handling, leading to degeneration of the spinocerebellar, dorsal column and corticospinal pathways as well as peripheral nerves. Clinically this causes progressive gait ataxia with absent or markedly reduced deep-tendon reflexes (hyporeflexia), together with other features such as pes cavus and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

735894.long_answer: Human papillomavirus (HPV) is a prevalent sexually transmitted infection. Certain HPV types infect the cervical epithelium, producing inflammation that presents clinically as cervicitis, and persistent infection with high-risk oncogenic strains (e.g., HPV-16, HPV-18) drives malignant transformation of cervical cells, making HPV the principal etiologic agent of cervical cancer.

871148.long_answer: Mutations in the NOTCH3 gene cause CADASIL (Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Sub-cortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy), a hereditary small-vessel disease. Defective NOTCH3 signaling injures smooth muscle cells in cerebral arterioles, leading to thickened and fragile vessel walls, recurrent ischemic strokes, and other cerebrovascular events.

874011.long_answer: Familial Mediterranean fever is caused by mutations in the MEFV gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 16p13.3 on human chromosome 16. This autosomal-recessive gene defect accounts for the high prevalence of the disease among Mediterranean populations, including Assyrians.

807935.long_answer: Vici syndrome is caused by recessive mutations in the EPG5 gene (Ectopic P-granules autophagy protein 5). The EPG5 locus is situated at 18q12.3 on human chromosome 18, so chromosome 18 harbors the gene responsible for the immunodeficiency seen in Vici syndrome.

753235.long_answer: Glycogen storage disease type 0 results from deficiency of the liver isoform of glycogen synthase, encoded by the GYS2 gene. The human GYS2 gene is located on chromosome 12 (cytogenetic band 12p12). Therefore, chromosome 12 harbors the gene responsible for the deficient liver enzyme in GSD-0.

378404.long_answer: The most prevalent form, leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I, arises from mutations in the ITGB2 gene encoding the β2-integrin (CD18) subunit. ITGB2 is mapped to human chromosome 21 (region 21q22.3), making chromosome 21 the chromosomal location responsible for the commonest LAD variant.

657099.long_answer: Factor V Leiden is caused by a single-nucleotide mutation (Arg506Gln) in the coagulation factor V gene (F5). The F5 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 1 at band 1q23, so the mutation resides on chromosome 1, leading to the hypercoagulable state characteristic of Factor V Leiden.

557666.long_answer: The ichthyosis hystrix variant that presents with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss is caused by pathogenic mutations in the GJB2 gene, which encodes the gap-junction protein connexin-26. GJB2 mutations disrupt intercellular communication in both epidermal keratinocytes and cochlear cells, producing the characteristic hyperkeratotic skin (ichthyosis hystrix) together with bilateral hearing impairment.

146159.long_answer: Mutations in the COL7A1 gene, which encodes type VII collagen, cause dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa. In this disorder, skin blisters form after minimal trauma and heal with pronounced atrophic or hypertrophic scarring, especially on exposed areas such as the face, leading to the characteristic facial scarring seen in affected patients.

708388.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the SCN1A gene, which encodes the α-subunit of the neuronal voltage-gated sodium channel Nav1.1, are the primary cause of Dravet syndrome—a severe developmental epileptic encephalopathy. Patients with SCN1A mutations typically present in infancy with febrile and afebrile seizures that evolve into multiple seizure types alongside cognitive and motor impairments, firmly linking SCN1A mutations to a neurological disorder in which seizures are a defining symptom.

937080.long_answer: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, an overgrowth disorder evident at birth (macrosomia, macroglossia, organomegaly), is produced by mutations or imprinting defects in the 11p15.5 region (genes such as CDKN1C, IGF2, H19) located on chromosome 11.

792413.long_answer: Fibrin is generated when the blood-borne precursor fibrinogen is cleaved by thrombin. All three fibrinogen polypeptide chains—α (FGA), β (FGB), and γ (FGG)—are encoded by a tight gene cluster on the long arm of human chromosome 4 (region 4q28-q31). Thus chromosome 4 contains the genes whose products assemble into fibrin during blood clotting.

428915.long_answer: Missense or truncating mutations in the POLR3A and POLR3B genes, which encode the two largest subunits of RNA polymerase III, cause the hypomyelinating leukodystrophy known as 4H/Pol III-related leukodystrophy. This disorder (4H, ADDH, TACH) was originally described as ‘CAMFAK-like’ because it presents with childhood-onset cerebellar ataxia, mental retardation, peripheral neuropathy and other features characteristic of CAMFAK syndrome.

805664.long_answer: Björnstad syndrome is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the BCS1L gene, which encodes a mitochondrial complex III assembly factor. The BCS1L gene is located on human chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q33–q35); therefore, chromosome 2 carries the gene responsible for Björnstad syndrome.

666245.short_answer: Xq (long arm of the X chromosome)
666245.long_answer: Recurrent microduplications involving the long arm of the X chromosome, particularly the Xq28 region (e.g., MECP2 duplication syndrome), are a well-established cause of X-linked intellectual disability. Thus, duplications on the Xq arm are characteristically associated with this condition.

791298.long_answer: Congenital aniridia is most commonly caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PAX6 transcription factor gene. PAX6 is located on the short arm of human chromosome 11 (region 11p13). Thus, the chromosome harboring the gene responsible for aniridia is chromosome 11.

518036.long_answer: Untreated maternal hypothyroidism increases the risk of placental abruption—the premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall. Abruption acutely disrupts fetal oxygen and nutrient supply, leading to fetal hypoxia, stillbirth, or neonatal death, thereby contributing significantly to perinatal mortality.

946088.long_answer: Mutations in the RMRP gene, which encodes the RNA component of mitochondrial RNA-processing endoribonuclease (RNase MRP), cause cartilage-hair hypoplasia. This mitochondrial disorder disrupts chondrocyte growth and leads to metaphyseal chondrodysplasia, producing marked skeletal deformities such as short-limbed dwarfism, bowed long bones and spinal curvature.

680701.long_answer: Several patients described with the syndrome of anonychia-onychodystrophy accompanied by brachydactyly type B and ectrodactyly have also been diagnosed with pseudohypoparathyroidism. This endocrine disorder (Albright hereditary osteodystrophy) characteristically produces shortening of the 4th and 5th metacarpal (and metatarsal) bones, the same skeletal feature noted in these individuals.

167905.long_answer: Down syndrome (trisomy 21) is well documented to carry a high prevalence of ocular motility disorders: 20–50 % of affected individuals develop esotropia or another form of strabismus. Brown’s syndrome, by contrast, is itself a specific mechanical subtype of strabismus rather than a systemic condition that increases general risk. Consequently, Down syndrome is the syndrome classically associated with a higher overall risk of developing strabismus.

718199.long_answer: The classic triad of ectrodactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, and facial clefts defines EEC (Ectrodactyly-Ectodermal Dysplasia-Clefting) syndrome. Pathogenic variants in the TP63 gene, which encodes a p53-family transcription factor crucial for limb and ectodermal development, are the well-established molecular cause of EEC syndrome. Therefore, TP63 is the gene associated with this skin and developmental disorder.

783421.long_answer: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a hereditary disorder of enamel formation. Among the genes identified, pathogenic variants in FAM83H (Family with sequence similarity 83 member H) are reported most often, making FAM83H mutations the single most frequent known genetic cause of this enamel-defect disorder. Loss-of-function or truncating mutations in FAM83H disrupt the maturation/mineralization stage of enamel development, producing the characteristic hypocalcified enamel seen in many affected families.

198039.long_answer: Nijmegen breakage syndrome is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the NBN (previously NBS1) gene. This gene is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 8 at band 8q21.3; therefore, the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 8.

257744.long_answer: Tricho-hepato-enteric syndrome is most commonly produced by loss-of-function mutations in the TTC37 gene. TTC37 transcripts are detectable in cells from amniotic fluid and other fetal tissues, and the gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 5 (band q15). Hence, chromosome 5 is the chromosome that harbours the gene expressed in amniotic fluid and linked to this syndrome.

540775.long_answer: Mutations in the PAX6 gene are the established cause of aniridia, an eye condition characterized by partial or complete absence of the iris. Aniridia can lead to a spectrum of visual impairment—from relatively mild reduction in acuity to severe vision loss—due to associated complications such as cataract, glaucoma, and foveal hypoplasia. PAX6 encodes a transcription factor critical for ocular development; loss-of-function variants disrupt normal eye formation, explaining the variable but often serious impact on vision.

409890.long_answer: Familial Alzheimer’s disease type 3 is caused by autosomal‐dominant mutations in the presenilin-1 (PSEN1) gene, which is located on human chromosome 14 (band 14q24.3).

367292.long_answer: Acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis (also called acromelic frontonasal dysostosis) is now known, in most patients investigated, to result from heterozygous missense mutations in the gene ZSWIM6.  ZSWIM6 (Zinc-finger, SWIM-type-containing 6) is mapped to cytogenetic band 5q12 on the long arm of chromosome 5 (GRCh38 coordinates ≈ chr5:58.7-59.1 Mb).  The recurrent hotspot mutation p.Arg391Cys/His in this gene has been repeatedly documented in affected individuals, establishing ZSWIM6 as the principal gene responsible for the disorder.  Because the causative gene is situated on chromosome 5, the statement that the major gene associated with Acrofrontofacionasal dysostosis is located on chromosome 5 is supported by current genetic evidence.

419535.long_answer: Waardenburg anophthalmia syndrome results from pathogenic variants in the PAX3 gene. PAX3 is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q35–q36). Hence, the gene responsible for this syndrome resides on chromosome 2.

777051.long_answer: Hartnup disease, the classic disorder characterized by defective intestinal and renal absorption of neutral (non-polar) amino acids, is caused by mutations in the SLC6A19 gene encoding the B⁰AT1 transporter. The SLC6A19 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 5 (5p15), so chromosome 5 carries the gene responsible for this absorption defect.

277149.long_answer: Acrocyanosis is seen much more frequently in children and young adults, especially adolescent females, and is seldom observed in individuals older than thirty years. Thus, its prevalence is high in the younger age group and rare beyond the third decade.

493557.long_answer: Mutations in the AR gene, which encodes the androgen receptor on the X-chromosome, cause androgen insensitivity syndrome. This disorder was formerly described as male pseudohermaphroditism because individuals with a 46,XY karyotype develop female or ambiguous external genitalia despite having testes. Thus, the AR gene is the gene classically linked to the condition once termed pseudohermaphroditism.

916631.long_answer: Mutations in the DPM3 gene, which resides on human chromosome 1 (band 1q22), cause DPM3-CDG—a congenital disorder of glycosylation. Loss of DPM3 impairs the synthesis of dolichol-phosphate-mannose, producing defective N-linked glycosylation and inadequate O-mannosylation of α-dystroglycan. Therefore, the relevant gene is on chromosome 1.

535694.long_answer: Mitochondria are the organelles responsible for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP generation, the primary energy-producing process required for normal cellular activities, including those of ovarian and gonadal cells that are impaired in XX gonadal dysgenesis.

364344.long_answer: Carnitine palmitoyl-transferase I deficiency is produced by pathogenic variants in the CPT1A gene, which is mapped to band q13.3 on human chromosome 11.

444555.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the centrosomal gene CENPJ (also called CPAP) are a known cause of autosomal-recessive primary microcephaly (MCPH6). The same gene can give rise to Seckel-syndrome–type primordial dwarfism, in which patients show severe growth retardation and the characteristic Seckel ‘bird-like’ facial appearance. Thus, CENPJ mutations link microcephaly with a Seckel-syndrome-like clinical picture.

865659.long_answer: Marshall–Smith syndrome is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the NFIX gene (Nuclear Factor I X). NFIX is mapped to cytogenetic band 19p13.2 on chromosome 19, making this chromosome the location of the gene responsible for the syndrome.

978202.long_answer:
Waardenburg anophthalmia syndrome (also called anophthalmia-syndactyly or ophthalmo-acromelic syndrome, OMIM #206920) is an extremely rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the SMOC1 gene. Since Waardenburg’s first description, a small number of affected families have been documented in the medical literature. Among them are:

• Italy – Several Italian kindreds have been published. Early reports include Caramia et al. (1992) and Neri et al. (1998), each describing Italian sibships with the full anophthalmia-limb‐malformation phenotype. In the mutation-identification study by Okada et al. (Nature Genetics, 2011), one of the 11 consanguineous families carrying a homozygous SMOC1 frameshift variant was of Italian origin.

• Lebanon – Teebi et al. (1993) reported two Lebanese siblings with the typical constellation of anophthalmia and limb defects. A second Lebanese family with a homozygous SMOC1 nonsense mutation was included in the Okada et al. (2011) cohort. Additional Lebanese case notes have appeared in regional clinical-genetics case series.

Because peer-reviewed case reports and molecular studies document affected individuals from both countries, it is established that Waardenburg anophthalmia syndrome has indeed been reported in Italy and in Lebanon.

827845.long_answer: Spasmodic dysphonia is a focal laryngeal dystonia marked by involuntary muscle spasms of the vocal‐fold muscles. Familial cases have revealed heterozygous mutations in the THAP1 gene (DYT6), which encodes a transcription-regulating DNA-binding protein. Pathogenic THAP1 variants disrupt normal neuronal transcriptional control and are therefore regarded as a potential genetic cause of this voice disorder.

202108.long_answer: Cystinuria results from loss-of-function mutations in two amino-acid transporter genes: SLC3A1, which encodes the rBAT heavy subunit, and SLC7A9, which encodes the b(0,+)AT light subunit. Defects in either gene impair the renal and intestinal reabsorption of cystine and the dibasic amino acids ornithine, lysine and arginine, leading to their elevated urinary excretion and the formation of cystine kidney stones characteristic of the disease.

834696.long_answer: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) frequently includes conotruncal congenital heart defects such as truncus arteriosus, tetralogy of Fallot and interrupted aortic arch. These malformations are readily detected by fetal or post-natal echocardiography, and without timely surgical correction they result in a very high infant mortality rate, making the cardiac lesion the principal life-threatening component of the syndrome.

866658.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the NIPBL gene cause Cornelia de Lange syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by variable limb-reduction defects that can include congenital absence of one or both hands (oligodactyly or amelia) together with moderate-to-severe intellectual disability. NIPBL encodes a cohesin-loading factor; loss-of-function mutations disrupt normal embryonic development, producing the combined limb and neurodevelopmental manifestations observed in affected patients.

419504.long_answer: Histidinemia results from loss-of-function variants in the HAL gene, which encodes histidine ammonia-lyase (histidase). Cytogenetic and sequencing studies place HAL on the long arm of human chromosome 12 (12q23-q24). Therefore, chromosome 12 carries the gene whose defect causes histidinemia.

348332.long_answer: The lifelong, asymptomatic peeling of the outermost epidermal layer seen in acral/peeling-skin syndrome results from loss-of-function mutations in the TGM5 gene, which encodes the enzyme transglutaminase 5. This epidermal transglutaminase is essential for cross-linking proteins during cornified envelope formation, and its deficiency destabilizes corneocyte cohesion, producing continuous shedding of the stratum corneum.

152425.long_answer: Fucosidosis results from loss-of-function mutations in the FUCA1 gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme α-L-fucosidase. Genetic mapping and sequencing studies have located FUCA1 to band p36.11 on human chromosome 1. Therefore, chromosome 1 carries the gene whose mutation causes fucosidosis.

224413.long_answer: Acrospiromas are benign adnexal skin tumours that show eccrine-sweat-duct differentiation. Current histogenetic models indicate that they arise when pluripotent stem cells located in the basal layer of the epidermis/acrosyringium differentiate abnormally along the eccrine duct lineage, giving rise to the tumour.

106619.long_answer: In pica, amylophagia refers to the compulsive ingestion of starch. Cornstarch, a refined starch commonly added to sauces and desserts as a thickening agent, is the substance most often reported in this form of pica, where individuals consume it in raw, non-nutritive form.

608964.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive loss-of-function mutations in the VPS33B gene (vacuolar protein-sorting 33B) disrupt intracellular vesicle trafficking. This causes ARC (arthrogryposis–renal dysfunction–cholestasis) syndrome, a multisystem genodermatosis characterized by congenital arthrogryposis, renal Fanconi-type dysfunction, neonatal cholestasis, and ichthyosis.

634442.long_answer: The 7th-century Byzantine surgeon Paul of Aegina (Paulus Aegineta) gave the earliest known operative description for congenital imperforate anus. In his medical compendium he advised making a cruciate incision through the obstructing membrane and keeping the opening patent with tents or tubes—history’s first recorded surgical management of this anomaly.

770125.long_answer: Mutations in the OPA1 gene cause autosomal dominant optic atrophy (ADOA), a hereditary optic neuropathy in which retinal ganglion cells degenerate. Loss of these cells and ensuing optic nerve atrophy lead to progressive, often early-onset vision loss. Thus, an OPA1 mutation is directly linked to a disease that specifically targets retinal ganglion cells and impairs vision.

434397.long_answer: Latanoprost, a prostaglandin F2α analogue used for glaucoma in Sturge-Weber syndrome, can stimulate hair follicles and prolong the anagen growth phase, producing marked eyelash and periocular hair overgrowth. This drug-induced excessive hair growth is termed hypertrichosis.

325995.long_answer: Severe congenital neutropenia is treated with recombinant granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF). G-CSF is encoded by the CSF3 gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 17 (17q21). Hence, the chromosome that carries the gene producing this therapeutic protein is chromosome 17.

446919.long_answer: The heterozygous p.Pro250Arg missense mutation in the FGFR3 (fibroblast growth factor receptor-3) gene is classically responsible for Muenke syndrome, a disorder marked by coronal craniosynostosis and variable syndactyly. The same FGFR3 p.Pro250Arg change has also been documented in families presenting solely with fourth–fifth metacarpal synostosis, demonstrating that this single gene mutation underlies both isolated metacarpal fusion and the craniosynostosis-syndactyly syndrome.

784931.long_answer: Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) is usually produced by an aldosterone-secreting adenoma arising in the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal cortex, the layer responsible for physiological aldosterone synthesis.

926369.long_answer: Moderate-to-high myopia is the principal predisposing factor for pigment dispersion syndrome. In myopic eyes the longer axial length and posteriorly concave iris increase contact between the iris pigment epithelium and the lens zonules, liberating pigment granules that accumulate in the trabecular meshwork and can raise intraocular pressure.

500788.long_answer: Williams syndrome is caused by a contiguous-gene microdeletion at band q11.23 on chromosome 7. The ~1.5-Mb deletion removes several genes, including ELN (elastin), leading to the characteristic cardiovascular, cognitive, and facial features of the disorder.

247441.long_answer: Northern epilepsy syndrome (also called progressive epilepsy with mental retardation) is produced by a missense mutation in the CLN8 gene. CLN8 is mapped to the short arm of chromosome 8 (8p23). Hence, the pathogenic missense mutation resides on chromosome 8.

847227.long_answer: Mutations in the DLD gene, which encodes the E3 subunit dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase, impair branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex function. This enzyme defect prevents proper catabolism of branched-chain amino acids, leading to the characteristic accumulation of leucine, isoleucine, valine, and their keto-acids seen in maple syrup urine disease (particularly the E3-deficient, or type III, form).

175506.long_answer: The skeletal dysplasia cartilage-hair hypoplasia—later shown to be caused by mutations within or adjacent to the non-coding RNA gene RMRP, the RNA component of RNase MRP—was first described in the 1960s by the medical geneticist Victor A. McKusick, after whom the disorder’s ‘McKusick type’ designation is named.

404507.long_answer: The classic syndrome in which the central (median) rays of the hands and feet fail to form—producing ectrodactyly or “split hand/foot malformation,” often seen in EEC syndrome—is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion, typically caused by heterozygous mutations in the TP63 gene. Hence, a single mutant allele is sufficient to produce the trait, and it shows vertical transmission with variable expressivity.

785055.long_answer: The gene encoding type II collagen is COL2A1, which is located at cytogenetic band 12q13 on human chromosome 12; this locus directs synthesis of the major collagen found in hyaline cartilage.

220178.long_answer: 3-M syndrome (an autosomal-recessive disorder marked by severe pre- and post-natal growth retardation and characteristic facial dysmorphia) is most frequently caused by loss-of-function mutations in the CUL7 gene. CUL7 encodes a cullin family scaffold protein that is part of an E3 ubiquitin-ligase complex; disruption of this gene accounts for the majority of genetically confirmed 3-M cases, making CUL7 the mutation most commonly associated with the syndrome.

764635.long_answer: Mulibrey nanism—a very rare congenital syndrome marked by generalized lipodystrophy together with microcephaly, growth failure and multiorgan involvement—is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the TRIM37 gene on chromosome 17q22–q23. TRIM37 encodes a tripartite-motif E3 ubiquitin-ligase; pathogenic variants disrupt normal protein function, leading to the characteristic lipoatrophy and neurodevelopmental features observed in affected individuals.

889921.long_answer: International DSD guidelines and tumor-risk reviews consistently report that partial androgen insensitivity syndrome (PAIS) with undescended testes carries an estimated lifetime germ-cell tumour risk of roughly 15 %. This reflects the higher propensity for intratubular germ-cell neoplasia and seminoma in cryptorchid testes of PAIS patients compared with complete AIS, yet lower than in dysgenetic gonads.

868488.long_answer: Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata type 1 is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the PEX7 gene, which encodes the peroxisomal PTS2 receptor. The PEX7 gene is mapped to human chromosome 6 (cytogenetic band 6q23-q24). Thus, chromosome 6 is the chromosome that carries the gene responsible for this disorder.

126865.long_answer: Diffuse non-epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (Unna-Thost type) is produced by missense mutations in the keratin 1 (KRT1) gene. KRT1 is mapped to the 12q11-q13 region of the human genome, so the disease-associated gene resides on chromosome 12.

870405.long_answer: In dextro-TGA the great arteries are switched, so the right ventricle ejects into the aorta and must support systemic circulation, whereas the left ventricle ejects into the pulmonary artery and only pumps to the lungs. Thus the right ventricle functions as the high-pressure systemic pump, while the left ventricle serves as the lower-pressure pulmonary pump.

329317.long_answer: A common genetic risk factor for age-related macular degeneration is variation in the complement factor H (CFH) gene. CFH is located at cytogenetic band 1q31 on human chromosome 1, making chromosome 1 the chromosome that carries this AMD-associated gene.

856037.long_answer: Classic autosomal-dominant monilethrix is produced by missense mutations in the type II hair-keratin genes KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86, all of which are clustered at cytogenetic band 12q13. Hence, the causative gene for monilethrix resides on human chromosome 12.

963300.long_answer: Woodhouse–Sakati syndrome is produced by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the DCAF17 gene (formerly C2orf37), which is mapped to cytogenetic band 2q31.1. Therefore, the causal gene resides on human chromosome 2.

866110.long_answer: The SMARCA4 gene (also known as BRG1), whose inactivation is linked to malignant rhabdoid tumours and other SWI/SNF-deficient cancers, is mapped to cytogenetic band 19p13.2 on chromosome 19.

696964.long_answer: Hypoprothrombinemia results from mutations in the F2 gene, which encodes coagulation factor II (prothrombin). The F2 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 11 (cytogenetic band 11p11.2), so chromosome 11 is the chromosomal site responsible for this bleeding disorder.

270081.long_answer: Mutations in the CYP1B1 gene cause primary congenital (infantile) glaucoma. This disorder is present at birth and the elevated intra-ocular pressure it produces can enlarge the globe (buphthalmos), thereby altering eye size. Hence, a CYP1B1 mutation is classically linked to a congenital condition that affects ocular size.

790917.long_answer: Cysticercosis is the disseminated larval infection produced by the pork tapeworm Taenia solium. Unlike simple intestinal taeniasis, the larvae (cysticerci) migrate through the bloodstream and can lodge in any organ, producing space-occupying cysts in the brain (neurocysticercosis), eye, skeletal muscle, and, though rare, the uterus and other pelvic structures. Because it can cause seizures, hydrocephalus, blindness, and even death, cysticercosis is regarded as the most severe disease attributable to any human tapeworm.

830043.long_answer: Usher-syndrome genes encode proteins that localise to the stereocilia of sensory hair cells in the cochlea (organ of Corti). Mutations disrupt these cochlear hair cells’ mechano-electrical transduction machinery, leading to the congenital sensorineural hearing loss characteristic of the syndrome.

473397.long_answer: Mutations in the WFS1 gene, which encodes the endoplasmic-reticulum membrane protein wolframin, are responsible for Wolfram syndrome (DIDMOAD), an autosomal-recessive disorder that typically presents with childhood-onset diabetes mellitus together with progressive optic atrophy and sensorineural deafness.

519913.long_answer: Type 1 Kabuki syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the KMT2D gene (formerly MLL2). KMT2D is mapped to cytogenetic band 12q13.12 on human chromosome 12. Mutations in this gene produce the characteristic features of Kabuki syndrome 1, which frequently include feeding difficulties and dysphagia, linking the chromosome location to the clinical presentation.

963239.long_answer: The fumarate hydratase (FH) gene, which encodes the Krebs-cycle enzyme fumarase, is located on human chromosome 1 (cytogenetic band 1q42.3). Mutations or deletions of this FH gene lead to reduced or absent fumarase activity, causing the metabolic disorder known as fumarase deficiency.
