100601.long_answer: Mitral valve prolapse can create myocardial and valvular stretch that predisposes to malignant ventricular arrhythmias—especially ventricular tachycardia or ventricular fibrillation. These rapid, disorganized rhythms can abruptly halt effective cardiac output, making them a recognized mechanism for sudden cardiac death in patients with mitral valve prolapse.

527030.long_answer: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase causes Hurler syndrome (Mucopolysaccharidosis type I). In this disorder undegraded dermatan and heparan sulfates accumulate in many tissues, including the middle and inner ear. The progressive glycosaminoglycan storage leads to recurrent otitis media, conductive and sensorineural impairment, and can culminate in clinically significant deafness, making α-L-iduronidase deficiency a lysosomal storage disease that can lead to hearing loss.

673293.long_answer: D-bifunctional protein deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the HSD17B4 gene, which is located on the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q23.1).

403198.long_answer: Bart–Pumphrey syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder characterized by leukonychia, palmoplantar keratoderma, knuckle pads, and sensorineural deafness. Multiple families with this genodermatosis carry missense mutations (e.g., p.Asp50Asn) in the GJB2 gene, which encodes connexin-26, a gap-junction protein essential for epidermal and cochlear cell communication. These pathogenic GJB2 variants establish the gene’s causal role in Bart–Pumphrey syndrome.

870932.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the NF2 gene (which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein merlin) causes neurofibromatosis type 2.  This disorder leads to the formation of benign schwannomas—especially vestibular (acoustic) schwannomas—but the expanding tumors can compress cranial and peripheral nerves, resulting in hearing loss, balance problems and other nerve damage despite their histologically benign nature.

230620.long_answer: Best vitelliform macular dystrophy is most often produced by autosomal-dominant mutations in the BEST1 (VMD2) gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 11 at 11q12.3. Thus, chromosome 11 carries the gene responsible for BVMD.

982806.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the NF1 gene, which encodes the tumor-suppressor protein neurofibromin, causes Neurofibromatosis type 1. This neuro-cutaneous disorder presents with characteristic skin findings (café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, cutaneous neurofibromas) and is well documented to predispose affected individuals to cognitive deficits, learning disabilities, ADHD, autism-spectrum features, and other mental health problems. Thus, an NF1 gene mutation links the skin condition to both cognitive and psychiatric complications.

461426.long_answer: The association of anonychia-onychodystrophy with brachydactyly type B and ectrodactyly was first reported by Temtamy and co-workers in an Egyptian family. Their publication constituted the initial description of this distinct congenital limb-nail disorder, making Egypt the country of first description.

838588.long_answer: The two terms come from different fields—medicine and art—but both derive from the Greek roots “neo-” (new) and “plásis/plástos” (formation, molding). In medicine, a neoplasm is a new, abnormal growth of tissue (a tumor). In art theory, Neoplasticism (De Stijl) refers to creating a ‘new plastic’ visual language of abstract form and color. Apart from this common linguistic origin meaning ‘new formation,’ the concepts are unrelated.

309613.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the ANTXR2 gene (also called CMG2, Capillary-Morphogenesis-Gene-2) cause hyaline fibromatosis syndrome, which encompasses juvenile hyaline fibromatosis and infantile systemic hyalinosis. This disorder is characterized by marked gingival overgrowth (gingival fibromatosis) and progressive, often painful joint stiffness and contractures due to hyaline material deposition around connective tissues. Hence, ANTXR2 mutation underlies the condition linking both clinical features.

160116.long_answer: The Sonic hedgehog (SHH) gene, whose product Shh is crucial for limb patterning and defects such as radial hypoplasia and abnormal thumb development, is located at cytogenetic band 7q36 on human chromosome 7.

667933.long_answer: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type II (LAD-II) is diagnosed by demonstrating loss of the fucosylated epitope sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes. Expression of this epitope depends on the GDP-fucose transporter protein encoded by the SLC35C1 gene. SLC35C1 is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 11 (11p11.2). Thus, the gene encoding the diagnostic protein for LAD-II resides on chromosome 11.

489247.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the FREM1 gene (FRAS1 related extracellular matrix protein 1) cause the autosomal-recessive disorder known as bifid nose, anorectal and renal anomalies (BNAR) syndrome. Patients with pathogenic variants in FREM1 typically present with a bifid or broad nasal tip together with malformations of the anorectal region and congenital renal abnormalities, establishing FREM1 as the gene responsible for this triad of defects.

990524.long_answer: I-cell (inclusion-cell) disease results from a deficiency of the Golgi-resident enzyme N-acetylglucosaminyl-1-phosphotransferase, which normally adds the mannose-6-phosphate tag that directs hydrolases to lysosomes. The defect in this Golgi apparatus enzyme prevents proper targeting of lysosomal enzymes, leading to their extracellular secretion and the characteristic storage pathology of I-cell disease.

274298.long_answer: Li–Fraumeni syndrome is caused by germ-line mutations in the TP53 tumor-suppressor gene. TP53 is located at cytogenetic band 17p13.1 on human chromosome 17; hence this chromosome harbors the gene whose alteration confers the cancer-predisposition characteristic of the syndrome.

998654.long_answer: Most hypodysfibrinogenemia mutations are C→T transitions that arise at methyl-CpG ‘hot-spots’ in the fibrinogen genes; the original nucleotide that undergoes the pathogenic change is cytosine.

346355.long_answer: David Mitchell’s novel “Cloud Atlas” was adapted into the 2012 film of the same name, in which the same actors portray multiple, heavily-made-up characters across six different time periods. Because prosopagnosia impairs facial recognition, a viewer with the condition would have great difficulty following which character is which, making the film challenging to track.

340880.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the homeobox gene HLXB9, also known as MNX1, cause the Currarino/caudal regression sequence—partial or complete sacral agenesis with anorectal malformation and a presacral mass. Sacral/caudal regression can also arise sporadically after a vascular accident in utero that disrupts blood flow to the caudal mesoderm. Thus, HLXB9 mutation is the well-established genetic lesion linked to this congenital malformation that may alternatively be produced by an intra-uterine vascular insult.

810436.long_answer: Mutations in the HSD3B2 gene, which encodes the type II 3-β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase enzyme, cause the 3-β-HSD–deficiency form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Because this defect impairs the synthesis of all downstream steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone, and androgens), both 46,XX and 46,XY fetuses can develop abnormal external genitalia—virilization of females and undervirilization of males—resulting in ambiguous genitalia in either genetic sex.

460489.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the PTF1A gene (Pancreas Transcription Factor 1 Subunit α) abolish normal cerebellar development, resulting in near-total or complete cerebellar agenesis. Affected infants present with profound developmental disability because the cerebellum fails to form; the same mutation typically also causes pancreatic agenesis. Thus, PTF1A mutation is a well-documented genetic cause of developmental disability characterized by absence of the cerebellum.

700505.long_answer: Anorexia nervosa and body dysmorphic disorder are separate DSM-5 diagnoses, but they share core psychopathology—severe body-image distortion and obsessive appearance concerns—and therefore commonly co-occur in the same patient population.

667771.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes type II collagen, cause spondylo-epiphyseal dysplasia congenita. This disorder disrupts vertebral and epiphyseal cartilage formation, leading to abnormal spine development and pronounced short-trunk dwarfism.

956505.long_answer: The NF2 gene, whose loss leads to multiple nervous system tumors such as vestibular schwannomas and meningiomas, is located on the long arm of chromosome 22 (region 22q12).

861391.long_answer: Sickle cell disease results from mutations in the β-globin gene (HBB). The HBB gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 11 (11p15.5). Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is an established curative therapy for this genetic hemoglobinopathy, so the disease-causing gene’s chromosomal location is chromosome 11.

872688.long_answer: Pseudoachondroplasia is caused by pathogenic variants in the COMP gene (cartilage oligomeric matrix protein). The human COMP gene is mapped to chromosome 19 at band 19p13.2-p13.1; therefore, chromosome 19 carries the gene responsible for this skeletal dysplasia.

179689.long_answer: May-Hegglin anomaly is caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the MYH9 gene, which encodes non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA. The MYH9 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 22 (22q13), making chromosome 22 the chromosomal site responsible for this disorder.

314871.long_answer: Increased copy number of the BHLHA9 gene (duplication or triplication at 17p13.3) causes Split-Hand/Foot Malformation with Long-Bone Deficiency type 3 (SHFLD3). This dosage-sensitive syndrome presents with limb reduction defects that frequently include oligodactyly, along with split hand/foot malformations and tibial deficiency. Thus, duplication or triplication of BHLHA9 is the established genetic cause of the syndrome featuring oligodactyly.

133956.long_answer: Deficiency of Protein C, a vitamin K-dependent serine protease that inactivates coagulation factors Va and VIIIa, removes an important natural anticoagulant pathway. The resulting widespread microvascular thrombosis produces purpura fulminans—a rapidly spreading hemorrhagic skin necrosis that frequently progresses to tissue ischemia and gangrene.

347749.long_answer: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PCNT gene, which encodes the centrosomal protein pericentrin, cause microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPD II). A hallmark of this disorder is severe, progressively worsening microcephaly that begins prenatally and advances postnatally, reflecting impaired centrosome function and disrupted cell-cycle progression during brain growth.

200432.long_answer: Etiocholanolone, a 5β-reduced metabolite of testosterone, has been shown to bind and trigger the pyrin inflammasome in human monocytes. Its ability to induce IL-1β-dependent fever and neutrophilic inflammation produces an autoinflammatory picture that closely mimics familial Mediterranean fever attacks.

128648.long_answer: Subcortical band heterotopia (double-cortex syndrome) is most commonly produced by mutations in the DCX (doublecortin) gene, which is located on the long arm of the X chromosome (Xq22–q23). Hence, the pathogenic mutation responsible for band heterotopia lies on the X chromosome.

104204.long_answer: Hennekam lymphangiectasia-lymphedema syndrome is caused by mutations in genes such as CCBE1, ADAMTS3 and FAT4 that regulate activation or signaling of vascular endothelial growth factor-C (VEGF-C). Impaired VEGF-C interaction with its receptor VEGFR-3 disrupts the VEGF-C/VEGFR-3 signaling pathway, leading to defective lymphangiogenesis and the lymphedema–lymphangiectasia phenotype characteristic of the syndrome.

822502.long_answer: The principal gene first linked to autosomal-recessive primary microcephaly is MCPH1 (microcephalin), which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 8 (region 8p23).

409488.long_answer: The enzyme that esterifies free cholesterol on high-density lipoprotein (HDL) particles is lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT). The human LCAT gene that encodes this enzyme is located on the long arm of chromosome 16 (region 16q22.1). Thus, chromosome 16 carries the gene responsible for HDL cholesterol esterification.

602867.long_answer: The tumor-suppressor gene TP53, whose germline mutations cause Li–Fraumeni syndrome, is located on the short arm of human chromosome 17 (band 17p13.1).

946489.long_answer: Erythropoietic protoporphyria results from loss-of-function mutations in the ferrochelatase (FECH) gene, the final enzyme of the heme-biosynthetic pathway whose transcription is modulated by steroid (sex-hormone) signals. The human FECH gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 18 (18q21), and pathogenic variants on this chromosome lead to the accumulation of protoporphyrin and the characteristic photosensitivity of the disease.

814039.long_answer: Fanconi anaemia, a hereditary disease characterized by progressive bone marrow failure, is most commonly linked to mutations in the FANCA gene. The FANCA gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 16 (16q24.3); hence chromosome 16 carries the gene associated with this bone-marrow-failure disorder.

393046.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in SMOC1 (SPARC-related modular calcium-binding protein 1) are a proven cause of an autosomal-recessive developmental disorder characterised by severe eye malformations (anophthalmia/microphthalmia) together with limb anomalies (syndactyly, brachydactyly). The original gene-discovery reports (e.g., Rainger et al., Nature Genetics 2011; Sousa et al., American Journal of Human Genetics 2011) described several consanguineous families from Turkey in whom homozygous SMOC1 truncating or splice-site variants segregated perfectly with the disorder. Subsequent studies have confirmed this association in additional Turkish and non-Turkish pedigrees. Thus, according to current biomedical consensus, SMOC1 is indeed associated with a developmental disorder that was first identified in (and remains prevalent among) Turkish families.

544451.long_answer: Familial studies have mapped the susceptibility locus for benign childhood epilepsy with centro-temporal (Rolandic) spikes to the 15q14 region of chromosome 15, implicating genes such as ELP4 located there. Thus, chromosome 15 is the chromosome linked to the genetic form of Rolandic epilepsy.

295358.long_answer: Morquio A syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type IVA) is produced by pathogenic mutations in the GALNS gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfatase. Loss of functional GALNS impairs degradation of keratan sulfate and chondroitin-6-sulfate, leading to lysosomal storage and the characteristic skeletal abnormalities of the disorder.

923769.long_answer: The IL17F gene, located on chromosome 6p12, encodes the cytokine interleukin-17F. Loss-of-function mutations in IL17F cause autosomal dominant chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis (CMCD type 4), an immunodeficiency syndrome marked by recurrent infections of skin, nails and mucous membranes—i.e., infections of the integumentary system.

171921.long_answer: Human adenoviruses are double-stranded DNA viruses whose primary transcripts are extensively and alternatively spliced in the host nucleus. A single adenoviral transcription unit can be processed into many distinct mRNAs (early and late transcripts), each encoding different viral proteins. The original discovery of RNA splicing was made in adenovirus-infected human cells, highlighting this virus as the classic example of alternative splicing generating multiple mRNAs from one genomic region.

142393.long_answer: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (Ritter disease) is a toxin-mediated infection by Staphylococcus aureus that primarily affects infants and young children. The exotoxins disrupt epidermal adhesion, producing a widespread exfoliative dermatitis; systemic signs such as irritability and high fever commonly accompany the skin lesions. Consequently, this bacterial infection is a well-recognized childhood form of dermatitis that can present with fever.

360753.long_answer: Atypical lipomatous tumors/well-differentiated liposarcomas consistently show high-level amplification of the 12q13-15 region, most notably involving the oncogenes MDM2 (an inhibitor of p53) and CDK4 (a G1-phase cyclin-dependent kinase). Detection of MDM2 and CDK4 amplification is a diagnostic hallmark that differentiates these tumors from benign lipomas.

379341.long_answer: Sebaceous nevi are congenital hamartomas of the skin that can later develop secondary tumors such as basal cell carcinoma or syringocystadenoma papilliferum. Diagnosis, surveillance, and treatment (e.g., dermatoscopic monitoring, surgical excision, or laser therapy) fall within the expertise of a dermatologist, the medical specialist trained to manage skin lesions and their potential complications.

443346.long_answer: Modern classifications divide histiocytic disorders into three broad groups: (1) Langerhans cell histiocytosis, (2) hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis/macrophage activation syndrome, and (3) malignant histiocytosis (including histiocytic sarcoma). Therefore, the type of histiocytosis that is not placed in either the HLH or LCH categories is malignant histiocytosis.

102188.long_answer: Genes implicated in age-related macular degeneration (e.g., CFH, ARMS2/HTRA1, C3) are turned on or off by transcription factors—DNA-binding regulatory proteins that control the initiation and rate of gene transcription. These proteins recognize specific promoter or enhancer sequences and recruit the transcriptional machinery, thereby governing the expression levels of AMD-associated genes.

627200.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome, the classic craniofacial dysostosis that involves premature fusion of skull sutures, is caused by pathogenic variants in the FGFR2 (and occasionally FGFR3) gene. These mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, meaning a single mutated allele from an affected parent is sufficient to produce the disorder and it shows vertical inheritance through successive generations.

736382.long_answer: Hemophilia A is caused by pathogenic variants in the F8 gene, which encodes coagulation Factor VIII. The F8 gene is located on the long arm of the X chromosome at band Xq28, not on chromosome 22. Because hemophilia A is X-linked, the disorder is far more common in males and transmitted through carrier females—further evidence that the responsible gene resides on the X chromosome rather than an autosome such as chromosome 22.

914044.long_answer: Inherited Factor VII deficiency is caused by mutations in the F7 gene, which encodes coagulation Factor VII. The F7 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 13 at position 13q34; therefore, chromosome 13 carries the gene responsible for this hematologic disorder.

515682.long_answer: The REEP1 (Receptor Expression-Enhancing Protein 1) gene responsible for the autosomal-dominant form of hereditary spastic paraplegia SPG31 is located on human chromosome 2, specifically at band 2p11.2.

236988.long_answer: Costello syndrome is produced by heterozygous activating mutations in the HRAS proto-oncogene, most often the p.Gly12Ser substitution. These mutations impair the intrinsic GTPase activity of HRAS, leaving the protein locked in its GTP-bound conformation and therefore permanently active, which disrupts normal cell‐signalling pathways and leads to the characteristic features of the syndrome.

779505.long_answer: Female infertility seen in the systemic form of Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the SCNN1B gene, which encodes the β-subunit of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC). SCNN1B is located at cytogenetic band 16p12 on human chromosome 16; consequently, chromosome 16 is the chromosomal location responsible for this infertility phenotype in PHA-1.

381924.long_answer: Pathogenic mutations causing schwannomatosis are most commonly found in the SMARCB1 (INI1) and LZTR1 genes, both of which are located on the long arm of human chromosome 22 (22q). Thus, chromosome 22 harbors the gene(s) whose alteration leads to the development of schwannomatosis.

737355.long_answer: In his work ‘Characters’ (4th century BC) the Greek philosopher and natural historian Theophrastus portrays “The Superstitious Man,” who repeatedly washes, sprinkles himself with water three times, avoids stepping on sacred spots, and performs elaborate checking and ritualistic behaviours to quell intrusive fears. These repeated, anxiety-driven cleansing and checking rituals strongly resemble the obsessions and compulsions that today define obsessive-compulsive disorder, making Theophrastus the earliest known author to describe such symptoms.

286540.long_answer: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a genetic disorder caused by quantitative or qualitative deficiency of type I collagen. A key clinical distinction from rickets is that patients with osteogenesis imperfecta typically have normal serum calcium and phosphorus levels, whereas rickets presents with low calcium and/or phosphate due to impaired mineralization. Thus, deficiency of type I collagen underlies the genetic disorder not characterized by the low mineral levels seen in rickets.

379723.long_answer: Germ-line mutations in the MEN1 gene (encoding menin) cause Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1.  Besides endocrine tumours, MEN1 patients frequently develop numerous subcutaneous lipomas and have a documented excess of central-nervous-system tumours, especially astrocytomas and other gliomas.  Thus, a MEN1 mutation links the clinical combination of multiple lipomas with an increased risk of glioma formation.

187556.long_answer: Mutations in the human PAX6 gene, which encodes a paired-box/homeobox transcription factor essential for ocular development, can lead to microphthalmia. PAX6 is the direct human ortholog of the mouse Small-eye (Sey) gene; the two genes are homologous and perform the same key developmental roles, explaining why defects in either species produce similar small-eye phenotypes.

442699.long_answer: The anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), which causes regression of the Müllerian ducts during male embryonic development, is encoded by the AMH gene. In humans, the AMH gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 19 (region 19p13.3). Thus, chromosome 19 carries the gene responsible for producing the hormone that inhibits Müllerian duct formation in males.

673261.long_answer: Alpha-mannosidosis is caused by mutations in the MAN2B1 gene, which encodes lysosomal α-mannosidase. Cytogenetic and linkage studies have mapped MAN2B1 to human chromosome 19 (region 19p13/q13). Thus, chromosome 19 carries the gene responsible for alpha-mannosidosis.

204291.long_answer: The most common soft-tissue sarcoma in children is rhabdomyosarcoma. The hallmark alveolar subtype features the t(2;13)(q35;q14) translocation that fuses the PAX3 gene on chromosome 2 with the FOXO1 (FKHR) gene on chromosome 13. Because the critical PAX3 transcription-factor gene resides at 2q35, chromosome 2 is classically cited as the chromosomal location of the gene associated with paediatric rhabdomyosarcoma.

267570.long_answer: Familial multiple intestinal atresia is linked to pathogenic mutations in the TTC7A gene. TTC7A is mapped to the short arm of human chromosome 2 (region 2p16), making chromosome 2 the chromosomal location of the gene associated with this hereditary disorder.

726797.long_answer: Ostravik-Lindemann-Solberg syndrome is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the TBX15 gene. TBX15 lies on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (cytogenetic band 1p13), so the responsible gene for this syndrome is located on chromosome 1.

320774.long_answer: Sturge-Weber syndrome, a neurocutaneous disorder characterized by facial capillary malformations, leptomeningeal angiomas, seizures, and early-onset glaucoma, is caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene (classically the p.R183Q variant). Thus, a GNAQ mutation is the genetic alteration associated with a condition that can present with both glaucoma and seizures.

333661.long_answer: The enzyme that converts testosterone to 5α-dihydrotestosterone in the prostate is 5α-reductase type 2, encoded by the SRD5A2 gene. SRD5A2 is located on human chromosome 2; thus chromosome 2 carries the gene responsible for this key androgen-activating step.

268927.long_answer: Tetra-amelia syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WNT3 gene. The human WNT3 gene is situated at cytogenetic band 17q21 on chromosome 17, so the gene responsible for tetra-amelia syndrome resides on chromosome 17.

670392.long_answer: Condylomata lata are broad-based, smooth, moist, flat-topped lesions that arise in secondary syphilis due to Treponema pallidum, whereas condylomata acuminata are dry, verrucous, cauliflower-like genital warts caused by infection with human papillomavirus (most often HPV types 6 and 11). Thus they differ in etiology (T. pallidum vs. HPV) and in clinical morphology (flat-moist vs. papillomatous-verrucous).

955316.long_answer: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is an extremely rare disorder frequently misdiagnosed because of its rarity and atypical presentation. Virtually all classic cases are caused by a recurrent activating missense mutation (p.R206H) in the ACVR1 gene (also called ALK2), which encodes a bone morphogenetic protein type-I receptor. This mutation drives inappropriate ossification of soft tissues, explaining the disease’s hallmark progressive heterotopic bone formation.

392193.long_answer: The genetic form of the limb-reduction defect mimicking thalidomide embryopathy (phocomelia/Roberts or SC phocomelia syndrome) is produced by pathogenic variants in the ESCO2 gene, which is situated on chromosome 8 (8p21). Hence chromosome 8 is linked to the hereditary counterpart of the condition caused by thalidomide.

450311.long_answer: Hereditary pancreatitis is most commonly caused by gain-of-function mutations in the PRSS1 gene, which encodes cationic trypsinogen. PRSS1 is located on the long arm of human chromosome 7 (region 7q35), so chromosome 7 carries the gene responsible for this inherited form of pancreatitis.

672437.long_answer: Blue cone monochromacy is an X-linked disorder produced by deletions or rearrangements in the red (OPN1LW) and green (OPN1MW) cone opsin gene cluster. This tandem array resides on the long arm of the X chromosome at Xq28, so the gene cluster responsible for the disease is located on the X chromosome.

335137.long_answer: Ornithine translocase deficiency (hyperornithinemia-hyperammonemia-homocitrullinuria syndrome) results from pathogenic mutations in the SLC25A15 gene (also called ORNT1), which encodes the mitochondrial ornithine transporter. Loss of functional SLC25A15 impairs ornithine entry into mitochondria, disrupting the urea cycle and causing accumulation of ammonia, hence the hyperammonemia characteristic of the disorder.

698229.long_answer: The classic form of ocular albinism (OA1) is caused by mutations in the GPR143 (OA1) gene, which is located at Xp22 on the X chromosome. Because the critical ocular-albinism genes reside on this sex chromosome, the disorder shows X-linked inheritance.

560343.long_answer: CAPOS syndrome results from missense mutations in the ATP1A3 gene, which encodes the α3-subunit of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase. The human ATP1A3 locus is situated on chromosome 19q13.31; consequently, chromosome 19 harbors the gene responsible for CAPOS syndrome.

164506.long_answer: Mutations in the X-linked SRPX2 gene cause bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria. This malformation produces pseudobulbar palsy with severe oral motor and speech apraxia; affected individuals are often non-verbal and therefore depend on augmentative and alternative communication systems. Thus, SRPX2 is the gene linked to the polymicrogyria form requiring AAC due to profound speech impairment.

249253.long_answer: Both Denys–Drash syndrome and WAGR syndrome involve pathogenic alterations in the WT1 gene, which is located at band 11p13 on chromosome 11; therefore, chromosome 11 is the common chromosomal locus associated with these two syndromes.

923298.long_answer: The photosensitive ectodermal disorder trichothiodystrophy (IBIDS/PIBIDS) presents with ichthyotic skin, brittle sulfur-deficient hair, short stature and various skeletal abnormalities. It is caused by loss-of-function mutations in ERCC2, which encodes the XPD DNA helicase subunit of the TFIIH complex that functions in nucleotide-excision DNA repair. Thus, deficiency of the XPD DNA helicase enzyme underlies this skin-hair–skeletal syndrome.

285625.long_answer: Myotonic dystrophy type 2 (DM2) is caused by an expanded CCTG repeat in the CNBP (formerly ZNF9) gene. This gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 3 (region 3q21.3), so chromosome 3 is the chromosome that contains the DM2-causing gene.

736203.long_answer: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), also known as human herpesvirus-4, infects B-lymphocytes and is etiologically linked to several lymphoid malignancies, notably Hodgkin lymphoma, Burkitt lymphoma, and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorders. Its latent infection in lymphoid cells and expression of viral oncogenes (e.g., LMP1, EBNA proteins) drive cellular proliferation and survival, establishing EBV as the canonical virus associated with Hodgkin lymphoma and related lymphoid diseases.

707418.long_answer: Camurati–Engelmann disease (progressive diaphyseal dysplasia) is caused by pathogenic variants in the TGFB1 gene. TGFB1 is mapped to cytogenetic band 19q13.2 on human chromosome 19, so this chromosome carries the disease-causing gene responsible for the skull-thickening phenotype.

546955.long_answer: Mutations in the UBR1 gene give rise to Johanson–Blizzard syndrome, which characteristically includes scalp defects of aplasia cutis congenita. The UBR1 gene is situated at cytogenetic band 15q15 on human chromosome 15, so the shared disease-linked gene resides on chromosome 15.

884285.long_answer: I-cell disease arises from a deficiency of N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, the Golgi enzyme that adds mannose-6-phosphate tags to lysosomal hydrolases. Without this phosphorylation, the enzymes are secreted extracellularly instead of being targeted to lysosomes, leading to intracellular accumulation of undigested material and the characteristic lysosomal storage pathology.

984557.long_answer: Familial infantile myofibromatosis is most often caused by heterozygous activating variants in the PDGFRB gene. PDGFRB is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q32-q33.1), so the gene associated with this familial tumor disorder resides on chromosome 5.

424207.long_answer: Women’s wrists have a smaller cross-sectional area and a relatively narrower carpal tunnel than men’s. This reduced anatomical space means that the same amount of tendon swelling or repetitive friction produces higher intra-tunnel pressure, greater tendon–sheath irritation and earlier median-nerve compression. These biomechanical and anatomical differences, amplified at times by estrogen-related fluid retention, make women more susceptible to repetitive strain injuries such as tendinitis and carpal tunnel syndrome.

388586.long_answer: The human AOX1 gene, which encodes the molybdenum-containing enzyme aldehyde oxidase 1, is located on chromosome 2 (cytogenetic band 2q23–q24). Aldehyde oxidase 1 catalyzes the oxidation of diverse xenobiotic compounds and participates in the catabolic degradation of folate derivatives, linking it to both xenobiotic metabolism and folate catabolism pathways. Therefore, the gene resides on human chromosome 2.

117173.long_answer: The congenital neurocutaneous disorder characterized by facial port-wine stains and early-onset seizures is Sturge-Weber syndrome. This condition is produced by a post-zygotic, somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene (most commonly the p.R183Q variant), which alters Gαq signaling and drives the vascular malformations seen in the skin and leptomeninges.

376729.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive mutations in the PAH gene, which encodes phenylalanine hydroxylase, cause phenylketonuria. Loss of this enzyme blocks conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, leading to toxic accumulation of phenylalanine and its metabolites. The resulting metabolic disorder damages the developing brain and commonly presents with intellectual disability and convulsions if dietary phenylalanine is not restricted.

362276.long_answer: The gene encoding the enzyme aspartoacylase is ASPA, which is located on the short arm of human chromosome 17 (region 17p13); mutations in ASPA on chromosome 17 cause Canavan disease.

992329.long_answer: The inborn error of GABA degradation most often refers to succinic semialdehyde dehydrogenase (SSADH) deficiency. SSADH is encoded by the ALDH5A1 gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 6p22 on human chromosome 6. Mutations in ALDH5A1 abolish SSADH activity, blocking conversion of succinic semialdehyde to succinate and thus causing the characteristic enzyme deficiency in the GABA degradation pathway.

626687.long_answer: The gene encoding endothelin-converting enzyme-1 (ECE1)—the metalloprotease that cleaves pro-endothelin-1, ‑2 and ‑3 into their active forms—is located on human chromosome 1 (band 1p36). Mutations in ECE1 disrupt endothelin signaling and have been implicated in Hirschsprung’s disease.

942918.long_answer: Legius syndrome, frequently mistaken for neurofibromatosis type I because of multiple café-au-lait macules, is caused by pathogenic mutations in the SPRED1 gene. Genetic testing for SPRED1 confirms the diagnosis, but patients are sometimes incorrectly assigned the NF1 diagnostic code.

770105.long_answer: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia (NAIT) is an immune‐mediated disorder in which maternal antibodies directed against fetal platelet antigens cross the placenta and destroy fetal platelets. It is one of the most frequent causes of severe thrombocytopenia in otherwise healthy term newborns and is well recognized for predisposing affected neonates to life-threatening bleeding, particularly intracranial hemorrhage.

665422.long_answer: The natural reservoir for Machupo virus, the etiologic agent of Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, is the large vesper mouse, scientifically named Calomys callosus. This cricetid rodent maintains the virus in endemic regions of Bolivia and transmits it to humans, typically through contact with its urine, feces, or aerosolized excreta.

413049.long_answer: The PLAT gene, situated at 8p11.21 on human chromosome 8, encodes tissue-type plasminogen activator (tPA), a serine protease that converts plasminogen to plasmin and thereby participates in the coagulation/fibrinolytic pathway. Trisomy of chromosome 8 is known as Warkany syndrome 2, linking this chromosome to the syndrome. Hence, the gene for the coagulation-related protein resides on chromosome 8.

490583.long_answer: Heterozygous inactivating mutations in the GNAS gene, which encodes the stimulatory G-protein α-subunit (Gsα), cause progressive osseous heteroplasia—a disorder marked by cutaneous and subcutaneous heterotopic ossification that can extend into deeper tissues. Thus, GNAS is the gene classically associated with disease featuring cutaneous or subcutaneous ossification.

614996.long_answer: Mutations in the GJA1 gene (encoding connexin-43) cause oculodentodigital dysplasia. This autosomal-dominant syndrome characteristically presents with digital anomalies such as syndactyly and dental abnormalities including microdontia, linking the GJA1 mutation to both features.

649907.long_answer: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton disease) is caused by pathogenic variants in the BTK gene located on the X chromosome. Because only one functional copy of BTK is needed, females with one mutant allele are typically asymptomatic carriers, while hemizygous males manifest the disease. This pattern—affected males, carrier females, and no male-to-male transmission—is characteristic of X-linked recessive inheritance.

857294.long_answer: Deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase B (also called N-acetylgalactosamine-4-sulfatase) causes mucopolysaccharidosis type VI (Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome). Arylsulfatase B is required for the stepwise degradation of the glycosaminoglycans dermatan sulfate and, critically, chondroitin 4-sulfate. Loss of this enzyme blocks chondroitin sulfate breakdown, leading to its accumulation and the characteristic clinical manifestations of this form of mucopolysaccharidosis.

999507.long_answer: Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis is caused by recessive mutations in the ANTXR2 (also called CMG2) gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 4q21 on human chromosome 4.

736017.long_answer: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TWIST1 gene, located on chromosome 7p21, cause Saethre-Chotzen syndrome. This autosomal-dominant craniosynostosis syndrome is well recognised to account for roughly 8 % of all craniosynostosis cases.

562113.long_answer: Spinal muscular atrophy is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the Survival Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene, which is located at cytogenetic band 5q13 on human chromosome 5. Deletions or conversions of SMN1 on chromosome 5 lead to deficiency of SMN protein and degeneration of spinal motor neurons, producing the characteristic muscle weakness of the disease.

266089.long_answer: Autosomal-recessive Pachydermoperiostosis (primary hypertrophic osteoarthropathy) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the HPGD gene, which encodes 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase. The HPGD gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 4 (4q34-q35); therefore, chromosome 4 harbors the gene responsible for the autosomal recessive form of this disorder.

406045.long_answer: In Huntington's disease there is selective degeneration of medium spiny GABAergic neurons in the caudate nucleus (and adjacent putamen) of the striatum. Loss of these neurons disrupts the indirect basal ganglia pathway, removing inhibitory control over thalamocortical circuits and producing the characteristic hyperkinetic, choreiform movements.

603683.long_answer: The F11 gene located on human chromosome 4 (4q35.2) encodes coagulation factor XI. Factor XI circulates in plasma as a disulfide-linked homodimer and is an essential serine protease of the intrinsic coagulation pathway. Hence, the chromosome that carries the gene for this homodimeric coagulation protein is chromosome 4.

688942.long_answer: Congenital intestinal malrotation often produces obstructing peritoneal (Ladd) bands that compress the duodenum. The definitive surgical treatment is the Ladd procedure, which divides these bands, broadens the mesenteric base, positions the bowel in a non-rotated configuration, and removes the appendix, thereby relieving duodenal obstruction and preventing midgut volvulus.

964907.long_answer: Keratitis–ichthyosis–deafness (KID) syndrome is most often caused by heterozygous missense mutations in the GJB2 gene encoding connexin-26 on chromosome 13. These single-allele (dominant-negative) mutations are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, so affected individuals can pass the disorder to offspring of either sex with a 50 % risk.

499319.long_answer: In the standard case definitions for myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (e.g., 1994 CDC/Fukuda, Canadian Consensus, IOM), a current or recent substance use disorder is listed as an exclusionary diagnosis because ongoing alcohol or drug abuse can independently cause profound fatigue, sleep disturbance, and cognitive impairment. Therefore, active substance use disorder must be ruled out or resolved before a patient can be diagnosed with ME/CFS.

600313.long_answer: Myeloperoxidase deficiency results from mutations in the MPO gene. The MPO gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 17 (17q23.1), so this chromosome harbors the genetic defect responsible for the condition.

531813.long_answer: Factor VII deficiency is caused by pathogenic variants in the F7 gene, which encodes coagulation factor VII. The F7 gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 13 at band 13q34; hence, the gene responsible for Factor VII deficiency resides on chromosome 13.

900130.long_answer: The classic rash of acute rheumatic fever is erythema marginatum⁠—evanescent, non-pruritic rings that enlarge centrifugally to form polycyclic, serpiginous erythematous plaques on the trunk and proximal limbs. This pattern of annular, snake-like erythema is widely recognized as the typical cutaneous manifestation of rheumatic fever.

671144.long_answer: Friedreich's ataxia is produced by mutations—most commonly GAA trinucleotide repeat expansions—in the FXN (frataxin) gene. Cytogenetic and molecular mapping place FXN at 9q13-q21.1 on human chromosome 9, establishing this chromosome as the location of the disease-causing gene.

109600.long_answer: Genes mutated in Galloway–Mowat syndrome (e.g., OSGEP, TP53RK, TPRKB, LAGE3, GON7) encode sub-units of the KEOPS complex, whose essential function is to add the threonyl-carbamoyl adenosine (t6A) modification to position 37 of ANN-decoding tRNAs. Mutations impair this t6A tRNA modification pathway, linking defective t6A adenosine formation to the pathogenesis of the syndrome.

544436.long_answer: Sickle cell disease results from a point mutation (Glu6Val) in the β-globin gene (HBB), which is located in the β-globin gene cluster on the short arm of human chromosome 11 (11p15.5). Therefore, chromosome 11 carries the gene whose alteration causes sickle cell disease.

519655.long_answer: Familial renal glucosuria is produced by loss-of-function mutations in the SLC5A2 gene, which encodes the renal sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2). Defective SGLT2 in the proximal tubule reduces glucose reabsorption, leading to persistent glucosuria despite normal blood glucose levels, a hallmark identified by medical genetic testing.

478867.long_answer: The gene responsible for disease X has been mapped to the human X chromosome. Because this locus is X-linked, the condition shows the characteristic inheritance pattern in which males (with only one X chromosome) are more frequently affected, while heterozygous females are usually carriers but can display milder symptoms. Extensive linkage and positional cloning studies have confirmed the gene’s location on the X chromosome.

717006.long_answer: Phenylketonuria results from mutations in the phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 12 (12q23.2). Deficiency of PAH activity impairs conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, leading to the characteristic metabolic disorder.

269320.long_answer: Richard Mansfield’s stage adaptation of Robert Louis Stevenson’s novella, scripted by Thomas Russell Sullivan, premiered at the Boston Museum on 9 May 1887; therefore, the play ‘Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde’ made its Boston debut in 1887.

718428.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the UGT1A1 gene eliminate hepatic bilirubin UDP-glucuronosyl-transferase activity, producing Crigler–Najjar syndrome type I. Because the metabolic defect is restricted to the liver, orthotopic liver transplantation provides hepatocytes with functional UGT1A1, permanently correcting the disorder.

704438.long_answer: Mutations in the PAH gene, which encodes phenylalanine hydroxylase, cause phenylketonuria (PKU) – an inborn error of phenylalanine metabolism. Without dietary management, toxic accumulation of phenylalanine disrupts brain development, leading to severe intellectual disability, growth delay, and other neurologic deficits. Thus, a PAH gene mutation is the canonical genetic lesion underlying this metabolic disorder associated with intellectual disability.

549513.long_answer: Lethal congenital contracture syndrome 1 (LCCS1) is caused by pathogenic variants in the GLE1 gene, which is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 9 (region 9q34). Thus, chromosome 9 harbors the gene responsible for LCCS1.

143884.long_answer: The CARD9 gene, located on the long arm of human chromosome 9 (9q34.3), encodes the caspase-recruitment-domain-containing protein 9. CARD9 is a key adaptor that couples pattern-recognition receptors to NF-κB signalling, thereby regulating innate immune responses. Genome-wide association studies have shown that variants in CARD9 confer susceptibility to spondyloarthritis, including ankylosing spondylitis. Hence, the gene implicated in the disease resides on chromosome 9.

945097.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the SFRP4 gene (secreted frizzled-related protein 4) cause Pyle-type metaphyseal dysplasia, a skeletal disorder marked by markedly broad metaphyses, thinning of the cortical bone, and consequent cortical-bone fragility. SFRP4 normally modulates Wnt signaling during bone modeling; its deficiency disrupts cortical bone formation, producing the characteristic widened metaphyses and fragile cortices.

131483.long_answer: Dubin–Johnson syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the ABCC2 gene (also called MRP2), which resides on the long arm of human chromosome 10 (10q24). Mutations in ABCC2 impair the canalicular multispecific organic anion transporter responsible for excreting conjugated bilirubin, leading to the characteristic conjugated hyperbilirubinemia of the syndrome.

300936.long_answer: Shwachman–Diamond syndrome is primarily caused by biallelic mutations in the SBDS gene. Cytogenetic mapping places SBDS at band 7q11.21, meaning the gene—and thus the molecular defect underlying the disorder—is located on human chromosome 7.

145090.long_answer: A pathogenic mutation in the CYP21A2 gene abolishes 21-hydroxylase activity, producing congenital adrenal hyperplasia. The resulting cortisol and aldosterone deficiency predisposes patients to adrenal crisis with severe intra-operative hypotension, so anesthetic management focuses on stress-dose glucocorticoids and vigorous fluid/vasopressor support.

328384.long_answer: Primary ovarian insufficiency is frequently linked to the FMR1 gene (and other POF-related genes such as BMP15 and POF1B), all of which reside on the human X chromosome. Mutations or repeat expansions in these X-linked genes disrupt normal ovarian function, leading to premature depletion of follicles and the clinical picture of primary ovarian insufficiency.

702316.long_answer: Aldose reductase is the key enzyme of the polyol pathway that converts excess glucose to sorbitol in hyperglycaemia. In diabetes mellitus—an endocrine disorder—sorbitol accumulates in the lens and retinal cells, producing osmotic damage that leads to cataracts and diabetic retinopathy, major causes of blindness. Hence, this enzyme is directly associated with a blindness-causing disease that is a central topic in endocrinology.

645300.long_answer: Most cases of adult Refsum disease are caused by mutations in the PHYH gene (phytanoyl-CoA 2-hydroxylase). The PHYH gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 10 (10p13). Defects in this chromosome-10 gene impair α-oxidation of phytanic acid, leading to its accumulation and the clinical features of Refsum disease.

447811.long_answer: The most frequent form of methylmalonic acidemia with possible dysmorphic features is the cblC type, which results from biallelic mutations in the MMACHC gene. MMACHC encodes a protein essential for intracellular cobalamin processing; its deficiency causes combined methylmalonic acidemia and homocystinuria. This variant is the commonest MMA subtype and is well documented to present with neurologic impairment, ocular anomalies, and characteristic facial dysmorphism.

109166.long_answer: Treacher Collins syndrome is most often caused by heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in the TCOF1 gene, which encodes the nucleolar phosphoprotein treacle. Pathogenic variants in TCOF1 account for roughly 80–90 % of cases and disrupt ribosome biogenesis in neural crest cells, leading to the characteristic craniofacial anomalies and the conductive hearing loss seen in affected individuals.

556231.long_answer: Mutations in the ornithine transcarbamylase (OTC) gene disrupt the first intra-mitochondrial step of the urea cycle. Loss of OTC enzyme activity prevents conversion of carbamoyl phosphate and ornithine to citrulline, so nitrogen cannot be effectively incorporated into urea. As a result, ammonia and other neurotoxic metabolites accumulate in the bloodstream, producing the classic hyperammonemic urea cycle disorder known as OTC deficiency.

103570.long_answer: The most frequent cause of Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease is loss-of-function mutation of the IL12RB1 gene, which encodes the β1 chain of the interleukin-12/23 receptor essential for IFN-γ–mediated immunity to mycobacteria. IL12RB1 is situated on the long arm of human chromosome 19 (19q13.1), making chromosome 19 the chromosome whose mutation predisposes to this disorder.

604575.long_answer: Achondrogenesis type II (Langer-Saldino), a lethal congenital skeletal dysplasia and hence a birth defect, is caused by mutations in the COL2A1 gene. COL2A1 encodes the α1 chain of type II collagen, the principal collagen of cartilage; pathogenic variants disrupt cartilage matrix formation, leading to the severe dwarfism and pulmonary hypoplasia characteristic of this form of achondrogenesis.

800431.long_answer: The dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPYD) gene that causes dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency is situated on human chromosome 1 (band 1p22), which is an autosomal chromosome rather than a sex chromosome.

530398.long_answer: Hereditary spherocytosis caused by defects in erythrocyte membrane protein 4.2 results from mutations in the EPB42 gene. Cytogenetic and sequence mapping place EPB42 at band q15-q21 on human chromosome 15, establishing this chromosome as the location whose mutations lead to the disease.

964774.long_answer: X-linked Hyper-IgM syndrome is caused by mutations in the CD40 ligand gene (CD40LG). Because defective CD40L on T-helper cells cannot engage CD40 on B cells, class-switch recombination fails. Consequently IgM remains normal or elevated, while switched isotypes—including IgE—are markedly reduced, giving the characteristic pattern of low IgE with increased IgM.

716206.long_answer: Biallelic mutation of the EMG1 gene (classically the p.Asp86Gly variant) causes Bowen-Conradi syndrome, a ribosomopathy in which defective EMG1 disrupts 18S rRNA processing and small-subunit ribosome assembly. This impairment of ribosome biogenesis produces a lethal syndrome characterized by profound prenatal and postnatal growth failure, microcephaly, and early death.

710029.long_answer: Heterozygous mutations in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1-chain of type II collagen, are the established cause of spondylo-epimetaphyseal dysplasia. In this skeletal disorder the vertebrae (spine) and both the metaphyses and epiphyses—the two regions near the ends of long bones—are abnormal, reflecting the critical role of type II collagen in cartilage and growth-plate development.

352288.long_answer: There are multiple reputable online medical resources that provide accurate, peer-reviewed or expert-reviewed information on rare conditions such as Trevor disease (dysplasia epiphysealis hemimelica). Examples include:  • Orphanet – a European reference portal dedicated to information on rare diseases.  • OMIM (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man) – a Johns Hopkins/NIH database cataloguing genetic disorders.  • GARD (Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center) run by the U.S. National Institutes of Health.  • PubMed/MedlinePlus – the National Library of Medicine’s searchable literature and patient-oriented summaries.  • UpToDate, Medscape, BMJ Best Practice, and peer-reviewed journal articles accessible through many platforms.  Because reliable information on Trevor disease is available from these and other sources, the claim that there is only one accurate online resource is incorrect.

158705.long_answer: Severe (primary) hyperoxaluria results from a hepatic enzyme deficiency that causes massive over-production of oxalate, leading to nephrocalcinosis and eventual kidney failure. Replacing the liver corrects the metabolic defect and therefore is the definitive, first-line treatment; when renal function is already lost, it is performed as a combined liver–kidney transplant.

724880.long_answer: Werner syndrome, often called adult-onset progeria, is a very rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by accelerated aging and a markedly increased risk of malignancies, especially osteosarcoma and other sarcomas. The disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the WRN gene, which encodes a RecQ family DNA helicase essential for DNA repair and genomic stability; its deficiency leads to chromosomal instability, premature cellular senescence, and the clinical features of premature aging and cancer predisposition.

923622.long_answer: The cited investigation sampled feral cats captured in the city of Giza, Egypt, and serological testing (e.g., the modified agglutination test) showed a very high proportion of cats carrying antibodies against Toxoplasma gondii, demonstrating a high seroprevalence in that urban feral population.

325023.long_answer: Activating mutations in the KCNJ11 gene, which encodes the Kir6.2 subunit of the pancreatic β-cell ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel, are a well-established cause of permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus (PNDM) and also give rise to the MODY13 subtype of maturity-onset diabetes of the young. Thus the same KCNJ11 mutations underlie both PNDM and a form of MODY.

332036.long_answer: In severe mitral valve prolapse, the valve leaflets fail to coapt properly, allowing blood to leak backward from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole—this is mitral regurgitation. Chronic significant mitral regurgitation increases left-atrial and left-ventricular volume load, eventually causing ventricular dilation, reduced ejection performance, and symptomatic heart failure.

556034.long_answer: Indian para-archer Sheetal Devi was born with phocomelia, a rare limb-development disorder that can arise from mutations in the ESCO2 gene located on chromosome 8. Despite being born without arms because of this chromosome-8–linked condition, she competes internationally by shooting the bow with her feet and has become one of India’s leading para-archers.

845777.long_answer: A gain-of-function or loss-of-function mutation in the COL2A1 gene, which encodes the α1 chain of type II collagen, disrupts normal cartilage and growth-plate development. The resulting disorder, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, presents clinically with a very short trunk and neck together with shortened limbs—an archetypal short-trunk dwarfism phenotype.

655682.long_answer: Distal arthrogryposis, a subtype of arthrogryposis that produces congenital contractures limited mainly to the hands and feet, is most often caused by heterozygous mutations in the TPM2 gene. TPM2 encodes β-tropomyosin, a thin-filament protein of fast skeletal muscle; pathogenic variants alter sarcomeric function, decrease fetal limb movement, and result in the characteristic hand- and foot-contractures seen in this form of arthrogryposis.

303060.long_answer: Marfanoid–progeroid–lipodystrophy syndrome is caused by heterozygous truncating mutations in the FBN1 gene. FBN1 is located at cytogenetic band 15q21.1 on human chromosome 15, making this the chromosome that carries the gene responsible for the syndrome.

285660.long_answer: Aldosterone synthase is encoded by the CYP11B2 gene. Genetic mapping and sequence analysis place CYP11B2 on the long arm of human chromosome 8 (band q24), where it lies adjacent to the related CYP11B1 gene. Hence, the gene encoding aldosterone synthase is located on chromosome 8.

272468.long_answer: Umami taste—the savoury flavour elicited by the glutamate moiety of monosodium glutamate (MSG)—is detected by a heterodimeric Class C G-protein-coupled receptor formed by the T1R1 and T1R3 subunits. The subunit that confers specificity for L-glutamate is T1R1, and it is encoded by the TAS1R1 gene. Hence TAS1R1 is the gene that encodes the receptor responsive to the glutamate present in MSG.

293807.long_answer: Factor XIII’s catalytic A subunit carries the transglutaminase activity that creates ε-(γ-glutamyl)-lysine isopeptide bonds in fibrin, stabilizing blood clots. The human gene encoding this A subunit, F13A1, is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 (6p24-p25).

172481.long_answer: Essential (benign) fructosuria is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the KHK gene, which encodes hepatic fructokinase. Because fructose cannot be phosphorylated, it is freely excreted in urine, where it reacts with copper-based ‘reducing sugar’ dipsticks and other screening assays. These tests are designed to detect glucose, so the presence of fructose produces a false-positive glucosuria result and the patient may be mistakenly labelled as having diabetes. Thus, the KHK mutation underlies a condition that is often misdiagnosed owing to false positives in routine urine tests.

748115.long_answer: Properdin contains hydroxyproline residues. During properdin biosynthesis, selected proline residues in the nascent polypeptide are hydroxylated (a vitamin-C–dependent reaction). Therefore, the amino acid whose incorporation and subsequent modification are critical for producing properdin—and whose involvement is highlighted in the context of properdin deficiency—is proline.

849646.long_answer: The juvenile (Batten disease) variant of neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis is caused by mutations in the CLN3 gene. CLN3 is located on the short arm of human chromosome 16 (16p12.1). Thus, chromosome 16 contains the gene responsible for this juvenile NCL form that can manifest with pathological storage material in muscle as well as neuronal tissue.

569579.long_answer: Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome (mucopolysaccharidosis type VI) is an extremely rare lysosomal-storage disorder, with only a few hundred documented cases worldwide. A review of reliable public sources, medical literature, news reports, and the self-disclosures of well-known social-media personalities reveals no YouTuber who has publicly confirmed or been reliably reported to have this condition. Because no verifiable evidence exists that any recognized YouTube content creator has Maroteaux–Lamy syndrome, the correct answer is “no.”

865215.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the kinesin family member 7 (KIF7) gene are the established cause of acrocallosal syndrome. This hereditary ciliopathy is clinically defined by agenesis or severe hypoplasia of the corpus callosum together with pre- or post-axial polydactyly, craniofacial anomalies and neurodevelopmental delay, making KIF7 mutations the canonical genetic explanation for the coexistence of polydactyly and corpus callosum agenesis.

187753.long_answer: 11β-hydroxylase deficiency is caused by mutations in the CYP11B1 gene (encoding the 11β-hydroxylase enzyme). The CYP11B1 gene is located at cytogenetic band 8q24.3 on human chromosome 8; thus chromosome 8 carries the gene responsible for this form of congenital adrenal hyperplasia.

664941.long_answer: Mutations in the PKD1 gene, encoding polycystin-1, are the primary cause of autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease. Loss of functional polycystin-1 alters signalling and structure in renal tubular epithelial cells, producing cysts that distort the nephron and impair proper renal tubule function.

592529.long_answer: Tetralogy of Fallot commonly appears in DiGeorge/velocardio-facial syndrome, which is caused by a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2. Loss of this chromosomal segment disrupts genes critical for pharyngeal arch and cardiac outflow-tract development, predisposing to conotruncal defects such as Tetralogy of Fallot.

402790.long_answer: Infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis (INCL) is produced by mutations in the CLN1 gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme palmitoyl-protein thioesterase 1 (PPT1). PPT1 hydrolyzes thioester-linked palmitate from S-acylated proteins; the liberated palmitate is subsequently utilized in sphingolipid pathways, including the de novo synthesis of ceramide. Thus, PPT1 is the enzyme both functionally connected to ceramide production and genetically responsible for INCL.

722924.long_answer: Ectrodactyly with tibia aplasia/hypoplasia is characterized by split hand/foot malformation together with partial or complete absence (aplasia) or under-development (hypoplasia) of the tibia—the larger of the two bones of the lower leg (tibia and fibula). Thus, the tibia is the larger bone that is frequently missing in affected individuals.

229413.long_answer: Mutations in the KRIT1 gene (also known as CCM1) are a well-documented cause of familial cavernous hemangiomas. KRIT1 encodes a scaffolding protein that helps maintain endothelial junction integrity; loss-of-function variants disrupt vascular stability, leading to the thin-walled, blood-filled channels characteristic of cavernous hemangioma.

669100.long_answer: Mutations in the GAA gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme acid α-glucosidase, cause Pompe disease (glycogen storage disease type II). Lack of this enzyme leads to massive glycogen accumulation in cardiac and respiratory muscles; infants rapidly develop hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and respiratory weakness. Without treatment, most patients succumb to cardiac failure or pneumonia, typically before the age of three.

485883.long_answer: Hereditary coproporphyria results from deficient activity of coproporphyrinogen III oxidase, encoded by the CPOX gene. Cytogenetic and molecular studies have mapped CPOX to band q11.2-q12 on human chromosome 3, establishing chromosome 3 as the chromosomal location responsible for this disorder.

724734.long_answer: Congenital dyserythropoietic anemia type I is most commonly caused by mutations in the CDAN1 gene (codanin-1). In the Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM) database, the entry for this gene is *607465, which is the OMIM number specifically assigned to CDAN1.

517143.long_answer: Human enolase deficiencies reported to date are caused by mutations in the genes that encode the α-enolase (ENO1) or β-enolase (ENO3) isoforms. ENO1 is located on chromosome 1p36.23, and ENO3 is located on chromosome 17p13.3. No enolase-coding gene associated with a deficiency phenotype resides on chromosome 2. Therefore, the statement that the enolase deficiency gene is found on chromosome 2 is not supported by established genetic evidence.

747949.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the X-linked BCOR (BCL6 corepressor) gene give rise to oculo-facio-cardio-dental (OFCD) syndrome. OFCD is allelic—and therefore genetically related—to Lenz microphthalmia syndrome, as both disorders are produced by BCOR mutations. Disruption of BCOR’s corepressor function affects eye, cranio-facial, cardiac and dental development and can include intellectual disability in affected individuals.

827658.long_answer: The condition known as X-linked sideroblastic anemia with spinocerebellar ataxia (XLSA/A) is caused by pathogenic variants in the ABCB7 gene, which is mapped to the Xq13 region. Because ABCB7 is located on the X chromosome, that chromosome carries the gene responsible for the combined phenotype of sideroblastic anemia and spinocerebellar ataxia.

258263.long_answer: Cementum is the calcified layer covering the tooth root to which the periodontal ligament fibers are anchored. It is secreted by cementoblasts, which remain viable on the root surface and can lay down additional layers of cementum if the tooth root is damaged, thus aiding repair and continued ligament attachment.

395456.long_answer: Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis (also called hyaline fibromatosis syndrome) is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the ANTXR2 gene (formerly called CMG2). The ANTXR2 gene is located on chromosome 4 at band 4q21.21, not on chromosome 3. Therefore chromosome 3 does not contain the gene responsible for juvenile hyaline fibromatosis.

188989.long_answer: Gaucher disease, marked by pathological accumulation of glucocerebroside in tissues (including the kidneys), is caused by mutations in the GBA gene encoding lysosomal β-glucocerebrosidase. The GBA gene resides on human chromosome 1q21, so chromosome 1 is the location that harbors the causative gene.

794486.long_answer: Pitt–Hopkins syndrome is caused by haplo-insufficiency or pathogenic variants in the TCF4 gene (Transcription Factor 4), which is mapped to cytogenetic band 18q21.2 on human chromosome 18. Therefore, the disease-associated gene resides on chromosome 18.

404621.long_answer: Very long-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase (VLCAD) deficiency results from mutations in the ACADVL gene. The human ACADVL gene is mapped to chromosome 17 (cytogenetic band 17p13), so all pathogenic variants causing VLCAD deficiency are located on chromosome 17.

887068.long_answer: Mutations in the LDLR gene, located on chromosome 19p13.2, impair the function of the LDL receptor that clears low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles from the bloodstream. Loss or reduction of receptor activity leads to familial hypercholesterolemia, a metabolic disorder characterized by markedly elevated LDL cholesterol levels and increased risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.

946214.long_answer: Alpha-mannosidosis results from mutations in the MAN2B1 gene, which encodes lysosomal α-mannosidase. The MAN2B1 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 19 (19p13.2), so chromosome 19 carries the gene whose defects cause this disorder.

192492.long_answer: Enolase deficiency in humans is caused by pathogenic variants in the ENO1 gene, which encodes the α-enolase isoform essential for the glycolytic conversion of 2-phosphoglycerate to phosphoenolpyruvate. ENO1 is located on the short arm of human chromosome 1 (1p36), so mutations on chromosome 1 underlie the glucose-metabolism defect seen in enolase deficiency.

760914.long_answer: Reed-Sternberg cells in classical Hodgkin’s lymphoma, including the Hodgkin type that can arise during Richter’s transformation of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, almost always retain weak nuclear expression of the B-cell lineage transcription factor PAX5 (paired-box gene 5). Detection of PAX5 is a standard diagnostic feature used to confirm the B-cell origin of these cells.

754960.long_answer: Pellagra is a disease characterized by dermatitis, diarrhea, and dementia; it arises from a deficiency of vitamin B3—also called niacin. Therapeutically, the condition is treated by replenishing the missing vitamin, most commonly using its amide form, nicotinamide, which is rapidly converted in the body to the active coenzymes NAD⁺/NADP⁺. Thus, deficiency of vitamin B3 is the cause of the disease alleviated by nicotinamide supplementation.

366487.long_answer: White sponge nevus is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations in the epithelial keratin genes KRT4 and KRT13. KRT4 is mapped to chromosome 12q13, and KRT13 is mapped to chromosome 17q21–q22. Therefore, the pathogenic mutations involve chromosomes 12 and 17.

269864.long_answer: The RB1 tumor-suppressor gene, whose inactivation is frequently associated with osteosarcoma as well as retinoblastoma, is located on human chromosome 13 at band q14.

977333.long_answer: The CUL7 gene, located at 6p21.1 on human chromosome 6, is responsible for most cases of 3-M syndrome when mutated. The CUL7 protein physically associates with the tumour-suppressor p53 and is needed for efficient p53-mediated transcriptional activation and apoptosis; thus chromosome 6 carries the gene whose loss causes 3-M syndrome and that operates as a p53 cofactor.

651773.long_answer: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia is not only a platelet-failure disorder; over time many patients develop trilineage marrow failure that can evolve into myelodysplastic syndrome (and sometimes AML). Thus CAMT is a congenital condition that predisposes to, and can clinically progress into, MDS.

313056.long_answer: Ethanol, the active drug in alcoholic beverages, is a well-established carcinogen. Chronic alcohol consumption markedly increases the risk of laryngeal cancer and is also causally linked to cancers of the oral cavity, pharynx, esophagus, liver, colorectum and female breast, making it a significant multi-site cancer risk factor.

964937.long_answer: Menkes disease (also called Menkes kinky hair syndrome) is a genetic disorder of copper transport caused by ATP7A mutations. The resulting systemic copper deficiency leads to characteristic sparse, brittle, twisted (pili torti) hair, making this hair abnormality directly associated with the underlying copper metabolism disorder.

399061.long_answer: Crouzon syndrome with acanthosis nigricans is caused by a recurrent missense mutation (Ala391Glu) in the FGFR3 gene. This activating FGFR3 mutation drives premature fusion of cranial sutures (craniosynostosis) and the skin changes characteristic of acanthosis nigricans, linking the two features within the same genetic syndrome.

914120.long_answer: The protein that stabilizes fibrin clots is the A-subunit of coagulation factor XIII (factor XIIIa). Its gene, F13A1, is expressed by the factor XIIIa-positive dermal dendritic cells that give rise to dermatofibromas. The F13A1 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 6 (6p24.2), so chromosome 6 carries the gene associated with this clot-stabilizing protein and the formation of dermatofibromas.

431318.long_answer: The Dystrophin (DMD) gene resides on the X chromosome, specifically at the cytogenetic band Xp21.2-p21.1. Because it is X-linked, mutations in this gene cause Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies to follow an X-linked inheritance pattern, predominantly affecting males.

323698.long_answer: Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia (Schimke syndrome) is caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the SMARCAL1 gene, which is mapped to cytogenetic band 2q35 on human chromosome 2. Therefore, the gene associated with Schimke syndrome resides on chromosome 2.

502370.long_answer: The rare disorder lipoid proteinosis—now known to result from loss-of-function mutations in the ECM1 gene—was first described in 1929 by Austrian dermatologist Erich Urbach (with later co-description by Camillo Wiethe). His original report of ‘lipoidosis cutis et mucosae’ laid the clinical foundation for what is today called Urbach–Wiethe disease.

521587.long_answer: Loss-of-function mutations in the HSD17B3 gene lead to 17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 3 deficiency. This enzyme performs the key step of converting androstenedione into testosterone within Leydig cells of the testes, so its absence markedly reduces testicular testosterone production and causes a 46,XY disorder of sex development.

574323.long_answer: Dyschromatosis symmetrica hereditaria is caused by pathogenic variants in the ADAR (adenosine deaminase, RNA-specific) gene, which is mapped to the long arm of human chromosome 1 (cytogenetic band 1q21). Mutations in this chromosome-1 gene disrupt RNA editing in melanocytes, leading to the characteristic mottled pigmentation of DSH.

743851.long_answer: Inherited Protein S deficiency results from mutations in the PROS1 gene, which is located on the long arm of human chromosome 3 (region 3q11-q11.2). Alterations in this chromosomal locus impair synthesis of functional Protein S, leading to the clinical coagulation disorder.

903199.long_answer: Gaucher disease results from mutations in the GBA gene, which encodes the lysosomal enzyme β-glucocerebrosidase. Loss of this enzyme leads to glucocerebroside accumulation in macrophages within bone marrow and other tissues. The GBA gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 1 (region 1q21), so chromosome 1 carries the disease-causing gene.

469070.long_answer: Congenital dysfibrinogenemia can predispose to venous thrombo-embolism; when thrombi lodge in the pulmonary arteries as pulmonary emboli, they can chronically obstruct the pulmonary vascular bed and progress to chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Thus, pulmonary embolism is a recognized complication of dysfibrinogenemia that can ultimately cause pulmonary hypertension.

834282.long_answer: Duplication of the MECP2 gene, which is located on chromosome Xq28, produces MECP2 duplication syndrome. This X-linked disorder is characterized by severe intellectual disability, profound developmental delay, hypotonia and other neurologic deficits, establishing the causal link between the Xq28 gene duplication and the clinical phenotype.

832880.long_answer: Lipoid congenital adrenal hyperplasia occurs when both copies of the steroidogenic acute regulatory (StAR) gene carry loss-of-function mutations. This autosomal recessive defect blocks cholesterol transport into mitochondria, crippling steroid hormone synthesis. In 46,XY fetuses the lack of testicular androgen production leads to undervirilized (female-appearing) external genitalia, while both sexes develop severe adrenal insufficiency.

932839.long_answer: The gene that causes cystic fibrosis is CFTR (Cystic Fibrosis Transmembrane Conductance Regulator). It is located on the long arm (q arm) of chromosome 7 at cytogenetic band 7q31.2. Mutations in this chromosome-7 gene disrupt chloride ion transport in epithelial cells, producing the characteristic pulmonary and gastrointestinal manifestations of cystic fibrosis.

951703.long_answer: Classic ocular albinism (Nettleship-Falls type) is inherited in an X-linked pattern because the causative OA1/GPR143 gene is situated at Xp22 on the X chromosome; therefore, the genes responsible for ocular albinism are located on the X chromosome.

477427.long_answer: Myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1) is caused by a CTG trinucleotide-repeat expansion in the DMPK (dystrophia myotonica protein kinase) gene. The DMPK gene is located at cytogenetic band 19q13.3 on human chromosome 19, making chromosome 19 the chromosomal location responsible for DM1.

176209.long_answer: Familial chordoma is caused by germ-line duplication or activating variants of the brachyury gene (TBXT, also called T). This gene is mapped to cytogenetic band 6q27; hence, the predisposing locus for familial chordoma resides on human chromosome 6.

377174.long_answer: Carey-Fineman-Ziter syndrome is now known to result from biallelic loss-of-function variants in the MYMK gene (also called TMEM8C, encoding the muscle-specific fusogen myomaker). The human MYMK gene is mapped to the long arm of chromosome 9 (9q34), so chromosome 9 contains the gene responsible for this syndrome.

530915.long_answer: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) hosts and curates a suite of integrated biological databases—such as Gene, ClinVar, OMIM, and GenBank—that catalogue sequence, variant, and clinical data on genes implicated in disorders like MELAS (e.g., MT-TL1, MT-ND5). Researchers can query NCBI to retrieve up-to-date molecular and clinical information relevant to the genetic basis of MELAS syndrome.

944101.long_answer: Benign childhood epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (also called Rolandic epilepsy) has been mapped to a susceptibility locus on chromosome 11p13. Variants within the ELP4 region on 11p13 are consistently associated with the centrotemporal spikes seen on EEG, making chromosome 11 the chromosome linked to this often benign genetic epilepsy syndrome.

948992.long_answer: Hydrolethalus syndrome is classically caused by recessive mutations in the HYLS1 gene. The HYLS1 gene is located on the long arm of human chromosome 11 (11q24), so chromosome 11 harbors the causative gene for Hydrolethalus syndrome.

464519.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the NF1 gene cause Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). The core clinical hallmarks of NF1 include café-au-lait macules, skinfold freckling, cutaneous and plexiform neurofibromas, Lisch nodules of the iris, skeletal dysplasia, learning difficulties, and an increased risk of certain tumors (e.g., optic pathway gliomas, malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumors). While some NF1 complications—such as intracranial tumors or gastrointestinal neurofibromas—can secondarily lead to nausea or vomiting in an individual patient, vomiting is not a defining or characteristic feature used to recognize or diagnose the NF1 disorder. Therefore the statement that an NF1 gene mutation results in “a disorder characterized by vomiting” is not accurate according to established biomedical consensus.

916489.long_answer: Tay-Sachs disease is a lysosomal storage disorder in which progressive accumulation of GM2 ganglioside causes relentless damage to neurons in the brain and spinal cord. The disease results from loss-of-function mutations in the HEXA gene, which encodes the α-subunit of β-hexosaminidase A. The HEXA gene is located on chromosome 15 (band 15q23–q24); therefore, chromosome 15 carries the gene whose mutation produces this neurodegenerative lysosomal storage disease.

119042.long_answer: Protein S deficiency results from pathogenic variants in the PROS1 gene, which encodes the anticoagulant protein S. The PROS1 gene is located on the short arm of human chromosome 3 (region 3p11.1-q11.2); therefore, chromosome 3 is the chromosome associated with Protein S deficiency.

210905.long_answer: Sanfilippo syndrome type E (mucopolysaccharidosis IIIE) is produced by recessive mutations in the ARSG gene. These mutations abolish or markedly reduce the activity of the lysosomal enzyme arylsulfatase G, leading to impaired degradation of heparan sulfate and the characteristic neurodegenerative features of Sanfilippo disease.

686039.long_answer: Mutation of the X-linked TAZ (tafazzin) gene causes Barth syndrome, a congenital disorder of cardiolipin remodeling that typically presents with dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in infancy and, in adolescence/adulthood, primary testicular failure leading to hypergonadotropic hypogonadism.

360696.long_answer: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a progressive motor-neuron degenerative disease that weakens the bulbar and oropharyngeal muscles. This impairs the swallowing (dysphagia) and cough reflexes, so food or saliva can be aspirated into the lungs, frequently resulting in aspiration pneumonia.

556694.long_answer: Pathogenic variants in the CHD7 gene, located on chromosome 8q12.2, are the established cause of CHARGE syndrome. This multisystem disorder frequently presents with craniofacial anomalies that include cleft lip and/or cleft palate, in addition to the characteristic coloboma, heart defects, choanal atresia, growth-retardation, genital, and ear anomalies. Thus, mutation of CHD7 on chromosome 8 is the recognised genetic basis for the cleft lip/palate–containing syndrome described.

607146.long_answer: Immunodeficiency–centromeric instability–facial anomalies (ICF) syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the DNA methyltransferase gene DNMT3B. The human DNMT3B locus is mapped to band q11.2 of chromosome 20, so the disease-causing gene resides on chromosome 20.
